evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into publishable engineering science with logging woven into the research, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in design and publishing an open guide offends no legal or social norms and is a somewhat unusual but welcome strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building three prototype systems with ablation studies is a significant research effort requiring substantial resources, though feasible for an AI lab, and it is closer to exploratory research than a quick compliance fix.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D, via logging design under performance and privacy constraints, which is closely related to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help design compliant logging with low performance and privacy cost, but it is a research programme that does not itself ensure the lab's systems meet Article 12 requirements, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Consolidating per-project logging into a shared service is a common, mundane engineering response that evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, merely centralized, and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial compliance approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two existing FTEs building a microservice on the current container stack with phased rollout is a modest, reasonably feasible change at low cost, though covering all pipelines takes some integration work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by auto-capturing the specified fields across high-risk projects.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared service capturing the Article 12(3) minimum fields would address the logging mandate substantially, but it does not clearly cover Article 12(2) risk-relevant event recording or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified internal logging schema with CI enforcement is a sensible and commonly expected response, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A standardized internal schema enforced by a CI lint rule is a new tool/process but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal standardization and CI checks are common engineering and compliance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-engineer-plus-compliance working group drafting over one sprint and adding a CI lint rule is a low-cost, non-radical change, though retrofitting existing projects takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by defining the required log fields and enforcing emitters.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared schema covering Article 12(2) and Annex III 1(a) fields with CI gating would substantially address the logging mandate, though it does not cover the technical documentation or retention aspects, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware that implements Article 12 minimums is the obvious, common response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice (middleware logging), with the lab's way of working essentially unchanged apart from designing logging in earlier.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into systems is a standard, legally expected approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging middleware integrated at design time with two sprints per research group is a modest, reasonably feasible engineering change rather than a radical or costly one.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, with the specific Article 12 requirements named.
evidence_effectiveness: Implementing the Article 12(3) logging fields in all high-risk systems would directly satisfy the logging mandate, though it addresses only logging and not wider compliance or R&D adaptation, and it mistakenly applies Annex III 1(a) minimums to all systems.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance reviews and shift-left design are a common, expected response, so the idea is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (gates, checklist) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Adding review gates and checklists to project templates is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: The plan amends an existing template, adds a one-page checklist, and runs a half-day workshop this quarter, which is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate and manage its cost within R&D, as an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Gates ensure logging is designed in and mapped to Article 12, which helps, but the proposal does not specify what logs are captured or ensure the technical mandate is fully met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding tamper-evident logging by design is a common, expected response to Article 12 and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces design-for-compliance and embeds instrumentation in the pipeline, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-by-design logging is a standard strategy that violates no norms and is welcomed by regulators.
evidence_implementability: A Q3 sprint prototype on two product lines is reasonably feasible, though integrating hooks into training and fine-tuning pipelines requires some engineering change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by building an Article 12(2)-aligned automatic logging layer, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A tamper-evident logging layer embedded in every high-risk system would substantially satisfy Article 12 logging requirements, though it covers only logging and not wider documentation or Annex III specifics, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging into a shared internal library is a standard, expected response that an experienced evaluator would see from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice delivered through a common tool, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging SDK with design-review gating is a common, norm-compliant engineering response to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_implementability: It consolidates existing partial loggers over one quarter with phased onboarding, which requires some organizational change but is reasonably feasible rather than trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by producing Article 12 logs and a single audit surface.
evidence_effectiveness: A unified schema covering timestamps, input references, database lookups, and human verification would, if adopted, directly deliver the Article 12 logging capability, though it addresses logging mostly for Annex III 1(a)-type fields and not the wider risk-event or documentation needs.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the experiment harness by default is a sensible idea that labs would commonly propose, so it is interesting but not rare or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Making log capture a default in every experiment run weaves logging into the science and links compliance to reproducibility, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Default logging for compliance and reproducibility is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a lightweight logging layer to an existing harness over two sprints is a modest, non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the specific Article 12(3) items, though it applies mainly to the R&D trial context.
evidence_effectiveness: It would capture the Article 12(3) minimum fields in experimental trials but does not address deployed-system logging, Article 12(2) event relevance, lifetime logging, or the human verifier identification, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate that many labs would propose, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, merely consolidated into shared infrastructure, and leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized reusable logging infrastructure is a common, sensible engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-to-four-engineer team building on the existing data stack with an API integrated at design time is reasonably feasible, though retrofitting existing projects and varied system types require some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal does X (shared logging middleware) to get the identified Y of automatic event recording for high-risk systems, which is directly the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer capturing events, timestamps and input-output references would, if built, directly deliver the Article 12(1) automatic logging capability across systems, but it does not by itself address Article 12(2) event relevance, Annex III-specific fields such as the reference database and verifying persons, or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code gates in CI/CD are a well-known DevOps pattern, so the idea is fairly common and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a pipeline gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding compliance checks to a CI pipeline is a common, widely accepted engineering practice that violates no legal or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends the existing GitLab CI with no new headcount, though writing static-analysis and schema-conformance checks takes some effort, so it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying log hooks and the Article 12(3) fields before progression.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging capability is built in early, but it verifies presence of hooks rather than guaranteeing sufficient traceability, retention, or covering all of Article 12, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding documentation tasks in sprints and rotating a steward is a sensible but familiar agile/docs-as-code practice with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a modest new process element (rotating steward, sprint deliverable) but still treats compliance as documentation practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Making documentation updates a sprint deliverable with a rotating steward is a common, norm-compliant internal process that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing Confluence-to-registry pipeline and spreads work across funded teams, so it needs only modest process changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of keeping the technical file current, which is related to but not the same as the stated logging mandate, so it applies indirectly.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping technical documentation current helps meet the documentation obligations in Recital 71, but it does not address the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing logging in from the start with kickoff templates and review gates is a very common, expected response to this mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice with process gates added, and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging and auditing releases is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires some process changes such as templates, review gates, and a dedicated engineer, but these are reasonably feasible measures at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (embed logging per Article 12) to get Y (compliant automatic event recording), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Building automatic logging of the Article 12(3) items into the architecture with review gates and release audits would, if done, satisfy the core logging mandate, though it addresses only the logging part and not wider R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Budgeting for compliance costs in project proposals is a fairly mundane and expected administrative response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance administration that leaves the lab's research approach unchanged, and it treats compliance as a cost item.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a required budget line to an internal grant-review template is a common governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It only requires amending a template and estimating costs, which is a non-radical change, though five-year estimates need some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of lifetime record-keeping obligations going unfunded, which is directly tied to meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It funds and plans for log retention and upkeep but does not itself make systems log events or meet Article 12 technical requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auditing existing infrastructure against regulatory fields and patching gaps is the common, expected response and is not imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is a standard gap analysis and patching of existing tooling that treats compliance purely as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting existing systems for compliance is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers over three months making pull requests into existing repositories with no new tooling is a modest, readily feasible effort with low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by mapping and implementing the Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would plausibly meet the logging requirements if executed, but it focuses on Article 12(3) fields (which apply only to Annex III 1(a) systems) and leaves out the Article 12(2) traceability purposes and the lifetime/documentation aspects, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into a shared ML pipeline is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Instrumenting the shared pipeline with hook-based loggers is a new tooling element, but it still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized automated logging is a standard engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers for one quarter using the existing framework and time-series store is modest, reasonably feasible work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, with a schema mapped to Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic event recording, but it leaves gaps such as Article 12(2) risk-relevant event selection, retention, and the human verification identities required for Annex III 1(a), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable drop-in logging service wired into CI is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging SDK/sidecar is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging infrastructure is a standard, uncontroversial approach that violates no norms, though storing input payloads raises minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: Building sidecar, gRPC ingestion, two SDKs, and CI integration is a moderate engineering effort and the one-day integration claim is optimistic, but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(1) automatic logging mandate for prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would largely deliver automatic event logging, but Article 12(2)-(3) specifics like risk-relevant events, traceability suited to purpose, and Annex III minimums need more than generic payload capture, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing compliance documentation for clients is fairly common transparency practice, with the differentiator framing adding mild interest but not surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A public whitepaper is a new element (a disclosure format) and frames compliance as a competitive differentiator, but it still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing compliance documentation is a common strategy, though disclosing sample log schemas could raise some security or IP concerns, it offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A quarterly document drafted by the compliance officer with engineering input and legal review is a modest, non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of communicating logging compliance to buyers, which relates to the stated problem but is not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A whitepaper does not itself implement automatic logging or meet Article 12; it only communicates and may support client due diligence, so it is a partial contribution at best.

evidence_originality: Open-source logging libraries for compliance are an expected, fairly common response, with only modest interest from the feedback loop into logging-efficiency research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and community offering but still treats compliance fundamentally as logging practice, with only slight stretching via the usage-data research loop.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source compliance tooling with an EU-friendly license violates no norms, though diverting lab resources to maintain public infrastructure is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A small team building a Python library with ONNX layers, integration guides, and partner validation is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial undertaking with some ongoing maintenance burden.
evidence_applicability: The proposal explicitly targets Article 12 logging requirements, so doing X (build compliant logging middleware) directly yields Y (meeting the stated logging mandate).
evidence_effectiveness: A middleware that automatically records use periods, reference databases, matched inputs, and verifier IDs would, if built, directly satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate including the Annex III 1(a) minimums, though the generic Article 12(2) event relevance remains partly unaddressed.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a validation research corpus is interesting and shows some imagination, though the data-reuse idea is not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making the mandatory logs a research asset, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing operational logs for research is somewhat unusual and raises data-protection and purpose-limitation concerns, though anonymization mitigates these and it does not offend sensibilities strongly.
evidence_implementability: It needs only an ETL stage on the existing SDK, the existing data warehouse, and one postdoc, which is a modest and reasonably feasible change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (extracting value from required logs and supporting post-market monitoring) that relates to the logging mandate but not the core question of how to meet it.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal assumes logs already exist and repurposes them for research and monitoring, so it does not itself ensure Article 12 compliance (event coverage, traceability, Annex III minimums), making it only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default SDKs with CI gates are a fairly standard, expected response to logging mandates, so the idea is sensible but not rare or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance basically unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared logging infrastructure with a CI gate is a common, norm-respecting engineering and compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires refactoring templates, building an SDK and adding a CI gate, which are some changes but reasonably feasible for a lab with existing prototyping templates.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by embedding the required log fields (timestamps, reference database, input match data) into builds.
evidence_effectiveness: Default logging plus an enforcement gate would largely satisfy the technical logging requirement, but it covers only some of Article 12 (e.g., no operator identification of verifiers, retention, or event relevance to risk and post-market monitoring), so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance gates in a staging/CI pipeline are a fairly expected response, though the replay-based verification of Article 12 event categories is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (an automated replay-harness gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice verified before deployment, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A pre-deployment compliance test gate is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a replay harness and schema/timestamp validators in a staging pipeline requires some engineering work but is reasonably feasible with existing CI/CD practice.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required event categories are logged before production.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify logging sufficiency for 12(2)(a)-(c) but covers only part of the mandate (not Annex III 12(3) specifics, retention, or runtime behavior), and synthetic replay may miss real-world risk events, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance tooling and publishing about it is interesting and shows some imagination in reframing compliance as research leverage, but it is not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning a compliance obligation into a research output and publication asset, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing compliance tooling and publishing on it is a somewhat uncommon but unobjectionable strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Using three postdocs and one engineer within existing grants over twelve months is reasonably feasible, though building a domain-agnostic library and writing a peer-reviewed paper requires some changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building and deploying compliant logging (do X to get Y, where Y is part of the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logging library covering Article 12(3) fields deployed across all active systems would largely meet the logging mandate, though it focuses on 12(3) fields and omits the Article 12(2) event-relevance and broader lifetime logging needs, making it a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Immutable audit logs and event sourcing are well-known patterns, so applying them as the primary architecture is interesting but not very surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reorganizes the lab's R&D architecture around logging so that traceability is built into the science workflow rather than added on, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Event sourcing and immutable audit logs are legitimate, norm-compliant engineering approaches, but making them the primary architecture is somewhat unusual, and the immutability may raise data-erasure concerns.
evidence_implementability: Re-architecting a production high-risk pipeline around an event-sourced core is a significant, costly change, though a three-month single-system prototype makes it difficult but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12's automatic logging and traceability mandate directly (do X: event-first logging, get Y: compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: An append-only, cryptographically chained event stream as the core architecture would, if built, directly deliver automatic lifetime event recording and traceability, though it does not address Annex III-specific fields or the documentation obligations in full.

evidence_originality: Public transparency standards and contractual audit rights are known practices, though framing compliance as a market differentiator is somewhat interesting and shows modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's business by turning logging into a market offering and partner-facing trust mechanism, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing a transparency standard and granting partner audit rights is somewhat unusual (exposure of logging details, IP/security concerns) but offends no norms and is consistent with regulatory sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a standard, adding audit-access clauses to contracts, and updating a public appendix quarterly requires some legal negotiation and process changes but no radical or costly technical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: The proposal documents and exposes logging architecture and retention, which relates to the logging mandate only indirectly (traceability and trust) rather than actually implementing the Article 12 logging capabilities, so it addresses an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help demonstrate and verify compliance and build trust but does not itself build the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A benchmark for log-schema sufficiency against Article 12 is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising since benchmarks are a familiar research format.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a public benchmark and shared research vocabulary) and shifts the lab toward researching auditability as a scientific property, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not fully redefine what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open, collaborative publication with legal scholars offends no norms, though it is a somewhat uncommon response to a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: Building annotated synthetic trace datasets, formal criteria with legal scholars, and open code is a significant but feasible research effort requiring collaboration and resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely knowing whether log schemas are sufficient for traceability, which relates to the logging mandate but does not directly implement logging in the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help assess log sufficiency but is only a partial solution, since it does not implement the lab's logging and the legal thresholds are hard to formalize in synthetic traces.

evidence_originality: A design-time traceability spec gate is a sensible but fairly expected shift-left compliance practice, only mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process artifact and review gate but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a required design document and peer review is a common governance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A one-page spec and two-engineer review layered onto existing design docs is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by mapping Article 12 event categories to data fields and retention paths.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help catch architectural logging gaps early but covers only design-stage mapping of Article 12(2), not actual implementation, Annex III minimums, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-instrumenting logging via an SDK wrapper in a base image is a sensible but fairly common engineering approach labs would expect, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (middleware SDK layer) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized logging middleware in dev tooling is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It refactors existing tracking hooks and uses a base Docker image, requiring some changes but being reasonably feasible within a sprint.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (auto-emit Article 12 structured logs) to get Y (logging mandate compliance), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would automatically capture events for prototypes and help meet the logging mandate, but it covers only technical logging capture and not retention, deployer-side obligations, or the risk-relevance of events, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as an open research corpus is unusual and imaginative compared with expected responses, though open datasets themselves are familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandatory logs into new scientific data resources and a new offering for the community, rather than treating them as a mere compliance burden.
evidence_acceptability: Open-science publication of anonymised data is a respectable practice, though releasing operational logs from Annex III systems could raise privacy and customer concerns, making it somewhat unusual but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: A four-person team building anonymisation tooling and quarterly releases is feasible, but de-identifying logs from deployed high-risk systems (GDPR, customer confidentiality, IP, re-identification risk) requires significant effort and cooperation.
evidence_applicability: The idea addresses the logs' secondary use and public trust, which relate only implicitly to how to meet the logging mandate, and it does not itself implement the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not satisfy the Article 12 mandate and only contributes tangentially (tagging events by 12(2) categories), with the legal and privacy risks making it unlikely to solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a longitudinal research corpus is an unusual, interesting reframing that shows some imagination, but it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science, turning a compliance cost into a research asset, though it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for internal research is a somewhat unusual strategy, but it raises data-protection and purpose-limitation questions only mildly and does not offend sensibilities, especially with a secure repository.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an analytics pipeline, a secure repository, and new statistical methods, which is a significant but reasonably feasible set of changes for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting added value from compliance logs, which relates to how the lab adapts its R&D to the logging mandate but is not the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal mainly repurposes logs for research and does not itself specify how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate, so it would contribute only partially to solving the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Retrofitting a logging module into existing pipelines is the most obvious, mundane response expected from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice added onto the current stack and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding an automated logging SDK in existing pipelines is a common, legitimate compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person pod building a lightweight SDK on existing infrastructure and leased storage is low-cost, incremental work, though hooking into orchestration layers takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X to get Article 12 logs).
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event logging directly addresses the Article 12 mandate, but the proposal omits what events are captured, retention, and the Annex III specifics, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code checks in CI are a fairly expected response, with only mild interest in tying them to specific Article 12 fields.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks for compliance are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It slots into existing CI/CD, though building a static-analysis tool that parses log-emission calls against a regulatory checklist requires some development effort and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by catching missing required log fields (do X to get Y, where Y is part of the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate checking schema coverage would help ensure required log fields exist, but it cannot verify that logs are actually recorded at runtime, are traceable, or fit the intended purpose, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the architecture by default and validating it against the Article 12 minimums is the obvious, expected response, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice (logging by design, pre-release testing) that treats compliance as a logging task and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging by design is a common, legally aligned compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a standard logging-layer specification into the SDLC requires some process and engineering changes across teams but is a reasonably feasible, well-understood measure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, using the Article 12(3) items (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier IDs) to produce compliant logs.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the logging mandate for the systems covered, though it does little for the R&D adaptation side and Article 12(2) event relevance is only lightly addressed, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a research dataset is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, but it is not highly surprising or unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the mandated log stream into research input, which is paradigm stretching, though it does not alter what the lab researches at large.
evidence_acceptability: Using compliance logs for internal safety research and post-market monitoring is a legitimate practice that offends no norms, though it is somewhat less common than plain logging, and it would need to respect data-protection constraints on the logged data.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight anomaly-detection pipeline on existing middleware logs plus a bi-monthly workshop is a small, reasonably feasible addition requiring some changes but low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly uses the Article 12(2)(a) risk-event logging and supports Article 72 post-market monitoring, so it connects to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, though the main benefit (research output) is partly an implied one.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help make use of logs and strengthen monitoring, but it does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated CI checks for compliance features are a fairly expected, sensible response that shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI gate with a test harness) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated pre-release gates are a common engineering and compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building CI integration tests with sandboxes, synthetic inputs, and restart cycles is reasonably feasible with standard engineering tooling and some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that logging capability exists in high-risk prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It reliably verifies that logging is active and persistent before release, but it does not decide which events or fields satisfy Article 12 or cover documentation and retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK enforced by CI is a sensible but very expected response among labs to a logging mandate, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely making it default, so it is slight stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal logging middleware and gating CI on it is a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A Python decorator library writing JSONL with a CI import check is cheap and non-radical, needing only modest engineering effort and some adoption discipline.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically capturing events across the lab's prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, standardized automatic event capture in every prototype would substantially meet the logging mandate, though it leaves out documentation, the Article 12(3) specifics, log retention and integrity beyond append-only JSONL, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating documentation as a living artifact tied to version control and audits is a common, widely recommended practice with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, apart from minor CI automation.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining living technical documentation with owners and audits is a standard, fully lawful compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning owners, adding CI triggers, and running quarterly audits requires some process and tooling changes but is reasonably feasible with existing engineering practice.
evidence_applicability: It directly solves an identified related problem (keeping technical documentation current) that is adjacent to, rather than squarely part of, the logging mandate; the link to logging is implied via Recital 71.
evidence_effectiveness: Up-to-date technical documentation addresses the documentation duty from Recital 71 but not the automatic event logging mandate in Article 12 itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using Article 12 logs as a substrate for sequential/Bayesian drift detection with provable false-alarm rates and open benchmarks is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but drift monitoring from logs is a fairly familiar idea, so it is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logs into a research program and public offering (open benchmarks, tools for deployers), changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than just adding a logging tool.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing synthetic benchmarks and building monitoring methods violates no legal or social norms and is a scientifically welcomed strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires statistical research expertise, synthetic log generation, and benchmark development, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial research effort with some resource commitment.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting value from Article 12 logs for post-market and operational monitoring (Art. 12(2)), which relates to but is not the core logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself implement the logging mandate and only helps with downstream use of logs for monitoring, so it contributes partially to meeting the logging obligation or adapting R&D.

evidence_originality: Interpretable-by-construction architectures with event hooks are an interesting, somewhat unusual compliance response but not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It ties logging into architecture design and research direction (loggable-by-design), changing the relationship between R&D and compliance rather than just adding logging tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a toolkit and publishing a paper is a legitimate, somewhat uncommon response that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team building a toolkit around a small model suite in one quarter is reasonably feasible but requires real research and engineering changes.
evidence_applicability: It targets Article 12(2) traceability directly, though the link to the lab's actual logging mandate is implied through research and community benefits rather than concrete compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: Inspectable internal state and event hooks would contribute to traceability but do not by themselves meet Article 12's automatic event logging obligations for the lab's deployed systems, so only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Combining regulatory documentation with ML venue disclosure norms is an interesting, somewhat imaginative pairing that is not the typical response, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a merged template) and links compliance to the lab's publication and research output, modestly changing how compliance relates to R&D, but it still essentially treats compliance as documentation practice.
evidence_acceptability: Aligning compliance documentation with publication norms violates no legal or social norms and is a somewhat unusual yet inoffensive strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building templates with the publications team and piloting on two projects is a modest, reasonably feasible change with low cost, though some disclosure tension (IP, confidentiality) may require work.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets technical documentation under Recital 71, which relates to the Act's record-keeping goals, but it does not address Article 12's automatic event logging mandate, so it solves an implied, related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Merged documentation templates would help with documentation compliance but leave the automatic logging requirement (Art. 12 events, traceability, post-market monitoring) unaddressed, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design in CI/CD is a well-known, expected response to such mandates, with only the sufficiency checker adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements such as design-time schemas and an automated sufficiency checker, but still treats compliance as a logging and documentation practice integrated in tooling, i.e. compliance-by-design that is fairly standard.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance into the development pipeline is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring CI/CD to require log schemas and auto-generate compliance artefacts in one quarter is a reasonable set of engineering changes, though it needs some real effort across teams.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate and adapting R&D workflow, with logs, documentation, and monitoring hooks tied to the regulation.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would give every system Article 12 logging capability by default, though Annex III-specific fields and judgments about the sufficiency of logs are not fully covered, so it is a strong but not guaranteed complete solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing position papers to influence regulation is a common response, though framing logging as a methodological advance for auditing adds a mildly interesting angle.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes logging as a research contribution and seeks to shape guidance, which modestly changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, but it adds no new compliance mechanism and does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing and engaging with standards bodies is a common, normatively unproblematic strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two researchers drafting a paper and presenting at a conference is low cost and non-radical, though peer-review acceptance is uncertain.
evidence_applicability: Writing a position paper on traceability relates to the logging mandate only indirectly, since it implies reputational and regulatory-influence benefits rather than directly meeting the Article 12 logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A paper and conference talk would not make the lab's systems log events or satisfy Article 12, so it is unlikely to solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: A reusable internal logging middleware is a common, mundane engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging library integrated at build time is standard compliance and logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal library with a project-lead mandate is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers prototyping within the existing CI/CD pipeline over one quarter is low-cost and involves non-radical changes, though a sprint-zero mandate adds some process change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a logging component that captures the Article 12(3) items (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier identities).
evidence_effectiveness: If adopted it would meet the logging mandate for Annex III systems, but it covers only the 12(3) minimum fields and does not address Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging from design with a dedicated architect is a common, expected response to this mandate and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard privacy/compliance-by-design practice that treats compliance as logging engineering, with a modest process addition but no change in how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging in by design is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: Assigning a logging architect per project and designing a telemetry schema in sprint zero is a moderate process change using ordinary engineering practice, reasonably feasible without radical cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building in the Article 12 logging elements, including the Annex III 1(a) minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would substantially satisfy the technical logging requirement, but it mostly mirrors the Annex III(1)(a) minimums and does not address broader Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or post-market monitoring use, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance tests in CI are a fairly expected DevOps-style response, though tying contract tests to project type and Article 12(2) purposes is a sensible touch that is not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a CI gate with contract tests) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Internal engineering gating violates no legal or social norms and is a common, accepted strategy.
evidence_implementability: It needs writing contract tests per project type and integrating a gate into existing CI/CD, which is reasonably feasible with some changes and modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D prototyping by catching logging gaps early.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would reliably ensure logging completeness and schema correctness, which addresses the logging mandate, though it does not cover retention, the Article 12(3) specifics or documentation beyond logs, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable shared logging infrastructure is a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging SDK is a common, uncontroversial engineering approach that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires one senior engineer for six months plus incremental onboarding, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial change rather than a trivially cheap one.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified log events.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared SDK would substantially deliver logging capability, but it covers mainly Art. 12(3)-style fields and leaves traceability-appropriateness, retention, and documentation partly unaddressed, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a CI regression-diff signal against a golden baseline is an interesting, somewhat imaginative repurposing, but it is not wholly unexpected for an AI lab.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns logging from a compliance chore into a development quality tool woven into the engineering workflow, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance without altering what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using CI gates and logs for regression checking is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight comparison service added to an existing CI pipeline with a dashboard report is reasonably feasible, needing some changes such as building baselines and the diff tooling.
evidence_applicability: It uses the Article 12 logs to catch risk-relevant events and thus addresses an implied problem of exploiting the logging mandate for R&D, rather than directly meeting the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps detect risk-relevant events during prototyping and leverages logs, but it does not itself satisfy the full logging mandate (retention, traceability, minimum content), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Continuous compliance testing in CI is a fairly common DevOps idea, sensible but not surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely automating verification without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing gates in CI pipelines are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses an existing harness framework and standard CI contract tests with schema validation, requiring only some added test and corpus work, so it is reasonably feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying Article 12(3) fields are present in every build.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging fields are correct and prevents regressions, but it only checks Article 12(3) fields and does not address the broader logging design, Article 12(2) relevance, or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance with CI gates is a fairly common and expected response, with only mild novelty in tying it to the Article 12(3) fields before model code.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (logging contract and CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance gate in the workflow with CI enforcement is a common engineering practice that offends no norms, though some researchers may find it mildly constraining.
evidence_implementability: Adding an intake template, tech-lead sign-off, and a CI check for log-emission stubs requires modest process and tooling changes that are readily feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate within R&D by requiring Article 12(3) fields be defined and emitted from the start of every sprint.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably ensure logging hooks exist in prototypes, but it covers only the logging capability (and Art. 12(3) fields apply only to Annex III 1(a) systems), leaving retention, log quality, and documentation to other measures, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging tests as CI pass/fail criteria is a sensible, known DevOps-style practice with some modest twist in replaying synthetic sessions, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (property-based tests, CI gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely automating its verification.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires writing test suites and pipeline stages, which is reasonably feasible with existing CI infrastructure, though defining synthetic sessions and the required event schemas takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring required events are actually recorded (do X to get complete logs).
evidence_effectiveness: CI gates verifying log completeness would reliably catch logging gaps in prototypes, but they address only verification of event emission, not retention, log design, or the wider compliance obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using compliance logs for deterministic replay debugging is a sensible and somewhat imaginative reuse, but log-replay tooling is a known concept and not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes how compliance relates to R&D by turning logging into a debugging asset that speeds iteration, which weaves logging into engineering work rather than treating it as overhead.
evidence_acceptability: A developer-side debugging tool built on logs violates no legal or social norms, though repurposing compliance logs for debugging is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing Jupyter debugging notebooks with a connector module that reads from existing middleware storage, so it needs some new development but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It uses the Article 12 logs (reference database, matched inputs, verifier overrides) for replay, which serves the implied problem of getting value from the logging mandate but does not itself deliver the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by exploiting and implicitly validating logs for traceability, but it does not ensure the logs are generated, complete, or compliant, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning the logging constraint into a publishable research agenda is interesting and shows some imagination but is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance tooling itself a research output, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking since it does not change what the lab researches broadly.
evidence_acceptability: Funding postdocs and a research program paired with compliance staff and publishing results violates no legal or social norms and is a somewhat unusual but inoffensive strategy.
evidence_implementability: Opening two postdoc positions within existing compute allocations and quarterly pairing with compliance is reasonably feasible, though hiring and 'idle' compute assumptions require some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets Article 12 logging and documentation-update needs for long-lifetime systems, which are part of the stated problem, though the means is research rather than direct implementation.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on lightweight logging with compliance grounding would help eventually but is only a partial, slow and uncertain solution to actually meeting the logging mandate now.

evidence_originality: Continuous documentation tied to project milestones is a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, only timing the writing across milestones.
evidence_acceptability: Living documentation files and milestone-gated updates are common, norm-compliant corporate compliance practice.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight template in an existing project-management tool updated at milestone gates is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the technical documentation requirement of Recital 71, which is related to the mandate but only implied for Article 12's automatic logging of events, so the problem solved is implied rather than directly the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with documentation obligations but does not provide automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log analytics for post-market monitoring is a fairly expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination beyond a sensible framing as an early-warning system.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (a streaming analytics pipeline with risk rules and dashboards) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring dashboards and alerts are common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms and aligns with regulatory expectations.
evidence_implementability: A small data-engineering team building a streaming pipeline with configurable rules is reasonably feasible, though defining risk rules and ingesting from deployed systems takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified part of the stated problem, using logs for risk identification and post-market monitoring, though it assumes logging already exists.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with Article 12(2)(a)-(c) monitoring uses of logs but does not itself ensure the systems technically record events or meet the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reconciling Article 12 logs with GDPR minimization via a DPIA and retention matrix is a sensible but fairly expected response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from many labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (DPIA, retention matrix, pseudonymization rules, secure archival) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional, legally prudent approach that violates no norms and is welcomed by regulators and stakeholders.
evidence_implementability: It requires cross-functional coordination and building secure archival infrastructure, which are reasonably feasible measures with some organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem, namely that Article 12 logs containing personal data collide with GDPR, rather than the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the data-protection side of logging and help avoid parallel GDPR enforcement, but it does not itself deliver the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A logging middleware SDK with tamper-evident append-only chained records is the standard, expected engineering response to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It deliberately decouples compliance from R&D and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, which is paradigm preserving standard logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Tamper-evident logging middleware is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities, though logging input data raises minor data protection concerns.
evidence_implementability: A middleware SDK hooking into the serving framework without model code changes is reasonably feasible, though building cryptographic chaining and integrating across pipelines requires some engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (auto-log Article 12 events, including the Article 12(3) items) to get Y (meet the logging mandate), which is explicitly part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic capture of events with tamper-evident storage would largely satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate, though it covers mainly inference and not wider documentation or Article 12(2) event-relevance judgments.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandatory Article 12 logs as a longitudinal drift-science research dataset is an unusual and imaginative angle that few labs would propose, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging feed the lab's science and open publication, stretching rather than breaking the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Aggregating and publishing field logs raises privacy, GDPR, confidentiality and customer-consent concerns, though anonymisation and open science are broadly accepted norms, so it is somewhat unusual but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: Building an anonymised cross-deployment aggregation pipeline with time-series analysis requires significant engineering, data-sharing agreements with deployers, and privacy work, but is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the 'adapt R&D accordingly' part of the problem by using the logs for research, an implied problem related to the stated one.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate (what to log, retention, traceability for Art. 12(2)); it exploits logs once they exist, so it only partially contributes to the problem.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a research corpus is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, but not wholly surprising or never expressed before.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging part of the science, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking since it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for internal research is somewhat unusual but offends no norms, though secondary use of personal data (verifier identities) raises mild GDPR questions.
evidence_implementability: It needs only three researchers and a data pipeline built on logs the lab must already produce, which is some change but reasonably feasible, though privacy limits on verifier identity data add friction.
evidence_applicability: It addresses how to adapt R&D around the logging mandate, an implied problem related to the stated one, but does not directly address how to meet the logging requirements themselves.
evidence_effectiveness: It makes use of the logs and adds research value but does not ensure the logging mandate is met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance gates and docs-as-code with CI are familiar patterns, though applying them to Article 12 is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces process elements (gate, CI-updated template) but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance design tasks into sprint cadence is a common engineering governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A sprint-one design gate with a version-controlled template and CI hooks is a process change using existing tooling, requiring some changes but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need to meet Article 12 logging and keep Recital 71 documentation current, and so directly relates to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses logging design and documentation currency but does not by itself cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or runtime logging quality, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance tests in CI are a fairly expected, engineering-standard response, so the idea is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (an automated CI stage) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding automated tests to CI is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A synthetic-request replay and assertion script on a staging endpoint is a modest, low-cost addition to existing CI pipelines.
evidence_applicability: The CI gate directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying the mandatory log fields are present in each build.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch logging regressions and help keep logs compliant, but it covers only the Article 12(3) minimums and does not address the broader traceability or Article 12(2) event-relevance requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Positioning compliance as a selling point is a fairly familiar business tactic and the one-page dossier is mundane, though somewhat interesting here.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by turning compliance into a competitive differentiator, a stretching move, though R&D itself is unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Marketing compliance in tenders with a mapping dossier violates no norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: A one-page dossier per product attached to tenders is a low-cost, non-radical change, assuming the logging capabilities already exist.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (leveraging compliance commercially, and documenting the mapping of logged fields to sub-articles) that relates to but is not the core logging response.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal markets existing logging capabilities but does not itself deliver or ensure the logging mandate is met, so it is at best a partial contribution to the problem of how to respond.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK for compliance is a common, expected response, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal compliance logging library is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared internal library with decorators and a standard scaffold is a modest engineering effort that fits existing workflows and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing event schemas matching Article 12(2)-(3).
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve much of the technical logging requirement and reduce rework, but it does not cover wider documentation, retention, or deployer obligations or judge which events are relevant, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating compliance documentation from experiment-tracking tools is a sensible and fairly expected response by ML labs, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (auto-generated templates from experiment trackers) and makes documentation a byproduct of research, but it still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Automating technical documentation from existing tools is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing MLflow tracker to emit structured artefacts is a modest engineering change using in-house tools, though it requires some data-engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the Recital 71 technical-documentation requirement and R&D burden, which relates to the stated problem, but does not directly address Article 12's automatic event logging, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reduce documentation burden and keep documentation current, but it covers only part of the mandate and does not deliver Article 12 event logs for traceability or monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging infrastructure is a mundane and expected response from labs facing this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-as-logging practice, consolidated into one tool, with no change to the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared middleware is a common engineering and compliance strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing experiment-tracking and serving stacks, phases rollout over two quarters, and stays within current headcount, which makes it reasonably feasible with some integration changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building a common event-recording layer, so do X to get Y holds with Y being part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A uniform logging layer capturing the Article 12(2) and 12(3) data points would substantially meet the logging mandate across high-risk projects, though it does not itself address documentation, retention, or R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalizing a quantitative similarity space for substantial modification is an unusual and interesting idea showing imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research problem integrated with the lab's science, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, but does not alter what the lab researches broadly.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research on compliance metrics is a legitimate, norm-respecting activity, though somewhat unusual relative to standard logging responses.
evidence_implementability: It requires a substantial research program with new metrics and perturbation experiments across biometric models, which is difficult and uncertain, and the brief says approval means committing resources rather than exploring, so it is a significant undertaking.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses detecting substantial modification, which Article 12(2)(a) links to logging, but it targets an implied compliance trigger problem rather than the logging mandate directly (what to log and how).
evidence_effectiveness: A substantial-modification metric would help the lab know when re-assessment is needed but does not itself deliver logging capability, so it only partially solves the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Combining homomorphic encryption with compliance logging is unusual and shows some imagination, but privacy-preserving logging is a recognized topic and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (cryptographic audit layer) but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving audit logging is legally and socially acceptable and aligns with data-minimization norms, though the cryptographic approach is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Homomorphic-encryption pipelines inside a model-serving stack are computationally expensive and difficult, and the proposal itself calls for prototyping and benchmarking, making this significant change but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 logging mandate, including the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which is an explicitly identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A logging layer that captures lifetime events and the required fields would satisfy the mandate, but homomorphic encryption adds a prototype risk and the proposal does not fully address how the logs stay usable for audit, so it helps substantially without being clearly complete.

evidence_originality: Version-controlled documentation with audits and alerts is common and mundane for compliance.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though with some process tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining living, version-controlled technical documentation with audits is a common compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires assigning a lead per project, a repository, quarterly audits and automated alerts, which are reasonably feasible measures involving some process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses documentation under Recital 71, which is related to record-keeping but not directly the Article 12 logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with technical documentation compliance but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Readiness audits with red/amber/green checklists derived from the regulation are a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A gap audit with RAG checklists is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal compliance audit and checklist is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint with one-page checklists and remediation folded into existing sprints requires only modest effort and non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The audit directly targets identifying and closing gaps against Article 12 logging requirements, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It identifies and sequences remediation but does not itself build the logging, so it is a helpful but partial solution, and it focuses narrowly on Annex III biometric items rather than the general Article 12(1)-(2) requirements.

evidence_originality: Treating the definition of relevant events as an interpretability research problem with causal-tracing perturbation experiments is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance logging a driver of interpretability research and addresses what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing a peer-reviewed taxonomy and offering regulators a scientific basis violates no norms, though a fundamental research programme is a somewhat unusual compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Running perturbation experiments across deployed prototypes and building a validated causal-tracing taxonomy for opaque systems is a difficult, expensive, long-horizon research effort, and the lab needs implementation resources now rather than exploratory research.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the ambiguity in what counts as an 'event relevant for identifying risk situations' under Article 12(2)(a), which is part of the logging mandate.
