evidence_originality: A centralized logging library with interceptors is a very common engineering response to a logging mandate, though well articulated.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standard engineering and compliance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared SDK and wrapping an existing inference pipeline requires some engineering change but is reasonably feasible and reduces per-project burden.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate across the lab's high-risk systems (do X to get automatic event recording).
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy Article 12(1) technical logging capability and support the 12(2) event categories, but it does not cover retention, documentation, or the Annex III-specific fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a reference logging framework is a fairly expected community response, though the cross-institutional benchmark dataset and overhead comparison add some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open framework, shared schema, benchmark study) and creates community offerings born from compliance, but still treats compliance chiefly as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source compliance tooling and shared standards violate no norms, though sharing cross-institutional logging data may raise some confidentiality questions.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular open-source framework plus community governance and a comparative study requires substantial effort but is reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by encoding paragraph 2 and 3 requirements into reusable components.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet the logging mandate for the lab and others, but the mapping of purpose-based recording and legal sufficiency remains partial, so it contributes rather than fully solves.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance testing in CI is a sensible and fairly familiar approach to regulatory checklists, interesting but not strikingly imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (test harness in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Testing logging before release violates no norms and is a common, well-accepted engineering and compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Writing scenario scripts and integrating them into existing CI pipelines is a non-radical change using existing QA staff, though edge-case scenario coverage takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements for Annex III biometric systems, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI-gated test suite would reliably verify that the four minimum recording requirements are met, but it covers only Article 12(3) and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging or documentation duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralised logging middleware or an SDK is a standard engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect from most labs, so it is common and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a plug-in SDK) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, which is slightly stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Standardised logging infrastructure for compliance violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: It needs a new SDK and retrofitting across all active projects within a short timeline, which is a reasonable but non-trivial engineering effort with some changes required.
evidence_applicability: It does X (standardised automatic logging middleware) to get Y (Article 12 compliant logs), and Y is directly part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer that records the Article 12(1)-(3) fields would, if built, directly satisfy the core logging mandate, though it does not cover the technical documentation or the question of how R&D should adapt.

evidence_originality: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (middleware) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging layer with an architecture-review gate is a common, norm-compliant corporate engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a middleware with a four-person team over two sprints and adding a review dependency requires some organizational change but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate with specific logging elements drawn from the regulation.
evidence_effectiveness: It would cover Article 12(3)-style items like timestamps, reference database queries and operator IDs, but not the broader Article 12(2) event relevance for risk identification, post-market monitoring, or documentation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Releasing an open-source Article 12 logging library is a sensible and somewhat interesting move, but open-source compliance tooling is a fairly expected response and is not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a shared open-source library and reference implementations) and a new offering born from compliance, yet it still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release of compliance tooling violates no norms and is a common, welcome strategy in the research community.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers and one researcher for six months is a modest, reasonably feasible resource commitment using standard software engineering.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, with Annex III use cases as validation, although the lab-specific decision is addressed only indirectly.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logging library would help meet the logging mandate, mainly for external groups, but it only partly solves the lab's own compliance and R&D adaptation problem.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking log schemas with fault-injection scenarios is an unusual and somewhat imaginative approach, though not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an open benchmark suite for log schemas) but still treats compliance as a logging-design practice, without changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source publication of methodology and synthetic benchmarks offends no norms and is a somewhat uncommon but acceptable strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a fault-injection scenario library and benchmark suite takes substantial engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with synthetic data.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of knowing whether log schemas are sufficient for Article 12(2) traceability, which relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab design adequate logging and give a principled design reference, but it does not itself implement logging or meet the mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using logs to drive post-market monitoring is the expected, mundane response that the regulation itself envisions, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (analytics team, triggers, escalation workflow) but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice without changing the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Post-market monitoring using Article 12 logs with incident escalation is a common, legally aligned strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires standing up a new analytics team, real-time log pipelines and threshold definitions, which is a reasonably feasible but notable change rather than a trivial one.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified post-market monitoring and operation-monitoring purposes of the logs named in Article 12(2), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to Article 12(2)(b)-(c) monitoring purposes but does not by itself deliver the logging capability or address R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging platform is an expected, sensible response that many labs would propose, with only modest framing around protecting research iteration speed.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (shared middleware/SDK) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving R&D's relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized, append-only audit logging is a common strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight SDK hooking into existing serving infrastructure with an append-only store is a reasonably feasible, moderate engineering effort that platform teams routinely do.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate while limiting burden on R&D, with explicit reference to Article 12(2) event types.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the automatic event recording required by Article 12 but is only a partial solution since it omits retention, Annex III-specific fields like the identification of verifying persons, and documentation/governance aspects.

evidence_originality: Treating log governance as a publishable research frontier is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not truly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new element (a governance research program) and turns compliance into a research topic and source of scholarly credibility, which changes how R&D relates to obligations, though it does not change what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Interdisciplinary research and publishing a position paper are unusual as a compliance response but offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A four-person group doing case-study analysis and writing a paper is reasonably feasible with modest resources and no radical organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely uncertainty about log scope and permissible use, which relates to the stated problem of how to respond to the logging mandate, rather than the direct need to build compliant logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A position paper and case studies would help de-risk decisions about log use and retention but would not itself deliver the logging capability the mandate requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in CI are a fairly common DevOps pattern, so this is interesting but not especially imaginative or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a blocking test stage to CI is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a test harness and synthetic traffic replay within the existing GitLab CI, which is reasonably feasible with some changes but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking that mandatory log fields exist before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A blocking CI gate that verifies Article 12 fields, types and chronological integrity would help ensure logging capability is present, but it covers only schema conformance of synthetic traffic and not retention, relevance of events, or the full compliance scope, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Documentation templates for compliance and reproducibility are common; pairing the two audiences is mildly interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new template format but still treats compliance as a documentation practice without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: An internal documentation template aligned with regulatory and peer-review norms violates no laws or sensibilities and is a common, welcome strategy.
evidence_implementability: A one-quarter working group of two researchers drafting and piloting a template is a modest, reasonably feasible change requiring no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It targets documentation clarity, which is an implied, related problem (Recital 71 documentation) rather than the identified logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The template addresses technical documentation (Recital 71) rather than the automatic event logging mandated by Article 12, so it only partially contributes to the stated logging problem.

evidence_originality: Feeding compliance logs into research hypothesis generation is an interesting, somewhat imaginative idea that is uncommon among typical logging responses, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance logging and R&D by making logs drive the lab's research agenda, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking since it does not rethink what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Reviewing anonymised log excerpts to inform research planning is a reasonable, somewhat unusual use of compliance logs that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only one postdoc per quarter and memo writing integrated into existing planning cycles, which is a reasonably feasible, modest change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to the logging regime by exploiting log data, which relates to the stated problem but not directly to meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate (no logging design, retention, or traceability measures) and only helps with adapting R&D, so it is at best a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Maintaining a living technical file with a template and quarterly review is a common, mundane compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard documentation practice using existing tools and templates, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation ownership, sprint updates and legal review are conventional strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses an existing GitLab wiki, a lightweight template and one designated engineer per project, so it is cheap and non-radical to implement.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation (Recital 71) and traceability evidence, which relates to record-keeping but not directly to Article 12's automatic event logging, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A maintained technical file helps with compliance evidence and traceability but does not deliver the automatic event logging the mandate requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a research dataset and open benchmark is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, but the idea of reusing operational data for research is not unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and creating new academic partnerships and outputs born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Academic partnerships and publishing are normal, though sharing anonymised log data raises some privacy and confidentiality concerns that are manageable and do not offend sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs data anonymisation, partnership agreements, and benchmark building, which are reasonably feasible but involve real effort and legal review of log data use.
evidence_applicability: The idea repurposes mandated logs for monitoring research and Article 72 post-market work, which relates to the logging mandate only by implication (a research benefit built on compliance data), not by meeting the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure Article 12 logging capability or compliance, but it helps by making logs useful for post-market monitoring and aligning compliance with R&D, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design gates and architecture reviews are a common, expected response to such mandates, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A lifecycle gate is a new process element, but it still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged, so it is at most slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Adding review checkpoints and compliance sign-off is a standard governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It folds into existing quarterly reviews with a small three-person panel, though quarterly timing could add some delay, so the change is modest.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets how the lab will ensure its systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-build spec review would help ensure logging is designed in, but it only checks the spec on paper and does not guarantee implementation or runtime logging quality, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Dedicated compliance budget lines are a fairly familiar overhead-allocation idea, with only mild interest in the fixed percentage framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a funding process but still treats compliance as logging/documentation practice and leaves the way research is done unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Earmarking a budget line for compliance is a conventional, norm-respecting financial practice, though a fixed 8% carve-out may draw some internal pushback from PIs.
evidence_implementability: Revising a budget template and briefing PIs at an annual retreat are non-radical, low-cost administrative changes, though funder acceptance of the line item is somewhat uncertain.
evidence_applicability: It funds logging, documentation and post-market monitoring infrastructure, which is an implied enabling problem related to meeting the logging mandate rather than directly producing logging capability.
evidence_effectiveness: Funding helps resource compliance work but does not itself design or implement the logs required by Article 12, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Using logs for drift detection is a fairly expected idea in ML monitoring, though framing it as a publishable research programme born from compliance shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making the compliance logs a research dataset and turning compliance into a source of scientific output, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Anonymised log analysis for monitoring and publishing methods violates no norms, though data-protection scrutiny on reusing logs warrants some care.
evidence_implementability: It needs a new research programme, anonymisation pipelines, and algorithm development validated against incident data, which is a significant but feasible commitment.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, making use of the mandated logs for risk detection and post-market monitoring, which relates to the stated problem but is not the core act of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift analytics on logs would help identify risk situations and support post-market monitoring (Art 12(2)(a),(b)) but does not itself deliver the logging capability or cover the other mandated logging requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating log traceability measurement as a new research subfield is unusual and imaginative compared with typical compliance responses, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research subfield, addressing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme on log quality and publishing it violates no norms and is a legitimate, if somewhat unusual, response to compliance.
evidence_implementability: Hiring two postdocs and building benchmark datasets from logged systems is a significant, costly commitment with uncertain payoff, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses how the lab adapts its R&D in response to the logging mandate, but only implies the need to meet the mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not itself implement the Article 12 logging capabilities and so contributes only partially, mainly by improving log quality and by redirecting research.

evidence_originality: Designing experiments around production log fields is a sensible idea with some imagination but resembles existing MLOps and experiment-tracking practice, so it is interesting without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It shifts compliance upstream into research design, which changes the relationship between R&D and logging obligations (logging woven into the science), but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized templates and CI checks for provenance are a common, norm-compliant practice that offends no sensibilities, though some researchers may find the added rigidity burdensome.
evidence_implementability: A one-page template and CI validation hook are low-cost, non-radical changes, though they require some cultural adoption and ongoing review.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by aligning research data schemas with required log fields, an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help with traceability and readiness but covers only research-phase records and not the full production logging capability or the other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating the regulation's logging requirement as a research object for measuring its performance cost is interesting and somewhat unusual, though the methodology is conventional benchmarking.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (experiments and benchmarks) and begins to tie compliance to what the lab researches, but it still treats logging as a practice to be measured rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Running internal controlled experiments is a normal research activity that offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: Paired benchmark experiments across five architectures are feasible with existing research resources but require significant effort, and Article 12(3) applies only to a specific Annex III category, which makes the setup somewhat awkward.
evidence_applicability: The proposal measures the performance costs of logging, which is only loosely related to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate, so it is an implied rather than direct solution.
evidence_effectiveness: Experiments quantifying logging overhead would not make the lab compliant and would at best inform later design choices, so it is unlikely to solve the problem.

evidence_originality: Shared logging libraries and auto-instrumentation are common, expected responses, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK scaffold) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal logging SDK built into prototype templates is a standard, legally compliant engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin middleware library pinned into an existing template hooking into the current inference pipeline requires some build effort but is reasonably feasible and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the required fields automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to logging compliance but only partially solves it, since it covers prototypes, relies on fixed schema, and Article 12(2) risk-relevant events and retention are not fully addressed.

evidence_originality: Documentation packs per Recital 71 are expected, and the tender-differentiator framing is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a versioned documentation pack linked to logging and repurposes compliance as a tender asset, which is a modest new offering born from compliance but does not change what the lab researches or how science is done.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining documentation and using compliance as a marketing asset in public tenders is a legitimate, norm-compliant business strategy.
evidence_implementability: Versioned repositories, release-cycle sign-off, and bundling into tenders use existing tooling and processes, requiring some process changes but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (technical documentation and traceability alongside logging, plus commercial value) rather than directly meeting the Article 12 logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: Documentation and linking to logs would contribute to Recital 71 traceability, but it does not itself specify the Article 12 logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Pre-release compliance testing against the stated legal minimums is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate with no surprising element.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that adds a verification step, leaving the lab's R&D way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A pre-deployment internal compliance audit gated by sign-off is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated compliance-testing team, scripted scenario suites, and staging environments, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial organizational addition.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate by testing the specific listed minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: Verifying Article 12(3) minimums before release would help ensure logging compliance, but it only tests for logging and does not itself build the logging capability or address Article 12(1)-(2) or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using compliance as a trust signal in procurement is a fairly familiar strategy, though it shows some imagination in exposing log metadata to clients.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a market offering (client-facing dashboard, white paper, sales narrative), changing the relationship between compliance and the lab's business, though not what the lab researches, which fits paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing white papers and offering transparency to clients is a common, norm-respecting strategy, though exposing log metadata needs care around confidentiality.
evidence_implementability: A white paper, a metadata dashboard and commercial briefings are reasonably feasible measures requiring some development effort and data governance but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, extracting business value from compliance, which relates to how the lab responds to the mandate but does not itself meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps monetize and leverage compliance but does not implement logging or adapt R&D, so it is only a partial contribution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Building logging into architectures as a first-class output is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing that is uncommon among lab responses, though tied to known interpretability techniques.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making traceability an architectural design constraint woven into the science, which is paradigm stretching and arguably touches what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme on architectures with built-in logging violates no legal or social norms and is an unusual but unoffensive strategy for compliance.
evidence_implementability: Redesigning model architectures and training pipelines and prototyping three variants is a significant, costly R&D effort, though not impossible, and the stated problem concerns committing implementation resources rather than exploration.
evidence_applicability: It aims to make event logging a native model output, which directly relates to the Article 12 logging mandate, though it frames the work as research rather than a compliance implementation.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, attention-trace and gradient-salience outputs only partly address Article 12's required event records (usage periods, reference databases, input data, persons), so it contributes partially.

evidence_originality: An open-source logging framework is a fairly expected response from an AI lab, though the open-license framing as shared scientific infrastructure is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a new element (a reusable open-source logging framework) and gestures at turning compliance into shared infrastructure, but it still treats compliance fundamentally as logging practice and does not change what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance tooling and releasing it openly is a common, norm-respecting strategy, with only minor concerns about disclosing proprietary details.
evidence_implementability: Building a framework around an existing serving stack with pluggable backends is reasonably feasible, but it requires meaningful engineering effort plus internal validation and open-source release processes.
evidence_applicability: The framework directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate, including the specified timestamped usage and reference database records.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, an Article 12-compliant instrumentation framework would meet the core logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it covers mainly Annex III 1(a) and says little about the broader traceability, risk-event, and post-market monitoring needs.

evidence_originality: Building shared logging middleware and design guidelines up front is a standard, expected response to a logging mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice, shifted earlier in the pipeline, without changing how the lab does R&D or its relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A design-time compliance directive with shared tooling is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building reusable middleware and issuing design guidelines requires some organizational and engineering change but is reasonably feasible with existing resources.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building Article 12(2)-tied logging into the lab's R&D process to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Standardized logging middleware tied to Article 12(2) categories would satisfy the logging mandate if executed, though it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics or documentation duties, making it a strong but not fully complete solution.

evidence_originality: Framing log categories as pre-registered falsifiable hypotheses is an unusual and imaginative idea that turns compliance into scientific inquiry, which few labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance monitoring part of the scientific method and publishing the resulting findings, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Pre-registration and statistical monitoring protocols are unusual in compliance but offend no legal or business sensibilities, and publishing findings may raise some confidentiality concerns without being unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: It requires a per-system protocol, real-time statistic computation in the logging pipeline, and researcher process changes, which is reasonably feasible but involves some real changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of how to use logging to identify risk, support post-market monitoring, and monitor operation under Article 12(2)(a)-(c), though the link to the basic logging mandate is somewhat implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Pre-registering hypotheses and configuring logs to compute risk-relevant statistics would help meet Article 12(2) traceability and monitoring goals, but it does not by itself cover the baseline automatic logging capability or the Annex III minimum logging items, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A tamper-evident, cryptographically chained append-only log for the Article 12(3) minimum data points is a common and expected response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice implemented as a software module, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Tamper-evident audit logging and pre-deployment validation are common strategies that violate no legal or social norms, though the log's biometric data raises minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: Append-only cryptographically chained logs and test harnesses are mature techniques, requiring a dedicated module and some integration work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It explicitly does X (capture the four mandated data points in a tamper-evident log) to get Y (Article 12(3) compliance), and Y is directly part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would directly satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it does not cover Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other high-risk systems or the wider R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Risk classification at project intake is a common, expected compliance response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process step (triage rubric and sign-off) but still treats compliance as a standard governance and logging practice, leaving R&D ways of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal triage and sign-off gates are common governance practice and offend no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A one-page rubric plus a sign-off gate at project inception is a lightweight, low-cost process change that needs no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: Scoping which projects trigger Article 12 obligations is an implied prerequisite to meeting the logging mandate, not the logging itself, so it relates indirectly to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps target compliance effort and avoid late redesign but does not itself build any logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware is a common and expected response with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard logging-as-engineering-practice approach, introducing a shared tool but leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance essentially unchanged, though embedding from first commit is slightly more than bolt-on.
evidence_acceptability: Building reusable compliance tooling is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging library with thin adapters is a moderate engineering effort using existing stacks, requiring some changes but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specific Article 12(3)(a)-(d) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would directly deliver Article 12 logging capability across prototypes, but it covers only logging (not documentation or the broader R&D adaptation, and Art. 12(3) fields apply only to certain Annex III systems), so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating documentation from experiment trackers is a fairly expected and well-known MLOps response, though tying claims in papers to training runs adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (a generator and structured metadata capture) but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice, and does not change the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Extending experiment tracking and generating documentation for regulators is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building on the existing experiment tracker makes it reasonably feasible, though a generator and validation against a regulator checklist require some development effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (technical documentation and traceability) rather than directly the Article 12 logging mandate of runtime event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with technical documentation under Recital 71 but does not address Article 12's automatic event logging of the system's operation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Minimal-sufficient logging with a regulation-to-hook mapping is an interesting and sensible angle, but not highly surprising among expected responses to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (formalised mapping, pluggable modules, publishable methodology) but still treats compliance fundamentally as a logging practice, though the auditability-as-design framing hints at slight stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Data-minimising compliance logging and publishing methodology violate no norms and are broadly acceptable to regulators and the public.
evidence_implementability: Building pluggable logger modules per Annex III category and a synthetic validation corpus requires significant engineering and research effort, but is feasible with moderate changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by defining and building logging modules that cover Article 12(2)(a)-(c) events, which is the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, mapping regulatory event categories to logging hooks would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it is framed as research and validated only on synthetic incidents and Article 12(3) specifics are only loosely covered, so it is reasonable but arguably not the complete solution.

evidence_originality: Dedicated compliance budget lines are a fairly expected organizational response, with the ring-fencing rationale being sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a funding and process element but still treats compliance as a logging/audit overhead phase, leaving R&D's relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Earmarking a compliance budget line and adding a work package to grant templates is a common governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires revising a template and budget policy, which is a modest administrative change at low cost, though 8-12% reallocation may cause some friction.
evidence_applicability: Ring-fencing budget for logging architecture and record maintenance directly addresses how the lab will meet the logging mandate, though it funds the work rather than specifying the logging itself, so the link is to an implied enabling problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Protecting resources and creating milestones helps ensure logging gets built and maintained, but it is only a partial solution since it does not define what to log or how to satisfy Article 12.

evidence_originality: Gap analysis and retrofit-versus-redesign triage is a common, expected response to a new regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance gap analysis that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A prioritization audit with traffic-light reporting is a common, norm-compliant management practice that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: A two-week audit by in-house senior engineers mapping event flows to Article 12 categories is low-cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (knowing where to spend compliance resources) that relates directly to deciding how to meet the logging mandate, rather than the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A triage audit only produces classification and cost estimates to guide budgeting, so it contributes to the solution but does not itself implement logging, making it a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared open-source compliance infrastructure is a reasonably known idea, though tailoring it to research-derived systems and the lab-consortium framing shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Consortium formation and positioning as an infrastructure thought-leader create new partnerships born from compliance, changing how the lab relates to compliance somewhat, though the core remains logging tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source consortia for shared compliance tooling are somewhat unusual for logging compliance but offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Modest resources (one postdoc FTE, compute credits) and a lightweight governance model are feasible, but coordinating a multi-lab consortium and aligning partners requires some organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building a shared logging-compliance layer, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer would help meet Article 12 and cut cost, but it is only a partial solution since the lab must still integrate it, address system-specific requirements, and the small resource commitment limits delivery.

evidence_originality: A gap-analysis audit with a taskforce is a standard, mundane compliance response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is conventional compliance and logging practice with no change to how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits and gap analyses are common, norm-abiding strategies that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: An eight-week cross-team taskforce with gap maps and platform-provided reference implementations is a reasonably feasible, moderate-effort organizational measure, not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would identify and help close gaps for biometric systems under development, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) and the 12(3) fields, not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Adding a design-review checkpoint and charter template section for logging is a sensible but fairly common shift-left compliance approach that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (charter section, reviewer) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review checkpoint and charter template revision are common governance strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires only a template revision, a training session, and one reviewer per charter, which are non-radical changes at low cost, though reviewer workload adds some burden.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets how to meet the Article 12(2) logging mandate by specifying logged events at design time, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is planned and reduces rework, but it only specifies and reviews rather than implementing logs, and ignores Art. 12(3) and legacy systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A log-ingesting monitoring dashboard is a mundane, expected response to this mandate, with only a mild tender-differentiator angle.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tool (dashboard) but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, leaving R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance monitoring dashboard is a common, legally sound strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing observability stack with Article 12 event categories within one quarter is reasonably feasible with some changes, though not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses Article 12(2)(b) and (c) logging for post-market monitoring and operational oversight, which is part of the stated problem, though it focuses on consuming logs rather than generating them.
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard helps monitoring and demonstrates compliance but only partially solves the logging mandate, since it does not itself specify what is logged, retention, or Annex III requirements.

evidence_originality: A compliance gap-analysis audit is a common, mundane response to a logging mandate with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A gap-analysis of existing logs against the Article 12(3) fields is standard compliance practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits of logs against legal requirements are a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week cross-functional inspection of existing pilot logs is easy, low-cost, and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12(3) logging minimums for biometric systems, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The sprint only identifies gaps for the Annex III 1(a) minimums and does not itself build logging or cover Article 12(1)-(2) generally, so it is a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking logging overhead across model architectures is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response, with some specificity but little surprising ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a benchmark and viability matrix as new tools but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal benchmarking and publishing an internal matrix violates no norms or sensibilities and is a common engineering strategy.
evidence_implementability: A two-week microbenchmark run on existing GPU cluster and test harnesses is low cost and non-radical, though it depends on an SDK from another proposal.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, namely assessing how logging per Article 12 affects R&D architectures and whether they can meet the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It only measures latency and memory overhead and flags problem architectures, so it contributes information toward compliance but does not itself implement logging or meet the mandate.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging libraries with build-time enforcement are a fairly expected engineering response, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK plus CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library with CI/CD enforcement is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small platform team building an SDK plugged into existing CI/CD gates requires some changes and effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly automates recording of the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields, which is part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver the mandated logging fields for Annex III systems, but covers only the 12(3) minimums (not the broader 12(2) traceability or non-Annex III systems or documentation), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralised, reusable logging infrastructure is a sensible and commonly expected response to this mandate, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable logging middleware is a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations, fitting slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared compliance infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A 3-4 FTE pod over two quarters hooking into an existing ML pipeline is a moderate, reasonably feasible commitment of resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-capturing the Article 12(3) fields and generic event logs.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, default-inherited logging would satisfy the logging requirement across projects, though 'generic event logs' may leave gaps in Article 12(2) traceability tailoring, so it is largely but not fully a solution.

evidence_originality: Gating projects on a compliance or design-time spec is a fairly familiar governance pattern (like privacy-by-design reviews), so it is interesting but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a traceability spec as a stage-gate kickoff requirement) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moved earlier, rather than changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate sign-offs and compliance templates alongside ethics review are common governance strategies that violate no norms, though a hard 'no spec, no build' gate may draw mild resistance.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing R&D governance, a template drafted with Compliance, and training within a quarter, requiring only modest, non-radical process changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping logged events to the article's specific purposes (a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: A spec requirement ensures logging is designed in and mapped to Article 12(2), which contributes substantially but does not itself implement logging capabilities, cover Article 12(3) specifics, or verify actual performance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a public community benchmark for drift detection is an unusual, interesting response that shows some imagination, though benchmark releases are familiar in ML.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning logging into a research offering and community positioning, stretching the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing benchmarks is a normal research practice, though releasing anonymised operational logs from deployments raises some data protection and confidentiality sensitivities that make it somewhat unusual rather than fully common.
evidence_implementability: It requires aggregating and anonymising logs, collecting ground-truth metrics quarterly, and building a rubric and release process, which is reasonably feasible but needs notable additional effort and customer/data permissions.
evidence_applicability: It relates to Article 12(2)(b) post-market monitoring and logging strategies, addressing an implied problem (better logging for monitoring) rather than the lab's direct compliance obligation.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark would help improve post-market monitoring research but does not itself fulfil the Article 12 logging mandate, so it is at best a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging middleware in CI/CD is a fairly expected response, with only mild interest in auto-generating schemas tied to Article 12(2).
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (middleware with auto schema generation) but still treats compliance as logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance logging in the build pipeline is a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a logging middleware into existing CI/CD pipelines requires some engineering changes and schema design but is reasonably feasible with standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by producing logs aligned to its categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially ensure technical logging capability exists, but it does not cover deployer obligations, retention, Annex III specifics, or whether the logged events are actually sufficient, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware for compliance is a common, expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice, though built into design, and leaves the lab's relationship between R&D and compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory logging middleware and tamper-evident storage are common, norm-compliant compliance strategies.
evidence_implementability: Building a reusable logging SDK with hooks and append-only storage is a reasonable engineering effort requiring some changes but well within standard practice.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the automatic logging requirement for high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Native automatic event logging across the lifetime would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not itself define which events or Annex III specifics are logged.

evidence_originality: Using logs for risk-trigger alerts and mock notified-body audits is a sensible but fairly expected response to Article 12(2), with only mild interest in framing logs as an early-warning asset.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (a monitoring unit, dashboards, simulated audits) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring units, dashboards, and mock audits are common compliance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Standing up a monitoring unit, analytics pipeline, and quarterly audits requires some new staffing and tooling but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of using logs for traceability, post-market monitoring, and operation monitoring under Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: It would meaningfully support Article 12(2) purposes of risk identification and post-market monitoring, but it does not itself ensure that systems technically record events, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a longitudinal research dataset is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though labs would plausibly think of logs as monitoring data, so it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the logging obligation into a source of scientific research, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Analyzing logs for research is somewhat unusual and could raise data-protection and deployer-confidentiality concerns, but it offends no norms if handled properly.
evidence_implementability: It builds on minimum log schemas and a time-series store with a quarterly analysis cycle, which is reasonably feasible, though access to deployer-held logs and data governance add some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of getting value from the logging mandate and adapting R&D to it, which relates to the stated problem though not directly how to meet the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It meets the minimum logging mandate and adds research value, but it does not itself address compliance depth such as retention, integrity, or traceability beyond the minimum schema, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A design-review gate with a checklist for logging specs is a common, sensible compliance-by-design practice that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process checkpoint but still treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review gate is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It only adds a half-day review to the existing calendar with a one-page checklist and ticket sign-off, so it is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by reviewing specs against paragraphs 2 and 3.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is designed in early, but it covers only the spec stage and does not itself deliver the logging capability, retention, or ongoing compliance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A quarterly checklist audit of the Article 12(3) minimum fields is a common, expected compliance response with little that is imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice (audit checklist, board escalation) that leaves the lab's way of working and its R&D-compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits with board escalation are a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A checklist audit run by legal and engineering staff each quarter is a modest, reasonably low-cost process requiring no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified Article 12(3) logging requirements, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit would help verify that the four mandatory fields are logged for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it only verifies rather than builds logging and covers just part of Article 12 (general logging, 12(2) purposes).

evidence_originality: Compliance test suites and CI gates are a fairly common, expected response to such a mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (test harness/gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A pytest-based harness run as a staging gate uses standard tooling and requires only modest, non-radical changes to the existing pipeline.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to ensure prototypes meet the Article 12 logging mandate (do X to verify logging, which is part of the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that logging works but does not itself implement logging, retention, or the broader Article 12(2) risk/monitoring requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Cryptographic hash-chain lineage for reference databases is an interesting, somewhat imaginative combination, though tamper-evident logging and data lineage are known ideas.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (hash-chain ledger, benchmark) and ties compliance logging to publishable reproducibility research, modestly changing the R&D-compliance relationship, though it remains largely a logging-centered tool.
evidence_acceptability: Hash-chained audit ledgers and publishing benchmarks are normal, uncontroversial practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a hash-chain ledger and a benchmark of degradation detection thresholds requires some new engineering and research work but is reasonably feasible with existing tools.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets Article 12(3)(b) reference-database logging for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is part of the stated logging mandate, though only for a narrow subset of systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the reference-database logging minimum for biometric systems but does not cover the other required logs (use periods, matched inputs, human verifiers) or general high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into architecture and gating releases on compliance is a common, expected response to Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standard module and review process but still treats compliance as logging practice, essentially standard privacy/compliance-by-design.
evidence_acceptability: A binding internal engineering standard with compliance sign-off is a common, norm-respecting corporate strategy.
evidence_implementability: A unified logging API with a three-person pod and release gating is a reasonably feasible set of engineering changes, though retrofitting existing builds and standardizing across all systems takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by building automatic event recording per Article 12 paragraphs 1 and 2.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially meet the logging mandate for the covered systems, but it omits Annex III-specific fields in paragraph 3, retention, and post-market monitoring details, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-project regulatory scoping or risk classification is a common and expected compliance step, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a scoping template and sign-off step but still treats compliance as a procedural gate before development, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged, though it introduces a new process element.
evidence_acceptability: A scoping template and compliance sign-off are common governance practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: A one-page template and a reviewer sign-off are low-cost, non-radical changes, though the two-week gate adds some delay.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of knowing which logging obligations apply and planning resources, which relates to the stated problem but does not itself implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Early classification helps allocate resources and avoid late surprises but does not deliver the logging capability itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance testing in CI is a sensible, somewhat known DevOps idea applied to logging; it is interesting but not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (log spec, CI gate) and shifts verification left, but still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations much.
evidence_acceptability: Adding definition-of-done criteria and CI checks is a common engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A YAML spec and a CI synthetic workload test require modest tooling and process changes that are reasonably feasible, though synthetic workloads for diverse prototypes take some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate within the lab's R&D by verifying required event types are captured, so do X to get Y where Y is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a CI-enforced log schema gate would ensure that Article 12(2)(a)-(c) event logging is built into every high-risk prototype, but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or log quality in production, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A documentation steward with periodic audits is a common, mundane compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation upkeep and internal audits are common, uncontroversial compliance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning documentation stewards and running quarterly audits are modest process additions using existing staff and no radical changes, so it is easy and low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation upkeep from Recital 71, which is related to but not the same as the Article 12 logging mandate, so it solves an implied rather than directly stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping technical files current helps overall compliance but does not itself implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandated logs as a shared public benchmark of post-deployment behaviour is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly unprecedented as a data-sharing idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logs into a research asset and creates new partnerships and offerings born from compliance, changing the relationship between R&D and obligations, though it stops short of redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Sharing anonymised logs under strict data-use agreements is a somewhat unusual strategy, and operators may worry about confidentiality and GDPR, but it does not offend sensibilities if properly governed.
evidence_implementability: Negotiating operator partnerships, de-identification, data-use agreements, a standardized repository and a public API is a significant, difficult undertaking that depends on third parties, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It exploits the logs the mandate creates to pursue an implied research benefit, which relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate but does not address meeting the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The corpus does not make the lab's own systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate, so it contributes at most a side benefit and does not solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Budgeting for compliance in grant applications is a sensible, somewhat interesting idea but fairly mundane and not very surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (grant template fields and workshop) but still treats compliance as logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Adding template fields and training PIs is a common administrative strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding four fields to a template and running a half-day workshop is low cost and a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (funding and planning for logging costs) that relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, rather than the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by budgeting for logging needs, but it does not itself build logging capability or meet the Article 12 mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Measuring the performance cost of logging is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response, with modest imagination in making it a design-time gate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (a benchmark suite and a sign-off gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Benchmarking logging overhead and gating architecture sign-off on it is a sensible engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms, though it is a slightly less common step than plain logging.
evidence_implementability: A microbenchmark harness comparing latency with logging on versus off is cheap and straightforward to build with existing tooling, though it needs some process changes to gate sign-off.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the performance cost of meeting the logging mandate, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging requirement, but it does not itself implement the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab budget and avoid late re-architecture for logging overhead, but it is only a partial solution because it neither designs the logs nor covers the content requirements of Article 12.

evidence_originality: Earmarking compliance budget lines and adding a review checkpoint is a sensible, familiar project-management move, which makes it interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template line and a review checkpoint, which are new process elements, and it ties logging resources to science funding, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Changing budget templates and adding peer-review gates is a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though researchers may grumble about overhead.
evidence_implementability: Updating a template and adding a committee checkpoint needs only modest administrative change, while the committed person-months are a real but reasonable cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely that logging compliance work is under-resourced or deferred, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting engineering time for logging would help ensure Article 12 work gets resourced, but it does not itself design or deliver the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the development toolkit from the start is a well-known 'compliance by design' response that an experienced evaluator would expect from many labs, so it is common rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a structured-logging framework and a gating requirement, which are new tools and processes, but it still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to its obligations in any deeper way.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging standards and lifecycle requirements in engineering practice is a common strategy that violates no norms, though researchers may grumble about the gating requirement.
evidence_implementability: Adopting an internal logging framework and a gating rule means changes to the toolchain and workflow, but these are reasonably feasible measures for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D to it, in the form of do X (log-native design) to get Y (Article 12 traceability).
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event logging in every prototype would help meet the logging mandate, but Article 12 applies to high-risk systems and the proposal does not address which events must be logged, the specific Annex III minimums, or documentation and retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging layer with a compliance gate is a sensible, expected response that many labs would propose, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a reusable middleware and test harness but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared logging middleware with a release gate is a conventional, fully lawful compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated engineering team, middleware integration into the existing serving stack, and a release-blocking test harness, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial set of changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specific Article 12(3) data items.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would generate the Article 12 logs and block non-compliant releases, but it does not address Article 12(2) risk-relevant events beyond the 12(3) minimum, or retention and post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance documentation into a queryable PROV-based knowledge graph exposed to external researchers is unusual and shows imagination, though knowledge graphs and provenance tooling are known and it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance documentation a community research resource, which is paradigm stretching rather than a new view of what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Exposing architectural decisions, data provenance and risk-management details externally could raise IP, security and confidentiality concerns, making it somewhat unusual and potentially offensive to sensibilities, though it is not unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing experiment-tracking infrastructure with an ontology layer and a read-only API, which requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the documentation and traceability requirements in Recital 71, which are part of the stated problem, though not the Article 12 logging mandate itself, so the problem it solves is implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the technical documentation mandate of Recital 71 but does not address Article 12's automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checkpoints in design reviews are a mundane, expected response with no especially surprising or imaginative element.

evidence_implementability: It reuses existing biweekly boards, a two-page checklist, and rotating internal staff, so it needs only low-cost, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by checking readiness against 12(2)(a)–(c).
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch logging gaps early but does not itself implement the logging capabilities or cover Article 12(1) and 12(3) fully, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Dedicated compliance budget lines are a mundane, expected response with little imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as an infrastructure and budgeting item and leaves the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance obligations unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Ring-fencing a budget line for compliance is a common, uncontroversial organizational practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Creating a cost centre and quarterly drawdowns requires only modest administrative changes at low cost, though the 8% allocation is a notable commitment.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (sustained resourcing for logging) that relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, rather than the logging requirements directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Funding protection helps sustain logging infrastructure but does not itself make systems log the required events, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A documentation owner with periodic reviews and stale-document checks is a mundane, expected compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Assigning documentation stewards and revision cycles is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires creating a role per product line and some automated changelog checks, which is a reasonably feasible organizational change rather than a trivial one.
evidence_applicability: It targets an implied related problem (documentation upkeep from Recital 71) rather than the explicit Article 12 logging mandate, so it applies indirectly.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses keeping technical documentation current per Recital 71 but does not itself deliver the Article 12 automatic event logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Storage-efficient append-only logging for long-lived edge deployments is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response and shows only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new reference architecture and benchmarking work but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A research track on log storage architecture violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: A six-month prototype and benchmarking effort requires dedicated engineering resources but is reasonably feasible with standard tools.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses Article 12(1)'s lifetime logging requirement by solving the storage and retention challenge of keeping logs over a long lifetime.

evidence_originality: Internal compliance audits are a common, expected response, though the reconstruct-from-logs test and the patch-survival check add a little interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds an audit process, but it still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
