evidence_acceptability: Centralised compliance infrastructure is a standard, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building one module on existing infrastructure with minimal-configuration APIs is a modest, reasonably feasible effort, though integrating across diverse projects will take some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building a reusable logging capability whose outputs correspond to Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared middleware that automatically captures timestamps, input references and verifier identities would meet the Article 12 minimum logging requirements for the lab's systems, but it addresses logging only and not wider compliance such as the 12(2) event relevance judgments or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A client-facing logging transparency dashboard and annual conformance white paper is somewhat interesting and a bit unusual, but transparency reports as compliance marketing are a fairly familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a competitive offering for clients (a new offering born from compliance), which changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's business, though not its research.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing anonymized log schemas and conformance status to clients violates no norms and is a common transparency/assurance strategy, though self-certification claims could raise minor concerns.
evidence_implementability: Building a read-only dashboard and a yearly report requires some engineering and process work on top of existing logging but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (demonstrating compliance and reputation/procurement benefits) related to the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate, rather than the logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It presupposes that logging is already implemented and only reports on it, so it contributes to demonstrating compliance but does not itself meet the logging mandate, making it a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Productizing mandatory logs as a client-facing monitoring dashboard is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, but compliance-as-product ideas are fairly commonly expected, so it is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by creating a new revenue-generating service born from compliance, which matches the paradigm-stretching anchor.
evidence_acceptability: Exposing monitoring data to clients is a common, transparency-oriented business strategy, though sharing incident logs raises some confidentiality concerns that remain manageable.
evidence_implementability: Building an API layer and client portal on existing log streams requires significant engineering work plus security and data-sharing safeguards, but it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly builds on Article 12(2)(b) logging and Article 72 monitoring, but it addresses a revenue opportunity rather than the core question of how to meet the logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard layered on logs would help demonstrate monitoring and transparency but does not itself ensure the logging requirements are met (event coverage, retention, traceability), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A sprint-embedded compliance gate with a checklist is a fairly expected shift-left compliance measure, though the replay tool simulating incident scenarios adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (gate, checklist, replay tool) but still treats compliance as a logging verification practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance checks in development sprints is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-hour gate in the sprint cadence with a checklist is a modest process change, though building the replay tool requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses verifying that logging captures events required by Article 12(2)(a)-(c), which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help catch logging gaps early for Article 12(2), but it covers only the prototype stage, ignores Article 12(3) specifics and lifetime logging, and relies on a single engineer, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using the lab's own models to monitor log integrity and turning compliance into publishable work is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (self-auditing modules using the lab's own models) and links compliance to publishable research, which partially changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, but it still centers on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: An internal research sprint building log-integrity tooling violates no legal or social norms and is a somewhat uncommon but unobjectionable approach to compliance.
evidence_implementability: A six-month sprint with two postdocs and existing synthetic-data pipelines is a reasonably feasible measure, though building reliable real-time anomaly detection for logs requires some new work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by verifying log completeness against Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, though it assumes logging exists and targets integrity rather than creation of logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help assure log completeness and reduce monitoring labor, but it is only a partial solution since it does not itself implement the core event recording or cover all Article 12 requirements.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware as a compliance-by-design measure is a common, expected response with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with logging added as a technical module and the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into standard engineering scaffolds is a common, norm-respecting strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two developers over one quarter to build reusable middleware is modest in cost and requires only non-radical changes to the workflow, though a mandatory dependency in all scaffolds needs some process change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building logging capturing the Article 12(2) events and the paragraph 3 data points.
evidence_effectiveness: A non-bypassable logging layer built into all high-risk templates would largely satisfy the logging requirement if implemented, though defining relevant events and the Annex III specifics still takes judgment, and it does not address wider R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandatory compliance logs as a scientific dataset for lifetime drift research is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logs into the science and turning the obligation into a research asset and positioning offering.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs containing biometric data for research raises GDPR purpose-limitation and privacy concerns, which somewhat offends sensibilities but is not totally unacceptable, though the approach is mostly benign.
evidence_implementability: It needs only two postdocs and a lightweight layer atop an existing pipeline, though it requires twelve months of data and data-governance work, so some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by exploiting the logs) that relates to the stated problem rather than the directly stated compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: It builds on the logging pipeline but does not itself meet the logging mandate; it only contributes by adding value to compliance, a partial solution to the stated problem of how to respond.

evidence_originality: A design-review gate requiring a logging architecture spec is a very common compliance-by-design response that an experienced evaluator would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint and checklist but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Stage gates with compliance sign-off are a standard, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a checklist, a sign-off process, and tracking, which are non-radical changes to existing pipelines, though some engineering overhead is involved.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring Article 12 event categories are captured in each project's design.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the gate would ensure systems have logging designs covering Article 12(2) categories, but it addresses only design-stage planning and not actual logging implementation, retention, or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a longitudinal research corpus is an unusual and imaginative reframing, though it is not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving mandated logging into the lab's scientific agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing logs for research and publishing preprints raises privacy and GDPR concerns, plus confidentiality issues over personal data and verifier identities, so it somewhat offends sensibilities; the claim that no non-EU lab can replicate it is also overstated.
evidence_implementability: Building an analytics pipeline over existing log streams and running robustness probes is a moderate extension of work the lab already does, though it needs engineering effort and data governance.
evidence_applicability: The proposal uses the mandated logs for research and does not directly say how to meet the logging mandate, so it addresses the 'adapt R&D accordingly' part through an implied benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not satisfy the logging mandate by itself, since it assumes the logs already exist, and it only partly addresses the problem by turning the logs into a research asset.

evidence_originality: Treating logging-overhead trade-offs as a publishable systems research question is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but performance benchmarking of instrumentation is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (benchmarks, publication) while still treating compliance as logging practice, though it does link compliance to the lab's research output somewhat.
evidence_acceptability: Benchmarking logging overhead and publishing the results is a normal research activity that violates no norms, though framing compliance as a paper is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: A six-month sub-project with two PhD students running ablation experiments on existing models is reasonably feasible, though it depends on the logging layer from Proposal 1 being built first.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely how much logging density the lab can afford in performance terms, which relates to meeting the logging mandate but is not the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It informs design choices about logging granularity and so helps, but it does not itself deliver Article 12 compliance, making it only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Cross-referencing genomics and climate-modelling data-management practice to define irreducible provenance is somewhat interesting and imaginative but not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a minimal provenance schema and research project) but still treats compliance as a logging/metadata practice, though it does reposition the lab as a methodological contributor.
evidence_acceptability: Literature synthesis and prototyping a schema is a normal, uncontroversial research activity that violates no norms, though the framing is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: It requires a research effort and prototyping against the existing registry on a live pipeline, which is reasonably feasible but involves some resource commitment and an exploratory orientation.
evidence_applicability: Defining which metadata fields satisfy Article 12(2) traceability directly addresses the logging mandate, though it focuses on provenance and only implicitly on event logs.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema derived from the Act helps determine what to record but is research-oriented, does not itself implement automatic event logging, and only partially solves the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design applied to logging is a very common, expected response and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (shared SDK, embedded engineers), and shifting logging from add-on to design-time integration changes how R&D and compliance relate somewhat, but it remains logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging in by design with review gates is a common, norm-conforming compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared SDK, review gates and embedded compliance engineers require significant process and staffing change but are reasonably feasible for a lab, so some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by making automatic event recording a built-in feature.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, built-in logging with gated sign-off would largely satisfy Article 12(1) and support traceability, though it does not specify which events or the Annex III minimums, so it is not a complete solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with update triggers and named owners is a common, mundane compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a versioned repository and update triggers but remains standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation governance with compliance owners and QA is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A versioned repository, update triggers and named owners are modest process changes that are readily feasible at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (documentation per Recital 71) rather than the identified logging requirement of Article 12 directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping technical documentation current is a real part of compliance but the proposal does not address Article 12's automatic event logging mandate, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Triaging in-flight projects by Article 12 obligation tier and sequencing remediation is a sensible but fairly expected project-management response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a process (self-assessment and sprint sequencing) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and prioritized compliance rollouts are common strategies that violate no norms, though deferring some compliance work could raise mild concern.
evidence_implementability: A four-week exercise with one-page self-assessments and sprint planning is low-cost and requires only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the directly stated problem of how to allocate scarce resources to meet the logging mandate, though it focuses on sequencing rather than the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps allocate effort and meet deadlines but does not itself build logging capability, and the paragraph 3 self-assessment applies only to Annex III point 1(a) systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance-by-design checklist at sprint planning is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checklist step to existing sprints but treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A planning checklist is a common, uncontroversial process that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing sprint cycle, a one-page template, and a small pilot on three projects, so it is low-cost with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by having leads identify required logging fields early.
evidence_effectiveness: A one-page checklist and architecture confirmation helps catch gaps early but does not itself build logging capability or ensure the logs satisfy the Article 12 requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log analytics with anomaly alerting is a fairly expected extension of logging, though framing it as turning compliance cost into a safety feature shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and a pipeline but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only adding analytics on top, with a slight nod to client-facing reporting.
evidence_acceptability: Post-market monitoring analytics is a normal, legally aligned compliance practice that offends no norms, though it carries some data-handling considerations.
evidence_implementability: Kafka, a time-series store, and SPC alerting are mature off-the-shelf components, but building per-system-type rules and a dashboard is still a real engineering effort requiring some changes and resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of using logs for the Article 12(2) purposes of risk identification, post-market monitoring, and operation monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meaningfully support Article 72 and 26(5) monitoring and risk detection, but it does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met (what to log, retention, Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable internal logging SDK that standardizes event capture is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and JSON schema but still treats compliance purely as logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal compliance library is a standard, uncontroversial business practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over six weeks to package existing patterns into a module is a modest, low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by producing records matching the Article 12 fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver the technical logging capability across projects, but it covers only Article 12(3) fields (which apply to specific Annex III systems) and not the broader 12(2) traceability purposes or other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using sequential change-point detection to operationalize 'substantial modification' is an interesting and somewhat imaginative link, though drift detection is a known monitoring approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (online change-point detectors) and ties a research program to compliance, but still treats compliance as a logging/monitoring practice rather than changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: It is a legitimate, non-controversial research and compliance strategy, though it frames a research effort as compliance which is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: It is a research project requiring new statistical methods and validation on deployment logs, which is a significant effort with uncertain results, though doable with existing data and expertise.
evidence_applicability: It addresses Article 12(2)(a) logging for identifying substantial modification, which is an implied sub-problem of the logging mandate rather than the core requirement of automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift detection would help flag substantial modifications but covers only one part of Article 12 and does not itself deliver the logging infrastructure, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal compliance teams, retention policies, and mock audits are a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audit and governance functions are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Chartering a small cross-functional team with policies and quarterly audits is a reasonably feasible, non-radical organizational change at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the problem of ensuring systems produce Article 12 logs and are retained and auditable, which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A governance and audit function would help verify and maintain logging compliance but does not itself build the technical logging capability or adapt R&D, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Provenance tracking and append-only experiment ledgers are common MLOps practice and a likely response, so the idea is interesting but not rare or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal extends existing experiment-tracking tooling with a lineage ledger, introducing a new element, but still treats compliance as a logging/documentation practice, though it does make compliance a by-product of R&D workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding provenance capture in internal pipelines is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing MLflow-style tooling, but restructuring the pipeline and versioning ledgers to dataset commits requires some engineering changes that are reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (documentation and traceability from Recital 71) related to the logging mandate, rather than directly specifying Article 12 runtime logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially support technical documentation and traceability, but it addresses R&D experiment records rather than Article 12 event logging of deployed high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging services with CI/CD gates are a standard, expected response to a logging mandate, so this is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as a logging engineering practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding tamper-evident logging and deployment gates is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging microservice with append-only storage and a CI/CD coverage gate is a moderate engineering effort that fits existing pipelines, so it needs some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building automatic event recording with timestamps and risk triggers.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would largely satisfy Article 12 logging requirements, but it does not cover the Annex III specific fields such as reference databases and verifier identities or the broader documentation needs, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: The 'traceability budget' metric and architecture-level logging hooks are somewhat unusual and show imagination, but tying compliance to interpretability research is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the science by making compliance a research agenda on architectures and interpretability, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not redefine what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Funding research and publishing open-source libraries violates no legal or social norms and is a respectable strategy.
evidence_implementability: Four funded positions over two years is a significant, costly commitment with uncertain results, and the brief explicitly says approval means committing implementation resources rather than exploring, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of making inference produce event-level records for Article 12(1), which relates to the stated problem though Article 12 asks for event logs rather than internal computation traces.
evidence_effectiveness: A two-year research programme yielding architectures and logging hooks would contribute to meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, but it is exploratory and does not by itself deliver compliant logging for current systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered log storage with indexing on Annex III fields is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response, with only mild interest in the SLA and benchmarking framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tiered storage architecture with query SLAs but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Robust log storage for regulatory inspection is a standard, uncontroversial approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a tiered storage stack and benchmarking it requires significant engineering effort and hardware budget, but it uses established technologies and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified lifetime logging requirement and the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses retention and retrieval of logs over the lifetime, which is a key part of the logging mandate, but does not cover what events to log, other Article 12 purposes, or non-Annex-III-1(a) systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using a CI gate to quantify cumulative drift against a compliance-locked release as a proxy for 'substantial modification' is an uncommon, somewhat imaginative idea, though CI gating itself is familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and weaves compliance determination into the engineering pipeline, but it still treats compliance as a process control rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Automated gating with Compliance owning thresholds and signed records is a reasonable governance practice that offends no norms, though quantitatively defining 'substantial modification' may be legally contestable.
evidence_implementability: Diffing weights and configs and computing distribution divergence in CI is feasible with existing MLOps tooling, but agreeing on thresholds and metrics requires some real changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, knowing when a change resets obligations under Article 12(2)(a), which relates to but is not the core logging requirement; the cited link between Article 12 and substantial modification is loose.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help detect modification-triggered obligations but does not itself deliver the Article 12 logging capability, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated model cards from tracking metadata are fairly well known, so this is interesting but not imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new pipeline element but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice without changing the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from experiment tracking is a sensible, common compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing MLflow tracking with a schema and a scheduled rendering job, which is reasonably feasible with modest changes.
evidence_applicability: It does X (auto-generate docs from metadata) to get Y (up-to-date technical documentation), which is an implied, related part of the record-keeping compliance problem rather than the logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Auto-generating technical documentation keeps it current, which addresses Recital 71 documentation upkeep but not the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A pre-market compliance review gate with a checklist and trained reviewers is a common, expected governance response to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged, adding only a sign-off step.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gates and audit sign-offs are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a checklist and training two engineers as reviewers is low-cost and requires only non-radical process changes.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets the identified problem of ensuring Article 12 logging and traceability obligations are met before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A review gate verifies logging compliance but does not itself build the logging capability, so it contributes to but only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Embedding a logging scaffold in starter templates is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response to the mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a middleware scaffold with adapter profiles) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standardizing logging via shared templates is a common internal engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing internal starter kit with a pluggable logging library is low-cost and non-radical for an ML lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the required logging capabilities into the lab's R&D process.
evidence_effectiveness: It would ensure automatic event recording and Annex III 1(a) fields in new prototypes, but it does not cover existing systems, deployment-time logging retention, or the Article 12(2) event-relevance judgments, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware/SDK is a fairly expected and mundane response from labs to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but treats compliance as logging practice and explicitly keeps the lab's way of working unchanged, which is standard compliance tooling with perhaps a slight new element.
evidence_acceptability: Building a shared compliance logging library is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A decorator-style SDK with a JSON schema is a moderate engineering effort that is reasonably feasible, though wrapping 'any' serving endpoint and defining relevant risk events involves some real work.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing events specified in paragraphs 2 and 3 (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: Standardized automatic event capture would substantially satisfy the logging requirement, but it does not on its own cover Annex III-specific fields such as reference databases or verifier identities, nor the broader documentation duties, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A dedicated post-market monitoring team with pause authority is a fairly expected, sensible response, interesting but not surprising or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A standing surveillance unit is a new organizational element but it still treats compliance as operational log monitoring without changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Hiring an internal monitoring team with escalation to regulators is a conventional compliance strategy that violates no norms, though pause authority may raise some internal friction.
evidence_implementability: Hiring three people and wiring them into an existing alerting pipeline is reasonably feasible with moderate cost, though granting pause authority requires some organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to use Article 12 logs for Article 79(1) risk identification and post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet Article 12(2) purposes of risk detection and post-market monitoring but does not itself deliver the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing log-sufficiency as an information-theoretic lower-bound problem is unusual and imaginative relative to typical compliance responses, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a research question for the lab, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations by weaving the science into logging, which is paradigm stretching rather than a break.
evidence_acceptability: Studying data minimisation versus logging is a legally and socially unobjectionable research activity that offends no norms, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: A fundamental research programme deriving information-theoretic lower bounds and running ablation studies on existing pipelines is a significant, expensive, uncertain effort, though not impossible, and it does not itself deliver the logging capability.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (how much to log under Article 12(3)(c) without over-collecting) that relates to the logging mandate but does not directly implement the required logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to the solution by informing proportionate logging design, but it is only a partial and long-horizon answer, and does not itself ensure the lab meets the mandate.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance gating through CI checks and linters is a fairly familiar DevOps pattern, with some interesting adaptation to Article 12 but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (sprint template, CI gate, linter, log-contract artifact) and modifies the R&D process, but it still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing how the science relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Gating builds on compliance checks is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no norms, though it may add some friction for researchers.
evidence_implementability: Updating the playbook, adding a board artifact, and writing a linter plugin are modest, reasonably feasible changes with some upfront architectural cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building the required log endpoints and checking events against the Article 12 checklist.
evidence_effectiveness: Front-loading the log schema and enforcing it with a CI gate would help the lab meet the Article 12 mandate for automatic event logging, but it addresses mainly technical logging capability and not the wider record-keeping and documentation duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning log-based reconstructability into a public benchmark is an unusual and interesting idea that shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance a source of research output, shared standards and partnerships with external labs.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open benchmark with external collaborators and a shared schema violates no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a harness and recruiting three external labs is feasible but requires coordination, a shared schema, and external buy-in, so some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It relates to the stated problem through traceability and log-based reconstruction, but the problem addressed (field-level reference point) is implied rather than the lab's own compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark does not itself make the lab's own systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate, so it contributes only partially at best, and its stated gains are mostly scientific reputation and IP.

evidence_originality: Turning the regulatory minimums into a typed schema is a sensible but expected and common response among labs, with only the CI-verifiable framing adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a schema and CI testing as new tooling but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A standard engineering approach to logging compliance that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: One engineer drafts it in a week and it is integrated into two existing projects during a normal sprint, which is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging minimums by mapping each of the four required items to a concrete schema emitted on every call.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a typed event schema wired into the serving path would satisfy the paragraph-3 minimums for Annex III 1(a) systems, though it covers only part of Article 12 (paragraph 2 event relevance, retention, and other systems are not fully addressed), so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a logging framework and turning compliance into reusable, licensable IP is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a product and reputational asset for the sector, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations (new offerings born from compliance).
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance framework and publishing a specification violates no norms, and is somewhat uncommon but inoffensive.
evidence_implementability: Two researchers at 30% time for twelve months in parallel with core research is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though it requires some changes and a year to deliver.
evidence_applicability: A logging framework for lifetime event capture directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate, though its main stated payoff is reusable IP and positioning rather than the lab's own compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema and framework would help the lab meet logging requirements, but it is only a partial solution since it omits the specific Article 12(2)-(3) content, retention, and integration into deployed systems.

evidence_originality: Automated conformance testing of logs against a reference schema is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response, with modest imagination in tying it to prototype-to-production handoff.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a log-fidelity conformance harness with pass-rate metrics) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in staging with metrics is a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Defining reference schemas per system class and building sprint-level conformance checks requires some tooling and effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by checking that required event types and Annex III minimums are captured.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch logging gaps early and help verify capability, but it only verifies logging rather than ensuring log content is adequate or covering the full compliance obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as a first-class computational primitive and mapping a cost-observability frontier is interesting and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the model science itself and turning the obligation into publishable research, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Research into observable architectures violates no norms, but committing scarce resources to open-ended research instead of compliance may somewhat strain sensibilities, so it is somewhat unusual yet inoffensive.

evidence_effectiveness: A multi-year research programme would contribute to future logging capability but does not by itself deliver Article 12 compliant logging now, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing logging up front in a checklist is a familiar 'compliance by design' move that is common and unsurprising.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK with declarative YAML event schemas is a fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, though the declarative framing is slightly interesting.

evidence_implementability: A thin wrapper over existing pipelines validated on two prototypes first is a modest-scale, reasonably feasible effort, though language-agnostic design and schema definition require some real engineering work.

evidence_effectiveness: It would enable automatic event recording across prototypes, which contributes substantially to Article 12 compliance, but it does not itself define which events satisfy Article 12(2)-(3), retention, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Directly implementing the statutory minimum log fields is the expected, mundane response to this mandate.

evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the four mandated log fields into the systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the Article 12(3) logging requirements for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it does not cover the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging for other high-risk systems or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance records into a publishable reproducibility framework is interesting and mildly imaginative, but not highly surprising.

evidence_effectiveness: A research-log template conflates Article 12's automatic event logging with documentation of algorithms and data (closer to technical documentation), so it only partially contributes to meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: A reference implementation of the mandated fields is the obvious, expected response and shows little imagination.

evidence_originality: A CI gate that validates log schema completeness is a sensible but fairly expected DevOps-style response to a logging mandate, interesting but not surprising.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking whether decision processes are reconstructable from logs alone is an unusual and imaginative way to turn Article 12 into a research question, though it is not wholly unprecedented given interpretability benchmarks.

evidence_acceptability: A public benchmark of auditability offends no legal or social norms and fits academic and regulatory sensibilities, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.

evidence_effectiveness: The benchmark would not itself make the lab's systems log compliantly under Article 12; it would at best inform what logging granularity is useful, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: The hash-chained append-only ledger adds some technical flair, but interceptor-based audit logging mapped to the Article 12(3) fields is a fairly expected response.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance-engineering and logging-maintenance costs as weighted criteria in internal funding scorecards is a somewhat unusual, mildly interesting governance tweak, but not surprising or ingenious.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by design with a review gate before merge is a very common, expected response to Article 12 from AI labs, so it is mundane.

evidence_originality: Linking sprint-log design decisions to Article 12 sub-paragraphs under version control is a sensible but fairly expected documentation/governance response, with only mild interest.
