evidence_originality: A reusable logging library integrated by design is the obvious, common response an experienced evaluator would expect from labs, with nothing surprising in it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging middleware with sprint-zero compliance review is a new tool and process, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, so it is standard practice or at most slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding mandatory logging in every build is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms and fits regulatory expectations.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared library with pipeline hooks and a sprint-zero review requires some engineering effort and process changes, but it is reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate, with specific reference to Article 12(3) fields and the compliance outcome.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would directly deliver automatic event recording under Article 12 across projects, though it addresses logging mainly and not broader documentation or post-market monitoring, so it is largely but not wholly a solution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated compliance documentation from CI is a fairly well-known idea, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling pipeline but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from CI pipelines is a sensible, norm-compliant practice that offends no sensibilities, though somewhat less common than manual documentation.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing CI/CD and experiment-tracking infrastructure with export hooks, so it needs some engineering changes but no new tooling or headcount.
evidence_applicability: It solves an identified related problem (documentation drift and traceability under Recital 71), which is related to but not the same as the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses technical documentation currency (Recital 71) and partly Article 12 logging, but does not itself implement event logging requirements like the Article 12(2)-(3) minimum logs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware with a decorator is a common, expected engineering response to this mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, so the lab's way of working is largely unchanged beyond a default library.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A Python decorator-based SDK with SQLite and Kafka back-ends is reasonably feasible but requires building, schema versioning, and adoption across teams, so it needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by recording events including the Article 12(3) minimum fields, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help meet logging requirements but is only a partial solution since it covers mainly Annex III 1(a) fields, leaves out retention, tamper-evidence, and other Article 12(2) event relevance, and does not cover non-intercepted paths.

evidence_originality: A compliance documentation unit with versioned records and quarterly audits is a standard, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard documentation and audit function separate from the R&D, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A dedicated compliance team, version-controlled repository and internal audits are common, norm-conforming practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Staffing three people and building a version-controlled repository with update triggers is a reasonably feasible, modest-cost measure requiring some process changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses keeping technical documentation current over the system lifetime, which is a stated Recital 71 compliance need, but it targets documentation rather than the Article 12 automatic logging mandate itself, so the problem it solves is related but only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation unit with update triggers and audits would help meet the documentation part of compliance but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware that is inherited by default is a sensible and fairly common engineering response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared SDK introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared internal infrastructure for compliance is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Three named engineers building an SDK on the existing containerised stack is a reasonably feasible measure that needs some changes but no radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate while protecting R&D time.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic capture of the Article 12(2) event categories would largely solve the logging mandate, though Annex III-specific fields and deciding what counts as relevant events still need work, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A time-boxed sprint to design a logging schema for the Annex III 1(a) minimums and publish it is a sensible but fairly expected lab response, with only mild interest from the publishable-contribution angle.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a reusable specification, a benchmarked prototype, a publication) but still treats compliance essentially as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging and sharing a specification internally and publicly violates no norms, though publishing may raise minor concerns about disclosure of biometric system details.
evidence_implementability: A six-week effort by two senior engineers on one live system is modest and reasonably feasible, though latency benchmarking and integration with a live system require some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, mapping each Article 12(3) item (a-d) to a schema element with an explicit latency constraint.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing and validating a schema that covers the four Article 12(3) minimums on a live biometric system would largely solve the logging mandate for that system and give a template for others, though it does not cover the full portfolio or the Article 12(2) event-relevance requirements beyond the minimums.

evidence_originality: Treating logging compliance as a CI test gate with property-based edge-case inputs is a somewhat unusual, interesting application, though CI testing of logs is a recognizable DevOps practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/process (CI gate with property-based tests) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a CI stage with property-based tests and a staging instance is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some engineering effort but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (automated test gate) to get Y (verified presence of required log events), which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch logging regressions for Article 12(2) events and thus contributes to, but does not by itself fully solve, the mandate (e.g., retention, Article 12(3) specifics, and design of logging remain separate).

evidence_originality: A controlled A/B experiment comparing logging-first versus retrofit effort is a somewhat interesting, empirical angle but not a surprising or ingenious response to the mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a parallel-track benchmark) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal engineering experiment with metrics violates no legal or social norms and is a common, conventional approach.
evidence_implementability: Running parallel sprint tracks across three system types duplicates engineering work and is costly, but it is reasonably feasible internally with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (deciding how to resource logging integration) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate, but does not itself implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help inform the choice between logging-first and retrofit, contributing to a partial solution, but it does not itself produce compliant logging and costs resources before any commitment to build.

evidence_originality: A shared compliance logging library integrated at design time is a standard, expected response among labs and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice (centralized tooling, compliance-by-design) that leaves the lab's research approach and its relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared tooling and design-review gates are common engineering governance strategies that offend no norms, though mandating them may draw mild researcher pushback.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight SDK and a design-review checkpoint are reasonably feasible with a platform team, but integrating across six active projects and standardizing schemas requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate (automatic event recording) across the lab's high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared SDK with event categories mapped to Article 12(2) and enforced at design review would, if built, deliver the core logging mandate across projects, though it does not itself cover Article 12(3) specifics, documentation, or retention governance beyond schema.

evidence_originality: Internal monitoring teams and mock audits are a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A standing compliance unit is a standard organizational compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance and audit functions are common, norm-abiding practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A three-person unit running monthly queries and a dashboard plus annual mock audits requires some hiring and organizational change but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of using logs for post-market monitoring and risk identification under Article 12(2), but it does not directly address how to build the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Monthly log review and mock audits would help exploit logs and catch risks, but they are only a partial solution because they do not make the system technically capable of automatic logging or cover the Article 12(3) minimum content.

evidence_originality: Provenance and experiment-tracking tools are well known, so an open-source logging layer is an interesting but fairly expected response with modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Open-sourcing the tool and treating it as a standing lab responsibility introduces new elements and partly shifts compliance into a community offering, but it still centers on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building and open-sourcing a logging/provenance tool under an MIT licence is a common, norm-compliant strategy, though open-sourcing regulatory-grade tooling is slightly less routine than purely internal compliance.
evidence_implementability: A middleware library integrated into existing experiment trackers is reasonably feasible but requires dedicated engineering and ongoing maintenance as a standing responsibility.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, explicitly targeting Article 12(3) minimums, though the focus on training-run lineage and biometric systems is somewhat narrower than the general Article 12 scope.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide automatic event logging and lineage that meets Article 12 needs, but it covers mainly the technical logging and not all compliance elements such as post-market monitoring processes or deployer-side obligations, so it is a substantial partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as longitudinal scientific datasets for drift research is an interesting, somewhat imaginative reframing, though drift detection with SPC is a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning logging obligations into a research program and new partnerships with deployers, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymized logs in partnership with deployers and publishing results is a somewhat unusual but legitimate approach that offends no norms, though data-sharing and privacy concerns need care.
evidence_implementability: Building statistical process control on log streams is technically feasible, but it requires deployer partnerships, data access agreements, and sustained longitudinal research, which is a significant undertaking with some changes needed.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, monitoring and post-market surveillance using logs, which relates to Article 12(2) purposes but not directly to the lab's own logging implementation.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift detection on logs would help post-market monitoring and risk identification, but it does not itself meet the core logging mandate (what to record, retention, traceability) so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auditing logs against the Article 12(3) minimum fields with an automated completeness script is a fairly expected compliance response, though the tie to the biometric sub-category is a modest specific touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds an audit script and an SLA but still treats compliance as ordinary logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal log audits and remediation SLAs are common, norm-conforming compliance strategies that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A weekly automated script that checks four fields and a policy SLA is low-cost and non-radical to build and run.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated logging mandate by checking that the Article 12(3) required fields are present in logs, although it applies only to the Annex III 1(a) biometric subset.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch missing fields but is only a partial solution, since it does not build the logging capability or cover Article 12(1)-(2) traceability and non-biometric high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: Treating lifetime logs as a longitudinal research corpus is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance logs a research asset and a source of publications, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for internal research and publishing white papers is a somewhat unusual but norm-respecting strategy, though data protection and confidentiality concerns are unaddressed.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight pipeline on existing logging infrastructure is reasonably feasible, but a multi-year program with tagging and annual publications requires some added resources and changes.
evidence_applicability: The idea builds on Article 12 logs and ties to Article 79(1) risk tagging, but its main output is research on drift, which is an implied rather than direct solution to meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It relies on logs existing and does little to ensure the logging mandate itself is met, so it contributes only partially to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance testing in CI pipelines is a fairly common, expected engineering response, with only modest imagination in the property-based testing detail.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (a CI/CD conformance gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated release gates for compliance are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing pytest suite and CI pipeline with a small QA team, so it is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that required Article 12 log fields are emitted.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch missing or malformed log fields but does not itself build the logging capability or cover broader risk-relevant events, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized log aggregation with anomaly dashboards is a mundane, widely expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging and monitoring infrastructure and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized log monitoring for compliance is a common, norm-conforming strategy, though central streaming of production logs raises minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: Deploying a streaming log pipeline with central store and dashboards is a significant but well-understood engineering effort requiring some changes and ongoing operation, though not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to meet the logging mandate and support post-market monitoring and risk identification stated in Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: Continuous ingestion and monitoring would substantially support Article 12 logging and Articles 72/26(5) monitoring, but it does not itself define what events must be logged or cover all obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in existing pipelines to avoid duplicate infrastructure is a common, mundane engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds logging hooks to existing pipelines and still treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logging into existing systems is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint per pipeline using existing Kafka and time-series infrastructure is a reasonably feasible, low-cost, non-radical change, though per-pipeline mapping effort is nontrivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: Mapping Article 12(2) trigger events to pipeline logs would contribute substantially to meeting the logging mandate, but it does not cover other obligations such as retention, Annex III specifics in full, or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A module that implements the Article 12(3) logging fields is the expected response to the mandate, though the immutable ledger adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a new tool (an immutable audit ledger with provenance tracking) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance logging with role-based access controls is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing feature stores and standard engineering such as ledgers and access controls, so it needs some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the specific Article 12(3) logging duties (reference database, matched input, verifier identity) and avoiding a retrofit.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully meet the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it does not address the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging or the broader R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Synthetic multi-year log load testing is a sensible engineering practice that is somewhat unusual to frame this way but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds testing tools and a synthetic-data generator but still treats compliance as logging infrastructure practice, so it is slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: This is a conventional engineering de-risking approach that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a synthetic generator and automated regression tests is a reasonably feasible, standard systems-engineering effort with moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: Stress-testing log storage for lifetime retention addresses the Article 12 requirement for logs over the system's lifetime, but the need for it is implied rather than stated in the mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Validating durability, integrity, and retrieval of logs helps ensure logs remain usable but covers only one part of the mandate (not what events to log, content, or monitoring use), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Phase-gate compliance checkpoints are a standard, mundane governance approach that an evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds process checkpoints but treats compliance as standard logging and review practice, leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Phase-gate reviews with a compliance officer as standing reviewer are a common governance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It only requires adding template fields and gates into existing sprint cadence, though some process change and reviewer capacity are needed, making it fairly easy with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab will meet the logging mandate by gating production on confirmed active logging, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Gates help ensure logging is in place before deployment, but the proposal does not specify what is logged or how Article 12 content requirements are met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mapping regulatory logging onto W3C PROV-O and publishing it as an open spec is an unusual and somewhat imaginative idea, but not wholly surprising since standards alignment is a known approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a shared open vocabulary and research infrastructure offering, changing the relationship between the lab's R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open standards and provenance schemas are legally and socially unobjectionable, with only mild unusualness in open-sourcing compliance tooling.
evidence_implementability: A small team over two quarters with reference implementations in two languages and validation on existing logs is reasonably feasible but requires dedicated resources and standards-adoption effort.
evidence_applicability: The schema directly maps Article 12's mandated event categories (use periods, reference databases, input matches, verifier identities) to a structured logging format, which is directly related to meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A standardized schema would help structure logs for compliance, but it does not itself implement automatic logging, cover Article 12(2) risk/post-market/monitoring purposes, or ensure traceability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Event-capture middleware for audit logging is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprising imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard logging middleware built on existing Kafka and OpenTelemetry tooling and treats compliance purely as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging on existing infrastructure violates no legal, social, or business norms and is a conventional strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over one quarter on already-deployed infrastructure with no new spend makes it a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly records the specific Article 12(3)(a)-(d) items (timestamps, reference database IDs, matched inputs, verifier identities), so it clearly addresses the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum logging items, but it covers mainly the Annex III 1(a) minimums and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) traceability purposes like risk identification and post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging middleware with tamper-evident storage and design-time embedding is the expected, mundane response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice, with only an engineering-timing emphasis (build in rather than retrofit), leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into systems and keeping tamper-evident records is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Middleware hooks, a standard schema, and immutable storage across all high-risk systems require significant platform engineering and coordination but are technically feasible with reasonably standard tools.
evidence_applicability: It does X (embed logging per Article 12(1)-(3)) to get Y (compliant automatic event recording), which is the explicitly stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding automatic, tamper-evident logging with per-category schemas directly satisfies the Article 12 logging mandate, so if done it would solve the main problem, though it does not address the R&D adaptation side.

evidence_originality: Quarterly internal sampling audits and compliance memos are a standard, expected governance response to a logging mandate, so the idea is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds an audit process and memo format but leaves R&D work unchanged and treats compliance as standard logging practice, which is paradigm preserving.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and documentation memos are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a standing instruction, a memo template and periodic sampling by existing compliance staff, which is a non-radical, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to verify that logs meet Article 12(2) purposes, which is part of the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Verifying log sufficiency would help ensure Article 12(2) traceability, but it does not build the logging capability itself or address Article 12(1) or 12(3), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Recurring log-integrity audits tied to a corrective-action register are a sensible but fairly expected compliance response, with only mild interest from gating releases on findings.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds an audit process but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and corrective-action registers are standard, uncontroversial governance practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Quarterly sampling audits by the compliance function are a modest, reasonably feasible process addition, though the release-gating requires some coordination with engineering.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by verifying completeness, integrity and Annex III 1(a) fields over the system lifetime, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logs remain compliant and usable for post-market monitoring, but it verifies rather than designs the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging microservice with OpenTelemetry and ClickHouse is a sensible but mundane and expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-as-logging-infrastructure approach that leaves the lab's R&D workflow and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized shared logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing Kubernetes stack, standard open-source tools, a thin SDK wrapper, and four redirected FTEs within the budget, making it reasonably feasible with some changes such as displacing the serving refactor.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly builds a logging service that captures the Article 12(3) fields, which is the identified logging mandate in the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a shared service capturing the mandated fields would cover the core Article 12 logging requirement, though it addresses mainly 12(3) (Annex III 1(a) systems) and not the broader 12(2) event relevance or documentation, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: A design-review gate for logging requirements is a common shift-left compliance practice that experienced evaluators would expect, with only a modest touch from the ticket-blocking sign-off.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard process step that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Design review gates are a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A half-hour checkpoint and a one-page diagram added to an existing sprint board is very cheap and non-radical to implement.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(2) logging mandate by mapping required events at design time.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch missing event types early but is only a partial solution, since it does not implement logging, cover Article 12(3) specifics, or ensure ongoing adequacy.

evidence_originality: Using schema evolution and model-version tagging for log durability is a sensible but fairly expected engineering answer, so it is interesting rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a storage and schema tooling layer but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Versioned, retained logs are a standard data-engineering approach that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Append-only schema-evolved stores like Iceberg or Delta Lake are mature off-the-shelf tools, so this needs some engineering but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, the lifetime recording obligation in Article 12(1) and its effect on R&D iteration.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the lifetime log readability piece of Article 12(1) but not the full logging mandate, such as event selection and the specific content requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared compliance logging SDK is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard reusable logging component that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal compliance library is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared internal logging library with default local JSONL storage and a scaffold pin is a modest engineering task using ordinary tooling and no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the paragraph-3 minimum log fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help standardize logging of the minimum fields, but it covers only paragraph 3 (Annex III 1(a) systems), ignores Art. 12(2) event relevance, retention, and integrity, and defaults to local JSONL, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Scaling compliance effort to development stage is a sensible and fairly expected response, showing some thoughtfulness but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint to an existing process and still treats compliance as logging practice, with only a modest tie to R&D workflow timing.
evidence_acceptability: Using existing stage-gate reviews and the regulation's own proportionality language is a common, norm-respecting approach, though minimal logging on prototypes is arguably fine since the Act applies to high-risk systems placed on market.
evidence_implementability: It needs only one added checkpoint in an existing stage-gate process plus a configurable logging schema, which is a modest change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate while adapting R&D, by tying log granularity to the intended-purpose language of Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: Staging log depth to lifecycle milestones would help calibrate logging to Article 12(2) proportionality but only partially solves the mandate, since it does not itself define the logging capabilities, retention, or content needed for compliance.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance design is a familiar idea (like privacy-by-design), making this a sensible but expected response with modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (workshop template, validation script, gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice integrated into process rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship much.
evidence_acceptability: A sprint-zero design gate with sign-off is a common, norm-respecting engineering governance practice, though the mandatory halt before coding may be mildly unusual.
evidence_implementability: A half-day workshop template plus a lightweight validation script and sign-off gate are low-cost, non-radical process additions.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping schemas to the paragraph 2(a)-(c) categories.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing the event taxonomy up front addresses the logging mandate for new prototypes and will help, but it covers only schema design (not runtime implementation, existing systems, or Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware in an MLOps pipeline is a standard, expected response with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice, inheriting it through tooling while leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in a deployment container is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Forking an existing base image and adding an event emitter wired to existing storage and tracking is a modest, non-radical change using current infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by automatically capturing the Annex III logging fields and events that Article 12 mandates.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet the technical logging requirement across prototypes but only partly covers the broader obligations such as appropriate-to-purpose event selection, documentation, and the Article 14(5) verifier identification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared internal logging layer for compliance is the common, expected response to this mandate and shows little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Centralizing logging in a reusable reference implementation is standard compliance engineering that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a shared internal logging standard with compliance officer review is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small systems group building a lightweight logging layer that hooks into existing inference pipelines without changing model architecture is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change, though it still takes real engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building the automatic event-recording infrastructure.
evidence_effectiveness: A consistent logging backbone would substantially meet Article 12's core requirement, but it leaves out the Annex III specifics, retention and other obligations, and its coverage is described only generically, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware with CI gating is a fairly common engineering approach to compliance, though the tidy architectural-default framing is sensible rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (auto-instrumenting SDK with CI enforcement) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: An internal SDK with CI checks and benchmark validation is a standard strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing internal packaging, decorators and CI, with a pilot on one pipeline, so only moderate non-radical changes are needed, though capturing all events automatically across training and inference takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting Article 12(1)'s automatic event recording mandate for high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic logging across high-risk modules, but it does not itself define which events satisfy Article 12(2)-(3), retention, or traceability content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Earmarking a fixed budget line for compliance is a fairly standard financial-governance move, though the fixed twelve percent ring-fence in project templates is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a budgeting process element but still treats compliance as a separate logging-related cost center, leaving the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Budget line items and quarterly reviews are common practices that offend no norms, though a flat percentage may draw some PI grumbling.
evidence_implementability: Revising a grant template and adding a quarterly review is a low-cost, non-radical administrative change that can be done quickly.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of funding and resourcing Article 12 compliance without distorting research, which relates to but is not itself the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Dedicated funding helps ensure compliance work gets done but does not itself design or deliver the logging capability, and a flat 12% may not fit projects, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Living, stage-gated documentation with a rotating steward is a sensible but familiar practice (model cards, experiment tracking), showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (living traces, steward role) but still treats compliance as a documentation practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation practices like this are common and violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Markdown traces, weekly reviews, and a rotating role are low-cost, non-radical changes that a lab can adopt easily.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified related problem of keeping documentation current throughout the lifecycle (Recital 71), which is part of the compliance context but not directly the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Living research traces would help meet the technical documentation and traceability aims of Recital 71, but they do not address Article 12's requirement for automatic event logging in the system itself, so the idea is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with diff-checks tied to weight changes is a common, mundane approach, with a slightly clever flagging mechanism.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice with a minor automation tool, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Version-controlled documentation with stewards and sprint updates is a common compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Version control, a steward role, and an automated diff-check are inexpensive and use existing tooling, requiring only modest process changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation kept current across the lifetime (Recital 71), which is related to the record-keeping mandate but does not itself implement the automatic event logging that Article 12 requires, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Up-to-date technical files help post-market monitoring and compliance verification but do not provide the automatic event logs Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging middleware with append-only storage is the obvious, expected response to a logging mandate and is common practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK/middleware) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized, immutable logging is a standard compliance strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building and integrating a shared SDK across all high-risk pipelines requires some engineering effort and changes but uses well-understood technology and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (build standardized automatic logging) to get Y (Article 12 compliant logs), which is the explicitly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A architecture-level logging middleware with immutable storage and lifetime retention would directly satisfy the Article 12 automatic logging mandate for the core events, though it does not cover risk-event identification logic, post-market monitoring processes, or human-verifier identification, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandatory logs as a longitudinal research corpus for drift and anomaly study is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving compliance logs into the lab's science and creating new scientific outputs born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Aggregating log streams across deployments raises data-protection, customer confidentiality, and purpose-limitation concerns even when anonymised, and Annex III 1(a) biometric logs include personal data, so it offends sensibilities somewhat.
evidence_implementability: It requires cross-deployment log aggregation, anonymisation pipelines, versioning infrastructure, and contractual or legal clearance, which is significant work but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, how to derive value from compliance logs, which relates to adapting R&D to the logging mandate but not to the core need of meeting it.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal reuses logs as a research dataset but does not itself deliver the Article 12 logging capability (what to record, retention, traceability), so it only contributes partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Retention schedules, ownership assignment, and periodic audits with sign-off are common, mundane governance measures an evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a lifecycle policy, archival triggers, and review processes, but still treats compliance as standard record-keeping practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Retention governance and documented oversight are conventional strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A policy, automated archival triggers, periodic reviews, and an officer sign-off are low-cost, non-radical changes that compliance teams can readily put in place.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (retaining and governing logs and documentation over the system lifetime per Recital 71) that relates to the logging mandate rather than the core requirement to enable automatic logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A retention and documentation governance framework would help with lifetime traceability and inspection readiness but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging capability Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: CI-enforced compliance checks are a known shift-left practice, though applying them to Article 12 fields is a mildly interesting tailoring.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (CI gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving R&D's relationship to obligations unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Build-time gating is a common engineering strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing CI pipeline with a static-analysis step and an integration test is reasonably feasible with some changes, though the 100 ms assertion and annotation conventions need setup.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by enforcing Article 12(1) and 12(3) requirements before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: It reliably ensures logging hooks and fields exist in artefacts but does not cover runtime log retention, risk-relevant event selection, or the other Article 12 purposes, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library with CI/CD enforcement is the standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable middleware and CI/CD gate but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance-by-construction tooling is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: An eight-week sprint to build a library and integrate it into architecture templates and CI/CD is a reasonably feasible, moderate change for an engineering lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by capturing the specific events (timestamps, inputs, reference-database queries, verifier actions) named in Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: A mandatory logging middleware built into every high-risk system would, if built, satisfy the Article 12 automatic-logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it covers logging only and not documentation or other obligations.

evidence_originality: Automated tests that check log schemas against a compliance checklist are a common, expected engineering response and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-testing tool that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged; at most it adds a minor new tool.
evidence_acceptability: Automated pre-production compliance testing is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A pytest-based integration test with synthetic calls and a schema checklist is cheap and quick to build with existing tooling and requires no radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The harness directly targets the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that the four required log fields are present and structured correctly, which helps compliance, but it covers only the 12(3) biometric subset and not Article 12(1)-(2) traceability or the quality of logging design, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as first-class research artifacts is a somewhat imaginative framing, but extending MLflow with structured logs is a fairly expected response among AI labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between research practice and compliance by weaving logging into the science itself, which is paradigm stretching, but it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Automated structured logging aligned with the regulation violates no legal or social norms and is a common, sensible strategy.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing MLflow pipeline with JSON-LD emission and registry versioning is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change, though per-inference logging adds some engineering work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate by emitting the specified fields (timestamps, reference databases, matched inputs, operator IDs) automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially meet the logging requirement and reduce burden, but it covers only logging, not the broader documentation, retention, or risk-based event requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared drop-in logging library is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a shared middleware package) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving R&D workflow unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal shared library for compliance is a standard, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin decorator API over existing inference servers built in two sprints is a modest, reasonably easy change, though matching diverse endpoints and crash recovery add some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate: do X (middleware) to get compliant logs, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would implement the Article 12 logging capability, including the 12(3) fields, across prototypes, but it only covers logging of those fields and does not address the broader 12(2) event-relevance or retention aspects, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A benchmark that unites regulatory log sufficiency with reproducibility criteria is unusual and shows imagination beyond typical compliance responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance logging double as experimental provenance and creating an open scientific offering from the obligation.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks are an accepted scientific practice, though releasing real deployment logs raises some privacy and confidentiality concerns that are somewhat unusual for compliance.
evidence_implementability: Curating high-risk configurations, generating synthetic and real logs, defining metrics, and releasing open tooling is a substantial, expensive effort that is difficult but feasible.
evidence_applicability: A benchmark scoring log sufficiency against Article 12 helps assess logging quality, which is an implied rather than directly stated need of the lab's problem of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark would help the lab and field evaluate log adequacy but does not itself implement logging in the lab's systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging requirements into research design and peer review is a sensible, somewhat unusual idea that shows some imagination but is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the scientific planning process so compliance becomes part of how research is designed, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance without altering what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Adding logging specifications to experiment templates and peer review is a sensible process change that violates no legal or social norms, though slightly less common than standard logging tooling.
evidence_implementability: It needs only template revisions and an added review step, which are reasonably feasible changes, though they require cultural adoption and the technical logging itself still has to be built.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by specifying Article 12(2) events, retention, and feedback in each experiment's plan.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is planned and reviewed, but it is a process measure that does not provide the technical logging capability itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI/CD compliance test harness for logging is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is interesting rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (automated test harness and CI/CD gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal pre-release compliance testing violates no legal or social norms and is a common, welcomed strategy.
evidence_implementability: Writing test cases per clause and adding CI gates requires a dedicated team and some process change but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying each sub-requirement before release.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would verify that logs meet Article 12 requirements, but it only checks logging capability and does not itself build the logging or address wider documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pricing compliance overhead into portfolio decisions is a sensible and somewhat unusual idea, but it resembles ordinary budgeting and is not ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance cost a criterion for deciding which research is funded or pivoted, which stretches the paradigm beyond logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Semiannual budget reviews with a compliance officer are a normal governance practice that violates no norms, though pivoting projects on compliance cost may be somewhat sensitive.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a simple cost model, existing committee processes, and compliance officer input, so it is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how Article 12 overhead affects R&D decisions, which relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A cost-weighted portfolio review helps decide which projects remain viable under logging obligations but does not itself build the logging capability or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a shared logging SDK into the MLOps platform is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with no surprising element.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice, merely centralizing it in a platform, and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging infrastructure and build-time mandates are common engineering strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Platform teams can build a shared SDK with schema validation, though it requires cross-team coordination and mandatory linking across projects, so some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, default logging with schema-validated Article 12(3) fields would meet the core logging mandate, though it addresses only the logging part and not documentation or broader R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Fault-injection style testing of logs for risk reconstruction is an interesting and sensible idea but not especially surprising or rare among expected responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new validation tool and process but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Testing logging adequacy with synthetic inputs is a sensible, norm-compliant practice, only slightly unusual in its emphasis on risk-event validation.
evidence_implementability: An ML validation team can build synthetic test scenarios and run them in sandboxes with existing skills, requiring some new work but no radical change, though calibrating adversarial scenarios and reconstruction scoring takes effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that logs capture events relevant to Article 79(1) risk identification.
evidence_effectiveness: It validates logging sufficiency but does not itself build the logging capability or cover all of Article 12, so it is a strong but partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Publishing a logging standard as a methods paper is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but open standards and schema proposals are not entirely unexpected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (an open standard and a publication) and turns compliance work into a research output and reputation asset, which changes the relationship between compliance and R&D somewhat, though it remains centered on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open specifications and peer-reviewed publication are accepted norms, though publicly releasing logging details may raise some confidentiality concerns, which are minor.
evidence_implementability: A small team over two quarters plus piloting and peer review is reasonably feasible, though journal acceptance is uncertain and the effort diverts staff resources.
evidence_applicability: Extending the Article 12 minimum fields into an open logging schema addresses the logging mandate directly, though the stated aim of intellectual leadership is more implied than the compliance itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A published schema would help standardize logs and could structure the lab's own logging, but it is only a partial solution because it does not by itself deliver the lab's compliant logging infrastructure or address risk-event capture.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as replay-based regression fixtures is an interesting and somewhat unusual repurposing, though log replay for testing is a known practice, so it is imaginative but not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes logs from a compliance artifact into a core part of the R&D quality pipeline, changing the relationship between compliance and R&D (logging woven into the science).
evidence_acceptability: Using production logs for testing raises data protection and anonymisation concerns and possible purpose-limitation issues, but it is a sensible practice that does not offend norms if anonymised.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing nightly CI with a replay job, but requires anonymisation, access to deployed-system logs, and divergence thresholds, which means some changes but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to make use of the mandated logs, which relates to but is not the direct problem of meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the Article 12 logging mandate (what to record, retention, traceability) and only contributes by exploiting logs for QA, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: A version-controlled living-documentation workflow on an existing wiki is a very common, mundane compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing Git notebooks and the wiki, needs no new software, and adds only a monthly review slot and a designated manager, so cost and change are low.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied related problem, documentation and audit-readiness, rather than the identified logging mandate, though it relates to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses technical documentation under Recital 71 but not the automatic event logging that Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Machine-readable provenance manifests via CI plugins are a fairly familiar approach (model cards, datasheets), though framing reproducibility as compliance infrastructure shows slight imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and weaves provenance into the code review and release workflow, but still treats compliance as a logging/documentation practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship much.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating provenance into code review and release is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small platform team building a lightweight CI plugin over existing trackers is a modest, reasonably feasible change at low cost, though lineage capture may need some work.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses meeting the logging/record-keeping mandate by generating provenance manifests from experiment trackers, though it conflates Article 12 event logs with technical documentation, so the fit is somewhat implied rather than exact.
evidence_effectiveness: Release-time manifests would help with documentation and traceability but do not provide automatic recording of events over system lifetime in deployed high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a corpus for 'failure archaeology' and an annual state-of-failure report is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly unprecedented given incident databases.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning Article 12 logs into an empirical research dataset and a standing research program on failure modes, which is paradigm stretching rather than just logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Analyzing own logs and publishing aggregated failure reports is a somewhat uncommon but unobjectionable strategy, though publication and privacy of log data need care.
evidence_implementability: Two postdocs and a structured incident database are a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though building the taxonomy and causal analysis across a portfolio requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (extracting value from logs and supporting monitoring/risk identification) that relates to the mandate, rather than the identified problem of implementing the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It makes use of logs and supports post-market monitoring but does not itself specify how to meet the logging mandate (what to record, retention, tamper-resistance), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware with schema contracts is a sensible but common developer-tooling response that an evaluator would readily expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK and templates) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal logging libraries and templates are a common engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It extracts existing production hooks into a versioned SDK and wires it into the template repo, which involves moderate engineering work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by providing pre-built log emitters and event schemas for new prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially ease and standardize logging in new prototypes, but it only partly solves the problem since it does not cover deployed systems, retention, Annex III-specific minimums beyond schemas, or broader compliance.

evidence_originality: Event-sourced WORM ledgers with auditor APIs are common, expected responses to logging mandates, with little surprising about them.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging architecture and leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable audit logging with retention controls is a conventional, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Event sourcing, WORM storage, a read-only API and SSO binding are established technologies that reuse existing infrastructure, though building a dedicated system needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified requirement in the stated problem, namely meeting the Article 12(3) minimum logging capabilities.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, the ledger would capture every Article 12(3) element (use period, reference database, matched inputs, verifier identity), but it addresses only the Annex III 1(a) biometric case and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared open logging ontology for cross-lab reproducibility is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, but standardization consortia are a familiar kind of response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (ontology, consortium, shared infrastructure) and creates a cross-lab offering born from compliance, yet it still treats compliance fundamentally as logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source, consortium-based standardization with permissive licensing is a collaborative approach that offends no legal or social norms, though somewhat less routine than in-house compliance.
evidence_implementability: Convening four to six labs to co-design and release an ontology with reference implementations requires coordination and significant effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets Article 12(3) logging fields directly but is aimed at the implied problem of reproducibility and broader impact rather than the lab's own compliance, so it applies by implication.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared schema covering Article 12(3) fields would help standardize logs but does not itself make the lab's systems log automatically or meet Article 12(1)-(2) obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate sign-offs for compliance are a common, expected response among labs, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A stage-gate compliance checkpoint is a new process element but still treats compliance as a logging practice separate from R&D, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Internal stage-gate reviews with compliance sign-off are a common governance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires amending stage-gate procedures and adding a recurring review, which are modest non-radical changes, though a 30-day re-review adds some burden.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying logging capabilities against Article 12(2)(a)-(c) before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A sign-off gate helps verify logging adequacy but does not itself build the logging capability or cover the full mandate (e.g., Article 12(3) specifics, retention), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing anonymized failure-case logs as a public benchmark is an unusual, interesting spin on a logging mandate that most labs would treat purely as internal compliance, though open data release itself is not unheard of.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance logging and the lab's science by turning compliance records into a research offering for external partners and the community, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing data derived from high-risk system logs publicly raises privacy, confidentiality, and GDPR concerns, though anonymization and ethics review mitigate this so it somewhat offends sensibilities but is not unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: It requires ethics review, robust anonymization, schema design, hosting and a methods paper, which is significant added effort and re-identification risk, but it is feasible with existing tools like Hugging Face.
evidence_applicability: It relates to the stated problem only indirectly by reusing logs for an adapted R&D benefit, which is an implied rather than identified problem and applies only in a special situation.
evidence_effectiveness: The idea does not itself make the lab's systems meet Article 12 logging requirements, so at most it contributes tangentially and could even add risk, making it unlikely to solve the stated compliance problem.

evidence_originality: A shared cross-project compliance pod with a dedicated internal funding line is a sensible organizational idea, but centralized compliance teams are fairly expected, so it is interesting rather than ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a permanent pod, a reclassified budget line) but still treats compliance as a logging-infrastructure practice, leaving the R&D approach itself unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reclassifying 15% of earmarked personnel costs to avoid renegotiation with funders could offend funder sensibilities or breach grant terms, so it is somewhat questionable though not totally unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: Forming a three-person team is easy, but reallocating earmarked funds and embedding across projects requires moderate organizational and financial changes, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of repeated ad-hoc compliance builds and staffing for logging, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate without directly specifying the logging solution.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared traceability team would help build logging capabilities efficiently but does not specify what logs are recorded or how Article 12 requirements are met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Version-controlled living documentation with stewards and release-triggered reviews is a very common, expected compliance response, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged, merely adding process.
evidence_acceptability: Internal documentation governance violates no norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Assigning stewards and linking doc updates to release triggers requires only modest process changes at low cost, though the 14-day cycle adds some burden.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied related problem (documentation upkeep and demonstrating compliance) rather than the directly stated logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses technical documentation (Recital 71) but not the automatic event logging mandated by Article 12, so it only partially solves the stated logging problem.

evidence_originality: Logging by design / compliance-by-design is a widely expected, mundane response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standard and shared middleware and shifts logging earlier into design, but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship fundamentally.
evidence_acceptability: A mandatory internal engineering standard for logging is a common, legally aligned strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building shared logging middleware and requiring it from the first sprint needs some process and engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with internal resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, built-in logging aligned with Article 12(2) would address the main logging mandate, though it omits Article 12(3) specifics and retention details, making it close to but arguably a full solution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Treating minimal-sufficient log schema design as a publishable research line is somewhat unusual and interesting, but it is not strikingly ingenious, since labs would more commonly just implement logging.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research output and a way to influence standards, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing preprints and engaging with interpretive guidance are normal, legitimate practices, though a 'minimal' logging stance might raise mild regulator eyebrows, it offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two researchers over twelve months on two existing pilot systems is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though it needs some staffing and process changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(2) logging requirement by determining what events to log, and it relates to the stated problem of how to meet the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help reduce uncertainty and inform schema design, but a twelve-month research effort on two systems is only a partial solution and does not itself deliver compliant logging across the portfolio, and minimization may risk under-compliance.

evidence_originality: Merging regulatory technical documentation with open-science reproducibility norms is somewhat unusual and interesting, but a documentation template is a fairly expected lab response and not highly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new format and partnership with an open-science group and reframes compliance as a scientific contribution, which modestly shifts the compliance-R&D relationship, though it remains a documentation practice.
evidence_acceptability: Standardised templates developed with ethics committees and open-science groups violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A six-week sprint and two-project pilot is reasonably feasible with some process changes, though coordinating external groups and institutionalising across all systems takes effort.
evidence_applicability: It targets documentation requirements in the recital, which relate only implicitly to the logging mandate in the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The template addresses Recital 71 technical documentation but not the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate itself, so it only partially solves the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Applying homomorphic tokens or differential-privacy noising to mandated biometric match logs is an unusual and thoughtful angle that shows imagination, though privacy-preserving logging is a known research area and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (privacy-preserving cryptographic or statistical log pipelines and threat models) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, so it only slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-protective logging and publishing threat models offend no norms and align with data-protection law, though noising mandated records could raise some regulatory questions.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping two architectures and publishing threat models is a bounded effort, but cryptographic or noised logs that stay auditable are difficult and require specialist expertise, so this takes significant change and is moderately difficult.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12(3)(c) logging mandate without creating a secondary surveillance dataset, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help resolve one tension for a narrow class of Annex III 1(a) systems, but it covers only a subset of the logging mandate and is exploratory, so it contributes only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A log retention and storage cost protocol is a mundane, expected operational response to a logging mandate, with little that is imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and IT governance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal protocols with DPO consultation and finance validation are common, norm-respecting business practice.
evidence_implementability: It is a document and process drafted by existing teams using current cloud contracts and the normal procurement cycle, so it is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied downstream problem (retention, access, and cost of lifetime logs) that relates to the logging mandate but is not the core requirement to enable automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: A retention, encryption, and cost protocol would help manage storage of logs but does not itself deliver the logging capability or traceability the mandate requires, so it is only a partial solution.
