evidence_originality: A shared logging library embedded in an SDK is a common, expected engineering response, with only mild interest from schema versioning alongside model code.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into shared tooling is a standard strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building and integrating a library into the existing SDK and getting prototypes to adopt it, which is reasonably feasible but involves some real engineering effort and changes.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly addresses the stated problem by automatically capturing Article 12(2) event types and the Annex III 1(a) minimum log fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, an automatic, versioned logging layer in the shared SDK would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not cover non-logging obligations or deployer-side retention.

evidence_originality: A log retention and access policy is a mundane, expected compliance response that most labs would produce.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging governance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retention and access-control policies are common, norm-respecting governance practices that offend no one.
evidence_implementability: Drafting an internal policy with encryption and role-based access is low-cost and uses existing compliance office capabilities with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses log retention, access and production on demand, which relates directly to meeting the logging mandate, though Article 12 itself does not set retention rules (that is Article 19), so the link is partly implied.
evidence_effectiveness: A retention and access policy helps with producing records for authorities and GDPR alignment but does not itself implement the automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A design-stage specification document with template and sign-off gate is a common, mundane compliance-documentation approach that shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and documentation practice that leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged, merely adding a template and gate.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory specification documents and sign-off gates are common governance strategies that violate no norms, though gating builds may draw mild engineering pushback.
evidence_implementability: A template, design-review step, and sign-off are low-cost, non-radical process additions that can be done quickly.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by defining what events are recorded and mapping them to the regulatory articles.
evidence_effectiveness: A per-system logging specification tied to Art. 12(2) and Annex III minimums, with sign-off gating, would contribute to meeting the mandate but is a planning/documentation step that does not itself ensure logs are technically implemented or retained.

evidence_originality: Reusing benchmark harnesses on production logs and presenting compliance output as publishable research is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle, but not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning post-market monitoring into a source of publications and grant narrative, though it stays within the lab's existing evaluation work rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing evaluation tools for monitoring and publishing aggregate findings is a reasonable strategy that offends no norms, though publishing production-derived data needs some care.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing harnesses, ten percent of compute and one shared analyst, so it is feasible with modest changes, though it depends on the logging middleware existing first.
evidence_applicability: It addresses post-market monitoring under Article 72, which Article 12(2)(b) says logging must support, so it relates to the logging mandate only indirectly, as an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet post-market monitoring needs, but it depends on a separate logging middleware and does not itself deliver Article 12 logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK for compliance is an expected, mundane response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with a shared tool but no change to how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A shared compliance library mandated across projects is a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal logging SDK and enforcing it at codebase level is a reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes but no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-capturing the specified event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the automatic recording obligation across systems, though Article 12(3) fields apply only to Annex III 1(a) systems and it does not cover log retention, appropriateness to purpose, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a shared longitudinal research corpus is unusual and imaginative, though the idea of data-sharing for research is not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making mandated logs a research asset and creating new offerings and partnerships born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Repurposing operational logs into a shared research corpus is unusual and raises data-protection and customer-confidentiality sensitivities, though anonymization and GDPR-compliant governance mean it is not totally unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year cross-system ingestion, anonymization and governance pipeline plus community dataset releases is a significant and expensive undertaking, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of how to get value from logging mandates, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly address how to meet the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself satisfy Article 12 logging requirements and offers only a partial, indirect contribution by leveraging logs once they exist.

evidence_originality: Mapping existing systems against regulatory requirements is the common, expected first step and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A gap audit against Article 12 fields is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A internal compliance gap audit is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint using existing engineers and existing observability tools is a low-cost, non-radical effort that is easy to implement.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by identifying which systems satisfy Article 12 and which do not.
evidence_effectiveness: An audit only diagnoses gaps and does not itself build the logging capabilities, so it contributes to but does not solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Append-only WORM storage with schemas mapped to the regulation's minimum fields is a common, expected response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging architecture and leaves the lab's R&D practice and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable append-only logs with role-based access and lifetime retention are a conventional, legally aligned approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-month prototype on existing WORM storage is reasonably feasible but requires some architectural changes and audit-latency testing, so it is not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate for biometric systems by specifying the four required fields and storage.
evidence_effectiveness: It covers the Article 12(3) minimum fields for Annex III 1(a) systems but not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) risk, post-market, and monitoring logging for other systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing compliance as an epistemological question about the information-theoretic limits of documenting learning systems is unusual and imaginative compared with typical lab responses, though not wholly unprecedented given existing interpretability and documentation research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It redirects what the lab researches, turning a compliance obligation into a fundamental research agenda and open standard-setting, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance and addresses the larger problem of what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing research openly and using case studies from own prototypes violates no norms, though disclosing high-risk prototype details might raise some confidentiality concerns, making it a somewhat unusual but inoffensive strategy.
evidence_implementability: A multi-paper theoretical and empirical research programme is expensive, long-horizon, and uncertain in outcome, which makes it a significant commitment of scarce resources, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (what documentation is epistemically achievable, per Recital 71) that relates to the stated logging mandate only indirectly, since Article 12 concerns event logs rather than model description.
evidence_effectiveness: A theoretical research programme on documentation limits would not itself deliver Article 12 automatic event logging, so it might inform documentation practice but is unlikely to solve the compliance problem of meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Schema evolution via registries is a well-known data engineering pattern, and applying it to AI Act logging is sensible and somewhat interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool and process (schema registry, migration tooling) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Schema registries and versioned data governance are standard engineering practice that offend no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Adopting Avro/Protobuf schema registries with migration tooling requires some engineering effort and process changes but uses mature, widely available tools and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely log schema drift across model iterations undermining lifetime traceability under Article 12(1), which relates to but is not the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A versioned schema registry with migration tooling would meaningfully sustain log continuity and traceability over the system lifetime, but it covers only one part of the logging mandate (not what to log, event relevance, or retention/access), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A post-market monitoring team with dashboards, weekly reports and escalation is a standard, expected response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a standard organizational function within ordinary compliance practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A dedicated compliance monitoring team reviewing logs is a conventional, norm-compliant business practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Standing up a permanent cell with a dashboard, reports and escalation protocol requires new staffing and tooling, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses identified Article 12(2) purposes (risk identification, post-market monitoring) tied to the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Continuous log review would help with post-market monitoring and risk detection, but it does not itself ensure the logging mandate of Article 12 is technically met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging library embedded in starter templates is a sensible, commonly expected response to a logging mandate and is not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging SDK built into the prototyping template is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standard internal engineering tooling that violates no legal, social or political norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin library with pluggable backends wired into an existing template is low-cost and requires only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the events specified in Article 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver the technical logging capability for every build, but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or the compliance and documentation aspects beyond logging, so it is a substantial partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating log-granularity as an architecture-evaluation axis with ablation studies is unusual and imaginative compared to typical logging-infrastructure responses, though not wildly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making traceability a scientific axis of architecture research, directly shaping what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open research on architecture and compliance violates no norms and is likely welcomed, though it is somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Running ablation studies across architectures is feasible for an AI lab but requires significant research effort, new metrics for log-informativeness, and uncertain timelines, which conflicts with committing scarce implementation resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (designing systems whose native logs support Article 12 traceability) that relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Studying how architecture affects log informativeness would inform better logging but is a research programme that only partially contributes to meeting Article 12 obligations, since the lab still needs to build actual logging now.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design and instrumentation templates are a well-known pattern, so this is a sensible but expected response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a template module with pre-wired schemas) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into development templates is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing internal prototyping template with a pluggable event-emitter module is a modest, non-radical change, though engineers must still wire domain-specific fields.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate through adapting R&D, with Article 12(2) categories explicitly named.
evidence_effectiveness: It would systematically give every prototype Article 12 logging capability, but it covers only the logging side (not retention, Annex III-specific minimums, or documentation), so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as an internal research dataset is an interesting and somewhat unusual reframing, but it is not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logs into the science (secondary research use), though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymised internal read-only logs violates no norms, though repurposing logs raises minor data-protection purpose-limitation questions.
evidence_implementability: Schema standardisation in two sprints plus streams and a dashboard are reasonably feasible using existing infrastructure, though cross-project standardisation takes some change.
evidence_applicability: Standardised schemas directly address the logging mandate, while the research-reuse benefit addresses an implied problem of adapting R&D and offsetting compliance cost.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help make logging useful and support audit defence, but it does not itself ensure the Article 12 logging requirements (events relevant to risk, post-market monitoring, Annex III minimums) are met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified, versioned log schema spanning model updates is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to lifetime logging, with only mild interest in the cross-version continuity angle.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a versioned schema and migration guide) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Schema design, retention planning and migration guides are standard, uncontroversial data-governance practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing object storage and a small cross-functional team with a data dictionary and prototype, so it needs only modest, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement of retaining logs over the system lifetime (Art. 12(1)) and supporting Article 72 monitoring, which are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A stable long-lived schema would help satisfy lifetime logging and post-market monitoring, but it covers only data architecture and not what events to capture or the other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Interpretable-by-construction and log-emitting layers are an interesting, somewhat imaginative framing of Article 12 compliance, but related ideas exist in the interpretability literature, so it is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the science of model design, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance and shaping what the lab researches, though it stops short of fully redefining the lab's agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into model architectures is a legitimate research approach that violates no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat more unusual than standard application-level logging.
evidence_implementability: Designing new architectures that emit intermediate representations by construction is a multi-year research effort with uncertain success and performance tradeoffs, so it is difficult and expensive though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the logging mandate and adapting R&D, explicitly aiming to meet Article 12 requirements through model design.
evidence_effectiveness: If achieved it would yield rich logs, but Article 12 mainly requires event logs such as usage periods, reference databases, and persons verifying results, which intermediate-representation logging does not fully cover, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalizing substantial-modification criteria as a research output is unusual and shows imagination, though it is not wholly surprising since others have looked at regulatory thresholds.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance ambiguity into publishable research and standard-setting influence changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, but it does not alter what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open preprints and aligning with regulatory guidance is a legitimate, norm-compatible strategy, though somewhat uncommon for compliance work.
evidence_implementability: Building a validated taxonomy and detection algorithms is a research effort with uncertain outcomes and moderate-to-significant cost, but it is feasible using existing sensitivity-analysis and drift literature.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the undefined substantial-modification boundary in Article 12(2)(a), which relates to the logging mandate but is not the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Defining and detecting substantial modification would help the lab know when logging obligations are triggered, but it does not itself deliver the logging mechanism, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gap assessments and prioritisation are common compliance-management steps, though the sunk-cost framing adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It links compliance cost to decisions about which projects to continue or restart, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations beyond treating it as logging practice alone.
evidence_acceptability: Portfolio audits and resource reprioritisation are legitimate management practices that violate no norms, though stopping projects may be somewhat sensitive.
evidence_implementability: A two-week gap assessment per project with a standard rubric and a consolidated board matrix within a quarter needs some effort but only modest, non-radical organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of deciding how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D by identifying where to retrofit versus restart.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit and reprioritisation would help the lab decide how to respond and adapt R&D, but it does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reference logging template mapped to Article 12(3) is a sensible, common engineering response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable logging SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal reusable compliance tooling with tests violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers in one sprint extracting hooks from an existing prototype is low cost and a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces the Article 12(3) logging fields (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier identities), which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the logging mandate for biometric Annex III 1(a) systems but not Article 12(1)-(2) for other systems or the wider R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using mandated lifetime logs as a longitudinal scientific dataset on drift is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning mandatory logs into a research instrument and research agenda, which stretches the paradigm, though it does not fully change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing anonymised aggregate findings from biometric system logs is somewhat uncommon and raises data-protection and deployer-confidentiality sensitivities, but it is not offensive.
evidence_implementability: It requires access to logs from two deployed biometric systems (likely operated by third-party deployers), multi-year commitment, and data-sharing agreements, which is significant difficulty though not impossible, with only one postdoc needed.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (getting research value from logging) that relates to the stated problem, but does not directly solve how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to adapting R&D around logging but would not itself ensure the lab meets Article 12 requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A log-completeness monitoring dashboard is a sensible, somewhat interesting observability idea, but monitoring log health with Kafka and Grafana is a fairly expected engineering response and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new tooling (streaming pipeline, alerts) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only with continuous verification of it.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring dashboards are a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Kafka and Grafana are off-the-shelf tools and a small pipeline per pilot is reasonably feasible with modest effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the problem, ensuring Article 12 event classes are actually recorded in production, though the needed logging itself is an implied prerequisite.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps verify that logs are captured but does not itself define what to log, retain logs, or meet the whole mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code tests in CI is a fairly well-known DevOps pattern applied to logging obligations, so it is interesting but not surprising or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (automated compliance test gate in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing of logging requirements is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Writing schema assertions and nightly test runs with tracker integration is low-cost and uses existing tooling, though defining assertions for the vague Article 12(2) categories requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required event categories are emitted during R&D prototyping.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging capability is present and catches gaps early, but it only verifies emission and does not itself design the logging, retention, or cover the other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing mandated logs as a natural experiment for drift research is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the logging obligation into a research platform, weaving logging into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Using operational logs for research and publishing is an unusual but non-offensive strategy, though privacy and data-protection concerns could arise.
evidence_implementability: Assigning a dedicated analytics team to mine existing logs for a multi-year research programme requires significant staffing, data governance, and sustained investment, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal uses logs as a research resource, which relates only implicitly to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate or adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: It does nothing to ensure the logging mandate is met (what to log, retention, traceability), so it contributes only a partial, byproduct benefit to compliance.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing monitoring infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, sensible, and mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal extends existing telemetry and middleware with gap analyses, treating compliance purely as logging practice and leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure and having project leads file gap analyses is a standard approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Incremental extension of existing pipelines with a six-week gap analysis is low cost and non-radical, though it relies on a referenced shared middleware from another proposal.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping existing telemetry to its specific paragraphs.
evidence_effectiveness: If carried out, auditing and patching existing telemetry against Article 12(2) and (3) would reasonably yield compliant logging, but it depends on telemetry sufficiency and does not address retention, integrity, or the scope of high-risk classification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging by default in a framework is a mundane and expected response to Article 12, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (logging middleware in templates) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely making it a default rather than changing the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building default logging into a shared SDK is a common, legally compliant engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing experiment-runner with middleware and project templates, which is a reasonably feasible change with modest cost, though it needs some engineering work and storage.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by making automatic event recording an architectural default.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet Article 1 automatic-recording requirements for prototypes, but it does not address Article 12(2) event relevance, Annex III-specific fields, retention, or post-market monitoring, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code and CI/CD documentation hooks are a fairly expected response for a tech lab, so the idea is interesting and sensible but shows only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving documentation and logging into the research pipeline rather than treating it as a post-hoc step, which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating compliance into engineering workflows is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building CI/CD hooks and metadata capture is reasonably feasible with existing MLOps tooling but requires some workflow changes and cross-team co-design.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly, producing the Article 12 logs and documentation.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatically generating logs and documentation at every pipeline stage would largely meet the logging and documentation mandate, though it conflates development-time documentation with Article 12's runtime event logging of deployed systems, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging middleware on existing monitoring to satisfy Article 12 is the standard, expected response and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging engineering and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging to meet a legal mandate is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person cell adding middleware on the existing monitoring stack within two sprints is low-cost and non-radical, though integrating into training and inference frameworks takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate via do X (embed loggers) to get Y (compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: Native logging of the Article 12(3) fields would meet the logging mandate for those systems, but it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or the R&D adaptation side, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automating substantial-modification detection in CI is a sensible and somewhat interesting idea, but MLOps-style gating is a fairly expected response to compliance mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI gate diffing model artifacts) but still treats compliance as a logging and review practice without changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: CI gates with sign-off and audit logs are a common engineering and compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a comparison service across weights, schemas, thresholds, and data lineage requires some real engineering and defining meaningful thresholds, but it is reasonably feasible within existing CI infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified element of the mandate, Article 12(2)(a) identification of situations involving substantial modification, with a clear do-X-to-get-Y mechanism.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help detect substantial modifications and record related events, but it covers only part of Article 12 (no general event logging, post-market monitoring, or Annex III minimums), and weight-diff similarity is a weak proxy for the legal 'substantial modification' test, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A drop-in decorator/SDK for logging is a common, expected response to a logging mandate with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, though it does introduce a new internal tool.
evidence_acceptability: Internal logging middleware with CI gating is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A Python decorator-based internal SDK with SQLite/Postgres backends and a CI import check is a modest engineering effort using standard tools, though instrumenting diverse pipelines takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically recording the specified event fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the technical logging capability, but it does not cover retention, tamper-resistance, risk-relevant event selection beyond Annex III 1(a) fields, or log review, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning a logging requirement into a community benchmark challenge is somewhat unusual and imaginative, though benchmarks are a familiar ML research device.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the obligation into a research output and community offering, shifting what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing public benchmarks and running community challenges is a normal, norm-respecting research practice, though anonymising real logs raises mild privacy concerns.
evidence_implementability: Curating labelled log datasets, defining metrics, and hosting an annual challenge is a significant, expensive effort requiring new infrastructure and labelling work, though clearly doable.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, risk-event identification under Article 12(2)(a), which relates to the mandate but not directly to the lab's own logging obligations.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark advances detection science but does not itself make the lab's systems log compliantly or satisfy Article 12, so it only partially contributes.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance testing in CI is a fairly common and expected DevOps response, so it is interesting but not unusual or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (CI compliance stage) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It adds a stage to an existing CI pipeline using standard schema validators, which is a modest, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically validating emitted logs against its requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: CI gates would catch schema, timestamp and retention gaps early, but they verify log format rather than ensuring the logged events are substantively sufficient for risk identification and monitoring, so they only partially solve the problem.

evidence_originality: Building logging middleware into a standard pipeline is a fairly expected engineering response, though the 'log-native prototyping' framing is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable SDK that makes logging the default architecture introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance logging in standard tooling is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK with pluggable emitters on an existing inference pipeline is a reasonably feasible engineering project requiring some changes but no radical shifts.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12's automatic event recording mandate while keeping R&D velocity high.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, default automatic event capture would address the logging mandate for prototypes, but it is only a partial solution since it does not cover high-risk-specific minimums, retention, or documentation requirements.

evidence_originality: Document control tied to CI/CD is a sensible and fairly expected compliance-tooling response, with only mild interest in the stale-document alerts.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (registry, CI/CD triggers, stale-document alerts) but still treats compliance as a logging/documentation practice separate from the R&D.
evidence_acceptability: A documentation and log-retention registry tied to compliance is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a CI/CD-linked document-control pipeline with a centralized registry requires some tooling and process changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses keeping records and logs current over system lifetime, which is part of the logging/record-keeping mandate, though it leans toward documentation (Recital 71) rather than Article 12 event logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help maintain documentation and log retention but does not specify what events are logged or ensure automatic event recording, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing observability tooling for compliance logging is a fairly expected, mundane response, with only mild interest in the inherit-by-default framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable middleware and default-inheritance schema modules but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing telemetry for compliance logging is a common, sensible engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Wrapping existing OpenTelemetry collectors with schema modules is a reasonably feasible extension of infrastructure already deployed, requiring some platform-team work but not radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate efficiently with limited resources.
evidence_effectiveness: A logging layer mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) would reasonably address the logging mandate, but it covers only logging and not wider obligations such as the Annex III 3 minimums or retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using compliance logs for longitudinal drift research is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but drift monitoring from production logs is a fairly expected idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning compliance logs into a research asset and a dedicated research node, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using operational logs for internal monitoring and research violates no norms, though possible data protection and purpose-limitation concerns on reusing logs are a minor caveat.
evidence_implementability: It needs a shared ingestion layer, schema normalization across projects, and a dedicated research team, which are significant but feasible changes, and the long-horizon data takes years to accumulate.
evidence_applicability: It uses Article 12 logs to serve an implied related need (post-market monitoring and research value) rather than directly solving the logging-compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Mining logs for drift supports post-market monitoring (Art. 12(2)(b)) but does not itself ensure the lab's systems technically record the required events, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Log-analytics dashboards for monitoring are a fairly expected response, though framing compliance logs as an operational capability is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, with a modest reframing of cost into capability, which fits slight paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Building a monitoring dashboard from compliance logs is a common, norm-respecting strategy.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing visualisation stack with one postdoc building a read-only panel, a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: The dashboard directly uses Article 12 logs to support post-market monitoring (Art. 72) and operation monitoring (Art. 26(5)), which are stated purposes of the logging mandate, though it does not itself implement the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps exploit logs for monitoring and risk detection but does not itself ensure logging capability or compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using a paying customer pilot to fund and amortize compliance work is a sensible and somewhat interesting idea but not especially surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a client-funded pilot and reusable template, which is a new commercial arrangement born from compliance, mildly stretching the compliance-R&D relationship, though it remains essentially logging implementation.
evidence_acceptability: A paid pilot with a bank customer and retained IP on the logging architecture is a normal commercial arrangement that violates no norms, though the bank-partner funding model is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing registry and alerting tools with only a new event-capture schema and verifier-identity module, funded by a partner bank, makes this a reasonably feasible set of changes rather than a trivial or radical one.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (implement Article 12(3) logging for the Annex III 1(a) system) to get Y (compliance with the logging mandate), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Retrofitting the biometric model to meet all four Article 12(3) minimums would solve the core logging mandate for that system and provide a template, but it covers only one system and not broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging for others.

evidence_originality: A log-conformance test harness that checks Article 12 event coverage is a sensible but fairly expected compliance-QA tool, mildly interesting without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (automated conformance testing) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving R&D's relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal automated QA of logging is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: A Python harness built on the existing observability stack and run nightly in staging is low-cost and requires no radical change, though defining 'sufficient fidelity' assertions takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, namely confirming the logging mandate is met, though it is a verification step rather than the logging capability itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that logs capture the Article 12(2) categories but does not itself implement logging, cover Article 12(3) minimums, or address wider R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Standardizing logging via a default SDK in templates is a sensible but common approach labs would expect, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (SDK with an Article 12 schema) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library mandated in project templates is a common engineering-governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Wrapping existing OpenTelemetry instrumentation and shipping it in an internal template repo requires some platform-team work but is reasonably feasible with modest change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by mapping events to Article 12(3) fields in every prototype.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help ensure logging capability exists across prototypes, but it covers only Art. 12(3)-type fields, not retention, risk-relevant event selection (12(2)), or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A pre-design compliance gate with checklist and sign-off is a very common governance response that labs would be expected to propose, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process gate and checklist but treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Governance gates and compliance sign-offs are common strategies that violate no norms, though blocking resources may cause mild friction.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist and a sign-off requirement are cheap and non-radical to introduce, needing only procedural changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by ensuring Article 12 requirements are reviewed before development starts.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is considered early but is only a partial solution since it does not provide the actual logging capabilities, and the checklist covers only Article 12(2) not the full mandate.

evidence_originality: Framing the compliance task as a formal taxonomy research project is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a formal taxonomy) and links compliance to research output, yet still primarily serves logging scope definition without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Academic research and publication of a classification framework violates no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual response to a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: A literature synthesis and validation against own deployments is a modest research effort needing some staff time but no major infrastructure, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: Defining what counts as a risk-relevant event directly addresses Article 12(2)(a) logging scope, but it addresses an implied need (clarifying scope) rather than delivering the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy would help decide which events to log but does not itself provide logging capability or satisfy the mandate, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Shared compliance logging middleware is a fairly expected response to a logging mandate, with only mild interest in the pinned-by-default enforcement.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (an SDK pinned in the base image) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library baked into the base image is a common engineering strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses metadata the containerised pipeline already captures and needs only a thin SDK and a base-image dependency, so it is easy and low cost, though it requires some build work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (automatic recording, Article 12 fields) in the lab's R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic event recording for prototypes, but it covers mainly Article 12(1) and the Annex III 1(a) fields, not the wider mandate such as retention, risk-relevant event selection or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance reviews are a very common, mundane response to regulatory mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint process but still treats compliance as a logging verification practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A internal review gate with sign-off is a common, norm-compliant governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs only an SOP, training two engineers, and a workflow tool integration, which is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of ensuring the lab's systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate checks logging coverage but does not itself build logging capability or address Article 12(1) and (3) or retention, so it contributes only partially.

evidence_originality: Log access control and pseudonymisation under GDPR-style governance is a common, expected response, though noticing the HR-privacy tension with verifier IDs is a modest touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: This is standard compliance and data-governance practice that leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retention policies, DPO involvement, role-based access and pseudonymisation are common, norm-conforming governance practices.
evidence_implementability: An SOP co-authored with the DPO plus role-based access on an existing log store is low-cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the Article 12(3)(d) requirement to log verifier identities and governs how those logs are handled, which is part of the stated logging-mandate problem, though it covers only one narrow piece.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet one sub-requirement (verifier ID logging) with privacy-aware access, but it does not deliver the logging capability itself or address the broader mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing Article 12 sufficiency as an information-theoretic and causal-inference optimization is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (entropy and causal metrics, formal criteria) and generalizable methodology, but still treats compliance as a logging practice question rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Research on minimal logging is legally and socially unobjectionable, though minimizing logs might raise mild regulator concerns about under-recording, so it is somewhat unusual but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: Defining and validating information-theoretic criteria for minimal sufficient logging is a significant, open-ended research effort requiring specialized expertise and uncertain outcomes, making it difficult though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It targets an implied problem (deciding which events to record to meet Article 12 without over-collection) that relates to the stated mandate, but it does not directly implement the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A formal criterion for sufficient traceability might help decide what to log, but it is a research program that does not itself deliver compliant logging and may not satisfy the specific minimums in Article 12, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: A feasibility and overhead benchmarking study for logging is a mundane, expected response, though the simulated five-year retention horizon adds slight specificity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Measuring logging overhead before committing to architecture is a common, sensible engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-month study by two engineers using load tests on existing production-like systems is a small, low-cost effort with no radical changes required.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, whether lifetime logging is technically viable at scale, which relates to meeting the logging mandate but is not itself implementing it.
evidence_effectiveness: It produces data to inform architecture decisions but does not itself deliver logging capability or compliance, so it is only a partial contribution, and the prompt says approval means implementation commitment, not exploration.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance logging schemas is an interesting and somewhat unusual idea, with the longitudinal dataset angle showing some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open schema registry, community-contributed corpus, new offering born from compliance) which modestly shifts compliance toward a public-good offering, but it is still fundamentally logging practice and does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source sharing of schemas, engagement with scientific panels and goodwill with authorities violate no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat uncommon strategy.
evidence_implementability: Three FTEs for one quarter is a modest, bounded investment using standard engineering skills, though community maintenance adds some ongoing effort.
evidence_applicability: Schemas covering Article 12(3) fields and an agent emitting conforming logs directly address the logging mandate, though much of the benefit targets other labs rather than the lab's own compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab meet logging requirements and aid others, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and general taxonomy, leaving intended-purpose traceability, retention, and integration with the lab's own systems unresolved, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checks in CI are a fairly common DevOps idea, so this is a sensible but expected response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Merge gates and contract tests are common engineering practice that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing pytest and CI infrastructure with contract tests and sandboxes, requiring some changes but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The CI gate directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required event categories are logged, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that logging capability exists and is complete for the Article 12(2) categories, but it does not itself design the logging, cover production behavior, or address Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open documentation standards and model-card-style approaches are well known, so this is interesting but not strikingly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a standard and tooling) but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice, though the open release adds an outward-facing offering.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open standard is a common, norm-compliant practice, though open release of documentation methodology might raise some IP concerns that are minor.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a standard, piloting on three projects, and building tooling plus open release requires a working group and software development, which is significant but feasible effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets technical documentation under Recital 71 rather than the Article 12 automatic logging mandate, so it addresses an implied, related problem (traceability/compliance documentation) rather than the logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation standard would help with traceability and compliance records but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution at best.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing monitoring telemetry for compliance logging is a sensible but fairly common and mundane response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces an annotation layer but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing monitoring infrastructure for compliance is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a thin annotation layer to existing dashboards within six weeks is a modest, non-radical change at low cost, though mapping schemas across projects takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by satisfying specific Article 12 recording requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the logging mandate, but it addresses only Article 12(3) fields and ignores Article 12(1)-(2) event relevance and the broader R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reconciling Article 12(3) logging with data minimisation via privacy-preserving techniques is an interesting and somewhat unusual angle, but it is a recognizable research direction and not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (cryptographic and differential-privacy schemes) and ties compliance to the lab's research and publication profile, yet it still largely treats compliance as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving research and publication is a common, norm-compatible strategy, though regulators may question anonymising records that must support traceability.
evidence_implementability: It is a research programme requiring significant cryptographic work and prototyping, and it does not commit to a deliverable compliance mechanism, so it is difficult and uncertain to implement.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(3) logging mandate for biometric systems, though only for the narrow Annex III 1(a) case and with a privacy sub-problem that is implied rather than stated.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with one aspect (privacy-compatible logging of match records) but not the general logging mandate, and k-anonymity on match records may conflict with Article 12's traceability purpose, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated CI gates for logging conformance are a fairly expected DevOps-style response to a logging mandate, though the Pact-style contract-test framing adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI contract tests) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI testing is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building on existing CI/CD pipelines with contract tests is reasonably feasible, though defining schemas for event classes and representative inputs requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D workflows (do X to verify logging conformance).
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify that systems emit required log event classes and so contributes to meeting the logging mandate, but it does not itself implement logging, cover retention, or address the broader documentation and monitoring obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered storage with schema versioning for long-term logs is a standard, expected engineering response to a lifetime logging mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging infrastructure and leaves the lab's R&D approach and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retaining structured logs internally is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms, although retention may raise data-protection questions that are not addressed.
evidence_implementability: A small team can prototype an internal microservice using well-established storage tiers at modest cost, which needs some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 requirement for logs over the system's lifetime, which supports post-market monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: Durable, queryable lifetime logs would help meet the retention and traceability part of the mandate, but the proposal does not decide which events to log, cover Annex III minimums, or address R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware/SDKs for compliance are a common, expected response to a logging mandate and show little surprise.

evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-capturing the required events and paragraph-3 fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would substantially satisfy the logging requirement, but it covers only logging capability and not other aspects such as retention, documentation, or appropriate-purpose scoping, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: A dedicated logging module mapped to Article 12(3) fields using OpenTelemetry is a sensible and expected response, with little that is surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a standalone capture microservice) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, so it is at most slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Building a compliance logging component with standard open tooling violates no legal or social norms and is a common, sensible strategy.
evidence_implementability: A two-sprint prototype on synthetic data and integration into the existing pipeline using OpenTelemetry is reasonably feasible with modest changes, though integration effort and the biometric data sensitivity add some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by capturing exactly the paragraph 3 items (timestamps, reference database, matched input, verifier identity) needed to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging requirements if implemented, but it does not cover the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event logging for risk, post-market monitoring, and operation monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A dedicated logging cell with a unified schema is the obvious, expected response to the mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging is a common, expected strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Retrofitting logging across all high-risk systems with a dedicated cell and unified schema is a significant engineering effort, but it is standard and feasible, so it needs some changes and reasonable measures.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing the required logging capabilities.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a unified schema covering Article 12(2)-(3) items would meet the logging mandate, though it does not address broader R&D adaptation or the need to scope which systems and events are relevant.

evidence_originality: Adding a compliance checkpoint to a stage-gate process is a common, expected governance response, with little that is surprising.

evidence_effectiveness: A design-time gate helps ensure logging is planned and avoids retrofits, but it is only a spec review and does not itself ensure logs are implemented, work, or cover 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging by design with CI/CD gates is a common, expected response to this mandate, showing little surprise.

evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logging middleware enforced by CI/CD gates would, if implemented, cover the core Article 12 automatic-logging mandate, but it does not address broader requirements such as event relevance for risk/post-market monitoring or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the ML framework so every model inherits it is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response, interesting but not surprising or ingenious.

evidence_acceptability: Automatic logging infrastructure to satisfy a regulation is a common, norm-compliant strategy with no offense to sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers for one quarter reusing the existing Kafka bus is a modest, reasonably feasible effort, though a framework refactor involves some real changes.

evidence_effectiveness: Framework-level logging would largely satisfy the logging requirement, but it does not itself cover retention, interpretation of risk-relevant events, or post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Templated event-schema specs mapped to Article 12 are a sensible, somewhat interesting approach but fairly expected from a diligent engineering team, showing little surprise.

evidence_effectiveness: It would help define what to log and tie events to Article 12(2)(a)-(c), but it addresses only the design-specification part of the mandate and not retention, runtime logging, or monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Adding compliance cost criteria to project prioritization is a sensible but fairly common governance move, showing little surprise.

evidence_implementability: It requires only a template and a committee criterion within an existing process, though estimating Article 12 effort accurately takes some work.
evidence_applicability: The idea addresses how the lab adapts its R&D to the logging mandate by costing Article 12 burden at intake, an implied problem (resource planning) related to the stated problem rather than meeting logging itself.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by design with a stage gate is a mundane, expected response to this mandate.

evidence_originality: Named documentation owners and periodic reviews are a common, mundane response to this kind of mandate.

evidence_originality: Immutable, time-partitioned append-only log stores are a standard engineering pattern and are what most labs would propose, so this is mundane though sensible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging infrastructure and leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Append-only logging with a retention policy is a common strategy that violates no norms, though data-protection concerns about retention are not addressed.
evidence_implementability: It is a scoped PoC on an existing deployment using off-the-shelf columnar and immutable storage technology, so it is feasible at low-to-moderate cost with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, the technical need to record events over the system's lifetime under Article 12(1).
evidence_effectiveness: A durable append-only log store that persists across retraining and versions would meet the Article 12(1) lifetime logging requirement, but it covers only storage persistence and not event selection, Article 12(2) relevance, or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as a co-design constraint studied through ablations is unusual and interesting with some imagination, but not strikingly surprising.

evidence_originality: A compliance dashboard that audits logs against regulatory obligations is a common, expected response with little that is surprising.

evidence_originality: A blocking compliance gate with a paragraph-mapped checklist and sign-off is a common, expected governance response to a logging mandate.
