evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing benchmarks and publishing papers offends no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated research group and long-horizon simulation infrastructure, which is a significant resource commitment but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the long-term quality of logging and post-market monitoring evidence, which relates to the mandate but does not directly implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not make the lab's own systems compliant and only contributes indirectly through evidence and reputation, so it is at best a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Unifying regulatory documentation with reproducibility records is a sensible but fairly expected idea, not ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (schemas, steward role) but still treats compliance as documentation and record-keeping practice, though it merges scientific and regulatory records slightly.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing version control and a documentation repository with rotating stewards is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing infrastructure with metadata schemas and a part-time rotating role, so only modest, non-radical changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It targets the documentation and record-keeping part of the mandate, which is related to but only implied by the logging requirement for events, so the problem it solves is an implied one.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses technical documentation and traceability from Recital 71 but does not provide the automatic event logging that Article 12 actually mandates, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Wrapping inference calls with logging middleware is a fairly common engineering pattern, though tailoring it to biometric-specific fields and researcher ergonomics is somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (middleware SDK) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely automating it for researchers.
evidence_acceptability: Automated internal logging infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: An internal library with context managers and async batching to an event store is a reasonably feasible, moderate-effort engineering task using standard techniques.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly records the Article 12(3)(b)-(d) fields (reference database, matched inputs, verifier identities), which is an identified part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, automatic stamping of the required fields would largely satisfy the biometric logging requirements, though it omits start/end timestamps in 12(3)(a) and the general Article 12(2) event logging, so it is strong but not complete.

evidence_originality: Adding CI gates that validate log schemas is a sensible but fairly expected DevOps-style response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/process (CI schema-validation gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI testing gates are a common engineering practice that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing CI runner and schema fixtures, requiring modest effort though fixtures per system class must be written and maintained.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the logging mandate by ensuring required event emissions exist and are well-formed during development.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch missing or malformed event emissions but does not decide which events are relevant, ensure retention, or cover runtime behavior, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing logging requirements up front as a gate is a sensible but fairly expected 'compliance by design' response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (design brief gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves R&D largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A design session, one-page template and compliance peer review are ordinary, uncontroversial governance practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A half-day session and a one-page template are cheap and need only modest process changes, though it adds a mandatory gate to every prototype.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping events to Article 12(2) criteria within R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure log design fits risk profile and is documented, but it covers only planning, not implementation, actual logging capability, or verification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Dedicating a resource carve-out to compliance work is a common, mundane management response with little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a staffing and budgeting item within standard practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Ring-fencing staff time with managerial sign-off mirrors existing practice such as safety-review hours and violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Ring-fencing a fixed share of headcount in next quarter's resource plan is an administrative budgeting change that needs no new technology, so it is easy and low-cost, though it does reallocate scarce senior capacity.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of resourcing logging work so the lab can meet the mandate, which relates to the stated problem only indirectly because it specifies no logging content.
evidence_effectiveness: It secures capacity and predictability but does not itself design or deliver the logging capabilities Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Quantifying proportionality and shaping regulatory interpretation is an unusual and interesting angle that shows some imagination, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a quantitative model, regulatory engagement) and a new institutional positioning, but still treats compliance as a logging-proportionality question rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Submitting to a consultation and publishing a preprint are legitimate, norm-compliant activities, though they are somewhat unusual for an R&D lab responding to a logging requirement.
evidence_implementability: Two sprints with a small team using public incident data is reasonably feasible, though the Article 71 database is limited and a defensible quantitative formula is difficult to build.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely how to interpret 'appropriate to the intended purpose' in Art. 12(2), which relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate but is not directly about implementing logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A proportionality formula and position paper might sharpen the lab's internal risk methodology, but it does not itself make any system log events, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the logging mandate, and it depends on the Commission adopting it.

evidence_originality: Assigning documentation owners and periodic audits tied to model version changes is a sensible but fairly expected governance response, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance governance workflow that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged and still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional compliance strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities and regulators would welcome it.
evidence_implementability: Assigning owners, update triggers and quarterly audits uses existing organizational processes at modest cost, with no radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of keeping records and documentation audit-ready, which relates to the logging mandate but does not directly specify how to meet the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps keep documentation and log review current but does not itself deliver the technical automatic logging capability Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by design rather than bolting it on is a widely expected, mundane response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with a design-phase tweak and no change to how the lab relates R&D to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Designing compliance-by-design logging is a common, legally aligned strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Defining a standard logging interface in design specs and using tamper-evident storage requires some process and architectural changes but is reasonably feasible with existing engineering practice.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: Native logging with defined event triggers and tamper-evident storage would largely satisfy Article 12's logging mandate, though it does not cover the documentation or the specific Annex III requirements in detail.

evidence_originality: Mapping existing systems to regulatory requirements is a common, mundane first step that an experienced evaluator would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A gap analysis of existing tooling against Article 12 is standard compliance practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A gap analysis is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week inventory by one senior engineer per project is low cost and non-radical, so it is easy to implement.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of deciding how to meet the logging mandate by determining what to build versus reuse.
evidence_effectiveness: The mapping only identifies gaps and avoids redundant builds; it does not itself deliver the logging capability, so it contributes to but only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Designing architectures where traceability is inherently built in and benchmarking logging overhead against accuracy is an interesting, somewhat imaginative framing, though 'privacy/explainability by design' research is not unheard of among lab responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making traceability a research variable that shapes what the lab researches, i.e., logging woven into the science, bordering on changing what the lab studies.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme on traceable architectures offends no legal or social norms and is a somewhat uncommon but sensible strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two senior researchers for eighteen months prototyping three architectures is a moderate, feasible commitment, though uncertain results and the no-accuracy-loss goal make it somewhat difficult.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of making systems technically able to log events by researching loggable architectures, which relates to the stated mandate but does not directly deliver Article 12 logs now.
evidence_effectiveness: Research prototypes over eighteen months would contribute to future logging capability but would not by themselves satisfy the logging mandate for current high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the model architecture and objective function as a jointly optimised 'log fidelity' term is an unusual and imaginative response, though the research-programme framing is somewhat expected for an R&D lab.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science itself (architecture and training objective) and generating community benchmarks, which is paradigm stretching rather than a change to what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Research into interpretable architectures and publishing benchmarks violates no legal, social or political norms and is somewhat unusual only as a compliance route.
evidence_implementability: Designing new architectures with joint optimisation of accuracy and log fidelity is a significant, expensive and uncertain research effort that is not a committed implementation, and the prompt says approval means committing scarce implementation resources rather than exploring whether an idea might work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly, with an explicit 'do X to get Y' link.
evidence_effectiveness: Article 12 only requires systems to technically allow automatic event recording, which ordinary logging already satisfies, and a research programme with uncertain outcomes would at best partially contribute to meeting the mandate (especially for existing systems and Annex III minimum fields).

evidence_originality: A centralized shared logging platform is a standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: A small three-person team within existing budget and a two-person-day SDK integration are feasible, though building a shared service still requires some real engineering change.
evidence_applicability: A centralized logging service directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate across the lab's high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Centralized ingestion, storage, and query would provide the automatic event recording and retention needed, but it does not by itself address which events are relevant (Art. 12(2)) or Annex III-specific fields, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Making traceability costs a mandatory budget line is a sensible, somewhat uncommon administrative angle, but it is a fairly predictable, mundane governance step rather than an ingenious one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (budget line item and template) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Itemizing compliance costs in budgets is a common, norm-respecting practice that offends no sensibilities, though sponsors may push back mildly.
evidence_implementability: A one-page template update to existing grant and project-charter processes is cheap and non-radical to implement.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the resourcing of logging and documentation, which relates to meeting the logging mandate but is not the technical logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It funds and makes visible logging costs but does not itself make systems log events or meet Article 12's technical requirements, so it only partially contributes to the solution.

evidence_originality: A centralised shared log-retention service on existing HPC storage is a common, mundane infrastructure consolidation that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as standard logging and storage practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised log retention is a common strategy that violates no norms, though access controls and data protection for logs are not discussed.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing Lustre storage and adding a lightweight query API is low-cost and non-radical to implement.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses Article 12's lifetime retention and post-market monitoring/audit access, which are parts of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with storage, retention and querying but does not address what events are captured, per-system logging capability, or Annex III minimum content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance tests in CI are a sensible but fairly expected approach that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool in the pipeline but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: CI/CD conformance testing is a common engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Pytest fixtures with mock endpoints and synthetic inputs are inexpensive and fit existing pipelines, requiring only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically verifying that log output contains the required fields and format.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify log conformance but does not itself design the logging, cover paragraph 2 event relevance or retention, or ensure the logs are useful for traceability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A traceability benchmark with a leaderboard is an unusual and interesting idea showing some imagination, though benchmarks are a familiar ML format.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (public benchmark and leaderboard) and shifts compliance toward shared research output and standards, modestly changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though still centered on logging.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks and leaderboards are a normal, uncontroversial practice in the AI community and offend no norms, though applying them to logging compliance is somewhat uncommon.
evidence_implementability: Curating 200 ground-truthed scenario pairs with a small cross-disciplinary team and annual publishing is reasonably feasible, though it needs some dedicated effort and expertise.
evidence_applicability: The benchmark directly targets the Article 12(2) logging requirements, but it mainly solves an implied problem (shared definition of appropriate traceability) rather than the lab's own decision on how to meet the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark would help the lab and field validate logging schemas but does not itself implement the lab's logging nor guarantee compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A gap-analysis and instrumentation sprint is the common, expected response to a logging mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It retrofits existing pipelines with log emitters, which is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logs within current budgets is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing clusters and tools, needs no new hardware, and fits in a six-week sprint at modest cost, so it is easy to implement.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping and filling logging gaps.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially advance logging compliance, but it is sketchy on retention, high-risk scoping, Annex III specifics, and ongoing R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Infrastructure-layer logging on repurposed telemetry is a sensible but fairly expected, mundane response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice with existing tooling and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure for compliance logging with encrypted append-only storage is a common, uncontroversial business and legal approach.
evidence_implementability: It reuses already-funded infrastructure and existing agents and storage, needing only schema templates and lightweight agents, so changes are modest and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the paragraph one logging mandate and the four Annex III 1(a) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide automatic event recording and the Annex III 1(a) fields, but it does not address Article 12(2) relevance of events, retention, or traceability design, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using the compliance obligation as a research topic on minimal-sufficient logging is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (selective-recording/compression research) and turns compliance cost into a publication and IP asset, but it still treats compliance fundamentally as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Research on efficient logging and publishing results is a somewhat uncommon framing but offends no norms, though selective recording could raise some regulator concerns about sufficiency.
evidence_implementability: One postdoc and one engineer on a six-month internal grant using an existing testbed is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets meeting Article 12 minimum logging requirements while reducing storage and privacy overhead, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It is an exploratory research thread that might reduce overhead but does not itself deliver the logging capability or guarantee compliance, so it only partially contributes to a solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized document and log archive with retention and access controls is the mundane, expected response to record-keeping mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as logging and documentation practice with no change to how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance records unit with tamper-evident log and document storage is a standard, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires provisioning a platform and staffing two people, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes rather than trivial or radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate and the documentation-retention requirement in Recital 71, which are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Archiving logs and documentation helps with retention and traceability but does not itself ensure that systems technically log the right events, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library integrated into existing pipelines is the most common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice layered on existing infrastructure, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging tooling is a conventional strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team over one quarter with incremental adoption on existing tracking infrastructure is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically capturing the event types required by Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a shared middleware capturing Art. 12(2) events would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though 'optional' adoption and the unspecified event definitions leave gaps, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Ring-fencing a budget line for lifetime compliance costs is a somewhat unusual financial angle but is a familiar budgeting practice, so it is interesting rather than ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new financial process but still treats compliance as a logging/maintenance practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Reserving budget for compliance is a sensible, common financial governance strategy that violates no norms, though taking a fixed percentage of grant money may face funder restrictions.
evidence_implementability: It requires finance-office process changes and a pooled-fund mechanism, which are reasonably feasible with modest organizational change, though grant rules may complicate it.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of funding the long-tail logging and documentation obligations, which relates to meeting the logging mandate but is not the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Funding helps sustain log storage and monitoring over the system lifetime but does not itself provide technical logging capability or ensure compliance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Conformance testing of log schemas in CI is a fairly expected, mundane response from labs, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool into the dev loop but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI testing of logging schema is a standard engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Writing parameterised pytest cases and adding them to an existing CI pipeline is a modest, low-cost change, though synthetic session replay and middleware hooks require some setup.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that Article 12(3) fields are present and correct.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies field presence and consistency but does not itself create logging, cover Article 12(2) event relevance, or non-Annex III 1(a) systems, so it is only a partial solution to the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the computational graph with a design-time audit gate is a sensible but fairly expected 'privacy/compliance by design' response, with some imagination but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Making traceability an architectural invariant woven into model design and prototyping changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal code-review gates and built-in logging violate no legal or social norms and are a common governance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Embedding event-emitters in inference pipelines and adding a review gate requires some engineering and process changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: Native logging would support Article 12(1)-(2) automatic event recording, but the proposal only addresses Article 12(3) on paper, which is mainly relevant to Annex III 1(a) systems, and does not cover retention or post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A competition that optimises for log richness and third-party reconstruction is unusual and shows imagination, though design competitions and auditability research are known concepts.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It makes logging an explicit design objective of the research itself, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, but it does not change what the lab researches at large, so it is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: An internal design competition offends no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Running three teams for six months to build a novel system is a significant resource commitment, and reconstructing reasoning without model weights is technically difficult, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely developing auditable logging architectures, which relates to the mandate but does not directly yield compliant logs for existing systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A single competition producing prototype architectures contributes to logging capability but does not itself ensure that the lab's production high-risk systems meet Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A middleware interceptor writing to an immutable store on an existing Kafka bus is the standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging infrastructure and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Logging inside the existing stack with immutable storage violates no legal or social norms and is a common compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two FTEs for a quarter reusing existing infrastructure is modest, though testing on three live systems in parallel with production adds some risk and effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by building a logging mechanism that records the Article 12(3) items (timestamp, input reference, match, verifier identity).
evidence_effectiveness: If built, an immutable middleware log would substantially meet the logging mandate, but it addresses only Annex III 1(a)-style fields and does little for Art 12(2) risk-event identification, post-market monitoring or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Cross-functional compliance liaison groups are a common organizational response, with little that is surprising or imaginative here.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Embedding compliance decisions within R&D teams' sprint planning changes the relationship between R&D and compliance somewhat, but it is mainly an organizational process for handling logging obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A cross-team working group funded by internal reallocation is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Fifteen percent of FTE from several people and a biweekly meeting is a modest, non-radical change funded within existing budget, though it does take some capacity from project work.
evidence_applicability: The pod directly maps logging obligations to R&D systems and sequences the work, which is part of the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It is a process and coordination mechanism that helps teams plan and embed logging, but it does not itself define or build the logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Version-controlled documentation repositories with owners are a common, expected response, with only the log-to-documentation cross-check being mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard documentation-management and compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, apart from adding automated consistency checks.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional compliance strategy that violates no norms and is readily acceptable to regulators and staff.
evidence_implementability: A repository, assigned owners and automated consistency checks are reasonably feasible with some process changes and moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses keeping technical documentation current and consistent with logs, which is part of the record-keeping compliance problem, though it centers on documentation (Recital 71) more than the Article 12 logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A living registry with cross-checks would help demonstrate compliance and traceability but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Prototyping the logging clauses to de-risk them is a sensible but fairly expected response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a logging engineering practice with a standard prototype process, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A time-boxed internal prototype to implement the legally required logging fields is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy.
evidence_implementability: A two-week spike by one engineer pair using an open-source model and the existing event bus is low-cost and a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly builds the Article 12(3)(a)-(d) logging capabilities, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A spike on a simplified pipeline only de-risks and informs architecture decisions rather than delivering full compliance, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: A standing post-market monitoring team reviewing logs is a common, expected response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a team and process but still treats compliance as a logging/monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A dedicated compliance monitoring team is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-person team running weekly anomaly-detection scripts on existing logs is a modest, affordable addition requiring some new staffing but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to use logs for Article 72 monitoring and Article 79(1) risk identification, though it presumes logging exists rather than building it.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with post-market monitoring and risk-signal detection but does not itself ensure the system's logging capability or the Article 12(3) minimum content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using statistical process control on logged drift to flag Article 79 substantial modification is an unusual and interesting angle beyond the typical expected logging-compliance responses, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning logging into a research track and a commercial offering, which is paradigm stretching rather than fully breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Research into drift detection and compliance dashboards offends no norms and is a somewhat uncommon but acceptable business strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires a new research track, model development on historical logs, and dashboard integration, which is a significant but feasible effort, and the legal definition of substantial modification is hard to operationalize statistically.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (identifying situations of substantial modification per Article 12(2)(a)) using logs, which applies to the stated problem via the logging purpose.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help detect substantial modification and support monitoring, but it does not by itself fulfill the core mandate of enabling automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation synced to commits is a well-known practice that labs would commonly propose, so it is mundane and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces an auto-sync documentation process, but it still treats compliance as a standard documentation and record-keeping practice, so the compliance relationship is unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Keeping technical documentation current and synced with experiment tracking is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a repository, an integration with the existing experiment-tracking tool, and one postdoc per project, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes rather than a trivial or radical one.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of documentation and record readiness for regulators, which is directly related to the record-keeping mandate, though it targets documentation more than logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would handle the technical documentation duty of Recital 71 well, but it does not address the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable library implementing the mandated minimum fields is the obvious, expected response to Article 12(3) and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice built as a component, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building mandated logging and validating against a mock audit is a common, norm-conforming compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: A two-quarter sprint with the platform team to build a reusable library is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some resources and changes but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the explicitly identified requirement of Article 12(3) minimum logging fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A module capturing the four Article 12(3) minimum fields would, if built, satisfy the specific logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it does not address general Article 12(1)-(2) logging for other high-risk systems or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory logs as a longitudinal research dataset is unusual and shows imagination, but the idea of reusing compliance data is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science, turning logs into research data, which is paradigm stretching but does not redefine what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Annotating logs and reusing them for research is a somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no norms, though reuse of logged data raises mild privacy and purpose-limitation questions.
evidence_implementability: Adding schema annotations and tags to log entries requires some engineering changes and cross-team partnership but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of extracting value from the logging mandate, which relates to how the lab adapts its R&D, but does not directly address how to meet the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab adapt R&D to the mandate and structured logs may aid compliance, but it is only a partial solution since it does not ensure Article 12 requirements are met and raises data-use issues.

evidence_originality: A stage-gate requiring logging architecture approval before development is a sensible but fairly expected compliance-by-design process step, with only mild interest from the framing around protecting research time.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a gate and template) but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing project charter workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Stage gates and design reviews are common governance strategies that offend no norms, though blocking development may cause mild friction.
evidence_implementability: It adds a one-page template to an existing charter process with a rotating review pair and a two-week window, which is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by preventing late retrofitting of automatic event recording for new high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It ensures logging is designed in early, which helps meet the mandate, but it does not specify what to log, ensure Article 12 content requirements are met, or cover existing systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default starter templates are a sensible, fairly common DevOps idea with little surprising about it, though tying fields to regulatory obligations adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling format (templates) but still treats compliance as logging practice added to the existing workflow, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance into project templates is a common, norm-compliant engineering practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring internal starter templates with a logging SDK, schema file, and checklist is a modest, non-radical change using existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate including the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably get logging hooks into new projects but does not cover existing systems, log quality, retention in operation, or other Article 12 aspects, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying schema contract testing and CI to logging is a sensible engineering idea that shows some imagination, but it is a familiar software practice carried over to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new tooling (versioned contracts, property-based fuzzing in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing CI and test frameworks and needs only modest engineering effort, with no radical change to how the lab works.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 requirement that logs be recorded and remain usable over the system's lifetime by preventing schema drift, which is an identified part of the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would guarantee schema compatibility across lifecycle changes but does not decide which events to log for risk, post-market monitoring, or operation oversight, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a reusable logging middleware wired into the standard development template is the obvious, expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice (logging by design) and leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging by design is a common strategy that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: A reusable middleware module integrated into an existing development template is a reasonably feasible engineering effort with moderate, one-time cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the required automatic event recording into the systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic lifetime event logging directly satisfies Article 12(1) and covers much of 12(2), but it does not specify the Annex III 3 minimum fields or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-differentiator through customer audit portals is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea but not highly surprising, as transparency dashboards are a known pattern.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the business by turning logging into a customer-facing offering and market differentiator, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Giving customers read-only access to their own system logs is a plausible, uncontroversial practice, though it is somewhat unusual and raises minor data-exposure concerns.
evidence_implementability: A thin REST API, dashboard, and per-customer scoping on top of an existing structured log store is reasonably feasible, though multi-tenant access control and contract scoping require some changes.
evidence_applicability: It builds on the Article 12 log contents (timestamps, matched inputs, verifier IDs) to address an implied problem of turning compliance into value, which relates to but is not the core mandate to log.
evidence_effectiveness: The client-facing API depends on a separate logging SDK to meet Article 12, so it adds transparency and customer value but does not itself satisfy the logging mandate, making it only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checks in CI/CD pipelines are a common and expected response, so the idea is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a CI/CD gate and automated log-simulation test, which are new tools and processes, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal engineering gates are a standard practice that offends no norms, though blocking merges may meet some developer friction.
evidence_implementability: Adding a checklist and automated tests to an existing CI/CD workflow is a modest, low-cost change that engineering teams routinely make.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by enforcing the specific Article 12(3) fields in development.
evidence_effectiveness: It would ensure Article 12(3) fields are built into prototypes, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and not the wider Article 12(1)-(2) logging needs or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Costing compliance into grant budgets is a reasonable but fairly mundane idea that shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (cost model) but still treats compliance as a logging practice to be budgeted, not changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A internal cost model attached to grant proposals is a sensible, transparent budgeting practice that offends no norms, though somewhat less common than standard compliance measures.
evidence_implementability: A finance analyst can build the model with existing benchmarks and pilot log-volume data and add it as a proposal attachment, requiring only modest process change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of funding the lifetime logging obligations, which relates to the stated problem but does not itself meet the logging mandate or adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab plan and afford Article 12 compliance but does not implement logging, so it is only a partial contribution to the problem.

evidence_originality: A shared OpenTelemetry-based logging service is a common, sensible engineering response that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tooling component but treats compliance purely as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging middleware is a standard strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Using existing OpenTelemetry components with two engineers over six weeks and a latency validation on two projects is a low-cost, non-radical build.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly targets the stated problem by capturing Article 12(2) event categories and Annex III 1(a) fields, so it is do X to get Y where Y is the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a shared logging layer would satisfy the technical logging mandate across projects, though it does not address documentation, retention, or human-verification identity capture, so it solves most but not the entire compliance problem.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library or SDK with defaults is a common and expected response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but still treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding default logging in internal tooling is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin internal middleware library imported through the existing scaffolding template is a modest engineering task needing some changes but no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(1) mandate for automatic event recording, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic logging in every prototype but does not by itself ensure that the logged events meet the Article 12(2) relevance requirements, Annex III minimums, or retention obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Requiring compliance budget lines in project proposals is a common, sensible project-management step with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A new template field and review criterion are a process element, yet compliance is still treated as a standard practice of resourcing logging.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a budget line and review criterion is a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though withholding funding may draw mild pushback.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a template change and reviewer guidance, though estimating costs by Annex III tier takes some expertise, making it reasonably feasible with modest change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (under-resourced logging implementation) that relates to meeting the logging mandate, rather than the logging requirements directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting for logging up front helps fund and plan compliance but does not itself design or deliver Article 12 logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated model cards are a known practice, so applying them to AI Act documentation is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI/CD doc generation) but still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation in CI is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing build pipeline and repository metadata, so it needs some tooling work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It clearly targets the documentation and keep-up-to-date requirements of Recital 71, which are related to but only implied by the logging mandate in the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the up-to-date technical documentation obligation but not Article 12's automatic event logging in the system itself, so it is only a partial solution, and the claim of guaranteeing compliance by construction is overstated.

evidence_originality: Automated log-compliance validators are a fairly expected, mundane response to a logging mandate, with little imaginative twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal self-auditing for regulatory compliance is a common strategy that offends no norms, though the survival framing is slightly off but not objectionable.
evidence_implementability: A validator running scheduled automated checks on existing logs within an existing monitoring pipeline is reasonably feasible with modest changes.
evidence_applicability: The tool directly checks that logs capture the four Article 12(3) minimum data points, which is an identified part of the stated logging-mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would detect logging gaps in Annex III biometric systems, but it only validates and does not build logging, cover other high-risk systems or Article 12(1)-(2) scope, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gating funding on compliance design is a sensible, somewhat familiar governance step (mirroring ethical review), showing modest imagination but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Adding a logging-architecture section to project intake changes when compliance enters R&D planning, but it is a checklist gate that still treats compliance as logging practice and does not alter the research itself.
evidence_acceptability: Intake gates mirroring existing ethical-review practice are common and offend no norms, though PIs may grumble about added paperwork.
evidence_implementability: Updating a grant-review checklist and returning incomplete proposals is a small, low-cost process change that can be done within a month.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how the lab adapts its R&D to the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring each project plans for the required events, storage and retention.
evidence_effectiveness: A one-page plan at intake helps ensure design-time logging but does not itself implement logging, verify adequacy, or cover existing systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left/design-time compliance is a well-known pattern that experienced evaluators would expect, so it is mundane to somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (architecture templates, ADR, design-review gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging into architecture templates and design reviews is a common, norm-compliant engineering governance practice.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint refactoring five architectures plus an ADR is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some process changes but no radical investment.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by designing the required event recording into new systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure Article 12(2) event categories are designed in, but it is only a partial solution since it omits Annex III 3 specifics, runtime verification, and ongoing retention and monitoring.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging middleware by design is a common, expected response to the logging mandate with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a modular middleware tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely built in rather than bolted on, so it only slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-by-design logging is a standard strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building middleware and retrofitting all in-flight projects requires significant engineering effort across the lab but is feasible with some changes and existing techniques.
evidence_applicability: It explicitly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging requirements and the specific minimum log fields.
evidence_effectiveness: Building tamper-evident logging middleware into all high-risk systems would directly deliver the Article 12 logging mandate including the Annex III 1(a) minimums, so it would solve the main problem if done.

evidence_originality: Reusing research documentation for regulatory purposes is a sensible and fairly common idea, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared template and merges science documentation with compliance, which modestly changes how the lab relates R&D to compliance, though it still treats compliance as a documentation practice.
evidence_acceptability: Consolidating documentation violates no norms, though auditors might question whether documents alone satisfy the logging mandate.
evidence_implementability: Restructuring existing documentation with a template and a quarterly refresh owned by the project lead is low-cost and requires only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the stated problem of meeting record-keeping obligations, but it targets technical documentation (Recital 71) and an implied need, not the automatic event logging that Article 12 requires.
evidence_effectiveness: A quarterly-refreshed document does not provide automatic event logs over the system's lifetime, so it helps with the documentation side only and is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a compliance-derived schema is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but standards-building and open-source tooling are familiar moves and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a public standard) and reframes compliance as a community-contribution offering born from compliance, which changes the relationship between R&D and obligations without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release under Apache 2.0 and community standards work violate no legal or social norms, though sharing training and validation records as seed data may raise some mild confidentiality concerns.
evidence_implementability: A small working group drafting a schema over two sprints and publishing a repository is reasonably feasible and low cost, though building community adoption and a reference implementation requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (having a common structure for logged/provenance data) that relates to the logging mandate, rather than directly specifying how the lab will meet Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: A public provenance schema seeded with the lab's own records would help standardize logging, but it does not itself implement automatic event logging in the lab's high-risk systems, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A stage-gate requiring a logging plan before funding is a sensible, somewhat expected 'compliance by design' response, with modest interest from tying it to grant review but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (intake gate and traceability spec) and shifts compliance upstream into project selection, but it still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal gating and checklist requirements are common governance practices that violate no norms, though researchers may grumble about added friction.
evidence_implementability: Amending an existing grant-review checklist and adding a one-page spec reviewed by engineering leads and the Compliance Officer is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by requiring Article 12(2) event categories to be planned from the outset of each project.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is designed in and avoids retrofits, but it covers only planning at intake and does not itself implement logging, verify it, or address the Article 12(3) requirements or existing systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Phased budget allocation and checklist gating are common, mundane project-management responses to a regulation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard project/budget management task and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Phased budgeting with risk-tier sequencing and release-gate checklists is a conventional, norm-respecting business and compliance approach.
evidence_implementability: Ring-fencing about 15% of engineering budget and adding checklist gates are non-radical, low-cost organizational changes, though retrofitting logging itself still requires effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of resourcing and scheduling Article 12 compliance without shocking R&D, which relates to but is not the direct logging design question.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps sequence and fund compliance but does not itself specify what logging to build, so it only partially solves the problem of meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Keeping documentation current through CI/CD triggers and assigned compliance engineers is a common, expected response to the documentation requirements, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a versioned documentation repository tied to CI/CD with update tickets, but it treats compliance as a standard documentation practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation maintenance with dedicated compliance staff and SLAs is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Linking documentation tickets to existing CI/CD and assigning compliance engineers requires some process changes and added staffing, but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets the technical documentation described in Recital 71, which is related to but not the same as the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it addresses an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A current technical file would help with traceability and post-market monitoring, but it does not deliver the automatic event logs Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance-by-design schema gate is a sensible, fairly common shift-left practice, with only mild interest in the YAML gate-zero framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new template and sprint gate but still treats compliance as a logging practice within the existing R&D workflow, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: A lightweight sign-off gate with a compliance liaison is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A YAML template and a sprint-planning gate require roughly two hours of design work per project and only minor process changes, so it is easy and cheap.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping events to Article 12(2) categories and Annex III 1(a) fields before build.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema gate ensures required events are instrumented, but it covers only design-time planning and not actual logging implementation, retention, or verification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mapping Article 12(3) fields to an append-only audit record is the obvious, expected response to the mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged, merely packaged as a module.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing mandated logging with tamper-evident storage is a conventional, legally aligned strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A logging module that serializes four defined fields to an append-only store is a bounded engineering task using standard components, requiring some changes but no radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing exactly the fields Article 12(3) requires for Annex III point 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging requirements but covers only that system category and does not address the general Article 12(1)-(2) event logging or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building an internal logging/observability toolkit for compliance is a fairly expected response, though packaging it as a publishable open-source asset for procurement adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a toolkit, dashboards, a methods paper) and a product angle, but still essentially treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the R&D–compliance relationship much.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source tooling, publication, and internal infrastructure violate no legal or social norms and are common strategies.
evidence_implementability: Two postdocs over a year atop an existing data lake is a reasonably feasible scope with some changes and no new headcount, though a year of effort is not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, with dashboards tied explicitly to the article's use cases.
evidence_effectiveness: A logging toolkit covering Article 12(2)(a)–(c) would substantially help meet the logging mandate, but it does not address all aspects (e.g., Annex III biometric minimums, retention, system-level integration), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a research corpus for a deployment-grounded failure-mode taxonomy is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logs into the science and turning a compliance obligation into a research dataset, which is paradigm stretching rather than changing what the lab researches fundamentally.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymised logs for research and publishing a taxonomy is an uncommon but non-offensive strategy, though data protection and confidentiality concerns add mild sensitivity.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an annotation pipeline, clustering methods, privacy anonymisation and publication processes, which are reasonably feasible but need some added resources and changes.

evidence_acceptability: Static analysis in CI is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an AST walker with taint tracking that reliably detects event emission across diverse prototype codebases requires meaningful engineering effort, though it is feasible with CI integration.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required event classes are emitted, mapped to each sub-clause.
evidence_effectiveness: A static linter can catch missing log points but cannot verify runtime behavior, log adequacy, or the full traceability purpose, so it contributes only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated documentation from experiment trackers is a fairly familiar approach, though tying it to Recital 71 is sensible and mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and a continuous process but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice, so it only slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: CI-based documentation automation with quarterly compliance review is a common, norm-respecting engineering practice.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing tools (MLflow, git CI, Jinja2) and a small maintenance role, so it requires some changes but is reasonably feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (keeping technical documentation current per Recital 71) rather than the explicitly stated logging mandate of Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Auto-generated living technical documentation would meet the Recital 71 documentation upkeep need, but it does not implement Article 12's event logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution to the logging problem.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a customer-facing dashboard is a fairly recognizable move that is interesting and somewhat imaginative but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as a product offering and client co-design, changing the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings (compliance-born new offerings), but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Exposing logs to deployers to support their Article 72 and 26(5) duties is a legitimate, norm-compliant strategy, though somewhat unusual in being packaged as a client feature (with a minor privacy/confidentiality consideration for exposing logs).
evidence_implementability: It builds on an existing logging layer with an API and lightweight front-end and a six-week pilot with two customers, which is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of responding to the logging mandate by using Article 12 logs for post-market monitoring and deployer obligations, though much of its benefit (market differentiation) is implied rather than the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard of logs helps downstream deployers and adds evidence, but it does not itself ensure the lab's logging meets Article 12 requirements (it presupposes the logging layer exists), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log analytics dashboards feeding post-market monitoring reports are a common, expected response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (dashboards, alerting, quarterly reports) but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance analytics team with dashboards and regulator-inspectable reports is a common, legitimate strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a permanent dedicated analyst team, real-time dashboards, and alerting rules, which is a significant but feasible investment short of radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (using logs for Article 12(2)(a)-(c) purposes and Article 72 monitoring) that relates to the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate, rather than the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Analytics on logs would help detect risks and support post-market monitoring, but it presumes the logging capability exists and does not itself meet the Article 12 logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Unifying research reproducibility records with compliance logging in one ledger is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but experiment tracking plus audit logs is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves compliance logging into the research workflow and repositions the lab as a reference implementation, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance beyond standard logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: A tamper-evident shared log store for compliance and reproducibility violates no legal or social norms and is a sensible, fairly common governance approach.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a platform service with CI/CD hooks across pipelines and engineering collaboration, which is reasonably feasible but involves real changes and cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event logging over training and evaluation would satisfy Article 12(1) for pipelines, but it does not explicitly address Article 12(2) event relevance or 12(3) specifics, and covers training logs rather than deployed-system operation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance checking is an interesting application of formal methods to logging requirements, though it is a recognizable compliance-as-code idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (formal specs, a CI gate, model-checking-style assertions) but still treats compliance as a logging-coverage practice rather than changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI pipelines are an uncommon but inoffensive strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a CI/CD gate with a small domain language and schema assertions requires some new tooling and effort, but it is reasonably feasible with existing engineering practices.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the logging mandate by verifying that logging covers the Article 12(2) event categories in prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch coverage gaps early but covers only schema-level checks of Article 12(2) and does not implement logging itself or address Article 12(3) or runtime behavior, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance testing in CI is a fairly common and expected idea, with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifting verification earlier in development.
evidence_acceptability: A CI/CD compliance test gate is a common engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Contract-test suites with synthetic traffic replay are reasonably feasible with existing CI tooling, though defining the required event schemas takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring logs meet Article 12(2) and 12(3) requirements, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably verify log completeness for Article 12 in prototypes, helping meet the logging mandate but not covering production logging, retention, or the broader obligations, so only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gating projects on a design-stage logging specification is a sensible but expected compliance-by-design approach, not a surprising or imaginative one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (intake gate and brief) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: A required logging brief at project intake is a common, norm-compliant governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It adds a one-page artifact and gate to an existing workflow with a part-time rotating reviewer, so it needs only modest, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated need to meet the logging mandate by building logging requirements into project start, solving an identified problem of late retrofitting.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging is designed early, but it only specifies logging and does not itself implement the technical automatic event recording or the Article 12(3) minimum content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance monitoring and doc generation is a fairly expected tooling response, with the LLM-assisted documentation sync adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (CI pipeline, LLM summarization) but still treats compliance as a logging and documentation practice, leaving R&D relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated log validation and documentation generation through CI is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy, though LLM-drafted regulatory documentation is slightly unusual but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight microservice on existing infrastructure with rule-based validators is feasible, but it needs some new development and LLM summarization quality control, so some changes are required.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting logging mandates and keeping documentation current under Recital 71 with a clear do-X-to-get-Y mechanism.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address Article 12(3) minimum checks and keep documentation current, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) and does not itself create logging capability or address Article 12(2) event relevance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared auto-instrumenting logging library using OpenTelemetry is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A logging SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged, fitting slightly paradigm stretching at most, and it is arguably standard practice.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised internal logging via a standard library violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building it in three weeks with standard lockfile and decorator adoption is low-cost and non-radical, though centralised storage and handling of varied prototypes adds a bit of work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate across the lab's prototypes while keeping R&D cycle times flat.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic logging of timestamps, reference database and matched inputs would meet the core logging mandate but does not cover Article 12(3)(d) human verifier identification, retention, or the risk-event relevance in 12(2), so it is a substantial partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance budgets in project funding is a sensible and somewhat uncommon angle, but it is a familiar 'shift-left' management idea rather than a surprising one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It moves compliance from an audit-time retrofit into the lab's funding and review cycle, changing the relationship between R&D management and compliance, though it adds no new technical elements.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting a compliance line item and reviewing it at quarterly checkpoints is a normal governance practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires modest changes to grant and milestone-review processes and coordination with the grants office, which is reasonably feasible but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: Funding logging and documentation from the start addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, though it works through budgeting and process rather than the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Guaranteed funding and checkpoint review help ensure logging gets built, but they do not specify what logs to capture or ensure technical adequacy, so this is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing an open-source reference implementation of compliance logging is a somewhat unusual and sensible idea, but open-sourcing compliance tooling is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning the compliance logging requirement into a published, citable research deliverable and standard-setting position changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release of compliance tooling violates no legal or social norms and is a common academic practice.
evidence_implementability: A three-month effort by two people using existing internal test data with no new infrastructure is a low-cost, modest change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate of Article 12(3) by building the specified log fields, though it applies only to the biometric systems covered by Annex III 1(a).
