evidence_effectiveness: A reference implementation only partially solves the lab's compliance problem since it covers only one category of high-risk systems and does not address the lab's own systems or general Article 12(1)-(2) logging.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design checklists with scaffold generation are a fairly common response, though auto-generated stubs add slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new template and scaffold tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moved earlier in the design process.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory design checklists and gated reviews are common engineering governance practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A design template, sign-off review, and stub-code generator are modest process and tooling changes that a lab can adopt at low-to-moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by ensuring logging and the Annex III 1(a) fields are designed in from the start.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is built in early but covers only design-stage process and not log content quality, retention, or operation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using compliance logs as a scientific instrument for drift research is unusual and shows some imagination, though the log-based monitoring idea is not entirely unexpected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning mandatory logs into a research programme with publications and a new research identity, which stretches the paradigm but does not wholly redefine what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open-access research and building internal benchmarks violates no legal or social norms, though open publication of findings is somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Creating a dedicated research thread, synthetic drift corpora and detector models requires significant staffing and effort but is feasible with reasonable changes.
evidence_applicability: The idea exploits Article 12 logs for drift detection, which relates to the post-market monitoring purpose of logging but does not directly address how to meet the logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not ensure the lab meets the logging requirements and mainly yields research output, so it contributes only partially to the problem.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance tooling is somewhat known, but pairing it with telemetry as a research dataset and reference-implementation positioning shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a public research contribution and turns telemetry into a reusable dataset, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance without altering what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building an open-source logging toolkit and releasing it under an open licence is a legitimate, norm-compatible approach, though publishing it externally is somewhat less common than purely internal compliance.
evidence_implementability: A two-person pod integrating a logging library into existing CI/CD within a quarter is reasonably feasible, although full documentation and open release add some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by implementing the Article 12 paragraph 3 elements in the lab's pipelines.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would meet the logging requirements for the covered systems, and the open release adds extra benefits, but it covers mainly the paragraph 3 biometric-type items and not wider R&D adaptation, so it is a strong yet not complete solution.

evidence_originality: A queryable log store with dashboards is a sensible and fairly expected response to the logging mandate, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (a queryable log store, API, dashboards) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: It is a standard, uncontroversial compliance infrastructure approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a partitioned append-only store, an SDK ingestion mapping, a REST API and three dashboards is a moderate engineering effort using well-understood technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses storing, retaining, and using automatic logs for Article 72 post-market monitoring and Article 12 traceability, which are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help make logs usable for monitoring and audits, but it does not itself define what events to log or cover all of Article 12 (e.g. Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging obligations as a research problem in provenance and interpretability is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations by turning compliance into publishable research and open-source outputs, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing research and open-sourcing tools violate no norms, though a slightly unusual framing for compliance work.
evidence_implementability: A small cross-functional team publishing papers and building open-source tools is reasonably feasible, though novel research on compression and causal insight carries some difficulty.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses Article 12 logging by building tools for compressing, querying and replaying logs, which relates to the mandate but is framed mainly as a research agenda, so it solves an implied rather than an identified compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on log compression and replay tools would help with log usability, but it does not itself ensure that systems automatically record the required events, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as research datasets on drift and degradation is an interesting, somewhat imaginative reframing, though dual-use of logging data is a fairly foreseeable response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science and turning compliance overhead into a research asset, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Using operational logs for internal research is a reasonable strategy, though data-protection limits on reusing logged input data are not addressed, making it slightly uncommon but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: It requires schema redesign and data-science collaboration plus extra storage and privacy handling, which is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly by designing log schemas.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing schemas that satisfy every regulatory minimum while adding research features would meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D, though the added research features are a bonus and Article 12 compliance details are only asserted.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as an empirical source for drift science is unusual and shows imagination, though it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research resource and a new research direction with deployer partners.
evidence_acceptability: Collaborative research with deployers on logs is a reasonably uncommon but non-offensive strategy, though data privacy and confidentiality of logs raise some sensitivities.
evidence_implementability: A three-year track requiring longitudinal log access from industry deployers and new statistical research is a significant, costly undertaking with data-sharing hurdles, but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making use of the mandated logs and detecting risk situations per Art. 12(2)(a)) that relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A drift-research track using logs would help the lab exploit logging data and anticipate Article 79 risk events, but it does not itself deliver the logging capability or satisfy the Article 12 mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as feedback for development is a fairly sensible and somewhat imaginative idea, but not surprising or especially ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance logging and R&D by feeding the logs back into the development loop, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for internal analytics with privacy-preserving aggregation is a somewhat uncommon but unobjectionable strategy that offends no norms, though secondary use of logs raises minor data-governance questions.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight ETL job on existing monitoring infrastructure and a dashboard in the existing experiment tracker requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to get value from mandated logs within R&D, which relates to adapting R&D to the logging mandate but not to the stated mandate-compliance core directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate (it assumes the logs already exist) and only adds a development-feedback benefit, so it contributes partially to the problem of how to adapt R&D.

evidence_originality: Turning log-based drift detection into an open benchmark is interesting and shows some imagination, but drift detection and open benchmarks are familiar research directions and not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making the compliance logs the object of research and a source of public scientific contributions, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open benchmarks with synthetic scenarios violates no legal or social norms and is a well-accepted research practice.
evidence_implementability: Building synthetic benchmarks and detection evaluations is a reasonably feasible research effort for an AI lab, though it requires dedicated staff and sustained work beyond routine compliance.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making mandated logs useful for Article 12(2) risk identification and monitoring) that relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate, rather than the direct need to meet the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on drift detection from logs would help interpret Article 12 logs for risk identification and post-market monitoring, but it does not itself implement the logging mandate or settle how the lab complies, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Assigning citable DOIs to compliance logs and framing them as open-science assets is unusual and shows some imagination, though it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logging into a reproducibility and publication asset and positions the lab as a reference implementation, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open sharing of logs that may contain personal data, verifier identities and sensitive reference databases raises privacy and confidentiality concerns, so it somewhat offends sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing containerised pipeline and metadata layers, but a schema generator, versioned repository and DOI minting are a considerable build that needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by auto-emitting records with the Article 12(3) elements, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic structured logging would substantially meet the mandate, but the proposal does not address the Article 12(2) event-relevance selection, retention, or the risks of openly sharing logs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating documentation drift as a measurable scientific phenomenon is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes a compliance obligation as a research question and changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and compliance, though it does not address what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Studying documentation drift internally violates no legal or social norms, though a research track on documentation is somewhat unusual for a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires standing up a research group, metadata capture on selected projects, and annual analysis, which are some changes but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It relates only tangentially to the stated problem via the technical documentation mentioned in the recital, and does not produce the required automatic event logs, so it has benefit only in a special situation.
evidence_effectiveness: Article 12 concerns automatic event logging, and this proposal addresses documentation currency (Recital 71) rather than logs, so it would not solve the logging mandate and is unlikely to meet the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs for debugging and incident replay is a sensible, fairly expected idea; it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (query layer and dashboards) and reframes logs as a debugging asset, but it still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal tooling project that reuses existing observability infrastructure violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin GraphQL layer on an existing observability stack with dashboard templates is a modest, low-cost build with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified need to use mandated logs for Article 72 monitoring, though much of its stated benefit is debugging, which is only implied by the compliance problem; it also misreads Annex III paragraph 3 as event types.
evidence_effectiveness: It makes logs queryable and supports post-market monitoring requests, but it does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met (what to record, tamper resistance, retention), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open standards for logging and audit trails are a known approach, so the idea is interesting and somewhat imaginative but not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance into a shared open standard and positioning the lab as a standard-setter changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations by making compliance a product and community offering.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a logging standard under an MIT licence with conformance tests violates no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat less common than simply building internal compliance logging.
evidence_implementability: Designing a schema, reference implementation, and conformance suite and prototyping it on two systems requires considerable but feasible effort and some changes to the lab's work, not a radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate by producing structured event logs designed to satisfy the stated requirements, including Annex III 1(a) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: A well-designed Article 12 logging schema would substantially meet the logging mandate, but a generic standard does not itself guarantee fit to each system's intended purpose or cover all Article 12 aspects, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance tooling is a fairly recognizable idea, interesting for its positioning angle but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new offering (public library and community resource) born from compliance, changing the lab's relationship to its obligation beyond mere internal logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing compliance tooling under a permissive licence is a legitimate, norm-conforming practice, though somewhat less common than internal solutions.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular library in the existing MLOps stack is feasible, but maintaining a public, versioned, multi-backend library with integration guides for several Annex III categories requires some significant effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly builds a logging library implementing Article 12(1)-(3), which is the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a library implementing the Article 12 logging requirements would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though legal sufficiency depends on per-system configuration and it does not address adapting R&D.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging in a reusable middleware is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (middleware) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library mapped to the regulation's articles is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building versioned middleware with hooks adopted during integration sprints is reasonably feasible but requires some engineering and changes to existing pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (Article 12 and Annex III 1(a) events) and the cost of doing so across projects.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would directly deliver Article 12 logging capability across projects, though it covers logging only and not documentation or other obligations, so it is nearly but not fully a solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing monitoring infrastructure for compliance logging is the most expected and mundane response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, merely reusing existing tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logging onto existing infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing event buses and aggregators with about two person-months of effort is cheap and involves only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the logging mandate by emitting the Article 12(2) event classes (risk triggers, post-market signals, operational telemetry), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Extending existing pipelines to emit the required event classes would largely meet the logging mandate, but it does not address Article 12(3) specifics, log integrity, or the lifetime retention details, so it is a strong but incomplete solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging in shared infrastructure is a common, expected response and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard logging practice implemented via a new middleware layer, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance middleware is a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy, though mandating it for all pipelines may cause some internal friction.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing experiment-tracking service as middleware is reasonably feasible, but a single sprint and mandatory traversal of all pipelines is optimistic and requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building automatic event logging per Article 12 into the lab's shared platform.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, platform-level middleware would largely satisfy the logging mandate across projects, though it covers mainly Annex III 1(a)-style fields and not the full risk, post-market monitoring, and oversight logging purposes, so it is mostly but not wholly complete.

evidence_originality: Using compliance logs as reproducibility and scientific audit assets is an interesting, somewhat imaginative reframing, but tying logging to MLflow experiment tracking is fairly expected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the scientific workflow so that compliance traces and research audit trails are one artefact, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Logging for compliance and reproducibility violates no norms, though making it the same artefact as scientific audit trails is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Adding instrumentation hooks to existing MLflow pipelines in one sprint is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes, though the schema design and no-opt-out enforcement add effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building automatic event logs mapped to the Article 12(2) categories.
evidence_effectiveness: Default structured logging mapped to Art. 12(2) would substantially meet the logging mandate, but it covers mainly the R&D/training pipeline rather than the deployed system's runtime logs and omits Art. 12(3) specifics, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing experiment-tracking infrastructure for compliance logs is a common, pragmatic response that an evaluator would expect from many labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice carried out with existing tooling, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing logging infrastructure for compliance records is a common, sensible strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a new schema, runtime container instrumentation, and field mapping, which are some changes but build on existing paid-for infrastructure and are reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the log store and mapping fields to the Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide automatic event logging mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c), but it does not address retention, integrity, or Annex III 3 minimums, nor the broader compliance response, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: The proposal restates the four Article 12(3) minimum logging items with an immutable log and a gap-flagging dashboard, which is exactly what labs would be expected to propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable audit logs with reviewer identification are common, legally required practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding an event log and a monitoring dashboard to existing pipelines is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by covering each Article 12(3) item for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging, but it covers only that subset and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) traceability for other high-risk systems or the R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A standing compliance team with periodic audits is a common, expected response to regulation and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standing team and audit process but still treats compliance as a separate logging and documentation practice and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A cross-functional compliance working group with audits and dual reporting is a common organizational strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reallocates four existing staff at twenty percent time with no new hires, which is a modest organizational change that is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of how to organize the lab to meet the logging mandate, though the link runs through process capacity rather than logging itself, so it sits between direct and implied.
evidence_effectiveness: A standing cell maintaining documentation templates and auditing prototypes for logging readiness would help the lab meet Article 12, but it supplies no technical logging mechanism itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging libraries with CI gates are a common, expected response from labs and are mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice, just built in earlier, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into architecture is a common, legitimate strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A reusable logging library with CI/CD test gates is a standard engineering effort requiring some changes and moderate work but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate with specific reference to Article 12(3) requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the embedded logging with test gates would directly deliver Article 12 logging capability, though it focuses on Article 12(3) items and less on the broader 12(2) event relevance, so it is a strong but not fully complete solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging hooks in SDK project templates is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response that many labs would propose, so it is common rather than ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (templates with middleware and a YAML manifest) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into internal tooling is a common strategy that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring an existing FastAPI template to add middleware is low-cost and non-radical for a lab that already has an internal SDK.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by instrumenting the Article 12(3) items (use periods, reference database, matched inputs, verifier identity) and avoiding retrofit costs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably cover the logging for prototypes, but it only partly solves the broader problem since it does not address production deployments, retention, or the wider R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Mining compliance logs for new failure taxonomies and sharing them openly is an unusual, imaginative angle that few labs would propose, though not wholly unprecedented as log analytics.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance-generated data into a source of scientific discovery and open community contributions, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal log analysis and publishing taxonomies is a somewhat unusual strategy, but publishing could raise data confidentiality or privacy concerns that are manageable and it offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs only two researchers at about 15 percent time and existing logs, which is a modest, reasonably feasible change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely getting value from compliance-generated logs and adapting R&D, which relates to but is not the stated logging-compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The workstream exploits logs that already exist but does not itself meet the Article 12 logging mandate, so it is at best a partial contribution to the problem of responding to the mandate.

evidence_originality: Treating the regulatory floor as a tender differentiator is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though audit-trail products and compliance-as-advantage are not entirely unheard of.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by turning logging into a commercial product and trust asset, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Tamper-evident logs and procurement-facing dashboards are legal and fit business norms, though marketing compliance as a differentiator is somewhat unusual but offends no one.
evidence_implementability: It uses two staff, an existing pilot contract and the current pipeline, so it needs only modest changes and is reasonably feasible at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems and goes beyond it, so it clearly applies to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Building a signed-event journal and dashboard would satisfy and exceed the logging requirements while offsetting costs, but it covers only biometric identity-verification systems and does not address broader Article 12 obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating log completeness as a build-failing test gate is sensible and somewhat unusual compared to typical documentation-based responses, but it is an application of familiar CI/testing ideas rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process (replay harness, build gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance beyond embedding checks.
evidence_acceptability: Automated quality gates in acceptance are a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A CI-style replay-and-audit harness with per-system checklists is a modest engineering addition that fits existing build pipelines, though scenario scripting for each prototype takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying required event types are emitted, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging completeness for event types but verifies only against a checklist and does not address retention, relevance of events to risk, or other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12 logging into a privacy-preserving, differential-privacy-aware log research line is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not wholly surprising since many labs would consider GDPR-compatible logging.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging a research output, publishable work and IP that differentiates the lab in tenders, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-conscious compliance research with publication and IP is a reasonable strategy that offends no norms, though it is slightly uncommon.
evidence_implementability: It uses a small slice of existing compute and no new capex, though differential-privacy log schemas that still meet traceability needs are technically nontrivial, so some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate and adapt R&D, while also addressing the implied GDPR tension, so it solves a directly related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A prototype research track at ten percent of one project's compute would only partially deliver compliant logging across the lab, and it covers biometric systems mainly, so it contributes but is not a full solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code gates in CI are a fairly expected response, though applying them to Article 12 schemas is somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool in the pipeline but still treats compliance as logging practice verified by checks, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a CI/CD compliance gate is a common engineering practice that offends no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires some pipeline changes and defining event schemas plus runtime smoke tests, which is reasonably feasible but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements, including the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, during R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch missing or malformed logging in prototypes, helping meet the logging mandate, but it does not address log content sufficiency, retention, or other obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Environment-tiered logging with promotion gates is a sensible but fairly expected DevOps adaptation, showing only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new workflow element (dual lanes and an automated gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice added around R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Gated release pipelines and separating dev from compliance environments are common engineering strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two-lane CI/CD with a config flag and automated gate checks needs some pipeline changes and immutable storage setup but uses established tooling, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate without crippling R&D, including the four Annex III data points.
evidence_effectiveness: A gated pipeline ensuring Article 12 logging is built and tested before release would address most of the logging mandate, though it covers only the engineering lane and not the wider compliance duties such as retention or the Annex III scope question, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating traceability constraints as a design variable and a publishable research question is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging requirements a research variable that shapes architecture choices and the lab's research agenda, though it stops short of fully redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Researching the effects of regulation and feeding results into standardisation is a somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Controlled comparisons on two representative tasks with varying logging variants are reasonably feasible for an AI lab, though they require dedicated research effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate, and its test cases (an Annex III 1(a) biometric pipeline) tie directly to Article 12, but it does not directly say how to meet the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A research programme comparing logging granularities would produce knowledge and some design guidance, but it would not itself implement the Article 12 logging capability, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance by design is a familiar idea, though treating timestamps and verification events as experimental variables adds some interesting imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the experimental design itself, which is paradigm stretching, but it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance into engineering and research practice and publishing a handbook violates no legal or social norms and is a sensible, uncontroversial strategy.
evidence_implementability: Writing a handbook and adjusting experiment design requires some process change and researcher buy-in but is reasonably feasible without major cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by embedding logging into R&D from the start, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding logs in experimental protocols would help produce compliant telemetry for prototypes, but it is a partial solution since it does not clearly cover deployed high-risk system logging, event relevance for risk and post-market monitoring, or retention.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance documentation into publishable open methodology is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance obligations and R&D by making compliance outputs into research contributions and public offerings, stretching the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing methodology papers is a normal academic practice, though releasing code and documentation openly raises some confidentiality and trade-secret sensitivities, making it somewhat unusual but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: Distilling compliance files into peer-reviewed papers and open benchmark suites for each milestone requires significant added effort, peer-review timelines, and IP/security vetting, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses Recital 71 technical documentation and implied reporting benefits but does not directly address the Article 12 automatic logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not produce automatic event logs or traceability required by Article 12, so it only contributes a partial benefit around documentation and reputation.

evidence_originality: Automated schema validation in CI is a fairly expected engineering response to a logging checklist, though the 'compile-time equivalent for compliance' framing is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI schema gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: JSON Schema assertions in an existing CI pipeline with a synthetic mock run are cheap and easy, needing only modest changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, meeting the paragraph-3 logging minima for Annex III 1(a) systems, with a clear do-X-to-get-Y link.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably verify that the Annex III 1(a) paragraph-3 minimum fields are present, but it covers only part of the mandate (not paragraph 2 relevance, retention, or non-1(a) systems, and it checks presence rather than whether the system actually logs correctly in production), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging libraries with OpenTelemetry exporters are a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable logging SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal compliance library is a standard engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: One sprint for two senior engineers to build a wrapper SDK with a template import is modest effort, though schema design and capturing the reference database hash and verifier identity need some integration work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by capturing the specified Article 12(3) fields automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a shared SDK that auto-captures the Article 12(3) fields would meet the logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it covers only the minimum fields for Annex III 1(a) systems and not broader Article 12(2) event relevance or documentation duties.

evidence_originality: Reusing mandated compliance logs as regression-test corpora is an interesting, somewhat imaginative reuse, though replay testing itself is known.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as an input to R&D (logging woven into engineering workflow), changing the relationship between compliance and R&D without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Replaying logged data in a sandbox for regression testing is a legitimate engineering practice, though privacy of logged personal data is a minor concern, so it is somewhat unusual but offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing test infrastructure but requires a replay scheduler, snapshotting of reference databases, and CI gating per risk class, which are reasonably feasible changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of how to derive R&D value from the mandated logs, which relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself satisfy the logging mandate (it depends on logs existing) and only partially addresses the problem by adapting R&D to exploit the logs, so it contributes but is partial.

evidence_originality: Compliance testing as a release gate is a fairly standard shift-left approach that an evaluator would expect, with only mildly interesting specifics like scenario-based triggers.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a test suite and release gate as a new process element but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing development lifecycle.
evidence_acceptability: Using QA gates and test suites to verify compliance before release is a common engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building test suites and scenario simulations and adding a release-blocking step, which is reasonably feasible with some process changes but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by testing that required events are captured (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: A release gate verifying Article 12 log capture would substantially ensure logging capability is built correctly, but it addresses only technical logging verification and not the broader response (e.g., R&D adaptation, retention, post-market use), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs for monitoring and drift analysis is a sensible and fairly foreseeable idea that shows some imagination but is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Treating compliance logs as research data assets changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, which is paradigm stretching, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for monitoring and analytics is a common, legitimate strategy, though data protection and purpose-limitation issues could arise, they do not offend norms here.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing pipelines and warehouse with one data scientist, requiring modest changes and reasonably feasible work.
evidence_applicability: Routing Article 12 logs into post-market monitoring and drift pipelines directly addresses the logging mandate and Article 12(2)(b)-(c) purposes, so the link to the stated problem is explicit.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the logging and monitoring purposes and make compliance useful, but it is only a partial solution because it does not by itself specify the required log content, retention, or traceability coverage.

evidence_originality: Building a log schema and secure storage for the mandated fields is the expected, standard response to this mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A schema with GDPR-aligned retention and access controls is a common, compliance-friendly strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-week prototype by the platform team against an existing pipeline with legal input is a modest, reasonably feasible effort, though encryption, retention policy and latency testing require some real work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by building the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields (timestamps, reference database, matched input, verifier identity) for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the specific Annex III 1(a) minimum logging requirements, but it covers only that category and not the Article 12(1)-(2) general traceability duties for other high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Schema-migration testing for long-retention logs is an interesting, sensible angle that few would propose here, but it is an application of known data-engineering practice rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new validation tool and process but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Testing log durability is a prudent, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms, though it is somewhat less common than basic logging.
evidence_implementability: Building a test environment with synthetic log replay and auto-generated migration scripts requires some new tooling and effort but is reasonably feasible with standard engineering.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (long-term log integrity over the lifetime) that follows from the Article 12 lifetime recording requirement but is not the stated logging decision itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Ensuring logs stay parseable and queryable over the system lifetime supports only the durability facet of Article 12, not deciding what to log or meeting the full mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK built on OpenTelemetry with CI gating is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response that labs would commonly propose, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (SDK, schema adapters, CI gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance basically unchanged, though it embeds logging from first commit.
evidence_acceptability: Internal standardized logging infrastructure with CI checks is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building on OpenTelemetry and existing serving stacks is reasonably feasible but needs some new shared infrastructure, adapters per risk category, and CI changes across teams.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by delivering automatic Article 12 logging with minimal disruption to R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would reliably produce automatic event logs for prototypes, but it addresses only the logging mandate and not the Article 12 content judgments (e.g., what events are relevant, retention, Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A gap audit and retrofit of legacy systems is a standard, expected response to a new logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The compliance matrix and risk-tiering are mild new process elements, but compliance is still treated as a logging retrofit with no change to how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Audit-and-patch prioritized by regulatory exposure is a conventional compliance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A bounded six-week sprint with one engineer per project and prioritized patching is reasonably feasible, though it needs staffing and touches multiple legacy codebases.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements by mapping paragraph-2 triggers to existing systems and patching gaps.
evidence_effectiveness: Auditing and retrofitting legacy prototypes would meaningfully close logging gaps for those systems, but it addresses only legacy systems rather than the full mandate (new development, documentation, retention, Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Assigning document custodians with a compliance file template is a common, mundane response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance governance that leaves the lab's R&D ways of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Designated compliance owners and per-system documentation files are common governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Naming a custodian and adopting a documentation template with quarterly reviews requires only modest organizational changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses keeping documentation and records current across the lifetime, which Recital 71 and Article 12 require, though it mostly covers documentation rather than the automatic logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with lifetime documentation and log-retention oversight but does not build the technical automatic event-logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging library shipped in project scaffolds is a common, sensible engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect from many labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance tooling with tamper-evident logs is a standard approach that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing telemetry bus with standard components such as append-only storage and object storage, making it a reasonably low-cost internal engineering project.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by emitting records that cover the 12(3) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would deliver the automatic event recording the mandate requires, but it only partly solves the problem because Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, and R&D adaptation remain outside it, and 12(3) fields apply only to Annex III 1(a) systems.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a longitudinal research dataset for drift early-warning is an unusual and imaginative angle that few labs would propose, though drift monitoring itself is a known topic.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logs as primary scientific data and changes what the lab researches, weaving the compliance obligation into the science and creating new partnerships, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Collecting anonymised logs from deployers for research is a reasonable, lawful strategy, though it raises some data-protection and data-sharing sensitivities (biometric context) that make it somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A two-year program requiring access to production biometric deployment logs through partners, plus specialised analytics, is expensive and difficult because of data-access, privacy and contractual hurdles, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal uses Article 12 logs to detect drift ahead of Article 79(1) risk situations, which addresses a purpose of the logging mandate, but it is a research program and does not directly tell the lab how to meet the logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift research on logs would help the lab's post-market monitoring and risk identification, but it would not by itself deliver compliant logging capabilities (Art. 12(2)-(3) minimums), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance-by-design gate in design review is a very standard and expected response, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint to existing processes while treating compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a review checkpoint to an existing design-review process is a common, norm-compliant governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing review process with modest overhead, though requiring schema specification before training begins demands some process change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by requiring logging schemas mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) before implementation.
evidence_effectiveness: A design-gate for logging would substantially help ensure logging capability is built in, but it covers only design planning and not the actual implementation, Article 12(3) specifics, or ongoing documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Classification audits of the portfolio are a mundane, widely expected first step in response to regulation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance scoping practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged and treats compliance as a separate task.
evidence_acceptability: A portfolio classification audit is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-week mapping by an existing regulatory-affairs liaison producing one-page sheets is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, knowing which systems carry logging duties, which relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate but is not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Scoping which projects trigger Article 12 and which log fields they need is a sensible prerequisite that helps allocate resources, but it does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mining compliance logs for failure taxonomies is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, but data-driven reliability analysis of logs is a fairly foreseeable use.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandated logs into a research asset and research direction, rather than treating them as a mere logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Using mandated logs for internal reliability research and staffing a postdoc track violates no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat less common than plain compliance.
evidence_implementability: A two-person postdoc track within an existing group is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though accumulating sufficient log corpora and recruiting add some difficulty.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the 'adapt R&D accordingly' part of the problem by leveraging logs, an implied related problem, but does not directly address how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate and is only tangential to compliance, so it contributes only partially to solving the problem of how to respond.

evidence_originality: Using anomaly detectors on inference logs to flag risk events is a somewhat unusual and interesting framing of Article 12(2)(a) that shows some imagination, but anomaly detection on logs is a known technique and not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (contrastive detectors) and ties compliance to the lab's research agenda by turning the obligation into a publishable research programme, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using internal monitoring data to build detectors and publishing the results violates no norms, though it is somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires an open research effort with uncertain calibration given scarce historical incident data, which makes it a significant and difficult commitment for a lab that needs committed implementation resources rather than exploratory work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets identifying risk-relevant events under Article 12(2)(a), which is part of the logging mandate, though it addresses event identification rather than the basic logging capability.
evidence_effectiveness: Detectors would help flag risk events and support post-market monitoring but would not by themselves deliver the full logging capability, retention, and traceability required, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Instrumenting API gateways with structured event emitters and an append-only store is the standard, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice with no change to how the lab works, explicitly avoiding redesign.
evidence_acceptability: Meeting the regulation's logging fields with tamper-evident storage is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Four engineer-weeks per module with existing API gateways is a modest, non-radical effort at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields for Annex III 1(a) biometric systems, which is the explicitly stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the automatic-recording and Article 12(3) minimum requirements for these modules, though it covers only two modules and not the broader 12(2) traceability purposes or lab-wide R&D.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code in CI is a fairly familiar idea, though applying it to Article 12 log schemas is a sensible and somewhat interesting application.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process (schema plus linter gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks and linters are a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing CI pipelines, though encoding the Article 12 requirements into a schema and writing a linter that detects inference paths lacking emitters needs moderate engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by detecting missing event types and gaps before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate checking for log emitters against a schema would help verify that logging capability exists, but it cannot ensure logs are actually recorded, retained and useful in operation, nor does it cover post-market monitoring or documentation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing compliance architecture and contributing to standards is a fairly known thought-leadership move, interesting but not surprising or highly imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (public dossier, open schema, standards contribution) and some new relationships with partners and standards bodies, but still treats compliance as logging documentation rather than changing R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing compliance documentation and contributing to standards bodies is a legitimate practice that offends no norms, though public disclosure of architecture is somewhat uncommon.
evidence_implementability: A one-quarter whitepaper and open-source schema authored by the compliance office with engineers is a modest, non-radical effort, though the standards submission adds some coordination.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (demonstrating compliance, market trust, defensible record) related to the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate, rather than the logging implementation itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It documents and builds trust around logging but does not itself implement the logging mandate, so it only partially contributes to meeting Article 12.

evidence_originality: Scoping and gap-auditing against a regulation is the most common, expected first response to a new mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A portfolio classification and gap audit is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal audit and classification exercise is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint using a template and internal audit is low cost and non-radical, though it needs some lab-lead time.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of deciding how to respond to the logging mandate by identifying which systems are in scope and where logging falls short of Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit only diagnoses scope and gaps and does not itself implement logging, so it contributes to but only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging as a default reusable pipeline component is a sensible but very common compliance-by-design response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with a tool integrated into CI/CD, and leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into the engineering pipeline is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A six-week sprint by one senior engineer to build a module and integrate it into existing CI/CD templates is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: The module directly produces the automatic event logging and Article 12(3) minimum fields that the mandate requires, so it addresses the stated problem head-on.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable embedded module would cover the core logging mandate for new systems, but it only partly addresses Article 12(2) event relevance, existing systems, and the broader documentation and retention duties.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK with decorator API is a sensible but expected engineering response that many labs would propose, so it is common rather than ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal tooling for compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a thin library wrapping existing middleware with SSO lookup is reasonably feasible with some engineering effort and modest change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by automating the specific Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would directly produce the Article 12(3) log fields across prototypes, but covers only logging and not documentation, retention, or Article 12(2) event relevance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI-integrated log schema validator is a sensible, somewhat expected engineering response, interesting but not surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (nightly build auditor) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI violates no norms and is a common, uncontroversial development practice.
evidence_implementability: A Python package running in nightly builds with synthetic replay is a small, low-cost addition to existing pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying required log fields during development.
evidence_effectiveness: It checks the log fields and would reliably catch schema gaps, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and not the broader Article 12(2) event-relevance or traceability adequacy, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design gates in the SDLC are a very common and expected response, making this mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (spec document, gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Design gates and compliance sign-offs are common governance practices that violate no norms, though engineering may resist the added friction.
evidence_implementability: It requires an SDLC revision, a new specification document, and sign-off processes, which are some changes but reasonably feasible with moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X, get compliant automatic logging by design), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A design-review gate requiring event schema, retention, and traceability specs before coding would substantially deliver Article 12 logging for new systems, but it does not cover legacy systems or verify the logs actually work, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking logging overhead is a sensible and fairly expected engineering response, with only mild interest in the cost-per-event table by granularity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The study introduces a benchmarking process and guidelines but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially intact, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Internal performance and cost benchmarking violates no legal or social norms and is a common engineering strategy.
evidence_implementability: A benchmarking project with internal guidelines uses existing engineering skills and moderate resources, requiring some effort but no radical change.

evidence_effectiveness: It would inform cheaper compliant logging configurations but does not itself implement logging or settle the broader compliance response, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Schema versioning for long-lived logs is a sensible, known engineering practice applied to the lifetime requirement, somewhat unusual in framing but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (schema registry, versioning, migration toolchain) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Schema versioning and data migration are common engineering strategies that violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A JSON-schema registry, version headers and migration scripts use standard tooling and require modest changes to middleware, so it is reasonably feasible at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (log readability over the lifetime) that is directly tied to the Article 12 lifetime and traceability requirement, though the problem is not explicitly stated in the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep logs readable and auditable across the system lifetime, but it addresses only one aspect of Article 12 compliance (not event selection, retention, or content), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using compliance logs for drift/anomaly early warning is a fairly expected and increasingly common idea, though framing it as turning obligation into research signal is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and reframes logs as productive research signal, which modestly shifts the compliance-R&D relationship but still centers on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Analyzing logs for monitoring and risk detection is a legitimate, uncontroversial use that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It relies on off-the-shelf stream-processing tools (Flink/Kafka Streams) and standard statistical process control, requiring some new build and integration but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly builds on the Article 12 event streams and ties to Article 79(1), 72 monitoring, and 12(3)(d) audit trail, addressing identified parts of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with identifying risk situations and post-market monitoring but does not by itself deliver the core logging mandate (what to record, retention, etc.), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable compliance templates or scaffolds are a common and expected response to logging mandates, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A code template with a compliance adapter is a new tool, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building standard compliance tooling into engineering workflows violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin wrapper adapter and template repo is cheap and non-radical to build and adopt, requiring only modest engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: The scaffold directly implements the four minimum logging fields of Article 12(3), which are an identified part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the Article 12(3) minimum logging for biometric systems if used, but it covers only Annex III(1a) systems and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging obligations or other high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware or SDK is a standard, expected answer to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.

evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared compliance infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.

evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, as in 'build shared middleware to get uniform Article 12 logs'.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging service would meet the Article 12 automatic-recording requirement across projects, but it covers only the logging mandate and leaves out other parts such as deciding which events matter for risk and post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in from the first design sprint (privacy/security-by-design style) is a common and expected response to the mandate, though applying the Annex III 1(a) minimums to all prototypes adds a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a mandatory traceability-layer spec gated at code review) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging by design and using the regulation's minimums as a baseline violates no norms and is a common, legally sound strategy.
evidence_implementability: Adding a spec requirement and code-review gate to the prototype pipeline requires some process and engineering changes but is reasonably feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly, with logging embedded in the prototype process as the means.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet the Article 12 logging mandate for the lab's high-risk prototypes and reduce retrofitting, but it does not address other aspects such as post-market monitoring, log retention, or what R&D to pursue, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging middleware with OpenTelemetry spans is a fairly expected and mundane response, though the extension with Annex III attributes is a sensible touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding standard middleware and using OpenTelemetry is a common engineering strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin decorator/context-manager SDK over existing inference APIs with OpenTelemetry is a modest engineering effort with low overhead and non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specific Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would largely satisfy the technical logging requirement, but it covers mainly Annex III 1(a) minimums and not the broader Article 12(2) event relevance or retention and documentation duties, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Scaffolding generators for compliance are a sensible but fairly expected tooling response, with a mildly interesting focus on the four Annex III paragraph-3 fields.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (scaffolder with typed schema and test stubs) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A internal scaffolding tool that wires in legally mandated logging fields is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: Building a CLI generator with schema and test stubs on top of existing logging middleware is a modest engineering task requiring some work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate, with do X (scaffold hooks) to get Y (compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: It would address only the paragraph-3 logging for biometric prototypes, and not Article 12(1)-(2) general logging or the broader decision on R&D, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as an R&D and monitoring data source is a sensible and somewhat imaginative framing, but it is a fairly foreseeable response and not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logs as an R&D asset feeding model improvement and procurement differentiation, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance without altering what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for monitoring and internal reporting is consistent with regulatory intent and offends no norms, though log data use may raise minor data protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: A small data-science team building anomaly-detection pipelines over an existing logging store is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some new work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses meeting Article 12 and Article 72 obligations by using the mandated logs for post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Mining logs for drift and risk situations would help satisfy post-market monitoring and risk identification but does not itself ensure the logging capabilities required by Article 12 are built, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance logging SDK or middleware wrapper is a very common, expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
