evidence_originality: An internal log schema standard is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal standards with review windows and design-review gates are a common, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: An eight-week drafting effort by three people plus a review window is a modest, non-radical change using existing design-review processes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12(2) logging mandate by defining which events count as relevant and how they are recorded.
evidence_effectiveness: A standard schema defining relevant events, fields, and retention would help meet the Article 12 logging mandate consistently, but it specifies logging rather than building the technical capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log-based monitoring dashboards with alerting are a fairly expected response, making it interesting but not unusual or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Log analytics, alerting and compliance reporting are common, norm-conforming compliance practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal analytics service ingesting log streams from all deployments with configurable rules and notifications requires significant engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of using logs for post-market monitoring and risk identification named in Article 12(2), i.e., do X to get Y where Y is part of the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A log-consuming monitoring dashboard supports Article 12(2)(a)-(c) purposes (risk identification, post-market monitoring) but does not itself deliver the logging capability, retention, or Annex III minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy/security-by-design style embedding of logging is a common, expected response to this mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice moved earlier in the lifecycle, with design gates and specs as modest process changes that leave the lab's R&D relationship to compliance basically unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-by-design and mandatory design gates are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building standardized logging modules and adding design-review gates requires some organizational and engineering changes but is a reasonably feasible, familiar compliance-by-design approach.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building automatic event recording into systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding logging by construction would largely satisfy Article 12 if done, though it omits specifics such as Annex III(1)(a) minimums, retention, and existing systems, so it is not a complete solution.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12 logging requirements into an open community benchmark is interesting and somewhat unusual, but it is not strikingly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates new offerings born from compliance (a benchmark, a reference role for the lab), changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations beyond mere logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source benchmarks and publishing in venues are uncommon as a compliance response but offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a benchmark atop existing logging infrastructure and maintaining versioned updates across Member States requires significant effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (ecosystem evaluation and reputation) related to the mandate, but does not directly address how the lab itself meets the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps test logging support and may inform the lab's own architecture, but it is only a partial solution and does not itself implement logging compliance.

evidence_originality: Building logging in from the start with a designated owner is the most common, expected response to this mandate and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Making logging a design input with design-review gates is standard privacy/compliance-by-design practice that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Updating internal engineering standards to meet a legal requirement violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Revising design-review standards and assigning a logging owner per team are non-radical process changes at modest cost, though retrofitting existing systems is not addressed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building the required event recording into systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would largely satisfy the logging obligation, but it is vague on specifics such as Article 12(3) minimum items, retention, and existing systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A documentation control program with audits and a central repository is a standard, expected compliance response and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice with unchanged R&D ways of working, only adding a repository and alerts within the existing paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Internal documentation governance and audits are common strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated team and tooling integration but these are routine, non-radical changes that are easy to implement, though the team adds some cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses documentation upkeep from Recital 71, which relates to the record-keeping mandate but is not the automatic event logging of Article 12, so it solves an implied, related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Version-controlled documentation helps traceability and compliance evidence but does not itself deliver automatic event logs, making it only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralised logging platform to avoid per-project duplication is a common and expected response, showing little ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice delivered through a shared tool, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised shared logging infrastructure is a common, normative engineering and compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing MLflow and on-prem storage with one senior engineer over six months and a thin SDK, which is reasonably feasible with some changes, though integration across projects and the capture of reference-database and verifier identity add effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X to get compliant logs, which is the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: A shared middleware capturing the Article 12(3) minimum fields with append-only logs would, if built, solve the core logging mandate, though it covers mainly the Annex III 1(a) minimums and not broader Article 12(2) event relevance or documentation, so it is a strong but not full solution.

evidence_originality: Hash-chained, compressed logs with privacy protection are an interesting and somewhat imaginative direction, but they are a fairly expected technical response among labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new protocol and an IP/differentiation angle, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging and optional publication are conventional, norm-respecting strategies, with only minor tension between data minimization and the mandated retention of records.
evidence_implementability: A six-month track with two postdocs, prototyping against an existing pipeline, is a reasonably feasible, moderate-cost undertaking, though it needs some dedicated research effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 minimum logging requirements for Annex III biometric systems, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A privacy-preserving hash-chained log would satisfy the logging minimums and address retention and privacy concerns, but it covers only Annex III biometric systems and a prototype internal standard, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Schema registries and tiered retention are well-known data-engineering practices, and applying them to compliance logs is sensible but expected rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a schema registry and infrastructure-as-code tooling but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standard engineering and records-management strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities and supports regulator auditability.
evidence_implementability: It needs data-engineering effort and prototyping on two pipelines this quarter, which is reasonably feasible with moderate change and cost, though lifecycle storage and schema versioning add some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to meet the logging mandate (Annex III(1)(a) fields, lifetime recording) that is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A versioned log schema plus tiered lifetime retention would substantially deliver Article 12's logging and lifetime traceability, but it does not by itself cover event selection for risk/post-market monitoring, Article 19 retention duties, or R&D adaptation, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Time-boxed retrofit of mandated log fields is a mundane, expected response, though the sprint framing is slightly practical.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice (add required fields to prototypes), leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged apart from CI/CD hooks.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logging to meet Article 12(3) via a time-boxed sprint is a common, legitimate compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers for eight weeks with CI/CD integration on two prototypes is a modest, reasonably feasible resource commitment with no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specific Article 12(3) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully meet the minimum logging requirements for the two prototypes but does not cover other systems, Article 12(2) event relevance, or broader R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Releasing compliance logs as a public benchmark corpus is an unusual and imaginative reframing relative to typical internal logging responses, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance logs into a shared public scientific resource and open tooling changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, creating a new offering born from compliance, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release of tooling and anonymized logs is somewhat unusual for compliance but offends no norms, though sharing logs raises modest confidentiality and privacy concerns.
evidence_implementability: A small team building a logging SDK around one prototype is feasible, though open-sourcing and releasing an anonymized log corpus adds some legal, privacy and engineering effort beyond routine changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by instrumenting event recording for the specified items (input data, reference databases, verification actions).
evidence_effectiveness: An SDK capturing Article 12(3) events would help meet the logging mandate, but it covers only one prototype and the Annex III 1(a) specifics, so it is a partial solution, and the benchmark release does not add compliance.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in the ML pipeline is a common, expected response to this mandate with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into engineering workflows is a standard, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding instrumentation hooks to an existing experiment-tracking stack is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change, though it takes some engineering effort across pipeline stages.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building Article 12 logging (timestamps, inputs, events) into the lab's workflows to meet the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Instrumenting all pipeline stages with structured logs aligned to Article 12(2) would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it leaves out details such as retention and identification of verifying persons, so it is not fully specified.

evidence_originality: Automated checking of required log fields in a release pipeline is a mundane, expected compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance testing practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal automated compliance test harness is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team building a test harness that checks four known log fields is a reasonably feasible, low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements for biometric systems, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that required fields are present but does not generate the logs, cover Article 12(1)-(2) general logging, or non-biometric systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance checkpoints are a very common and expected response to regulatory mandates, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged, merely adding a control point.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate compliance reviews are a common, norm-conforming governance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Appointing a compliance officer per group, a checklist template, and a sign-off hook in an existing project-management tool are modest process changes with low cost.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly addresses the stated problem of how the lab responds to the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying logging capabilities before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A review gate verifies that logging exists but does not itself build the logging capability or specify technical design, so it helps as only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A release gate with a cross-functional sign-off checklist is a very common compliance practice that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint and checklist process but treats compliance as standard logging and release practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Pre-release compliance reviews with sign-off panels are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small panel and checklist are a non-radical, low-cost change, though mapping the regulation to a checklist takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying Article 12 traceability requirements before release.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate would help verify that logging meets Article 12(2) requirements but does not itself build the logging capability or cover Article 12(1) and 12(3), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK built on OpenTelemetry is a common, expected response to a logging mandate with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice delivered via a tool, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using a shared, standards-based logging middleware is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two sprints to wrap the inference pipeline with an OpenTelemetry layer and pluggable backends is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the specific Article 12(3) items such as session times, reference database and input matches.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer would largely satisfy the technical logging requirement, but it omits identification of reviewing persons (Art 12(3)(d)), retention, and the risk-event logging of 12(2), so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Operationalising a vague legal term via statistical process control and publishing it as an open preprint is interesting and somewhat imaginative, though not wholly unprecedented in AI governance research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning a regulatory term into publishable science and open research output, rather than treating compliance as a logging practice only.
evidence_acceptability: Collaborating with legal and publishing a framework is a normal, norm-respecting approach, with only mild sensitivity around releasing incident data insights and legal interpretation publicly.
evidence_implementability: It requires cross-team collaboration, historical incident data analysis, and a research effort over time, which is reasonably feasible but involves notable effort and legal uncertainty about thresholds.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified element of the mandate, the Article 12(2)(a) requirement to record events identifying situations involving risk or substantial modification, making the link do X to get Y explicit.
evidence_effectiveness: Defining measurable criteria for substantial modification would help the lab meet Article 12(2)(a) logging purposes, but it addresses only one part of the logging mandate (not what to log overall, retention, or technical capability), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A recurring internal audit of documentation currency and log retention is a common, expected compliance response with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance governance that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged and treats compliance as routine process.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audit cadences are a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A quarterly review by an existing compliance cell requires only modest process additions and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of maintaining documentation and log retention over the system lifetime, which relates to the logging mandate but does not directly address how to technically meet Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps keep documentation current and logs retained, but it does not itself build logging capability or cover event-recording content in Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Packaging logging as a default dependency in starter templates is a sensible and fairly expected approach, with only mild interest in the compliance-by-default framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK in templates) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working largely intact.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding a shared logging library in templates is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers refactoring existing monitoring middleware into a pip package and adding it to starter templates is a modest, non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically recording start/end times, input references, and state at creation time.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the core logging capability requirement for new prototypes, but does not cover existing systems, Annex III-specific items like reference databases and human verifier identification, retention, or event relevance to risk, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance budget allocations are a fairly common and mundane response, though tying tranches to compliance milestones adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a financial governance mechanism but still treats compliance as a cost-handling practice, leaving the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Budget ring-fencing and milestone-tranche funding are ordinary governance practices that violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires amending an intake template and funding-release process, which is a modest administrative change building on existing gating practices.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, funding the cost of compliance, which relates to but is not the direct logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting for compliance helps resource logging work but does not itself create the technical logging capability Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating the logging mandate as an object of study for its effect on optimisation and generalisation is an unusual and imaginative angle that few labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a scientific research question and weaves logging into the experimentation platform, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, and it also shapes what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliant logging into the platform and running research on it violates no norms, though framing compliance as a research programme is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Restructuring the experimentation platform and running controlled comparisons across core architectures is a significant, costly effort, and the effect on gradient dynamics is uncertain, which makes this hard to commit resources to.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses Article 12(1) automatic event recording through default-compliant logging on the platform, though much of its stated aim (gradient dynamics research) is only implied to relate to the compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Making every run emit a compliant log stream by default would partly meet the logging mandate, but the research comparing logging-on and logging-off behaviour does not itself solve compliance, so it only contributes partially.

evidence_originality: Leveraging existing MLOps logs for compliance is a fairly common and expected response, with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It stays within standard compliance and logging practice, merely reusing existing tooling, though it does gesture at integrating logging with experimental records rather than treating it as a separate workstream.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing pipelines for compliance is a common, legitimate strategy that offends no norms, though regulators might question whether experiment logs suffice.
evidence_implementability: Building on existing experiment-tracking infrastructure with minimal added instrumentation and a gap audit is a modest, non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by auditing for gaps and adding instrumentation, though it conflates Article 12 logs with technical documentation.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially but only partially solve the problem, since training logs do not by themselves satisfy Article 12's deployment-time event logging for risk, post-market monitoring, and operation monitoring.

evidence_originality: Open-source compliance tooling is a fairly expected response, with some interest in the community-resource framing but little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an open-source shared toolkit) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though sharing it as a community resource slightly shifts how compliance is handled.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release of compliance tooling is a common, norm-compatible strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular Rust/Python framework with PyTorch and JAX hooks, mapping each sub-clause, and maintaining public releases is a substantial engineering effort but feasible for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: The toolkit directly implements the Article 12 logging requirements, which is the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A drop-in logging layer documented against Article 12(2) and (3) would plausibly meet the logging mandate for the lab's systems, but it does not itself address Article 12(3) specifics tied to Annex III biometric systems or the surrounding documentation duties, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log retention and retrieval infrastructure is a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs facing this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Encrypted storage, retention policies and regulator query interfaces are standard, uncontroversial compliance infrastructure that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-quarter project with IT, encrypted storage, a query interface and assigned owners is a reasonably feasible set of measures requiring some changes but no radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the mandate, keeping logs available and retrievable for traceability and regulator inquiries, though the retention step is implied rather than explicitly stated in Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Retaining and retrieving lifetime logs supports traceability and post-market monitoring, but it covers only storage and retrieval, not the event-recording capability, content specification, or other Article 12 requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing a common logging schema and SDK is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as logging practice and only adds a shared schema and SDK as new tooling, without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralizing a shared logging standard with a cross-team pod is a common engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A six-week pod of four people within the current sprint cadence producing a spec and thin SDK is low cost and non-radical, though adoption across teams needs some coordination.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by designing a schema covering the Article 12(3) minimums (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier IDs), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared schema and SDK would deliver the technical logging capability and meet Article 12(3) minimums if adopted, but it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Keeping a versioned, regularly reviewed technical file is a common, expected response to documentation requirements and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working and the R&D-compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining versioned technical documentation with named owners and periodic reviews is a standard, norm-compliant regulatory practice.
evidence_implementability: It requires a versioned repository, a named engineer per product line and quarterly reviews, which are reasonably feasible process additions rather than radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the Recital 71 requirement to keep technical documentation current and tie it to post-market monitoring, which is related to the logging mandate but concerns documentation more than the automatic event logs Article 12 mandates.
evidence_effectiveness: A living dossier helps with traceability and compliance evidence but does not itself implement the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared benchmark for log utility in monitoring is an unusual and interesting idea showing some imagination, though benchmarks as a concept are familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a new scientific offering and standard-setting role for the lab, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks and voluntary scoring are a legal, non-offensive practice, though inviting regulators and industry to adopt a lab-made standard is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Building a curated benchmark from anonymised incident reports, synthetic drift scenarios and adversarial traces with an open evaluator is a significant, costly effort requiring data access and cross-party buy-in, but is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (verifying log adequacy for post-market monitoring under Art. 12(2)(b)) that relates to the stated problem but not directly to implementing the lab's own logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark would help assess whether logs support monitoring but does not itself make the lab's own systems meet Article 12's logging mandate, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware layer is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard logging tool that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared logging middleware to meet Article 12 is a common, legally conforming compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two existing engineers building a middleware layer over current inference servers is a modest, reasonably feasible, low-cost change with no new headcount.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by recording the specific events Article 12 paragraphs 1-3 require.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, the middleware would satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address broader documentation or R&D adaptation and its coverage of non-Annex III needs is unclear, making it a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking logging overhead against record completeness is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, though benchmark suites are a familiar research format.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns logging into a measurable research axis and a community benchmark, which shifts the relationship between R&D and compliance somewhat, but it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing open benchmarks and publications offends no norms and is a somewhat uncommon response to a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: Building ten scenarios, instrumenting reference implementations and running controlled experiments across scales is a significant, costly effort, though it is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely understanding the cost and completeness trade-offs of logging, which relates to the mandate but does not directly implement the required logs.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark would inform logging design choices but would not by itself make the lab's own systems compliant with Article 12, so it contributes only partially.

evidence_originality: Building a reference logging implementation and test suite is the common, expected response to the mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: This is standard compliance engineering that implements the logging requirements and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged; the reusable test suite is only a minor addition.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging via a prototype and test suite is a standard, uncontroversial approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person, eight-week sprint on an existing pipeline is small, low-cost and reasonably feasible, though building the reference-database provenance and verifier-identity linkage will take some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an explicitly identified part of the stated problem, meeting the logging mandate through the specific Article 12(3) log categories.
evidence_effectiveness: Implementing all four Article 12(3) minimum log categories would directly satisfy the most prescriptive logging requirement, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) biometric subset and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning logging compliance into a client-facing, auto-generated transparency dossier used as a sales differentiator is somewhat unusual and interesting but not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates a new offering born from compliance and changes how compliance relates to the lab's business, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Delivering transparency documentation to clients and having legal review it is a somewhat uncommon but entirely unobjectionable strategy.
evidence_implementability: Generating a document from existing logging SDK metadata at each release and adding a legal review step requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of how to communicate and leverage compliance, which relates to but is not the core logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The dossier showcases and documents logging capabilities but does not itself implement the logging mandate, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: A shared compliance logging SDK with scaffold integration and fail-fast assertions is a common, expected response, with only slight cleverness in the compile-time conformance checks.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A standard shared library and scaffolding template introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library with CI checks is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a shared SDK in one sprint and wiring it into the scaffolding CLI is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though supporting three language stacks and CI schema validation adds some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building logging into every high-risk prototype (do X to get automated logs, which is part of the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: It would automate logging for prototypes and contribute substantially to Article 12(1) compliance, but it does not address retention, post-market monitoring or Article 12(2) risk-relevance, and the Article 12(3) minimums apply only to the Annex III 1(a) systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with ownership and deadlines is a standard, expected response, with the automatic deployment hold being only a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a documentation process with a deployment gate but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice, not changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining versioned, up-to-date technical documentation is a common, legally aligned compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A versioned repo with named owners and a deployment hold requires some process and tooling changes but is reasonably feasible within existing release cadences.
evidence_applicability: It directly solves an identified related problem (keeping technical documentation current), but that is adjacent to rather than the core logging mandate, making it a related implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the documentation upkeep requirement of Recital 71 but not the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Empirically testing whether mandated minimum log fields detect drift is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle beyond typical compliance responses, but not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (testbeds, sufficiency quantification) and links compliance logging to the science of model behavior, modestly changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, yet remains centered on logging.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme testing logging sufficiency with controlled perturbations on its own systems violates no legal or social norms, though positioning for regulatory revision is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Building instrumented testbeds and perturbation studies requires dedicated research effort and resources but is reasonably feasible for an AI lab, though the task says approval means committing implementation resources rather than exploratory funding.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, whether the logging mandate is adequate, which relates to but does not directly deliver meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not itself implement compliant logging and is exploratory, so it contributes only partially, mainly by informing internal monitoring and regulatory input.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code in CI is a known DevOps pattern, though applying drift and risk-onset checks to Article 12 logs shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (CI/CD log-validation gates) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only automating verification earlier in the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Automated quality gates in CI are a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy with no legal or social concerns.
evidence_implementability: Writing schema assertions and SPC checks in existing CI pipelines is reasonably feasible, though defining drift and risk signatures requires some effort and process change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying log completeness and risk-relevant events per Article 12(2)(a).
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure log quality in development builds but does not cover production logging, post-market monitoring, or human-oversight identification, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logs as a scientific instrument designed with the hypothesis is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, but 'compliance by design' is a fairly familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into hypothesis and experimental design, which is paradigm stretching, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Designing logs early with a named traceability role violates no legal or social norms and fits regulatory expectations, though it is slightly more than the bare-minimum approach.
evidence_implementability: It needs process changes and a new co-designer role per high-risk project, but these are reasonably feasible measures without major cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D practices, with a clear action producing traceable, useful records.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing logs early would help meet Article 12 and support post-market monitoring, but it does not specify the minimum logging elements or retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code tests in CI are a fairly common DevOps idea applied to logging, so it is sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI compliance checks are a common, norm-respecting engineering practice that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: It requires building schema-based fixtures per Annex III category and sandbox harnesses, which is some work but reasonably feasible with standard CI tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring systems technically emit the Article 12 required logs (do X to verify logging, which is part of the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch missing log event classes pre-merge, contributing to the logging mandate but not covering retention, content adequacy in production, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reconciling log retention with GDPR is a predictable and mundane compliance step that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, adding a policy document without changing how the lab works or how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Co-authoring a retention and GDPR policy with the DPO is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It is mainly a governance document and policy work with existing staff, which is low-cost, though per-category retention windows and access tiers need some technical changes.
evidence_applicability: The protocol addresses an implied problem related to the stated one, namely that Article 12 logs must be stored and handled without colliding with data-protection law, rather than the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by governing retention, access and pseudonymisation of logs, but it does not itself deliver the automatic event recording or the traceability content that Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing logging in from the start (privacy/security-by-design analog) is a familiar, sensible idea with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (traceability spec at kickoff, logging-first design) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches or how compliance relates to the science, though it does integrate logging into the research planning somewhat.
evidence_acceptability: Shift-left design and kickoff documentation are sensible, norm-compliant practices that offend no one.
evidence_implementability: Adding a traceability specification to project kickoffs and designing logging at the architecture stage requires process and pipeline changes but no radical investment, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring event recording capabilities exist in systems, tied to intended purpose as the Article requires.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help ensure logging capability exists and is appropriate to purpose, but it covers only design specification and not the specific content requirements, retention, or post-market use, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared internal logging library is a common, expected response, though forcing scaffold failure without it and version-locking schemas with model weights add a modest touch of imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and makes logging a default dependency in project scaffolds, but it still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Standard internal engineering practice that violates no norms, although mandatory scaffold failure may cause mild friction among researchers.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over six weeks and a monorepo template change is a low-cost, reasonably non-radical effort that is quite feasible with existing resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building the automatic event-recording capability the article requires.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared SDK enforcing Article 12(3) schema fields and persistent storage would, if adopted, deliver most of the technical logging capability, but it leaves out Article 12(2) event-relevance judgments, retention, and the non-logging documentation duties, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware with decorators is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging infrastructure and explicitly leaves researchers' way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging library for compliance is a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a lightweight library with a single decorator call that plugs into existing stacks is a modest, non-radical change, though tamper-evident storage adds some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate by capturing events in a tamper-evident store.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver the automatic event recording Article 12(1) requires, but it does not cover the Annex III-specific fields such as reference databases or identification of verifying persons, nor does it address the risk-relevance of events or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library baked into the dev framework is a common, expected response for labs, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK, schemas) and shifts logging earlier in prototyping, but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the R&D-compliance relationship much.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library with append-only storage is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an SDK, schemas, and multi-year append-only storage and making it default across Python and C++ repos requires some changes and moderate effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping event schemas to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) in the lab's R&D workflow.
evidence_effectiveness: It would give prototypes automatic lifetime event recording, but it covers mainly generic logging and not Article 12(3) specifics, retention details, or the adequacy of the logged events, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-CI-gate or shift-left checks are a familiar DevOps approach, so this is interesting but expected rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a process gate that still treats compliance as logging practice layered onto the existing workflow, introducing a checklist but not changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a CI-automated compliance checkpoint to existing sprints is a common, norm-respecting engineering practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing sprint cadence and CI with a three-item checklist and no new roles, so it is a low-cost, non-radical change, though log schema and doc tooling need some setup.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate (Art. 12 logs and up-to-date documentation) during R&D by ensuring traces exist at each milestone.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps prevent retroactive instrumentation and ensures logging exists, but it checks only schema conformance and flags rather than the substantive Art. 12(2)-(3) event content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating Article 12 logs as an experimental variable in a replication study is unusual and shows some imagination, though it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as an object of scientific study and links it to what the lab researches, but it does not change how the lab's R&D relates to its compliance obligations, so it introduces new elements while still treating compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Replication research on published papers and logging is a legitimate academic activity that violates no norms, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Re-running a benchmark suite of published high-risk AI papers under two documentation conditions is expensive and difficult, and it is a large research undertaking given that the lab needs to commit scarce implementation resources, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The study examines the effects of Article 12 logging on reproducibility, which relates only indirectly to the lab's decision on how to meet the logging mandate or adapt its R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: A research study would produce evidence about policy effects but would not make the lab compliant or settle how to implement logging, so it is unlikely to solve the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in CI pipelines are a fairly expected, mundane response, though mapping them to Article 12 sub-paragraphs is sensible, so it is merely interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (automated validation in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal automated compliance testing is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A schema-assertion harness run in existing CI is a modest build with low cost and non-radical changes to workflow, though mapping vague legal text to rules takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that prototypes' logs contain the required fields, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI-based validator checks logging output against Article 12 requirements and helps verify compliance, but it does not itself design the logging, retention, or cover post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as a design-time requirement (compliance by design) is a fairly common recommendation, though the compute-release gating adds a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes how R&D projects are scoped and funded so compliance is woven into the research design, and it links compliance to winning public contracts, which stretches the relationship between R&D and obligations without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Adding intake requirements and funding gates is a normal governance practice that offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a template change and a gating rule with no new headcount, though some researcher process change is required.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly by requiring Article 12(2) event emission at design time.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing in event recording helps meet the logging mandate, but it does not specify actual log content, retention, or Article 12(3) requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Assigning document owners and review cycles tied to change management is a very common, mundane compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance process practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Document governance and sign-off workflows are common strategies violating no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing change-management workflows and requires only a register and review triggers, so it is easy and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied related problem (documentation currency under Recital 71) rather than the directly stated logging mandate of Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping technical documentation current addresses Recital 71's documentation requirement but does not implement the automatic event logging mandated by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: An embeddable logging SDK wired into a prototype template is a sensible but common engineering response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK/sidecar) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding default logging tooling is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a Rust SDK with Python bindings and adding it to a template repo is a modest, reasonably feasible engineering effort with a sidecar design limiting disruption.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the Article 12(3) items as structured events.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the Article 12(3) minimums but covers only Annex III 1(a) fields and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) traceability, risk-event and post-market monitoring needs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying chaos-engineering to verify logging survives rapid prototype iteration is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process (recurring chaos drills) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Regular testing drills are a normal engineering and compliance-assurance practice that offends no norms, though the chaos framing is slightly uncommon.
evidence_implementability: It requires scripting scenarios and recurring effort each sprint, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial change to workflow.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying Article 12(2) events are captured during R&D iteration.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging robustness but only verifies logging and does not itself build the logging or cover documentation and other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory logs as a longitudinal research corpus for drift science is interesting and imaginative, though not wholly unexpected or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning compliance artefacts into a research asset and producing new community offerings, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing logs for internal analytics and publishing benchmarks is a somewhat unusual strategy that offends no norms, though publishing benchmarks derived from production logs raises data-protection and confidentiality questions that must be managed.
evidence_implementability: It needs an analytics pipeline, drift benchmarks, and curated open releases on top of the logging backends, which is a significant but feasible effort that goes beyond the compliance logging itself.
evidence_applicability: It is linked to Article 72 post-market monitoring, but it addresses an implied research benefit rather than the directly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself satisfy Article 12 logging requirements and only contributes indirectly through monitoring methods, so it is at best a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Using mandated logs as a basis for research on predictive risk-signal detection with partner data is uncommon and imaginative, though not wholly surprising given existing anomaly-detection and drift research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes logs from a compliance artifact into a research asset and changes what the lab researches (safety-monitoring science), altering the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Partnering with deployers to collect anonymised logs for research and publishing is a somewhat unusual but legitimate strategy, though data-sharing and confidentiality concerns may raise mild sensitivities.
evidence_implementability: An eighteen-month programme requiring two external partners, log access agreements, and validated temporal anomaly models is a significant, costly and difficult undertaking, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It targets identifying Article 79(1) risks and feeding Article 72 monitoring, which are the purposes of the logging mandate, but it doesn't directly address how the lab meets the logging requirement itself, so it addresses an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to making logs useful for risk detection and post-market monitoring but does not by itself provide the lab's logging capability or compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using a compliance-cost gate in project intake is a sensible, interesting process idea but resembles ordinary budget-planning practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a workshop and scoring step to the intake process but still treats compliance as a logging cost to manage, leaving the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A joint intake review workshop with the compliance team is a common governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires modest process changes, a recurring half-day workshop, and a scoring method, which is reasonably feasible within existing quarterly cycles.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (budget overruns from retrofitted Article 12 logging) that relates to but is not the direct logging requirement in the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A budget-scoring gate at intake helps plan for logging costs but does not itself deliver the logging capability, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Building logging into project templates is a sensible, fairly expected 'compliance by design' response and shows little surprise or ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (template scaffolding, pre-wired middleware) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moved earlier in the workflow, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Default tooling and templates are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing containerised build pipeline and template repository, so it needs only moderate changes and is reasonably feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the Article 12(1) logging mandate and the Annex III 1(a) fields, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably cover logging capabilities in new prototypes, but it does not address existing systems, Article 12(2) event relevance, log retention, or production deployment, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance requirements into grant charters with a contingency funding pool is a sensible but fairly expected governance move, with modest imagination in the funding mechanism.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (mandatory logging work package in project charters) but still treats compliance as logging practice, though it moves logging into project planning rather than weaving it into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Amending an SOP and using a contingency pool is a common administrative strategy that violates no norms, though PIs may grumble about added overhead.
evidence_implementability: It requires only an SOP/template amendment and a contingency fund allocation, which are non-radical changes, though the pool needs institutional funding and the work packages need real effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how the lab organizes itself to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring logging design is planned and funded in R&D projects.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by ensuring logging is planned and budgeted early, but it is only a process safeguard and does not itself specify what to log or deliver compliant logging capabilities, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI gate that tests logs against Article 12 fields is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response, with some interest in the synthetic edge-case harness but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI compliance gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI are a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a test-harness container and CI check requires some engineering work and defining per-risk-class field schemas, but it is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that prototype logs contain the Article 12 fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch missing mandatory log fields early but cannot judge whether logged events are truly relevant or cover organizational duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal pre-deployment compliance review gates are a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A pre-release compliance gate with a checklist is a standard governance process that still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves R&D ways of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gates are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A checklist-based review office with a two-week audit window is reasonably feasible with modest process additions, though the delay adds some burden.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of verifying that systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate verifies logging but does not build the logging capability or address R&D adaptation, so it contributes to rather than fully solves compliance, and the checklist wrongly leans on Article 79 and operator-verification items beyond Article 12's scope.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging microservice with write-once storage and cryptographic chain-of-custody is a sensible but fairly expected response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a shared tamper-evident logging service but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized, tamper-evident logging is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared service and integrating it across every high-risk system in the portfolio requires significant cross-team change and cost, though it is feasible with standard technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by providing automatic event recording for high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a standardized logging layer would fulfill Article 12(1)-(2) for the lab's systems, though it does not explicitly cover Annex III 1(a) minimums or adapt R&D, so it is nearly but not fully complete.

evidence_originality: Structured event logging via middleware and append-only streams is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Instrumenting pipelines with logging middleware is a standard, uncontroversial compliance approach that violates no norms, though storing biometric match data and verifier identities raises minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: Lightweight middleware wrappers around existing scoring functions are reasonably feasible, but restructuring serving pipelines and capturing reference DB versions and verifier identities requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate for biometric systems by naming each required field and mapping it to a mechanism.
evidence_effectiveness: Emitting the four Article 12(3) fields into an append-only stream at each inference would fully satisfy the Annex III 1(a) logging mandate if done, though it does not address the broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging or R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated log fields as observable experimental variables is an imaginative and uncommon angle compared with typical logging-infrastructure responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science itself so records double as experimental evidence, which is paradigm stretching, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing a methodological framework and drafting internal protocols violates no norms, though framing compliance as research design is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A methods group drafting an internal protocol is feasible with some changes, but peer-reviewed publication and reworking experimental design around log schemas takes real effort and is outside the lab's control.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (aligning R&D practice with logging requirements and reusing the records) that relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D, rather than directly meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Treating log fields as experimental variables could make compliance records do double duty, but it is mostly a research-methods framework that does not itself deliver the Article 12 logging capability, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left log-completeness testing is a fairly common and mundane DevOps approach, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a scripted verification tool but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing workflow, so at most slightly stretching; arguably preserving, but the new mandatory gate is a new process element.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance tests in release gates is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding automated log-field checks to an existing CI/CD pipeline is a modest, low-cost change using standard tooling, though defining the checks takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying required log fields are captured before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that logs are present and well-formed but does not itself design logging or cover runtime, retention, or risk-relevant event coverage, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized, continuously updated documentation system with stewards and quarterly audits is a common, mundane compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a centralized platform, stewards, and audits but treats compliance as standard documentation practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation management with audits is a standard strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a new platform and process roles, but these are reasonably feasible changes using existing sprint structures and compliance functions.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation (Recital 71) rather than the automatic event logging mandated by Article 12, so it solves an implied, related problem rather than the stated logging problem directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Up-to-date documentation helps with compliance and inspections but does not provide automatic event recording or logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalizing event-relevance for Article 12(2) as a theoretical research problem with drift thresholds is an unusual, interesting angle that shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research question feeding the lab's theoretical core, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than merely adding logging tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Research-oriented compliance work violates no norms, but regulators and managers may find a theoretical programme an unusual response to a compliance deadline.
evidence_implementability: A multi-step research programme deriving formal threshold conditions across existing deployments is a significant, uncertain undertaking that goes beyond committing implementation resources to a deliverable.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(2) requirement of deciding which events are relevant to record, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Formal criteria for event relevance would help define what to log but do not deliver the logging mechanism, retention, or Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Consolidating compliance logging onto existing MLOps monitoring is a common, expected response with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds no new elements beyond extending tooling and still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing monitoring infrastructure for compliance is a common, sensible business practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing dashboard and data pipeline with log storage and retention is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the logging and post-market monitoring mandate of Articles 12 and 72, which is the stated problem, by extending existing infrastructure to store event logs.
evidence_effectiveness: Event-log storage, retention scheduling and query interfaces would meet much of Article 12's recording obligation, but it does not specify which events are logged, nor does it address Article 12(2) traceability or Annex III-specific minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Defining semantically meaningful events and positioning the lab as the authority is a somewhat unusual and thoughtful angle, but standardization-oriented taxonomy work is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (an event taxonomy and reference specification) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, not changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Producing a reference specification for regulators and engineers violates no norms and is a common, welcome kind of compliance-supporting activity.
evidence_implementability: Surveying architectures and formalising and validating a taxonomy needs substantial research effort and expertise but is reasonably feasible with moderate resources.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets what events must be logged under Article 12(2), which is an identified part of the logging mandate the lab must meet.
evidence_effectiveness: A validated event taxonomy and log granularity specification would materially help determine and meet Article 12(2) obligations, but it is a methodological study and does not itself implement logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking storage architectures before committing is sensible engineering but a fairly common, mundane approach to logging requirements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a benchmarking process but still treats compliance as a logging infrastructure practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A internal sandbox benchmarking experiment is a standard, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a sandbox cluster, synthetic workloads, and simulation of multi-year volumes, which are reasonably feasible with some effort and cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (avoiding storage bottlenecks for lifetime log retention) that relates to the stated logging mandate rather than the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help pick a storage architecture, which is only one partial piece of meeting the logging mandate (no event definitions, content, or governance).

evidence_originality: Linking open-science release tiers to compliance documentation is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (tiered release policy, documentation generator) and ties compliance to research-sharing practice, but still largely treats compliance as documentation/logging practice, so it is slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Open-science sharing with tiered release policies and documentation tooling is a somewhat unusual but non-offensive strategy that respects legal norms.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a tiered release policy and an automated documentation generator, piloted on two projects this quarter, involves some tooling and process changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It targets an implied problem, reconciling open-science practice with documentation obligations, which relates to but is not directly the logging mandate; it also misreads Recital 71 as rewarding openness.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses documentation currency and versioning with log schemas, but does not itself implement Article 12's automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in pipelines are fairly known, but tying them to the substantial-modification trigger for logging baselines shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool-like element (a CI gate) into the workflow but still treats compliance as a logging and documentation practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Gating deployments with sign-off in CI/CD is a common, norm-compliant engineering and compliance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing CI runner with configurable rules and diff reports, though defining and tuning substantial-modification criteria and thresholds takes some work, so it needs some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified part of the mandate, detecting situations of substantial modification named in Article 12(2)(a), so it solves an identified problem related to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate would catch substantial modifications and force re-validation logging, which helps with Article 12(2)(a), but it leaves unaddressed the core logging mandate (what to log, retention, post-market monitoring), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Versioned living documentation with stewards, change-trigger alerts and quarterly audits is a very common, expected compliance response, with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's R&D workflow and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation stewards and internal audits are conventional strategies that violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Versioned repositories, alerts and designated stewards are low-cost, non-radical changes using existing tooling, though they require some process discipline.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation requirement in Recital 71 directly, but Article 12 concerns automatic event logging and the proposal does not address logging itself, so the link to the stated logging mandate is only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Up-to-date documentation helps compliance and traceability, but it does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a reusable logging library is a fairly expected response, though open-sourcing it and positioning it as a reference implementation aligned with standards bodies adds some interesting, somewhat unusual twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open-source library, standards-forum engagement, tender positioning) and turns compliance into a reusable asset and market position, but still treats compliance primarily as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing under an EU-friendly licence and engaging standards bodies violates no norms and is a common, welcome practice.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers for one quarter is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though it requires some changes such as standards engagement and documentation.
