evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing logging schemas for common high-risk categories.
evidence_effectiveness: A reference logger would meet the logging requirements for common categories and reduce cost, but it covers only the most common categories and not wider obligations like documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning logging transparency into a public white paper used as a sales asset is somewhat unusual and interesting, but publishing documentation for marketing is a familiar tactic, so it is not truly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new element (public white paper and contract appendix) and reframes compliance as a market differentiator, yet the lab's R&D and logging practice stay essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing transparency documentation and including it in contracts is a common business strategy that offends no norms, though disclosure of logging details needs security vetting.
evidence_implementability: Writing and quarterly refreshing a document with marketing and engineering is low-cost and requires only non-radical process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, turning compliance into a commercial benefit and customer transparency, which relates to the response but does not directly meet the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not implement or ensure the automatic logging capability required by Article 12, so it only contributes a partial benefit around communication and market positioning.

evidence_originality: Publishing an open traceability standard as a community benchmark is a somewhat unusual and interesting move that shows some imagination, but standards and reference implementations are a known response pattern.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the lab's relationship to compliance from consumer to knowledge-setter and treats traceability as research methodology, creating new offerings born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Open publication and engagement with conformity-assessment bodies violate no norms and are welcomed practice, though sharing prototype details is mildly unusual.
evidence_implementability: A three-person working group drafting a schema and releasing GitHub implementations is reasonably feasible, but gaining community adoption and regulator uptake requires considerable effort beyond the lab's control.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12 logging requirements by defining a metadata schema (timestamps, lineage, versioning, human identifiers) and validating it on the lab's own Annex III 1(a) prototypes, though much of the effort is aimed at community standard-setting.
evidence_effectiveness: A published schema with reference implementations would help the lab's own logging compliance but does not itself implement logging in its systems or guarantee conformity-assessment acceptance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building traceability into experiment tracking and reusing the logs as a failure-mode dataset is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but wrapping MLflow-type trackers with schemas is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Weaving logging into the experimental process as the default record and mining the logs for science changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, which fits paradigm stretching, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using standard experiment trackers and mandating their use for compliance violates no norms, though a mandate may draw some researcher friction.
evidence_implementability: Wrapping existing orchestration tools with structured schemas is reasonably feasible, but refactoring training pipelines and mandating use next quarter involves some real engineering change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping event schemas to 12(2)(a)-(c) and the Annex III minimums, so it solves an identified problem tied to the stated one.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially meet the logging requirements for R&D-stage systems, but Article 12 concerns deployed system logging capability, and experiment logs may not ensure the deployed system's lifetime automatic logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12 logs into a public benchmark for detecting Article 79(1) risk events is an unusual and imaginative reframing that few labs would propose, though benchmarks as a format are familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making the regulatory logging requirement a shared research problem and creating new partnerships with regulators and participants.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing anonymised traces and co-developing rubrics with regulators is an uncommon but not offensive strategy, though data-sharing and confidentiality concerns exist.
evidence_implementability: Anonymising real deployment logs, annotating risk episodes, and hosting annual evaluations requires significant effort, privacy/legal review, and ongoing resources, but is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, understanding what logs can reveal about risk, which relates to the logging mandate but does not directly implement the required logging capabilities.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to research on log utility but would not by itself meet the lab's own logging obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Schema versioning and tiered retention for logs is a sensible but expected engineering response, with only modest insight in linking it to substantial modifications.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces some new tooling and formats but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Versioned schemas, immutable object storage and tiered retention are common engineering practices that violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires data-engineering effort for schemas, lifecycle rules and migration tooling, which is reasonably feasible with standard cloud technology but is more than trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(1) mandate for automatic logging over the system's lifetime and the 12(2) traceability purposes, so it solves an identified problem tied to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A versioned schema and retention architecture would make logs durable and interpretable across modifications, but it does not itself decide which events to log or cover the Annex III 3(a)-(d) minimum content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compiling logging semantics into execution graphs as research is unusual and shows imagination, but the 'native vs bolt-on' framing is a fairly familiar idea in auditability discussions.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging a native architectural research topic rather than a bolt-on, though it stops short of redefining what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Architectural research into auditable systems violates no norms and is an uncommon but entirely acceptable response to regulation.
evidence_implementability: Building three reference architectures with logging compiled into execution graphs is a significant, costly research effort with uncertain outcomes, and the lab needs committed implementation resources rather than exploration.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly, with the clear X (native logging architecture) to Y (automatic event recording) link.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, it would help meet the Article 12 automatic logging requirement and lower overhead, but it addresses only part of the mandate (what events to log, retention, minimum fields) and is a research prototype rather than a compliance solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation tied to commits and release gates is a mundane, widely expected response to documentation duties.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though a release gate adds a minor process element.
evidence_acceptability: Keeping technical documentation current with a release gate is a common, uncontroversial compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning writers per product line and adding a release gate are modest process changes with reasonable cost, not radical.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (documentation currency per Recital 71) rather than the Article 12 automatic logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the technical documentation upkeep from Recital 71 but does not implement the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tamper-evident hashed logs in a dedicated pipeline are a predictable, mundane response to the logging requirement.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with isolation of the biometric logs and no change to how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: A dedicated, legally coordinated audit pipeline with retention and access controls is a standard compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a dedicated pipeline and extending existing provenance tooling, which means some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) logging minimums with tamper-evident logs, but it covers only the biometric subset and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging across other high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: Tying documentation updates to milestone reviews is a sensible but fairly common idea that an experienced evaluator would expect, with a small touch of insight on staff rotation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checklist to existing stage-gate meetings and treats compliance as a documentation practice, so the lab's way of working is largely unchanged, though it does embed documentation in the research milestones a little.
evidence_acceptability: Using existing review meetings and assigning ownership to lab managers violates no legal or social norms and is a common governance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing meetings and adds only a checklist and assigned owners, so it is easy and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of keeping documentation current under Recital 71, which is related to the mandate but not the logging itself, making it an implied fit.
evidence_effectiveness: It keeps technical documentation current but does not address the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance telemetry as a new category of open scientific data with shared anonymization schemas is an unusual and imaginative angle that few labs would propose in response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning compliance logs into research data and partnerships with universities, which is paradigm stretching rather than a new view of what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Sharing de-identified data under data-use agreements is a somewhat uncommon strategy, but privacy, confidentiality and GDPR concerns about releasing operational logs make it slightly sensitive though not offensive.
evidence_implementability: It requires only two researchers, a pilot on one system class and a limited release to three partners, which is a reasonably feasible scope though anonymization and legal review add some effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal concerns using mandated logs as shared scientific data, which relates to the logging mandate only indirectly and does not directly address how to comply with Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Publishing a whitepaper and a de-identified corpus would not make the lab's systems meet the logging requirements, so it is unlikely to solve the stated compliance problem and at most contributes marginally.

evidence_originality: Wrapping services with logging sidecars and append-only stores is a familiar engineering pattern, and applying it to biometric match auditing is a sensible but expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (a sidecar or decorator layer) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Tamper-evident audit logging is a common, regulator-aligned strategy that violates no norms, though biometric logging raises some data-protection considerations that stay manageable.
evidence_implementability: Sidecar or decorator integration through configuration with no model refactoring is reasonably feasible with moderate engineering effort, though capturing verifier identity and database versioning needs some integration work.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly captures the Article 12(3) minimum logging items (reference database, input data, match results, verifier identity), which is an identified part of the stated logging-mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If deployed, it would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) logging minimums with tamper-evident storage, but it covers only biometric systems and not the Article 12(2) relevance of events or the wider compliance duties, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding automatic structured logging in experiment tooling is a sensible and fairly expected response, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (a telemetry layer, an append-only event store) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though it moves logging into the research pipeline rather than the deployed system.
evidence_acceptability: It is a standard engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing MLflow harness with mandatory telemetry and an append-only store is a reasonably feasible set of engineering changes, though it requires some workflow changes for researchers.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, with a clear X (native logging) leading to Y (compliance-ready records).
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the logging mandate by providing traceability and documentation, but it covers only the R&D pipeline and not the deployed system's Article 12 event logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Productizing compliance tooling as open-source is an interesting and somewhat unusual move, but compliance-tooling vendors and open-source logging libraries are fairly familiar, so it shows some imagination without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance into a distributable product and a market offering changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations (new offerings born from compliance), which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release with permissive licence and compliance documentation violates no norms, though usage analytics in a distributed library might raise mild privacy concerns, which are manageable and generally accepted.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team over one quarter is a reasonable, feasible commitment, though maintaining a public SDK and supporting clients adds some ongoing change and cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building the logging capability and mapping it to each sub-paragraph.
evidence_effectiveness: An SDK implementing Article 12 schemas internally would credibly meet the logging mandate for the lab's own systems, though it does not itself address the Annex III 3 minimums beyond documented functions or broader record-keeping, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logging into a client-facing differentiator is unusual and shows some imagination, though assurance dossiers are a familiar commercial move.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by making logging a product feature and sales asset, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Exposing log architecture to clients under contract is somewhat unusual and raises confidentiality and data-protection questions, but it offends no norms and is commercially sensible.
evidence_implementability: A one-page brief and a read-only gated endpoint on existing logs require some cross-team work and security considerations but are reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (leveraging compliance for client assurance and market position) that relates to how the lab responds to the logging mandate but is not the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself implement Article 12's automatic event logging; it only exposes and markets logs that must already exist, so it is at best a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a scientific dataset for studying real-world AI reliability is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not completely unprecedented, since the field already uses deployment monitoring data.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making regulatory logs a source of research and a new research line, which stretches the paradigm, though it does not rethink what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing deployment logs for research raises data protection, confidentiality, and customer-consent concerns, which offend sensibilities somewhat, though anonymisation mitigates this and the idea is not unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: Pooling anonymised production logs across projects and building new statistical and causal methods needs significant new data infrastructure, governance, and research effort, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal uses the Article 12 logs as a research dataset, which relates to the logging mandate only implicitly and does not directly address how to meet the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not by itself satisfy the logging mandate (what to log, retention, traceability) but contributes value by exploiting the logs, so it is only a partial solution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Formalising a minimal sufficient log set via causal information-flow metrics is an unusual, imaginative framing that few labs would propose in response to a logging mandate, though not entirely unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new theoretical elements and ties research into compliance, but it still ultimately treats compliance as logging design rather than changing what the lab researches or how compliance relates to R&D.
evidence_acceptability: A research study to define minimal logs violates no norms, and regulators and organizations would find it acceptable, though minimizing logs could raise some eyebrows about compliance sufficiency.
evidence_implementability: Deriving rigorous causal information-flow bounds for arbitrary high-risk architectures is a difficult, open research problem requiring significant effort, though synthetic-workload validation is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of what events are relevant under Article 12(2) and how to meet the logging mandate with appropriate granularity.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, theoretical bounds would inform what to log but would not itself implement logging or satisfy Article 12 obligations, so it only partially solves the problem and results may not map to legal sufficiency.

evidence_originality: Reusable shared logging middleware is a common, expected engineering response to a logging requirement, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling (centralized logging middleware) that treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralizing compliance tooling and adopting it at design review is a common strategy that breaks no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building one SDK in two sprints and integrating it into existing CI/CD requires some engineering change and adoption effort but is reasonably feasible, with the two-sprint estimate somewhat optimistic.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, with explicit mapping to Article 12 fields and to the cost of compliance for R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging SDK that captures the Article 12(1)-(3) events would, if built, meet the core logging mandate, though it leaves out the documentation and post-market monitoring processes the regulation also touches.

evidence_originality: Using self-monitoring OOD/anomaly detectors to generate Article 12 logs is an interesting and somewhat imaginative link, but anomaly detection for monitoring is a familiar concept in the field.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (auxiliary detector models, a signal class, benchmarks) and ties compliance to research output, yet still treats compliance as a logging mechanism rather than changing the lab's relationship to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building on-system monitoring and structured alert logs is a legitimate, norm-conforming research and compliance approach that offends no sensibilities, though framing it as replacing human audit is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Developing benchmark datasets and reliable OOD detectors that run in real time as auxiliary models is a substantial research effort with uncertain outcomes, and the approval context requires committing resources to implementation rather than exploration.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12(2)(a) by building detectors that flag risk-relevant events and feed Article 72 monitoring, which is an identified part of the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Self-run anomaly detectors would contribute to meeting 12(2)(a) event recording, but they are a research programme that does not cover the basic logging mandate (12(1), 12(3)) and their detection reliability is uncertain, so the solution is only partial.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK with declarative config is a mundane and expected response for a lab facing a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, which is paradigm preserving, perhaps slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal compliance tooling is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin middleware agent hooked into existing pipelines with YAML config is reasonably feasible and needs some platform-team work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate across the lab's R&D prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: A default-on logging middleware that captures the Article 12(2) event classes would largely meet the logging mandate, though it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or the wider documentation duties, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-source compliance tooling is a fairly foreseeable response for research labs, with some interest in the benchmark and schema-standardisation angle but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Releasing an open-source toolkit with co-maintained partners and a publication introduces new elements and turns compliance into a community offering and reputational position, stretching the compliance-R&D relationship, though it remains fundamentally about logging.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release with academic partners and publication violates no norms, though releasing a toolkit to the wider field is somewhat uncommon for compliance responses and may raise minor IP concerns.
evidence_implementability: Building a toolkit, benchmark suite, partner co-maintenance and a peer-reviewed paper within eighteen months is a significant resource commitment for a lab with scarce implementation resources, though feasible.
evidence_applicability: The toolkit directly addresses Article 12 logging, including the paragraph 3 minimum fields, so it solves an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab and others instrument prototypes for logging, but it is only a partial solution, since it covers just schemas and tooling and not the lab's own deployment, retention, or oversight obligations, and the open release adds no compliance guarantee.

evidence_originality: Reframing mandatory logs as a longitudinal scientific dataset with an open benchmark is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance logs a source of scientific data and research outputs, i.e. logging woven into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Using the lab's own deployment logs for research and open-sourcing a toolkit is somewhat unusual but offends no legal or social norms, though publishing the dataset raises mild privacy and confidentiality questions.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting lab deployments and building change-detection algorithms validated with fault injection is reasonably feasible but requires additional research effort, data governance, and engineering beyond baseline logging.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of making logs useful for post-market monitoring and risk identification under Article 12(2), which relates to but is not the direct logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The approach would improve post-market monitoring capability but does not itself ensure the lab meets the Article 12 logging mandate, so it contributes only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning post-market monitoring log analysis into a publishable research programme with shareable modules is interesting and somewhat unusual, but not wholly surprising as a response to the mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance a research output and creating partner-adoptable offerings born from the obligation.
evidence_acceptability: Research on monitoring methods and sharing modules with partners offends no legal or social norms and is a reasonable strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two senior researchers and a data engineer for eighteen months is a sizeable but reasonably feasible commitment for an R&D lab, though generalising to partners adds difficulty.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets using logs for post-market monitoring and operation monitoring under Article 12(2)(b) and (c), though it does not itself address how to implement the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Anomaly-detection on logs would contribute to monitoring and traceability aims but does not cover the core logging capability, event recording requirements, or Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance reviews are a standard, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (milestone gating) but still treats compliance as a logging and documentation review practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gates and sign-offs are a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though they may meet some engineering resistance.
evidence_implementability: Adding milestone review gates with an assigned compliance reviewer is a modest process change using existing staff and sprint structures, though it requires some new roles and coordination.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging and record-keeping mandate by reviewing log design, documentation currency, and monitoring hooks during development.
evidence_effectiveness: Gate reviews would contribute substantially to compliance but do not themselves build the logging capability or guarantee technical adequacy, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware with OpenTelemetry is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D workflow essentially unchanged apart from a design-gate registration step.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized shared logging layer is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing container orchestration with an OpenTelemetry collector by two platform engineers is a modest, reasonably feasible change using standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (automatic recording of event categories) across systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would automate event logging required by Article 12 but does not address the content of what events are relevant, retention, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution to the broader response problem.

evidence_originality: A CI gate that tests log conformance is a sensible, fairly expected DevOps-style response to a logging mandate, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (automated CI conformance test) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building test scenarios and a pipeline stage requires some effort but uses standard CI tooling and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses verifying that logs meet Article 12 requirements, which is part of meeting the logging mandate, though it covers only (a)-(c) fields and not the logging capability itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps verify and maintain log conformance but does not build the logging itself and cannot fully judge relevance of events or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: An open benchmark for logging compliance quality is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, but benchmarks and open releases are a familiar research response and it is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (benchmark, open publication) and turns compliance into a research output and community offering, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations somewhat.
evidence_acceptability: Open research releases and benchmarks violate no norms, though publishing under an open license is a somewhat unusual compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building reference implementations, test scenarios, and a public release is a substantial but reasonably feasible research project for an AI lab.
evidence_applicability: Building reference implementations of the Article 12(3) sub-requirements directly addresses meeting the logging mandate, though the benchmark and publication parts are only implied to serve the lab's own compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: Reference implementations help the lab meet Article 12(3) for Annex III 1(a) systems, but the benchmark covers only that narrow scope and does not address Article 12(1)-(2) or the lab's broader R&D, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging by construction at the inference layer is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, though 'logging built-in' and observability instrumentation are fairly familiar notions.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new architectural element (log-native inference layer) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a logging architecture and building tamper-evident logs violates no legal or social norms, though open-sourcing internal pipelines is somewhat less common than standard compliance.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting every transformer block and internal decision node with tamper-evident emitters on current pipelines requires significant engineering change and risks performance overhead, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need to meet the logging mandate by producing structured automatic event records, though the open-source and research-community framing is tangential.
evidence_effectiveness: Logging at every internal node would help meet Article 12 event recording, but Article 12 requires event-level traceability, not internal activations, so it is a partial solution and does not address the lab's decisions on use-period or reference-database fields explicitly.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing observability infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, sensible and expected response, not imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds middleware to the existing stack but treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, even though it frames compliance as a byproduct of SRE monitoring.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding automatic logging in the serving stack using existing observability tools is a common, norm-compliant engineering approach.
evidence_implementability: It needs a middleware layer built over two sprints on existing Kubernetes and Prometheus/Grafana infrastructure, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes at low marginal cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the automatic logging mandate, including the Article 12(3) minimum items such as use period, input data and match outcomes.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic per-inference logging of timestamps, input references and match outcomes would satisfy much of Article 12(1) and 12(3), but it does not clearly cover risk-situation identification, post-market monitoring needs, human verifier identification, or log retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance stage-gates and design reviews are a very common and expected response to a regulatory mandate, with the cost-of-retrofit argument being mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice using a checkpoint review, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate reviews are a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though the gate may add some friction for project leads.
evidence_implementability: A one-page spec and a two-person standing review panel are a small, non-radical process addition that fits into existing sprint planning at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying logging architecture before phase progression.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate would help ensure logging design meets Article 12, but it only checks design specs and does not itself implement logging, retain logs, or cover other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Soak-testing log integrity with simulated multi-year cycles, crashes, database migrations and verifier turnover is a somewhat unusual and sensible idea, but it borrows from standard reliability testing and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a time-accelerated test rig in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated nightly testing of logging middleware is a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a Python test harness with time-acceleration scripts and CI integration requires moderate effort but uses existing tooling and is reasonably feasible, though simulating realistic migrations and crashes takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, which is meeting the logging mandate over the system's lifetime with reliable records.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify that mandatory logs are never dropped and stay queryable, which helps with Article 12 but is only a partial solution because it does not define what to log or address the lab's wider R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: A centralized shared logging layer is a common, mundane engineering response that evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as logging practice and only centralizes it into a shared platform, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging middleware that meets Article 12 requirements is a common, legally compliant strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a standardised logging SDK into existing serving infrastructure is reasonably feasible but requires platform work across projects, so some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specific mandated events.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the logging requirements of Article 12 including the Annex III 1(a) minimums, though it covers only logging and not wider documentation or R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Unifying research provenance with compliance logging is sensible and somewhat imaginative, but fairly expected among thoughtful responses and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves compliance logging into the scientific workflow, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations by merging reproducibility with regulatory records, without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Extending an eval framework with provenance metadata and reproducibility is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-sprint extension of an existing framework led by a senior researcher is low-cost and non-radical, though capturing verifier identity and matched inputs in research runs needs some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified part of the stated problem, the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging fields and how to adapt R&D to them.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding the four Article 12(3) fields into every eval run would meet the minimum logging for Annex III 1(a) in the research harness, but it covers only research/evaluation runs rather than the deployed system's lifetime logging (Art. 12(1)-(2)), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left design review gates and checklist updates are a very common and expected response, so the idea is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checklist item and workshop but treats compliance as logging practice within the existing process, leaving the lab's way of working basically unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Design-review gates and workshops are common governance strategies that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Updating templates and running a half-day workshop is low cost and a non-radical change to existing processes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by requiring event taxonomy and log schema design up front in R&D, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging capability is designed in, but it covers only design planning and does not itself deliver the logging, retention, or verification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design as a design-review gate is a very common, expected response to the mandate (privacy/security-by-design analogue), so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template and checkpoint to existing proposal forms but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a design-review checkpoint is a common governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page template added to the existing proposal form and reviewed by the existing governance board is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate through R&D adaptation by specifying logging before modelling begins.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure new systems have logging specified but does not itself implement Article 12 event recording, cover existing systems, or address minimum content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging microservice mandated across all pipelines is the most obvious, expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice built into the development process without changing how the lab relates R&D to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into architecture is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging service with schema templates is reasonably feasible but requires integrating it into all inference and training pipelines, which means some engineering changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building automatic event recording into systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a mandatory logging layer with timestamps, input references and operator identities would largely satisfy Article 12 logging, though it covers only part of the broader compliance picture such as post-market monitoring relevance and retention.

evidence_originality: Automated, versioned documentation tied to CI/CD is a common, expected response to documentation mandates, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (documentation-as-code pipeline) but still treats compliance as a record-keeping practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation and record retention is a standard, legally aligned compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Documentation-as-code with CI/CD hooks is reasonably feasible using existing tooling, though it needs engineering effort and integration across model versions.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the technical documentation and record-keeping requirements in Recital 71 and supports post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated compliance problem, though it targets documentation rather than the Article 12 event logs themselves.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with documentation and audit readiness but does not implement the automatic event logging that Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code gates in CI are a common and expected response, with only the claim of zero retrofit cost adding any flair.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tool (lint gate, conformance report) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI and sign-off checklists are common engineering governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing CI pipeline with a lint step and a checklist is a modest change at low cost, though parsing diverse logging configs takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: The CI/CD gate directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D by enforcing the required log fields before EU deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A build gate would help ensure schema conformance, but it only checks that logging configuration is present and does not verify that events are actually recorded or retained, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log-based monitoring dashboards with alerting are a common, expected response, though mapping alerts to specific articles adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A monitoring dashboard aligned with legal obligations is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Built by three people on the existing observability stack in two sprints, it needs some new work but no radical change, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need for using logs for post-market monitoring and operation monitoring under Articles 12, 72 and 14, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard supports post-market monitoring and oversight checks but does not itself make systems generate compliant logs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A two-tier log policy with hash-chained aggregated summaries for pre-deployment iterations is a somewhat unusual and thoughtful idea but not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes how R&D iteration relates to compliance by tiering logging by lifecycle stage, though it remains largely a logging-policy adjustment rather than reshaping what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Governance board policy with legal review is a common corporate approach, though reducing log fidelity might raise some regulatory eyebrows.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a policy and adding legal validation gates is reasonably feasible with moderate process changes and hash-chained tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate while adapting R&D practice, specifically the tension between lifetime logging and exploratory research.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help manage the retention burden and the transition gap, but aggregated summaries for R&D iterations may not satisfy Article 12 if prototypes count as high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gap analysis or inventory mapping against regulatory requirements is a common, expected first step and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A telemetry-to-Article-12 gap audit is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal audit and gap matrix is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-week audit using one-page inventories from infrastructure leads and a compliance engineering gap matrix is low cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by determining which Article 12(3) fields are already satisfied and which need new instrumentation.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit only identifies what logging exists versus what is missing and does not itself implement the logging mandate, so it contributes to but only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Inventorying systems, assigning owners and running periodic audits is a standard, expected compliance response with little imaginative or surprising content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice, and the lab's way of working and R&D approach remain unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance registers and audit cadences are common, norm-conforming governance practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A four-week inventory, a register, named owners and quarterly audits are administrative processes needing modest staff time and no radical change to the lab's work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of deciding how to respond to the Article 12 mandate by determining which systems are covered and verifying log schemas, though the technical logging implementation is left implicit.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps scope and verify logging obligations and prioritize effort, but it does not itself build the logging capability or ensure the technical requirements are met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging layer built into the architecture is the obvious, mundane response most labs would give.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, a shared module with no change in how the lab's R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding native logging to meet a legal mandate is a common, conventional compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared telemetry and log-emission layer across all high-risk systems requires some engineering changes, but it is a reasonably feasible, standard software measure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building the mandated event-recording capability.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the logging requirement, which is the core of the mandate, though it does not address the broader documentation or Annex III specifics beyond a general mention.

evidence_originality: Privacy-preserving logging is a recognized topic, but positioning the lab as a reference voice at the logging-versus-data-minimisation intersection is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (cryptographic, differential-privacy, MPC layers) and turns compliance into a research and publication agenda, partly changing the lab's relationship to compliance, but it still centers on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving techniques and publishing research are widely accepted and violate no norms, though the claim of getting ahead of regulators is mildly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Funding several PhD/postdoc teams to prototype MPC and anonymisation is expensive and difficult, and it is exploratory research rather than a committed implementation, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (GDPR conflict with logging personal data) related to the stated problem, and Article 12(3) is named explicitly, though Annex III 1(a) scope is narrow.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would address the GDPR tension in logging, which is a real part of meeting Article 12, but it does not itself deliver the basic logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware built into development templates is a common, expected response to this mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, merely moving logging earlier in the process.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging in by design is a common, compliance-aligned strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a middleware layer and embedding it in the standard development template is a reasonably feasible engineering change requiring some platform investment but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building a module that captures the Article 12(3) minimum items.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable embedded logging layer would, if built, satisfy the core logging requirement across high-risk systems, though it covers mainly the 12(3) items and not all of Article 12(2) event relevance or the documentation duties, so it is nearly but not fully complete.

evidence_originality: Adding a compliance cost estimate to project funding gates is a sensible but fairly expected governance response, with a mildly interesting twist of pairing failing projects to share infrastructure.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a budget template and gate) but still treats compliance as a logging cost to be managed, leaving R&D practice largely unchanged, though the pairing of projects slightly stretches it.
evidence_acceptability: A budget line item in proposal review is a common, uncontroversial management practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It only requires adding a two-page template to the existing proposal form and using existing quarterly reviews, which is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (budgeting for the logging mandate to avoid mid-project overruns) that relates to the stated problem but does not itself implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab plan and fund Article 12 compliance but does not produce logging capability, so it is only a partial contribution to the solution.

evidence_originality: Versioned log envelopes with checkpoint IDs, data hashes, and schema migration are a sensible and somewhat imaginative application of familiar MLOps ideas to the lifetime-logging requirement, but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (envelope format, migration toolchain) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Technical log versioning and schema migration violate no norms and fit regulatory expectations of traceability.
evidence_implementability: Building a log envelope standard and migration tooling requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with existing versioning and data-lineage tooling.
evidence_applicability: The protocol directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 mandate for logs over the system's lifetime by keeping logs coherent across model retraining and swaps.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would keep lifetime logs traceable across system changes, but it covers only the continuity aspect and not the full range of event selection, retention, or Article 12(3) content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging platform with CI checks is a sensible, common engineering response and not particularly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-infrastructure practice that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged, though it adds a platform tool.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised shared infrastructure and CI gating are common engineering strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A six-person platform squad building a middleware logging service integrated with existing CI/CD is a substantial but reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes to workflow.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate by building logging capability into systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver the technical logging capability and consistency across projects, but does not itself define which events are relevant for risk, post-market monitoring, or Annex III minimums, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging by design and default middleware is the standard, expected response and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, merely moved earlier into the architecture, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging in by default is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Embedding logging middleware in the serving stack and auditing prototypes in 90 days requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible, not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (embed automatic logging) to get Y (Article 12(1) compliance), which is the explicitly stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Default automatic logging would substantially satisfy Article 12(1), but it does not address the 12(2) relevance scoping, Annex III 12(3) specifics, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a compliance reference implementation is an interesting, somewhat unusual move, but it is not highly surprising and similar reference-implementation ideas are plausible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by turning compliance into a public asset and a market position, going beyond treating it as internal logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing open-source compliance tooling violates no norms and is well received, though it is a somewhat unusual strategy for a lab.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team over eighteen months is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, although it requires ongoing maintenance and legal diligence.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 logging mandate by building a reference implementation covering all four Article 12(3) fields for Annex III 1(a) systems, though it is framed as a public good rather than strictly the lab's own compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would deliver compliant logging for biometric verification systems and so would solve the lab's logging obligation for that category, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) and leaves general Article 12(1)-(2) logging for other systems as a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized, schema-versioned, append-only log store is a standard and expected response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (versioned event store) but still treats compliance purely as logging infrastructure without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Append-only, versioned log retention is a conventional, legally aligned practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Deploying a partitioned columnar store with a schema registry and archival policy uses mature off-the-shelf technology, requiring some engineering effort but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by retaining logs across system lifetime to support post-market monitoring and risk reconstruction.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially contribute to meeting Article 12 retention and traceability, but it covers storage only and does not define which events to capture or address the other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checks in CI are a mundane, expected response, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool-like process (CI assertions) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, which is at most slight stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Using CI tests to check compliance is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Schema validation wired into an existing GitHub Actions pipeline is low cost and a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking that required log fields exist (do X to get verified log completeness).
evidence_effectiveness: Automated schema assertions in CI would verify that mandated Article 12(3) fields are emitted, which contributes to compliance but does not itself implement logging, cover Article 12(1)-(2) general event recording, or address other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Analyzing logs for drift and risk signals for post-market monitoring is an expected, fairly standard response, though sensibly tied to Article 79 criteria.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (streaming analytics, alerts, dashboards) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Post-market monitoring and reporting to notified bodies is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Streaming analytics, alerting and dashboards on an existing log store are reasonably feasible with standard data-engineering tools, though they require some new build effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(2) purposes of identifying risk situations and facilitating post-market monitoring, which are part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would make the logs useful for monitoring and risk detection, but it does not itself satisfy the logging capability requirements such as the Annex III minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Schema-validation gates in CI are a common, expected DevOps approach to compliance logging, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI gate/log contract) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks for log compliance are a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Defining a log schema and adding a CI step with synthetic workload is a reasonably feasible addition to existing pipelines, though building the contract and workloads takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring systems meet the Article 12 logging requirements, with do X to get compliant logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch missing or malformed logs pre-deployment, helping meet the logging mandate, but it does not address which events matter, retention, or runtime behavior, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Merging scientific reproducibility records with compliance documentation is a sensible and somewhat familiar idea that is interesting but not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It links compliance documentation to the research workflow by making experiment tracking serve both science and regulation, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance modestly, though it remains documentation practice.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized documentation that serves both reviewers and regulators violates no norms and is a common, welcome strategy, though mandatory outputs may cause minor researcher friction.
evidence_implementability: A three-person group drafting a schema in one quarter, piloting on two projects and integrating into an existing tracking pipeline is a reasonably feasible plan with some process changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal documents training, testing, validation and data provenance to meet Recital 71's documentation needs, which relates to the logging/record-keeping mandate but targets technical documentation rather than the automatic event logs of Article 12 itself, so it addresses an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Unified experiment records would help with technical documentation and traceability but do not provide automatic runtime event logging of deployed high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Infrastructure-level default telemetry is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces no new elements beyond a standard logging retrofit and treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building default logging into shared infrastructure is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Patching container orchestration and data-lake ingestion over two sprints using existing infrastructure is a moderate, reasonably feasible change at low incremental cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the identified requirement of automatic event logging under Article 12(1), which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Default telemetry at the infrastructure layer would generate automatic event logs for training and inference, a major part of Article 12(1), but it does not by itself ensure the Article 12(2) event relevance, the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, or the traceability that fits the intended purpose, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK enforced by CI is what an experienced evaluator would expect from labs, so it is mundane, with only slight interest in the build-fail enforcement.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged, though the SDK is a new element.
evidence_acceptability: An internal logging library enforced through CI is a common, legally compliant engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-sprint Python/C++ middleware with a decorator API and a CI check is a reasonably feasible, non-radical build, though integrating across varied pipelines needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified items such as timestamps, reference-database pointers, input data, and operator IDs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would automate event capture for prototypes but only partially solves the mandate, since it doesn't address retention, risk-relevant event selection, post-market monitoring, or Annex III-specific fields beyond a generic mention.

evidence_originality: Log analytics dashboards and anomaly alerts for post-market monitoring are an expected, fairly standard extension of logging, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (streaming analytics, dashboards, automated reports) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for monitoring and regulator reporting is a common, legally aligned strategy, though continuous surveillance of logs may raise minor data protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an event-streaming pipeline, dashboards, thresholds and automated reporting on top of another logging system, which is a significant but feasible engineering effort with some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the logging mandate's stated purposes (Art. 12(2)(b),(c), Art. 72 post-market monitoring, Art. 79(1) risk), so it solves an identified problem related to the stated one.
evidence_effectiveness: Analytics on logs would meaningfully support monitoring and risk detection, but it presupposes the logging architecture and does not itself satisfy the logging requirement, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Release gates and compliance attestations are common and mundane responses that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, a review gate added to the lifecycle, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance release gate with sign-off and audits is a conventional governance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires a new checkpoint, a template, and audit routines, which are some process changes but reasonably feasible with existing QA and compliance staff.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying required log fields are captured before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate verifying log capture, immutability, and retention would largely ensure logging compliance, though it covers only logging and relies on attestation, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Versioning and linking artifacts to logs is a fairly standard MLOps and documentation approach, though the monitoring-triggered review cycles add mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new pipeline and a living knowledge-base framing but still treats compliance as record-keeping practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common, uncontroversial internal governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a structured pipeline linking artifacts and logs plus new review processes, which is reasonably feasible with existing tooling but needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (keeping documentation current and linked to logs, from Recital 71 and Article 72) that relates to the logging mandate rather than the explicit logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Linking model versions, datasets, and validation reports to log entries with monitoring-triggered reviews would help meet documentation and traceability needs, but it centers on technical documentation and does not itself deliver the automatic event logging Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Implementing the enumerated Article 12(3) fields in a dedicated module is the obvious, expected response to the mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice built as a product module, leaving the lab's R&D and compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building mandated logging with legal counsel validation is a common strategy that violates no norms, though it must handle data-protection concerns.
evidence_implementability: A four-person pod prototyping within a quarter on an existing pipeline is reasonably feasible with some changes and moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It explicitly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, meeting the logging mandate for biometric-ID tools, with a clear do-X-to-get-Y link.
evidence_effectiveness: Building the four Article 12(3) capture functions directly satisfies the specific minimum logging requirements for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it does not cover the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging or broader R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Making logging a differentiable, co-optimized structural part of the network is unusual and imaginative compared with typical logging-pipeline responses, though not wholly unprecedented in interpretability/provenance research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the science and architecture of the models (compliance shapes what the lab researches), changing the R&D-compliance relationship, though it stops short of redefining the lab's whole research agenda.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme on compliance-enabling architectures offends no legal or social norms and is an uncommon but acceptable strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires launching open-ended research with two working groups and uncertain outcomes, which is expensive and difficult, and it does not produce deployable logging soon, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It targets the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by changing R&D, but the link to the specific Article 12 requirements is indirect and implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if it worked, in-network trace tokens would only partly satisfy Article 12's event-logging requirements (period of use, reference databases, human verifiers), which need conventional system-level logs, so it helps only partially and is speculative.

evidence_originality: Pricing compliance overhead into project prioritisation is an unusual and sensible angle that most labs would not state in response to a logging mandate, but it is not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal changes how compliance cost feeds into R&D portfolio prioritisation, linking compliance obligations to what the lab researches, though it does not alter the logging itself, so it stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Cost-weighted project prioritisation is a normal management practice that offends no norms, though it may meet some resistance from researchers whose projects score badly.
evidence_implementability: Adding an overhead coefficient to existing resource estimates before the next funding round needs some process change but is reasonably feasible with existing planning tools.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of compliance costs eroding R&D budgets, which relates to adapting R&D to the logging mandate but is not the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps manage budget impact and funding decisions but does not itself deliver the logging capability the mandate requires, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code testing of logs in CI/CD is an interesting and sensible idea but fairly expected among engineering-minded labs, showing only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (declarative assertion harness in CI) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated checks in CI are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Writing assertion rules and adding a pipeline step is reasonably feasible with existing CI tooling, though encoding legal semantics into rules requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying logs satisfy the requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch logging gaps in prototypes but does not itself create the logging capability or cover Annex III specifics or broader obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A public benchmark for logging adequacy is an unusual and somewhat imaginative idea, though benchmarks as a community tool are a familiar format in AI research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates a new offering born from compliance obligations, changing the lab's relationship between R&D and compliance by producing a community standard rather than just logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: A public benchmark for logging adequacy is an uncommon but norm-respecting community initiative, though sharing annotated log traces raises some privacy concerns it addresses via privacy metrics.
evidence_implementability: Curating annotated traces from multiple model families, defining rubrics, and hosting an annual open evaluation platform is a significant, expensive undertaking that goes well beyond the lab's own compliance resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (shared measurement of Article 12 conformity) that relates to the stated logging mandate, but not the lab's own decision on how to meet it.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark for scoring others' logging does not by itself make the lab's own systems meet Article 12, so it only contributes partially at best and arguably is unlikely to solve the lab's compliance need.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging SDK with CI gates is a standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice via a shared tool and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging library with CI enforcement is a common engineering compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building an SDK in a four-week sprint on the existing serving stack with CI gates is a reasonably feasible set of changes, though not trivial across all product lines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by embedding the required event fields in every high-risk prototype.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would reliably provide the Article 12 logging capability, but it covers mainly the paragraph 3 schema (which applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems) and not the broader paragraph 2 traceability, documentation, or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Operationalizing substantial modification with quantitative thresholds in promotion pipelines is a sensible and somewhat unusual angle, though not ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (threshold tables, automated gates) and embeds compliance into the R&D pipeline, but still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal threshold-setting with compliance officer involvement violates no norms, though defining substantial modification is legally governed and thresholds might diverge from regulator interpretation.
evidence_implementability: A working group plus pipeline gates is reasonably feasible, but defining quantitative thresholds for varied model classes and integrating automated checks requires some real effort and change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab operationalizes Article 12(2)(a) substantial-modification identification, which is an identified part of the logging mandate and R&D adaptation problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Thresholds and automated gates help the lab identify when modifications trigger compliance records, but they cover only one slice of Article 12 (not the logging capability itself, 12(2)(b)/(c), or Annex III minimums), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-template with CI enforcement is a sensible, fairly expected response to this mandate and shows little surprise beyond competent engineering.
