evidence_implementability: An inventory and ticketing process uses existing staff and counsel at modest cost and requires no radical change, though a full portfolio audit takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of knowing which systems need Article 12 logging, which relates to the stated problem but does not itself implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It identifies gaps and organizes remediation but does not itself build logging, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A reusable shared logging middleware is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard engineering approach to compliance as a logging practice, with a shared tool but no change in how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared infrastructure funded from a common budget is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses an existing microservice and cluster with two engineers for six months, which is a modest, reasonably feasible effort requiring some changes to project design phases.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly implements the Article 12(1) automatic logging and the Annex III point 1(a) minimum fields, which are the core of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a shared logging layer would satisfy the logging mandate across projects, though it does not address Article 12(2) event relevance tailoring, retention, or documentation in depth, so it is strong but somewhat partial.

evidence_originality: Dedicated compliance documentation offices with accountable owners are a common and expected response, with only mild interest from the log-event-triggered review.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds an organizational unit and review triggers but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice separate from the R&D itself.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance documentation function with named owners and periodic reviews is a conventional, uncontroversial governance approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Setting up a dedicated office with embedded staff across all product lines requires organizational change and ongoing headcount, but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Recital 71 documentation and traceability requirement, which relates to the logging mandate only by implication rather than being the stated logging problem itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A lifetime documentation office would help keep technical documentation current and audit-ready, but it does not itself build the automatic event logging that Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Performance-regression gating in CI is a well-known engineering practice, and applying it to logging overhead is a sensible but fairly mundane combination with some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new test/gate element but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Latency budgets and CI gates are common engineering strategies that offend no norms or legal sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing CI performance gates and production telemetry, requiring only modest additional instrumentation and test setup, so it is reasonably easy and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (logging overhead degrading system performance) that is related to, but not directly part of, the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI latency gate protects performance against logging overhead but does not itself deliver the logging mandate (event capture, traceability, Annex III minimum fields), so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Turning post-market monitoring logs into an open longitudinal dataset on deployment drift is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes the compliance logging obligation as a source of research data and scientific output, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Monitoring deployed systems and publishing benchmark reports is a reasonable practice, though open release of operational data raises some privacy and confidentiality concerns without offending norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a cross-team group, automated ingestion infrastructure, per-system drift metrics, and agreements with external pilot partners, which is a significant but feasible effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly uses Article 12 logging for post-market monitoring, but much of its stated benefit (open research data, scientific impact) is an implied add-on rather than meeting the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Continuous log collection and drift tracking contribute to monitoring compliance, but the proposal does not address required log content, Annex III minimums, or retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design templates are a fairly standard, expected response, with little that is surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a template and checklist as a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach basically unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusable project templates and compliance-by-design are common, uncontroversial engineering strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: A versioned repository with diagrams, checklists and sample tests is low-cost and a non-radical change for an R&D team.
evidence_applicability: The template directly targets the Article 12(3) minimum logging capabilities, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging floor for new projects, but it covers only Article 12(3) items, not Article 12(2) event logging, existing systems, retention, or other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware/SDKs are a common and expected response to a logging mandate, so the idea is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance tooling approach that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged, though it introduces a shared tool.
evidence_acceptability: Shared logging middleware is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin SDK in the existing inference stack with configurable schemas is a reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes but not radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically capturing the mandated event fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially solve the logging capture requirement across prototypes, but does not cover retention, documentation, or the fact that Annex III-specific fields vary by system and deployer context, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging modules with sprints and unit tests is the common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance engineering that builds logging into the codebase, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance logging and testing is a conventional strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires a cross-team effort and a dedicated sprint per release, which is some change but reasonably feasible within normal engineering processes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly implements the Article 12 logging mandate, building the specific logging fields required by Article 12(3) into the systems, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, native logging with tests would satisfy the logging requirement, though it assumes Article 12(3) fields apply to all systems (they are specific to Annex III 1(a)) and does not cover the broader Article 12(2) traceability purposes, so it is largely but not entirely a full solution.

evidence_originality: Directly implementing the statutory minimum fields is the expected, mundane response, with the reference-vendor positioning being only a modest add-on.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged, with only a mild procurement-positioning angle.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields with encrypted, access-controlled storage and internal audits is a common, norm-compliant strategy.
evidence_implementability: A thin middleware layer at the API boundary writing four defined fields is a reasonably feasible measure, though ledger, access control and audits add some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by recording the exact fields Article 12(3) requires for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging requirements but does not cover the Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other high-risk systems or the R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution to the broader problem.

evidence_originality: Retained, queryable audit log storage is a common and expected response to a logging mandate, with only the registry co-location adding minor interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard log archiving and query practice that leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An append-only, queryable log archive is a standard, uncontroversial compliance infrastructure choice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a time-partitioned log store integrated with an existing model-release registry requires some engineering work and storage cost but uses mature, reasonably feasible technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate's lifetime retention and post-market monitoring needs by providing storage and query of logs, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve retention and retrieval for lifetime logs but does not address what events to log, the Article 12(2) relevance of recorded events, or the technical documentation duties, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware at a gateway is a fairly expected engineering response, though the declarative per-system-type schema adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (middleware plus YAML schema) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging middleware with declarative configuration is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a middleware plugin, schema system, and durable write-ahead logging into the existing gRPC stack, which is some change but reasonably feasible, not trivial or 'zero-cost'.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces automatic event recording including Article 12(3) fields, which is part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would structurally satisfy automatic recording for inference-time events, but it covers mainly Article 12 logging and not broader obligations like documentation or ensuring the logged events support risk identification and post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mapping the Article 12(3) fields to backend logging is the most obvious, expected response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance logging to meet a legal mandate is a common strategy that violates no norms, with the minor caveat that logging verifier identities raises routine privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: Modifying backend APIs and mapping user journeys requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible, though blocking outputs until fields are captured adds moderate effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by implementing the four Article 12(3) minimum logging fields in biometric verification workflows.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, capturing all four mandated fields as a prerequisite would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) logging requirement, though it does not cover Article 12(1)-(2) general event logging for risk and post-market monitoring, so it is mostly but not wholly complete for the mandate.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in CI pipelines are a fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, though the framing as a pass/fail gate is somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI test gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing gates are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A pytest suite with synthetic queries against a throwaway instance is cheap and uses standard tooling, requiring only non-radical changes to the pipeline.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying the specified log content before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate verifying the Article 12(3) fields would reliably catch missing logging fields, but it covers only the minimum fields for Annex III point 1(a) systems and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event-relevance, retention, or post-market monitoring needs, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Risk-tiered prioritization of compliance work by regulatory category is a common and mundane response that evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice scheduled within the existing pipeline and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Tagging projects by regulatory category and prioritizing engineering sprints is a common, uncontroversial project-management practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only tagging in the next planning cycle and reallocating sprints within the existing funding envelope, which is a non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements (including the 12(3) sub-log specifications) by organizing R&D work accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: Sequencing projects by Annex III exposure and front-loading logging design for biometric systems would help meet the Article 12(3) mandate, but it is a planning measure that does not itself implement logging for all high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance reviews with checklists are a very common response to regulatory mandates and show little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that adds a checkpoint without changing how the lab does R&D or how it relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A pre-deployment compliance gate with checklist and sign-off is a common, conventional governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a one-page checklist and a review step in the lifecycle, which is a modest process change, though it adds some workflow and sign-off burden.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets verifying Article 12 logging requirements, which is the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate would catch logging gaps before release, but it only verifies and returns systems for remediation and does not itself build the logging capability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Allocating a fixed share of project hours to compliance upkeep is a common and mundane project-management response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a budgeting process but treats compliance as a separate overhead activity and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged, so it is at most slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Reserving budget for compliance is a standard, uncontroversial management practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A budget policy with an eight percent cap can be adopted next quarter with modest change and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified related problem, deferred and rushed documentation and log maintenance, which falls within the lab's compliance response, though it is not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Reserving hours for documentation and log upkeep would help keep records current across the lifetime but does not itself implement the logging capability or its required content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log analytics dashboards for post-market monitoring are a fairly expected response, though the framing of compliance as a customer-facing differentiator adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (dashboards, queryable repository linked to model versioning) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, with only a modest nod to compliance-as-offering.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal monitoring dashboards and sharing capability with regulators and customers is a common, norm-compliant strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a new analytics platform, repository, and role-based dashboards plus cross-team effort, which is feasible but a moderate undertaking.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need to use logs for post-market monitoring under Article 12(2)(b), which is part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Analytics over logs would meaningfully support post-market monitoring but does not itself ensure the automatic-recording capability or cover Article 12(1) and 12(2)(a),(c) or Annex III minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a longitudinal corpus for deployed-AI reliability science is an imaginative and relatively uncommon reframing, though drift detection from logs is a known practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging a source of scientific data and a new research direction, stretching the paradigm without redefining what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for internal research is somewhat unusual and could raise data-protection and purpose-limitation questions, but it offends no sensibilities if handled properly.
evidence_implementability: It builds on logging already mandated and adds an archive pipeline plus standard drift-detection methods, but a multi-year program with dedicated research teams requires some real resource commitment.
evidence_applicability: The proposal implies the logging mandate is met and then exploits the logs for research, which addresses the 'adapt R&D' part of the problem but not the mandate compliance itself directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by turning logs into research value and monitoring, but it does not by itself ensure Article 12 compliance (event selection, retention, traceability) so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A dedicated post-market monitoring or log analytics team is a predictable response to the mandate, so it is mundane, with only modest interest from the real-time drift detection.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (a team, a data lake, anomaly pipelines) but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal surveillance units that support compliance are a legitimate business practice that regulators and boards would welcome, and they violate no norms, though the log data may raise some privacy questions.
evidence_implementability: Standing up a dedicated team, a data lake and real-time anomaly detection across all deployed systems is a significant organizational and technical investment, though feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need to use logs for Article 72 and Article 26(5) monitoring, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A centralized log pipeline with anomaly detection and a dedicated team would address the risk-identification, post-market monitoring and operational-monitoring purposes of Article 12(2), but it does not itself ensure that systems technically record events, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a log verification and export tool as a market differentiator is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new offering born from compliance (open-source reference tool, positioning as market differentiator), which changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing an open-source compliance toolkit and running customer workshops is legal and uncontroversial, though somewhat less common than purely internal logging practice.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team over two quarters with a permissive licence and a one-day workshop is a reasonable, feasible commitment requiring some new work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate, including the Annex III 1(a) fields, by providing verification and export of log records.
evidence_effectiveness: The toolkit helps deployers verify and export logs, but it does not itself ensure the system's automatic event recording or the lab's R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a logging wrapper library is a fairly expected response, though dual-use as a citable research output and funding narrative adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and an open-source release, but still treats compliance essentially as a logging practice without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance tool under MIT and claiming grant credit violates no norms and is a somewhat uncommon but inoffensive strategy.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building on existing internal tooling over one quarter is a modest, reasonably feasible effort with low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by recording events, reference databases, and verification actions aligned to Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: A wrapper library would substantially help with logging but cannot fully solve the mandate, since Article 12(3) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems and a drop-in wrapper may not capture all risk-relevant events or identify persons in verification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open standards for documentation are an interesting and somewhat unusual response but not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the lab's relationship to compliance by turning it into a field-shaping offering and reference position with regulators and collaborators.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source documentation templates and standards submissions are legally and socially welcome, though the open release and standards push are somewhat less routine than plain internal compliance.
evidence_implementability: A small team drafting a schema, validating it on two systems and submitting a position paper is reasonably feasible, though standards-body engagement takes some extra effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets Recital 71 technical documentation rather than Article 12 automatic logging, so it addresses a related implied problem instead of the stated logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with documentation compliance but does not provide event logging capability, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: A financial cost model with budget reallocation is a fairly mundane, expected management response to a compliance mandate, though tying it to trimming speculative projects adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process (cost model, budget reallocation) but still treats compliance as a logging/infrastructure cost, without changing how R&D relates to compliance beyond funding trade-offs.
evidence_acceptability: Budget planning and board presentation are common, norm-respecting corporate strategies that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A twelve-week internal analysis and a budget revision are easy, low-cost, non-radical changes, though trimming projects requires some internal negotiation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of resourcing the logging mandate, which relates to but is not directly the stated problem of how to meet the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A cost model and funding ring-fence would help ensure resources exist for logging but does not itself deliver the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A dedicated compliance logging suite mapped to the regulation's minimums is the expected, mundane response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-driven logging with access controls and data minimization is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a structured log schema with write-once storage and access controls is standard engineering requiring some new development but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building logging that meets the specific Article 12(3) minimums (timestamps, reference database, matched input, verifier identity).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the Article 12(3) logging floor for Annex III 1(a) systems, though it does not cover Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other high-risk systems, so it is mostly but not wholly the solution; it would solve the main problem for biometric systems.

evidence_originality: Productizing logs as a trust signal is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle, but transparency dashboards are a familiar pattern and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logging into a customer-facing product offering and procurement differentiator, changing the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings (a new offering born from compliance).
evidence_acceptability: A customer-facing, consent-based read-only log portal offered in a licensing tier is a somewhat uncommon but unobjectionable strategy, though exposing verifier identifiers raises some data-protection sensitivity that consent agreements address.
evidence_implementability: Building a lightweight API and web interface atop existing logging middleware is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some new development and access-control work, but not radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to respond to the logging mandate by building on the logs, though its main stated aim (procurement differentiation) is an implied rather than core compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps make logs verifiable and exportable and adds business value, but it does not itself implement the logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging into a reusable middleware with thin adapters is a common, expected engineering response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging middleware is standard compliance tooling that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A central shared compliance platform is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A team of three building it in six months on existing containerised infrastructure with thin adapters is reasonably feasible, though it requires some changes across projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (Article 12(3) fields) while protecting research headcount, both part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would capture the Article 12(3) items across all high-risk systems and so would largely solve the logging mandate, though it covers less of Article 12(2) event relevance and the documentation duties in the recital.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK/middleware is the most obvious, commonly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (shared SDK) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, though it is a modest step beyond purely ad hoc logging.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised compliance tooling is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK requires platform engineering effort and integration across pipelines, but it is a reasonably feasible, standard software measure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate: do X (build a logging layer) to get Y (Article 12-compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a middleware capturing Article 12(2) events and 12(3) fields would directly deliver the logging capability, though it does not cover technical documentation or all system types, making it a strong but not wholly complete solution to the mandate.

evidence_originality: A schema validator in CI for mandated log fields is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (a JSON schema and a CI validator) but treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated validation of required logs is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A scoped sprint using existing tooling, an event bus and a small Python library is low cost with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum log fields in Article 12(3) but does not address the general logging in Article 12(1)-(2), so it is only a partial solution to the overall mandate.

evidence_originality: Treating log schemas as publishable interpretability research is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and creating publishable outputs from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Open schemas and publication with legal counsel input violate no norms, though treating logs as research is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Designing schemas, prototyping across three systems, publishing, and iterating with counsel requires some changes and moderate effort but is reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need of meeting the logging mandate by defining event taxonomies for Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: A schema covering Article 12(2) events would contribute to meeting the logging mandate but does not by itself implement logging or address Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance requirements into design documents and review gates is a common, mundane engineering practice that most labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A design-doc template with a review gate is a new process element, but it still treats compliance as ordinary logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Design-review gates and documentation templates are standard, norm-conforming practice that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: A template and a design-review checkpoint are low-cost additions to existing processes and need no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by specifying the required Annex III 1(a) fields up front.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is planned and prevents rework, but it covers only design specification, not actual implementation, verification, or the broader Article 12 scope, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding traceability into model architecture as a design principle is an unusual and imaginative response compared with the typical add-on logging approach, though it echoes existing interpretability research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the regulatory constraint into an internal design principle woven into the science, and it stops short of redirecting what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Interpretable-by-design architectures raise no legal or ethical objections and fit regulator and industry norms, though the approach is somewhat unusual for a lab.
evidence_implementability: A six-month prototype by a three-person team is modest in cost, but the architectures carry research risk and may incur accuracy or overhead tradeoffs before they reach production, which means significant change with uncertain delivery.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the logging mandate by building traceability into biometric models, which is the stated problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: If achieved, self-documenting inference paths would substantially satisfy event recording, but Article 12 needs event logs such as usage periods, reference databases and reviewer identities, which interpretability instrumentation alone does not provide, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-release validation checklists for compliance are a common, expected response, with only mild framing as drills.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a testing process but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Pre-release testing and sign-off gates are a conventional, uncontroversial quality practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It adds a QA protocol with synthetic scenarios and a checklist to existing release processes, which takes some effort but is reasonably feasible with no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that required events are captured.
evidence_effectiveness: Validating logging against each Article 12 sub-paragraph before release would help verify compliance, but it only checks logging capability and does not itself build the logging or cover documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-deployment compliance checkpoints are a standard, expected response to regulatory mandates and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, adding only an audit step.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gates before deployment are a common, norm-respecting governance practice.
evidence_implementability: A three-person review cell and a go/no-go certificate are a modest process addition using existing staff, so it needs some changes but is reasonably feasible and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying logging adequacy before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A review gate verifies and catches logging gaps but does not itself build logging capability or cover post-deployment, so it is a partial solution that contributes to compliance.

evidence_originality: Keeping technical documentation up to date with named owners and version control is a common, expected response, not surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A documentation steward and version-controlled revision cycles are standard compliance process practice that leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, with only mild new process elements.
evidence_acceptability: A documentation maintenance process is a conventional strategy that violates no norms and is welcomed by regulators.
evidence_implementability: Assigning stewards and using existing version-control repositories is low-cost and requires only non-radical process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the Recital 71 technical documentation requirement, which is related to but not the Article 12 automatic logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Maintaining current documentation contributes to compliance but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated conformance tests and CI-style gates for compliance are a fairly expected response, with only mild interest in applying them to early prototypes.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (gate and test suite) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A sprint-level compliance checkpoint with automated testing is a common engineering governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an automated replay test suite and adding a gate to sprints, which is a reasonably feasible measure involving some process changes rather than radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying Article 12 event capture during R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch logging gaps early and reduce retrofit cost, but it covers only Article 12 logging capture and not the wider mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building compliance logging into research tooling early (shift-left) is a fairly sensible idea that experienced evaluators would expect from some labs, with only some imagination shown.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the experimental process itself rather than retrofitting, but it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: The approach is a common engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms, and it explicitly preserves researcher autonomy.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing training harness with a structured-event logger and versioning schema is reasonably feasible, though it requires some engineering changes across research code.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly, by building Article 12 logging into the lab's pipeline.
evidence_effectiveness: Instrumenting research pipelines with Article 12-aligned logging from the start would meaningfully support the logging mandate, but it does not cover deployed-system specifics like Annex III 3(a)-(d) fields or post-market monitoring processes, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auditing existing systems against requirements to find gaps is a common, mundane first step that any experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A gap audit with a checklist and tracker is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Gap audits and compliance checklists are common strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week audit with liaisons and a simple tracker is low-cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of determining what logging is missing and prioritizing scarce engineering resources, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit would identify gaps and focus effort but does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Building monitoring analytics on top of logs is a sensible and fairly expected response, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new team and analytics tooling but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring analytics that feed a risk register are a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small data science team with streaming dashboards and SPC alerts needs some new staffing and infrastructure but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(2)(a)-(c) purposes of using logs to identify risk situations and support post-market monitoring, which are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Analyzing logs for drift and Article 79(1) risk triggers supports post-market monitoring and risk management, but it does not itself deliver the logging capability, the Annex III minimums, or documentation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Documentation lifecycle management with stewards and audits is a mundane, expected compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation stewardship and audits are common, uncontroversial compliance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning a compliance steward per project and using version-controlled repositories with quarterly audits needs some process changes and staffing but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied related problem (documentation upkeep for traceability) rather than the explicit logging requirement of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal covers technical documentation upkeep from Recital 71 but does not address the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandated logs as a longitudinal research dataset is interesting and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the logging obligation into a research data source and a new research agenda on operational AI behaviour.
evidence_acceptability: Using mandated logs for reliability research and publication is legitimate, though it raises some data-protection and confidentiality questions that make it somewhat unusual rather than purely standard.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated data-science pod, long-term data retention and sustained analysis over months and years, which is a significant but feasible commitment.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (extracting value from compliance logs) that relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate but does not solve the logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: The programme does not itself make the lab's systems meet the logging mandate; it only exploits logs once they exist, so it contributes at most a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Instrumenting all research experiments with deployment-grade logging from inception is a sensible and somewhat interesting idea, but similar to common MLOps and reproducibility practice, so it is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the research process itself, which changes how compliance relates to R&D, but it does not change what the lab researches or add new partners or offerings.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding audit logging in research workflows is a legally and socially unobjectionable strategy, though mandating it across all experiments is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A thin logging agent added to the existing MLOps stack with an append-only store and a handbook update is a reasonably feasible set of changes, though it needs some engineering and process work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, and the idea is to do X (build logging into the pipeline) to get audit-ready traceability.
evidence_effectiveness: It would make experiments and deployments traceable and cut retrofit work, but it does not cover the Article 12 specifics such as event relevance, the Annex III minimums, or deployment-time logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging infrastructure via telemetry agents is a standard, expected response to the logging mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared middleware layer is a new tool, but it still treats compliance purely as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, so it is at most slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on an existing time-series store and container orchestration, requiring some refactoring but reasonably feasible measures with amortized cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the automatic logging mandate (do X to get Article 12 compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, standardized automatic event recording across all high-risk systems would meet Article 12(1) and (2) logging capability, though it does not address what events are relevant or the Annex III minimums, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A time-boxed feasibility spike with cost modeling and a go/no-go recommendation is a common, mundane engineering practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A feasibility study of logging architecture and storage costs treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal feasibility study violates no norms or sensibilities and is a common business strategy.
evidence_implementability: A four-week effort by one senior engineer and one DBA is low cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, whether lifetime logging of Annex III 1(a) fields is viable and affordable, which relates to the logging mandate but is not itself the logging response.
evidence_effectiveness: It would inform the decision and reduce risk but builds no logging capability, so it contributes only a partial solution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Dashboards that ingest logs and flag risks are an expected, common response for labs, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A log-analytics dashboard is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring dashboards developed with legal counsel are a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal ingestion pipeline, rules engine and reporting is a significant engineering effort but uses standard, reasonably feasible technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified Article 12(2)(b) and 72 monitoring and risk-flagging obligations, which are part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It supports post-market monitoring and risk detection but does not itself ensure the systems technically record events per Article 12(1) or the Annex III minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs for longitudinal model-ageing research is an interesting and somewhat imaginative move that is unusual among labs' responses, but not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making the logging layer a research instrument co-developed with the science group, which is logging woven into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Building richer-than-minimum logging and publishing aggregate longitudinal studies violates no norms, though use of deployment logs for research raises mild data-governance questions.
evidence_implementability: Co-developing the logging layer with the ML science group and embedding distribution statistics, calibration metrics, and decision-boundary snapshots requires significant engineering and storage effort but is feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly designs the Article 12 logging schema (satisfying minimum fields and supporting post-market monitoring), so it addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate, though its main stated payoff is research publication.
evidence_effectiveness: Enriched logs would satisfy and exceed Article 12 traceability and monitoring needs, but the proposal does not detail how compliance is verified and focuses on research value, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design and shifting left is a common, expected response to such a mandate, and it shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a review gate and upfront specification step but still treats compliance as logging practice, though shifting it into the design stage slightly stretches the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Security/compliance-by-design gates are a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: Adding logging specs and a review gate to the existing SDLC is a process change within normal engineering practice, needing some changes but little cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring logs are specified against Article 12(2) criteria.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing logging in upfront and validating schemas against 12(2) would substantially help compliance, but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or legacy systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gap analysis before remediation spending is a very common, mundane response to a new regulation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A gap audit against Article 12 is standard compliance practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A gap audit is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week audit with one senior engineer per team is low cost and non-radical, so it is easy to implement.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (knowing the delta before committing resources) that relates directly to meeting the logging mandate, though the gap matrix is not the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit would not itself deliver logging capability, but it is a reasonable step that contributes to a solution by sizing the retrofit.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default tooling with CI enforcement is a fairly expected response and is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (schema as an architectural artifact, default middleware, CI gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice, with the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in a shared framework and enforcing it via CI gates is a common engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building middleware, a canonical schema, and CI checks requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building in the logging capability (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: Default logging middleware with CI gates would make prototypes technically capable of automatic event recording, but it does not cover production deployment, retention, or the Annex III-specific fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design with a kickoff compliance gate is a fairly expected response that experienced evaluators would anticipate, with little surprising or ingenious about it.

evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (extracting value from compliance logs) that relates to how the lab adapts its R&D to the logging mandate, rather than the identified problem of meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal makes use of logs once they exist but does not itself deliver the logging capability or meet Article 12 requirements, so it only partially contributes to solving the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Front-loading compliance design into the first sprint and auto-updating docs via CI hooks is sensible but resembles familiar shift-left and docs-as-code practice, so it is interesting rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (a sprint gate, CI-driven documentation) but still treats compliance as logging and documentation practice within the existing R&D workflow.
evidence_acceptability: A sprint-one design gate and version-controlled documentation are common engineering strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a modest change to sprint cadence plus some CI tooling, which is reasonably feasible with existing engineering practices and no added headcount.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by designing the event schema per Article 12(2) and keeping documentation current per Recital 71.
evidence_effectiveness: If carried out it would substantially ensure logging coverage and up-to-date documentation, but it does not cover runtime log retention, the Annex III specifics, or the quality of logs, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated CI regression tests for log-field presence are a sensible but fairly expected application of standard DevOps practice to compliance, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI compliance gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a CI stage with synthetic requests and assertion scripts is a modest, low-cost change to existing pipelines, though it needs a staging endpoint and test harness.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of ensuring the logging mandate's Article 12(3) minimum fields are present and correct in builds.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch logging regressions for the listed fields but does not itself design the logging, cover retention, or address the broader Article 12 obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using compliance as a marketing differentiator is a fairly common, expected response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates a new offering (compliance dossier as a sales asset) born from compliance, modestly changing how compliance relates to business, but R&D itself is unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Marketing compliance in tenders is a common practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Producing a one-page dossier per product mapping logged fields to sub-articles and attaching it to tenders is a low-cost, non-radical documentation task, assuming the logging already exists.
evidence_applicability: It addresses market positioning, which is only implied by the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate or adapting R&D, and does not itself implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It presumes logging capability already exists and does nothing to meet the mandate, so it would contribute only a minor partial benefit and probably would not solve the stated problem.

evidence_originality: A reusable internal logging library with decorators is a common, sensible engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect from many labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged, so it is at most slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized internal tooling for compliance violates no norms or sensibilities and is a common business practice.
evidence_implementability: It needs some engineering effort to build and integrate with existing pipelines, but it is reasonably feasible, though the claim of one day of integration is optimistic.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing event schemas matching 12(2)-(3).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would give consistent automatic event logging across prototypes, but it covers only logging mechanics and not the content judgments, retention, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating compliance documentation from experiment trackers is a fairly expected response, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process that weaves compliance into the research workflow as a byproduct of training runs, but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice rather than changing the lab's relationship to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from existing tooling is a sensible, non-controversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing MLflow tracker to emit structured artefacts is a reasonably feasible modest engineering effort using current tools.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of documentation burden and compliance bookkeeping tied to the regulation, though the documentation is adjacent to the Article 12 logging mandate itself, making the link implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Auto-generated documentation from experiment trackers would help meet Recital 71 technical documentation needs but does not address Article 12's event logging of deployed system operation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging in a common middleware layer is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging middleware is a new tooling element but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, which fits slightly paradigm stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Shared infrastructure and phased rollout are standard engineering strategies that violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing tracking and serving stacks, phases rollout over two quarters, and stays within existing headcount, though building a cross-team telemetry bus requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified data points.
evidence_effectiveness: A uniform logging layer capturing Article 12(2) and 12(3) data points would substantially meet the logging mandate, though it does not by itself address documentation, retention, or per-system purpose-appropriateness, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalizing a quantitative similarity metric for substantial modification is an unusual and interesting, imaginative framing that few labs would propose in response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a metric and benchmark) and ties research to compliance triggers, stretching the relationship between R&D and compliance beyond plain logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Developing a metric and publishing results is a legitimate research activity that violates no norms, though regulators may not accept a lab-defined standard as binding.
evidence_implementability: It requires a multi-dimensional research program with controlled perturbation experiments across biometric models, which is a significant, difficult and uncertain effort for a resource-constrained approval.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of detecting 'substantial modification' referenced in Article 12(2)(a), which relates to logging and compliance triggers but is not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A substantial-modification metric would help the lab decide when logging and compliance obligations are triggered, but it does not implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying homomorphic encryption to compliance logging is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, but privacy-preserving logging is a known research direction and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tools (cryptographic pipeline) and a publication thread but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving audit logging violates no norms and regulators would likely welcome it, though homomorphic encryption is somewhat unusual for logs.
evidence_implementability: Building a homomorphic-encryption pipeline inside a production model-serving stack is technically difficult and expensive, with latency and storage overheads, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets Article 12 automatic event recording and the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A cryptographic logging layer would satisfy the logging mandate and reduce data retention risk, but encrypted logs may complicate auditability and verification, and the proposal covers only logging rather than wider compliance, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Version-controlled living documentation with a designated lead and quarterly audits is a mundane, expected compliance response to Recital 71 rather than an imaginative one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice (documentation ownership, audits, alerts) that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation governance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A documentation repository, a designated lead role, and milestone alerts use existing tooling and are low-cost, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the technical documentation upkeep in Recital 71, which is related to but not the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate that the stated problem centers on, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with documentation currency and traceability but does not implement automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance gap audit with red/amber/green checklists is a very common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, merely checking and remediating logging.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and checklists are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint with one-page checklists and slotting remediation into upcoming sprints is low cost and requires non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The audit directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by inventorying gaps against Article 12(3) requirements across projects, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: An audit and sequenced remediation helps identify and close gaps but is only a partial solution, since it does not itself build logging capabilities or cover Article 12(1)-(2) general requirements and non-Annex III systems.

evidence_originality: Treating the definition of 'relevant events' as an epistemological research problem is unusual and shows imagination, though interpretability-for-audit research is not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research question about what the lab studies (interpretability for audit), changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations and addressing the larger problem of what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing a taxonomy and doing research on interpretability-for-audit violates no norms, and regulators would welcome it, though committing to a fundamental research programme as a compliance response is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year fundamental research programme with perturbation experiments across deployed prototypes and causal-tracing methods is expensive and difficult, though not impossible, and is not a quick compliance implementation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified, directly related problem: what events Article 12(2)(a) logging should capture to identify risk situations.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to specifying what to log for risk identification, but it is only a partial solution, since it does not implement the logging, covers only 12(2)(a), and yields uncertain research outcomes on a long timeline.

evidence_originality: An open synthetic log benchmark with injected-fault ground truth is an interesting and somewhat imaginative response, though dataset releases are a familiar research move.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a research offering and reputational position for the lab, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations by creating a new output born from the mandate.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing a synthetic open dataset is a somewhat unusual compliance response but offends no legal or social norms and avoids privacy issues.
evidence_implementability: Building synthetic log generators and ground-truth annotation pipelines is a substantial but feasible engineering effort using known simulation techniques, requiring some dedicated resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (advancing post-market monitoring research tied to Art. 12(2)(b)) that relates to but is not the lab's stated problem of meeting the logging mandate or adapting R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: The corpus does not make the lab's own systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate; it only supports external research on monitoring, so it is at best a tangential contribution.

evidence_originality: Standardized shared logging SDKs are a common, expected response to logging mandates, with a plugin interface being only mildly thoughtful.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but treats compliance purely as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library mandated in repo templates is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-week prototype by two engineers against two projects is modest, though mandating it across all new repo templates requires some organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate with a concrete intervention producing compliant logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would implement automatic event logging and Article 12(3) minimums but does not cover the wider record-keeping, technical documentation, or retention obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal compliance audits of logs are a mundane, expected response with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal audit cell sampling logs against Article 12 purposes is a common, norm-compliant governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a small team of three people and scripted checks on existing log stores, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes with modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying logs map to Article 12(2) purposes, though it audits logging rather than creating it.
evidence_effectiveness: Verification would help catch gaps but does not itself build the logging capability or cover the R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable compliance logging library is a common, expected engineering response to the mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, though the gating of project kickoffs and the log-ready-from-day-zero framing nudge slightly beyond standard practice.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal platform tooling and project gating are common engineering strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A 2-3 person team building a library with SQLite and object-store backends and gating kickoffs is reasonably feasible, requiring some process changes but no radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate (do X, get Article 12(2) traceability).
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging SDK with append-only storage and event-to-category mapping would meet the Article 12 automatic-recording mandate for prototypes, but it covers only logging and not the documentation, Annex III specifics, or other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Native structured event logging and publishing guidelines is a sensible and somewhat interesting idea, but it is a fairly expected response by labs to a logging mandate and shows limited surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (native architectural patterns, APIs, open guidelines) and weaves logging into the engineering science, turning compliance into a publishable contribution, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open design guidelines and building logging into the architecture is a legal, uncontroversial approach, though framing compliance as a research program is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Building a reference framework on the existing serving stack with component-level instrumentation and benchmarking is feasible but requires significant engineering and research effort, so some changes are needed rather than low-cost ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, with an explicit link to Article 12(1)-(2).
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would produce a logging capability that satisfies Article 12(1)-(2), but it does not address Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or documentation, so it solves most but not all of the logging mandate; it is mainly a contribution toward the solution.

evidence_originality: Log-fed monitoring dashboards with anomaly detection are a common, expected response, making the idea mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a monitoring cell and anomaly detection tooling but still treats compliance as a logging and surveillance practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A monitoring cell with dashboards for post-market surveillance is a conventional, regulator-aligned approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires creating a dedicated team, dashboards, and anomaly detection pipelines, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified need to use logs for post-market monitoring and risk identification, which is directly tied to Article 12(2)(a)-(c), part of the stated mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Dashboards on logs help with Article 12(2)(a)-(c) monitoring purposes but do not themselves ensure the logging capability, content, or the minimum Annex III logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design and compliance gates at design review are standard, widely expected responses and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, adding a checklist and gate without changing how the lab does R&D or its relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A logging-by-design checklist with a compliance gate at architecture sign-off is a common governance practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires adding a specification section and a review gate to existing design processes, which is a reasonably feasible change rather than a radical one, though it adds some process overhead.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring logging capability is specified and built into high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing logging in upfront would help satisfy Article 12 but does not itself guarantee the logs meet the specific required content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logging into an open-source tool and research publication is interesting and shows some imagination, but logging harnesses and experiment tracking are fairly familiar ideas.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging a first-class output of science and creating a publishable research contribution and standards-setting position, but it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release and publication are common, norm-respecting strategies, though releasing compliance tooling openly may raise minor IP or security considerations.
evidence_implementability: Extending the orchestration layer with an event-schema module is feasible with existing MLOps staff, but building a polished open-source tool plus a peer-reviewed paper demands some significant changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly delivers automatic event logging (timestamps, reference databases, inputs) as Article 12 requires, which is the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A native logging harness would substantially satisfy the logging mandate for the lab's runs, though it covers only part of broader compliance (e.g., deployed-system logs, person identification, retention) and relies on adoption.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandatory logs as a longitudinal drift-research resource is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance logs into a research dataset changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations, so logging feeds the science rather than sitting beside it, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing biometric-related event logs for research raises purpose-limitation and data-protection concerns, and Article 12 logs are meant for traceability and monitoring, so this offends sensibilities somewhat even with anonymisation.
evidence_implementability: Ingesting anonymised log streams into a versioned repository and running a small data-science subgroup is reasonably feasible, though anonymising biometric match records and legal clearance add some difficulty.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D around the logging obligation by gaining research value from the logs, which relates to the stated problem only indirectly.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself deliver the logging mandate (what to log, retention, integrity); it only exploits logs once they exist, so it is at best a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design scaffolding templates are a fairly expected, mundane response, though somewhat useful and interesting in its specifics.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (scaffolding CLI) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using project templates to build in regulatory logging fields is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A scaffolding CLI with templates and schemas mapped to an ORM is ordinary engineering work that can be built at low cost without radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the paragraph 3 logging mandate in the lab's high-risk projects by pre-wiring the required fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the Article 12(3) logging schema requirement for Annex III 1(a) prototypes but covers only part of the mandate (not general Art 12(1)-(2) logging, retention, or non-biometric systems), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK with CI enforcement is a common, expected response to this mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that introduces a reusable tool but still treats compliance as a logging layer, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance middleware and build-gating are common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-sprint middleware build with CI/CD gating is reasonably feasible but requires some changes to the serving stack and integration across pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (do X to get automatic logs, which is the stated problem).
