evidence_originality: Append-only cryptographically chained logs and compliance gates in CI/CD are sensible and somewhat interesting but are a fairly expected response among technically minded labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (chained logs, CI/CD coverage gates) and embeds compliance in the engineering pipeline, but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-by-design logging with immutable storage is a common, norm-respecting strategy, though privacy and retention tensions are not discussed.
evidence_implementability: Rebuilding inference and training pipelines with gateway agents, immutable storage and deployment gates is a significant engineering change and cost, though achievable with existing tools.
evidence_applicability: It explicitly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements, naming the specific events and Annex III 1(a) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, automatic tamper-evident logging covering Article 12(2) events and Annex III 1(a) minimums with CI/CD coverage gates would directly satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address the broader R&D adaptation or documentation duties.

evidence_originality: Centralized, default-on logging infrastructure is a common and expected engineering response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (shared SDK, immutable store) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Built-in logging with compliance-reviewer access violates no norms and is a standard strategy, though logging inputs from first testing may raise minor data-privacy concerns.
evidence_implementability: Building and maintaining a universal SDK wrapping all training and inference endpoints with an immutable store requires substantial engineering work but is reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by providing automatic event recording across all high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A platform-level SDK that automatically logs timestamps, inputs, reference databases and verification actions would, if built, satisfy the core Article 12 logging mandate, though event relevance to Art. 12(2) risk identification and the Annex III 1(a) person-identification field need tailoring.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as research data is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, but it is a fairly foreseeable move and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science, turning a regulatory cost into a research instrument, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Repurposing operational logs for research is a somewhat unusual strategy that raises possible data-protection and purpose-limitation questions, but it does not offend sensibilities if handled properly.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing event-bus and metrics pipelines with metadata tagging and a curated dataset, which is reasonably feasible with some changes, though governance and access controls add effort.
evidence_applicability: The idea builds on the identified logging mandate under Article 12(1) to get an implied benefit (research value from the compliance data) that relates to the 'adapt its R&D accordingly' part of the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Tagging logs with metadata and reusing them for research would help the lab satisfy Article 12(1) logging and generate research value, but it does not itself ensure the 12(2) event-relevance or Annex III minimum content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Earmarking compliance costs in project budgets is a common, expected organizational response and is not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a budgeting process element but still treats compliance as a logging cost to be managed, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A mandatory budget line item in internal grant templates and portfolio reviews is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Revising a template and adding a review checkpoint is a modest process change, though a ten percent budget cap and re-scoping of projects add some friction.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (funding and resourcing logging compliance) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate, rather than the logging requirements directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting for logging up front ensures funding exists but does not itself produce the technical logging capabilities Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Dedicated compliance budget lines are a common, mundane governance response that an evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard administrative compliance measure that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though it embeds compliance in budgeting.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting for compliance is a common, legitimate practice that violates no norms, though framing it to funders is slightly strategic.
evidence_implementability: Adding a required budget line, updating a committee policy, and training grant writers are modest administrative changes that need no new technology and cost little.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, that logging work gets underfunded, which relates to meeting the logging mandate but does not itself build logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It secures resources for logging design and upkeep but does not specify what to log or ensure Article 12 technical compliance, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in at design time (privacy/compliance-by-design applied to logs) is a very common and expected response to Article 12, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice with architecture review sign-off, leaving the lab's way of working and its R&D-compliance relationship essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A standing engineering directive for compliance-by-design violates no norms and is a common, conventional strategy.
evidence_implementability: Adding a logging middleware to the reference stack and a schema sign-off step in design review requires some process changes but is reasonably feasible and not costly.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the Article 12(1)-(3) logging requirements, including the specific Annex III fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would largely satisfy the logging mandate, but it covers only logging capture and not retention, log quality, or broader R&D adaptation, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Staged schema tiers tied to maturity gates with CI enforcement is a sensible, somewhat thoughtful shift-left approach, but it is a fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (tiered schemas, CI gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using CI checks and milestone-based gates is a common engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing sprint milestones and CI tooling, requiring schema design and check scripts but only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D workflow by ensuring the full log set exists before release.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably ensure logs are in place at release and avoid late retrofitting, but it covers only the logging-capability side and doesn't address which events are relevant or the documentation and monitoring obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates in release pipelines are a common, expected response, so the idea is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging verification practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance checkpoints and release sign-offs are standard governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses a checklist, a small audit pod, and integration into the existing release tool, which needs only modest, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying compliance before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A release gate verifying logging against Article 12 would catch deficiencies, but it only checks logging outputs and does not itself build the logging capability or address Article 12's wider aims, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging as an automatic side-effect in CI/experiment tooling is an expected, mundane response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (middleware hooks) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automatic, append-only logging built into the pipeline is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding logging middleware to an existing Docker/CI experiment runner is a modest, non-radical engineering change using standard tooling, though capturing fields like verifier IDs and reference databases may need some extra work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate with minimal disruption to R&D, with a clear do-X-to-get-Y link.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would produce the Article 12 logs for prototypes, but it only partly solves the problem since it covers the narrow Annex III 1(a) fields, applies to prototypes rather than deployed high-risk systems, and does not address broader logging and traceability needs.

evidence_originality: Hot-warm-cold tiered log archiving is a common, mundane engineering response that evaluators would expect from labs facing this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building tiered log storage to satisfy a legal logging mandate is a standard, uncontroversial engineering approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building and load-testing a purpose-built storage layer, which is reasonably feasible with existing columnar and tiered storage technology but needs some dedicated effort and cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of retaining and retrieving logs over the system lifetime as required by Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Storage and retrieval infrastructure with a schema mapped to Article 12(2) would support the lifetime logging obligation but does not by itself decide what events to log or cover documentation and other compliance elements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging framework with tamper-evident append-only storage is the common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with a shared library and append-only logs, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance largely unchanged, apart from compliance-by-design from the prototype stage.
evidence_acceptability: Building standard compliance logging into systems is a common, legally sound practice that offends no norms, though retention of verifying-person identities raises minor privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: A shared library hooking into inference pipelines with an append-only store is reasonably feasible engineering, but retrofitting all prototypes and ensuring tamper-evidence requires some changes and cost.
evidence_applicability: It explicitly does X (embed a logging framework) to get Y (Article 12 compliance), which is the identified core of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared, tamper-evident logging library embedded from prototyping would, if built, directly deliver the Article 12 automatic-logging capability including the 12(3) minimum fields, though it covers logging only and not the wider R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Treating minimal sufficient logging as an information-theoretic research problem is unusual and shows imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.

evidence_acceptability: Collaborating with legal scholars and balancing privacy with traceability violates no norms, though a research-first response to a compliance mandate is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: It needs interdisciplinary collaboration, formal methods, and empirical evaluation over an open-ended research timeline, which is significant effort and uncertain, and the lab wants committed implementation not exploration.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets how to meet Article 12 logging by defining what events must be logged, which is part of the stated problem, though it is framed as a research workstream.
evidence_effectiveness: Log-sufficiency criteria would help the lab decide what to log but a research program does not itself deliver compliant logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code tests in CI are a fairly expected response, with mild interest in tying it to prototype builds and tenders.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (CI gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI compliance checks are a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small pytest plugin in a sandboxed container within existing CI pipelines is low cost and non-radical, though defining synthetic edge-case inputs takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying Article 12 log content before release.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that logs have required fields but cannot ensure that the events logged are truly relevant to risk or post-market monitoring, nor does it build the logging itself or cover deployment, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Writing immutable provenance rows keyed on session ID in a feature store is a sensible but fairly standard audit-logging approach, with the reuse for debugging and drift detection a mild added interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a pipeline asset and storage design but still treats compliance as logging practice, though the reuse for debugging and drift detection slightly stretches it.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable audit logging for regulatory compliance is a common strategy, though logging identified natural persons raises minor data-protection considerations that are manageable.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing feature-store layer with an append-only table and storage-tier retention is a reasonably feasible change, though a synchronous write before each inference adds latency and engineering work.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly implements the Article 12(3) minimum logging items (reference database, matched input, verifying person, plus session timing), which is an identified part of the stated logging-mandate problem.

evidence_implementability: Adding a sign-off stage in the SDLC is a process change requiring director buy-in and some reviewer effort, but no new technology, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by requiring logging design and traceability mapping to Articles 79(1), 72 and 26(5) before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-deployment review gate with veto power would help ensure logging specs exist and map to the Article, but it checks designs rather than building logging capability or verifying runtime behavior, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing logging as a publishable research question is interesting and somewhat imaginative, though 'compliance as research asset' is a fairly foreseeable response from R&D labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and creating publication and influence channels born from compliance, but it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source publication and peer-reviewed research on logging offend no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated working group, benchmarks across diverse architectures, and open-source publication, which is a significant but reasonably feasible commitment.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12's logging mandate by designing log schemas that satisfy it, so it solves an identified problem related to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Developing log schemas across model families would plausibly satisfy the logging mandate, but it centers on research outputs and does not specify the concrete Article 12(2)/(3) event content, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized shared logging platform is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with nothing surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces no new relationship between R&D and compliance; it is standard consolidated logging infrastructure with the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized internal logging platforms are a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires committing about 40% of a two-person infrastructure team's sprint capacity and a simple schema API, which is reasonably feasible though it adds some burden to a small team.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by providing event ingestion, querying, and retention across high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help with logging infrastructure and audit-readiness, but it does not itself define which events must be logged per Article 12(2)-(3), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a research dataset for drift detection is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though drift monitoring on logs is fairly familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the logging obligation into a research data source feeding retraining, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using mandatory logs for internal drift analytics is a legitimate, norm-respecting practice, though somewhat beyond plain compliance, and it does not raise legal or social concerns.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an analytics pipeline and drift detectors over the central log collector, which is reasonably feasible with existing ML engineers but involves some new work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting value from the required logs and supporting monitoring under Article 12(2), which relates to but is not the core logging-compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift research on logs does not itself satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate, so it only contributes partially, by exploiting logs once they exist and aiding post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: Log analytics dashboards for monitoring are a familiar idea, though framing compliance as a client-facing service adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance into a product offering for clients changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and its obligations, which stretches the paradigm, though it still centers on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Offering monitoring dashboards to clients is a common business strategy that violates no norms, though client data handling needs care.
evidence_implementability: Building a hosted streaming pipeline with dashboards and alerting requires dedicated engineering and analyst staff and notable cost, but uses standard, proven technology.
evidence_applicability: The dashboard directly targets Article 72 post-market monitoring and Article 26(5) operational monitoring, which are the purposes the logging mandate serves, though it addresses use of logs rather than generating them.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab use logs for monitoring and compliance demonstration, but it assumes the logging capability already exists and does not itself satisfy Article 12's recording requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware with CI-template defaults is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and CI integration but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A internal logging SDK aligned to the regulation text is a common compliance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A drop-in decorator library built in one sprint and inherited via CI templates is low-cost and non-radical, though the claimed hour-per-integration and one-sprint timeline are optimistic.
evidence_applicability: It does X (build logging middleware) to get Y (automatic event recording per Article 12), which is directly the stated logging-mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would directly deliver automatic event logging for prototypes, but covers only Article 12(2) categories generically, skipping retention, traceability appropriateness, and other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Periodic internal compliance audits are a standard, expected response, with synthetic event injection a minor technical touch, so the idea is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging and audit practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal self-audits with board reporting are a common, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses an internal compliance team, a test script in staging, and a corrective-action register, all of which are modest, reasonably feasible additions to existing processes.
evidence_applicability: The audit directly targets verifying that logging captures the Article 12(2)(a)-(c) event categories, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A recurring audit with synthetic-event tests and corrective actions would help confirm and maintain conformity, but it only verifies logging rather than designing it or addressing broader R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: CI-based compliance testing is a fairly well-known pattern, and applying it to Article 12 is sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool-like process (a compliance gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Adding automated compliance checks to CI is a common engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses the lab's existing test runner with pytest fixtures and synthetic sessions in nightly runs, so it is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by checking emitted logs against the Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It catches missing or malformed log fields early but checks schema only, and does not ensure that the right events are logged, nor retention, nor the content of what is logged, so it only partly solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a longitudinal research corpus for performance drift is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly unprecedented given existing drift and monitoring research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logs as a scientific resource and redirects what the lab researches, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, with a new research agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Sharing anonymized logs via partnerships is a fairly normal research practice, though data-protection and confidentiality concerns may raise some sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires partnerships with deployers to obtain twelve months of anonymized production logs, which is difficult and slow, and the lab's own logs would not exist yet, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It uses mandatory logs as a research corpus, which only loosely relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate or adapting R&D, offering a benefit in a special situation.
evidence_effectiveness: The research track mines logs for drift science but does not itself make the lab's systems meet Article 12 logging requirements, so it would at best contribute marginally to the compliance problem and is unlikely to solve it.

evidence_originality: Versioned documentation with owners and quarterly audits is a common, mundane compliance response expected from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard documentation governance process (owner, repository, audits) that leaves the lab's way of working and compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: This is a conventional compliance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A documentation owner, central repository and quarterly audits are low-cost and require only non-radical process changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses keeping technical documentation current per Recital 71, which is related to the compliance problem but is not the automatic logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A maintained technical file helps traceability and compliance checks but does not deliver the Article 12 automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A default-on shared logging library in the project template is a common, mundane engineering approach to logging requirements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and template but still treats compliance as standard logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in standard templates is a common strategy that violates no norms, though capturing inputs and outputs by default may raise minor data-handling concerns.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing observability stack and template with standard tools like Parquet and object storage, requiring modest changes and low cost.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly implements automatic event logging (timestamps, versions, inputs/outputs), which is the core of the Article 12 logging mandate stated in the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would give automatic logging across prototypes, but it does not address the Article 12(2) event-relevance requirements for risk, post-market monitoring, or Annex III specifics like reference databases and human verifier identification, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Schema registries and log retention tiers are well-known engineering practice, so applying them to compliance logging is sensible but mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard tooling and logging practice addition that leaves the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal versioned log registry with retention tiers is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers can build it in one sprint on existing Postgres infrastructure, so it is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by keeping logs interpretable over the system lifetime (Article 12(1)) and supporting post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would keep logs interpretable across redeployments and so contribute to meeting the lifetime logging and monitoring requirements, but it covers only schema/retention and not what events to log or how to analyze them, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating traceability as a design constraint at the hypothesis stage, on par with power analysis, is a somewhat unusual and interesting framing, though 'compliance by design' gates are a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the design of the science itself, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance beyond mere logging practice, though it introduces mainly a process gate rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: An internal review gate with sign-off is a common governance strategy that offends no norms, though treating it like power analysis is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: It requires adding a review gate, a template, and a compliance liaison role, which are modest process changes but with some friction for researchers and staffing needs.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, mapping explicitly to the Article 12(2) categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging architecture maps to Article 12(2) categories and avoids retrofits, but it addresses design specification rather than actually delivering the technical logging capability or the Article 12(3) minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Directly implementing the Article 12(3) minimum fields with a compliance test suite is the obvious, mundane response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as a logging retrofit mapping requirements to components, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing the mandated logging fields is a standard, legally expected compliance response that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding four defined log fields to an existing verification workflow with a test suite is a bounded product-engineering change requiring some modification but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the specific minimum logging requirements for biometric systems, but it does not cover Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other high-risk systems or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized, indefinitely retained, queryable log storage is a common and mundane response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: This is standard logging and storage infrastructure that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized log retention is a common, conventional compliance strategy that offends no norms, though indefinite retention may raise minor data-protection questions.
evidence_implementability: A partitioned time-series store with batched gRPC log emitters and disabled garbage collection uses standard infrastructure, though it needs some new build-out and integration across deployments.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to keep automatic logs over the system's lifetime and make them available for audits, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Retaining and querying logs over the system lifetime would substantially support Article 12 traceability, but it does not by itself define which events to log or cover the content requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying differential privacy and homomorphic encryption to compliance logs is unusual and shows imagination, though privacy-preserving logging is a recognizable direction rather than a surprising one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a source of publishable R&D output and ties logging design to the lab's research, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than only adding a tool.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving research that supports compliance and reduces GDPR exposure offends no norms, though it is somewhat less common than standard logging approaches.
evidence_implementability: It needs two postdocs and about eight percent of discretionary research budget with a defined six-month deliverable, which is a reasonably feasible measure, although homomorphic encryption on logging of biometric matches is technically hard.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(3) requirements for recording input-data matches and verifier identities, which are part of the stated logging mandate, while also addressing the related GDPR tension.
evidence_effectiveness: The project explores whether privacy-preserving techniques can satisfy Article 12(3) logging, but it is a six-month research exploration that only partly addresses the logging mandate, and the stated problem requires committing to implementation rather than exploring feasibility.

evidence_originality: Schema versioning is a well-known practice in data engineering; applying it to AI Act logs is sensible but not very surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process and tooling for schema evolution but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a familiar data-engineering governance practice that violates no norms and fits regulatory expectations.
evidence_implementability: Semantic versioning, compatibility mappings, and a PR checklist requirement are modest changes using existing engineering practice, though they need some tooling and process discipline.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (keeping logs interpretable across substantial modifications over the system lifetime) that relates to Article 12's lifetime logging and Recital 71, but does not itself meet the core logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Schema versioning helps keep records usable over time but is only a partial solution, since it does not decide what events to log or satisfy the Article 12(2) and 12(3) content requirements.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements into an open, shared benchmark with external submissions is an unusual and interesting idea, though not highly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates new partnerships and a public offering born from compliance, changing the lab's relationship to its obligations beyond internal logging practice, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open-licensed benchmarks with partner institutions violates no norms and is an accepted research practice, using synthetic data to avoid privacy problems.
evidence_implementability: Building a benchmark, reference implementation, and partner coordination requires significant but reasonably feasible effort by an evaluation group, not trivial and not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses Article 12(3) logging requirements directly, but its main stated benefit is community impact rather than meeting the lab's own logging mandate, so it applies via an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark only helps validate logging designs and does not itself implement logging in the lab's systems or cover Article 12(1)-(2), so it is a partial contribution at best.

evidence_originality: Documentation-as-code tied to model versioning is a well-known MLOps practice (model cards, automated docs), so it is a mundane, expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces an automation step but still treats compliance as a documentation/record-keeping practice, leaving the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Auto-generating versioned documentation inside an existing MLOps pipeline is a common, norm-respecting practice that offends no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing MLOps tooling with scripts pulling metadata into an internal repository, so it needs only modest, non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Recital 71 technical-documentation and keep-up-to-date requirement, which is part of the record-keeping mandate, though it does not address Article 12 event logs themselves.
evidence_effectiveness: It would keep technical documentation current and so contribute to compliance, but it is only a partial solution because it does not provide the automatic event logging required by Article 12(1)-(3).

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a reliability meta-dataset is unusual and shows imagination, though the idea of mining operational logs is not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandated logs into a research corpus, so logging is woven into the science, but it does not redirect what the lab researches at large.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for research is somewhat uncommon and raises data protection and customer-ownership questions, but it does not offend sensibilities if properly governed.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated analytical workstream, cross-deployment data access rights, and new ML methods, which is significant but feasible change.
evidence_applicability: The idea exploits the logs required by Article 12 but mainly addresses an implied benefit (research value) rather than the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not satisfy the mandate itself but contributes by extracting value and potentially risk precursors from logs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Native architecture-level logging is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, but is a recognized direction (privacy/observability by design) and not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Weaving logging into the architecture itself changes the relationship between R&D and compliance (traceability becomes a design property of the science) but does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging natively into model architectures is a legitimate, norm-respecting approach that offends no legal or social sensibilities, though it is somewhat less common than standard instrumentation.
evidence_implementability: Co-designing schemas per system family and prototyping embedded recorders with overhead measurement requires significant engineering change and research effort, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedded event recording would contribute substantially to compliance, but as a design-research project with trade-off exploration it yields only partial coverage of specific Article 12 requirements and is not a full solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance testing in CI is a fairly well-known DevOps pattern and an expected response, though the build-failure framing is sensible, making it merely interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI-based log conformance tests) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations, fitting slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks are a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing Jenkins pipeline and parameterised scripts with a staging endpoint, requiring modest effort and no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements within the lab's R&D by catching gaps early.
evidence_effectiveness: Verifying required log fields and timestamp consistency on each commit helps meet the logging mandate but only covers format and completeness, not full traceability, retention, or other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Measuring logging overhead against a latency SLO is a standard, mundane engineering step that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal performance benchmarking in staging is a common engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting two existing prototypes in staging and running benchmarks is cheap and requires only modest, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified part of the problem, namely whether the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields can be captured within latency constraints in the biometric pipeline.
evidence_effectiveness: Benchmarking log overhead only produces information to inform an architecture decision and does not itself implement logging, so it is at most a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A reusable embedded logging component with CI/CD gating is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice via a tool, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into the engineering pipeline is a standard, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Developing a configurable SDK and integrating it into CI/CD requires some engineering effort and changes but is reasonably feasible, not radical.
evidence_applicability: It does X (embed logging module) to get Y (Article 12 compliant logs), which is the explicitly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logging SDK enforced in CI/CD would, if built, directly satisfy the Article 12 automatic logging mandate including the 12(3) minimums, solving the main problem.

evidence_originality: A shared logging infrastructure layer is a standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (reusable middleware with schema templates) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves R&D ways of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance-by-design logging is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building and mandating a microservice across all pipelines with per-category schemas requires meaningful platform engineering effort and integration changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a logging layer that records the events Article 12(1)-(3) requires.
evidence_effectiveness: A centralized middleware that automatically captures the required events would largely satisfy the logging mandate if built, though it relies on the middleware being correctly adopted and on Article 12(3) items being applicable only to certain Annex III systems.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK with decorators is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (SDK/decorator) but treats compliance purely as logging infrastructure, with the lab's way of working unchanged, which is roughly standard practice with a slight new element.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared tooling for compliance is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared library maintained by platform engineering with a decorator is reasonably feasible, though supporting both Python and C++ stacks and a central collector requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by automatically emitting Article 12 event fields across all prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve much of the logging requirement if implemented, but it only covers the logging mechanics and not the other parts such as deployer-specific scope, Article 12(2) relevance judgments, retention, or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Separating research from deployment with a readiness gate is a fairly common and expected compliance response, showing only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a structural pipeline split and a gate, which changes how R&D relates to compliance obligations somewhat, but it still treats compliance as logging practice applied at a later stage.
evidence_acceptability: Tiered compliance by deployment stage is a common, normative approach, though reliance on lighter regimes for prototypes may draw some regulatory scrutiny.
evidence_implementability: A checklist gate and an automatically activating observability layer require some pipeline changes but are reasonably feasible with existing engineering practices.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab meets the Article 12 logging mandate and adapts its R&D by gating full logging at deployment readiness, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet obligations at deployment and spare exploratory work, but it is only a partial solution because it leaves the logging design itself unspecified and risks gaps, such as Article 12(1) technical capability and the logging needed for systems nearing deployment.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware is a standard, expected response to a logging mandate, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a shared tooling layer that treats compliance as logging practice, introducing a new tool but not changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized logging layer mapped to regulatory minimums is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A six-month build by three engineers plus two-week integration sprints per system is a moderate, concrete effort requiring some changes but clearly feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, doing X (middleware) to get Y (Article 12 compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements across systems, but does not address wider Article 12(2) traceability or other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Piggybacking compliance logging on existing MLOps tooling is a common, expected response from AI labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice with the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though the 'byproduct of normal development' framing is slightly integrative.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure for compliance is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing experiment-tracking and CI/CD tooling with log hooks and a retention scheduler is a modest, non-radical change at low incremental cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements, including auditing gaps against 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the logging mandate of Article 12(1)-(2) and retention, but it covers only development pipelines and does not address deployed-system event logging or the Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design shared logging infrastructure is a common and expected response, with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice implemented as a shared service, leaving the lab's way of working and relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into the architecture is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared logging microservice and integrating it across product squads requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X to get compliant logging), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging service that automatically records events across the lifecycle and captures the Annex III minimums would, if implemented, address the core Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not cover the documentation or R&D adaptation aspects.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware over existing pipelines is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (shared middleware) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared compliance infrastructure is a conventional strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers for six months with adapters to existing infrastructure and three pilots is a reasonably feasible, moderate-sized effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate across the lab's systems, with a clear do-X-to-get-Y link.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatically capturing Article 12(2)(a)-(c) events across pipelines would largely meet the logging mandate, but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or documentation, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Default logging middleware integrated at initialisation is the obvious, expected response to Article 12 and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice implemented as middleware; it introduces no new relationship between R&D and compliance, so the lab's way of working is essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building default logging into systems is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A six-week sprint by two senior engineers reusing existing experiment-tracker infrastructure and code templates is a modest, reasonably feasible change with low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing automatic event recording including timestamps and reference-database queries.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to meeting Article 12 but is only a partial solution since it omits the full Article 12(2) purpose-driven event relevance, identification of verifying persons, log retention, and documentation, so it helps but does not fully solve.

evidence_originality: A design-review gate for logging requirements is a common, mundane shift-left compliance practice that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a design-review sheet to an existing kickoff template while still treating compliance as logging practice, with no change to how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review checkpoint is a standard process that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It only adds a one-page sheet to an existing template and a senior engineer review, so it is cheap and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets meeting the Article 12(2)(a)-(c) logging mandate by specifying event coverage at design time, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging design is considered early but covers only prototype design, not implementation, Article 12(3) specifics, or retention and verification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalising substantial-modification detection through drift metrics is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle, but it is not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (formal thresholds, certification procedure) and ties compliance to the lab's research, but it still treats compliance as a logging-trigger practice rather than changing the lab's relationship to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A lab defining its own modification thresholds and publishing them is a somewhat unusual but entirely legitimate strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing drift-detection work and runs on three in-house pipelines, but formalising thresholds and certifying substantial modification is a significant research effort, so some changes and reasonably feasible measures fit.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied problem, deciding when logging obligations are renewed, that relates to the stated logging compliance problem, though Article 12(2)(a) itself does not set renewed logging obligations.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses only one narrow trigger (substantial modification) and does not itself deliver the logging mandate, so it contributes to a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in at design time as a gated engineering standard is a very common 'compliance by design' response that an experienced evaluator would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a standard and a review gate but treats compliance as ordinary logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal engineering standards and architecture review gates are common, norm-compliant strategies that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a spec and adding a review gate is a non-radical change, though applying it to all high-risk models from the first sprint requires some process adjustment.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the Article 12(3) logging elements in system designs.
evidence_effectiveness: A mandatory gate ensuring automated logging of the specified items would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it focuses on Article 12(3) items (specific to Annex III 1(a)) and does not address log retention or the Article 12(2) purposes in depth, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Prototyping the most demanding logging clause is sensible and well-structured but a fairly expected way to respond to the mandate.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a failure-event corpus is an unusual and interesting reframing that shows imagination, but it is not wholly unprecedented, since labs already mine incident data.

evidence_effectiveness: It does not by itself meet the logging mandate, which still has to be implemented, but it offsets the compliance cost and improves R&D, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware enforced by a deployment gate is a common, sensible engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect, with little surprise.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging in shared pipeline infrastructure is a common, sensible engineering approach that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.

evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer that automatically captures timestamps, input provenance and risk-event flags would deliver the core Article 12 automatic-recording capability across systems, though it does not itself cover Article 12(3) specifics like reference databases or verifier identity or retention and review processes, so it is largely but not completely a solution.

evidence_originality: Automated schema validation in CI is a sensible, well-known DevOps pattern applied to compliance, interesting but not surprising.

evidence_originality: A shared, reusable logging middleware is a very common and expected engineering response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise or imagination.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in CI are a fairly expected, mundane response, with replaying synthetic traffic adding only modest interest.

evidence_effectiveness: It would verify log field completeness for Annex III 1(a) systems, which helps meet the mandate, but it does not itself create logging, cover Article 12(2) relevance, retention, or other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logs as a data source for detection research is interesting and shows some imagination, but log analytics for monitoring is a fairly foreseeable response.

evidence_originality: Risk classification and prioritization is a mundane, expected response to such a mandate.

evidence_originality: Standard logging libraries and CI gates are a common response that labs would be expected to propose, so it is interesting but not surprising.

evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would provide automatic event recording for prototypes, which contributes substantially but does not by itself cover Article 12's purpose-appropriate event selection, retention, or Annex III minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized reusable logging/monitoring module is a common, expected response, though packaging it with its own SLA is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a reusable shared logging component, a new tool that still treats compliance as standard logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A reusable logging/telemetry module tied to Article 12 and 72 is a standard, legally unobjectionable compliance approach that offends no norms.

evidence_originality: Building automatic, tamper-evident logging into the prototyping SDK is a sensible and fairly expected engineering response that labs would commonly propose, though the build-time schema validation against Article 12 categories adds mild interest.

evidence_effectiveness: Article 12 applies to deployed high-risk systems' event logging, while this logs R&D experiment runs and so only partly addresses the mandate, helping with traceability and documentation but not guaranteeing the deployed systems' logging capabilities.

evidence_originality: Dedicated compliance teams and contractor-built frameworks are standard, expected responses with little surprising about them.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code tests in CI are a fairly known idea in the reference class, though applying it specifically to Article 12 fields is sensible and somewhat interesting rather than surprising.

evidence_effectiveness: It would catch missing Article 12 logging fields early, helping with the logging mandate, but it covers only the Art. 12(3) biometric fields and not retention, post-market monitoring use, or the broader logging requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Event taxonomies for non-discrete architectures with a criterion separating informative from bureaucratic logs is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.

evidence_originality: Pre-release compliance gates with mapping matrices are a standard, expected response, with little surprising about them.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK with decorators is a standard, expected engineering response and shows little surprise.

evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.

evidence_originality: Versioned living documentation with periodic gap audits is a common, mundane compliance response.

evidence_originality: Cross-mapping logging obligations to GDPR is a sensible and fairly expected compliance step, interesting but not surprising.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code checks in CI are a fairly common idea, though tying it specifically to the four Article 12(3) fields is a mildly interesting application.

evidence_effectiveness: A schema and toolkit would help satisfy Article 12 logging but it does not itself guarantee the lab's own systems meet the mandate (e.g., Annex III point 1(a) minimum fields, retention), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_applicability: It directly targets how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D, though the link to specific Article 12 outputs is implied rather than explicit.

evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning compliance logs into a scientific asset and positioning the lab as a data provider, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing de-identified logs openly is somewhat unusual and raises GDPR, confidentiality and IP sensitivities, though it does not flagrantly offend norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an ontology, versioned archive, de-identification pipeline and release governance, which is a significant and costly change though feasible.
evidence_applicability: The idea builds on the logging layer and implies benefits for post-market monitoring, but the open-data release addresses an implied rather than identified part of the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Extending the logging layer with semantic tagging would help meet Article 12 traceability and post-market monitoring, but the open-data archive mostly serves research goals and does not by itself solve the full logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Documentation owners, trigger-based reviews and audits are a common, expected compliance response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance governance with a new owner structure but leaves the lab's R&D workflow and compliance relationship essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A documentation governance office is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Creating a small cross-functional cell with named owners, trigger-based reviews and quarterly audits is a modest organizational change using existing resources, though it needs some staffing and process setup.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (documentation upkeep from Recital 71) rather than the directly stated logging mandate, so it applies via an implied link.
evidence_effectiveness: It keeps technical documentation current per Recital 71 but does not address the automatic event logging mandate of Article 12, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Front-loading a bounded spike and a one-page memo mapping events to Article 12 triggers is a somewhat unusual, sensible process idea, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (a timeboxed log-surface spike before architecture review) and moves logging design earlier in R&D, but it still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A lightweight engineering gate before architecture review is a common practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-day timebox, a stub model, a fixed test corpus and a one-page memo are cheap and non-radical, though it depends on a scaffold from another proposal.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by mapping event types to Article 12 paragraph 2 criteria for new architectures.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by identifying loggable events early, but a stub-model spike on an unproven system gives only partial coverage of the full logging obligation, so it is not a complete solution.

evidence_originality: Deployment gates and automated pre-release checklists are a familiar compliance and CI/CD practice, so the idea is fairly mundane despite the tidy framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a scripted validation step to an existing release workflow while still treating compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Release gates are a common, uncontroversial strategy that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing release approval workflow with a scripted validation check is low-cost and non-radical to build.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate by checking the four specified logging elements before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-release gate verifying the Article 12(3) logging fields would help ensure those minimum capabilities exist, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and the Article 12(1)-(2) event-logging and lifecycle needs remain unaddressed, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Folding compliance checks into existing QA and test cycles is a common, expected response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It embeds log-conformance checks into existing sprints and test harnesses, which is standard shift-left compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating compliance criteria into normal testing violates no legal, social, or business norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing harnesses and staff with only two added test criteria per sprint, so it is easy and low-cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D processes by generating compliance evidence during development.
evidence_effectiveness: Test criteria verify that logs are generated and traceable, which helps, but it does not by itself define what events to log, retention, or the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware built on open-source event sourcing is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with only the review-gating schema validator adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared tool and a schema-validator gate but still treats compliance purely as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared infrastructure and review gating are common, norm-respecting engineering and governance practices.
evidence_implementability: Three engineers embedding open-source tooling into the existing containerised stack is a reasonably feasible, modest-cost effort, though retrofitting all prototypes needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the Article 12(3) fields across lab systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would cover the Article 12(3) minimum fields and gate pilots on them, but it addresses only the Annex III 1(a) minimum items and not the broader Article 12(2) traceability, retention, or documentation needs, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-source compliance tooling is a fairly expected response, with the science-rationale documentation adding mild interest but not surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (open-source middleware with scientifically useful schema) and partly links logging to science, but still treats compliance fundamentally as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building and open-sourcing a compliance logging tool violates no legal or social norms, though open-sourcing is a somewhat less routine choice than purely internal compliance.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team over two quarters is a reasonable, bounded commitment, though open-source documentation and a richer schema add some extra work beyond the baseline.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building a logging tool for the lab's own system.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would satisfy Article 12 logging for the lab's system and likely cover the main compliance need, though it does not address Annex III specifics or broader R&D adaptation explicitly.

evidence_originality: Building shared logging infrastructure for compliance is a fairly expected response among labs, with the reuse and time-to-market framing being sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable middleware platform but still treats compliance as logging practice, with only a mild framing of turning obligation into infrastructure that does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A reusable internal logging platform is a common, norm-respecting engineering and compliance strategy with no legal or social concerns.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated platform team and architectural integration across every high-risk system, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial change with some cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building automatic lifetime event logging validated against Article 12 paragraph 2, so the intervention clearly yields compliance with the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, architecture-level logging middleware with risk-trigger hooks and post-market monitoring feeds would largely satisfy Article 12, though it omits the Annex III 1(a) specifics and documentation aspects, so it is close to a full solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the pipeline by default is a sensible and fairly expected 'compliance by design' response, with a mildly interesting reproducibility angle but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Embedding logging by default into R&D pipelines so experiments become auditable artifacts begins to change how compliance relates to research, though it remains essentially a logging tool and not a change to what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source, auditable logging infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A small internal team building middleware that wraps existing training and evaluation harnesses is reasonably feasible, requiring some changes but no radical investment.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by generating the required log data (timestamps, reference data, input, operator IDs).
evidence_effectiveness: Native, immutable logging of the Article 3 items would largely satisfy the logging mandate if done, but it focuses on R&D pipelines and leaves deployed-system logging, retention, and event-relevance for risk and post-market monitoring only partly covered, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building automatic logging into the architecture from design with a shared schema and review gates is the standard, expected response to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice (logging by design, architecture gates) that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged and does not alter the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory engineering requirements, architecture review gates, and compliance logging are common strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a shared schema, platform team work, and gating processes across the portfolio, which are reasonably feasible but involve some real changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (embed auto-logging with a schema and validation) to get Y (meet the Article 12 logging mandate), which is explicitly part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native automatic logging validated against Article 12(2)(a)-(c) would address the core logging mandate, though it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics or the R&D adaptation aspect fully, making it a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: A reference prototype with a checklist mapping fields to regulatory text is a sensible but expected compliance response, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a prototype and a mapping checklist but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building a reference compliance implementation is a common, norm-abiding strategy with no legal or ethical offense.
evidence_implementability: A two-engineer plus one-researcher pod over eight weeks using existing test data is modest and reasonably feasible, though it is a dedicated project requiring some resources.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly builds a prototype logging pipeline capturing the Article 12(3)(a)-(d) fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A reference implementation and compliance checklist would substantially help but covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and Article 12(1)-(2) general logging, so it is a partial solution for the lab's overall response.

evidence_originality: A unified telemetry layer reusing existing infrastructure is the expected, mundane engineering response, with only a mild reuse-and-amortise framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard logging module that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging built on existing infrastructure is a common, conventional compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing Kafka streaming and observability infrastructure with a refactor by the platform team, so it needs some changes but no new procurement, which is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the Article 12(3) minimum logging items (usage periods, reference database, matched inputs, verifier identities), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimums for the Annex III 1(a) systems, but it only partially covers the broader Article 12(1)-(2) traceability purposes and the R&D adaptation question.

evidence_originality: Design-time compliance checkpoints and checklist sign-offs are a common, expected response, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a design gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A kickoff design review with a checklist template and peer sign-off is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a two-hour meeting and a one-page template added to the existing checklist, so it is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping events to the three Article 12(2) categories during design.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure the Article 12(2) event categories are considered early, but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, the logging implementation itself, or ongoing verification, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shifting compliance left into project planning is a sensible and fairly expected idea that shows modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process step (a template and gate) but still treats compliance as a logging-practice checklist without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A chartering-stage compliance checkpoint using an existing review form is a common governance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a one-page template and a part-time liaison already on staff, so it is a small, non-radical change to existing process.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of late-stage rework and misalignment with Article 12, which relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate in R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It prompts teams to plan for Article 12 logging but does not itself build the logging capability or guarantee compliant records, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-derived benchmarks are an unusual and interesting idea that shows some imagination, but benchmark-as-standard-setting is a familiar research move.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a research and publication offering and brings in academic partners, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source releases and standard-setting efforts offend no norms, though a benchmark of this kind is somewhat uncommon for a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Building a benchmark with a labelled corpus from incident databases plus synthetic fault injection, and releasing it open-source, requires significant effort and data curation but is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, how to assess log quality against Article 12, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly implement the lab's logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark would not itself make the lab's own systems meet the logging mandate, so it contributes only partially, mostly through measurement and reputation.

evidence_originality: Applying change-point detection to mandated logs is an interesting and sensible idea, but it is a fairly expected extension of monitoring research rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (drift detection methods) and redirects some R&D toward log-based safety science, but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only slightly stretching the paradigm.
