evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard audit and verification practice that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits and mock inspections are a common, norm-abiding governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two compliance engineers running semi-annual drills and filing tickets is a modest, reasonably feasible addition requiring some process change but little cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly tests whether logging meets Article 12(3) minimums, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies and remediates logging but does not itself build the logging capability or address Article 12(1)-(2) design, so it is a partial solution that helps ensure compliance.

evidence_originality: A compliance gap audit is a standard, expected first response to any new regulation and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits by cross-functional teams are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs staff time across all high-risk systems but involves no radical change and is reasonably feasible with existing engineering and compliance staff.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping current capabilities to specific Article 12(2) and 12(3) requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A gap audit with a remediation plan helps the lab find and plan fixes for logging shortfalls but does not itself build the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging middleware that reuses existing infrastructure is the most common, expected response to a logging mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice with no change to how the lab does R&D, so it preserves the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging middleware into existing serving infrastructure is a standard, uncontroversial compliance approach that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Retrofitting an event hook into each endpoint and reusing the existing time-series store requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible, though the claim of near-zero cost is optimistic.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (auto-capture Article 12 events in logs) to get Y (logging compliance), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event logging would meet the logging mandate technically, but it leaves out retention, log integrity, and the Annex III-specific fields, and it does nothing about R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code CI gating is a known DevOps pattern, so it is a sensible but fairly expected response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (gates, static analysis, template repo) but still treats compliance as logging practice integrated into the existing workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Build-failing gates are common engineering governance and violate no norms, though some engineers may chafe at the friction.
evidence_implementability: Adding an SDK, template repo and a CI static-analysis lint step requires some engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: The gate and CI check directly produce Article 12 logging capability (Annex III fields) in high-risk prototypes, which is the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would reliably ensure logging is present in prototypes, but it only checks for presence of fields and not log quality, retention, or the broader Article 12(2) event relevance, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance stage gates are a common, expected response to regulatory mandates and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, adding only a checklist and gate.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate sign-offs and checklists are common governance strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist and sign-off gates are low-cost, non-radical additions to existing milestone processes, though remediation sprints add some schedule burden.
evidence_applicability: The idea directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking logging requirements at each R&D stage (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: Gated checkpoints verifying logging against Article 12(2) and Annex III 1(a) would help ensure logging gets built, but they only verify and do not design the logging capability itself, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing logging-native architectures is a sensible and somewhat expected 'privacy/compliance by design' analogue, interesting and showing some imagination but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal weaves logging into system architecture and the science itself (hooks in training loops, provenance layers), changing the relationship between R&D and compliance beyond treating it as a logging add-on, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-by-design architecture is a conventional, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building three reference architectures in two quarterly sprints is feasible with internal testbeds, though it requires significant engineering change and the timeline is optimistic.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12 mandate of automatic event logging over system lifetime by building it into architectures, with Annex III 1(a) specifically covered.
evidence_effectiveness: If achieved, native logging would meet the logging mandate, but the proposal focuses on prototypes and overhead benchmarking in testbeds and does not cover the specific Article 12(2)/(3) content requirements or post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a reference implementation of the Article 12(3) minimums is a sensible, fairly expected response, with only modest imagination in making it a forkable template.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A forkable reference implementation is a new artifact but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliant logging on an internal prototype is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Four weeks on an existing prototype with a shared SDK is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified paragraph-3 logging requirements, which are part of the mandate, though only for the biometric subset.
evidence_effectiveness: It would only help for the Annex III 1(a) biometric case and would not cover general Article 12(1)-(2) logging across the lab's other systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Generating log schemas from model cards via a rules engine is a sensible tooling idea but a fairly expected automation response to compliance burden, with only some imaginative touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: An internal tool that derives compliant log schemas with human review for edge cases violates no legal or social norms, though automated schema generation is slightly less routine than manual compliance.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers prototyping in six weeks using an existing YAML model-card format and a rules engine is a reasonably feasible measure, though encoding the regulatory mappings accurately requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: The tool directly produces the Article 12 logging fields the lab must meet, so it does X to get Y where Y is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema generator would settle which fields to log, but it does not ensure logs are actually recorded, retained, or sufficient for traceability and post-market monitoring, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable internal logging framework is a sensible and fairly common engineering response to compliance, with some interest in the per-Annex-III configurability but little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a unified logging API) but still treats compliance as logging practice, though it does embed logging into training and inference pipelines, which stretches the practice slightly.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal compliance standard is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small team building an API and retrofitting two prototypes in one quarter is a reasonably feasible measure that needs some changes but no radical resources.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building a unified logging framework that satisfies 12(1)-(3).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a standard framework embedding automatic event logging with per-category granularity would satisfy the logging mandate across systems, though it does not address the broader documentation or monitoring duties, so it is close to a full solution for the logging problem.

evidence_originality: Building an internal log retention and export platform is the obvious, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal logging service with encryption and data sovereignty is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A containerised pipeline with retention policies, encryption and export APIs uses well-understood tooling, though it needs some DevOps effort and ongoing maintenance.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to keep and serve logs over the system lifetime that the logging mandate requires.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide lifetime log storage and audit exports, which contributes to Article 12 compliance, but it does not define which events to record or address the Article 12(2) and 12(3) content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Storing, indexing and analysing logs for post-market monitoring is a fairly expected response from labs, though the early-warning framing adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (analytics dashboards, anomaly detection on logs) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Retaining logs and monitoring them is a common, norm-compliant strategy, though long lifetime retention may raise data-protection questions that the proposal does not address.
evidence_implementability: It requires provisioning secure storage and a dedicated analytics team, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial set of changes using existing IT infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of handling mandated logs and feeding Article 72 post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the logging, retention and post-market monitoring duties but does not by itself address the Article 12 capability to record events or the specified minimum log content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Async ring-buffer logging with latency benchmarking is a standard, mundane engineering pattern that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an async logging prototype and documenting overhead in the technical file is a common, norm-compliant engineering and compliance approach.
evidence_implementability: A ring-buffer with batched async flush and a p99 benchmark against a baseline is a modest engineering effort requiring some work but reasonably feasible with existing infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12(3) logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems without harming real-time performance, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It demonstrates technical viability and overhead for capturing logs, but it is a proof-of-concept that covers only capture performance and not full compliance such as the content of the fields, retention, or identification of verifying persons, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing operational logs as a longitudinal scientific dataset is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into experimental design and making compliance data the backbone of research.
evidence_acceptability: Treating compliance logging as research infrastructure offends no legal or social norms and is a sensible business practice.
evidence_implementability: Rebuilding the serving stack and embedding schema design into protocol review across all research teams is a significant, costly change, though a shared instrumentation library makes it feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: Capturing every event with schema discipline would satisfy the logging mandate and add research value, but it does not explicitly address Article 12 minimums such as reference databases, persons verifying results, or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK baked into scaffolding is a fairly standard compliance-by-design approach, interesting but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK as architectural default) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building a shared logging library as a default dependency is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-engineer internal library team building an SDK that plugs into existing prototype scaffolding is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though schema design and integration take some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, with explicit reference to the Article 12 and Annex III 1(a) requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would largely satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it covers mainly the minimum fields and not wider documentation, event relevance tuning, or other high-risk categories, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning a compliance mandate into open, citable community schemas is uncommon and shows some imagination, though standardised schemas are a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging a research output and a source of scientific standing, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open schemas under an open licence is a somewhat unusual compliance strategy, but it breaks no legal or social norms and is welcomed in research culture.
evidence_implementability: Drafting versioned JSON-LD schemas and publishing them is reasonably feasible, though it needs extra effort in design, peer review and community adoption beyond the internal logging build.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified need for Article 12-compliant event logging by formalising the paragraph 2(a)-(c) event categories, though the reproducibility and publication benefits are only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Schemas would help structure the logs Article 12 requires, but they do not implement the logging capability itself and add little to the actual mandate, so the idea only partly solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Reserving a fixed share of project hours for compliance in charters is a fairly familiar governance and budgeting device, though the audit sampling and explicit trade-off framing add mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process element (charter line item, funding gate, audits) but still treats compliance as a logging and documentation practice without changing how research relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Project charters, funding gates, and budget audits are common management strategies that offend no norms, though a fixed cap may irk researchers.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a policy rule, a charter template change, and quarterly sampling audits, which is a non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The idea addresses an implied problem, resourcing compliance work, which relates to the stated need to meet the logging mandate, rather than directly specifying how to log.
evidence_effectiveness: Reserving hours helps resource logging work but does not itself ensure that logs meet Article 12 technical requirements, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Quarterly audits with a designated officer and a checklist are a very standard governance response that experienced evaluators would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging and audit practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a Log Officer role, a checklist, and a quarterly schedule, which are non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by verifying that Article 12 logging continues over system lifetime, including Article 72 data flows.
evidence_effectiveness: Audits and escalation would help sustain compliance but do not themselves build the logging capability or cover the design side, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-deployment compliance testing and audit trails are a common, expected response among labs, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a test script and dossier process but treats compliance as standard logging and verification practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal pre-deployment audit and verification of logging against the regulation is a standard, uncontroversial compliance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires creating a test script, a joint Compliance/QA step and dossier archiving, which are reasonably feasible process additions but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements, including the specific paragraph 3 fields, and demonstrating compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: Verifying that logs capture required events checks compliance but does not itself build the logging capability or cover the full mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance as a driver of interpretable-architecture research is interesting and shows imagination, but the 'logging by design' and interpretability themes are fairly familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science of model design and making compliance a research agenda, which is paradigm stretching and arguably addresses what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in model architecture and publishing the research violates no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping three new architectures with natively emitted computation traces is a significant, expensive research effort with uncertain outcomes, not a quick compliance measure.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the logging mandate directly (Article 12 logging, benchmarked against 12(3)), though the architecture-level traces go beyond the event logs the article actually requires, so the link is partly implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Native trace emission could help with traceability, but it is a research programme that only partially covers Article 12 (period of use, reference database, human verifier identity are not architecture-level) and may not deliver compliant logs.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging scaffolds or middleware in project templates are a common, expected response to a logging mandate and show little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-logging tooling approach that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building standard logging middleware into a shared prototype template is a common engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing experiment-tracking framework with middleware and a single-dependency scaffold, so it is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified Article 12(1) automatic-recording obligation, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic event recording for prototypes, but it does not cover the Article 12(2) relevance requirements, the Annex III minimums, retention, or documentation, so it only partly solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Versioned documentation with quarterly reviews and audit trails is a common, mundane response to the mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A versioned documentation system with a document-control team is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Document control and audit trails are common strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Document management systems and ownership assignments are readily available and need only modest process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses technical documentation upkeep from Recital 71 rather than the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it relates to the problem only indirectly, though the audit trail is loosely related.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to compliance by keeping documentation current but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance into a product feature is a recognizable strategy, somewhat interesting but not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by creating a new product born from compliance, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Commercializing compliance tooling is a legal, normal business practice that offends no sensibilities, though it is somewhat less common than simply complying.
evidence_implementability: Extracting an existing logging stack into an SDK and piloting with two customers requires some engineering and productization work but is reasonably feasible, though it depends on a first proposal being built.
evidence_applicability: The idea mainly addresses an implied problem (monetizing and gaining credibility from compliance) rather than directly meeting the logging mandate, which relies on the separate first proposal.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure the lab meets Article 12 but contributes by funding and strengthening the logging infrastructure, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A retrofit of logging using an open-source agent on existing infrastructure is the common, mundane response expected from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in existing prototypes using open-source tools and documenting it in the technical dossier is a common, compliant strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team, six weeks, and reuse of the existing Kubernetes monitoring stack make this a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified Article 12(3) fields, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet the logging requirement for the three prototypes, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and only existing prototypes, not Article 12(2) traceability or future systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating log entries as first-class typed event objects in an append-only store is a sensible but fairly expected approach that shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new structure (typed event objects, schema inheritance) but still treats compliance as a logging practice built into the architecture rather than changing the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Structured, append-only event logging documented in architecture records is a conventional, norm-compliant engineering response to a legal mandate.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring the serving microservice and data pipeline to emit typed event objects requires some architectural changes but is reasonably feasible with existing engineering resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the specific Article 12(3) fields as structured records.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields and make logging a structural property, though it covers only the Annex III 1(a) scope and not the broader Article 12(2) event relevance or R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: A reusable reference template for the Article 12(3) logging fields is a sensible but common engineering and compliance-by-design response that many labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a reusable golden pipeline template and published logging contract) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reference implementations and compliance-by-design templates are common strategies that violate no norms, though biometric identity logging raises minor privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: Building a Dockerised service on the existing matching stack with OpenAPI docs is a reasonably feasible engineering task requiring some changes, though integrating verifier identity capture takes work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by emitting the exact four data points mandated in Article 12(3) for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully solve the 12(3) minimum logging requirement for biometric systems if adopted, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging mandate across the lab's other work, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging by design with a standard middleware and release gate is a very common, mundane response to Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that treats compliance as logging and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged apart from a gate.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into system architecture as a mandatory internal gate is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared middleware layer and internal spec maintained by a small platform team is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some process changes but not radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, with X (native logging layer) producing Y (Article 12 compliance).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a native logging layer with defined event types and Annex III fields would substantially meet the Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not address broader R&D adaptation or the Article 12(2) purposes in detail.

evidence_originality: A client-facing dashboard of aggregated log summaries is a somewhat unusual and interesting angle on Article 12, but it is not strikingly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new offering born from compliance, turning logging into a procurement differentiator, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Read-only, anonymised, access-controlled summaries with full logs kept under custody respect GDPR and contractual norms, so the strategy offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building on existing logging middleware with role-based access is reasonably feasible and needs only moderate change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate through a transparency layer, but the dashboard solves an implied problem (client assurance and market positioning) rather than the core logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The dashboard does not itself implement Article 12 logging capabilities such as event recording or the Annex III minimums, so it helps only as a partial contribution to the solution.

evidence_originality: Red-team style audit of logs is an interesting, somewhat imaginative twist on standard compliance checks, though mock audits are fairly familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (simulated regulatory inquiry) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits and mock inspections are common, legitimate practice that offends no norms, though the log-only reconstruction framing is slightly distinctive.
evidence_implementability: A semiannual cross-functional exercise on one system per cycle needs some staff time and process setup but no radical change or major expense.
evidence_applicability: The audit directly tests whether Article 12 logs enable reconstruction of risk events, modifications, and verification chains, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It detects and remediates logging gaps but does not itself design or build the logging capability or address R&D adaptation, so it is a helpful partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK with CI-gated enforcement is a sensible and fairly expected engineering response, with only mild imaginative touches like per-risk-category schema templates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (SDK, schemas, CI gating) but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal shared libraries and CI checks are common engineering practice that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a dual-language SDK, schema templates per risk category, and CI enforcement requires a dedicated platform team effort and some process change, but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (do X to get automatic logs, which is the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, standardized automatic event logging in every prototype would largely satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not itself address the specific minimum fields or retention, so it is close to a full solution.

evidence_originality: Shifting-left compliance design into project planning is a common, expected response, though the rotating engineer gate is a mildly interesting detail.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process element (design checkpoint and workshop in each sprint) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only moved earlier, without changing what the lab researches or how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A planning workshop and sign-off gate is a common governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A half-day workshop and a spec section require modest process changes and a rotating engineer from an existing pool, though the code-review gating adds some friction.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by ensuring logging requirements are designed in rather than retrofitted.
evidence_effectiveness: Scoping logging early would help meet Article 12 for new projects but does not address existing systems, the actual log content, or the technical logging itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Inserting compliance reviews into phase gates with a checklist is a common, mundane governance approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint and rotating record-keeper role into existing processes, treating compliance as standard documentation practice with the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using existing phase gates, rotating staff, and a checklist violates no norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: It relies on existing tooling and personnel with a half-day workshop and a single-page template, so it is easy and low cost to implement.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses documentation and record-keeping review (Recital 71 technical documentation) but only implies the Article 12 automatic logging mandate, so it solves a related, implied problem rather than the logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation checklist review helps ensure technical files are clear and complete but does not create automatic event logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware reusing existing infrastructure is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared middleware logging layer is a new tool but still treats compliance purely as logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure and standard middleware agents violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Deploying lightweight agents on existing endpoints and storage is low cost and non-radical, though integrating across all projects takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the automatic event-logging mandate (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic structured event logging with timestamps and reference-database queries would meaningfully address Article 12 logging, but it omits input-match data, human verifier identification, and risk-event relevance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging into shared middleware built on existing observability tooling is a common, sensible engineering response that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that consolidates tooling without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging for compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing Prometheus and Loki infrastructure with one platform team build in a quarter, though each project must adapt its manifests, so some changes are needed but cost is low.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly implements the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing timestamps, reference-database identifiers, input hashes, and verifier records, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A single schema and audit point would largely satisfy the logging requirements if built, but it covers mainly the Annex III 1(a) minimums and does not address documentation, risk-relevant event selection, or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design logging from the earliest prototype is a very common and expected response, not particularly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds templates, gates and roles but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged, though it does embed logging into the design process slightly beyond bolt-on.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-by-design logging is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Revising design templates, adding review gates, and assigning a logging engineer per team are moderate process changes with some added cost but clearly feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building automatic event recording into all high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native logging with sign-off gates would largely meet the Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not address specifics like Annex III minimum items or retention explicitly.

evidence_originality: Durable versioned log storage is a sensible, expected engineering response to lifetime logging mandates, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (versioned store) but still treats compliance as logging infrastructure practice.
evidence_acceptability: Retention, access controls and auditor query APIs are conventional, legally aligned practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A schema-versioned columnar append-only store with tiered compression and role-based access uses mature technology but requires building a dedicated infrastructure layer, so some changes and moderate effort are needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of keeping logs across the system lifetime (Art. 12(1)) and supporting post-market retrieval (Art. 72).
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve lifetime log durability and retrieval, but does not decide which events to log or cover the broader compliance and R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and git-based compliance tracking is a fairly known practice, though the automated diffs that flag invalidated descriptions add mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and processes (git-linked documentation, automated diffs) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice, though it does fold compliance into routine workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Version-controlled documentation with named-owner sign-off is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Git tooling and a ten-day sign-off rule are reasonably feasible with modest changes by existing research-ops staff, though the automation to detect invalidated descriptions takes some building.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (keeping technical documentation up to date per Recital 71) rather than the directly stated logging mandate, and it misattributes the documentation duty to Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Version-controlled living documentation would keep technical documentation current, but it does not implement the automatic event logging Article 12 actually mandates, so it solves only part of the problem.

evidence_originality: Centralised reusable logging middleware is a common, expected engineering response to such a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice with shared tooling, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a shared internal logging module to meet Article 12 is a common, legitimate compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building middleware on existing infrastructure with standardised APIs is reasonably feasible, though it needs some integration changes across projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by auto-capturing the logs Article 12 requires.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would deliver the automatic event recording and minimum Article 12 fields, but it covers mainly the technical logging and not wider documentation or risk-relevant event definitions, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance into a client-facing differentiator is interesting and shows some imagination, but transparency dashboards and compliance reports are fairly familiar ideas.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a market offering and competitive differentiator, which changes the relationship between the lab's activity and its compliance obligations without altering what it researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing transparency reports and compliance dashboards is a fairly common, uncontroversial practice, though certifying conformance for every client deployment and sharing log schemas is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Building a read-only status dashboard and writing an annual white paper requires some new tooling and processes but is reasonably feasible given logs already exist.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, proving and communicating logging compliance to clients and procurement, which relates to the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate but is not the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A client-facing dashboard and transparency report only demonstrate logging conformance and do not themselves implement the automatic event recording Article 12 requires, so they contribute to compliance but are only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning mandatory logs into a client-facing monitoring dashboard product is a somewhat unusual and interesting idea that shows some imagination, but 'compliance as a product' is a fairly familiar framing and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by creating a new revenue-generating service born from compliance, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking the lab's research focus.
evidence_acceptability: Exposing logs to clients raises confidentiality and data-protection concerns, yet offering monitoring services is a normal business strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an API layer and client portal over existing log streams requires notable engineering effort, data-access and security controls, but is reasonably feasible with standard technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly builds on Article 12(2)(b) and Article 72 logging and monitoring obligations, but the identified benefit (revenue, reputation) is an implied rather than stated part of the compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard built on log streams would help with post-market monitoring and transparency but does not by itself ensure the logging mandate is met (event coverage, retention, traceability), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance checks in development cycles are a familiar response, and the replay tool adds only a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (gate, checklist, replay tool) but still treats compliance as a logging verification practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A sprint checkpoint with a checklist is a common, uncontroversial process control that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-hour gate, a checklist, and a replay tool require modest changes to the sprint cadence, though building the replay tool against live log streams takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D by verifying that required events are captured.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate that verifies logging covers Article 12(2)(a)-(c) events would help meet the logging mandate, but it checks only prototypes at one stage and does not itself build logging, cover Article 12(3) specifics, or address documentation and lifetime logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using in-house models to self-audit logs and turning compliance into publishable research is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as publishable research and funding leverage, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than just adding a logging tool.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research on compliance tooling violates no norms, though using models to audit logs for a regulated system is a slightly uncommon approach that should not offend regulators.
evidence_implementability: A six-month sprint with two postdocs and existing synthetic-data pipelines is modest and reasonably feasible, though building reliable real-time anomaly detection requires some new effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (log reliability and completeness for post-market monitoring) related to the logging mandate, benchmarked against Annex III 1(a) fields, rather than the directly stated need to meet the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: Anomaly detection on log completeness would help assure log integrity but does not itself implement the core logging mandate (event recording, retention, Article 12(2) relevance), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable compliance middleware in project scaffolds is a fairly standard, expected engineering response, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (middleware, scaffold dependency) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into templates and gating code review on it is a common, sensible engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A reusable middleware built by two developers in one quarter and integrated into project scaffolds is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some process change but not radical investment.
evidence_applicability: The idea directly implements automatic event logging, which is the identified requirement in Article 12 and the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A non-bypassable logging layer capturing Article 12(2) events and Annex III 1(a) data points would, if built, address the core logging mandate for the lab's high-risk systems, though it does not itself cover other obligations like documentation.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory Article 12 logs as a scientific dataset for longitudinal drift research is an unusual and interesting reframing that shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging woven into the science and turning the obligation into a research asset.
evidence_acceptability: Analyzing own operational logs and publishing findings is a reasonable strategy, though privacy and biometric data concerns under GDPR add some sensitivity but do not offend norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds a lightweight analytics layer on an existing logging pipeline with two postdocs, so it needs modest changes and cost, though it must wait twelve months for data.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by leveraging logs, but does not itself meet the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab get value from compliance logs but does not solve the compliance mandate itself, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates and design reviews are a standard, expected response to a regulatory mandate and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint and a spec format but treats compliance as standard logging practice, with the lab's research approach unchanged, which is largely paradigm preserving.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate reviews and compliance sign-offs are common, uncontroversial corporate practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A design-review gate with a compliance-drafted checklist and sign-off uses existing governance structures and needs only process changes and modest engineering effort, though it requires some changes to the pipeline.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by requiring a spec that covers all Article 12(2) event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate ensures logging is designed in and checked before pilot, which contributes substantially, but it covers only the design spec rather than the actual implementation, the retention, or the Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a longitudinal robustness research corpus is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, but the idea of mining deployment telemetry for drift is fairly familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making mandated logs a core research dataset and turning compliance into a scientific asset, which is paradigm stretching, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Secondary research use of logs containing personal data and input data raises GDPR purpose-limitation and confidentiality concerns, and publishing from deployment data may offend customers somewhat, though it is not wholly unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: Building an analytics pipeline over existing mandated logs and running scheduled probes is reasonably feasible with some added engineering and data governance effort.
evidence_applicability: It uses the Article 12(3) log streams to produce research value, which relates to the stated problem of how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate, though the benefit (research output) is an implied rather than directly identified compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal builds an analytics pipeline over the logs, but it does not itself ensure that the logging mandate is met (coverage, retention, Article 12(2) event relevance), so it contributes only partially to the solution and mainly addresses the 'adapt R&D' half.

evidence_originality: Studying logging overhead trade-offs as a publishable research question is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but a performance benchmarking study is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a research-framing of compliance instrumentation, modestly changing how compliance relates to R&D, though it remains centered on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: A research sub-project with open benchmarks and a paper offends no norms, legal sensibilities, or business practices.
evidence_implementability: Six months with two PhD students on existing model families is modest, though it depends on the logging layer from Proposal 1 being built first.
evidence_applicability: Benchmarking logging overhead addresses an implied problem (understanding the performance cost of meeting Article 12 logging) that relates to the mandate but is not itself the act of complying.
evidence_effectiveness: It would inform how to tune logging density but does not itself implement logging or satisfy the mandate, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Drawing on genomics and climate-modelling data-management practice to define minimal provenance is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a formal minimal provenance schema and a methodological contribution) but still treats compliance as a logging/metadata practice.
evidence_acceptability: A research project to formalise provenance schemas and prototype them against an existing registry violates no legal or social norms, though framing it as a methodological contribution is slightly uncommon.
evidence_implementability: Literature synthesis and prototyping two or three schemas on an existing registry is a reasonably feasible, modest-cost effort, though formalising an 'irreducible' schema is somewhat open-ended.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, deciding what to record to satisfy Article 12(2), which relates to the stated logging mandate, though it focuses on provenance metadata rather than event logs directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema defining which metadata to record would help determine what the logs must contain, but it is research-stage, does not itself implement automatic event logging, and covers only part of the compliance need.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by design through a shared SDK, review gates and embedded compliance engineers is the standard 'compliance by design' answer an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (SDK, review gates, embedded engineers) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Engineering-integrated logging with review gates and compliance sign-off is a common, norm-respecting strategy that violates no laws or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared SDK, review gates and a compliance engineer per squad require some process change and moderate cost, but are reasonably feasible measures.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(1) logging mandate by enabling automatic event recording across systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, built-in logging with review gates would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not specify event content for Article 12(2) and 12(3) and relies on execution quality, so it is mostly but not fully a solution.

evidence_originality: Keeping documentation continuously updated is a standard, expected response to Recital 71 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though it adds a repository and triggers.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining living technical documentation with named compliance owners is a common, fully legitimate compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A versioned repository, update triggers, and named owners require some process changes and tooling but are reasonably feasible with existing QA resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the technical documentation requirement in Recital 71, which is related to but not the Article 12 automatic logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Up-to-date documentation helps traceability and compliance but does not implement automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Risk-tiered audits and prioritized remediation are what an experienced evaluator would expect, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance project-management process that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Triage and prioritization of compliance work is a common business practice that offends no norms, though deliberately deferring some compliance work is mildly sensitive.
evidence_implementability: A four-week self-assessment and sequenced sprints use existing staff and ordinary project management, so it is easy and low cost with no radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of scarce implementation resources versus the logging mandate, though it applies to the Article 12 obligations only indirectly via prioritization (and the deferral may conflict with obligations).
evidence_effectiveness: It helps allocate scarce resources and sequence work, but it does not itself build the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checklists and design-phase checkpoints are a common, expected response, with nothing surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-by-design process step that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a checklist checkpoint to an existing sprint cycle is a common, norm-compliant project management practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist piloted on three projects within the existing sprint cadence is low-cost and requires only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by adapting R&D planning so that required logging fields are specified up front.
evidence_effectiveness: A planning checkpoint that identifies needed Article 12 log fields and confirms the architecture can emit them helps ensure logging capability, but it is only a process step and does not itself build the logging or cover the full mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using SPC-based anomaly alerting over logs for post-market monitoring is a sensible, fairly expected extension of logging, interesting but not surprising or rare among labs' responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (streaming pipeline, SPC alerting, dashboard) while still treating compliance as logging practice, though it reframes logs as safety intelligence without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Monitoring production logs for safety and reporting to clients is a common, norm-respecting strategy with no legal or social concerns.
evidence_implementability: Kafka plus a time-series store and alerting dashboards are mature off-the-shelf tools, so this requires some new infrastructure and rule definition but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets identified obligations in Articles 72, 79(1), and 26(5) that the logging mandate serves, though the core logging capability itself is assumed rather than addressed.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially support post-market monitoring and risk detection but does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met at the system level, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging library with a schema and retention settings is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance tooling approach that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged and treats compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging SDK is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over six weeks building a reusable Python logging library is a modest, non-radical change that fits existing pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces Article 12 logs, which is the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver the logging capability, but it targets only Annex III 1(a) fields and not the broader Article 12(2) event-relevance, traceability, or documentation needs, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying sequential change-point detection to operationalize 'substantial modification' is interesting and somewhat unusual, but drift detection is a well-known approach in ML monitoring.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (online change-point drift detectors) and ties a research project to compliance, but it still treats compliance as a logging/monitoring practice rather than changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A research project on monitoring tools violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy for a lab.
evidence_implementability: Developing and validating adaptive online detectors is a research effort requiring significant work, though it is feasible with existing statistical methods and deployment logs.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified part of the stated problem, event recording for identifying substantial modification risks, though it frames Article 12 as implicitly requiring detection, which is an implied link.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift detection would help identify situations of substantial modification under Article 12(2)(a), but it covers only one logging purpose and does not meet the broader logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: An internal log governance and audit function with mock regulator inspections is a common, expected response to the mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance governance and audit practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance and audit functions are a common, norm-conforming strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Chartering a small cross-functional team to write retention policies and run quarterly mock audits requires some organizational change but uses ordinary, reasonably feasible measures.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that records are produced and retained, though the retention and audit focus is somewhat implied rather than the technical logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Governance and auditing help verify and sustain logging compliance but do not themselves build the technical automatic logging capability Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Experiment tracking with data lineage and append-only ledgers is well known; the framing of compliance as a by-product is mildly interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and processes but still treats compliance as logging/documentation practice, though it does weave documentation into the research workflow somewhat.
evidence_acceptability: Provenance tracking and audit-ready experiment records are common, norm-compliant practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing MLflow-style tracking with an append-only versioned ledger is reasonably feasible with some pipeline changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely documentation and traceability of development, which relates to the stated logging mandate via Recital 71 rather than directly meeting Article 12 operational logs.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic lineage and provenance capture supports technical documentation and traceability under Recital 71, but it does not address Article 12's event logging of deployed high-risk systems (risk situations, post-market monitoring, Annex III 1(a) minimums), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized append-only logging with deployment gates is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as a logging practice, adding tooling (microservice, deployment gate) without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A shared tamper-evident logging service with CI/CD gating is a standard, legally aligned engineering response that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared microservice with append-only storage and a CI/CD test gate requires real engineering effort across all pipelines but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by recording sessions and risk-relevant events.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would largely satisfy the logging requirement, though it only partially covers items like the Annex III 1(a) specifics (reference database, matched inputs, verifier identity) and does not address R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: A 'traceability budget' metric and tensor-level logging hooks born of compliance are unusual and imaginative, though the link between interpretability and logging is somewhat familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It ties logging to what the lab researches by making traceability an architectural property and a research contribution, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme with doctoral hires and open-source publication violates no legal or social norms, though a research-heavy response to a logging mandate is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A two-year programme with four research positions and speculative architecture-level logging hooks is expensive and uncertain, and the lab says approval means committing implementation resources rather than exploring.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting Article 12(1) automatic event logging and adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achievable, tensor-level traces and benchmarks on a few standard tasks only partly deliver Article 12's required event logs, such as use periods, reference databases and human verifiers, so it contributes but is not a full solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered log storage with latency SLAs is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a lifetime logging mandate, with only modest imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tiered storage architecture with query SLAs but still treats compliance as a logging infrastructure practice, leaving the lab's R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a robust log storage architecture for regulatory inspection is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A prototype benchmarked before committing hardware budgets is reasonably feasible, though decade-scale storage with sub-second queries and under 1% write overhead requires some real engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 lifetime log retention and retrieval requirement, including the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the storage and retrievability side of logging but does not decide what events to log, address post-market monitoring processes, or cover other compliance needs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using a CI gate to operationalize substantial-modification thresholds is an interesting and somewhat imaginative application, though CI gating and drift detection are known techniques.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process and ties compliance to commit-time engineering workflow, but still treats compliance as a logging/monitoring practice without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Gating promotion on compliance-owned thresholds with signed records is a reasonably familiar governance practice, though a bit unusual for R&D, and offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Diffing weight hashes and configs in CI is feasible with existing pipelines, though defining quantitative substantial-modification thresholds and gating merges requires some process and tooling changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, knowing when a model change is a substantial modification, which relates to Article 12(2)(a) and the lab's compliance response rather than the logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate that detects substantial-modification drift supports Article 12(2)(a) event identification but does not deliver the core logging mandate (automatic event recording, traceability, post-market monitoring), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Documentation-as-code generated from experiment metadata is a fairly well-known approach (model cards from MLflow), so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/process (doc generation pipeline) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from tracking metadata is a common, norm-compliant practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing MLflow tracking with a schema and a scheduled rendering job, which is a modest engineering change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified Recital 71 requirement that technical documentation be kept up to date, which is related to but not the core logging mandate of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would keep technical documentation current, which helps, but it does not address the Article 12 event logging mandate itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-release compliance gates with checklists are a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance review practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged and treats compliance as a checkpoint.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance checkpoints and sign-off gates are common governance strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a checklist and training two engineers as reviewers is a low-cost, non-radical change, though it adds a mandatory gate to the release process.
evidence_applicability: A pre-release review gate directly targets the stated problem of how the lab meets the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying compliance before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A review gate only verifies logging compliance and does not build logging capability, so it contributes to the solution as a partial measure rather than solving the whole problem.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default logging templates are a fairly expected response, with the adapter-profile selection adding only modest interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (scaffold and adapters) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliant logging into internal starter templates is a common, norm-respecting engineering practice that offends no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing internal starter kit with a pluggable logging adapter requires some development work but is reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate in the lab's R&D by making logging automatic at prototype creation.
evidence_effectiveness: If adopted, it would automatically wire Article 12 logging, including Annex III 1(a) fields, into new prototypes, but it covers only new systems, not existing ones, and does not address retention, post-market monitoring use, or human-verifier identification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A drop-in logging middleware/SDK for compliance is a very expected, common engineering response to Article 12, with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (SDK with JSON schema) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, which is slightly paradigm stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding standard compliance tooling into engineering workflows is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a decorator-based middleware with a schema is reasonably feasible with moderate engineering effort, though wrapping any serving endpoint universally is somewhat ambitious.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate while preserving R&D velocity (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: A standardized logging layer would address the logging mandate for events in 12(2) and 12(3) in prototypes, but it does not cover deployment-level retention, the Annex III specifics like reference databases and verifier identities automatically, or the documentation obligations, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Dedicated monitoring units for deployed systems are an expected response to Article 12/72, so the idea is fairly common with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a team and an alerting workflow but still treats compliance as log consumption and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A post-market surveillance team with escalation and pause authority is a common, norm-compliant governance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Hiring three people, wiring them into existing alerting, and granting pause authority is a reasonably feasible organizational change requiring some cost and process adjustment but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses using Article 12 logs to identify Article 79(1) risks and support post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute meaningfully to monitoring and risk detection but does not itself deliver the logging capability or cover R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing log-sufficiency as an information-theoretic problem with lower bounds per risk category is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly unprecedented given privacy-utility research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It makes compliance a research question and changes what the lab researches, relating R&D to obligations, but it stops short of fully redefining the lab's overall research agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Academic research on privacy and logging offends no norms and is a legitimate, somewhat uncommon response to a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: Fundamental research deriving formal bounds is difficult and uncertain, and approval here means committing resources to work with no near-term compliance deliverable, though ablations on existing pipelines are feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (balancing Article 12(3)(c) logging with data minimisation) that relates to the mandate but not the stated need to meet the logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would inform how much to log and reduce over-collection, but it does not itself deliver a working logging mechanism meeting Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance gates and CI checks are a fairly familiar DevOps pattern, with only mild novelty in tying them to an Article 12 linter.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (sprint template, CI gate, linter, log-contract artifact) but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing agile workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Gating builds on compliance and front-loading architecture work are common engineering strategies that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Updating a playbook, adding a board artifact, and writing a linter plugin are modest, reasonably feasible changes, though the linter and schema work take some effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab meets the Article 12 logging mandate by defining event schemas and enforcing log endpoints via a CI gate and linter against the Article 12 checklist.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, front-loaded logging architecture with automated enforcement would largely ensure systems technically support automatic event recording, though it does not cover documentation, retention, or the substance of what counts as relevant events.

evidence_originality: A public benchmark scoring how well system internal state can be reconstructed from logs alone is an unusual and imaginative response, though not wholly unprecedented as a benchmark idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logging into a research and field-level offering with external partners, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, but it stops short of redirecting what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks with collaborating labs and open data are broadly accepted scientific practice and offend no norms, though the IP framing is mildly self-serving.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers, synthetic tasks and three partner labs are modest, but coordinating a shared schema across external labs and defining a valid reconstructability metric takes real effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the logging mandate only indirectly, since the benchmark helps assess log quality but does not itself get the lab's own systems to meet Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Publishing an external benchmark would not by itself deliver Article 12 logging in the lab's systems, so it is unlikely to solve the stated problem and at most helps tangentially.

evidence_originality: Mapping the Article 12(3) minimums to a typed event schema enforced in continuous integration is a sensible but expected response that many labs would give, so it is common rather than ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a typed schema and CI checks but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged, which is at most slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing the mandated logging fields in a schema is a common compliance strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
