evidence_implementability: A small team of four writing and piloting a spec over two quarters and submitting a paper is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some resource commitment but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (logging schema design and standardization, reputation) related to the mandate rather than directly meeting the logging obligation.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure the lab's own systems meet Article 12 logging requirements, though piloting internally contributes partially, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing production logs as regression fixtures is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing of a compliance obligation, though replay testing is a known technique.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance logging and R&D by weaving the logs into the lab's testing and release process, but does not address what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Replaying anonymised production logs in CI is a reasonable engineering practice that violates no norms, though it needs care with data protection and anonymisation, making it a slightly unusual but acceptable strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a log-sampling and replay pipeline and anonymisation extending existing nightly CI, which is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It uses the logs mandated by Article 12 for a purpose (regression testing) that is only implied by the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, rather than meeting the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure the logging requirements of Article 12 are met but adds value from the logs and aids post-market monitoring, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Version-controlled living documentation on an existing wiki with a designated owner is a common, mundane compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It uses existing tools and standard documentation practice and leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation ownership and periodic reviews are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It piggybacks on existing Git and wiki infrastructure with one owner per project and a monthly review slot, so it needs no new purchases and only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation and record-keeping under Recital 71, which is related to but not the same as Article 12's automatic event logging, so it solves an implied rather than directly stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A living-documentation workflow helps with traceability and audit readiness but does not provide the automatic event logging Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Provenance manifests in CI are an interesting, somewhat familiar idea (model cards, ML metadata) with modest imagination in framing reproducibility as compliance infrastructure.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI manifest plugin) but still treats compliance as logging/documentation practice, though it weaves it into the release workflow somewhat.
evidence_acceptability: Provenance manifests reviewed in code review are a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small platform team building a CI plugin on top of existing experiment trackers is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes to workflow.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets generating records and documentation (logs, validation records, lineage) for compliance, which is related to the logging mandate, though it focuses on released artifacts rather than runtime event logs of deployed high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Auto-generated manifests from experiment trackers would help with technical documentation and traceability but do not provide automatic event logging over a system's lifetime, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mining logs as a failure taxonomy with an annual state-of-failure report is an interesting, somewhat imaginative reuse of compliance data, but analyzing incident data is a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logs into a standing research program and published output, changing the relationship between R&D and Article 12 obligations so logging feeds the science, though it does not change what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Analyzing operational logs and publishing aggregate failure reports is a legitimate, norm-compatible practice, with only minor confidentiality and data protection concerns to manage.
evidence_implementability: Two postdocs and a structured incident database are modest, reasonably feasible resources, though it depends on logs already existing and on access to deployed-system data.
evidence_applicability: It uses Article 12 logs to serve the implied need of risk identification and post-market monitoring, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly address how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with post-market monitoring and identifying risk situations but does not itself deliver the logging capability the mandate requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware and template scaffolding is a common, mundane engineering response to such a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, packaged as a library, with the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging SDK is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It extracts existing production logging hooks into a versioned package and wires it into the template repo, which is reasonably feasible and low cost with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by providing Article 12 log emitters for prototypes, though the stated benefit of saved setup time is partly an adjacent efficiency gain.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with the technical capability to log events, but it covers only part of the problem, since it does not decide which events matter, retention, or Annex III specifics beyond schemas.

evidence_originality: An immutable event-sourced ledger mapped to Article 12(3) fields is a sensible, expected engineering response, with only mild interest in the SSO binding.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a specific tooling architecture (event-sourced WORM ledger, auditor API) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how the lab's R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable audit logging with retention policy and SSO integration is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy, though biometric data storage raises some privacy considerations that are not addressed.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing SSO and standard WORM and event-sourcing technology, requiring a moderate dedicated system build that is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement of Article 12(3) logging items (period of use, reference database, matched input, verifier identity).
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would record all four Article 12(3) minimum items for biometric identification systems, solving the core logging mandate for that product line, though not Article 12(1)-(2) for other systems.

evidence_originality: An open cross-lab logging ontology tied to reproducibility is somewhat interesting and imaginative, but standardized log schemas and consortium-built open standards are a fairly expected response, so it shows some imagination without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (an ontology, consortium, and reference implementations) and reframes logs as shared scientific infrastructure, but it still treats compliance essentially as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source consortium standards with permissive licensing are common, norm-conforming strategies that offend no sensibilities, though publishing log structures may raise some confidentiality questions.
evidence_implementability: Convening four to six labs to co-design an ontology and produce reference implementations requires significant coordination effort and time, but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (standardizing log formats, reproducibility) related to the logging mandate, and the Article 12(3) fields apply only to Annex III 1(a) systems, so the link is indirect rather than a direct fix.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared schema would help standardize log fields, but it does not itself make the lab's systems log automatically or meet Article 12 obligations, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: A compliance gate memo in a stage-gate process is a very standard, expected response to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice layered onto existing procedures, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A stage-gate compliance checkpoint is a common governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a compliance sign-off gate to existing stage-gate procedures requires modest process amendment and staff time, not radical or costly change.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets verifying that logging meets Article 12(2) requirements, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It ensures review and sign-off but does not itself build the logging capability or technical content, so it is a partial solution that helps verify compliance.

evidence_originality: Publishing logged failure events as an open benchmark is unusual and shows imagination, though open datasets from deployments are a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logs into a public research offering and extends the lab's scientific reach, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, though it does not redefine what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing deployment-derived records publicly raises privacy, confidentiality and GDPR sensitivities, and may offend somewhat, although anonymization and ethics review mitigate this.
evidence_implementability: It needs ethics review, anonymization pipelines, schema design and publication, which is some added work but reasonably feasible once logs exist, though the risk of re-identification and IP or confidentiality review adds difficulty.
evidence_applicability: It uses logged data for external research, which only implicitly relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate or adapting R&D, so it addresses an implied downstream benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: Releasing an anonymized failure dataset does not itself deliver the Article 12 logging capability or compliance, so at best it is a tangential partial contribution and arguably does not solve the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Shared compliance teams and budget line reallocation are interesting organizational moves but fairly predictable, with some imagination in the funding decoupling.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new organizational structure and funding line but still treats compliance as logging infrastructure practice, not changing the R&D-compliance relationship fundamentally.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding a compliance team is common, but reclassifying 15% of R&D personnel costs as regulatory infrastructure could raise accounting or funder-compliance concerns, offending sensibilities somewhat.
evidence_implementability: Forming a three-person team is feasible, but cross-project embedding and budget reclassification need organizational and funder negotiation, requiring some changes.
evidence_applicability: A shared team to build logging/traceability compliance directly addresses how the lab meets the logging mandate, though the logging specifics are implied rather than stated.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared pod avoids duplicated compliance builds and helps meet logging requirements, but it is only a partial solution since it does not specify what gets logged or how Article 12 requirements are technically satisfied.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with stewards and review triggers is a common, expected compliance response, with the fourteen-day cycle as the only slightly specific touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice, with the documentation process added alongside R&D and no change to how the lab works or relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation governance programs are a common, norm-compliant corporate compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Version-controlled documentation with designated stewards and release-triggered reviews uses existing practices and needs only modest process changes, so it is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation (Recital 71), which is related to the logging mandate but is not the logging requirement in Article 12 itself, so it solves an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It contributes to demonstrating compliance and traceability but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in from the first sprint via shared middleware is a sensible, widely expected 'compliance by design' response that labs would commonly give, with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standard, shared logging layer and process but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged, though integration into design reviews adds a slight stretch.
evidence_acceptability: An internal engineering standard for logging violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Shared middleware and a technical specification are standard engineering work that a lab can build with moderate effort, though requiring it from the first sprint for every prototype involves some process change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the event-recording capability into R&D, with the outcome tied to Article 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the core logging mandate of Article 12(1)-(2) if implemented, but it omits the Article 12(3) minimum items and does not cover other aspects such as retention, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Treating minimal-sufficient logging as a publishable research line is somewhat unusual and interesting, but the expected lab response is a logging implementation, and this is only a moderately imaginative twist rather than a surprising one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the obligation into a research output and standards-influence activity, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing preprints and engaging in interpretive guidance discussions violate no norms, though minimizing logs might raise mild regulator sensitivities, so it is somewhat unusual but inoffensive.
evidence_implementability: Two researchers over twelve months using existing pilot systems is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment requiring some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified related problem, namely determining what logging satisfies Article 12(2) and reducing compliance uncertainty, though the immediate mandate to implement logging is only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: A research programme yields findings only after twelve months and does not itself deliver compliant logging now, so it contributes partially to meeting the mandate rather than solving it.

evidence_originality: Standardized documentation templates are common, but tying them to open-science reproducibility norms shows some imagination without being truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance documentation as a contribution to scientific infrastructure and builds new partnerships born from compliance, changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Combining compliance documentation with open-science norms is somewhat unusual but offends no sensibilities, though sharing templates raises minor IP caution.
evidence_implementability: A six-week sprint with existing internal committee and an external working group, then a two-project pilot, requires some coordination changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The template directly addresses Recital 71 documentation requirements, but it does not address the Article 12 automatic logging mandate that is the core of the stated problem, so it solves a related implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with technical documentation and credibility but would not deliver automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying homomorphic tokens or DP noising to mandated biometric match logs is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle that few labs would propose, though the techniques themselves are well known.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (privacy-preserving tooling, threat models) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Studying privacy-preserving logging is a legitimate, norm-respecting approach, though noising or tokenizing mandated match data could raise questions about whether logs still satisfy the legal requirement, making it somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping two architectures and publishing threat models is feasible for a lab, but making cryptographic or DP techniques preserve evidentiary fidelity for biometric matches is difficult and needs significant engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified problem, the tension between the Article 12(3)(c) mandated logging of match input data and the data-protection risk, which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal is exploratory research that would at best yield a prototype and analysis, helping with Article 12(3)(c) compliance and privacy risk only partially rather than solving the logging mandate for the lab.

evidence_originality: Log retention and cost protocols are a common, expected response to a logging mandate, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging administration that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A storage, encryption, and access-tier protocol with DPO consultation and finance validation is a standard, uncontroversial governance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It is a document drafted by existing IT and finance teams tied to existing cloud contracts and the normal procurement cycle, requiring only modest changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of log storage, security, and cost that relates to meeting the logging mandate, but it does not itself produce the logging capability.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help manage retention, privacy, and cost of logs but is only a partial solution since it does not implement the logging or cover the Article 12(2) event recording.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware built into the SDK is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, though schema versioning alongside model code is a modest touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging middleware embedded in the SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building standard logging infrastructure to meet a legal requirement violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a shared library into an existing SDK is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change, though capturing Annex III-specific data and retention policies requires some engineering work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified event types and minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, automatic structured logging of Article 12 events and minimums would largely solve the logging mandate, though it does not address broader questions like retention duties or what R&D to pursue.

evidence_originality: A log retention and access policy is a very common, expected compliance response, so it is mundane and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance governance (retention, encryption, RBAC) that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal retention and access-control policies aligned with GDPR are common strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a policy by the compliance office is low cost and non-radical, though aligning retention with lifetime and updates takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (log governance, retention, GDPR tension, and production on request) that relates to the logging mandate but not the identified core requirement of technically enabling logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A retention and access policy helps ensure logs can be produced and protected but does not itself implement the automatic logging capability or event coverage required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Requiring a design-phase specification document with sign-off gates is a common, mundane compliance approach that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A per-system Logging Specification template is a documentation-and-sign-off process that still treats compliance as ordinary logging practice without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: A mandatory design document with sign-off is a conventional governance strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires only a template, design-review integration, and a sign-off step, which are non-radical changes at low cost, though a gate before testing adds some process burden.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by defining which events are logged mapped to Article 12(2) and Annex III minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging requirements are planned and documented, but a specification does not itself implement logging capability or ensure it works, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing benchmark evaluation harnesses for drift monitoring and turning compliance into publications is a moderately imaginative angle, though drift monitoring itself is familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance outputs a source of publications and grant narrative, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Post-market monitoring reports and publishing findings are legitimate, but publishing from production traffic samples may raise data-privacy and confidentiality concerns, so it is somewhat unusual yet not offensive.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing evaluation harnesses with ten percent compute and a shared analyst and needs no new hires, though it depends on production log availability and a middleware that must exist first.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem (post-market monitoring under Article 72 as a purpose of logs), though it relies on logs produced elsewhere.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift analysis on production log samples supports Article 72 post-market monitoring but does not itself deliver the Article 12 automatic event logging and depends on another proposal's middleware, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable internal logging SDK enforced at codebase level is a sensible but very common engineering response that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, centralized as a library, and leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal shared tooling for regulatory compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a lightweight SDK wrapping inference pipelines is a routine platform-engineering task, though enforcing it across all projects requires some integration changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements, with explicit reference to 12(2) and 12(3) elements.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would automatically capture the mandated log categories and so would largely solve the logging mandate, though it is not enough alone for broader obligations like retention and documentation, and Annex III 3(d) personnel identification depends on workflow.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a shared longitudinal research corpus released to the community is an unusual and imaginative reframing that few labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making mandated logs a source of science and outside partnerships, and it also affects what the lab researches, which counts as paradigm breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing operational logs from deployed systems, even anonymized, raises GDPR, customer confidentiality, and security sensitivities, but data sharing for research is an accepted practice and is not outright unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year pipeline with anonymization, governance, customer data rights, and periodic public releases is a significant and costly undertaking, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal uses the Article 12(1) logs mandated by the regulation, but its main output is a research corpus rather than a way to meet the logging mandate, so it addresses an implied, related problem (adapting R&D around the mandate).
evidence_effectiveness: It does not help satisfy the logging requirements themselves, and it adds data-protection and confidentiality burdens, so it contributes only partially at best to the lab's response to the mandate.

evidence_originality: Gap audits and compliance matrices are the common, expected first response to a new regulation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance gap analysis that leaves the lab's way of working and the R&D-compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A internal compliance gap audit is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint using existing engineers and observability tools is low-cost and non-radical, easy to carry out.
evidence_applicability: A gap audit against Article 12 minimum fields directly addresses the stated problem of deciding how to meet the logging mandate, though it is a diagnostic step rather than the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit identifies where engineering is needed but does not itself implement logging, so it contributes only a partial solution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Append-only immutable logs with RBAC and retention policies are a standard, expected response to Article 12 and show little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a tiered WORM storage architecture but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable compliance logging with access controls is a common, norm-conforming strategy, although long retention of biometric data raises some privacy tension that is not addressed.
evidence_implementability: A three-month spike on existing WORM object storage is a reasonably feasible measure, though it requires some changes to deployment topology and pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by covering the four Article 12(3) fields and the lifetime retention for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, the architecture would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum fields and support audit retrieval, but it covers only the biometric subset and not Article 12(1)-(2) general logging or the broader documentation duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating documentability of stochastic learning systems as an epistemological research question is an unusual and imaginative response compared with typical logging-tool proposals, though not wholly unprecedented given existing interpretability and documentation literature.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research question about what the lab researches and publishes, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations and addressing the larger problem of research direction.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open research and setting community standards violates no legal or social norms and is broadly acceptable, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: A fundamental multi-paper research programme needs substantial researcher time and has uncertain outcomes, making it a significant and costly commitment but not impossible, and it is not a near-term implementation of a mandate.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely what documentation can be achieved, which relates to Recital 71 and the logging mandate but not to concrete Article 12 logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A theoretical research programme on documentation limits would not itself deliver the automatic event logging Article 12 requires, so it is at best a partial, indirect contributor and unlikely to solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Applying schema-registry versioning to compliance logs is a sensible but fairly expected data-engineering answer, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standard data-engineering tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves R&D workflow essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Schema registries and versioned data migration are common engineering strategies that violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Avro/Protobuf registries are mature tools, but adopting them with backfill and migration tooling across model teams requires some changes and moderate effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, log continuity and auditability as systems evolve, which relates to the logging mandate but is not the stated problem of meeting the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Schema versioning keeps historical logs usable over the system lifetime, which helps with Article 12(1) traceability, but it does not decide what events to log or cover the Article 12(2) relevance requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A post-market monitoring team with dashboards, thresholds and escalation is a common, expected response with little imaginative surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging and monitoring practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A dedicated compliance monitoring unit reviewing logs is a conventional, legally aligned practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires hiring a permanent team and building a dashboard and escalation protocol, which is reasonably feasible but involves some real organizational change and cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(2) purposes of risk identification, post-market monitoring and operation monitoring that the logging mandate serves.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by using logs for monitoring and escalation, but it does not itself make the systems technically log events or define what to log, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging middleware embedded in a starter template is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, though tying schemas to model cards is a small touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional, standard engineering and compliance approach that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin library integrated into an existing starter template is low-cost and non-radical, and is easy to build and adopt.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building a library that captures the event categories in Article 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a shared SDK would deliver technically present automatic logging across builds, but it covers only part of the problem (it ignores Article 12(3) specifics, retention, and deployer-side use, and a schema alone does not show relevance of the events logged).

evidence_originality: Treating log-informativeness as an architecture-dependent property to study through ablations is uncommon and imaginative, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes traceability as a scientific axis of architecture research, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance and affects what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A publicly shared research programme on architecture and logging offends no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Running controlled ablations across architectures needs significant compute, research staff, and a new metric for log-informativeness, so it is difficult and costly but possible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of making systems natively produce better logs, which relates to the logging mandate but is not a direct way to meet Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute knowledge that helps future compliance but does not by itself deliver logging capability now, so it is only a partial and long-term solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into a prototyping template is a sensible, fairly expected approach (observability by design) with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a pluggable emitter module in the template) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Standard engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities, though mandating it for every prototype may meet mild pushback.
evidence_implementability: Extending an internal prototyping template with a pluggable module and pre-wired schemas is a reasonably feasible, moderate change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X to get Article 12 event recording) and the R&D adaptation part.
evidence_effectiveness: A default instrumentation layer with schemas for each Article 12(2) category would meaningfully deliver the logging capability, but it does not cover Article 12(3) minimums, retention, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a research resource is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is a fairly intuitive idea that many labs would raise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Treating mandated logs as an internal research dataset changes the relationship between compliance and R&D (logging woven into the science) without redefining what the lab researches, so it is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Internal secondary use of logs is a fairly common strategy, though logs containing personal data raise GDPR purpose-limitation concerns that anonymisation only partly addresses.
evidence_implementability: Standardising schemas and adding read-only streams and a dashboard is reasonably feasible using existing infrastructure, though the two-sprint timeline across all projects is ambitious.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by deriving research value, which directly relates to the stated problem, though the compliance benefit is implied rather than stated.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with the logging mandate by standardising schemas and supporting audit defence, but it does not itself specify what must be logged under Article 12 and so only partly solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Long-lived, version-aware log schemas are a sensible but fairly expected response to lifetime logging requirements, so it is interesting rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a unified schema and migration guide but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Data architecture and retention schema design is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A small team drafting a schema and prototyping on existing object storage is a modest, low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(1) lifetime logging requirement and Article 72 post-market monitoring query needs, which are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses log continuity across model versions and post-market monitoring but does not cover which events to log, risk identification, or other Article 12 content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Interpretable-by-construction and self-logging architectures are somewhat unusual as a response to Article 12 and show imagination, but the interpretability idea itself is known in the literature.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the science of model architecture, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of changing what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Regulators, auditors and research communities would welcome this; it violates no norms, though it is a somewhat uncommon route to compliance.
evidence_implementability: Developing new architectures with formal log-emitting layers that match standard performance is a difficult, expensive, uncertain research effort that needs significant change, and the lab needs a committed implementation path rather than exploration.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building logging into the model and validating the logs against Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: If achieved, models that natively emit structured logs would satisfy Article 12's automatic event recording, but it is a research programme that covers only part of the mandate (e.g., use periods, reference databases, human verifier identities) and need not deliver compliance itself, so it contributes rather than fully solves.

evidence_originality: Developing formal criteria for substantial modification using distributional-shift methods is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but it is a fairly foreseeable research-oriented response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a research agenda and standard-setting activity, changing the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open preprints and contributing to standard-setting is a norm-compatible, somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Developing and validating formal criteria and detection algorithms is significant research work with uncertain outcomes, though it is not impossible and builds on existing literature.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely defining the substantial-modification boundary that triggers Article 12(2)(a) logging, which relates to but is not directly the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A formal modification taxonomy would help the lab decide what to log and when, but it is only a partial solution because it does not implement the logging capability and the taxonomy may not match regulatory interpretation.

evidence_originality: Compliance gap audits are a common response, though the framing around sunk-cost and retrofit-versus-restart adds some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a rubric and resource-allocation matrix, and links compliance to which projects the lab continues, which moderately touches what the lab researches, but it still treats compliance as a gap-assessment practice.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and portfolio reviews are common governance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week gap assessment per project and a board presentation within a quarter is a modest, reasonably feasible process requiring some effort from project leads.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (allocating scarce resources across projects facing Article 12 obligations) that relates to the stated problem of how to respond and adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit and reprioritisation helps the lab decide where to retrofit versus restart, but it does not itself build logging capability, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK/template is a sensible and fairly expected response, interesting but not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK with tests) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal reusable compliance logging template is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers extracting existing prototype hooks into an SDK in one sprint is low cost and a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging requirements for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It fully covers the Article 12(3) fields for biometric systems but not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event logging or other system types, so it is a partial solution to the mandate.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a longitudinal research dataset on drift is unusual and imaginative compared with typical compliance responses, though not wholly unprecedented as a monitoring idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the logging obligation into a source of scientific output, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing anonymised aggregate findings from biometric system logs is a somewhat unusual strategy that raises data-access and privacy concerns, but it does not offend norms if anonymised and agreed with operators.
evidence_implementability: It needs access to logs from two deployed third-party biometric systems, a multi-year commitment, and an analyst, which is a significant and uncertain undertaking, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal uses Article 12 logs for a research programme, which relates to the logging mandate only by implication, since it does not directly say how the lab will meet the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute scientific value and use logs for monitoring, but it does not ensure the lab's own systems comply with Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Monitoring log completeness as an observable engineering metric is somewhat interesting and shows modest imagination, but observability tooling for logs is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (a streaming dashboard with alerts) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: An internal monitoring dashboard is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Kafka plus Grafana with alert rules is standard, inexpensive tooling, though per-pilot setup and defining the event-class checks take some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by detecting dropped Article 12 event classes in production.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help verify that logs are captured, but it does not itself create the logging capability or cover documentation and other obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code and CI tests for requirements are fairly well known, so the idea is interesting but not surprising or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (compliance gate in prototyping) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Schema-assertion tests in nightly CI with blocking tickets use standard engineering tooling and need only modest, non-radical changes, though defining assertions for each Article 12(2) category takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D by verifying the required event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch logging gaps in prototypes and so contribute to meeting the logging mandate, but it only verifies emission and does not itself cover log retention, content adequacy, or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a natural experiment for drift science is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance obligations and R&D by turning logging into a source of research and publications, which stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing findings from operational logs is a legitimate research strategy, though possible data-protection and confidentiality concerns make it somewhat unusual without offending sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year programme with a dedicated analytics team and access to deployed-system logs is a significant, costly change though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It does something with the logs (research on drift) that relates to the logging mandate only implicitly, addressing an implied benefit rather than the identified compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: Mining logs for drift research does not itself make the lab's systems generate compliant Article 12 logs, so it only contributes to the stated problem at best and is mainly a downstream use of logs.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing telemetry and doing a gap analysis is a very common, pragmatic response that labs would typically give, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as logging practice built on the existing infrastructure, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Extending existing infrastructure and running internal gap analyses is a standard business strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Incremental upgrades on existing pipelines with a six-week gap analysis are low cost and non-radical, though the patching of shared middleware requires some engineering work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping existing telemetry to paragraphs 2 and 3 and patching gaps.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to compliance but is only a partial solution, since telemetry built for debugging may not meet traceability needs and it depends on another proposal's middleware and ignores broader R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in a shared SDK with auto-wired templates is a common, expected response, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-by-default logging practice that adds tooling but still treats compliance as logging, leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building default logging into a shared SDK is a common engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing experiment-runner with middleware and project templates is a reasonably feasible change requiring some engineering work but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses Article 12(1)'s automatic recording requirement, which is part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would give automatic logging across prototypes, but it does not cover Article 12(2)-(3) specifics like risk identification, post-market monitoring, or Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automating compliance documentation via CI/CD hooks is a fairly expected 'compliance-as-code' response, interesting but not surprising among lab responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (CI/CD hooks, automated metadata capture) and shifts compliance from post-hoc to integrated in the research workflow, but still treats compliance as logging and documentation practice.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating compliance into engineering workflows is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires co-designing pipeline hooks and metadata schemas across teams, which is a reasonably feasible but nontrivial change to existing workflows.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by automatically generating event logs and technical documentation per model iteration.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, automatic logging and documentation at every pipeline stage would reasonably satisfy Article 12's record-keeping, though it does not cover specifics such as Annex III use-period logs for deployed systems or post-market events.

evidence_originality: Building logging into training and inference frameworks is the common, expected response to Article 12 and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Embedding logging middleware in existing pipelines is a standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in existing infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-person cell integrating middleware on the current monitoring stack in two sprints is a low-cost, non-radical change, though the scope may be somewhat optimistic.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly implements the automatic logging mandate, including the four Article 12(3) fields, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Native logging validated against the Article 12(3) fields would meet the logging mandate, but it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance for risk, post-market monitoring, or the broader adaptation of R&D, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automating change detection in CI with deploy holds is a sensible, familiar MLOps pattern, interesting but not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI diff gate) but still treats compliance as a logging and review practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance basically unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Gating deployments on automated checks and sign-off is a common engineering governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building it requires defining substantial-modification thresholds and similarity metrics across weights, schemas, and data lineage, which takes some real engineering but is feasible within existing CI infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, recording events that identify substantial modification as Article 12(2)(a) requires, by building a deploy-gate to produce the record.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch and log substantial modifications under Art. 12(2)(a), but it covers only one part of the logging mandate (not runtime event logs, post-market monitoring, or Annex III minimums), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Drop-in logging middleware with decorators and CI gating is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (an SDK) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal logging SDK with CI enforcement is a common engineering strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A decorator-based library with SQLite/Postgres backends and CI checks is reasonably feasible, though building and maintaining it for all pipelines and capturing fields like verifier IDs needs some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements while preserving the lab's R&D cadence.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help meet the logging mandate, but it is only a partial solution because it does not cover log retention, governance, or Annex III-specific semantics, and automatic capture of reference database and verifier identity is assumed rather than shown.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12(2)(a) risk-event identification into a public anomaly-detection benchmark with an annual community challenge is unusual and shows some imagination, but benchmarks and challenges are a familiar research format, so it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It brings in new elements (benchmark, community challenge, external partners) and shifts the lab's compliance work toward research on monitoring science and public outputs, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing public benchmarks and running challenges is a common, norm-respecting research practice, though the use of anonymised real logs raises mild privacy and confidentiality concerns.
evidence_implementability: Curating labelled log sequences, defining metrics, and hosting an annual challenge needs substantial data, labelling effort, and anonymisation work, which is expensive and difficult but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses Article 12(2)(a) risk-situation identification from logs, which is an implied related problem, but it does not directly deliver the lab's own logging capability.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark helps the field and may improve detectors, but it does not make the lab's systems log compliantly, so it is only a partial contribution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance testing in CI is a familiar, mundane approach an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice embedded in existing tooling, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance checks in CI are a common, uncontroversial DevOps practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a validation stage to an existing CI pipeline is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes, schema definitions, and replay tooling but no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying Article 12 compliance of emitted logs during development.
evidence_effectiveness: Automated CI checks verifying log schemas, timestamps and retention would help ensure logs meet Article 12, but they do not by themselves provide the logging capability or cover everything (e.g., relevance of events, Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK baked into the pipeline is a sensible and expected engineering response, not especially surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK/middleware) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the lab's relationship between R&D and compliance in a major way.
evidence_acceptability: Automatic logging middleware as a default architecture is a common, norm-compliant approach that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK/middleware hooked into the standard inference pipeline is a reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by making automatic event recording the default in prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic logging but captures only generic fields and does not cover risk-situation identification, post-market monitoring specifics, or Annex III minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A versioned documentation and log registry with CI/CD-triggered staleness alerts is a sensible but fairly expected compliance-tooling response, with only modest imagination in tying doc updates to retraining events.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (CI/CD-linked document control and automated alerts) but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A document-control registry integrated with engineering workflows is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a centralized registry and CI/CD-triggered pipelines requires some engineering changes and process integration but uses established tooling and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Recital 71 requirement that documentation be kept up to date and logs retained, which is part of the stated logging-mandate problem, though Article 12 logging content itself is only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation current and manage log retention, but it does not address the Article 12 technical capability of automatic event recording or specify which events to log, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing observability tooling for compliance logging is a fairly predictable, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice with a new tooling approach, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing telemetry infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, legitimate engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Wrapping existing OpenTelemetry collectors with schema modules requires some platform-team work but builds on deployed infrastructure, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping to the 12(2)(a)-(c) event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help deliver the technical logging capability by default across projects, but it does not by itself cover Article 12(3) specifics, log retention, or the relevance judgments needed for traceability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using mandated Article 12 logs as a longitudinal research dataset for drift detection is an interesting and somewhat unusual repurposing, though drift monitoring itself is a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning compliance logs into a research asset and a new research program, going beyond standard logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Aggregating logs across deployed systems for research raises some data-protection and customer-consent sensitivities, but it is a broadly accepted kind of monitoring practice.
evidence_implementability: It requires a shared ingestion layer, schema normalisation across projects, and a dedicated research node, plus access to deployed-system logs, which is a significant but feasible undertaking.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making use of logs for monitoring and research value) related to the mandate rather than the directly stated need to comply with logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate (what to log, retention, traceability) but would contribute by building on compliant logs and aiding post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a monitoring dashboard on top of Article 12 logs is a fairly expected and sensible response, with a mildly interesting framing of compliance cost as operational capability but nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (analytics dashboard) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged apart from a funding narrative.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring dashboards for compliance logs are a common strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Repurposing existing visualisation tools with one postdoc building a read-only panel is low cost and non-radical, though calibrating drift thresholds per system is some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly uses Article 12 logs to serve post-market monitoring and operation monitoring purposes named in Article 12(2)(b) and (c), though it addresses the use of logs rather than the core logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The dashboard would help exploit logs for monitoring but does not itself implement the logging capability or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using a paid customer pilot to fund and produce a reusable logging compliance template with retained IP is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a partnership and a commercial offering born from compliance, changing how compliance relates to R&D funding, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A paid pilot with a bank customer and retained IP on logging architecture is a normal business arrangement that violates no norms, though the bank's data and biometric sensitivities need care.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing registry and alerting tools with only a new schema and verifier-identity module, and an existing customer funds engineering, so the changes are modest, though finding a bank and handling biometric data adds some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate for an Annex III 1(a) system with specific requirement-level mapping, and also addresses the R&D budget impact.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would meet the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements for the biometric system and create a template, solving the main compliance problem for that class, though it only partially covers other high-risk systems and Article 12(1-2).

evidence_originality: A log-conformance test harness is a sensible but fairly expected tooling response to a logging mandate, with only modest imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (conformance testing) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing of logs is a conventional QA practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A Python harness built on the existing observability stack and run nightly in staging needs some new development but no radical change, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required event categories are captured.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies log coverage but does not itself produce the logging capability, and checking whether events are 'relevant' is hard to automate, so it helps only as a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging into shared templates via OpenTelemetry is a sensible and fairly expected engineering approach, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a default logging SDK in prototype scaffolds) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Making a shared logging library a mandatory default is a common engineering governance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing OpenTelemetry instrumentation and an existing template repository, requiring only moderate platform-team effort and some schema work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate with specific Article 12 fields and an implementation mechanism.
evidence_effectiveness: A default logging layer mapped to Article 12(3) fields would meaningfully contribute to meeting the logging mandate but only covers part of it (Art. 12(3) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems, with no coverage of retention, documentation, or production systems beyond prototypes).

evidence_originality: Compliance gates and checklist-based stage reviews are a very common, expected response to regulatory mandates, with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a procedural gate but still treats compliance as a checklist-style logging practice separate from the science, leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal governance checklists and sign-off gates are common corporate compliance practice that violates no norms, though blocking resources may cause mild friction.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist and sign-off requirement is low-cost and non-radical to implement, though it adds some process overhead to project initiation.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by catching gaps early in R&D projects.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-design gate checking logging readiness against Article 12(2) would help ensure logging is designed in, but it is only a process check and does not itself deliver the technical logging capability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a formal academic taxonomy of risk-relevant events is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not ingenious or surprising enough to be unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a formal taxonomy and publishable research output) and reframes compliance as regulatory science, but it still treats the task as defining what to log rather than changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Research and publication of a classification framework offends no legal or social norms, though a lab might see it as an unusual use of scarce implementation resources.
evidence_implementability: It needs a research effort, literature synthesis and validation against deployments, which is a significant resource commitment with a delayed and uncertain payoff, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of defining which events are risk-relevant under Article 12(2)(a), which relates to the logging mandate only indirectly, since it does not itself deliver logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy would help scope what to log for one of three purposes, but it is only a partial contribution and does not implement logging capabilities, so the mandate stays unmet.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware baked into base images is a sensible and fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized internal tooling and dependency pinning are common strategies that offend no norms, though mandating it may cause mild friction with engineers.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing containerised pipeline metadata and a base Docker image, requiring some engineering effort but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate across the lab's high-risk systems, with fields mapped to Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic event recording for prototypes (Art. 12(1) and the listed fields) but does not cover the wider obligations such as Article 12(2) relevance of events, retention, or production deployment, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-deployment compliance gates are a common, expected response to regulatory mandates and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A review gate with an SOP and sign-off is a new process element, but it still treats compliance as a logging-verification practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal review checkpoint with sign-off is a standard governance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs only an SOP, two trained reviewers, and a project-management tool integration, which are non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets verifying that the logging mandate in Article 12(2) is met, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate would help catch logging gaps before deployment but does not itself build logging capability or cover Article 12(1) or (3), so it solves only part of the problem.

evidence_originality: Retention policies, role-based access, and DPO involvement are common, mundane compliance responses, though the focus on verifier-ID privacy is a slightly thoughtful angle.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is a governance SOP with access controls and pseudonymisation for logs, which is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's research workflow unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Data-governance policies co-authored with a DPO are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Writing an SOP and configuring role-based access on a log store involves only modest, non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the mandate (handling Article 12(3)(d) verifier-identification logs) but 3(d) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems, so relevance to the general problem is narrower, making it a related implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address only the privacy and governance of one logging element (verifier IDs under 3(d)) and does not deliver the automatic event logging mandate itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing log sufficiency as an information-theoretic and causal-inference optimization problem is unusual and shows imagination, though not entirely unprecedented in auditability research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (formal metrics, entropy-based event selection) and makes auditability science part of the lab's research, shifting compliance from logging practice toward research, though it still centers on logging.
evidence_acceptability: Researching minimal logging is socially and legally acceptable, though regulators may be wary of 'minimal' logging framed as reducing records, which is a slightly unusual stance.
evidence_implementability: It is an open-ended research program requiring specialized expertise and uncertain results, and it commits scarce resources without a guaranteed compliance deliverable, making it difficult though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the question of which events must be logged to meet Article 12 traceability, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A formal criterion for minimal sufficient logging would help determine what to log and avoid over-collection, but it is a research output that only partially delivers actual compliance (implementation, retention, and the Article 12(3) fields are still needed) and the legal sufficiency is not guaranteed by a mathematical criterion.

evidence_originality: A log overhead benchmarking study is a standard, expected engineering response, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as a logging engineering practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal engineering feasibility study with load testing and board sign-off is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only two engineers for three months using production-like load tests, which is a reasonably feasible, modest-cost effort with no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, whether lifetime logging is technically viable at scale, which relates to meeting the Article 12 logging mandate but does not itself deliver logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would only inform architecture decisions and would not itself implement logging or achieve compliance, so it contributes only partially, and it is an exploratory study rather than a commitment of implementation resources.

evidence_originality: Open compliance schema registries are an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, with the longitudinal community dataset angle adding interest, but it is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open registry, community contributions, dataset) and a new offering born from compliance, stretching the relationship between R&D and compliance without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing compliance tooling and engaging regulators and scientific panels is a legitimate, norm-respecting approach, though somewhat less common than internal compliance, and it creates no offense to sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Three FTEs for one quarter to build schemas, a Python agent and a white paper is a modest, reasonably feasible effort requiring some changes but no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by providing structured logs for the Article 12(3) fields, though much of the stated benefit targets other labs rather than the lab itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging schema and agent would help the lab meet Article 12 logging requirements but covers only the schema/format part of compliance (not retention, event relevance determination, or other duties), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code in CI is a well-known DevOps pattern, so it is sensible but not surprising or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (merge-blocking compliance tests) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance fundamentally unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks and contract tests are standard engineering practice that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing pytest infrastructure and containerized sandboxes, requiring modest test-writing effort and no radical change, though defining the schemas and synthetic inputs takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that required events are recorded, though it addresses verification rather than the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate verifying that logs cover Article 12(2) event categories would help ensure logging capability exists, but it does not itself design the logging, address retention, Article 12(3) specifics, or post-deployment behavior, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open standards and living documentation are fairly familiar ideas in AI governance (model cards, datasheets), so this is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a standard, tooling, open release) and some new offerings born from compliance, but still treats compliance as documentation practice rather than changing how R&D is done.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open documentation standard with an open license violates no legal or social norms, though open release may raise some IP concerns, and it is a fairly unusual but inoffensive strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires a working group, three pilots, and tooling development, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets technical documentation under Recital 71, which is related to the record-keeping mandate but not the automatic logging required by Article 12, so it solves an implied rather than directly stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Living documentation would help traceability and compliance but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing monitoring dashboards for compliance logging is a sensible and fairly common integration approach that labs would readily expect, so it is merely interesting at most.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds an annotation layer but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only reusing existing monitoring tools rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Leveraging existing infrastructure and mapping to legal requirements is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
