evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified Article 12(1) lifecycle logging requirement and the 12(2) traceability purposes, which are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet the retention and traceability aspects of Article 12 but does not cover what events to log or the broader R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tying funding releases to compliance sign-off is a familiar stage-gate practice, so it is interesting but not unusual or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new verification nodes to existing project-management templates but still treats compliance as logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate compliance reviews are a common business practice and violate no norms, though gating funding may cause some friction.
evidence_implementability: It amends existing budget-release templates with two review nodes, which is a modest change using existing structures and staff.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate within R&D by making conformance checks part of development phases.
evidence_effectiveness: Gating funding on demonstrated logging readiness would help ensure Article 12 conformance is built in early, but it covers process governance rather than the logging mandate itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared internal platform or SDK for compliance logging is a standard, expected response that shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a platform and API tooling but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralizing compliance infrastructure in an internal platform team is a common, uncontroversial organizational strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires reallocating about 12% of engineering headcount to a four-person squad and getting every project to integrate, which is a reasonably feasible measure with some organizational change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building a shared logging schema, SDK, and retention pipeline.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared service would deliver automatic event logging and retention across projects, but it does not by itself cover which events are relevant, the Annex III minimums, or the wider documentation duties, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared reusable logging library is the standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as logging practice with a tooling consolidation, leaving the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged, though it adds a new shared component.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small internal pod building a library that plugs into existing experiment-tracking and CI/CD tooling without new headcount requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building the specified logging capabilities.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatically capturing the Article 12(3) minimums by default would meet much of the logging mandate, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimums and not the broader Article 12(2) event relevance or the documentation and R&D adaptation aspects, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared internal logging/MLOps infrastructure is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise or ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A centralized internal logging platform is a standard compliance engineering approach that treats compliance purely as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralizing shared internal tooling and amortizing costs is a common business strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two existing MLOps engineers reusing current pipeline infrastructure over six months is a modest, low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(2) logging mandate across high-risk projects.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging service would address the Article 12 automatic event-recording requirement, but it does not cover the Annex III-specific minimums, documentation, or retention and so is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance documentation as publishable scientific artifacts is unusual and shows some imagination, though documentation-as-code and reproducibility ideas are known.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by merging documentation with research output (documentation-as-code, peer review, open science), which stretches the paradigm but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sharing of high-risk system details may raise security, trade-secret, and confidentiality concerns, but the strategy is somewhat uncommon rather than offensive.
evidence_implementability: Setting up a structured documentation repository with version control and review is reasonably feasible, though aligning formats with journal standards and handling IP and confidentiality needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the dual maintenance burden of documentation, which relates to the compliance response but is not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with technical documentation requirements but does not address automatic event logging under Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design gates and schema templates in architecture review are a common, mundane response to such a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance process step (checklist gate and templates) that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review gate for compliance is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing sprint-zero checklists, four one-page templates, and a two-hour workshop, so it is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by mapping templates to Article 12(3)(a)-(d) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging fields are designed in early, but it covers only Article 12(3) fields (not 12(2) event relevance, retention, or actual implementation), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Quarterly audit of logs against a checklist is a common, mundane compliance response with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Internal compliance audits are standard practice and leave the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits violate no norms and are a widely accepted governance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Hiring two auditors with read access and scripted queries is a modest, non-radical change at relatively low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets verifying that logs satisfy Article 12(2)(a)-(c), which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Auditing verifies logging gaps are found and fixed but does not itself build the logging capability, so it is a helpful partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a longitudinal observational dataset for drift detection is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes mandatory logs as a research dataset woven into the lab's science, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not redirect what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for research is somewhat uncommon and raises possible data-protection and purpose-limitation questions, but it does not offend sensibilities if handled properly.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting three pilot deployments and applying standard change-point and embedding analyses is reasonably feasible, though it needs deployment access and some added effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of turning logging obligations into value and detecting substantial modification, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly implement the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not itself meet the logging mandate and only helps with Article 12(2)(a) risk identification, so it contributes to the solution only partially.

evidence_originality: Reallocating staff from a lower-priority project to a compliance team is a common, mundane resourcing response to a new regulation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard logging and engineering function handled by a separate platform group, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal resource reallocation with joint reporting to the Compliance Officer is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Reassigning four FTEs within a flat headcount via a board decision is reasonably feasible, though descoping milestones and creating a new cross-project group require some organizational change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to resource and meet the Article 12 logging mandate by creating a standing compliance-engineering pool for logging infrastructure.
evidence_effectiveness: Dedicated staffing for logging infrastructure would help meet Article 12 but it names no specific logging capabilities or event types, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Native logging libraries with CI gates are what experienced evaluators would expect from labs, so it is common and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces an SDK and CI/CD gates but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into the architecture with CI/CD compliance gates is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A mandatory SDK, stage hooks and CI/CD gates across every high-risk system require cross-team engineering and some pipeline changes, but are reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate, with the specific Article 12(3) fields named explicitly.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would directly satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate, though it covers the Annex III 1(a) minimums more than the broader traceability purposes, so it is largely but not wholly complete.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance documentation as a publication appendix is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though documentation templates are a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new template and workflow and ties compliance documentation to publishing and grant practice, which modestly changes how R&D relates to compliance without altering what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation standards and publication practices violate no norms and are widely accepted by funders and reviewers.
evidence_implementability: A template drafted by one group, piloted on two projects, and then required in grant proposals is a modest process change, though the claim of zero marginal cost is optimistic.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets technical documentation under Recital 71 and traceability, which relates to the stated problem, but it does not address Article 12's automatic event logging mandate directly, so the problem it solves is only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Documentation templates would help with technical documentation and compliance verification but do not deliver automatic event logs, so the proposal is at best a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI-enforced stage gate for logging completeness is a sensible but fairly expected shift-left compliance measure that shows modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (stage gate with automated CI check) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate compliance checks are a common practice that violate no norms, though gating client demos may cause mild friction.
evidence_implementability: Adding a CI check and stage gate with a remediation buffer requires some pipeline changes and schema definitions but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring prototypes produce logs covering the 12(2)(a)-(c) categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging capability during development but covers only prototypes, does not guarantee log content quality, retention, or the Annex III 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Capturing verifier identity through an authenticated sign-off in existing review tooling is a common, expected response to Article 12(3)(d).
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds an authenticated sign-off step to existing review tooling but still treats compliance as ordinary logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Authenticated sign-off logging is a standard, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A single sign-off screen added to an existing interface with structured log lines is a small, low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified requirement, recording the natural persons who verify results, which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy only the verifier-identification item of Article 12(3)(d), which applies to a narrow Annex III 1(a) category, and leaves the broader logging mandate unaddressed, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Release gates, compliance checklists, and CI-enforced checks are common, expected responses with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A pre-deployment logging gate with a checklist and CI block is a standard compliance process that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance sign-offs and CI gates are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing pull-request and deployment workflow with a one-page checklist and automated CI blocking, which requires only non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by validating the logging schema against Article 12(2) and Annex III 1(a) requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate would reliably ensure that logging is designed and checked before deployment, but it verifies schema documentation rather than guaranteeing runtime log quality or lifetime coverage, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12 compliance into a marketable badge with a machine-readable manifest for procurement is an unusual, somewhat imaginative angle, though compliance-as-differentiator is a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by making compliance a product and market differentiator, creating new partners and offerings born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Partnering with a notified body and issuing a branded conformance label is a somewhat unusual but legitimate business practice, though a private badge could be mistaken for official CE-type conformity, which is a mild risk.
evidence_implementability: It requires negotiating with a notified body, building an audit checklist, and running a certification program plus a manifest format, which is a significant but feasible undertaking.
evidence_applicability: It addresses how to respond to the logging mandate, but mostly through marketing and attestation rather than building logging, so it solves an implied related problem (commercial positioning).
evidence_effectiveness: A badge helps with demonstrating and capitalizing on compliance but does not itself implement the logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding traceability natively in architecture via mandatory trace tokens is unusual and imaginative compared with typical logging-wrapper responses, though related interpretability work exists.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance a first-class research problem and embedding logging into model architecture, which addresses what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Research into architectures for traceability violates no norms and is legally and socially acceptable, though somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Redesigning neural architectures with trace tokens and validating them is a significant, expensive, uncertain research effort that is difficult but not impossible, and it doesn't deliver compliance for near-term deployed systems.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12 logging requirements, explicitly validating against the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, so it solves an identified problem tied to the stated one.
evidence_effectiveness: If achieved, native layer-level tracing would satisfy automatic event recording, but it is a research programme that covers only part of the mandate (e.g., system-level logs, period of use, reference database, human verifier identity) and wouldn't itself solve the lab's compliance decision, so it contributes partially.

evidence_originality: Compliance test suites are a fairly expected idea, interesting but not surprising or especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and shared artifact but still treats compliance as logging practice, with limited change to the lab's R&D-compliance relationship, though the open-source offering edges toward a new offering.
evidence_acceptability: Open, public release of compliance tooling is a norm-consistent and welcome strategy that offends no sensibilities, though somewhat beyond routine practice.
evidence_implementability: Building containerized test environments with synthetic event injection across diverse live systems is a significant engineering effort but feasible with some resources.
evidence_applicability: The harness directly targets verifying that logging meets Article 12's sub-clauses, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A test harness validates logging but does not itself build the logging capability, so it contributes to compliance as a partial solution rather than solving it fully.

evidence_originality: Tiering logging depth by regulatory category is a sensible but fairly expected compliance approach that an experienced evaluator would anticipate, with little surprising or ingenious about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a decision matrix and release gating but still treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Risk-proportionate compliance mapped to legal text and reviewed by counsel is a common strategy that offends no norms, though minimal logging for non-Annex III systems could draw mild scrutiny.
evidence_implementability: A one-page matrix, quarterly legal review, and checklist gates are low-cost, non-radical additions to existing release processes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate in a way that is proportionate, and also protects R&D capacity.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses scoping of logging obligations but does not itself deliver the logging capability or the Article 12(2) traceability, so it only partially solves the mandate.

evidence_originality: Compliance gap audits and prioritized remediation are common and mundane responses that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A gap analysis with phased retrofits is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A gap audit with prioritized, phased upgrades is a common compliance strategy that offends no norms, though deferring lower-priority gaps might raise some legal concern.
evidence_implementability: A one-week mapping per project lead and funding three retrofits per year uses existing staff and a phased approach, so it needs only some changes and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements in existing systems by mapping against the 12(2) and 12(3) checklists and upgrading.
evidence_effectiveness: It identifies gaps and fixes only the top three, deferring the rest, so it contributes to meeting the logging mandate but is only a partial solution and does not itself design the logging.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware/SDK is a common and expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with only modest touches like default PII encryption.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but treats compliance as standard logging practice, centralizing it as infrastructure without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Shared logging infrastructure with encrypted PII violates no norms or sensibilities and is a conventional strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a plugin SDK with fixed schemas per Annex III category and hooks for varied architectures requires some real engineering effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X, get compliant logs) with explicit reference to Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared SDK that automatically captures the Article 12(3) fields would meet much of the logging mandate, but it covers mainly the point 1(a) Annex III minimum fields and not the broader Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or documentation, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A provenance ledger for the statutory minimum fields is a mundane, expected response to Article 12(3), with only the regulator-response framing adding a bit of interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a schema and audit process but treats compliance purely as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A provenance ledger with audit sampling is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy, though logging verifier identities raises minor privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: Defining a schema with data governance, writing entries atomically at match-time and running quarterly audits requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with existing practices.
evidence_applicability: The idea does X (log the specified fields) to get Y (meet the identified Article 12(3) logging requirements), which is directly part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Recording match, reference database version, input data and verifier identity at match-time directly implements the Article 12(3) minimums for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it does not cover Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other high-risk systems or the lab's R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Prioritising compliance work by sprint reallocation and a cost-avoidance model is a mundane, expected response with little imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging implementation work with resource scheduling and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Prioritising legally mandated compliance work through a costed steering-committee proposal is a common, norm-respecting business strategy.
evidence_implementability: Reallocating about 15% of engineering capacity and deferring minor features for a quarter is a moderate, reasonably feasible prioritisation change that needs steering-committee approval.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by implementing and testing the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields on biometric-identification lines to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the most prescriptive minimum logging fields but covers only Article 12(3) and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event logging or other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Keeping technical documentation current with named owners and review cycles is a mundane, expected compliance response with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance record-keeping practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation stewardship and controlled repositories are common compliance strategies that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Assigning documentation stewards, quarterly reviews and a version-controlled repository are routine records-management measures that need little change or cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation upkeep of Recital 71, which is related to the record-keeping mandate, but it does not address the Article 12 automatic event logging that the stated problem centers on.
evidence_effectiveness: Up-to-date documentation helps part of the record-keeping requirement but does not provide the automatic event logs Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gap audits and readiness triage are common compliance responses, with only the grant-cycle alignment adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is a gap audit and prioritization matrix that treats compliance as a logging-remediation practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though the grant-cycle sequencing adds a modest new process element.
evidence_acceptability: A cross-team audit with prioritization into existing backlogs is a standard, uncontroversial management practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week audit and slotting fixes into existing sprints without new headcount is low cost, although absorbing the actual remediation work into existing backlogs may be optimistic.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of determining how to meet Article 12 logging requirements across the lab's high-risk projects by assessing gaps and planning fixes.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit and sequencing would help identify and schedule remediation but does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution to meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Documentation schemas and standards participation are fairly expected responses, with modest imagination in tying a publishable open schema to the biometric paragraph-3 pilot.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open schema, peer-reviewed methodology) and a standards-shaping role, but still treats compliance as documentation practice rather than changing how R&D is done.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open documentation methodology and engaging in standards discourse is a legally and socially unobjectionable, though somewhat research-oriented, approach to compliance.
evidence_implementability: A twelve-month project with two postdocs, a paper and a schema is a moderate, reasonably feasible investment, though it needs dedicated staff and does not itself deliver logging quickly.
evidence_applicability: It targets Recital 71 technical documentation, which is related to but not the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it addresses an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation schema would contribute to traceability but does not implement automatic event logging or the paragraph-3 logging minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal log audits and compliance dashboards are what an experienced evaluator would expect, with a slight twist of the client portal.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (an audit function and a client portal) but still treats compliance as logging verification practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and client transparency reporting are common, norm-conforming compliance strategies, though a client-facing portal is a mild extra.
evidence_implementability: An internal audit office with semi-annual sampling and a read-only aggregate metrics portal needs some new staff and tooling but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The audit directly checks that logs capture the events required by Article 12(2)(a)-(c), which is an identified part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Spot-checks of 20% of deployments verify logging works but do not build or design the logging capability itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Validation testing of logs is a fairly expected, sensible response to such a mandate and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a test suite process but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Release-gating QA testing for compliance is a common, norm-conforming strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building automated test scenarios in staging and adding a sign-off gate requires some effort and process change but is reasonably feasible with existing QA staff.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem of meeting Article 12's logging mandate by testing that logs capture required events and fields.
evidence_effectiveness: Testing verifies log adequacy but does not itself build the logging or cover all compliance duties, so it is a helpful partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library with CI/CD gates enforcing required log fields is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, though sensible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a library and build gates but still treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged, though shifting left slightly adds new tooling elements.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance in the build pipeline is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adopting a shared logging library and adding CI/CD checks is low-cost, uses standard tooling, and requires only non-radical changes to engineering workflow.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring required log fields are captured in every high-risk system.
evidence_effectiveness: It would go a long way to ensure logging compliance for new projects, but covers mainly Article 12(3) fields, ignores existing systems, and does not address the broader 12(2) traceability purposes or log quality, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a longitudinal research observation window is unusual and shows some imagination, but drift analysis on logs is a fairly recognizable idea rather than a surprising one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by treating mandated logs as primary research data, weaving logging into the science, though it does not alter what the lab broadly researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using mandated logs for internal research is a legitimate strategy that offends no norms, though data protection and purpose-limitation concerns for deployment logs add minor caveats.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting two prototypes and running a six-month pilot with standard sequence and anomaly-detection methods is reasonably feasible, though it requires a pilot deployment and sustained effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by reusing compliance logs as research data, which relates to but is not directly the stated problem of meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Instrumenting prototypes with Article 12 logging and analyzing the logs would partly meet the logging mandate, but it is primarily a research study and does not by itself deliver the full compliance capability (e.g., minimum Annex III logging content, retention, traceability design).

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance via project templates and lint rules is a fairly common, sensible approach with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (scaffolding template) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifting it earlier in development.
evidence_acceptability: A starter-repo template with lint rules and a kickoff checklist is a common engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Templates, CI lint rules, and a checklist are low-cost and non-radical, though the two-week retrofit of in-flight projects requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate by building log hooks into prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging capability exists but does not specify which events are relevant for Article 12(2) or Annex III minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance linter/CI quality gate for log conformance is a sensible and somewhat interesting idea, but automated compliance checks in CI are a fairly expected response among labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process (automated conformance gate, reusable client-facing asset) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, with a slight hint of new offerings.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks and handoff reports are a common, uncontroversial practice that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A Python package wrapping existing schema definitions integrated into CI is reasonably feasible with moderate effort, though encoding Article 12 requirements into checks takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to confirm the lab's logs meet Article 12 requirements, i.e., do X (lint logs) to get Y (verified conformance).
evidence_effectiveness: It would help verify that logs contain required fields and timelines, but it does not itself create the logging capability or address the substantive Article 12 content like risk-relevant events, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using logging mandates as a basis for longitudinal event-significance research is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes the compliance logging obligation as a research programme and a publishable contribution, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme that instruments deployed systems and publishes findings is a legitimate, non-offensive strategy, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires instrumenting two deployed systems, running quarterly cohorts over a long period, and building classifiers, which is a significant and costly commitment with delayed payoff relative to a compliance deadline.
evidence_applicability: It targets the identified Article 12(2)(a) requirement of recording events that identify risk situations, which is directly part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Learning which events matter would improve the logging schema for Article 12(2)(a), but it does not by itself deliver the baseline logging capability or cover 12(2)(b), 12(2)(c) or the Annex III minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A standardized, non-bypassable logging SDK embedded in the dev framework is the most obvious, expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice built into existing frameworks, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Built-in default logging for compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating an event-capture SDK into an existing standard development framework is a reasonably feasible, non-radical engineering change at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate, producing automatic logs for traceability, which is an identified part of the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the Article 12(1) and 12(2) automatic-event-recording mandate broadly, but it is vague on Annex III 1(a) minimums such as reference database and verifier identification and on retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance cost into grant-review scoring is a somewhat unusual and sensible administrative idea, but it is not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Budgeting a mandatory traceability work-package and scoring proposals on how efficiently they absorb compliance overhead changes how compliance relates to R&D funding decisions, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Budget line items and revised review templates are common internal governance practices that violate no norms, though scoring on overhead absorption may cause mild friction among teams.
evidence_implementability: Revising a grant template and adding a budget line is a non-radical administrative change, though sizing the percentage and enabling shared infrastructure requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the implied problem of resourcing and funding logging and documentation compliance, which relates to the stated problem of how to respond to the mandate but does not directly specify the logging mechanisms.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure resources exist for logging and monitoring work, but it does not itself implement logging or satisfy Article 12 technical requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing Article 12 ambiguity as an open research problem with a publishable framework is unusual and shows imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a research question and reorients part of what the lab researches, changing the relationship between R&D and obligations, though it stops short of reworking the lab's core agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing a research framework and engaging with regulatory guidance is a legally and socially acceptable, if somewhat uncommon, response that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team producing a formal framework is reasonably feasible, though validating it across architectures against failure-mode benchmarks is substantial work with uncertain outcome.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified gap of what events must be logged under Article 12(2)(a), which is part of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A framework for event selection would help define what to log but does not implement logging or cover the other Article 12 requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware or shared compliance libraries are an expected, mundane response to a logging mandate and show little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared tool and pipeline gate but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a shared internal logging layer and making it a pipeline dependency is a common engineering and compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers for one quarter plus a pipeline template change is a modest, reasonably feasible investment, though integrating across diverse systems requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by providing automatic event recording across systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared middleware that auto-captures Article 12(1)-(2) event logs would, if built, meet the core logging mandate for new builds, though it does not cover legacy systems or Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance checks into stage-gate reviews is a common and expected response, so it is mundane rather than imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a gate note) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged, so it is slightly stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a design-document checkpoint is a common governance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It only amends an existing stage-gate review with a one-page note and a five-day joint review, which is a non-radical, low-cost process change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of ensuring logging capability is built in to meet the logging mandate, via an explicit process step.
evidence_effectiveness: Early logging design review helps with Article 12 but does not itself implement logging or cover the specific content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing experiment-tracking data for compliance is a sensible idea that is fairly expected and shows modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Making traceability a byproduct of experimentation changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating logging into existing experiment trackers is a sensible, norm-respecting compliance approach that offends no legal or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing tools like Weights and Biases with lightweight agents, requiring some toolchain changes but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by producing automatic event logs and documentation aligned with Article 12 and Recital 71.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially support logging and documentation, but Article 12(3) fields are specific to Annex III 1(a) systems and experiment logs do not capture deployed-system runtime events, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Scoping logs to relevant events by intended purpose is a sensible but fairly expected response to the Article's wording, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a documentation and process step that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Co-authoring taxonomies between compliance and engineering with annual review is a standard, norm-respecting governance practice that also supports data-protection concerns.
evidence_implementability: It needs cross-functional effort per product line and periodic review but uses existing staff and no radical technical change, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of deciding which events are relevant to log under Article 12(2) and ties them to Articles 79(1), 72, and 26(5).
evidence_effectiveness: A purpose-calibrated event taxonomy would define what must be logged under Article 12(2), which is a core part of compliance, but it does not itself implement the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in a shared pipeline or experiment tracker is the common, expected response and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal centralizes logging in the existing MLOps platform, which is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's research way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandating a common platform backend for new high-risk projects is a conventional engineering governance step that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting an existing platform in a two-week sprint with no added headcount is mostly non-radical, though the timeline may be optimistic and some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing automatic event recording including the Annex III minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging backend would largely satisfy the technical logging requirement, but it does not cover other aspects such as deployer-facing logs in deployed systems, retention, or the relevance of events to risk and post-market monitoring, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware or an SDK with regression tests is a very common and expected response to this mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Logging is built in at sprint zero, which is an architectural step, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Standard engineering and compliance-by-design practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers building an SDK that teams integrate at project start is a reasonably feasible measure that needs some process change but no radical resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the specific Article 12(3) log elements into the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared tamper-evident logging layer capturing timestamps, input references and verifier identifiers, with regression tests, would substantially meet the Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not cover technical documentation, post-market monitoring processes or the other Article 12 purposes (risk identification, Article 26(5) monitoring), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A model-agnostic middleware logging layer is a fairly expected, mundane response to Article 12, with only mild interest in reusing it across products.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, with only a mild reuse-by-default framing.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging is a common, legally aligned strategy that violates no norms, though biometric identifier logging is routine under the Act.
evidence_implementability: A modular logging layer prototyped by a small team in two quarters on an existing pipeline is a reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes but no radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specified log fields (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If built, the layer would capture the Article 12(3) minimum items and directly satisfy the logging mandate for the biometric system, though it covers only the Annex III 1(a) case and not broader R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Using funding tranches as a compliance lever is a somewhat unusual and sensible idea, but it is a recognizable application of stage-gate governance rather than a surprising one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D funding and compliance by making compliance a condition of project progress, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gated funding with compliance checkpoints is a fairly common governance practice that violates no norms, though tying disbursements to compliance over science milestones is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: It adds two checkpoints to existing workflow using existing tooling with no new procurement, so it is a non-radical, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (ensuring projects actually implement logging before resources are spent) that relates to meeting the logging mandate, rather than directly specifying what to log.
evidence_effectiveness: Gating funding on logging integration and documentation completeness would help ensure Article 12 conformity in funded projects, but it is a governance mechanism that does not itself build the logging or cover the full set of mandated capabilities, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying the Article 12 event-schema discipline to internal R&D runs is a somewhat unusual and interesting angle, but it is not highly surprising since reproducibility logging is a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the scientific method itself, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: A lab-wide logging and reproducibility policy is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Lightweight logging hooks with a single flag and a lab policy require some changes to pipelines and workflow but are reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal solves an implied problem (building logging culture and reproducibility) that relates to the stated problem but does not directly address the deployed-system logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: Logging internal experiments helps traceability and documentation, but Article 12 concerns logging in deployed high-risk systems, so this contributes only partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware built into pipelines is a common, expected response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-engineering logging practice with no change to how the lab's R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding tamper-evident logging as a mandatory build dependency is a common compliance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building reusable logging middleware with a dedicated platform squad and integrating it into every pipeline requires some real engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified log items.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a standardized logging layer would solve the main logging requirement, though it addresses only Annex III 1(a) items and not the broader risk-relevant event scope or retention, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little novelty.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice with shared tooling, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized logging service to meet Article 12 is a common, legally compliant strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated four-person pod for two quarters and retrofitting pilot projects, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial change on existing infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate across high-risk projects (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging service would deliver the automatic event recording and standard schema Article 12 requires, but it does not by itself address the risk-relevant event content, retention, or the Annex III specifics, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance audits with test harnesses and remediation backlogs are a standard, expected response to a regulatory mandate, so the idea is common.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and QA practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits are a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building test harnesses and running cross-functional audits requires some staffing and process additions but is reasonably feasible with existing roles.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring the lab's systems meet the Article 12 logging requirements by checking logs against the regulatory checklist.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-release audit verifying logs capture Article 12(2) and (3) events would substantially help meet the logging mandate, but it only verifies logging rather than building it and quarterly cycles may not align with every release, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy-preserving and blockchain-based audit logging are known ideas in the field, so combining them is interesting and shows some imagination but is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (privacy-preserving architectures, on-chain trails) and links compliance to publishable research, but still treats compliance essentially as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging research and publishing methodology offends no norms, though on-chain audit trails and differential privacy on logs are somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A working group building three prototype schemas including on-chain audit trails is a significant undertaking requiring specialized expertise and resources, though feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the logging mandate (Article 12 automatic lifetime event recording and traceability) by prototyping and evaluating logging schemas, though it is framed as research rather than direct compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: Prototyping schemas in synthetic scenarios would contribute to a logging solution but does not itself deliver compliant production logging, and the differential privacy and on-chain elements may conflict with traceability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware layer built on existing infrastructure is the common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a middleware tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, though it is somewhat of a new element.
evidence_acceptability: Standardizing compliance tooling in the development pipeline is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over three sprints reusing existing message-bus infrastructure is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified events across the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A standardized logging layer mandated in all new prototypes would largely meet the logging requirement, but it covers mainly Annex III 1(a)-style fields and does not address risk-identification relevance, retention, or already-shipped systems, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking the performance overhead of mandatory logging fields is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a benchmarking spike and per-field cost measurement but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Measuring the cost of legally mandated logging violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: A minimal prototype loop with instrumentation and measurement is a small, low-cost spike that requires only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified problem, that Article 12(3) logging may degrade performance of biometric systems, which is part of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Quantifying overhead helps budgeting and design but does not itself deliver compliant logging, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Tiered logging with a toggle and promotion gating is a sensible, fairly expected engineering solution with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (tiered SDK) and a gate but still treats compliance as logging practice applied to prototypes, only slightly stretching the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Internal instrumentation libraries and promotion gates are common engineering strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an OpenTelemetry-compatible SDK with profiles and a pipeline gate is a moderate engineering effort using existing tooling, requiring some changes but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate while adapting R&D workflow to it.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially contribute to logging compliance and avoid retrofits, but does not cover other obligations like retention, Annex III specifics, or deployer-side monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as longitudinal research datasets is an unusual and imaginative reframing that converts a cost into an asset, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science, making compliance data the experimental record, which is paradigm stretching rather than a change in what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using biometric-system logs for secondary research raises data protection and purpose-limitation concerns under GDPR, which offends sensibilities somewhat though it is not wholly unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting pipelines to emit logs is required anyway and quarterly analyses are modest, though privacy limits on biometric log data and the needed analytic infrastructure demand some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (how to turn compliance logging into R&D value), which relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate rather than directly meeting it.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal uses logs for research but does not itself ensure Article 12 compliance (logging capability, minimum Annex III items), so it only partially contributes to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Treating logging and provenance as first-class scientific outputs embedded in experimental design is somewhat interesting and shows some imagination, but 'compliance by design' is a fairly expected response among labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Weaving logging into the research protocol changes the relationship between R&D and compliance (logging woven into the science), which is paradigm stretching though not changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Adopting a design template and committee submission is a common governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A mandatory design template and committee review for new projects is a reasonably feasible process change at modest cost, applying prospectively to new projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, specifying events, reference databases, and verifiers mirroring Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help meet logging obligations and avoid retrofitting, but it covers only new projects, and mirroring Annex III 1(a) is not relevant to every system, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: An interceptor layer writing append-only records of reference database version, match inputs, and verifier identity is a direct, expected implementation of Article 12(3) and is mundane for labs responding to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a specific tool but explicitly leaves the core matcher and R&D workflow unchanged, treating compliance as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable append-only logging of compliance data is a standard, uncontroversial approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: An interceptor layer with append-only storage, tested on an existing rig without redesigning the matcher, is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the logging mandate by capturing exactly the items Article 12(3)(a)-(d) require for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging requirements, but it does not address the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging for other high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Inventorying and classifying systems by regulatory risk tier is the most common first step an evaluator would expect from labs, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A scoping audit of projects against the Act's classification criteria is standard compliance practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal audit with legal involvement is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A six-week sprint with a small team of two engineers, a legal advisor and the proposer is low cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: Determining which projects are high-risk and which logging obligations apply addresses an implied prerequisite of the logging mandate, though it does not itself implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps target resources and identifies obligations but is only a partial solution since no logging capability is actually built and it is a one-time exercise.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as longitudinal research data is unusual and shows imagination, though it is not wholly surprising since drift monitoring from logs is a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research data asset, so logging is woven into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing anonymised compliance logs for drift research and monitoring is somewhat unusual and raises data-protection and purpose-limitation questions, but it does not offend sensibilities and is broadly acceptable.
evidence_implementability: It needs a log-to-dashboard pipeline, per-deployment SPC charts, anonymisation, and training of early-warning classifiers, which are reasonably feasible but involve some real changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly uses the Article 12 logs to support post-market monitoring and anticipate Article 79(1) risks, which is part of the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal supports Article 72 monitoring and risk detection but does not itself implement the logging mandate (what to record, retention, traceability), so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Retrofitting pipelines with automated, tamper-evident logging is the most common and expected response to Article 12, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal wraps existing orchestration tools with logging hooks and explicitly calls itself an engineering-integration task, so it treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance logging in engineering infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Four engineers over one quarter using existing tools like MLflow and Kubeflow is a modest, reasonably feasible effort, though retrofitting every pipeline and getting tamper-evidence right takes some real changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by producing the logs Article 12 requires.
evidence_effectiveness: Automated event capture mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) and validated against Annex III minimums would, if done, largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address adapting R&D or retention, oversight, and other related obligations.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code testing is a fairly familiar idea, though encoding each Article 12 obligation as a CI assertion is a sensible, mildly interesting application.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and process (CI compliance tests, auto-filed documentation) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifted earlier.
evidence_acceptability: Using CI tests and merge gates for compliance is a common engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Writing parameterised pytest assertions and CI gates is feasible with existing tooling, though it requires building synthetic session injection and staging integration.
evidence_applicability: The harness directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by testing that required log fields are produced during R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify technical logging capability and catch gaps early, but it does not itself design the logging, cover non-testable obligations such as relevance to risk situations, or address broader compliance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalizing 'substantial modification' as provable geometric feature-space criteria is an unusual and imaginative approach beyond typical labs' logging responses, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (mathematical criteria, open-source library) and links R&D theory to compliance, partly changing the relationship, though it still centers on logging practice and thresholds.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release and rigorous criteria offend no norms, though regulators may not accept lab-defined thresholds as legal definitions, making it somewhat uncommon but acceptable.
evidence_implementability: Deriving provable conditions, validating on incident data, and building a library requires a theoretical team and significant effort with uncertain success, making it difficult but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12(2)(a), operationalizing logging for identifying risk situations and substantial modifications, which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Formal criteria for modification thresholds would help detect relevant events but address only one of the logging purposes and not the full mandate (post-market monitoring, operation monitoring, Annex III minimums), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tying compliance checks to existing funding-gate reviews is sensible but a fairly expected governance response, with only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a mapping document and process step but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged, which is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a checklist item to an existing internal review board is a common governance step that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Using the existing board at about fifteen minutes per meeting is a low-cost, non-radical change that is easy to put in place.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D by making Article 12 fields visible during research.
evidence_effectiveness: A paper-based mapping surfaces gaps early but does not itself build the automatic logging capability, so it only partially solves the mandate.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design is a common, expected response to this mandate, with a logging impact assessment as a minor twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is the standard compliance-by-design practice that treats compliance as logging practice with a new review step, only mildly changing the lab's workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Designing logging in from the start is a widely recommended, norm-compliant approach (privacy/security by design) that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires adding a log module and a design-review deliverable, which means some process changes but is reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by making logging part of R&D design (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help ensure logging capability exists, but it is high-level, does not specify what events or Annex III minimums, and does not address documentation or monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK wired into CI is a sensible but very common engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a logging practice and merely introduces a tooling element (SDK, CI default) without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared tooling and CI defaults are standard, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-sprint build with a defined schema and CI integration is reasonably feasible, though it requires building pluggable backends and adapting every prototype branch.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the specified log fields into prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would implement the Article 12(3) logging fields and automatic recording across prototypes, but it covers only the paragraph-3 Annex III 1(a) fields and not the broader Article 12(2) traceability purposes, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Dedicated documentation or compliance staff funded from overhead is a fairly familiar response, though framing it as lifetime stewardship is somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new organizational unit and funding model but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Funding a permanent documentation team from overhead is a common, norm-respecting organizational strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Hiring two permanent FTE and shifting their cost to overhead is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though it needs institutional budget approval.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (the lifetime documentation upkeep from Recital 71) rather than the logging mandate that is the stated focus.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep technical documentation current but does not address the automatic event logging mandate of Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing traceability as an information-theoretic compression problem with provable lower bounds on log size is unusual and imaginative compared with typical logging-compliance responses, though not wholly unprecedented in interpretability/auditing research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a research agenda about what the lab studies (theory of auditability), changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, but it does not alter the lab's operational compliance practice itself.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open proofs and reproducible experiments about regulatory traceability violates no legal or social norms and is a normal academic activity.
evidence_implementability: A theory research programme needs specialist talent and has uncertain, long-horizon results, and proving bounds for transformers and MoE models is difficult, so it is hard to commit resources to as a dependable deliverable.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of knowing what must be logged for traceability, which relates to the logging mandate, but it does not directly say how to meet Article 12 now.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if successful, lower bounds on log size would only inform logging design and would not itself deliver compliant logs, and Article 12(3) minimums do not require reconstructing decision paths, so it is at best a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Using MLflow/DVC-style experiment tracking for compliance is a sensible but fairly expected response that shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and reframes compliance as a by-product of experimental practice, but it is still essentially a logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and obligations in a deep way, though the by-product framing weaves logging into the science slightly.
evidence_acceptability: Experiment tracking for traceability is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating existing open-source metadata tools into current cluster workflows within two sprints is reasonably feasible with some changes at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D by explicitly mapping fields to Article 12(3) and Recital 71.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic structured logging of runs mapped to Article 12(3) and Recital 71 would contribute substantially to meeting the logging and documentation mandate, but it covers mainly development-side records rather than the deployed system's event logs over its lifetime, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using compliance logs as a longitudinal research dataset is unusual and shows some imagination, though a seasoned evaluator could foresee it as a repurposing idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning mandated logs into primary research data and publications, which stretches the paradigm but does not redefine what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing anonymised benchmarks and papers is a somewhat unusual but non-offensive strategy, though secondary use of logs raises modest privacy and confidentiality concerns.
evidence_implementability: It needs a multi-year programme, an analytics team, and data governance, which is a significant but feasible commitment given that logs must exist anyway.
evidence_applicability: It directly uses Article 12 logs and links to Article 72 duties, adapting R&D to the mandate, though the research benefit is an implied rather than stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It contributes by leveraging logs and supporting Article 72 monitoring, but it does not itself define how to meet the logging mandate (content, retention, minimums), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing existing telemetry into a centralized log store is a common, mundane response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice using existing tooling, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Consolidating logs on existing infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing monitoring infrastructure and adding schema fields is a non-radical, low-cost change, though mapping all systems into one canonical schema takes some engineering work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(1) automatic recording requirement and the Annex III fields.
evidence_effectiveness: A unified append-only store with the required fields would satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it does not address broader needs such as event relevance to risk or post-market monitoring in depth.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design logging frameworks and open-sourcing are known approaches, though the telemetry-for-science angle adds some imaginative interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Embedding logging into the architecture and treating compliance as a reusable research asset changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, but does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building a compliance logging framework and open-sourcing it violates no legal or social norms, though open-licensing the spec is a slightly uncommon choice that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: A four-person team with two pilots in an existing biometric line is a reasonably feasible, moderately resourced effort, though building a full reference framework and open spec involves some real changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate with specific captured items matching Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: The framework would record the Article 12(3) items and embed logging, which would meet the logging mandate if implemented, though it addresses logging mainly for the biometric line and not all Article 12(2) purposes explicitly.

evidence_originality: Living documentation tied to a model registry is a well-known, mundane compliance and MLOps practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces some new process elements like registry-triggered review tickets but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation governance and audits are common, uncontroversial compliance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning owners, linking version-controlled docs to a model registry with auto-triggered tickets, and running quarterly audits are reasonably feasible changes using existing tooling.
