evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers building an SDK wrapping existing serving infrastructure is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though not trivially low-cost across eight projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by automatically capturing the Article 12(2) event categories while protecting research time.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the automatic event recording capability, but it does not define which events are relevant or address documentation, retention, or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-first experimental design with log completeness as a validity criterion is unusual and shows some imagination, but 'compliance by design' is a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Weaving logging into experimental design and treating missing logs as experimental invalidity changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: It is a somewhat uncommon internal methodology that offends no legal or social norms, though researchers may resist the added constraints.
evidence_implementability: Defining schemas at the hypothesis stage and wiring them into cluster workflows requires real process and tooling changes, but these are reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D by producing Article 12-conformant logs from the start of each experiment.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially ensure logging capability and avoid retrofitting, but it covers only the logging mandate for experiments, not deployment-time logging details such as Annex III minimums or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware layer is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tool (middleware) but still treats compliance purely as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance logging is a standard, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing time-series database and serving stack with a modest team over six months, which is reasonably feasible but involves some changes across pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the 12(2)(a)-(c) event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: A unified capture layer would substantially meet the logging requirement across systems, but it does not cover the Article 12(3) specifics, log retention, or the documentation side, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and model-card style documentation are fairly familiar, though unifying it explicitly with research reproducibility standards shows modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving documentation into the scientific record, but it introduces no wholly new elements or rethinking of what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Merging compliance documentation with research-integrity practice is a sensible, norm-respecting approach, though somewhat less common than separate compliance tracks.
evidence_implementability: A documentation template version-controlled alongside code and linked from reports needs some process changes and discipline but uses existing tools and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem, technical documentation and traceability, rather than the explicit automatic event-logging mandate that is the core of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses the documentation side (Recital 71) well but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging that Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as research data is an interesting idea that shows some imagination, but it is a fairly foreseeable move and not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science, so compliance data becomes research input.
evidence_acceptability: Using production logs for internal research is a somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no sensibilities, though data-protection questions could arise.
evidence_implementability: One postdoc and 15% of the GPU cluster over six months on existing deployments is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes, not radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting added value from mandated logs, which relates to but is not the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate or adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Repurposing logs for anomaly-detection research does not itself deliver the logging capability Article 12 requires, so it only partly contributes to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging middleware with an open-source reference implementation is a fairly expected response, though releasing it as a demonstrative artefact is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a reference architecture, logging by construction, open-source artefacts) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, with only a mild nod to partner demonstration.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging and open-sourcing a reference implementation is a common strategy that violates no norms, though open-sourcing might raise minor IP or data-exposure questions.
evidence_implementability: Integrating lightweight middleware into an existing serving stack and benchmarking overhead requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building logging middleware that captures the Article 12(3) elements (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier identities).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, built-in schema-driven logging would satisfy the logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems, though it addresses only logging and not the broader record-keeping, post-market monitoring, or relevance-to-risk event requirements.

evidence_originality: A shared public yardstick for log fidelity is interesting and shows some imagination, but benchmark-building is a familiar research move and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a research and community-offering product (benchmark, reference-point role), changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, though it does not change what the lab researches broadly.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open benchmark and open-licensed tooling is a legitimate, unobjectionable approach, though somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Building synthetic scenarios, instrumenting open-weight models, and releasing a CI harness requires substantial but feasible engineering effort and some resource commitment.
evidence_applicability: The benchmark measures whether logs capture Article 12(2) event categories, which is an implied, related need for meeting the logging mandate, though it targets community measurement rather than the lab's own compliance directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab verify and improve its own logging and aid others, but it is only a partial solution since it does not itself implement the lab's logging or adapt its R&D.

evidence_originality: Tying documentation updates to release gates is a common, expected response to technical documentation requirements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice that treats compliance as a process add-on and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though the release-blocking gate adds a small new element.
evidence_acceptability: Release-gated documentation is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a documentation owner per project, a template, and a release-gating hook in the versioning system, which are some process changes but reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It solves an identified problem, stale technical documentation, which is related to but distinct from the logging mandate, so it applies only implicitly to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping the technical file current addresses Recital 71 documentation, but the stated problem is the Article 12 automatic logging mandate, so it only partially contributes.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates in release pipelines modeled on safety reviews are common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A checklist and sign-off gate is standard compliance process that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal review gates are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist and a sign-off step in an existing release pipeline is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by verifying logging capabilities before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A release gate checking logging against Article 12(2) purposes would help ensure compliance but is only a partial solution since it does not build the logging capability itself or address Article 12(3) specifics.

evidence_originality: A purpose-built logging module mapped to the four listed fields is the obvious, expected response to Article 12(3), so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as a logging practice with a standard module and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a compliance logging module to meet the regulation's explicit minimum fields is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A dedicated logging service with tamper-evident storage, QA test cases and legal review is a reasonably feasible set of engineering changes, not radical or very costly.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified logging mandate by doing X (build the four-field logging) to get Y (compliance with Article 12(3)), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the module would satisfy the specific Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it does not cover the broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as research data is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, but dual-use logging and shared data lakes are fairly familiar ideas and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes logging from a compliance cost into shared scientific infrastructure woven into the lab's research, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: The strategy is a sensible engineering approach that offends no norms, though mixing compliance logs with research use may raise some data governance and privacy questions that are manageable.
evidence_implementability: Building a unified schema, tamper-evident archive and shared data lake requires coordinated engineering effort and some changes across project groups, but is reasonably feasible with standard tools.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by designing a unified event schema and tamper-evident compliance archive, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the compliance archive would satisfy automatic event recording and traceability, though the proposal does not detail the specific Article 12(2)-(3) event content, so it is mostly but not fully a solution to the whole mandate.

evidence_originality: A literal implementation of the four required fields as a demo artifact is the common, expected response, with only minor interest in the mock auditor query validation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice with a conventional schema, storage, and test process, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliant logging and validating it against a mock auditor suite is a standard, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over three weeks with a defined schema and a mock auditor test suite is a modest, low-cost, non-radical effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (build the Article 12(3) logging store) to get Y (compliant logging capability), which is explicitly part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Implementing the four Article 12(3) fields as a queryable store would meet the prescriptive logging mandate only for Annex III 1(a) systems, leaving Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other high-risk systems and the lab's wider R&D unaddressed, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-default in internal frameworks is an obvious and widely expected response, with some sensible framing as a configuration toggle but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (auto-instantiated logging in the SDK) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance into developer tooling is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing base framework with a telemetry module is a reasonably feasible engineering change that requires some SDK rework but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by automatically generating Article 12 logs (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs) for high-risk systems, including the Annex III 1(a) field set.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, default-embedded logging would meet the core logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it omits human verifier identification under 3(d), the appropriateness of logging to intended purpose, and retention or production-deployment concerns, so it is close to but not a full solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logs as first-class experimental output is a sensible, somewhat interesting framing, but the content (timestamps, logs in CI/CD) is fairly expected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It explicitly weaves logging into the research record so compliance is no longer separable from science, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building automatic logging into development pipelines is a legally compliant, widely acceptable engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a mandatory logging stage to CI/CD and restructuring pipelines requires some changes and platform work but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by generating the Article 12 log elements automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to logging compliance but conflates training-run logs with deployed-system lifetime logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by default via SDK middleware and templates is a sensible, fairly expected 'compliance by design' response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a default SDK scaffold with pre-wired logging middleware) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only moving it earlier in the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Standardizing logging in internal tooling is a common engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring the base framework and creating schemas and templates takes real engineering effort, but it is reasonably feasible and uses internal resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic-logging mandate by pre-wiring the Article 12(3) minimum fields into every new project.
evidence_effectiveness: A default scaffold would structurally ensure logging exists in new projects, but it does not cover existing systems, Article 12(2) event relevance, log retention or integrity, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Public transparency reports are a familiar corporate practice, and applying one to logging is mildly interesting but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a reporting format but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing transparency reports and attaching summaries to contracts offends no legal or social norms, though disclosing logging details publicly may raise some security or IP concerns.
evidence_implementability: Drafting an annual report with engineering and legal review and attaching a summary to contracts is low-cost and requires no radical change, though a customer log-retrieval mechanism may need some work.
evidence_applicability: The report documents how logging is implemented and what is logged, which relates to the logging mandate only indirectly, since it supports transparency and an implied goal of demonstrating compliance rather than building the logging capability itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A public report does not itself create or ensure the automatic event-recording capability Article 12 requires, so it only contributes partially, mainly as a signaling and customer-access aid.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK built into the architecture by default with CI/CD checks is the obvious, expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, introducing no change to how the lab's R&D relates to its compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging in by default is a common strategy that violates no laws, norms, or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared SDK integrated during normal development sprints and CI/CD is a reasonably feasible measure needing moderate engineering effort but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing the required automatic event recording and specific fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the technical logging requirements, though it leaves other aspects like log retention, use of logs, and non-Annex III contexts only partly covered, so it is mostly but not fully a solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging-design reviews and validation gates into project lifecycle stages is a fairly common shift-left compliance practice that labs would be expected to propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (sprint checkpoints and gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the R&D relationship to compliance basically unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Lifecycle reviews and stage gates are common, conventional management strategies that violate no norms, though PIs may grumble about overhead.
evidence_implementability: Adding checkpoints to existing planning templates requires some process change and retrofitting of Gantt planning to sprints but is reasonably feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by ensuring logging capabilities are designed and validated before testing or deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: Early design reviews and validation gates help ensure logging exists but do not specify what to log or cover Article 12 content requirements, so they only partially solve the problem.

evidence_originality: Shift-left, instrumentation-first and compliance-by-design approaches are a fairly common response, so this is interesting but not rare or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (reordered pipeline, definition-of-ready gate, early compliance review) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Reordering development and adding checklist gates is a common engineering-governance strategy that violates no norms, though developers may grumble about the added upfront process.
evidence_implementability: It requires changes to workflow, checklists and review practices but no major new technology or large cost, so it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by preventing costly retrofit of logging, which is an identified problem tied to compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: Building the logging layer first and gating tickets on an approved log-event schema would substantially help meet the Article 12 logging mandate, but it covers only the development-sequencing part and not documentation, retention, or the specific minimum logged items, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating event definition across architectures as a research question is unusual and shows some imagination, though it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It ties logging definition to the lab's interpretability research mission, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, but does not redefine what the lab researches overall, so it stretches rather than breaks the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme to define loggable events violates no norms and is a legitimate, common-sounding strategy for a lab.
evidence_implementability: Running controlled logging-granularity experiments across transformer and RL systems is a significant research effort that is expensive and difficult but feasible for an AI lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the ambiguity of what counts as an event under Article 12(2), which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help clarify what to log and support compliance, but it is a research programme yielding a taxonomy rather than a complete logging solution, so it contributes only partially.

evidence_originality: Turning logging compliance cost into an open benchmark dataset is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research output and publishable contribution, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than just adding a logging tool.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open benchmark of compliance costs is somewhat unusual but offends no legal, social, or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Redirecting one postdoc and a small GPU allocation for a year to instrument five existing models is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the cost and design of meeting the logging mandate within budget, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: The benchmark would build compliant logging stacks on five models and inform architecture choices, but it measures overhead rather than itself delivering full compliance across the lab's work, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking logging overhead and releasing an open suite is a sensible, somewhat interesting idea, but it is not especially surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes the regulatory constraint as a research question that yields citable output and reputation, which modestly changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it mostly adds a new process of benchmarking.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing benchmarks and a preprint on compliance overhead is a normal research activity that offends no norms, though treating compliance as a research question is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: It uses two existing postdocs, no new hires, and a two-quarter preprint timeline, so it is cheap and non-radical to carry out.
evidence_applicability: It measures the overhead of Article 12 logging, which relates to the mandate only by supplying implied information for deciding how to meet it, not by implementing the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Benchmarking overhead helps the lab and others choose logging tiers, but it does not itself deliver compliant logging or cover the content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized reusable logging module is the obvious, mundane response most labs would give to Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library with mandated integration is a common, norm-compliant engineering and compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared library and adding an architecture-review gate and QA checks requires some process changes and engineering effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically recording events, including the paragraph 3 minimum data.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the technical logging capability but does not cover the event-relevance judgments, retention, human-verifier identification, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance documentation into an open community standard is interesting and somewhat unusual, but open templates and model-card-style standards are a familiar response, so it is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (an open schema, a community standard, new partners and positioning) that shift compliance from internal practice toward a public good, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance modestly, though it remains documentation-focused.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing documentation standards offends no norms, though releasing it publicly is somewhat uncommon for a compliance response, so it is largely acceptable.
evidence_implementability: A small team drafting a schema over two quarters, piloting on three publications and releasing it openly is a reasonably feasible, modest-cost plan.
evidence_applicability: It addresses documentation requirements from Recital 71, which are related to the mandate, but Article 12 concerns automatic event logging, so the logging mandate is only indirectly addressed.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation template would help with technical documentation but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Building shared logging libraries and enforcing them via scaffolding is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response, with modest imaginative flair in blocking instantiation without logging.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (scaffold-integrated logging library) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A standard internal engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineer-weeks for schema plus wiring into a scaffolding CLI is low cost and non-radical, though the schema scope and retrofitting are mildly uncertain.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate with specified event types tied to 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would ensure technical logging capability in every prototype, but it does not address Article 12(3) specifics, retention, adequacy of events for traceability, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Lifecycle cost line items in project budgets are a fairly expected administrative response, though tying them to tranche release adds a small interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new funding-template element, but it treats compliance as an administrative cost line and leaves the lab's R&D and compliance relationship largely unchanged, so it only slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting for maintenance and annual spend reviews are common, norm-compliant management practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Revising the cost-model and project charter templates is a modest internal administrative change that the grants office can make within a quarter at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of paying for lifetime logging and documentation upkeep, which relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, rather than the logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting for lifetime log storage and documentation upkeep helps fund the logging and record-keeping obligation but does not itself make systems log events or capture the required content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance logs as a scientific dataset for studying drift and feeding continuous learning is uncommon and imaginative, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and creating new partnerships born from the obligation.
evidence_acceptability: Aggregating anonymised logs with partners is a somewhat unusual strategy, and data protection and confidentiality concerns raise some sensitivities, but it is not offensive.
evidence_implementability: It needs partner agreements, anonymisation pipelines, aggregation infrastructure and dashboards, which is significant effort but reasonably feasible for a lab with deployed systems.
evidence_applicability: It uses the mandated Article 12 logs to build a research resource, which addresses the 'adapt R&D accordingly' part of the problem but only implies an answer to how the lab meets the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not ensure the logging mandate is met (capabilities, coverage, retention), so it is a helpful partial contribution that leaves core compliance unsolved.

evidence_originality: Compliance gap audits are the most common and expected first response to a new regulation, making this mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A gap assessment is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A gap audit reported to the board is a conventional strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week review by four existing staff with a single document output is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of determining where current systems fall short of Article 12 logging requirements, though the 'four mandatory log categories' only apply to Annex III 1(a) systems, which is a limited fit.
evidence_effectiveness: A gap audit identifies non-compliance and prioritises remediation but does not itself implement logging, so it contributes only a partial solution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a standard, mundane engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging practice with shared infrastructure and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared centralized logging infrastructure is a common, normative engineering and compliance approach that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Reusing idle storage nodes from the existing HPC allocation and a lightweight ingestion API is a modest, non-radical change that is reasonably cheap, though cross-team integration takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: Automatic event recording across all high-risk systems directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate that is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared substrate would provide automatic logging, but the proposal does not specify which events are captured (Art 12(2) traceability, Annex III minimums, retention, integrity), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable shared logging library integrated into CI/CD is a common, mundane engineering response to such a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging dependency is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared tooling funded from existing budgets is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing containerised CI/CD and current maintenance budgets makes it low-cost and non-radical to implement.
evidence_applicability: The module directly implements Article 12(1) automatic logging and the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which are explicitly part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If deployed across all high-risk builds it would satisfy the core logging requirements, though it covers Article 12(2) event relevance only implicitly and Annex III 1(a) fields apply only to some systems, so it is near-complete rather than fully comprehensive.

evidence_originality: Turning the logging mandate into an open-source benchmark suite on long-term log integrity is an unusual and interesting idea that shows some imagination, though not wholly unprecedented as a research-contribution strategy.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance a source of scientific output and a new offering (benchmarks, papers) rather than only a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing benchmarks and publishing papers are legitimate, norm-consistent scientific practices that offend no sensibilities, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated research group and months-long simulated deployment scenarios, which is a significant resource commitment but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (building evidence base for log integrity and post-market monitoring) that relates to the logging mandate but does not directly address how the lab complies.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark suite and publications do not make the lab's own systems meet Article 12 logging requirements, so it contributes only partially to the problem.

evidence_originality: Unifying regulatory documentation with internal reproducibility records in version control is a sensible but fairly common idea that labs would readily propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces metadata schemas and a doc-steward role but still treats compliance as record-keeping practice, not changing the relationship between R&D and compliance much.
evidence_acceptability: Using shared documentation and rotating roles is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing version control with schemas and a rotating steward role is low-cost and non-radical, though keeping docs current requires discipline.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses record-keeping and documentation requirements in Recital 71 and maps to Article 12 fields, though it centers on technical documentation more than automatic event logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with documentation and traceability but does not itself provide automatic event logging at runtime required by Article 12(1) and 12(3), so only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Wrapping inference calls with logging middleware is a fairly expected engineering response, though the first-class metadata and zero-burden framing is a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK) but still treats compliance as logging practice, though it embeds it in researcher workflow, making it slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Automatic logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial engineering approach that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: An internal SDK with context-managers and middleware wrapping inference calls is a modest engineering effort using standard tools, requiring some changes but not radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(3) logging fields (reference database, matched input, verifier identities) and the lab's need to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve record-keeping for biometric systems under 12(3), but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and does not address Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or the lifetime logging of non-biometric systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using CI tests to validate log schema emission is a sensible, fairly expected DevOps-style response to logging mandates, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (CI gates with schema fixtures) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing gates are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing CI runner and requires writing schema-validation fixtures per system class, which is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by catching missing or malformed event emissions during development.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure events are emitted with correct structure but does not decide which events are relevant, ensure retention, or cover deployed behavior, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Design-upfront reviews are a familiar practice, so applying one to log taxonomy is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a gate and brief template) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the lab's R&D relationship.
evidence_acceptability: A design-gate and documentation process is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A half-day design session, a one-page template and peer review by an existing compliance lead are low-cost, non-radical process additions.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D processes accordingly by tying design to Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logs match Article 12(2) risk criteria, but it is only a planning step and does not itself implement logging capability or the Article 12(3) minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Ring-fencing compliance staff is a mundane, expected organizational response with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging work handled by resource allocation and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Dedicated resource allocation with sign-off controls is a common managerial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Ring-fencing a fixed share of headcount through the next quarter's resource plan is an administrative change with existing precedent (safety-review hours), so it is reasonably feasible with some reallocation cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely resourcing and schedule predictability for logging work, which relates to the stated problem of meeting the mandate while adapting R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Staffing capacity helps build and maintain logging but does not itself define or deliver the Article 12 logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalising proportionality as a quantitative risk-based function and feeding it to the consultation is an unusual, somewhat imaginative response compared with typical logging-implementation proposals, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the lab's relationship to compliance by making it an active contributor to interpreting the standard and a reference source, going beyond logging practice, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Contributing to regulatory consultations and publishing open-access research is a normal, legitimate practice that offends no norms, though it is somewhat less common for a lab.
evidence_implementability: A small team over two sprints using public incident data is feasible, though calibrating a defensible formula on limited incident data and the consultation timing add some difficulty.
evidence_applicability: The study aims to define what 'appropriate' logging granularity means under Art. 12(2), which relates to the logging mandate, but it produces a policy position and an internal methodology rather than directly implementing logging, so the link is to an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A formula and position paper would clarify proportionality and help the lab calibrate its logging, but it does not itself deliver logging capability and depends on regulators adopting it, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with owners and periodic audits is a common, expected response to the mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance governance with a few process elements added and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation ownership and internal audits are common governance practices that offend no norms and fit regulators' expectations.
evidence_implementability: Assigning owners, setting update triggers, and running quarterly audits needs only modest process changes and some staff time.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of record-keeping and traceability for audits, though the link to the logging mandate itself is implied rather than stated.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation owner and review triggers help keep records current and audit-ready, but the proposal says nothing about the technical logging capability Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design is a very expected, standard response to this mandate and shows little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, merely shifting timing to design-phase, with the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Designing logging in from the start is a common, sensible compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a standard logging interface into design specs and using tamper-evident storage requires some process and architecture changes but is reasonably feasible with existing engineering practices.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building automatic event recording into systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Native, standardized, tamper-evident logging would largely satisfy Article 12 if executed, though it does not by itself address the specific event-relevance content, retention, or Annex III minimums, so it is mostly but not fully complete.

evidence_originality: Mapping existing tooling to regulatory requirements is a common, mundane first step that most labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice (gap analysis) that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged and treats compliance purely as logging.
evidence_acceptability: A gap analysis against regulatory requirements is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week inventory using existing engineers and tools is low-cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of deciding how to meet the logging mandate by determining what must be built versus what already exists.
evidence_effectiveness: The mapping helps identify gaps and avoid redundant builds but does not itself deliver the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Observability-by-design research is somewhat known in explainability circles, but framing compliance as a scientific frontier shows imagination without being truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making traceability a first-order design variable and research question, shaping what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Treating traceability as a research program is an unusual but inoffensive strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two senior researchers over eighteen months prototyping three architectures is a significant, expensive, uncertain research commitment, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate only indirectly, by solving an implied problem of making architectures inherently loggable.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if the research succeeded, it would not deliver the Article 12 logs needed now and would only partially contribute, with uncertain accuracy-free outcomes.

evidence_originality: Embedding the logging requirement into the model objective and architecture is unusual and imaginative compared with typical external logging responses, though not wholly unprecedented given interpretability research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the science itself and changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance a research objective, stretching the paradigm but not changing what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Research into interpretable, self-logging architectures and publishing benchmarks violates no legal or social norms and is a well-regarded research direction.
evidence_implementability: Redesigning architectures with joint optimisation of accuracy and log fidelity is a significant, uncertain research effort requiring substantial resources and is exploratory rather than a committed deployable measure.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 logging mandate by designing models that natively emit event logs, which is part of the stated problem of meeting logging requirements and adapting R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: If achieved, native decision-relevant logging would satisfy automatic event recording, but Article 12 requires specific traceability events (risk situations, post-market monitoring, Annex III minimum fields like reference database and verifier identity) that model-emitted logs alone would not cover, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging into a shared platform service is a common, expected engineering response and is not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A centralized logging microservice is standard compliance infrastructure that treats Article 12 as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal infrastructure funded from an existing shared-services line is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a small three-person team and a lightweight SDK with a two person-day integration, which are reasonably feasible measures within the existing budget, though building a centralized platform requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate across the lab's high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A central service with an SDK would supply the automatic event recording and storage Article 12 requires, but it does not by itself define which events to log or address Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Budgeting for compliance is a fairly mundane idea, though framing it as a visible line item in sponsor negotiations adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a budgeting process element and links compliance costs to project approval, but it still treats compliance as an administrative overhead and leaves the science unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a mandatory budget line for compliance costs is a common, uncontroversial administrative practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A one-page template update to charter and grant processes is a low-cost, non-radical change, though sponsors may need to accept the added costs.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the resourcing of compliance work, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate but is not the technical logging response itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Funding logging and documentation is helpful but does not itself build the logging capability or meet Article 12's technical requirements, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Shared centralised log retention on existing infrastructure is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A centralised log-storage service is a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised log storage on existing infrastructure is a standard strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing HPC and Lustre storage with a lightweight query API is low-cost and non-radical, though lifecycle policies and the API need some building.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified Article 12 requirement of lifetime log retention and supports post-market monitoring and audits, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses retention and queryability over system lifetime, but it does not specify what events to log, the logging capability itself, or integrity and access controls, so it only partly solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance testing in CI is a sensible and fairly expected DevOps-style response, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI/CD conformance tests) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing of logs in CI violates no norms and is a common engineering strategy that developers and regulators would accept.
evidence_implementability: Pytest fixtures with mock endpoints and synthetic inputs are inexpensive and fit existing CI pipelines, requiring only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying Article 12 log content continuously.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably verify log fields and format, but it covers only the paragraph 3 minimum fields and not the broader Article 12 duties (risk-relevant event selection, traceability appropriateness) or the logging mechanism itself, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A traceability benchmark for logging schemas is an interesting and somewhat imaginative response, uncommon among typical logging-implementation responses, but not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a public benchmark and leaderboard) and shifts compliance toward a shared research artifact, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance modestly, though it still centers on logging.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks and leaderboards are broadly acceptable, though publishing them as a regulatory-interpretation vehicle is somewhat unusual and does not offend sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Curating 200 ground-truthed scenario pairs with a small cross-disciplinary team and an annual leaderboard is a moderately sized effort requiring some new resources and expertise but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The benchmark targets Article 12(2) logging for risk identification and post-market monitoring, which is related to the mandate, but it serves the field's shared standards rather than directly fulfilling the lab's own logging obligation (an implied problem).
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark would help define 'appropriate traceability' and test logging schemas, contributing to a partial solution, but it does not itself implement compliant logging in the lab's systems.

evidence_originality: Retrofitting existing pipelines with structured log emitters after a gap mapping is the common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is a standard gap analysis and instrumentation of existing pipelines, treating compliance purely as logging practice with no change to how the lab works.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logs within existing budgets and infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A six-week sprint on existing Kubernetes clusters with no new hardware and no capital request is low-cost and a non-radical change, though retrofitting legacy pipelines may take more effort than planned.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by identifying missing event types and instrumenting systems to record them.
evidence_effectiveness: If carried out it would substantially deliver Article 12 logging capability, but it is light on specifics such as log retention, integrity, and traceability tied to risk and post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing telemetry and data infrastructure for compliance logs is a common, pragmatic response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice using existing infrastructure, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Infrastructure-level logging with encrypted append-only storage is a conventional approach that violates no norms, though repurposing experiment-reproducibility storage may raise minor data-governance questions.
evidence_implementability: Reusing already-provisioned infrastructure and lightweight agents avoids procurement and requires only modest extensions, so it is easy and low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building the automatic event-recording infrastructure Article 12 requires, including the Annex III 1(a) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: Infrastructure-layer logging with append-only storage would largely satisfy the logging mandate, but it says little about relevance-of-events under Art. 12(2), retention, or traceability design, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Optimizing logging efficiency and publishing on it is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is a fairly expected research-turned-compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a research project and publication angle but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though turning compliance into publication and IP edges toward changing the relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Minimizing logging overhead while meeting legal minimums and publishing results is a common, norm-respecting strategy.
evidence_implementability: One postdoc and one engineer for six months on an existing testbed is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though it is research with uncertain outcomes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12's minimum logging requirements and the storage and privacy overhead of meeting them, which is part of how the lab should meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A research thread on selective recording would at best reduce the cost of logging and would not itself deliver compliant logging, so it is only a partial contribution, and selective recording risks conflicting with the requirement to record events.

evidence_originality: A document and log management system with access controls and retention alerts is a common, mundane response to a record-keeping mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A records platform with a staffed unit is standard compliance infrastructure and treats compliance as a logging and record-keeping practice without changing how R&D works.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized records management with tamper-evident storage and a compliance-reporting records unit is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Provisioning an internal platform and staffing a two-person unit requires some investment and changes but is reasonably feasible with existing technology.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging and documentation retention mandate in Article 12 and Recital 71 by building infrastructure to store logs and documentation over the system lifetime.
evidence_effectiveness: Archive infrastructure would help meet the retention and up-to-date documentation requirements, but it does not itself ensure that the right events are logged per Article 12(2) or the Annex III 1(a) minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library integrated into existing experiment tracking is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling that treats the mandate as a logging practice and leaves the lab's research workflow unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance infrastructure adopted incrementally is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team building an optional layer over one quarter within existing infrastructure is a non-radical, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate across high-risk systems (do X to get automated Article 12 logging).
evidence_effectiveness: A shared middleware capturing Article 12(2) event types would substantially meet the logging mandate, but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Dedicated maintenance reserve funds are a familiar budgeting device, so applying one to logging obligations is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It leaves compliance as standard logging practice and only adds a budgeting mechanism, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Ring-fencing a maintenance budget pool is a common, legitimate financial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a finance-office policy and a percentage allocation at project close-out, which is a modest administrative change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of funding lifetime logging and documentation obligations, which relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate but does not directly implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Securing funds for long-term log storage and monitoring helps sustain compliance but does not itself deliver logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated CI testing of log schemas is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI test suite) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using CI tests for compliance verification is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Writing parameterised pytest cases and adding them to existing CI is a non-radical, low-cost change, though synthetic session replay needs some setup.
evidence_applicability: The harness directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that Article 12(3) fields are present and correct (do X to get verified compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure log quality and catch schema drift but does not itself create logging for Article 12(1)-(2) events or cover non-Annex III 1(a) systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging by design is a fairly familiar 'compliance by design' idea, with modest imaginative elements like computational-graph-level emitters and an audit-first gate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making traceability an architectural invariant integrated into prototyping and useful for science, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into design and adding review gates is a sensible, norm-compliant approach, though somewhat more architecture-centric than typical wrapper-based compliance.
evidence_implementability: Embedding event-emitters in inference pipelines and adding a code-review gate requires some changes to engineering workflow and architecture but is reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building automatic event recording into systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic logging and a compliance gate, but Article 12(3) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems, and the proposal does not address retention, post-market monitoring links, or Article 12(2) appropriateness, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A competitive internal design challenge optimizing for log richness and third-party reconstruction of reasoning is unusual and shows imagination, though design competitions are a known format and the idea is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes logging from a compliance add-on into a primary design objective of the lab's research, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of changing what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal competitions and auditability-focused research offend no legal or social norms, though the unusual framing is somewhat uncommon.
evidence_implementability: Running three teams for six months to build a novel system is a significant resource commitment, and reconstructing reasoning from logs without weights is technically difficult, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly by treating logging as a design objective.
evidence_effectiveness: It would yield exploratory architectures and insights but does not itself deliver compliant logging for the lab's production systems, and the reconstruction goal goes beyond Article 12 requirements, so it contributes only partially.

evidence_originality: An inference-logging interceptor on an event bus with an immutable store is a common, mundane response expected from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice via a middleware module and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an in-house logging middleware on existing infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two FTEs for a quarter reusing the existing Kafka bus is a low-cost, non-radical change, though integration testing on live Annex III systems adds some effort.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly builds automatic event logging (timestamp, input reference, output match, verifier identity) that maps onto Article 12's stated logging mandate, including Annex III point 1(a) items.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, immutable structured logs of these fields would satisfy the core Article 12 logging requirement, though it leaves out broader risk-event logging for 12(2) and R&D adaptation, so it is largely but not wholly complete.

evidence_originality: Cross-functional compliance committees are a familiar response to regulatory mandates, so the idea is mundane even if sensibly framed.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (the pod) but still treats compliance as a logging-obligation mapping practice, though embedding it in sprint decisions slightly stretches the way of working.
evidence_acceptability: A cross-team compliance working group funded by internal reallocation is a common organizational strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires some time allocation (15% FTE per participant) and process changes but uses existing budget and standard meeting structures, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate within R&D by mapping obligations and integrating them with sprint work, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The pod helps identify and sequence logging obligations early but does not itself design or implement logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation registries are a common, expected compliance response, with the log-to-documentation consistency check adding only slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a registry and automated cross-checks but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice without changing how R&D works.
evidence_acceptability: A version-controlled documentation registry with assigned owners is a common compliance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Standard repository tooling plus assigning owners and automated cross-checks needs some process changes but is reasonably feasible at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (keeping documentation consistent with logs and demonstrating compliance) rather than the logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with the technical documentation and traceability side of Recital 71 but does not itself implement the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A time-boxed feasibility spike for logging is a common, mundane engineering response to a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice with a prototype, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Prototyping compliance logging is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week prototype by one engineer pair using an open-source model and the existing event bus is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate, which is the stated problem, by building the required log fields.
evidence_effectiveness: A spike on a simplified pipeline de-risks the hardest clause but only partially solves the full compliance problem, which also covers Article 12(1)-(2) and production systems.

evidence_originality: A dedicated team reviewing logs with anomaly detection is a common, expected organizational response to monitoring obligations and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a staffed unit and scripts but treats compliance as standard logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance monitoring team with incident registers for regulators is a conventional strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Hiring four staff and running weekly automated scripts is a reasonably feasible, moderate-cost change that requires no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets identified purposes in Article 12(2)(a)-(b) by using logs to detect risk situations and support post-market monitoring, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A review unit for logs addresses Article 12(2) purposes (risk identification, post-market monitoring) but does not itself deliver the logging capability or the Article 12(3) minimum fields, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using logged drift and distribution-shift statistics with process-control models to flag Article 79 substantial modification early is an unusual, imaginative idea, though not wholly unprecedented given drift monitoring exists.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research track and a commercial offering, but it does not alter what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Monitoring logs for drift and offering a compliance product violates no laws or norms and is a somewhat unusual but inoffensive strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated research track, modeling work on historical logs, and dashboard integration, which is significant effort and uncertain since substantial modification is a legal concept hard to map to statistics, but it is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, detecting substantial modification from logs under Article 12(2)(a), which relates to the stated logging mandate but is not the core requirement of enabling logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Early-warning drift signals would help flag possible substantial modifications but do not themselves satisfy the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Continuously updated documentation tied to model versions and synced with experiment trackers is a sensible, commonly expected MLOps-style response, so it is interesting but not imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process (living documentation synced to experiment tracking) but still treats compliance as a documentation and record-keeping practice without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A standard documentation-as-code practice that violates no norms, though dedicating postdocs to documentation may be somewhat unwelcome to researchers.
evidence_implementability: Assigning a postdoc per project and auto-syncing a repository with existing tracking tools is reasonably feasible with moderate staffing cost and some tooling work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, keeping records and technical documentation audit-ready, though it is mostly adjacent to the logging of events itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the technical documentation requirement of Recital 71 but does not address the automatic event logging mandate in Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a module for the four mandated fields is the obvious, mundane response a lab would be expected to give.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing mandated logging fields and validating via mock audits is a common compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-quarter sprint building a reusable library with the platform team is a reasonably feasible, moderate change rather than low-cost or radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the Article 12(3) minimum fields for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging requirements but covers only Article 12(3), not the general Article 12(1)-(2) event logging for other high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory logs as a longitudinal research dataset is an unusual and imaginative reframing, though not wholly unprecedented, since operational telemetry is often reused.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and turning the obligation into a research asset.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing logs for research is somewhat unusual and may raise data-protection and purpose-limitation concerns, but it does not clearly offend norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding schema annotations and condition tags with the platform team is a reasonably feasible change, though data governance and privacy constraints add some effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to respond to the logging mandate by annotating Article 12 logs and repurposing them for R&D, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Schema annotation would make logs more useful and traceable, but it does not itself ensure the Article 12(2) and 12(3) coverage requirements are met, so it contributes only partially to compliance.

evidence_originality: A pre-development gate requiring logging architecture sign-off is a fairly familiar compliance-by-design / design-review practice, though framing it as protecting research momentum adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a gate and template) but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing project charter workflow.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review gate is a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though some researchers may dislike added gatekeeping.
evidence_implementability: It adds a one-page template to existing charter processes with a two-week review by rotating staff, requiring modest changes and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate (automatic event recording) and avoid costly retrofitting in R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate ensures logging is designed in early, which helps meet Article 12 for new systems, but it does not address existing systems, actual log content, retention, or ongoing verification, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default templates are a sensible and fairly expected engineering response, with some thoughtfulness in the schema-to-obligation mapping but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (scaffolding templates) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only moved earlier in the workflow, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Using internal starter templates and checklists is a common engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring internal GitLab templates and adding an SDK and schema file takes modest effort and few changes to existing workflows, though keeping the schema mapped to regulatory obligations needs some upkeep.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate, including the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, in the lab's R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Starter templates with built-in logging hooks, schemas and sign-off would make new high-risk prototypes log-capable by default, but they do not cover existing systems, retention beyond templates, runtime verification, or the other compliance elements, so the idea is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying schema-contract testing and fuzzing to lifetime log compatibility is a somewhat imaginative, interesting angle, though rooted in standard CI/software-testing practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (versioned schema contracts with property-based CI tests) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI is a conventional engineering practice that offends no norms and is fully legally and socially acceptable.
evidence_implementability: Versioned JSON schemas, property-based tests, and CI gating use common tooling and require modest changes to existing engineering workflows.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied but related problem, keeping the lifetime logging requirement of Article 12(1) satisfied despite system changes, which fits the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It reliably addresses only one risk (schema drift over the lifetime) and does not ensure the logs capture the events required by Article 12(2)-(3), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging middleware built into a development template is a common, expected response to this mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice and treats compliance as a logging task without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Building automatic logging into the architecture is a common, legally aligned strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A reusable middleware module and development template require some engineering changes and upfront investment but are reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(1) logging mandate by building automatic event recording into every system.
evidence_effectiveness: A lifetime event-recording layer covering inputs, outputs, risk triggers and verification would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though Annex III specifics and retention are not detailed, so it is mostly but not fully specified.

evidence_originality: Exposing Article 12 logs to clients via an API as a market differentiator is a somewhat unusual and interesting reframing of compliance, but not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a customer-facing offering, changing the relationship between compliance and the lab's business (a new offering born from compliance), which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Giving clients read access to their own system logs under contract is a sensible practice that offends no norms, though privacy of verifying persons' IDs and confidentiality need handling.
