evidence_implementability: It builds a thin REST API and dashboard on top of an existing logging SDK with contract-scoped access, which is reasonably feasible with some changes, though multi-tenant access control and data scoping add work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of leveraging logging obligations for business benefit, which relates to how the lab responds to the mandate rather than directly meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself satisfy the logging mandate (it depends on Proposal 1's SDK) but adds a partial contribution by making logs usable and producing commercial value from compliance.

evidence_originality: Compliance checks in CI/CD pipelines are a well-known approach, so this is common and mundane, with only mild interest in the pre-demo gating.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces an automated test and gate but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working largely intact, which is slight stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: A CI/CD compliance gate is a common engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a checklist and automated log-simulation test to existing CI/CD is a modest, low-cost change, though applying it to every prototype needs some setup.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (gate on logging fields) to get Y (compliance with the Article 12 logging mandate), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure Article 12(3) fields are implemented in prototypes, but covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and not the broader logging, retention, or documentation obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Costing compliance into proposals is a sensible but fairly mundane financial planning idea with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a financial tool but treats compliance as a cost of logging practice, leaving R&D ways of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting compliance costs into grant proposals is a common, uncontroversial financial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A finance analyst building a cost model from existing benchmarks and pilot log-volume estimates, then attaching it to grant applications, is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (funding recurring log-related costs) that relates to the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate, rather than the logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A cost model helps the lab budget for Article 12 obligations but does not itself deliver logging capability or compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized OpenTelemetry-based logging layer is a common and expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging middleware is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a conventional strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers prototyping over six weeks with an existing open-source base and a validated latency target is modest and reasonably feasible, though integration across all projects needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, including the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a schema-versioned shared logger covering Article 12(2) categories and Annex III fields would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though identification of verifying persons and the reference database depend on integration details.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in shared templates or SDKs is a common, expected response to logging mandates, with little surprising or imaginative content.

evidence_acceptability: An internal logging library inherited through standard project templates is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.

evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic logging capability, but it does not by itself ensure that events are relevant to Article 12(2) purposes or cover the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Adding a compliance budget line to project templates is a sensible but fairly common governance step that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.

evidence_acceptability: Requiring budget lines in proposal templates is a routine, common management practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a form field and review criterion is a non-radical change, though accurately estimating by Annex III tier takes some expertise.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, funding and planning for logging obligations, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate rather than the logging requirements directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting for logging infrastructure helps resource compliance but does not itself build the logging capability or satisfy Article 12 content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated documentation from repository metadata is a known practice, so it is interesting but not surprising.

evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation in CI/CD is a sensible strategy that violates no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat less common than manual documentation.
evidence_implementability: Adding a doc-generation job to an existing CI/CD pipeline that reads model cards and configs from the repository requires some tooling and process changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied related problem (keeping technical documentation up to date per Recital 71) rather than the Article 12 logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps keep technical documentation current but does not implement Article 12's automatic event logging itself, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Automated log-completeness checking against Article 12(3) is a fairly expected and sensible response, with little that is surprising or imaginative.

evidence_acceptability: An internal compliance self-audit tool is a common strategy that violates no norms, although the framing about institutional survival is mildly self-interested.
evidence_implementability: Building a log validator with scheduled weekly runs and an escalation path is a reasonably feasible engineering task using existing pipelines, with some changes needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging requirements for biometric systems, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help detect logging gaps for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it covers only the minimum fields of Article 12(3) and does not address the wider logging mandate in Article 12(1)-(2), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gating funding on compliance documentation is a sensible but fairly common governance approach, showing little surprise or ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a process step into R&D intake that links compliance to funding decisions, modestly changing the relationship, but it remains a standard compliance process rather than a rethinking of the research itself.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a checklist section to grant review mirrors the existing ethical-review gate and violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Updating a checklist and adding a one-page section is a low-cost, non-radical change that can be done within a month.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab will meet the Article 12 logging mandate by requiring logging architecture planning at project intake, which is a direct response to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A planning gate helps ensure logging is designed in early but does not itself implement logging capabilities or cover existing systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left design-time compliance with ADRs is a well-known, standard practice and would be an expected response from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces an architecture-first template and decision record but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Architecture templates and design-review requirements are common strategies that violate no norms and are acceptable to stakeholders.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint refactoring five architecture documents and adding an ADR requirement is a modest, low-cost change that is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the logging mandate by embedding Article 12(2)(a)-(c) event categories into system architecture designs, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing event recording in as a first-class component would help meet Article 12, but it omits Article 12(3) specifics, verification of log content, and the documentation and post-market processes, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design middleware is the expected, common response to Article 12 and is not surprising.

evidence_acceptability: Embedding tamper-evident logging to meet a legal mandate is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building modular logging middleware and retrofitting all in-flight projects requires a cross-functional team and some significant changes, but is reasonably feasible with standard engineering.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X, get Article 12 compliance).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native tamper-evident logging capturing the Article 12(3) fields would directly satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address the broader Article 12(2) purposes or documentation, so it is near-complete for the logging requirement.

evidence_originality: Reusing scientific documentation to satisfy regulatory paperwork is a fairly sensible and expected efficiency move, with some interest but little surprise.

evidence_acceptability: Consolidating documentation under the project lead violates no norms, though relying on a quarterly refresh without a compliance team may raise some regulatory eyebrows, it remains a common and acceptable strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared template and assigning ownership to project leads requires modest process change at low cost, using documentation that already exists.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the stated problem of meeting record-keeping obligations, but it targets the technical documentation described in Recital 71 rather than the automatic event logging that Article 12 requires, so it applies to an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A maintained technical file would help with documentation and traceability, but it does not provide automatic event logs over the system lifetime, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open provenance standards and metadata schemas are known ideas, though framing Article 12 as a seed for a community standard is somewhat interesting.

evidence_acceptability: Open-source standards releases under Apache 2.0 are a common, norm-compliant practice, though releasing seed training and validation records needs data-governance care.
evidence_implementability: A small working group drafting over two sprints and publishing on a public repository is low cost and modest change, though adoption and the actual logging integration remain outside its scope.
evidence_applicability: It addresses logging/record-keeping by extending Article 12 minimums into a provenance schema, but the stated aim is a community standard, so the link to the lab's own compliance need is implied rather than directly stated.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema and reference implementation would help structure records, but it does not itself deliver Article 12 automatic event logging in the lab's high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance gating at project intake is a fairly common governance idea that an experienced evaluator would expect, though it is sensible and not outright mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Embedding a logging-architecture requirement into project intake changes when compliance enters R&D (design constraint rather than post-hoc fix), but it is a checklist/process addition that still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a checklist and joint review with the Compliance Officer is a common governance practice that violates no norms, though researchers might grumble about overhead.
evidence_implementability: It only requires amending the grant-review checklist and a one-page spec reviewed by existing staff, which is a non-radical, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring event categories are planned for in each R&D project, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It ensures logging is planned but does not itself implement logging, cover existing systems, or guarantee the logs meet Article 12 in operation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Phased budgeting and compliance checklists are mundane and predictable responses to a regulatory mandate, with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance project management that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Risk-tiered phased budgeting with release-gate checklists is a common, uncontroversial corporate strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Phasing budget, ring-fencing about 15% of engineering spend, and adding checklist-based release gates are ordinary planning and governance changes that need little new technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to resource and sequence meeting the Article 12 logging mandate while protecting R&D, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It funds and sequences the work and adds gating, which helps, but it specifies no logging design or technical means, so it is only a partial solution; the deferral of lower-tier systems may also risk deadline non-compliance.

evidence_originality: Versioned documentation tied to CI/CD with update tickets and assigned compliance engineers is a common, expected response to Recital 71.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a CI/CD-linked documentation workflow but still treats compliance as a standard documentation and record-keeping practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date technical documentation and assigning compliance owners is a conventional strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing tooling (repositories, CI/CD, tickets) with modest staffing additions, so it requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified documentation requirement in Recital 71, which relates to but is not the core of the logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping technical documentation current helps with Recital 71 and post-market monitoring but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging mandated by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing the logging schema up front as a gate is a sensible shift-left practice that is interesting but not especially surprising or rare.

evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping events to Article 12(2) categories and Annex III 1(a) fields before build.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure the required events are instrumented, but it only specifies a schema and does not cover implementation, retention, or verification of the logs, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A module that captures the mandated Article 12(3) fields is the obvious, expected response to the mandate, with the tamper-evident store a mild embellishment.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a specific tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice separate from the core R&D, so it is at most slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Building a logging module that records the legally mandated fields in a tamper-evident store is a standard, norm-compliant way to meet the regulation.
evidence_implementability: Intercepting a matching pipeline and writing four structured fields to an append-only store is a bounded, reasonably feasible engineering task, though tamper-evidence and a query interface add some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems by recording exactly the required fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging requirements if built, but it does not cover the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging for other high-risk systems or the R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logging into a publishable open-source toolkit and procurement asset is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but building logging tooling is a fairly expected response.

evidence_acceptability: Building internal tooling, publishing, and offering it to clients violates no norms, though the open-source and publication angle is mildly uncommon.
evidence_implementability: Two postdocs for one year on the existing data lake is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though a year of work and diverting researchers from research is not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to meet the logging mandate for the Article 12(2)(a)–(c) use cases, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A logging and query toolkit with dashboards would help meet the Article 12 logging mandate, but it only partly solves compliance, since it does not specify which events to log or how to cover Article 12(3) or the retention duties.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a scientific dataset for a failure-mode taxonomy is unusual and shows imagination, but the idea of mining logs for failure analysis is not entirely unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes mandated logs as a primary research corpus, changing the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations and influencing what the lab researches, though it stops short of fully redefining the lab's mission.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymised operational logs for research and publication is a somewhat unusual strategy that raises data-protection and confidentiality issues but does not offend sensibilities if properly managed.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an annotation pipeline, clustering methods, anonymisation, and peer-reviewed publication, which is a significant but feasible effort for a research lab, and it depends on having deployed systems with log data.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of extracting value from the logging mandate, but it does not itself address how to meet the logging requirements, so it relates to the stated problem only indirectly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help adapt R&D to the mandate and generate benefits from logs, but it contributes nothing to actually satisfying Article 12 compliance, making it only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware with pluggable backends is a common, expected engineering response and is mundane.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design gates and reusable logging libraries are a well-known, expected response, so this is only mildly interesting rather than surprising.

evidence_acceptability: A design-gate review and shared logging libraries are common, norm-respecting engineering governance practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a shared library, a review gate, and process changes, which are reasonably feasible but need some organizational change and platform-team effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(1) automatic logging mandate by building logging into systems from the start.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially ensure the automatic recording capability exists, but it does not specify which events to log per Article 12(2)-(3) or cover retention and other duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-aware benchmarks for log quality are relatively unusual and show some imagination, but benchmark suites are a familiar research format.

evidence_implementability: Curating synthetic scenarios, a scoring rubric, and an annual release with community contributions requires sustained effort and expertise, but it is feasible without radical organizational change.

evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark would help evaluate log quality but does not itself make the lab's own systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in CI/CD middleware using existing brokers and storage is a common, mundane engineering approach to compliance logging.

evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would produce the required logs, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) fields in test builds and does not address lifetime logging in deployed systems or the Article 12(2) event-relevance requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-project compliance gates and impact assessments are a familiar governance tool, so the idea is interesting but not imaginative or surprising.

evidence_originality: Reusable compliance middleware is a conventional and expected engineering response, with nothing surprising about it.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance monitoring telemetry as research data is a somewhat interesting dual-use angle, but drift monitoring for post-market monitoring is a fairly expected response.

evidence_implementability: Wrapping existing endpoints with a lightweight telemetry layer and storing results in an existing data lake involves modest changes and is reasonably feasible.

evidence_originality: Privacy-by-design-style embedding of logging with architecture review gates is a common, expected response to this mandate.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design with shared logging libraries and gated reviews is a common and expected response, showing little surprise.

evidence_effectiveness: A shared middleware that automatically logs timestamps, reference databases, matched inputs and verifier identities from the first sprint would, if done, address the main Article 12 logging mandate including the Annex III 1(a) minimums.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging into a shared internal library with a CI/CD gate is a common, mundane engineering response to such a mandate.

evidence_effectiveness: Baking log emitters, viewer and retention checks into default dev scaffolds would make logging capability present in nearly all prototypes, but it covers only Article 12 technical logging and not the content requirements, the documentation, or the deployer-side obligations, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Schema validation in CI/CD is a familiar compliance-as-code pattern, with only mild interest from applying it to Article 12 fields.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool-based gate but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only shifted earlier in the pipeline.
evidence_acceptability: Build-time gating checks are a common engineering practice that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing GitLab runners and JSON Schema, requiring modest template authoring per system category and no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring every AI service emits the required log events before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably enforce log field presence and format, but it cannot verify that the logged events are actually relevant, sufficient for traceability, or retained, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checkpoints at project intake are a familiar governance pattern, so the idea is sensible but mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process step but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged, so it slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate reviews at project intake are a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though some engineers may dislike the added friction.
evidence_implementability: A one-page plan and a two-person biweekly panel is a small process addition requiring few resources and no radical changes, though it adds some overhead to intake.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by ensuring Article 12 event types and modification triggers are specified before R&D starts.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-funding logging plan gate helps ensure logging is scoped early, but it only covers planning and does not itself build the logging capability or meet the Article 12 mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging component is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice via a shared module, leaving the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared, immutable logging module with compliance sign-off is a standard, norm-respecting way to meet a legal logging mandate.
evidence_implementability: Building a standalone internal logging service and linking it into pipelines requires some engineering and process changes but is reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified log fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would cover the Article 12(3) minimum fields and reduce non-conformity risk, but it addresses only logging (not Article 12(2) event relevance tailoring or broader documentation), so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared internal logging library baked into project templates is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response, though the template-default angle is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a shared SDK embedded in repo templates) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal shared tooling and default templates are common engineering practice that offends no norms, though logging input payloads raises minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: A thin Python/TypeScript SDK with decorators and template pinning is a modest, reasonably feasible platform-team effort, though integrating with diverse prototypes takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the automatic logging mandate and adapting R&D to it, with clear X (SDK) leading to Y (automatic logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would automatically capture the Article 12(3) items (timestamps, reference DB, input data, verifier identity) across prototypes, but it covers only part of the mandate (e.g., risk-event identification, retention, post-market monitoring needs), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in at the design stage (privacy/compliance by design) is a very common and expected response, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a logging-first design template and design-gate schema reviews but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: It is a standard, norm-respecting compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities or laws.
evidence_implementability: Adding a spec template and design-gate reviews to the existing pipeline is a modest process change achievable at low cost, though it requires some engineering adjustment.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, including the specific Article 12(3) items.
evidence_effectiveness: Designing logging in from the start would substantially help meet the mandate, but it covers mainly Annex III 1(a) items and does not address broader R&D adaptation, retention, or legacy systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A living, version-controlled documentation repository with designated stewards is a common and expected response to the documentation requirement, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It keeps compliance as a documentation practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though it adds stewards and diff review.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional compliance strategy that violates no norms and is welcomed by regulators and clients.
evidence_implementability: Assigning stewards and using version control with compliance review needs some process changes but is reasonably feasible with existing tools.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified need for up-to-date technical documentation in Recital 71, which relates to the record-keeping problem, though it does not directly address the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping technical documentation current helps meet Recital 71 but does not address Article 12's automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building analytics and alerting on mandated logs for post-market monitoring is a sensible but fairly expected response that labs would commonly propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (analytics pipeline, alerting) but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal log monitoring with compliance review is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Requires a dedicated data-engineering team and new tooling, which is a significant but reasonably feasible investment using standard threshold-based alerting techniques.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses Article 12(2)(a)-(c) purposes of identifying risks and facilitating post-market monitoring, though it presumes logging exists and does not itself specify how the logging mandate is met.
evidence_effectiveness: Analytics on logs would help with monitoring and risk detection but is only a partial solution since it does not cover logging design, retention, or the Annex III minimum logging content.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance evidence into a procurement differentiator is interesting and shows some imagination, but transparency packages are a fairly familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a market offering and reputation asset, which changes the relationship between the lab's work and its compliance obligations (a new offering born from compliance).
evidence_acceptability: Sharing evidence with customers and notified bodies while protecting proprietary internals is a legitimate, somewhat unusual practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Templated disclosure packages and a short training module are modest additions to existing compliance work, though they depend on logs and documentation already existing and require per-release refreshes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of demonstrating Article 12 conformity to partners and regulators, which is related to but not the core logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A disclosure package demonstrates conformity but does not itself implement the logging capability, so it addresses only the evidence side of the mandate and is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing existing monitoring for compliance is a common, expected response and not imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice using existing tools, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing observability infrastructure for compliance is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing tools with thin adapters and flat spend is reasonably feasible with some changes, though mapping metrics to event categories takes work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by reusing existing infrastructure to produce Article 12 logs.
evidence_effectiveness: Mapping existing monitoring metrics to Article 12(2) categories would help meet the logging mandate, but training-loss and latency metrics are mostly not the deployed-system event logs Article 12 targets, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared default logging library is a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging library with append-only storage is a common engineering approach that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over one sprint building a decorator layer on existing registry and tracker, distributed via the base Docker image, is a modest and reasonably easy change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (automatic recording of events) while preserving prototyping speed.
evidence_effectiveness: It would give automatic event logging across pipelines and so substantially meets Article 12 paras 1-2 for the lab's systems, though it does not itself cover para 3 specifics, risk-event identification content, or retention and other compliance duties, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance gap audits are the standard expected first response to a new regulation and are mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A internal compliance audit is a common, uncontroversial business practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Project leads mapping existing telemetry against specific articles is a low-cost process using existing staff and budget cycles, requiring non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified need to know where systems fail Article 12(2) and 12(3) requirements, which is directly tied to the logging mandate, though the gap-finding is a precursor to the stated problem of meeting it.
evidence_effectiveness: A gap audit identifies shortfalls and prioritizes remediation but does not itself build the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Cost modeling in project intake is a sensible but fairly predictable governance tool, with some interest in tying it to Article 12 operational costs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D selection and compliance obligations by making lifetime logging cost a criterion for what research gets funded, which stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Cost-planning gates in project intake are a legitimate, uncontroversial management practice, though weighting compliance overhead in scientific funding is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Adding a financial template and a scoring criterion to an existing grants intake process is a modest, non-radical process change, though estimating multi-year log costs takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of resource commitment under the logging mandate (long-term costs of Article 12), which relates to the stated problem of how to respond and adapt R&D, but it does not itself meet the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab avoid overcommitting resources and adapt its R&D portfolio, but it does not implement logging or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A gap audit with a compliance matrix and remediation owners is the most standard, expected first response to a new regulatory mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits with legal counsel are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A six-week cross-team working group and inventory require modest coordination and effort but no radical change, so it is easy to implement at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of determining whether systems meet Article 12 logging requirements, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit identifies gaps and assigns remediation but does not itself implement logging, so it contributes only partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as R&D data is a fairly foreseeable and not unusual idea, though the framing of a compliance cost as an asset shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning compliance logs into a research asset feeding development cycles, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymized logs for internal analytics and monitoring is a sensible, legally mindful practice that offends no norms, though data-protection questions about log reuse need care.
evidence_implementability: A small cross-functional team building an ingestion and analysis layer atop existing logging middleware is reasonably feasible, requiring some new work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: Feeding mandated logs into post-market monitoring and risk-management documentation addresses the implied problem of making the logging mandate useful, though it does not directly say how to meet Article 12's logging requirements themselves.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab get value from logs and support post-market monitoring, but it is only a partial solution because it assumes the logging itself is already built and does not ensure Article 12 compliance.

evidence_originality: A public Article 12 log benchmark is an unusual and interesting idea showing imagination, but benchmark datasets are a familiar research format and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates a new output (public benchmark) born from compliance, extending the lab's relationship to compliance into a research contribution for the ecosystem, which stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing de-identified synthetic log corpora openly is an uncommon but norm-respecting research practice, though publishing derived internal telemetry carries some confidentiality considerations.
evidence_implementability: Generating, de-identifying, hand-annotating, and publishing a corpus with an evaluation harness and white paper requires significant effort and expense, though it is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (ecosystem tooling and research on observability) related to Article 12, but does not directly address how the lab meets its own logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not make the lab's own systems log compliantly, so it contributes little to solving the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Scaling compliance effort to regulatory exposure is a fairly common and expected response, with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged apart from a triage memo.
evidence_acceptability: Risk-proportionate compliance via an internal memo is a common, legally grounded approach that offends no norms, though minimal-tier logging must still satisfy Article 12(1)-(2).
evidence_implementability: An internal memo, kickoff-review tier assignment, and tying engineering allocation to tiers requires only modest process changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate (Article 12(2) vs 12(3) scope) and manage the cost of adapting R&D, which are parts of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Tiering logging depth to risk class would help meet Article 12 proportionately, but it only allocates effort and does not itself deliver the logging capabilities, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code linting in CI is a fairly expected response, though mapping coverage to specific sub-clauses adds some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal CI check is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an AST and taint-tracking analyzer that maps to legal sub-clauses is nontrivial engineering, but it is reasonably feasible with existing tooling and CI integration.
evidence_applicability: The linter directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by checking that required event classes are emitted in prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: Static analysis can catch missing log points but cannot verify runtime behavior, log adequacy, or the traceability purpose, and Article 12 covers only part of compliance, so it is a helpful partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated documentation from experiment trackers is a fairly common idea, and applying it to Recital 71 is sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new pipeline tool and moves documentation from batch-at-release to per-commit, which is a modest workflow change but still treats compliance as a documentation practice separate from the science.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation with quarterly compliance review is a common, norm-compliant strategy, though quarterly review may be light.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing tools (MLflow, Jinja2, git CI) with modest template maintenance, so it is reasonably easy and low-cost to implement.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses keeping technical documentation current under Recital 71, which is related to the logging/record-keeping mandate but targets documentation rather than automatic event logs, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Living documentation would help traceability and compliance but does not implement Article 12 automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Productizing logs as a client dashboard is an interesting and sensible idea but fairly commonly expected, showing some imagination without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logs into a client-facing product offering with anchor-customer co-design, changing the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings (compliance-born new offerings), though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Exposing logs to deployers and packaging compliance as a feature is a reasonable business strategy, though real-time exposure of logs raises some data-protection and confidentiality considerations without being offensive.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing logging layer with an API and lightweight front-end and a six-week pilot with two customers, which is a modest, feasible effort.
evidence_applicability: The dashboard directly uses Article 12 logs and ties them to Articles 72 and 26(5), but it mainly addresses deployers' needs and market positioning rather than the lab's own logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It builds on the existing logging layer and supports evidence documentation, but it does not itself ensure the lab's logging meets Article 12 requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building analytics dashboards and alerting on top of compliance logs is a fairly expected, mundane response that experienced evaluators would anticipate from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (dashboards, alerting, a dedicated analyst team) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Proactive monitoring and filing reports for regulator inspection is a common, norm-conforming compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated permanent analyst team, real-time dashboards, and alerting infrastructure, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial investment atop existing logging middleware.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem by using logs to meet Article 12(2)(a)-(c) purposes and Article 72 documentation.
evidence_effectiveness: Analyzing logs against Article 12(2) purposes would meaningfully support risk identification and post-market monitoring, but it does not itself deliver the logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Merging research reproducibility records with compliance logs is a sensible and somewhat imaginative idea, though experiment-tracking ledgers are fairly familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and positioning the lab as a reference implementation, but does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Unified logging for compliance and reproducibility is a sensible, norm-respecting approach, though somewhat less common than separate compliance tooling.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared tamper-evident log store with CI/CD hooks across high-risk pipelines is a platform engineering effort requiring some changes and reasonably feasible measures, not radical or impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically recording events in the lab's pipelines.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic tamper-evident logging at training and evaluation steps would substantially satisfy Article 12(1), but it records experiment provenance rather than the deployed system's operational events (Art. 12(2) risk, post-market monitoring, Art. 26(5)) and the Annex III 1(a) specifics, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code and shift-left checks are known ideas, but applying formal property specs to Article 12 traceability coverage is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tools and processes (spec language, model-checking gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice verified in the existing development loop.
evidence_acceptability: A CI/CD compliance gate that checks logging coverage is a legitimate engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms, though the formal-spec approach is somewhat less common than ordinary checklists.
evidence_implementability: Formalizing Article 12(2) requirements into a domain language and model-checking against event schemas needs significant tooling and expertise, though it is feasible within a CI pipeline, and 'intended purpose' parsing is hard.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that logging configurations cover the Article 12(2) events.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help catch coverage gaps early but only checks schema coverage of events, not that logs are actually generated, retained, or sufficient (e.g., Annex III minimums), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code tests in CI are a fairly familiar idea, so applying them to Article 12 is interesting but not very surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool in the pipeline but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifting verification earlier, which is slight stretching.
evidence_acceptability: A CI/CD compliance test gate is a common engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a contract-test suite, synthetic traffic replay and build-pipeline integration, which are reasonably feasible changes but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements by checking log completeness in development builds.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that logs contain the required fields, which helps meet the logging mandate, but it does not create the logging capability or address the substantive appropriateness of the logged events, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Requiring compliance design artifacts at project intake is a common shift-left practice that an experienced evaluator would expect, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process gate and artifact but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A lightweight intake gate is a standard governance approach that violates no norms, though some researchers may resist added process.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing intake workflow and a rotating 0.2 FTE reviewer from existing staff, which is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab meets the logging mandate by requiring a logging architecture brief before development begins, so the action maps onto the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A one-page brief gate at intake would help ensure logging is designed in early, but it only covers planning and does not guarantee the technical logging capability or the Article 12 content requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automating compliance checks and documentation sync is an interesting, sensible idea but is a fairly expected response among compliance-tooling proposals.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (CI pipeline, LLM summarization) but still treats compliance as logging and documentation practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance monitoring and documentation generation is a socially and legally unobjectionable, fairly common compliance strategy, though LLM-drafted regulatory documentation may raise mild accuracy concerns.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight microservice on existing infrastructure with rule-based validators is reasonably feasible, but LLM-generated documentation and integrating across deployments require some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified mandate to meet logging requirements and keep Recital 71 documentation current, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help verify logging minimums and keep documentation current, but it only checks logs rather than ensuring the system technically logs, and the Article 12(3) minimums apply to only one Annex III category, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared auto-instrumenting logging library with OpenTelemetry export is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice packaged as tooling, leaving the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging via a shared library is a common strategy that violates no norms, though centralized storage of matched inputs raises minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a decorator-based OpenTelemetry exporter in three weeks using existing lockfile dependency workflows is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-emitting timestamps, reference-database version, and matched inputs (do X to get Y, where Y is the logging mandate).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would cover the automatic event recording requirement across prototypes, but it is mostly a partial solution because it doesn't address identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring, human verifier identification, or retention and relevance judgment per intended purpose.

evidence_originality: Building compliance costs into project budgeting is a fairly common, sensible approach, mildly interesting but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (funding gates and budget lines) but still treats compliance as logging and documentation practice rather than changing the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting compliance as a funded line item and reviewing it at quarterly checkpoints is a conventional governance practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires modest changes to the grant and milestone-review process and coordination with the grants office, which is reasonably feasible without major cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of retrofitting logging and documentation late, which relates to how the lab meets the logging mandate, rather than directly specifying logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Funding and checkpointing logging design helps ensure it gets done but does not itself specify or implement the logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing a compliance logging reference implementation as an open-access research deliverable is a somewhat unusual and interesting angle, though open-sourcing reference code is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance into a citable research output and a standard-setting position changes the relationship between compliance and R&D (new offering born from compliance), stretching the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a reference implementation and publishing documentation is a fairly common, norm-respecting practice, with only minor concerns over presenting it as the standard.
evidence_implementability: Two staff over three months using internal test data with no new infrastructure is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though assuring compliance fidelity and maintaining open-source code adds some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified Article 12(3) logging requirements (timestamps, reference database, match inputs, verifier identity) that are part of the stated mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver compliant Article 12(3) logging only for the biometric Annex III 1(a) case and does not address Article 12(1)-(2) logging for the lab's own systems broadly, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A design-time checklist with auto-generated stub code is a sensible but fairly common compliance-by-design approach, with only mild interest from the code scaffolding.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a template and scaffold tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moving it earlier in the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: A mandatory design sign-off gate is a common engineering governance practice that offends no norms, though some developers may resist the rigidity.
evidence_implementability: Building a template, a stub generator, and a review step requires some tooling and process change but is reasonably feasible with modest cost.
evidence_applicability: The template directly addresses how the lab meets the logging mandate by requiring event schema, storage, and Annex III 1(a) fields to be defined at design time.
evidence_effectiveness: It would ensure logging is designed in from the start and covers the mandatory fields, but it addresses only design-stage process and not runtime log content adequacy, retention, or post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a scientific instrument for drift research is interesting and shows some imagination, though drift detection and log analytics are familiar ideas.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making mandated logs the object of the lab's research and a source of publications and identity, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open-access research and using logs for monitoring offends no norms, though using compliance logs as research data is somewhat unusual and raises minor data governance questions.
evidence_implementability: Building a research thread with synthetic drift benchmarks, detector models and publications requires significant staffing and effort, but it is feasible for an AI R&D lab and builds on logs it must already produce.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by turning logs into research value, which relates to but is not directly the stated problem of meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself deliver the logging mandate (it presumes logs exist), so it only contributes to a partial solution by leveraging logs for post-market monitoring and research identity.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance tooling is a fairly expected response, though reusing the telemetry as a research dataset and positioning as a reference implementation adds some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance cost into an external research contribution and reference implementation changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations somewhat, with logging becoming a research output and a partnership offering.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release with regulators and other labs is a norm-respecting approach, with only minor questions about exposing telemetry data that might contain sensitive inputs.
evidence_implementability: A two-person pod integrating into existing CI/CD in one quarter plus documentation and release is reasonably feasible, though building a conformant, publishable toolkit takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by instrumenting inference pipelines to produce Article 12 logs.
evidence_effectiveness: A logging library implementing the Article 12 elements (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier IDs) would meet the core logging mandate, though it covers mainly paragraph 3 for Annex III 1(a) systems and not broader risk-event logging, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: A log store with query API and dashboards is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces tooling but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, which is close to paradigm preserving.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal log infrastructure for compliance officers is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping an append-only columnar store, schema-mapped ingestion, a REST API, and three dashboards is reasonably feasible with standard technology though it needs some engineering resources.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by building storage, query, and reporting for Article 12 logs and Article 72 post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A queryable lifetime log store would help make logs usable for monitoring and traceability, but it covers only the storage and consumption part of compliance, not the event-capture content or documentation requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance logging as a publishable provenance and interpretability research programme is somewhat unusual and imaginative, though not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging a research subject and producing open-source outputs, which stretches the paradigm but does not redefine what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open-source logging research tools and working papers violates no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual way to respond to a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: A small cross-team group building new log compression, querying and replay tools is feasible but requires considerable research and engineering effort beyond simply implementing logging.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses Article 12 logging by building tools for querying and replaying logs, but its main aim is research output, so it solves an implied problem related to compliance rather than directly delivering the required logging capability.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on log compression and replay tools would help with log usability and traceability but does not itself guarantee that the lab's systems meet the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as research datasets is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though repurposing logs for analytics is a fairly foreseeable response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and turning compliance overhead into a research asset, but does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for research is somewhat unusual and raises minor data-governance and privacy considerations, but it offends no sensibilities and violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending log schemas with extra statistical fields and coordinating with data science requires some design changes and collaboration but uses ordinary engineering and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate while adapting R&D, with an explicit X (design logs as research datasets) leading to Y (compliance plus research asset) which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Logging satisfying every regulatory minimum would meet the mandate, and the research reuse adds value, but the idea mostly addresses the adaptation angle and leaves compliance details such as retention and verification mostly unspecified, so it contributes substantially rather than fully solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Using mandated logs as a longitudinal empirical resource for drift research is imaginative and relatively unusual among lab responses, though not wholly unprecedented given existing drift monitoring work.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning logging data into a research resource and creating partnerships with deployers, and it sets a new research direction (drift), which approaches changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Research partnerships and publication are normal, though sharing live-system logs with outside labs raises some data-protection and confidentiality sensitivities without being offensive.
evidence_implementability: A three-year track requiring access to deployers' live logs, partnerships, and dedicated research staff is a significant, costly, uncertain commitment, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the 'adapt its R&D accordingly' part of the problem and ties to Article 79(1) risk events, but the problem solved (drift science) is implied rather than the identified compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate (no logging capability design for the lab's own systems), so it is at best a partial contribution to the stated problem of how to meet the mandate and adapt R&D.

evidence_originality: Reusing mandatory compliance logs as a feedback corpus for retraining is a sensible and somewhat unusual idea, but not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving the logs into the development loop so compliance spend doubles as research data, which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for internal analytics with privacy-preserving aggregation is a fairly standard practice, though repurposing logs raises minor data-protection questions.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight ETL job on existing monitoring infrastructure and an existing experiment-tracker UI is reasonably feasible with modest changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting extra value from the mandated logs, rather than directly meeting the logging mandate, so it relates to the stated problem only indirectly.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps adapt R&D to the mandate but does not itself deliver compliant logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a substrate for drift-detection science is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but not wholly surprising given existing monitoring research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research agenda and public contribution, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks and research on monitoring are unusual as a compliance response but offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building synthetic drift benchmarks and detection algorithms and publishing open harnesses is a reasonably feasible research effort for an AI lab, though it requires dedicated researcher time.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, making logs useful for risk identification and monitoring, which relates to the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate and adapting R&D, but it does not directly state how to meet logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A drift-detection research programme does not by itself make the lab's systems log events or meet the Article 12 mandate, so it would contribute only partially, by exploiting logs for Art. 12(2)(a)-(c) purposes like risk identification and post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into citable, DOI-assigned open science artifacts is an unusual and imaginative twist beyond typical logging responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logs a reproducibility and publication asset and positioning the lab as a reference implementation, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open publication of logs that may contain identities of natural persons and sensitive reference data raises GDPR and security sensitivities, making it somewhat uncommon and potentially offensive to norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing metadata layer within a containerised pipeline is reasonably feasible, but schema generation, versioned repositories, and DOI minting require some real engineering changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by auto-emitting Article 12 records (timestamps, reference databases, matched inputs, verifier identities), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: An automated logging layer would substantially satisfy Article 12 record-keeping, though publishing logs openly with DOIs ignores confidentiality/data protection issues and the Annex III 1(a) scope, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Treating documentation drift as a measurable research phenomenon is an unusual and somewhat imaginative reframing, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning a documentation obligation into a research question, though it does not change what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research on documentation practice offends no norms or laws, though it is somewhat uncommon as a response to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_implementability: Recording documentation-update metadata for selected projects and running an annual analysis requires modest changes and a small research track, which is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem, keeping documentation up to date throughout the system lifetime, which is adjacent to but not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses technical documentation currency (Recital 71) rather than the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it only partially contributes to compliance.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandated logs as a debugging asset with a query layer is a sensible and fairly expected idea, with some interest but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and reuses compliance data for debugging, but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal tooling on compliance logs violates no norms or sensibilities and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Reusing the existing observability stack with a thin GraphQL layer and dashboard templates is a reasonably feasible build requiring modest changes.
evidence_applicability: The tool is built on the mandated Article 12 logs and explicitly serves Article 72 post-market monitoring, but its main stated payoff (faster debugging) is an implied rather than a directly stated part of the compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A query layer helps use logs for post-market monitoring but does not itself ensure the logging capabilities, content, or retention that Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a logging standard with conformance suites is a sensible idea that shows some imagination, though similar open-standard efforts are fairly expected and it is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Publishing an open standard turns compliance into a new offering and positions the lab as a standard-setter, which changes its relationship to compliance, but it still centers on logging and does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source standard-setting under an MIT licence is a legitimate, non-offensive strategy, somewhat uncommon for compliance but violating no norms.
evidence_implementability: Designing a schema, a reference implementation, and conformance test suites, then prototyping on two systems, takes significant effort but is reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate by producing a schema meant to satisfy the requirements, and it tests the schema on an Annex III 1(a) biometric system.
evidence_effectiveness: A well-built standard would help the lab and others meet logging requirements, but it covers only part of the problem, since it does not address the lab's wider R&D adaptation and its adoption and legal sufficiency are uncertain.

evidence_originality: Open-source compliance tooling is a fairly foreseeable response that labs and vendors commonly propose, so it is interesting but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Open-sourcing a logging library turns compliance into a community offering and positions the lab as an infrastructure partner, which changes the lab's relationship to compliance beyond internal logging practice, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing under a permissive licence and publishing guides is a norm-compatible, well-accepted strategy, with only mild unusualness for a lab's proprietary concerns.
evidence_implementability: Building a generic, schema-versioned, pluggable library plus public guides for multiple Annex III categories is a significant effort beyond internal compliance, but it can be done within the existing MLOps stack.
evidence_applicability: The library directly implements Article 12(1)-(3) logging requirements, which is the explicitly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A modular logging library would fulfil the logging mandate if built well, but the proposal does not address the broader Article 12 purposes such as risk-event identification and post-market monitoring, or the lab's R&D adaptation, so it is mainly a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware is a sensible and commonly expected engineering response, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice packaged as a library, leaving the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal compliance tooling is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building an internal library adopted during integration sprints is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some engineering changes but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly implements the Article 12 logging mandate, capturing the exact events named in Article 12(2) and Annex III 1(a), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, standardised hooks would meet the logging requirements across projects, though it does not address wider obligations like documentation or retention, so it solves the main logging problem well but not everything.

evidence_originality: Retrofitting existing monitoring pipelines for compliance logging is the most common and mundane response expected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing monitoring infrastructure to comply is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building on existing event buses and aggregators with about two person-months and no new tooling is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by adding emitters for the specified event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: Extending existing logging infrastructure to emit the Article 12(2) event classes with lifetime retention would largely meet the logging mandate if executed, though it omits Annex III 1(a) specifics and the definition of which events are relevant, making it close to a full solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing compliant logging in shared platform middleware is a common, sensible engineering response that most labs would expect, with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice implemented via existing experiment-tracking tooling, leaving the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building mandatory logging middleware is a common strategy that violates no legal, social, or political norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing tracking service is reasonably feasible, though a single sprint for platform-wide mandatory middleware is optimistic and requires some changes to pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate across the lab's high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer would substantially deliver automatic event recording, but it covers only some Article 12 elements (e.g., it omits human verifier identification and risk-situation event relevance, and the Annex III 1(a) specifics are only partially addressed) and does not address broader documentation or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as reproducibility assets is a somewhat unusual and interesting framing, but experiment tracking is familiar, so it shows only some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Making compliance logs and scientific audit trails the same artefact changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Logging by default with no opt-out for high-risk branches and reusing the logs for scientific audit is a legal, norm-respecting approach that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: Adding hooks to existing MLflow pipelines in one sprint and defining a schema is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though mapping events to Article 12(2) takes some design work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, with the schema mapped to the explicit categories in Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: It would give the lab automatic event recording tied to the Article 12(2) purposes, but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, the system's runtime logging in deployment, or documentation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing ML tracking and data lake infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, pragmatic response that many labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reuses existing experiment-tracking infrastructure with a new compliance schema, which is standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing internal infrastructure for compliance logging is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
