evidence_implementability: It builds on infrastructure the lab already pays for, though it still needs a new schema and instrumentation of each deployed runtime container, so it involves some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing and mapping events to the stated purposes.
evidence_effectiveness: A compliance-event schema fed by runtime container logs mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) would meet much of the logging mandate, but it leaves out Article 12(3) specifics, retention, and integrity, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: It restates the statutory minimum as a logging system, which is a common and expected response with only a mildly useful dashboard check.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging with a dashboard monitor and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing the statutory minimum logging for Annex III 1(a) systems with named reviewers is a common, norm-conforming compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an immutable log and a dashboard tied to biometric pipelines, which is reasonably feasible but needs some engineering changes rather than being trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly maps each of the four Article 12(3) data points to a logging mechanism, addressing the identified mandate to meet the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would fully satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum for those systems, but it does not cover Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other high-risk systems or the R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A standing cross-functional compliance working group with periodic audits is a common, expected organizational response to a regulatory mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a team and audit process but treats compliance as a separate logging and documentation practice, leaving the lab's research approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance working group with joint reporting is a standard, uncontroversial governance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses four existing FTEs with 20% time blocks and no new hires, which requires modest reallocation and is reasonably feasible at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by maintaining Article 12 documentation and auditing logging readiness.
evidence_effectiveness: Template maintenance and pre-advancement logging audits would help the lab meet Article 12 but do not themselves build logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging libraries with CI gates are a standard, expected response and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a library and a test gate but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged beyond building it in earlier.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance logging in the architecture and CI/CD is a common, norm-abiding strategy with no legal or social objections.
evidence_implementability: Building a reusable logging library and adding a CI/CD test gate is reasonably feasible engineering work, but it requires changes across every pipeline and configurable schemas for each Annex III category.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building automatic logging that captures the Article 12(3) elements (period of use, reference database, matched input) and by gating releases on traceability tests.
evidence_effectiveness: A standardized, CI/CD-gated logging library would substantially satisfy the logging mandate if built, though it does not cover the identification of verifying natural persons in detail or Article 12(2) risk-relevant event selection beyond the schemas.

evidence_originality: Logging middleware and project templates are a fairly expected, mundane response to a logging mandate, though the manifest-based scaffolding is a sensible touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (templates/middleware) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging hooks in internal SDK templates is a common, norm-respecting engineering practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring an existing FastAPI serving template with a middleware and YAML config is a modest, reasonably low-cost change using existing infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate without retrofitting, with X (templates) yielding Y (instrumented logging) that is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab meet logging requirements in prototypes by default, but it covers only part of the problem (e.g., Annex III 1(a) fields, retention, lifetime logging for deployed systems, and the non-prototype R&D adaptation) so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a research resource for failure taxonomies is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning compliance-generated logs into a source of scientific discovery that feeds model redesign, which stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Using operational logs for research and publishing open taxonomies is unusual but offends no norms, apart from minor data-protection and confidentiality considerations to handle.
evidence_implementability: It needs only two researchers at about 15 percent time querying logs that already exist, which is a small, non-radical change, though it presumes a log lakehouse is in place.
evidence_applicability: The proposal does not meet the logging mandate itself; it uses logs after the fact to find failures, which only implicitly relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab get research value from compliance logs and supports post-market monitoring, but it does not ensure the logging mandate is met, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Using audit trails as a tender differentiator is an interesting and somewhat unusual framing that shows some imagination, but it is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning compliance into a commercial offering born from the logging obligation, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Treating logging as a marketable trust feature for public-sector clients is somewhat unusual but offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two staff prototyping inside an existing pilot contract, reusing the current verification pipeline and adding a signed journal and dashboard, requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems and the implied problem of compliance cost, so it applies clearly to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet and exceed the Article 12(3) logging requirements for one use case and offset costs, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and does not address the lab's wider logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-CI-test is an interesting and sensible idea but is a fairly expected shift-left move that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (an automated replay-and-audit harness and build gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely intact, though it does shift logging into the prototype acceptance process.
evidence_acceptability: Quality gates in build pipelines are common strategies that offend no norms, though slowing sign-off may draw minor resistance.
evidence_implementability: Building a replay harness with scripted scenarios and per-system checklists requires some engineering effort but uses standard CI/testing practice and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required event types are actually emitted.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch missing event types early and strongly support compliance, but it covers only completeness of event emission, not log retention, appropriateness of the checklist, or Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy-preserving logging is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing of compliance as research output, but it is a fairly foreseeable idea and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research line, IP, and a tender differentiator, but it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging that complies with Article 12 and GDPR, published as research, violates no norms, though a research-track response is somewhat less common than plain compliance.
evidence_implementability: It uses about ten percent of one existing project's compute budget with no new capital expenditure, so it needs only modest changes, although differential-privacy-aware log schemas are nontrivial research.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12 logging mandate, specifically the Annex III 1(a) biometric requirements, and adapts R&D to it, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help satisfy the logging mandate for biometric systems while limiting GDPR exposure, but it is a prototype research track that only partly solves the lab's overall response, and it covers only biometric systems.

evidence_originality: A CI/CD gate that enforces logging-schema compliance is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with only modest novelty in tying it to Article 12 and Annex III 1(a) fields.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (automated pipeline gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated build checks for regulatory compliance are a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: Adding static-analysis and runtime smoke-test stages to an existing CI/CD pipeline requires some changes and effort to define schemas and tests, but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring prototypes meet the Article 12 logging mandate during R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate would catch missing or malformed logging early but does not itself deliver the logging capability, retention, or other record-keeping aspects, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Separating dev and compliance environments with a CI/CD gate is a sensible and somewhat interesting approach, but it resembles standard environment-promotion and compliance-as-code practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (two lanes, automated gating) but still treats compliance as a logging practice added at handoff, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance essentially intact.
evidence_acceptability: The approach is a common DevOps and compliance strategy that violates no norms, though deferring full logging until late may raise mild regulator concern about Article 12's lifetime logging requirement.
evidence_implementability: It requires building interceptors, immutable storage, and a CI/CD check, which are reasonable changes using existing DevOps tooling, though the config-flag switch may hide integration complexity.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate while adapting R&D workflow, with an explicit mechanism (two-lane gating) and outcome (no system ships without tested logging).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the gate would ensure logging architecture is embedded and tested before release, but it covers only Annex III point 1(a) data points and does not address the broader Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or ongoing monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging requirements as a design variable that shapes architecture is interesting and somewhat imaginative, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging constraints a driver of research questions and architecture choices, which is paradigm stretching and approaches addressing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Studying regulatory constraints as research questions and publishing findings offends no norms, though a research-led response to compliance is somewhat less common than standard compliance.
evidence_implementability: A research programme with controlled comparisons on two tasks is feasible with existing lab resources, but it requires building multiple system variants and measurement infrastructure, so it involves some changes and moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the 'adapt its R&D accordingly' part of the stated problem directly, but it does not directly deliver the logging mandate itself, so the link is partly implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would generate knowledge on logging trade-offs that informs compliant design, but it is exploratory and would not by itself implement compliant logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating timestamps and verification events as first-class experimental variables is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but 'logging by design' is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into experimental design itself, stretching the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging into experiment protocols and publishing a handbook violates no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat more unusual than plain compliance tooling.
evidence_implementability: Writing a methodology handbook and building logging in from the start requires some process changes to R&D workflows but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, producing audit-ready telemetry from the start.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help produce compliant logs for research prototypes, but it addresses mainly the R&D-stage logging and does not by itself fully meet Article 12 obligations for deployed high-risk systems (e.g., Annex III specifics, retention, monitoring).

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance documentation as open-access methodology publications is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance output a scientific contribution, which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open publication of training data provenance and validation protocols may raise IP, security, and confidentiality concerns, offending some sensibilities, though publishing research is a normal academic practice.
evidence_implementability: Distilling documentation into peer-reviewed papers per milestone with open code and test harnesses requires significant extra effort, review delays, and legal vetting, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets Recital 71 technical documentation and loosely Article 12, but it addresses documentation rather than the logging mandate, so it solves an implied, related problem (publishing as a byproduct of compliance).
evidence_effectiveness: Publishing methodology papers would not itself implement automatic event logging, so it contributes little to meeting the logging mandate and may even conflict with confidentiality needs.

evidence_originality: Schema validation of logs in CI is a fairly expected, mundane response, though framing the checklist as a compile-time equivalent is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool-like element (CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks of required log fields are a common engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Encoding four fields as a JSON Schema assertion in an existing CI pipeline with a synthetic test is cheap and mostly non-radical, though building a mock biometric end-to-end run takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the paragraph-3 logging minima for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably verify the Article 12(3) minima for point 1(a) systems, but it covers only part of the mandate (not paragraph 1-2 event relevance, retention, or non-1(a) systems), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging wrapper library with OpenTelemetry exporters is a very common engineering response to logging requirements and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a new tool but treats compliance as a logging practice, only making it more efficient and leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared tooling for compliance logging is a standard, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers and one sprint to build a wrapper SDK is low cost and non-radical, though the schema design and capturing the verifier identity and reference database hash add some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, explicitly mapping to 12(3)(a)-(d) fields (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a shared SDK that captures the Article 12(3) fields would meet the core logging mandate, but it covers only the 12(3) minimum fields (which apply to Annex III 1(a) systems) and not the broader 12(2) event relevance or documentation requirements, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log replay for regression testing is known, but applying mandated compliance logs as free regression coverage is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance logging and R&D by turning logs into part of the development and testing workflow, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Replaying logged data for regression testing is a legitimate engineering practice, though it must handle privacy and data-retention constraints on the logged inputs, so it is somewhat uncommon but offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing test infrastructure but requires a replay scheduler, sandboxing, snapshotting of reference databases, and per-risk-class merge gating, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate by extracting value from the logs, which relates to the stated problem though it does not directly meet the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It reuses logs to improve validation but does not itself ensure that the logging mandate of Article 12 is met, so it contributes only partially to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Compliance testing as a release gate is a common, expected response, sensible but mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a test suite and a gate but still treats compliance as logging practice, a standard process within the existing way of working.
evidence_acceptability: Release gates and compliance testing are standard engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a logging-completeness test suite as a release gate fits into existing QA and CI/CD pipelines with moderate scripting effort, so it needs some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements by verifying the specific 12(2)-(3) events.
evidence_effectiveness: Verifying that required log events are captured before release would contribute strongly to meeting the logging mandate, but it does not itself build the logging or cover post-deployment monitoring and retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs for monitoring and research is a sensible but fairly foreseeable idea that shows some imagination without being truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Routing compliance logs into the lab's research and drift-analysis pipelines changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging feed the science, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing logs for internal monitoring is a common strategy, though any personal data in the logs raises minor purpose-limitation questions, so it is largely but not fully norm-neutral.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing analytics infrastructure with one data scientist and a structured event feed, which makes it a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate while also tying into post-market monitoring (Art. 12(2)(b)), though the research-asset framing is a side benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: It would support Article 12 traceability and monitoring goals, but it says nothing about log content, retention, integrity, or the Annex III specifics, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A log schema with encrypted storage and retention policy is the expected, mundane response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance engineering (schema, storage, retention) that leaves the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a compliant log schema with GDPR-aligned retention and legal input is a standard, norm-respecting compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: A four-week prototype by the platform team against an existing pipeline is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some engineering changes but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the four minimum Annex III 1(a) log fields that Article 12(3) mandates, which is part of the stated logging problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the biometric-specific logging minimums, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) traceability for other high-risk systems or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Replay testing of schema migrations is an interesting, somewhat imaginative angle on lifetime retention, but it borrows from standard data-engineering practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/test environment but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Testing log durability is a sensible, uncontroversial engineering and compliance practice that offends no norms, though slightly uncommon in its thoroughness.
evidence_implementability: Building a dedicated test environment with synthetic log replay and auto-generated migration scripts requires some new effort but is reasonably feasible with existing engineering skills.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (logs must remain usable over the system's lifetime per Article 12(1)) which relates to the logging mandate but is not explicitly stated as the core problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure long-term log integrity and parseability but is only a partial solution since it does not decide what events to log or cover the Article 12(2)/(3) content requirements.

evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, automatic structured logging gated in CI would reasonably satisfy the logging mandate across prototypes, though schema content for Annex III specifics and legal adequacy still depend on adapters, so it is strong but not fully complete.

evidence_originality: A legacy-system inventory, gap audit, and prioritized retrofit is a mundane, expected response that experienced evaluators would anticipate from most labs.

evidence_effectiveness: It would help close gaps in legacy systems but is only a partial solution since it ignores new development, log retention, and Annex III specifics and prototypes may not even be high-risk.

evidence_originality: Custodian roles and compliance file templates are a common, expected response that shows little imagination.

evidence_originality: A reusable compliance logging SDK with scaffold integration and smoke tests is a sensible but expected engineering response, not especially imaginative.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a research dataset for drift early-warning is unusual and imaginative, though drift detection from monitoring data is a known field, so it is not wholly unprecedented.

evidence_effectiveness: Studying drift from logs does not by itself satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate (what to record, retention, traceability) and only contributes indirectly, so it is a partial solution at best.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance gates and privacy/security-by-design checkpoints are a familiar and expected response, so this is common and unsurprising.

evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by requiring logging schemas mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) before implementation, so it solves an identified problem tied to the stated one.
evidence_effectiveness: A design-gate for logging schema would substantially ensure logging capability is built in, but it only covers design planning and not actual implementation, verification, or the documentation and other obligations, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Scoping projects against regulatory categories is a common, mundane first step any experienced evaluator would expect.

evidence_acceptability: Design reviews and checklists are standard engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A half-day review, a checklist item in an existing template and a one-page schema document are low-cost, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by defining the events to log, risk situations and post-market monitoring access.
evidence_effectiveness: Front-loading logging design helps meet Article 12 but does not itself ensure the logs satisfy the required content, retention or Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating documentation from experiment-tracker metadata is a fairly common, expected response (docs-as-code, model cards), so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI/CD documentation plugin) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from existing pipeline metadata is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It relies on standard tools (MLflow hooks, Jinja2 templates, CI) and needs only modest changes, though mapping metadata to the required documentation sections takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified related problem, keeping technical documentation current, which comes from the recital and sits next to, but is not the same as, the logging mandate in the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with the Recital 71 technical documentation but does not address Article 12's automatic event logging (risk situations, post-market monitoring, operation monitoring), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mapping logging granularity to intended purpose follows Article 12(2) directly and turning compliance into a publication is a somewhat expected move, though mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a proportionality taxonomy and reference guide) and mildly links compliance to publishable research, but still fundamentally treats compliance as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: A internal research-based guideline to right-size logging is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: One postdoc and two months of compute within an existing grant is a modest, reasonably feasible resource commitment with no radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of deciding how much and what to log under Article 12(2) in a way directly related to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy and checklist would help calibrate logging to intended purpose, contributing to compliance but not itself implementing the logging capability or covering the full mandate.

evidence_originality: Adding a compliance-cost line item to portfolio scoring is a sensible but fairly expected budgeting move, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new scoring process and begins to influence what the lab researches by weighting proposals by compliance cost, modestly changing the R&D-compliance relationship without breaking the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Internal portfolio rubrics with cost accounting are a common governance practice that offends no norms, though discouraging high-risk work due to compliance cost might raise slight concerns.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a cost template and a tweak to quarterly review processes, which are non-radical changes requiring minimal resources.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses how the lab adapts its R&D to the logging mandate by costing Article 12 burden into project prioritisation, which is an implied rather than direct solution to meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It makes compliance costs visible in funding decisions but does not itself deliver logging capability or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a longitudinal research asset for drift studies is an interesting, imaginative reframing that goes beyond typical compliance responses, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving mandated logging into the science itself, which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Retaining production logs for research is a somewhat unusual use that could raise data protection and purpose-limitation concerns, but it does not offend sensibilities if governed properly.
evidence_implementability: Building an ingestion pipeline and long-term retention store is a sprint-scale engineering effort with some changes and costs, but it is reasonably feasible, though the longitudinal research program adds more work.
evidence_applicability: The proposal builds an ingestion pipeline and retention store for lifetime logs, which directly addresses the logging mandate, though it frames the main payoff as research value rather than compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: Persistent lifetime log ingestion and retention would help satisfy Article 12's lifetime recording and support post-market monitoring, but it says nothing on required log contents, Annex III minimums, or traceability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: An open benchmark built from Article 12(3) logs is unusual and imaginative for a response to a logging mandate, though open benchmarks and challenges are familiar, so it is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logging into an open research resource and external partnerships, which changes the relationship between compliance and R&D, but it does not address what the lab researches at a larger level.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing log streams derived from biometric verification, even anonymised, raises GDPR, re-identification and the confidentiality of deployer data, which offends sensibilities somewhat, though the open-science aim is not unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: It requires partner coordination, schema standardisation, anonymisation of biometric logs, open licensing and running a challenge, which is a significant and costly change, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It uses the Article 12(3) fields as its data structure and so relates to the mandate, but the outcome it aims for, field-wide scientific impact, is only an implied benefit relative to the stated compliance decision.
evidence_effectiveness: The benchmark does not itself make the lab's systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate, so at most it contributes to the lab's R&D response and does not solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Centralised log repositories with query templates for auditors are a common, expected response to logging mandates, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A centralised log aggregation dashboard introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving R&D's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal log aggregation and audit-ready querying is a common strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an ingestion layer with standard JSON schemas and a searchable repository is reasonably feasible with existing engineering tools, though it requires some build effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to support Article 12(2) traceability and post-market monitoring objectives through usable logs.
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard organizes and exploits logs for traceability and audits but does not itself ensure that systems automatically record the right events, so it only partially solves the mandate.

evidence_originality: A scaffold generator that bakes Annex III 1(a) logging fields into project templates is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response (compliance-by-template), showing only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (project generator with middleware) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automating mandated logging via templates violates no legal or social norms and is a common, welcome compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a scaffold and middleware for a narrow category is a reasonably feasible internal tooling project requiring some changes to workflow but no radical effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring the four specified Article 12(3) fields are recorded, with the output being part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably satisfy Article 12(3) fields for 1(a) prototypes, but covers only that Annex III category and not general Article 12(1)-(2) event logging across other high-risk systems, nor verifier identity capture beyond the scaffold, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated CI/CD testing of logging requirements is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response, with some interest in replaying synthetic sessions against the log stream.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a compliance gate in the pipeline) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI/CD is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It plugs into the existing pipeline as a test stage, though building the harness and synthetic session replay takes moderate effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that required log events (timestamps, reference DB, match inputs, verifier IDs) are emitted.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that logs fire and catches omissions early, but it does not design the logging itself, cover the Article 12(2) risk and monitoring purposes, or address the full mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance logging wrappers and open-source tooling are a common, expected response, with a mapped-documentation touch that is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and an open-source release but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal logging tool and open-sourcing it under MIT is a common, norm-respecting strategy, though publishing compliance tooling is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team over one quarter, targeting existing PyTorch and JAX pipelines with no architecture changes, is a modest and reasonably feasible effort at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The library directly targets the stated problem by producing structured event logs that satisfy Article 12 paragraphs 1-3, so it does X to get Y, where Y is the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A wrapper emitting schema-validated logs would meet the generic logging requirement if built, but it cannot cover Annex III 1(a)-specific items like the reference database or the identities of verifiers without extra work, and it does not address risk-relevance judgments, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: An open reference implementation for Article 12(3) logging is a sensible and fairly expected response, with some community value but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an open-source toolkit) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release under an EU-compliant license for compliance tooling is a common strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A small engineering group building a minimal toolkit with synthetic data and two external deployers is feasible with modest resources, though it requires partner coordination and some new effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the explicit Article 12(3) logging obligations, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the Annex III 1(a) logging requirements if built, but it covers only the biometric subset and not Article 12(1)-(2) for other high-risk systems or the lab's R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK with CI/CD enforcement gates is a common and expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance engineering practice, with logging treated as a build requirement and no change to how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory engineering standards with build gates are a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an SDK and CI gates requires some platform engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with common tooling.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a shared logging SDK and CI/CD gates to meet the Article 12 logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native logging in every system with build gates would solve the main logging-compliance problem, though it focuses on the Article 12(3) fields, which strictly apply only to Annex III point 1(a) systems, and it does not cover the Article 12(2) event-relevance requirements.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a monitoring product is a fairly recognized idea and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making a regulatory cost a product offering, which is a paradigm stretch, but it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for transparency and customer reporting is a somewhat unusual strategy but offends no norms, though sharing client log data raises some privacy questions that are not addressed.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers prototyping a log-analytics service that feeds an existing portal is a modest and reasonably feasible change, though real-time anomaly detection and exposing client data add some work.
evidence_applicability: The proposal builds on Article 12 logs and Article 72 post-market monitoring, but its main aim is a client-facing product and reputation benefit, so it addresses the logging mandate only by implication.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by making use of logs for monitoring and could aid post-market monitoring, but it does not itself deliver the logging capability or the compliance requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared compliance cost center is a fairly expected organizational response, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new organizational element but still treats compliance as a support/logging function separate from the science, leaving R&D practice unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared-cost services with chargebacks are a common organizational strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-FTE shared service funded by reallocating eight percent of existing overhead and reusing existing servers requires some organizational change but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate (logging stack, documentation, regulator requests) through resourcing.
evidence_effectiveness: It would organize and resource logging and documentation upkeep, but it does not itself specify what to log or ensure the technical logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Integrating compliance documentation into notebook workflows and peer review is a sensible, somewhat unusual idea but resembles existing documentation-as-research practices such as model cards and datasheets.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making regulatory documentation a first-class scientific output weighted equally with statistical validity in peer review, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Researchers may bristle at weighting documentation equal to statistical validity, but the approach violates no laws or norms and is broadly acceptable.
evidence_implementability: Amending protocol templates and review criteria requires some process and cultural change plus added documentation effort, but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Recital 71 documentation and traceability requirements by embedding them in R&D workflows, though it addresses technical documentation more than Article 12's automatic event logging specifically.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding documentation in experimental protocols would help meet record-keeping and documentation obligations but does not itself deliver the automatic logging capability Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Triaging exploratory versus regulated work with scaling logging is a fairly expected response, though the threshold-based boundary adds some interesting thought.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a classification framework and tiered metadata layer, new process elements, but still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Proposing unlogged research could raise regulatory concerns and the compliance officer's scrutiny, but internal scoping with consultation is not totally unacceptable and offends sensibilities only somewhat.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a classification framework and a lightweight metadata layer requires moderate effort and some engineering, which is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab should adapt its R&D to the logging mandate by defining when Article 12 obligations attach, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A scope-classification framework with thresholds and scalable metadata would help the lab apply logging only where needed, but it does not itself deliver Article 12 logging capabilities and rests on a contestable reading that pre-deployment prototypes fall outside scope, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logging in CI is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response that labs would commonly propose, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (CI test harness) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI is a common practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It plugs into the existing CI runner with pytest-style checks and a lightweight log reader, so it is easy and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by catching missing or malformed logs before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate verifying that log fields are populated and queryable helps ensure logging capability but covers only Article 12(3) fields and not the broader mandate (relevance of events, retention, R&D adaptation), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the architecture from the start (privacy/security-by-design style) is a very common, expected response to a logging mandate and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reference spec and a design gate but still treats compliance as standard logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance logging in design processes and gate reviews is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires drafting a specification, adding design-gate reviews and integrating a module into the shared framework, which is reasonably feasible, though it needs some process changes and retrofitting of existing systems.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by defining event schemas, timestamps and retention aligned to Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: A mandatory embedded logging module with defined schemas and a ship-blocking gate would largely satisfy Article 12(1)-(2) but does not address Article 12(3) specifics, post-market monitoring, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code tied to release pipelines is a well-known DevOps/MLOps practice and an expected response, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (documentation engineers, automated regeneration tied to CI/CD) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation and release gates are common engineering strategies that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing CI/CD and experiment-tracking infrastructure, requiring some process changes and a new role per squad, which is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses technical documentation upkeep from Recital 71, which is related to the logging mandate only implicitly, since Article 12 concerns automatic event logs rather than the technical file.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep the technical documentation current but does not implement the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: ML-based anomaly detection on logs is a fairly familiar idea, though framing it as a publishable byproduct of compliance adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (ML anomaly classifier) but still treats compliance as a logging and review practice, with the publishable angle only a minor extension.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal anomaly classifier over logs is a common, legally and socially unobjectionable engineering approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over six months within the existing budget is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though it is a prototype needing scaling later.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (the operational burden of reviewing logs under Article 12(2)(b)) related to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, rather than the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reduce review burden for post-market monitoring but does not itself provide the logging capability or satisfy Article 12 requirements, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: A shared reusable logging layer is a sensible, common engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs, with the reuse-across-grants framing adding only mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice delivered via a shared tool, treating compliance as logging infrastructure without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal logging infrastructure to comply with the regulation is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing Kubernetes observability stack with a small named team over two quarters, which is a reasonably feasible, moderate-cost effort though not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging requirements (do X, get automatic logs that satisfy Art. 12(1)-(3)).
evidence_effectiveness: A uniform logging middleware capturing events, timestamps, reference-database pointers and verification metadata would meet Article 12's logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it does not address other obligations, so it solves the main logging problem if implemented.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code gates in CI are a familiar idea, so this is interesting but not unusual or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged, so it is only slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI are a common engineering strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a schema-validation step to existing Jenkins/GitLab CI pipelines is a modest, non-radical change using standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying required log fields are present.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging completeness at prototype stage but only covers schema checks on replayed sessions, not the full logging capability, retention, or broader obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Productizing compliance tooling is a known commercial move, but framing it as an Article 12-mapped SDK add-on shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's business by turning a compliance obligation into a product offering for customers, which is a new offering born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Packaging logging as a licensed SDK is a normal commercial practice that violates no legal or social norms, though bundling for lock-in is mildly unusual.
evidence_implementability: It requires productizing an internal module with a standard API, documentation, and licensing, which is reasonably feasible but involves real product-team effort and support.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the lab's logging mandate only indirectly, since the main benefit is a commercial offering that helps clients with deployer-side reporting, an implied problem related to the stated one.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not itself ensure the lab's systems meet Article 12 and only helps clients' reporting, so it is a partial contribution at best, though the underlying logging module is presumably built anyway.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware with code-review gates and logging-by-design is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Although framed as 'native' rather than post-hoc, it remains standard compliance-by-design logging practice that treats compliance as a logging engineering matter and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms and is readily accepted by regulators, buyers, and engineers.
evidence_implementability: Adopting a shared middleware library and review gates requires some engineering changes and process adjustments but is reasonably feasible with existing practices.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the specified log elements into systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging middleware with design-phase gates would, if done, meet the Article 12 automatic-logging mandate for high-risk systems, though it focuses on Article 12(3) fields and does not cover R&D adaptation or the broader 12(2) event relevance fully.

evidence_originality: An internal reference implementation and cookbook for regulatory logging is a common, sensible engineering response that shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, packaged as snippets, and leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal compliance tooling and documentation is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a minimal service on the existing stack is a low-cost, non-radical effort with a clear scope.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12(3) mandatory logging fields for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is a named part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A tested reference implementation and cookbook would substantially help teams comply for Annex III 1(a) projects, but it covers only that one category and the generic Article 12(1)-(2) logging duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging SDKs are a standard, expected response to this mandate and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable SDK and design-review step but remains standard compliance and logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Logging by design with design-phase specification reviews is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a reusable SDK and adding a design-review gate requires some engineering effort and process changes but is reasonably feasible within a systems-engineering team.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building automatic event logging covering Article 12(2)(a)-(c) into every high-risk system the lab develops.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a reusable logging layer with schemas agreed at design review would satisfy the core Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not address Annex III-specific minimums or log retention explicitly, so it is largely but not fully complete.

evidence_originality: A 'loggability score' as an architecture-selection criterion is unusual and shows imagination, though it is not entirely surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making loggability a research criterion that shifts which architectures the lab pursues and deploys, weaving compliance into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Benchmarking models on a new axis offends no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual compliance response for a lab.
evidence_implementability: Defining formal loggability criteria and benchmarking several architecture families head-to-head requires a substantial research program with new metrics and significant compute, making it expensive and difficult but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It targets the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate, tied explicitly to Annex III point 1(a) logging elements, though it aims at architecture choice rather than direct logging implementation.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab choose architectures that are easier to log, but it does not itself produce the logging capability, record-keeping, or the Article 12 minimum requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Risk-to-logging-depth mapping is a sensible, somewhat interesting idea but fairly expected as a compliance methodology, showing limited surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It stays within logging practice by developing a methodology for granularity, though it frames compliance as a differentiating asset and publishes norms, mildly stretching the relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Internal standard development with optional publication violates no norms and is a common, legitimate compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: A small team over two sprints prototyping on three existing deployments is a modest, reasonably feasible effort requiring some resource commitment.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets how to meet Article 12(2)'s requirement of logging appropriate to intended purpose, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A scoring framework for logging granularity helps determine proportional logging but does not itself implement logging or cover Article 12(3) minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in CI are a common and expected response, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice folded into existing pipelines, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Release gating via automated tests is a common engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a schema-conformance test step to an existing release pipeline is reasonably feasible with modest changes and standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging requirements through a clear 'do X to get Y' mechanism.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate verifying Annex III 1(a) minimum log fields helps ensure logging compliance but covers only part of the mandate (Art. 12(1)-(2) event relevance, retention, post-market monitoring), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Standardized logging middleware with a design-stage gate is the common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice built into engineering without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building automatic logging into system architecture is a standard, fully lawful compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A logging SDK, integration tests and a review gate require some engineering changes and process additions but are reasonably feasible rather than radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing the specified log contents.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native logging with completeness tests and review gates would largely satisfy Article 12, though it assumes the Annex III 1(a) items apply to all systems and does not address broader documentation or retention.

evidence_originality: Logging middleware with decorators and schema validation is a fairly expected response, with only mild interest in the automatic mapping to Article 12 categories.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance essentially unchanged apart from decoupling it from research velocity.
evidence_acceptability: Reusable logging middleware and append-only stores are common engineering strategies that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A decorator-based library with SQLite/Parquet storage is feasible with ordinary engineering, though the claim of zero code changes and automatic mapping to Article 12 categories requires some real effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate for the lab's prototypes (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If built, automatic structured event capture mapped to Article 12(2) categories would meet the core logging mandate, though it does not address Article 12(3) specifics or log retention and integrity, so it is largely but not fully a solution.

evidence_originality: Adding compliance line items to grant proposal forms and sequencing projects by risk tier is a sensible but fairly expected project-management response, so it is merely interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a planning and scheduling process that links compliance workload to project intake, which modestly changes how R&D is organized but still treats compliance as a workload to be managed rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Risk-based planning and intake checklists are common governance practice that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a form field and a capacity calendar entry to an existing review process needs only small, low-cost changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, resourcing and scheduling for compliance, which relates to the stated problem of how to respond, but it does not directly address how to meet the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Planning and sequencing would help allocate resources but would not itself produce logging capability, so it is only a partial contribution to the solution.

evidence_originality: A benchmark of logging overhead is a reasonable and somewhat unusual idea, but it is a fairly standard research-style response without a surprising twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (a benchmark and leaderboard) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the relationship between R&D and obligations unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open, reproducible benchmarks is a common, norm-compliant research practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires running controlled ablations on open-source models across several model classes plus public release, which is feasible with moderate compute and engineering effort but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: The benchmark measures the overhead of logging under Article 12 but does not itself implement logging, so it only addresses an implied sub-problem (knowing compliance costs) of how the lab should respond.
evidence_effectiveness: Overhead data would inform design choices and help the lab and others, but it does not by itself deliver compliant logging, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance documentation as a research contribution on epistemic transparency is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes how the lab relates research to compliance by treating documentation as a scientific output, which stretches the paradigm, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal workshops and an open peer-reviewed paper are normal, uncontroversial activities, though publishing may raise mild IP concerns.
evidence_implementability: Workshops and drafting templates are low-cost and feasible, though peer-reviewed publication needs some extra effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets Recital 71's technical documentation, which is only implicitly related to the Article 12 logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem rather than the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Documentation templates and rubrics would help with technical documentation, but they do not deliver automatic event logging, so they offer only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Requiring compliance cost lines in project proposals is a common, mundane governance idea with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard administrative compliance-planning step that leaves the lab's research approach and its relationship to compliance largely unchanged, though it does bring logging into the design phase.
evidence_acceptability: Adding budget and planning fields to intake forms is a common governance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs only three added form fields and a committee rule, which is a non-radical, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely unplanned compliance cost and resource allocation, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate but is not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting for logging at the charter stage helps fund and plan compliance but does not itself build the logging capability or satisfy Article 12's technical requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library embedded in the ML toolchain is the obvious, mundane response most labs would give to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with logging added as tooling and no change to how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building a standardized logging module into the development stack is a common, legally sound compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a reusable module, defining an event schema, and making it a mandatory pipeline dependency, which is reasonably feasible but needs some real engineering change.
evidence_applicability: It does X (build native logging covering Article 12 categories) to get Y (compliance with Article 12(1) and 12(2)), which is explicitly the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, automatic logging of all Article 12(2) event categories by default would directly meet the logging mandate, though Article 12(3) specifics and the 'appropriate to purpose' calibration are not addressed in detail.

evidence_originality: A design-review gate with a checklist and compliance sign-off is a common, expected compliance-by-design response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process step and checklist but still treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach basically unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Sprint-zero checklists and compliance sign-off are common strategies that violate no norms, though mandatory sign-off may cause mild friction.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a half-day workshop, a checklist, and a compliance engineer's sign-off, which are small additions to the existing workflow.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by specifying log events tied to the Article 12(2) sub-clauses before building.
evidence_effectiveness: A design-time schema step would help ensure the right events are captured, but it only specifies requirements and does not itself deliver logging capability, retention, or verification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Built-in, tamper-evident, append-only logging at the gateway is the standard response an evaluator would expect and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as logging practice using familiar tools like a microservice and append-only store, with the only shift being log schema as a sprint deliverable, so it preserves the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Building automatic, tamper-evident logging into the architecture is a common, legally aligned compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires redesigning the training and inference stack and adding a logging microservice and append-only store, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes though not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing automatic event logs.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the Article 12(1) automatic-recording mandate, but it does not explicitly cover the Article 12(2) event purposes or the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, or the R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying differential privacy to compliance logs is an interesting and somewhat imaginative combination, but privacy-preserving logging is a known research direction.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (privacy middleware, benchmarks) and links compliance to frontier privacy research, but still treats compliance as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging is a legitimate, somewhat unusual approach that offends no norms, though it risks tension with Article 12's traceability expectations.
evidence_implementability: Building a DP/homomorphic-encryption middleware and benchmarking it across vision, LLM, and retrieval models is a significant, expensive research effort, and it is framed as a research project rather than a committed implementation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (logging may conflict with data protection or privacy) that relates to the logging mandate rather than the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if built, it addresses only the privacy side of logging and does not by itself deliver the required logging events or Article 12(3) content such as input data matches, so it is a partial contribution to the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Standardized logging middleware inherited at scaffold time is a sensible but common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice delivered as infrastructure, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a common engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a thin SDK with pipeline integration is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though a truly project-agnostic schema across diverse systems may need some adjustments.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by embedding automatic event recording in every high-risk system (do X to get logging capability).
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer inherited by all high-risk systems would directly deliver Article 12(1)'s automatic event recording, but it does not address Article 12(2)-(3) content specifics, retention, or R&D adaptation, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Measuring the performance cost of mandated logging is an interesting and somewhat unusual framing, but it is not especially ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a research program that treats compliance as an object of study, shifting the relationship between R&D and compliance somewhat, but it remains an experiment on logging overhead rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Running paired experiments and publishing findings violates no legal or social norms, though logging every forward pass goes beyond what Article 12 requires.
evidence_implementability: Training paired models up to frontier scale with per-forward-pass logging is expensive and difficult, requiring significant compute, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal studies the performance cost of logging, which only loosely relates to how the lab should meet the logging mandate or adapt its R&D, so it is an implied/indirect link at best.
evidence_effectiveness: A research program measuring performance costs would not itself deliver compliant logging or resolve the lab's decision, and it is exploratory research rather than a solution, so it is unlikely to solve the problem.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default instrumentation with CI gates is a well-known DevOps pattern and an expected response, making it interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A default-on SDK is a new tooling element but still treats compliance as logging practice, though 'build property' shifts timing slightly.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in the build pipeline is a sensible, legally aligned and common engineering approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging middleware plus CI gates inside an existing internal MLOps toolkit is a reasonably feasible set of changes, though it requires building and integrating the SDK across prototypes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified fields (timestamps, reference database, input matches).
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably produce the required logs for prototypes, but it covers only Article 12(3) fields for point 1(a) of Annex III, omits the identification of verifying persons (the fourth field, Art. 12(3)(d)), and does not address Article 12(2) event logging, retention, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Checklist-based pre-release compliance audits with sign-off are common and mundane responses to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A release gate with a checklist and sign-off is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gates are a common strategy that violates no norms, though the self-assessment and reputation-shielding framing is slightly self-serving but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: A checklist and sign-off step can be added to an existing release process at low cost with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that logging capabilities satisfy Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-deployment gate verifying logging against Article 12(2) would help ensure compliance but does not itself build the logging capability, address Article 12(3) specifics, or cover ongoing lifetime logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mapping existing documentation artifacts to regulatory text via a gap audit is a sensible and expected response, with little surprising or ingenious about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a documentation bridge protocol but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Interviews, audits of past prototypes, and an internal white paper are ordinary, norm-respecting organizational practices that offend no one.
evidence_implementability: Twelve interviews, five audits, and a year of co-design is a modest, low-cost effort, though it takes some researcher time and coordination.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the stated problem of how to adapt R&D to the record-keeping mandate, but mostly via documentation rather than the automatic logging capability, so the link is somewhat implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would only produce a gap analysis and a documentation protocol, contributing partially but not delivering the automatic event logging Article 12 requires.

evidence_originality: Documentation lifecycle ownership with periodic review is a common, mundane compliance response that most labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working and the R&D-compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Assigning documentation owners, quarterly reviews and tamper-evident storage is a standard, fully norm-compliant governance practice.
evidence_implementability: It requires process setup, role assignment and a document management system, which are reasonably feasible measures with some organizational change but no radical cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the related technical-documentation requirement from the recital, which is implied by but not the same as the logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Up-to-date technical documentation addresses Recital 71 but does not implement the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance testing in CI is a fairly expected, sensible engineering response to a logging mandate, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a CI test gate for logging) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI gates are a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing CI runners and test fixtures, requiring modest work to write per-category fixtures, so it is easy and low-cost.
