evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required log events are emitted.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch missing or malformed logs in prototypes and so contribute substantially, but it checks only format and presence, not whether logs are adequate for risk identification or post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code tests in CI pipelines are a fairly well-known engineering practice, so applying them to Article 12(3) fields is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A CI-integrated conformance test suite is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing gates in CI are a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Schema assertions and behavioural checks wired into an existing pull-request pipeline are reasonably feasible with modest changes to existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified requirement of producing the Article 12(3) minimum log fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify the four minimum Annex III log fields but covers only Article 12(3) for biometric systems, not the general logging mandate in 12(1)-(2), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a longitudinal research corpus on drift and degradation is unusual and imaginative, though the idea of reusing logs for analysis is not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning mandated logs into a scientific dataset and a research program, which stretches the paradigm but does not change what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing aggregated findings from logs raises confidentiality, data protection, and IP concerns that somewhat offend sensibilities, though anonymization and aggregation mitigate them.
evidence_implementability: It requires dedicated senior researchers per project, curation infrastructure, anonymization, and multi-year horizons, which is a significant and costly change though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by repurposing logs, which is an implied benefit related to the stated problem, but it does not directly address meeting the Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It adds value from logs the lab must keep anyway but does not itself ensure compliant logging capabilities, so it contributes only partially to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Framing Article 12 compliance as a research problem of emergent and compound failure mode detection is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, though anomaly detection for monitoring is a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research agenda feeding engineering specifications and standards authorship, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than just adding logging tools.
evidence_acceptability: A research project on detecting risk events to meet Article 12(2)(a) and contribute to standards is a legitimate, norm-compliant approach, though somewhat more research-oriented than the typical compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Building novel detectors, taxonomies per system class, and validation against post-market monitoring is a significant, expensive, uncertain R&D undertaking, and the proposal itself admits no published methodology exists.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified Article 12(2)(a) requirement for recording events relevant to identifying risk situations, which is part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Detecting risk-relevant events would help satisfy Article 12(2)(a) but does not by itself cover the full logging mandate (automatic recording, lifetime logging, Annex III minimums), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Risk-tier inventory and proportional compliance effort is a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice (classification register and budget allocation) that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Risk-tier classification and proportionate logging effort is a standard, legally aligned compliance approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-month internal audit run by the compliance officer feeding a register and budget spreadsheet needs modest effort and no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of deciding how much logging each system needs, which relates to the stated decision on how to meet the logging mandate, though Article 12 applies only to high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Classification and scoping helps allocate logging effort but does not itself build the automatic logging capability Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy-preserving logging architectures are an interesting approach with some imagination in tension between audit logging and data minimisation, but similar ideas are fairly expected from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (architecture variants, design guide, publication) and reframes compliance as a research contribution, but still treats compliance mainly as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-minimizing logging with data-protection counsel and publication of a design guide violates no norms, though differential-privacy logging and publication are somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping three logging variants and benchmarking them is a sizable engineering and research effort requiring some changes and cross-functional work with counsel, but it is reasonably feasible for an AI lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building logging architectures mapped to paragraph 1-3 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would yield a ready-to-deploy logging layer that satisfies Article 12 requirements, but it focuses on biometric Annex III 1(a) and a research prototype may only partially cover all systems and the lab's full compliance response.

evidence_originality: Integrating compliance logging into experimental design is interesting and sensible but is a fairly predictable 'compliance by design' response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science itself so that compliance becomes a by-product of methodology, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding documentation standards in templates and review gates is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It adds checklist items to existing experiment templates and peer-review gates, which is a modest process change at low cost, though it requires some cultural and tooling adjustment.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by making experiment outputs satisfy Article 12 logging (timestamps, reference database identifiers, verifier metadata) as part of the lab's R&D process.
evidence_effectiveness: If adopted, it would produce Article 12-compliant logs for new experiments, but it covers only new high-risk experiments and does not address runtime logging in deployed systems or existing ones, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A public benchmark for logging adequacy is an unusual and imaginative response compared with typical internal logging implementations, but benchmark-as-contribution is a known pattern, so it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance into a research and public-goods offering (a benchmark used by vendors and regulators), which changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release and collaboration with regulators violate no norms, and the approach is somewhat unusual for a compliance response but unoffensive.
evidence_implementability: Building a taxonomy, synthetic and real-system test cases with ground-truth risk events, and a public evaluation suite is a significant, costly effort that needs scarce resources and cross-domain expertise, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified ambiguity of 'appropriate to the intended purpose' in Article 12(2), which relates to how the lab meets the logging mandate, but the benefit is mostly implied and indirect for the lab's own compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not by itself make the lab's own systems log events per Article 12, so it contributes only partially to the mandate by clarifying the standard and enabling audits.

evidence_originality: Instrumenting pipelines with OpenTelemetry-style logging for compliance is a mundane, expected response, with only mild framing about dual use for debugging.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, though it uses some tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logging into existing MLOps pipelines is a common, legally compliant strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Using two existing DevOps engineers and OpenTelemetry-style tooling on current Kubernetes with no new hardware is a low-cost, non-radical change, though a six-month sprint implies some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (embed automatic logging) to get Y (meeting the Article 12 logging mandate), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the logging mandate's technical capture of events like timestamps, reference DBs, matches and verifier identities, but omits retention, traceability scoping, risk-event identification and documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging library with standard schemas is the common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (shared SDK) but treats compliance as a logging engineering practice and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandating a shared internal dependency is a common engineering governance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK and mandating it in architecture reviews requires some engineering effort and coordination but is reasonably feasible for a platform team.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, with schema fields mapped explicitly to paragraph 3 items.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging SDK with standard schemas mandated across all high-risk projects would, if adopted, directly deliver the Article 12 automatic-logging capability, though it leaves out other aspects such as retention, risk-based event selection, and documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing documentation templates and standards is a fairly familiar move in the community, so it is interesting but not imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an open shared template and standard) but still treats compliance as documentation practice, with the lab's R&D unchanged, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open documentation template with a position paper is a somewhat unusual but entirely uncontroversial and norm-respecting strategy.
evidence_implementability: A small working group drafting and publishing a template in one quarter, tested on the lab's own documentation, is a modest, reasonably feasible effort with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses technical documentation (Recital 71 and clarity), which is only implied and adjacent to Article 12's logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation template does not implement automatic event logging, so it would contribute only partially to the logging mandate and would not solve the stated problem.

evidence_originality: A standardized template mapping the four Article 12(3) fields into inference wrappers is the obvious, expected response to the mandate, with little that is imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice with a template and an audit, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standard engineering and audit practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Hard-coding four capture points into existing wrappers and a two-week audit is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the exact Article 12(3) minimum fields for biometric systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum for biometric systems but covers only that point 1(a) Annex III scope and not Article 12(1)-(2) general event logging for other systems or the wider compliance picture, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing the compliance documentation standard as an open public artifact is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance into a public scientific offering and sector-wide framework changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance template is somewhat unusual, and it may raise IP or disclosure concerns, but it offends no norms and is broadly welcome.
evidence_implementability: It needs a small interdisciplinary team, a versioned repository and quarterly peer review, which means some added process but is reasonably feasible with modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation and traceability side of the mandate, which is related to but only implied by the logging requirement of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation template mapping Article 12 records to rationale and protocols would help with traceability and documentation, but it does not itself build the automatic logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging service with config-driven declarations is a common, mundane engineering response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice, with the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a common engineering strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two sprints of one senior engineer integrating into an existing containerised stack is modest, though some changes to pipelines are needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (automated logging platform) to get Y (Article 12 logging compliance), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging service capturing the Article 12(3) data points would meet the core logging mandate if built, though it does not address broader Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or documentation, so it is a strong but arguably partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging via interceptors/middleware is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with modest imagination in the 'invisible to the prototyping loop' framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK middleware) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely automating it, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding automatic logging in tooling is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an SDK-level interceptor/middleware with a time-series store is a reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes to the toolkit, though full automatic Article 12 coverage across all prototypes is nontrivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate (Article 12 logs) for the lab's R&D systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help produce event logs, but it is only a partial solution since Article 12 specifics (risk-relevant events, Annex III biometric minimums, identification of verifying persons) and retention/governance need more than generic metadata capture.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging requirements into design-review gates and checklists is a very common, expected compliance response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It applies standard compliance and logging practice (checklist, audit, designated lead) without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating regulatory logging into design review is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a checklist update, a sixty-day audit and assigned leads, which are some changes but reasonably feasible within existing processes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building Article 12 logging into R&D pipelines.
evidence_effectiveness: If carried out, built-in automatic logging covering timestamps, input references and risk flags would largely satisfy the Article 12 mandate, though it does not address Annex III-specific items like reference databases or verifier identification.

evidence_originality: Differentiable audit trails and log-emitting attention are imaginative and unusual compared with typical logging-infrastructure responses, though auditable and interpretable AI research is a known area.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into the research agenda itself, addressing what the lab researches and introducing new elements.
evidence_acceptability: Reframing compliance as a publishable research programme violates no norms, but it is a somewhat unusual response to a logging mandate and does not offend sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Forming a small group and prototyping log-emitting attention mechanisms and differentiable audit trails is a significant, uncertain research effort that is expensive and difficult, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It aims at the implied problem of producing automatic event logs natively, which relates to the stated logging mandate but is not a direct compliance measure.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if successful, research prototypes of log-emitting architectures would only partially address the need to meet Article 12 logging requirements now, such as the minimum logs and traceability, so it contributes but is not a full solution.

evidence_originality: Internal mock-inspection audits of compliance outputs are a common, expected response, with only mild interest from the scenario-based edge-case scripting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a recurring internal audit process but treats compliance purely as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits are a standard strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Quarterly scripted tests by an existing team are a reasonably feasible measure requiring some process changes but no radical investment.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets verifying that logs meet the Article 12(2) and (3) requirements, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies and catches gaps in logging but does not itself build the logging capability or address R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Structured limitation or model-card-style disclosure is a familiar practice, so applying it to publications is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process (a publication gate and taxonomy) but still treats compliance as documentation practice, and arguably drifts away from logging altogether.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a limitation matrix and a pre-submission review gate to publications is a common, norm-compatible internal policy that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: It requires only a template and a review step, so it is cheap and non-radical, though it needs some process change and co-author buy-in.
evidence_applicability: It addresses Recital 71's documentation of capabilities and limitations, which relates only loosely to the Article 12 logging mandate and to the lab's publications rather than its high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Publication limitation matrices do not create automatic event logging under Article 12 and would not satisfy the logging mandate, so it is unlikely to solve the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Mining compliance logs for drift detection is an interesting, somewhat imaginative reframing, though drift detection and log-based monitoring are known ideas and not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandated logs into a scientific instrument and creating partnerships with deployers, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Collaborative research on operational logs is a reasonable strategy, though biometric log data raises privacy and data-sharing concerns that are manageable but somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: It requires partnerships with two deployed high-risk installations, multi-month data collection, and building and validating detectors, which is a significant but feasible research undertaking with some access and data-sharing hurdles.
evidence_applicability: It directly uses Article 12(2)(a)-(c) logs to serve risk identification and monitoring, but the problem it solves (drift detection) is an implied benefit of the logging mandate rather than the stated compliance problem of meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift detection on mandated logs would help identify risk situations and substantial modifications, but it is a research effort that only partially addresses the broader need to meet the logging mandate itself.

evidence_originality: A per-project event taxonomy workshop tied to Article 12(2) is a sensible but fairly expected compliance-process response, with modest interest but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (Event Taxonomy Sheet and workshop gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A workshop and one-page sheet reviewed at an existing gate is a common governance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a meeting, a one-page template, and a gate review, which are non-radical and low-cost changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement that logs record events relevant to risk, post-market monitoring, and operation, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Defining relevant events helps meet Article 12(2) but does not itself implement automatic logging or the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered or environment-dependent logging is a fairly familiar pattern, though tying it to promotion gating for compliance is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool pattern (mode-switch adapter) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A tiered logging adapter with feature-flag promotion is a conventional engineering approach, though a one-day retention cap on prototypes is slightly unusual and not offensive, since Article 12 applies to high-risk systems in the market.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing feature-flag infrastructure and a single interface with two backends, which is a reasonably feasible measure with modest changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate while preserving R&D iteration speed, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is in place at promotion, but it only partially solves the problem since it doesn't define which events to log, Annex III specifics, or retention/integrity details, and it assumes prototypes are out of scope.

evidence_originality: A log-monitoring dashboard with threshold alerts and periodic reports is a fairly expected tooling response to Article 12 and Article 72, so it is common though sensible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool layer on top of existing logging but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring dashboards and compliance reporting are conventional strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a querying interface and staffing a compliance-ops team, which is some change but reasonably feasible atop existing logging infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to use logs for Article 72 post-market monitoring and Article 26(5) monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Surveillance of logs would support post-market monitoring and operational oversight, but it does not itself implement the logging mandate or cover the full requirement set, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a logging layer on existing experiment tracking is a common, expected response with only a mild reuse-as-asset framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a logging practice with a standard tooling retrofit, though it mentions reuse for reproducibility, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Instrumenting pipelines with automatic logs to meet Article 12 is a standard, legally compliant strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two sprints of one engineer layered on existing experiment-tracking infrastructure is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building automatic event logging with Article 12 minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: Logging at ingestion, inference, and human verification with retention policies would largely meet Article 12, though it assumes the Annex III-specific fields and Article 12(2) event relevance are fully captured and does not address broader documentation, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: A lifetime log-retention cost model is a sensible and somewhat unusual angle focused on budgeting, but it is not especially ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (a cost calculator) and budgeting step, yet still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach largely unchanged, though it does tie compliance to proposal funding.
evidence_acceptability: Internal financial modeling and a required calculator in proposals is a common, uncontroversial management practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: An operations analyst surveying log volumes and building a calculator is a modest, low-cost task requiring only non-radical process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the cost of retaining logs, which relates to the logging mandate but does not itself meet the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps budget for log storage but does not implement logging, define what events are recorded, or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Aligning reproducibility standards with regulatory traceability to eliminate dual documentation is interesting and somewhat imaginative but not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Merging research provenance and compliance documentation into one artifact changes the relationship between R&D practice and compliance, weaving traceability into the science itself.
evidence_acceptability: Unified documentation and reproducibility practices violate no norms and are welcomed by researchers and regulators alike.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight manifest co-designed with compliance engineering requires some process and tooling changes across papers and reports but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the record-keeping/traceability and technical documentation obligations of Recital 71 and Article 12, though it focuses more on documentation than on automatic event logs.
evidence_effectiveness: A unified provenance manifest would help with traceability and documentation but does not itself deliver the automatic runtime event logging Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A logging SDK with schema registry and CI gate is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with only modest imaginative touches like 'compliance-native from day one of prototyping'.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (SDK, schema registry, CI gate) and shifts logging earlier into prototyping, but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Standard engineering tooling and CI gating are common practices that violate no norms, though a hard gate may draw some developer pushback.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers in six weeks with a middleware decorator and CI gate is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though adoption across services and schema design require some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need to technically allow automatic logging of events across the lab's systems, which is the core of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would make automatic event recording systematic and audit-ready, which contributes substantially, but it does not address the specific Article 12(2)-(3) event content, retention, or non-high-risk research scope, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized reusable logging infrastructure enforced through CI/CD is a very common and expected response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared middleware layer is a new tool, but it still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, which fits slightly paradigm stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory shared tooling and CI/CD gates are standard engineering governance that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs two engineers plus a liaison on an existing Kubernetes stack, which is reasonably feasible, though integrating heterogeneous pipelines will require some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 automatic logging requirement across the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, automatic event capture in every system would meet the Article 12 logging mandate, but it does not itself define which events are relevant or cover the Annex III minimums, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance documentation as publishable reproducibility material is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle, though not wholly unprecedented given model cards and datasheets.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and research by weaving documentation into scientific output and turning compliance into a competitive merit signal, stretching the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing documentation alongside releases and aligning it with peer-review norms offends no legal or social sensibilities, though publishing may raise confidentiality concerns, so it is mildly unusual but acceptable.
evidence_implementability: Creating templates and co-authoring documentation at milestones requires some process changes and researcher time but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the documentation requirements in Recital 71 and Annex III 1(a) fields, which relate to the mandate, but it barely addresses the automatic logging requirement of Article 12 itself, so it solves an implied, related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Templated documentation would help satisfy the technical-documentation side of compliance but would not by itself deliver automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Versioned git-based documentation is somewhat interesting and the publication angle is a modest twist, but docs-as-code is a familiar idea and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process (versioned living documentation tied to retraining plus a publication) but still treats compliance as documentation/record-keeping practice, not changing how R&D relates to obligations much.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date documentation and publishing methodological findings violates no legal or social norms, though publication needs care around confidentiality.
evidence_implementability: A pilot on one model line using existing git tooling is reasonably feasible, though tying to retraining cycles and peer-reviewed publication requires some process changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied related problem (documentation upkeep over the lifetime) rather than the identified Article 12 logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses the technical documentation lifetime requirement in Recital 71 but not the automatic event logging mandate of Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking time-series, columnar, and object-storage options for log retention is a mundane, expected engineering response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A short internal engineering evaluation of storage stacks to meet a legal logging requirement is a common strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week benchmarking spike of off-the-shelf storage options is cheap and easy, requiring no radical change.
evidence_applicability: The spike directly targets building durable, retrievable logging infrastructure for Article 12(1) and Article 72 post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It only produces a prototype and a decision memo, so it helps de-risk architecture choice but is a partial contribution that leaves content of logs, Article 12(2)-(3) coverage, and production implementation unsolved.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a marketable monitoring offering is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising since compliance-tech products are a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by redirecting research teams to build monitoring products born from logging obligations, though it does not rethink what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reallocating research toward compliance-monitoring products and commercializing it violates no norms and is a somewhat uncommon but inoffensive business strategy.
evidence_implementability: Repurposing two existing research teams to build anomaly-detection tooling is reasonably feasible, though productizing and gathering enough labelled log data requires some real changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (how to use and recoup cost from logs and support post-market monitoring) related to the stated problem of responding to the logging mandate, rather than the logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself ensure the Article 12 logging mandate is met; it builds on logs and helps with Article 72 reporting and offsets cost, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying differential privacy to compliance logs is an interesting and somewhat imaginative combination that is unusual among likely lab responses, but not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (DP wrappers, benchmarks) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though it also opens a research publication track.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging with open benchmarks is a socially and legally welcome approach, though noising mandated logs may raise some regulatory questions, so it is somewhat unusual but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: Designing local differential privacy wrappers and benchmarks needs substantial research effort and expertise, and the tension between DP noise and logs that must be accurate for traceability makes it difficult though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It targets an implied problem, the privacy tension created by Article 12(3) logging, which relates to but is not directly the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses only the biometric Annex III 1(a) logging subset and the privacy-leakage side effect, so it contributes to meeting the logging mandate but is not a full solution.

evidence_originality: A reference implementation with logging emitted at decision points is a sensible, expected approach, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as logging practice, adding a structured event-bus architecture and a compliance test suite as new tools but leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a compliant biometric system with the mandated logs is a standard, norm-respecting response to the regulation.
evidence_implementability: Shipping a working biometric system with an event bus, human-review UI and a compliance suite requires substantial engineering effort, but it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the specific logging mandate in Article 12(3)(a)-(d).
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would implement the Article 12(3) logging fields for one Annex III category, but it covers only that category and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) mandate across the lab's systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A living technical dossier with owners is the obvious, common response to Recital 71 and offers little that is imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice, though it adds a few process elements, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date technical documentation is a standard, expected compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning documentation owners and a versioned repository with release-linked triggers is a modest process addition using existing tooling, though keeping it continuously current takes ongoing effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation, which is related to the logging mandate via Recital 71 but is not the logging requirement itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with traceability and compliance evidence but does not itself implement automatic event logging under Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design and logging SDKs are a common, expected response, so it is sensible but mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A log-first checklist and SDK are new tools but still treat compliance as logging practice, with the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Designing logging in from the start is a common, regulator-friendly strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A log-first architecture checklist and an internal SDK are reasonably feasible measures requiring some engineering effort and process changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X: design-time logging, to get Y: Article 12 compliance).
evidence_effectiveness: Built-in logging directly delivers the Article 12 capability and would substantially meet the logging mandate, though it does not address broader documentation or the Annex III-specific content beyond SDK fields, so it is mostly but not fully complete.

evidence_originality: Treating logs as primary experimental data and part of the scientific protocol is an interesting reframing, but embedding logging in the pipeline is a fairly expected response, so it is unusual without being truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science itself (logging as part of the experimental protocol), which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in research workflows is a legitimate, somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no norms, though researchers may resist added protocol burden.
evidence_implementability: A shared harness logger and a canonical taxonomy across teams require some pipeline changes and cross-team coordination, but are reasonably feasible with lightweight tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D by building automatic event recording into prototypes and the shared harness.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to meeting Article 12 automatic recording, but it is vague on the specific required events (risk situations, post-market monitoring, Annex III minimum fields) and on deployed systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code checks in CI are a fairly familiar idea, though mapping logged fields to specific regulatory sub-paragraphs adds a little interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool and registry but still treats compliance as logging practice, with no change to the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in code review are a normal engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a custom registry and PR-diff tooling, which is some work, but it is reasonably feasible with existing CI infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: The tool directly targets how an R&D lab can keep its logging compliant with Article 12(2) while it changes architectures and pipelines, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch logging regressions at code-review time, but it does not itself build the logging or cover Article 12(3) or the other obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Assigning audit IDs to human verifiers is an obvious, mundane response that experienced evaluators would readily expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with HR and legal procedures added and no change to how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Recording verifier identity for accountability is a standard, legally grounded practice, and the proposal explicitly handles data-protection concerns, so it violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Enrolling verifiers with unique audit IDs and linking their actions to logged events needs a modest workflow and some system integration, which amounts to reasonably feasible changes rather than a radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified, explicit logging requirement (verifier identification under Art. 12(3)(d)), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It fully addresses only Article 12(3)(d) for one Annex III category, so it is a partial contribution to the broader logging mandate and not a full solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized compliance budget line is a fairly familiar administrative move, though framing it as converting variable costs to predictable fixed costs is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a budgeting restructure that treats compliance as an overhead cost and leaves the lab's research and logging practice essentially unchanged, though it does introduce a new funding process.
evidence_acceptability: Central cost pooling is a common, uncontroversial budgeting strategy that violates no norms, though PIs might mildly grumble about the eight per cent top-slice.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing staff and data-centre contracts with only a budget reallocation, making it easy and low cost to implement.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (funding the recurring costs of logging and documentation) that relates to, but is not directly, the mandate to meet logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Pooling funding for documentation and log retention helps pay for compliance but does not itself create logging capability or meet Article 12's technical requirements, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design from the first sprint is a common, expected response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from AI labs, and it is sensible but unsurprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standard logging-by-design middleware practice but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, at most slightly stretching the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into engineering architecture is a common, legally compliant, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Thin middleware with standard event schemas wired in at architecture review is cheap and feasible, requiring only modest process changes to prototyping workflows.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building automatic event logging into R&D from the start (do X to get logging compliance).
evidence_effectiveness: A scaffold-level logging layer mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) would give high-risk prototypes the automatic event recording the mandate requires, but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or technical documentation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI/CD gate that lints log schemas and replays synthetic calls is a sensible, fairly expected 'shift-left compliance' response, with only mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (linter, replay test, CI gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI/CD are a common engineering strategy that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a schema linter and a replay test in an existing CI pipeline requires some changes but is reasonably feasible with modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying log completeness before production.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably verify that required log events are emitted and queryable, but it does not itself define which events are relevant or address retention and other duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using zero-knowledge proofs for log verification and framing compliance as a trust differentiator is unusual and shows imagination, though privacy-preserving logging is a known research direction.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by redirecting research toward compliance-driven techniques and turning the obligation into a product offering with new academic partners.
evidence_acceptability: Funding doctoral research and academic partnerships and pursuing privacy-preserving compliance is legally and socially unobjectionable, though somewhat unusual as a response to a logging mandate.
evidence_implementability: Funding two PhD positions and a university collaboration on zero-knowledge proof verification of logs is a significant, expensive, long-horizon research commitment that is difficult but not impossible, and it is not a quick path to compliance.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem related to the mandate, namely recording Article 12 events without exposing sensitive biometric data, rather than the direct logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Privacy-preserving logging would help in sensitive Annex III 1(a) contexts but is only a partial solution, since it does not cover the core logging mandate across systems and the research may not deliver in time.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and automated model-card generation are fairly common, so the idea is sensible but not very imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (automated doc generation in CI/CD) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging-style practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated, continuously updated technical documentation is a conventional, regulator-friendly compliance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Embedding metadata extraction into CI/CD with a dedicated engineer requires some tooling and process changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the Recital 71 documentation-currency requirement, which is related to but not the Article 12 logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping documentation current helps with compliance and post-market monitoring but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable shared logging infrastructure is a sensible, commonly expected platform-engineering response, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging library is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal platform library is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers for one quarter wrapping existing registry and pipeline tools is a modest, reasonably feasible investment, though integrating into every system takes some change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate across the lab's high-risk systems (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide consistent automatic event logging across systems, but it does not itself define which events satisfy Article 12(2) or the Annex III minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared, reusable logging library across projects is the obvious, standard engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice, implemented as infrastructure, and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance tooling with PI-led rollout is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers and a one-quarter integration across all active projects requires some real changes and retrofitting effort, but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It does X (build shared logging middleware with the Article 12(3) minimums) to get Y (compliant automatic event recording), which is an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable middleware implementing the Article 12 logging capabilities would directly satisfy the logging mandate, but it covers mainly the technical logging and not documentation or the Article 12(2) event-relevance judgments, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK is the standard, expected response to a logging mandate, so it is common and mundane despite being sensible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tooling element but still treats compliance as ordinary logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal logging middleware package is a common, norm-abiding engineering response to a logging mandate that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a versioned schema and interceptor library shipped as an internal package requires some engineering effort but is reasonably feasible, not trivial since schemas for Article 12 vary by system.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate with automatic structured logs for lab prototypes while preserving R&D speed.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would provide automatic event logging for prototypes, helping meet Article 12 but only partially since it does not address high-risk classification, Annex III specifics, retention, or deployer monitoring needs.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a compliance logging library is a fairly expected response that is interesting for its publication and funding angle but not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and a publication framing but still treats compliance as logging practice, so it is only slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance tool under a permissive licence is a somewhat uncommon but entirely inoffensive strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers can prototype a wrapper library in one quarter using existing CI/CD, which is a reasonably feasible, modest change though maintaining it and handling retention adds some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces compliant logs, which is an identified part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A logging wrapper would meet the Article 12(2) event-recording mandate for inference calls but does not cover Article 12(3) minimums, model-internal events, or the R&D adaptation side, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Risk-based prioritization of compliance work by time-to-market is a mundane, expected response with little imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice and only reshuffles resources, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Portfolio triage by deployment exposure is a common management strategy that offends no norms, though lightweight stubs for exploratory work are mildly risky.
evidence_implementability: A one-day board and a 15% FTE reallocation are administrative changes within the lab's control, feasible with some disruption to other projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to allocate engineering resources to meet the Article 12 logging mandate, which is an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Prioritizing logging engineering for near-deployment projects helps meet the mandate where it bites but defers coverage and leaves details of what to log unaddressed, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared internal logging library is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though centralization adds a small new element.
evidence_acceptability: Mandated internal tooling with code-review enforcement is a conventional strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small platform team maintaining a versioned SDK with integration in sprint one is reasonably feasible with moderate effort and some process changes.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly automates capture of the Article 12(3) log fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) logging requirements across projects, but it covers only Article 12(3) fields and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) traceability or lab R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A pluggable logging/observability middleware is a standard engineering response that evaluators would expect from most labs, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (a platform logging library) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging infrastructure is a conventional, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building adapters for PyTorch, TF and custom C++ plus an append-only store is a reasonably feasible engineering effort with some changes, though not trivial or low-cost.
evidence_applicability: It explicitly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by doing X (middleware) to get Y (automatic event recording per Article 12(2)), which is directly part of the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable auto-capture layer directly delivers the Article 12(1) automatic recording and covers the 12(2) event purposes, but it does not by itself define which events matter, retention, or the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design with architecture review gates and merge blocking is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a review role and merge-blocking gate but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-by-design with review gates is a conventional strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a logging module, a designated reviewer and a merge check is a modest process change using standard engineering tooling, though it requires some cross-team adaptation of prototypes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly does X (embed logging with Article 12(3) fields) to get Y (compliant automatic event recording), which is an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Building a logging module into every prototype with a gatekeeping reviewer would directly deliver the Article 12 logging capability, but it covers only the logging mandate (and applies Article 12(3) to all systems though it only binds Annex III 1(a)), and it omits documentation, retention and the other Article 12(2) event purposes, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Design-stage compliance review (shift-left, privacy-by-design style) is a common and mundane approach with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process step but still treats compliance as logging practice scoped by a memo, leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged, though it does shift compliance earlier into design.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance review gate at project intake is a common governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It slots into the existing quarterly review calendar with a two-day review and a one-page memo, so it is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by identifying which events must be logged in new high-risk projects.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps scope logging requirements for new projects but does not implement logging, cover existing systems, or ensure the technical capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-default templates with CI enforcement are a fairly common and expected engineering response to a logging mandate, though the mapping to Article 12(2) is a sensible touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a scaffold template, CI gate, workshop) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only shifting it earlier in the workflow rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Internal engineering standards, CI checks and training workshops are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a template, adding a CI check, and running a two-day workshop is a modest, reasonably low-cost change within existing monorepo infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring high-risk prototypes emit event logs from the start.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably ensure logging capability exists in prototypes but covers only part of the problem, leaving log content adequacy, retention, and Annex III specifics and deployment-time requirements unaddressed.

evidence_originality: Append-only cryptographically chained logs and volume benchmarking are standard engineering practice, though the cost-curve framing is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It uses familiar tools such as time-series stores and hash chaining and treats compliance purely as logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable logs and feasibility prototyping are common strategies that violate no norms, though access controls for verifier identities touch ordinary privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: A bounded prototype using off-the-shelf storage technology with small benchmark scales is readily feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by prototyping storage and retrieval of the specific Annex III 1(a) records Article 12(3) requires, though as a feasibility prototype rather than the full compliance solution.
evidence_effectiveness: A bounded prototype and cost curve would only contribute to meeting the lifetime logging obligation, as it de-risks retention but does not itself deliver compliant production logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered hot/cold log archiving is a common, mundane approach, with only mild tagging by Article 12 purposes.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Tiered retention and archival is a common, uncontroversial data-management practice that violates no norms and is agreed with legal counsel.
evidence_implementability: Tiered storage with lifecycle policies built on existing HPC file-management tools is a routine, low-cost extension of current infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It solves an identified, directly related sub-problem (retaining logs over system lifetime affordably) within the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses only the storage-cost aspect of lifetime retention and does not itself ensure logs capture the required events or meet Article 12(2)/(3) content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralised log aggregation with access controls is a common, expected response to logging mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance infrastructure approach that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised audit logging is a conventional strategy that violates no norms, though retention and access across projects may need data-protection care.
evidence_implementability: Two sprints per quarter with existing engineering and a Legal check is a reasonably feasible, moderately scoped effort using established technology.
evidence_applicability: The platform directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by aggregating, retaining, and making logs auditable across high-risk deployments.
evidence_effectiveness: Centralised tamper-evident retention would substantially support Article 12 traceability and audit, but it does not itself ensure the systems log the right events (Art. 12(2)/(3) content), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK built in from the start is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that leaves the lab's research approach and its relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized internal logging libraries and compliance-by-design are common, uncontroversial engineering strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK and enforcing it via code review requires some engineering effort and process change but is reasonably feasible for a lab with a platform team.
evidence_applicability: The idea directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the required log fields into every system.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logging SDK enforced via code review would, if implemented, directly deliver the automatic event recording Article 12 requires, though it covers logging only and not wider documentation or post-market duties, and it conflates Article 12(3) Annex III 1(a) items with all systems.

evidence_originality: Reusing mandated logs as a longitudinal drift research dataset is an unusual and interesting angle that shows some imagination, though drift monitoring itself is familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning logging obligations into a research resource, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking since it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymised logs for internal research is a reasonable strategy, though data-protection and purpose-limitation concerns may raise some questions, it offends no major norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a data-governance and anonymisation pipeline plus analytics, which means some real changes but is reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to benefit from the logging mandate, which relates to the stated problem but not directly to meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met (what events to log, retention, traceability); it only adds value on top of compliance, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Publishing open documentation templates for transparency is a fairly familiar open-science idea (model cards, datasheets), though framing regulatory documentation as an open reproducible-science asset shows slight imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance documentation into an open-science asset and thought-leadership offering, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance somewhat, stretching the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Open documentation is broadly acceptable, though publishing documentation of high-risk systems may raise some confidentiality and IP concerns, it is not offensive to norms.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight metadata schema and generation scripts are reasonably feasible with some changes to workflow and effort for public maintenance.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (documentation quality and traceability under recital 71) that relates to, but is not directly, the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation template and tooling would help with record-keeping and technical documentation comprehensibility, but it does not itself implement automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalising the legal notion of substantial modification as a change-detection problem distinguished from benign drift is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle that is unusual among logging responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (detectors, benchmark corpus) and ties compliance to the lab's research agenda and regulators, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance beyond plain logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Research on detecting substantial modification and sharing benchmarks with regulators violates no norms and fits compliance practice, though it is somewhat uncommon for a lab to take it on.
evidence_implementability: Building a labelled corpus of model updates with ground truth and training detectors in weight and behaviour space is difficult, because the legal threshold is undefined and ground-truth labels are hard to establish, though it is feasible with significant effort.
evidence_applicability: It targets the Article 12(2)(a) requirement to log events identifying substantial modification, but the intervention is a research study on detecting modification rather than directly meeting the logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A reliable detector of substantial modification would help the lab's logging flag relevant events, but it covers only one part of Article 12 and does not provide the general logging capability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Productizing compliance logging as an SDK for partners is a somewhat unusual and interesting commercial angle, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning a compliance cost into a product offering and new partner relationships, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Offering compliance tooling to deployers violates no norms, though marketing it as lock-in and a differentiator is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Building an API-based recorder, SDK and mapping documentation requires a dedicated sprint track, product support and legal mapping, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial set of changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly builds an automatic event-recording logging module, which addresses the Article 12 logging mandate, and extends it to deployers' Article 26 obligations.
evidence_effectiveness: A configurable event recorder built alongside the core systems would substantially deliver Article 12 logging, but it does not specify which events are logged (risk situations, post-market monitoring, Annex III minimums), so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing regulatory documentation as open science and peer-reviewed case studies is unusual and shows some imagination, though it is not wholly unprecedented given model cards and datasheets.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning documentation obligations into publishable scientific output and new collaborations, which stretches the paradigm but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing anonymised documentation where IP permits is a somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no norms, though confidentiality and security concerns need care.
evidence_implementability: Writing up documentation to a higher standard and submitting anonymised case studies is reasonably feasible, though it needs extra effort and IP and legal review.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to treat documentation obligations and gain value from them, which relates to the stated problem only loosely and not to logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not address the Article 12 logging mandate (automatic event recording) and only touches on the documentation in Recital 71, so at best it contributes marginally to compliance.

evidence_originality: A shared canonical logging schema is a common, expected response to Article 12, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standardized schema as an internal spec but treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal standardization and open-source specs are common practice and violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small working group drafting a YAML spec and linking it to onboarding documentation is low-cost and non-radical to implement.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by defining the fields Article 12 requires for consistent logging across projects.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared schema covering the Article 12(2)-(3) fields would help with the logging mandate but is only a partial solution since it does not address the other logging requirements or how R&D adapts.

evidence_originality: Reusable internal reference architectures and standardised compliance templates are a common, expected response, with no surprising element.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance engineering that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal standard architectures with mandatory adoption are a common, uncontroversial engineering governance strategy.
evidence_implementability: A small team can draft it in two sprints and validate it on two projects using ordinary engineering processes, so it is a modest, reasonably feasible change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate, with event schemas, retention, and Annex III minimum fields, to get conformant logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable Article 12 logging reference architecture would, if adopted, meet the logging mandate across projects, but it covers only logging design and not wider compliance or R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing model architectures whose attention or gating emit schema-aligned event records as native outputs is an uncommon and imaginative reframing of logging, well beyond the expected bolt-on logging responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making loggability an architectural research constraint and turning the regulation into a frontier research question about what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance into model design violates no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual strategy for meeting a logging mandate.
evidence_implementability: Developing new transformer variants with a dedicated group and benchmarking them is a significant, expensive, uncertain research effort, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate (automatic event recording) while adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: If achievable it would deliver traceability by construction, but the benefits of interpretability and generalization are speculative and it may not capture all Article 12 requirements such as the Annex III items, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Studying the performance cost of compliance logging is an interesting and sensible idea but a fairly predictable response, showing modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a benchmark suite and research framing but still treats compliance as logging practice, only turning it into a publishable study.
evidence_acceptability: Benchmarking logging overhead and publishing results is a common, legitimate research practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting existing models with logging layers and running A/B benchmarks at three scales requires some engineering and compute but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (understanding performance costs of logging) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Measuring overhead informs design trade-offs but does not itself deliver the logging capability, so it only partially contributes to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A schema-contract CI gate is a sensible but fairly conventional application of existing data-contract practice, with mild imagination in tying it to lifetime traceability.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (contract and gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D works.
evidence_acceptability: Pipeline gating with sign-off exceptions is a normal engineering governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A versioned schema registry, CI emission of schemas, and a pipeline gate are standard DevOps tooling requiring some changes but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of maintaining lifetime logging continuity under Article 12(1) across prototype-to-production handoff.
evidence_effectiveness: It prevents schema drift between environments but does not ensure the logs capture the right events for Article 12(2) or 12(3), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal audits and mock-regulator drills are common and mundane responses to a compliance mandate, with only slight flavor from the random log-window sampling.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged and treats compliance as logging verification.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits and mock regulator drills are common, well-accepted practice that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Quarterly sampling and table-top exercises require some staff time and cross-team coordination but only modest, reasonably feasible changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets verifying that logging meets Article 12(3) minimum fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
