evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance logging is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a standard logging SDK into existing serving infrastructure is reasonably feasible with some engineering changes and moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (do X, get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer capturing the Article 12(1)-(3) events would, if built, deliver the core logging mandate, though it does not address documentation, post-market monitoring processes, or R&D adaptation beyond logging.

evidence_originality: Merging reproducibility provenance with regulatory logging is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Weaving the compliance log fields into the research workflow and publications changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, stretching the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging metadata and provenance in research runs is a sensible, norm-compliant approach that offends no sensibilities, though slightly less common than plain compliance logging.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing eval framework over two sprints with a senior researcher is a modest, reasonably feasible change requiring some engineering but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces the Article 12(3) minimum log fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, though only for research/benchmark runs rather than deployed systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet logging requirements for the lab's evaluation runs but does not cover logging in deployed high-risk systems or Article 12(2) event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left logging design in templates and checklists is a fairly common, expected response to such a mandate, though sensible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a design-review gate and schema deliverables but still treats compliance as logging practice, though shifting it earlier into design, so it introduces new process elements without changing the R&D-compliance relationship fundamentally.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review gate, updated checklists and a workshop are common practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires only updating existing templates, adding a gate, and a half-day workshop, which are non-radical, low-cost changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by avoiding late discovery that required log fields cannot be produced.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging capability is designed in early, but it does not itself implement logging, retention, or cover post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing logging in early (privacy/compliance by design) is a common, expected response, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a logging-specification template and design-review checkpoint, a new process element, but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a template to an existing proposal form and review step violates no norms and is a common governance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing governance board and proposal form with a one-page template and no new procurement, so it is easy and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by requiring logging specs for new high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging capability is designed in for new systems, but it does not cover existing systems, actual log content requirements, or ongoing operation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a mandatory shared logging layer into all systems is the most obvious and common response to Article 12, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging microservice with schema templates is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandating a logging component as a build criterion is a common, uncontroversial engineering governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging microservice with schema templates is a routine engineering effort, though integrating it across all training and inference pipelines requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: The idea directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building automatic event recording into every high-risk system.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would largely satisfy the technical logging requirement, but it covers only the logging part and not documentation or the lab's R&D adaptation, and it says little on event relevance for risk or post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated, versioned documentation generated from CI/CD is a sensible and fairly expected response by AI labs, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (documentation-as-code tied to CI/CD) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation and record retention is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a documentation-as-code store with CI/CD hooks needs some engineering changes but uses existing DevOps practice and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the technical documentation requirement from Recital 71 and substantial modification tracking, which is related to but not the Article 12 event-logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with documentation and audit readiness but does not provide the automatic event logging Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code gating in CI is a well-known pattern and is what an experienced evaluator would expect, so it is somewhat mundane though sensible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a build gate and conformance report) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves R&D itself unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding compliance gates to CI/CD is a common, legitimate engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends the existing CI pipeline with a lint step and a checklist, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes, though defining a schema and parsing diverse logging configs takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by enforcing required event types before EU deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging capability exists in prototypes, but a schema lint cannot verify runtime logging, retention, or Annex III-specific content, so it is only a partial solution to the full mandate.

evidence_originality: Dashboards and alerting on logs are a common, expected response to a logging mandate, with only the mapping of alerts to specific articles adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A monitoring dashboard is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, which fits level 2 at most, though it is largely standard practice.
evidence_acceptability: Monitoring dashboards with legal-aligned alerts are a common strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers and one analyst building on existing observability infrastructure in two sprints is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by using Article 12 logs to meet post-market monitoring (Article 72) and human-verification obligations, though it presumes logging exists and is aimed at deployed systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with monitoring and compliance evidence but does not itself implement the logging mandate or adapt R&D, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered logging with hash-chained provenance is a sensible, somewhat imaginative adaptation, but differentiating logging by lifecycle stage is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a governance protocol and hashed summaries but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only separating R&D from deployed systems, without changing how the science is done.
evidence_acceptability: Reducing log fidelity for internal R&D might be questioned by regulators, but the approach is a common risk-based governance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A governance board drafting a policy, plus legal validation and hash-chained summaries, requires some process changes but is reasonably feasible with existing resources.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab should meet the Article 12 logging mandate while adapting R&D, via a two-tier log policy tied to the deployment transition.
evidence_effectiveness: A tiered policy with legal validation before deployment would help close gaps for high-risk systems, but it is only a partial solution because it leaves open whether reduced-fidelity R&D logs satisfy the obligations and it covers neither technical logging capability nor the Article 12(2) event requirements.

evidence_originality: Mapping existing systems to regulatory requirements via a gap matrix is a common, mundane compliance step.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance gap analysis that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gap analysis is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-week inventory with one-page submissions and a gap matrix is a low-cost, non-radical internal exercise using existing staff.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by determining which required fields are already covered and which are not.
evidence_effectiveness: A gap audit identifies what logging exists versus what is missing but does not itself create the logging, so it is a helpful partial step toward meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Compliance registers with named owners and periodic internal audits are common, mundane responses to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance inventory and audit practice that treats compliance as a governance process and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal inventories, ownership assignment and audit gates are common strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-week inventory and quarterly audits require modest process additions and staff time, but no radical changes or heavy expense.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the need to determine which Article 12 logging obligations apply and to verify log schemas, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A register, classification and audit cadence would help the lab identify and verify Article 12 obligations, but it does not itself build logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a shared telemetry and logging module to satisfy Article 12 is the most common, expected response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is a standard compliance approach of building a shared logging layer into systems, treating compliance purely as logging practice with no change to how the lab works.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding mandated logging violates no norms or sensibilities and is a conventional compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging layer is a reasonably feasible engineering measure, though integrating it across all pipelines and validating each model variant requires some changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the automatic event recording required by Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native logging capturing the Article 12 event categories would meet the core logging mandate, though it does not cover retention, documentation, or R&D adaptation beyond logging.

evidence_originality: Privacy-vs-logging tension is a fairly expected concern, though the MPC and tiered-retention angle plus positioning as a reference voice shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (cryptographic, MPC, differential privacy layers) and a research track that turns compliance into publications and reputation, partly changing the R&D-compliance relationship, but it still centers on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Investing in privacy-preserving compliance research and publishing findings violates no norms and is a sensible strategy.
evidence_implementability: Staffing two or three PhD/postdoc teams on cryptographic prototyping is expensive and uncertain, a significant commitment though not impossible, and it is closer to exploratory research than a committed implementation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the GDPR tension implied by Article 12 logging of input data and personal identities, which is an implied problem related to meeting the logging mandate rather than the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Privacy-preserving logging would help the lab log compliantly, but it is exploratory research, does not itself deliver the logging capability, and is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging by design into a standard template is a very common, expected response to this mandate, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable middleware logging module built into development templates is a new tool but still treats compliance as standard logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance logging in engineering standards violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: A middleware layer and template require some platform engineering effort and changes across projects, but are reasonably feasible with standard engineering.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by satisfying Article 12(3) minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would largely solve the logging mandate for high-risk systems, though it covers mainly Article 12(3) items and not broader traceability or R&D adaptation fully, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance cost line items in project approval are a fairly mundane governance move, with only the pairing of failing projects to share infrastructure adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template and review step and pairs projects to share infrastructure, which slightly changes how R&D selection relates to compliance cost but still mostly treats compliance as a logging overhead to be budgeted.
evidence_acceptability: Budget gates in funding review are a common governance practice that violates no norms, though deferring projects may cause some friction.
evidence_implementability: It adds a two-page template to the existing proposal form and a quarterly review, which is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: The idea addresses the cost of meeting Article 12 logging by budgeting for it at project approval, which is an implied problem (funding compliance) related to the stated decision, not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps avoid mid-project budget surprises but does not itself deliver logging capability or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Schema migration and versioned logging for model changes is a sensible and somewhat uncommon angle for a lab response, but it is an extension of known data-versioning practice and is not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements such as the envelope format and migration toolchain but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Versioned, hash-linked audit logs are a conventional engineering and compliance practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an immutable envelope format and a forward-migration toolchain requires some engineering changes but uses standard versioning and schema-migration techniques, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses a real but implied problem, log continuity across retraining that follows from Article 12's lifetime requirement, rather than the explicitly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The protocol keeps logs coherent and traceable across model changes, which helps meet the lifetime logging mandate but does not itself define which events to log or cover the whole compliance response, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralised logging middleware with CI/CD enforcement is a sensible, commonly expected response and shows little surprise or ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging platform with CI/CD gates introduces a new tool and process but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised internal infrastructure and CI gating are standard engineering practices that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated six-person squad and integration across all project teams, which is a reasonable but real organisational change and cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate across the lab.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide the technical logging capability across projects, but it does not by itself define which events are relevant under Article 12(2) or cover the Annex III-specific minimum fields, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Default-on logging middleware as an architectural invariant is the standard, expected response to Article 12 and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice built into the stack, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging in by default is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a logging middleware layer to the serving stack and auditing prototypes within 90 days requires some template and pipeline changes but is reasonably feasible with standard engineering.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(1) automatic logging mandate by implementing it in the development stack.
evidence_effectiveness: Default automatic event recording would satisfy Article 12(1) and make a major contribution, but it does not specifically address the Article 12(2) event relevance or Annex III 12(3) minimum content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a compliance reference is somewhat unusual and interesting but not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new offering (public reference and positioning as compliance authority) that shifts compliance from burden to market differentiation, stretching the relationship between R&D and compliance beyond plain logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing open-source compliance tooling violates no norms, though publishing it openly is somewhat less common than keeping it in-house.
evidence_implementability: A team of three over eighteen months is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though it requires dedicated staff and ongoing maintenance.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the logging mandate by building a reference implementation covering all four Article 12(3) fields for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A reference codebase would help the lab meet the Annex III logging requirements for biometric systems, but it addresses only that subset and not Article 12(1)-(2) generally or the lab's broader R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized append-only, schema-versioned lifetime log store is a common and expected engineering response to Article 12, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A tamper-proof log store with retention policies is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Deploying a partitioned columnar database with a schema registry and archival policy uses established technology but requires moderate engineering effort and some infrastructure change.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (lifetime event store) to get Y (traceability for post-market monitoring and Article 79 risk identification), which are explicit parts of Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Retaining tamper-evident, version-tagged logs over the system lifetime would substantially address the logging mandate, but it does not itself define which events to log or cover the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated schema-validation tests for logs in CI is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice added to an existing pipeline, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI violates no norms and is a widely accepted strategy.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing GitHub Actions and standard schema validation tools, so it is easy and cheap to implement with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The harness directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that the fields required by Article 12(3)(a)-(d) are present in the logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch missing or malformed mandated log fields, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimums and does not address the broader Article 12(1)-(2) traceability, retention, or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log-based drift monitoring and alerting is a well-known MLOps practice and an expected response, though tying thresholds to Article 79 criteria is a modestly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new tooling (streaming analytics, dashboards) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Post-market monitoring and reporting to notified bodies is a common, legally aligned strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building streaming analytics and dashboards on an existing log store is feasible with standard tools but requires some team effort and defining thresholds.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of making use of logs for post-market monitoring and risk detection that Article 12(2) names, which relates to but is downstream of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Analytics on logs support Article 12(2)(a)-(c) purposes (risk identification, post-market monitoring), but it does not itself deliver the core logging capability or the Annex III minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated schema-contract testing in CI is a well-known engineering practice applied straightforwardly to logging compliance, so it is common and mundane for this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (CI gate and log contract) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Pre-deployment automated checks are a standard engineering strategy that violates no norms and is welcomed by compliance and engineering stakeholders.
evidence_implementability: Defining a JSON schema and adding a CI step with a synthetic workload is inexpensive and fits existing pipelines, requiring only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The CI gate directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying required log fields are emitted before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably catch missing or malformed log fields but does not address which events are relevant under Article 12(2), log retention, or the R&D side, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Unifying experiment-tracking records for peer review and regulatory documentation is a sensible but fairly expected response that shows only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new schema and a mandatory pipeline output, but it still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice and does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: An internal documentation standard that serves both science and compliance violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: A three-person group drafting a schema in one quarter, piloting it on two projects, and folding it into an existing tracking pipeline is reasonably feasible and needs only moderate change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation and traceability needs in Recital 71, which relate to the stated problem but are not the Article 12 automatic event-log requirement, so the fit is implied rather than direct.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal targets Recital 71 technical documentation and does not address Article 12's automatic event logging over the system's lifetime, so it only partly solves the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Building logging into shared infrastructure so telemetry is emitted by default is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is standard compliance logging via infrastructure patching, and the lab's research approach and its relationship to compliance stay unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Default infrastructure-level logging is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Patching orchestration and ingestion over two sprints on existing hardware is a modest, low-cost change, though it is somewhat optimistic about retrofitting all pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(1) automatic event logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver automatic logging but does not specify which events Article 12(2) requires, or cover retention, traceability and deployed-system obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal logging wrappers with CI gating are a common, sensible engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect from many labs, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging SDK with CI enforcement introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory shared tooling and build checks are common engineering governance that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A Python/C++ middleware with a decorator API and CI check is reasonably feasible in two sprints, though integrating across varied pipelines needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by automatically capturing events such as timestamps, inputs, reference databases, and operator IDs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver Article 12 logging capability across prototypes but only partially solves the problem, since it leaves open the retention, risk-relevant event selection, and non-prototype production systems.

evidence_originality: Turning logs into monitoring analytics for post-market surveillance is a sensible and fairly expected extension, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (streaming analytics, dashboards, anomaly alerts) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for internal monitoring and regulator reporting is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a streaming and analytics layer on top of a separate logging architecture plus risk thresholds and automated reports, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial data engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(2)(b),(c) purposes of post-market monitoring and operational monitoring, which belong to the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially support monitoring and post-market obligations but depends on a separate logging layer and does not cover the core logging mandate or other requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates and attestation checklists are common and mundane responses to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance checkpoint and audit practice that leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance review gate with sign-off and audits is a standard, widely accepted governance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a new checkpoint, template, and audit process, which are some process changes but reasonably feasible with modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by turning Article 12 requirements into an acceptance test.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate verifying log fields exist would substantially ensure the logging mandate is met, but it verifies rather than builds the logging capability and doesn't address Article 12 details like appropriate traceability, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Artifact versioning and living documentation linked to monitoring is a fairly familiar MLOps idea with modest imaginative framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a pipeline and review cycles and frames records as a living knowledge base, but it still treats compliance as record-keeping practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Versioning and documentation management tied to compliance is a conventional, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a pipeline that links artifacts to logs requires some new infrastructure and process changes, but it is reasonably feasible with existing MLOps tooling.
evidence_applicability: It targets the implied problem of keeping technical documentation current over the system's lifetime (Recital 71), which relates to the logging mandate but is not the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Linking model versions, datasets, and validation reports to log entries with monitoring-triggered reviews would help keep documentation current, but it mainly covers the documentation and traceability side and does not itself implement the automatic event logging that Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Directly implementing the enumerated statutory logging items in a compliance module is the common, expected response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-logging build that leaves the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building the Article 12(3) logging functions and validating with EU legal counsel is a standard, fully lawful compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-person pod prototyping within a quarter on an existing pipeline is reasonably feasible but requires some new engineering and legal validation work.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the specific Article 12(3) logging requirements, with X (build the module) yielding Y (compliance) that is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Implementing the four mandated Article 12(3) capture functions would directly satisfy the logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) biometric systems, though it does not cover Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other systems.

evidence_originality: Differentiable logging co-optimized with task loss and trace tokens in the computation graph is an unusual and imaginative idea that few labs would propose in response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and architecture itself and by redirecting what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Research programmes on compliance-oriented architectures offend no norms, though they are somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Open-ended research on novel architectures with uncertain outcomes is expensive and difficult, and it is not a committed implementation path for meeting the mandate, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making logging and traceability native to the system) that relates to the stated logging mandate, though the link to concrete Article 12 compliance is indirect.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on architectures with intrinsic tracing might eventually support logging, but it is exploratory and would not by itself deliver the Article 12 automatic event recording the lab must have in place, so it is at best a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Pricing compliance overhead into a prioritisation matrix is sensible and somewhat interesting but not especially surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new scoring element and links compliance cost to what the lab prioritises researching, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance beyond logging practice, though not radically.
evidence_acceptability: Weighting projects by compliance cost is an uncommon but reasonable budgeting practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding an overhead multiplier to resource estimates before the next funding round is a modest process change using existing project-management routines, though re-scoring every project takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to logging obligations by budgeting for them, but does not itself address how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps allocate resources and protect research budgets but does not implement logging or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code and automated test gates are a fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, though the declarative assertion encoding adds some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI/CD assertion suite) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in pipelines are a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Encoding rules as assertions in an existing CI pipeline is reasonably feasible, though translating legal semantics into rules and building trace fixtures requires some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by automatically checking that logs satisfy Article 12 obligations.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI-integrated conformance harness would catch logging gaps against Article 12 requirements, but it only verifies logging semantics and does not address the broader compliance response (documentation, Annex III specifics, R&D adaptation), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking compliance-oriented logging is unusual and shows some imagination, though benchmark initiatives are a familiar research format.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new offering (a public benchmark) born from compliance and shifts the lab's relationship to the obligation toward community standard-setting, stretching the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Open community benchmarks are a socially and legally acceptable, somewhat uncommon strategy, though sharing annotated log traces raises mild privacy and confidentiality concerns.
evidence_implementability: Curating annotated traces across model families, defining a rubric, and hosting an annual open evaluation platform requires substantial effort and external participation but is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (having a measurable standard for Article 12 adequacy) that relates to, but is not directly, the lab's decision of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark for external scoring would help the community compare logging but does not itself make the lab's own systems log compliantly, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware with merge-blocking CI checks is a standard, expected engineering response and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK plus CI gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging SDK with CI gates is a common, norm-conforming compliance engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over a four-week sprint on the existing serving stack with CI gates is a reasonably feasible, modest-cost change, though a language-agnostic versioned SDK across all prototypes requires some adaptation work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, with the specific Article 12 paragraph 3 fields as its target outcome.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would meet the logging mandate for the Article 12(3) schema across prototypes, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and not broader Article 12(2) event relevance or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Operationalizing 'substantial modification' as quantitative thresholds with automated promotion-pipeline gates is a sensible, somewhat interesting angle that few labs would foreground, but it is not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (threshold tables, automated gates) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice, not changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A internal working group and pipeline gates violate no norms, though thresholds must be defensible to regulators, so it is a common, acceptable strategy.
evidence_implementability: Convening a working group and adding automated checks to an existing pipeline requires some changes and defining defensible thresholds is hard, but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified problem tied to Article 12(2)(a), determining when changes constitute substantial modification and trigger documentation, which is part of the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with one piece of compliance (identifying substantial modification events and managing documentation burden) but does not address the core logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Templated scaffolding with logging hooks is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response, with only mild imagination in pre-populating Annex III fields at prototype inception.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (scaffold, CI lint) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal scaffold package with CI linting is a common engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing experiment-tracking decorators and standard CI tooling, so it needs some platform-team work but is reasonably feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (automatic event recording and Annex III 1(a) minimum fields) within R&D workflows.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would ensure logging capability exists in all new prototypes, but it covers only the Article 12 technical logging hooks and not retention, existing systems, or the other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A provenance-logging microservice with an append-only log is a common, expected response to this mandate, with only a small touch in the synchronous crash-safe write.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard logging service added to the stack and leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Logging a reference database version, match inputs, and verifier identity is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A Postgres-backed microservice with an append-only log built in one sprint is a modest, reasonably feasible addition, though the synchronous call into the inference path requires some changes to the pipeline.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the identified paragraph 3 requirements (reference database, matched input data, verifier identity), which are part of the stated logging-mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses only Article 12(3) for Annex III 1(a) systems and omits the general logging duties in paragraphs 1-2 (risk events, post-market monitoring), and it does not record the period of each use, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning the undefined traceability requirement into a standardized auditability benchmark is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but benchmark-building is a familiar research move.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research agenda and public offering (benchmarks and leaderboard) tied to what the lab researches, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open benchmark and leaderboard for auditability violates no legal or social norms and is a welcome contribution, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Building and releasing a public benchmark suite with curated scenarios across several task types and a defined reconstruction-fidelity metric is a significant, costly research effort, though feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: The benchmark relates to traceability that logging under Article 12 supports, but it does not itself make the lab's systems log or comply, so it solves an implied, related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark would not by itself meet the logging mandate or the lab's own compliance, so it contributes only a partial solution at best.

evidence_originality: Periodic compliance audits with checklists and risk-register findings are common and mundane responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal quarterly audit of logs is a common, norm-compliant governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a checklist, an analyst and a recurring process, which are modest changes using existing compliance structures.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets verifying that Article 12 logging requirements are met, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Auditing verifies log completeness but does not itself build the logging capability or address R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default scaffolding is a fairly expected, well-known developer-tooling approach, though the per-Annex III packaging adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (templates, CI checks) but still treats compliance as logging practice added to the lab's existing workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Project templates and CI validation are common engineering practices that violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Scaffold templates, monorepo packages, and CI checks use standard internal tooling and require some upfront building but no radical change, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D by pre-binding the log schema into new prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It reliably ensures logging is present from the start of new projects, but it does not cover existing systems, log content adequacy for risk identification, retention, or documentation upkeep, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered retention schedules and role-based access for logs are common and mundane governance measures.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and governance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Cross-functional retention and access policies with IT security and DPOs are a common, norm-compliant corporate strategy.
evidence_implementability: Drafting policies and embedding them as middleware configuration requires some coordination and changes but is reasonably feasible without radical cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (managing, retaining and securing logs once generated) rather than the directly stated mandate of enabling automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: Retention and access governance helps preserve log evidence and limit personal-data exposure, but it does not itself produce the logging capabilities Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A logging SDK built on OpenTelemetry is a sensible and fairly expected response, with mild interest in the compliance-as-byproduct framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely making it less burdensome for developers.
evidence_acceptability: Using a standard logging library and OpenTelemetry is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin decorator-based wrapper on existing OpenTelemetry tooling needs no model changes and is easy to adopt, though building and maintaining the SDK takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (auto-emit conformant logs) to get Y (meeting the Article 12 logging requirement), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, an SDK that auto-emits logs covering the Article 12(3) fields (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier IDs) would largely solve the logging mandate, though it does not address documentation or retention.

evidence_originality: Treating Article 12 event categories as a signal space for drift-detection research is an interesting, somewhat imaginative reframing, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research agenda, but it does not alter the broader question of what the lab researches in a fundamental way.
evidence_acceptability: Using compliance logs as a research data source and hiring postdocs to study drift offends no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires hiring two postdocs and a multi-year commitment, which is a significant resource commitment, but it builds on logs already generated and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making use of logs and adapting R&D to the mandate) that relates to the stated problem, but it does not directly address how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The research line does not itself ensure that logging meets Article 12 requirements; it only exploits logs that exist, so it contributes only partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Open-source compliance-checking tools are a fairly expected response, but releasing a verifier as a sector reference point and a way to engage regulators is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal creates a new offering (an open toolkit) and a new relationship with regulators and clients that comes out of compliance, which stretches the paradigm beyond ordinary logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release and regulator engagement break no norms, though publishing tooling built on internal log fixtures could raise minor IP or confidentiality concerns.
evidence_implementability: Two postdocs prototyping over one quarter using internal logs is a modest and reasonably feasible effort, though a general verifier against vague legal minimums is harder than it sounds.
evidence_applicability: The tool verifies that log output meets Article 12 minimums, which is directly tied to the logging mandate, though its main aim is sector-wide positioning rather than the lab's own compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: A conformance verifier would help the lab check its own logs and show compliance, but it only partially solves the problem because it does not build the logging itself and Article 12 requirements are loosely specified.

evidence_originality: Automated schema validation in CI is an interesting and sensible idea, but it is a fairly expected DevOps-style response and not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI schema-validation gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a pre-promotion compliance check is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires authoring schemas per system class and adding a containerised validator job to existing CI, which is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by checking that the minimum fields are emitted before promotion.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logs contain required fields but only addresses schema completeness, not the broader logging mandate such as retention, traceability appropriateness, or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Releasing compliance logging as open community infrastructure is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but open-source tooling itself is a familiar approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a shared scientific offering born from the regulatory obligation, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, but does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing compliance tooling under MIT is a somewhat uncommon but unoffensive strategy, with minor sensibilities around releasing it publicly and claiming 'compliance' for others.
evidence_implementability: Building and maintaining a public toolkit with two engineers and a researcher is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial commitment beyond just internal logging.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X to get compliant logs), including the Annex III 1(a) specifics.
evidence_effectiveness: A harness wrapping models with Article 12 logging, Annex III 1(a) schema validation and verification audit trails would, if built, satisfy the core logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it does not cover documentation or the other obligations or the R&D adaptation question.

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance as a research asset is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but evaluation frameworks and open benchmark publication are fairly familiar in the field.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning compliance documentation into a research output and scientific contribution, stretching the paradigm rather than treating it as mere logging.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing evaluation frameworks and baseline results as open research violates no laws or norms, though open publication of failure modes of high-risk models is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Building a standardized probe suite covering edge cases, distribution shifts and adversarial perturbations plus publication requires substantial effort and expertise but is feasible for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: The proposal documents capabilities and limitations (a technical documentation concern from Recital 71), but Article 12 is about automatic event logging, so it only addresses an implied related problem and does not directly tackle the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A probe suite and published evaluation would not produce automatic event logs over the system lifetime, so it contributes only marginally to meeting the logging mandate and is unlikely to solve it.

evidence_originality: Living, version-controlled documentation with automated diffs is a sensible but fairly expected response that experienced evaluators would anticipate from labs, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (version-controlled repository, automated documentation diffs, embedded compliance engineer) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date technical documentation and audit trails is a common, legally aligned practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires tooling, automated diff pipelines, and a dedicated compliance engineer per project, which is some change and cost but reasonably feasible with existing version-control technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the documentation and record-keeping requirements in Recital 71 and the logging mandate by tracking changes with timestamps, though it focuses mainly on documentation rather than Article 12 event logs of system operation.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation current and support audits, but it is only a partial solution since it does not provide the automatic event logging of system operation required by Article 12(1)-(3).

evidence_originality: Auto-instrumentation SDKs for logging are a familiar and expected response, so the idea is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared logging libraries and instrumentation SDKs are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing serving harness with a thin decorator layer and one import per project, which is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the required events and the paragraph-3 minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would ensure the logging requirements are met across new systems, though it addresses only logging capability and not retention, legacy systems, or wider compliance, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A formal event ontology for AI traceability is interesting and shows some imagination, but ontology and standardization efforts are a fairly expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a formal ontology and shared vocabulary) and some external partnerships, but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Collaborative standards-oriented working groups with academics and compliance staff are somewhat uncommon but offend no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A small working group with two pilot deployments is reasonably feasible, though cross-category Annex III coverage and external partners add some difficulty and the output is a conceptual deliverable needing further work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely the ambiguity about which events count as relevant, which relates to the stated logging problem but is not an explicit step in meeting it.
evidence_effectiveness: An event taxonomy would help define what to log under Article 12(2) but does not itself implement logging capabilities, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A pre-coding compliance gate with sign-off at sprint zero is a fairly common 'compliance by design' response that labs would readily propose, though it is sensibly specified.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a process checkpoint and checklist but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifting its timing earlier in the lifecycle.
evidence_acceptability: Review gates and sign-offs are standard governance practices that offend no norms or sensibilities.

evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly by validating log specs against Article 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure log specifications cover Article 12(2) event categories early, but it does not itself implement logging, cover Art. 12(3) specifics, or ensure runtime behavior, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK or middleware is the standard, expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, and the lab's way of working is largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin Python/PyTorch decorator-based layer with standard backends is cheap and easy to build, with integration under half a day per prototype, although the PyTorch-specific design limits some generality.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building in automatic event recording, timestamps, and reference-database pointers.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logging SDK would satisfy the automatic-recording mandate of Article 12(1) for prototypes, but it only partly covers the whole response, since it leaves out the 12(2) event-relevance judgments, retention, and the Annex III-specific minimums.

evidence_originality: A standardized logging SDK retrofitted across systems is the obvious, expected response of an AI lab to this mandate, with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, merely adding a module.
evidence_acceptability: Building a standardized logging module to satisfy a legal mandate is a common, fully legitimate compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A dedicated squad building an SDK and retrofitting existing pipelines is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial change requiring some resources and engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging requirements by recording the specified data items.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native tamper-evident logging covering Article 12(2) events and Annex III 1(a) minimums would directly satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address broader R&D adaptation or retention issues.

evidence_originality: Treating lightweight, cryptographically chained log formats for edge deployments as a research programme is unusual and shows some imagination, but compressible and tamper-evident logs are a known idea.

evidence_acceptability: Funded research on compliance tooling and chained logs violates no norms and is a normal, if somewhat unusual, strategy.
evidence_implementability: A small PhD team prototyping and benchmarking on existing infrastructure is reasonably feasible, though research outcomes are uncertain and must be integrated into middleware.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, making lifetime logging feasible on constrained deployments cheaply, which relates to the logging mandate but is not the core act of meeting it.
evidence_effectiveness: A minimal-schema logging format would help with the storage and bandwidth side of compliance, but it is only a partial solution and depends on a separate middleware proposal and on what is actually required.

evidence_originality: A reusable shared logging middleware is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane despite being sensible.

evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer would meet the logging requirements across projects, but it covers mainly Article 12(3) fields and does not address broader aspects like Article 12(2) risk-event identification or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Documentation owners and audit registers are common, mundane compliance practice with little surprise.

evidence_effectiveness: A documentation lifecycle program would help with traceability and compliance verification but does not implement the automatic event logs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating traceability as a research contribution is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly unprecedented in reproducibility discourse.

evidence_acceptability: Updating internal publication standards is a mild, norm-compatible strategy, though somewhat uncommon in framing, and offends no sensibilities.

evidence_effectiveness: Adding traceability sections to papers and review checklists does not itself deliver Article 12 automatic event logging in high-risk systems, so it is at best a partial contribution to the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the pipeline from the start is the common, expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination.

evidence_acceptability: Integrating compliance logging into existing infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing infrastructure and lightweight middleware with no redesign of core models, making it an easy, low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by capturing timestamps, input-output records and reference-database tracking, which are Article 12 elements.
evidence_effectiveness: Native logging in the pipeline would largely satisfy the technical logging requirement, but it does not cover the full Article 12(2) event-relevance scoping, retention, or Article 14(5) verifier identification, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging middleware with configurable schemas and an immutable store is a common, expected response to this mandate.

evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing events automatically in the lab's pipeline.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver the automatic event recording Article 12(1) requires, but it covers only logging and does not address wider compliance, such as the Article 12(3) specifics or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared centralized logging service with an internal SDK is a common, mundane engineering response that most labs would expect to give.

evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.

evidence_effectiveness: A shared log store would substantially support the logging requirement, but it does not itself cover the specific event-relevance content, retention, or Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Self-documenting architectures tied to interpretability are an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, though related ideas exist in interpretability literature.

evidence_acceptability: Publishing research on interpretable, self-logging architectures offends no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual response to a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: Two postdocs for eighteen months building a novel architecture is a significant, uncertain research effort, and the lab needs to commit resources now with no commercial readiness promised.
evidence_applicability: The idea addresses traceability and logging under Article 12 only indirectly, via future research that would eventually help systems meet the logging requirement, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not give the lab compliant logging now and the benefits are speculative, so it is unlikely to solve the actual decision of how to meet the mandate, though it could contribute long term.

evidence_originality: Named owners with periodic reviews and deployment freezes are a familiar governance pattern, making the idea mundane.

evidence_effectiveness: Keeping dossiers current helps compliance and traceability but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandated logs as a research dataset is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is a fairly intuitive idea and not truly surprising.

evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for research is somewhat unusual and raises data-protection and purpose-limitation concerns (personal data of verifiers, input data), though it does not offend sensibilities outright.
evidence_implementability: Standardising log schemas and building mining pipelines requires some engineering changes and data-science effort, but it builds on logging that is already mandated, so it is reasonably feasible.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK is a common, expected response to a logging mandate with little surprise.

evidence_effectiveness: A shared drop-in logging layer would deliver the automatic event recording Article 12(1) requires across systems, but it does not cover documentation, risk-relevance of events, or retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Adaptive sampling of compliance logs is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle, but minimizing logging overhead is a fairly expected response from labs.

evidence_originality: A dedicated compliance monitoring team reviewing logs is a sensible and fairly expected organizational response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new organizational element (a standing monitoring cell with alerts and a risk register) but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Creating an internal compliance team reporting to the audit committee is a common governance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires hiring or reassigning staff, building alerting infrastructure, and sustaining near-real-time review, which is a significant but feasible commitment.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(2) purposes of identifying risk situations and supporting post-market monitoring, which are part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would actively use logs to identify risk situations and support post-market monitoring, but it does not itself ensure the systems technically produce compliant logs, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in default tooling is a sensible and fairly expected response, with a mildly interesting 'structurally impossible to ship non-compliant' framing.

evidence_acceptability: Standard engineering-governance practice that violates no norms, though mandatory tooling may mildly constrain researchers.

evidence_originality: A review gate with PR-template checklists mapping log fields to code emission points is a common, mundane compliance practice that most labs would propose.

evidence_originality: Embedding a reusable logging library in project templates is a sensible, widely expected engineering practice with little surprise.

evidence_effectiveness: A default logging library would meet much of the Article 12 technical logging requirement for new prototypes, but it does not cover existing systems, the Article 12(2) risk and post-market monitoring relevance, or retention and governance, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a failure-mode knowledge base is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, though not wholly unprecedented.

evidence_originality: Built-in logging hooks with sidecar emitters and append-only stores are a mundane, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.

evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice, adding only a template and test harness without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal reference implementation for regulatory compliance is a common, norm-respecting strategy.
evidence_implementability: A two-engineer sprint on existing standard middleware producing an internal template is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12(3) logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the logging requirement for biometric-ID systems but covers only Article 12(3) for that category, not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging libraries and compliance-by-default templates are a fairly expected engineering response, so it is interesting but not surprising or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (default-on logging SDK in starter templates) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Default-on logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin SDK with decorator hooks and YAML config is a modest engineering effort that fits existing templates and requires non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-capturing the required event categories while preserving R&D speed.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the automatic-recording capability for new prototypes, but it covers only the technical logging capability and not legacy systems, deployer-side logging, retention, or the Annex III 1(a) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A dedicated internal operations/compliance unit is a mundane, expected organizational response to such a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that keeps research unchanged and simply assigns logging duties to a separate team.
evidence_acceptability: Centralizing log retention and post-market monitoring in a small internal team is a common organizational strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Reassigning two existing staff, hiring one analyst, and using the existing storage cluster requires only modest, non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The team directly addresses log retention, retrieval, and Article 72 post-market monitoring, which are part of the stated logging-mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A three-person team on existing storage helps own retention and monitoring but does not itself ensure that systems technically record events or that logs capture the Article 12(2) event types, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Budgeting lifetime log-storage and documentation costs as explicit line items is a sensible, somewhat interesting finance-side angle, but cost accounting for compliance is a fairly expected response and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (compliance line items in business cases) but still treats compliance as logging overhead to be costed, not changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Lifetime cost budgeting is a common, uncontroversial financial practice that offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: Adding budget line items with finance, calibrated from pilot estimates and applied at the next budget cycle, requires only modest process changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, resourcing long-term log retention and maintenance, that relates to the stated mandate rather than directly specifying how to meet the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps fund and sustain logging and documentation over time but does not itself deliver the logging capability or meet Article 12's technical requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a standing longitudinal research instrument is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not wholly surprising since reusing telemetry is a recognizable idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as permanent research infrastructure, changing the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations (logging woven into the science), though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal logging infrastructure to meet the law and reusing it for research offends no norms, though research access to logs needs privacy care, which makes it a somewhat uncommon but acceptable strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated systems team and instrumentation at several boundaries plus a query API, which is a significant but feasible engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly, with the compliance outcome explicitly named.
evidence_effectiveness: Meeting the Article 12(3) minimums with lifetime event capture would meet the logging mandate and add research value, but the proposal is thin on Article 12(2) traceability purposes and on retention and governance, so it is a strong but incomplete solution.

evidence_originality: Simulated regulator inspections that try to reconstruct operational history from logs alone are a somewhat unusual and sensible audit idea, but internal compliance audits and mock inspections are a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process (log-reconstruction red-teaming) but still treats compliance as a logging and audit practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and mock inspections are common, legitimate compliance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A semi-annual internal exercise needs an audit team, scenario scripting and some effort, but it requires only reasonable changes and no new technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring Article 12 logging compliance, including the 12(3) minimum fields and paragraph 2 traceability.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies and finds gaps in logging but does not itself build the logging capability, so it contributes only partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A centralized shared logging middleware is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared tool and gate but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized logging middleware with a code-review gate is a common, legitimate engineering compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers over six weeks plus a pipeline gate is a reasonably feasible set of changes, though it requires some process change and dedicated staffing.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building the logging capability for all high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a shared logging layer with a gate would largely satisfy Article 12 technical logging, but it may not address system-specific event relevance or Annex III minimums without further tailoring, so it is strong but arguably not complete.

evidence_originality: Inventorying and classifying AI systems against risk tiers is the most common first step any lab would propose for AI Act compliance, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A compliance matrix reviewed quarterly is standard compliance practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A systematic internal inventory and review is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning postdocs to catalogue prototypes and maintain a spreadsheet-style matrix is low-cost and requires no radical change, though it consumes some staff time.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied prerequisite problem (scoping which systems need Article 12 logging) that relates to the stated problem rather than the logging mandate directly.
