evidence_implementability: Two engineers prototyping in six weeks using an existing YAML model-card format is a modest, reasonably feasible effort, though encoding legal obligations into rules takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by producing the required log fields, including Annex III 1(a) items.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help define the minimum fields and reduce ambiguity, but it covers only schema definition, not actual logging infrastructure, retention, or the interpretation of 'appropriate' traceability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized, reusable logging framework is a sensible and fairly expected response, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable internal standard and embeds logging into pipelines, but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal reference logging standard is a common, legitimate compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A small team building a unified API and retrofitting two prototypes in one quarter is reasonably feasible but involves real engineering changes and latency trade-offs.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by building a unified logging framework that satisfies Article 12(1)-(3) for every high-risk system the lab ships.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a native, configurable logging API embedded in training, deployment and inference pipelines would largely solve the logging mandate, though it leaves some interpretive questions such as what counts as relevant events and retention to be settled.

evidence_originality: An in-house logging platform with retention and audit export is a very common, expected response to Article 12, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal logging infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a containerised pipeline with retention, encryption and export API requires some engineering effort but is reasonably feasible for a DevOps team.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate through automatic recording and availability of logs across the system lifetime.
evidence_effectiveness: Lifetime log capture, retention and export would contribute to meeting the logging mandate but does not address event relevance per Article 12(2) or Annex III specifics, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log storage with anomaly dashboards is a fairly expected response to the mandate, with only modest value in framing logs as an early-warning capability.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds tooling such as analytics and dashboards but still treats compliance as logging infrastructure, though it links logs to post-market monitoring, so it is slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Log retention and monitoring for compliance is a conventional, norm-abiding strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires provisioning new storage, lifecycle policies and a dedicated analytics team with near-real-time dashboards, which is a significant but feasible investment using existing IT partnerships.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by storing and analysing Article 12 logs and feeding them into Article 72 post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Tamper-evident lifetime storage and log analytics would meet retention and monitoring needs, but it does not itself ensure that systems record the right events or address the R&D adaptation, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Async ring-buffer logging with latency benchmarking is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a prototype and benchmark process but still treats compliance purely as a logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Engineering benchmarking and documenting the results in the technical file violates no norms and is a common compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Ring buffers with batched async flush to object storage are standard, low-cost engineering that can be prototyped quickly on an existing reference model.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Annex III 1(a) logging fields (period of use, reference database, matched input, verifier identity) without harming real-time performance, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It is a proof-of-concept that de-risks the technical feasibility of logging but does not cover the full mandate, such as the other high-risk categories, retention, or the identification of verifiers, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a longitudinal research dataset is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not wholly surprising since it parallels existing ideas on observability and MLOps.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Logging schemas are designed during protocol review and operational logs become a scientific dataset, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: The approach is lawful and consistent with norms, with only mild friction from researchers' process changes, making it fairly uncommon but inoffensive.
evidence_implementability: Rebuilding the serving stack and embedding schema design into every team's protocol review is a significant, costly change, though feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (automatic recording of events over system lifetime) and adapting R&D to it.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared instrumentation library enforcing event-level capture of timestamps, input hashes and more would, if done, satisfy the Article 12 automatic-logging mandate and add value beyond it, so it would solve the main problem.

evidence_originality: A reusable compliance logging library is a fairly obvious and expected response, though the zero-config default framing is sensible rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moving it earlier into the architecture rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal shared logging library is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-engineer team building an SDK and integrating it into existing scaffolding is a modest, reasonably feasible effort with some changes to existing projects.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specific items listed in Article 12(3), including timestamps, database pointers, input references, and verifier identities.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a default-embedded logging layer would largely satisfy the logging mandate, but it covers mainly the Annex III 1(a) minimums and leaves some of the Article 12(2) event-relevance judgment and the log retention and governance questions open, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing open schemas as citable research is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, but standards-sharing is a known idea and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logging into publishable research output and community standards, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open specifications and publications are normal in research and violate no norms, though releasing logging designs openly may raise minor IP or security concerns.
evidence_implementability: Drafting and publishing schemas is feasible with moderate effort, but peer-reviewed publication and adoption need some resources and time, so it is reasonably feasible rather than trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by defining event categories, and adds the related aim of reproducibility.
evidence_effectiveness: Formal schemas covering Article 12(2)(a)-(c) would help meet the logging mandate, but they do not by themselves implement logging in systems or cover the other obligations, so the solution is only partial.

evidence_originality: Budget set-asides and compliance cost line items are a familiar project-governance practice, with only mild interest in making the trade-off explicit to funders.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a governance process (charter line item, funding gate, audits) while still treating compliance as an overhead cost separate from the science, not changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Budget ring-fencing and audits are common management strategies that offend no norms, though a fixed cap might draw some researcher grumbling.
evidence_implementability: Adding a charter line item, a gate check, and quarterly sampling audits uses existing governance structures and requires modest, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab resources and governs Article 12 logging work by reserving hours for logging, documentation, and monitoring tooling, though it targets budgeting rather than the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Reserving hours helps ensure logging work gets done and is auditable, but it does not itself build the logging capability or guarantee compliant logs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Periodic audits with a compliance officer are a mundane, expected response to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Quarterly audits, a designated officer and escalation deadlines are standard governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a checklist, a Log Officer role and an audit schedule, which are reasonably feasible organisational changes without major cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses keeping logging functional over system lifetime and supporting post-market monitoring, which is part of the Article 12 mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Auditing catches logging drift and gaps but does not itself design the logging or define what events to record, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-deployment compliance testing of logs is a mundane, expected response that shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, merely adding an audit step.
evidence_acceptability: Internal pre-deployment compliance audits and test scripts are a common, normatively unproblematic strategy.
evidence_implementability: It needs a QA/compliance test step and test scripts, which is a modest process addition using existing teams and not a radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that logs capture the required events and paragraph 3 fields.
evidence_effectiveness: Verification testing helps confirm compliance but does not itself build the logging capability or address how R&D adapts, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Architecture-native auditability is a somewhat unusual and imaginative framing, though related to existing interpretability and traceability research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science itself and redirecting what the lab researches, which is paradigm breaking.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme to build logging into architectures violates no laws or norms, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping three novel architectures with native trace emission is a significant, expensive, uncertain R&D effort, and the lab needs committed implementation resources rather than exploratory funding.
evidence_applicability: It targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging and adapting R&D, directly referencing Article 12(3) data requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, research prototypes benchmarked against Article 12(3) would only partially meet the logging mandate for deployed systems, with no assurance of covering Article 12(2) event types or lifetime logging.

evidence_originality: Default instrumentation baked into project templates is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable scaffold but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized, template-based logging infrastructure is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing experiment-tracking framework with middleware and a single dependency in the scaffold, so it is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate: do X (scaffold logging) to get automatic recording capability.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic event recording (Art. 12(1)) but does not address the Art. 12(2) relevance of events or the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Versioned document control with quarterly reviews is a common, mundane response to technical documentation requirements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Document control and audit trails are common, uncontroversial compliance practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A versioned document-management system with an assigned owner and scheduled reviews uses standard tooling and modest process change, though it needs a dedicated team.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified documentation-currency requirement from the recital, which is related to but not the same as the logging mandate in the stated problem, so the problem it solves is implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully address the technical-documentation upkeep in Recital 71 but not the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance infrastructure into a market product is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is a fairly familiar compliance-as-a-feature move rather than a surprising one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Creating a new product offering born from compliance changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and its obligations, which is paradigm stretching though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Packaging compliant logging as a commercial SDK for deployers is a legitimate, somewhat uncommon business strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires extracting the logging stack into a standalone SDK with configurable schemas and piloting with two customers within a quarter, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial change that depends on a prior logging build.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the logging mandate only indirectly, because it builds on an assumed logging stack and aims at commercialization, so it solves an implied problem related to the stated one.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself satisfy Article 12 obligations for the lab's own systems and mostly adds revenue and reputational benefits, so it would contribute only partially to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Embedding an open-source logging agent into existing prototypes using current Kubernetes monitoring is a mundane, expected compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard logging retrofit and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logging with existing tools is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team, six weeks, open-source tooling and existing infrastructure make this low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by implementing the Article 12(3) logging fields in the lab's high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet the specific Article 12(3) logging items for three prototypes but covers only Annex III 1(a)-type fields and not broader Article 12(2) event relevance, lab-wide R&D adaptation, or retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating log events as typed first-class objects in an append-only store is a sensible and fairly common engineering pattern (structured logging, event sourcing), so it is interesting but not imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (typed event schema, architecture-decision records) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though it does embed it structurally in the architecture.
evidence_acceptability: Structured audit logging and documenting design decisions in ADRs are common, norm-conforming strategies that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring the serving microservice and adding an append-only store is a reasonably feasible set of changes requiring some engineering effort but not radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate, with each element mapped to the Article 12(3) requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Emitting structured event records with timestamps, reference database, matched inputs and verifier identity into an append-only store would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields and Article 12(1) automatic recording, though it does not address the broader Article 12(2) purposes or other obligations, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Golden-path templates for compliance logging are a familiar engineering pattern, so the idea is interesting but not imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable reference implementation is a new tool/format, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusable compliance templates and published logging contracts violate no norms or sensibilities and are common strategies.
evidence_implementability: Building a Dockerised service on an existing matching stack with OpenAPI docs is a reasonably feasible, moderate-effort engineering task.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified Article 12(3) logging mandate for biometric systems, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging items for biometric projects but does not cover the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging needs for other high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by design with a shared middleware and a release gate is the standard, expected response of a lab to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It preserves the existing paradigm by treating compliance as logging practice and only moving it earlier in the design process, with no change to what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging and an internal compliance gate is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a platform team, a logging spec and a mandatory release gate, which are some changes but reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by producing automatic logs covering Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, automatic native logs with Annex III 1(a) fields would largely satisfy the Article 12 mandate, though the proposal does not detail how it covers risk-event identification or post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: A client-facing log transparency dashboard is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not ingenious or surprising enough for the top level.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logging into a client-facing offering and procurement differentiator, which changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings, though R&D itself is unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Role-based access, anonymised aggregates and retention of full logs under GDPR-compliant custody violate no norms and are a sensible, fairly uncommon strategy.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building on existing logging middleware is a modest, reasonably feasible effort with some new work on access control and privacy.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, evidencing Article 12 readiness to clients, which relates to the stated problem but is not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate, which the underlying middleware must do, so it contributes only partially, mainly by demonstrating traceability and adding commercial value.

evidence_originality: Red-team style audit of logs as a traceability test is an interesting and somewhat imaginative twist beyond typical logging implementation, though audits are familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (simulated inquiry audit) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: An internal semiannual audit simulating a regulatory inquiry is a legitimate, somewhat uncommon compliance practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a cross-functional team and recurring effort plus remediation tracking, but uses existing logs and ordinary audit processes, so it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses verifying that Article 12 logging actually supports traceability, which is part of how the lab must meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch logging gaps and drive remediation, but it only tests and does not itself build the logging capability or cover R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a logging SDK with CI enforcement is a sensible, commonly expected engineering response, with only modest imagination in the 'from day one' scaffolding framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a shared SDK with schema validation and CI gating) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal shared libraries and CI checks are common engineering strategies that offend no norms, though merge-blocking may cause mild friction.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK and CI gate requires platform team effort and adoption across projects, which is a moderate change but reasonably feasible with standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D by providing automatic event recording in prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic event logging across prototypes, but it does not by itself cover Article 12 purposes like risk-situation identification, post-market monitoring, or Annex III specific fields, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shifting compliance left into planning is a common, expected response from labs, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a workshop and a gate but keeps compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A half-day design workshop and a code-review gate are ordinary, uncontroversial project-management practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a modest process change and a rotating compliance engineer from an existing pool, which is reasonably feasible but adds some workload and gating to every project.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building logging design into R&D from the start.
evidence_effectiveness: Scoping logging early would help meet Article 12 but does not itself deliver the logging capabilities, cover the specific content requirements, or address post-deployment upkeep, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Phase-gate compliance checklists with designated reviewers are common and mundane, with little that is imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance process layered onto existing workflow, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a documentation review step to existing phase gates with a rotating record-keeper is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing phase gates, PM tooling and personnel with only a half-day workshop and a one-page checklist, so cost and change are low.
evidence_applicability: It targets the documentation and record-keeping part of the stated problem and is related to compliance, but the Article 12 logging mandate is only implied or touched, not directly solved.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses documentation quality under Recital 71 but does not implement automatic event logging required by Article 12 (technical logging capability, Annex III minimums), so it is only a partial solution at best.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware reusing existing infrastructure is a common, expected response to the mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard logging infrastructure that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Deploying a lightweight middleware agent and reusing existing GPU cluster and data lake storage requires some engineering changes but no new procurement, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing events, timestamps, and reference-database queries.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic event recording, but it does not itself address risk-situation identification, retention, human verifier identity, or input-match data fully, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging into one shared middleware is a common, sensible engineering consolidation that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A unified logging middleware is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal logging infrastructure is a standard, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing Prometheus and Loki tooling, needs no vendor procurement, and requires only a one-quarter build plus manifest changes by project leads, which is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by providing the Article 12(3) minimum fields and a single audit point.
evidence_effectiveness: A single schema capturing timestamps, reference databases, input hashes and verifier records would substantially meet Article 12 logging needs, though it covers mainly Annex III 1(a) items and not retention, risk-event identification or post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: Building logging in from the start (compliance by design) with design-template changes and review gates is a very common, expected response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds process elements (templates, review gates, dedicated engineers) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging into design and sign-off is a standard, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: It requires revising templates and gates and assigning a logging engineer to each team, which are some changes and reasonably feasible measures rather than radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the automatic logging requirement by building the capability into R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Native logging in every high-risk build would substantially satisfy Article 12's logging mandate, though it does not detail what events are logged or retention, so it is mostly but not fully specified.

evidence_originality: Durable, versioned, access-controlled log storage is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to lifetime logging mandates, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a schema-versioned append-only store with tiered compression and access controls) but still treats compliance as a logging infrastructure practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Append-only audit stores with role-based access and retention policies are common, norm-respecting strategies that raise no legal or social concerns.
evidence_implementability: Building a custom columnar store with schema versioning, tiered compression, and a query API is a substantial engineering effort, though feasible using existing storage technologies, so it needs some changes and moderate resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified part of the stated problem, namely keeping logs across the system lifetime and making them retrievable for post-market monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the lifetime retention and retrieval portion of Article 12 and Article 72 but does not by itself define what events to log or cover the full mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code with version control and auto-diff flagging is a known DevOps/MLOps practice applied to compliance, so it is interesting but not ingenious or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and process (git-mapped documentation, automated diffs) but still treats compliance as a documentation/record-keeping practice without changing the lab's R&D relationship to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Version-controlled documentation with named owner sign-off is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing git tooling and a research-ops team with modest scripting and a sign-off process, requiring non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses keeping technical documentation current, which is in Recital 71 and related to record-keeping, but Article 12 itself mandates automatic event logs, so it solves an implied rather than the directly stated logging problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation up to date but does not provide the automatic event logging, traceability of operation, or post-market monitoring that Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralised reusable logging middleware is a mundane, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, merely centralised, and leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging module is a common, lawful compliance strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building one middleware against existing infrastructure with standardised APIs and minimal configuration is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the required log elements (timestamps, input references, verification actors).
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to meeting the logging requirements across systems, but it covers only the minimum Annex III 1(a) items and not the broader risk, post-market and monitoring event recording or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-differentiator transparency reporting is a fairly recognizable idea, though somewhat imaginative in its client-facing portal form.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (client portal, transparency report) and turns compliance into a market offering, which stretches the compliance relationship but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A transparency dashboard and annual conformance report are legitimate, norm-respecting business practices, though somewhat less common than plain internal logging.
evidence_implementability: Building a read-only dashboard and annual white paper requires some engineering and certification effort but is reasonably feasible, though certifying every client deployment adds burden.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (demonstrating compliance and gaining market benefit) related to the logging mandate rather than the core requirement of building the logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself implement the logging capabilities required by Article 12; it only demonstrates and publicizes them, so it contributes partially at best.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a marketable monitoring product is imaginative and somewhat unusual, but the idea of a monitoring dashboard is fairly familiar and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance logging the basis of a new commercial offering, which matches the 'new offerings born from compliance' example of paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Productizing compliance monitoring as a client service is somewhat unusual but offends no legal or social norms, though exposing logs to clients raises some confidentiality questions.
evidence_implementability: Building an API layer and client portal over existing mandatory log streams requires some real engineering work and data-governance changes but is reasonably feasible with known technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified logging for post-market monitoring (Art 12(2)(b)/Art 72) and how to respond to the mandate, though the revenue goal is an adjacent implied benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: A client dashboard would leverage logs and support post-market monitoring but does not by itself ensure Article 12 logging capabilities are met (event coverage, retention, traceability), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A sprint-embedded compliance gate with a checklist is a fairly expected response, though the replay tool simulating incident scenarios against live logs adds a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (gate, checklist, replay tool) but still treats compliance as logging practice verified within the existing workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Internal verification gates and checklists are common strategies that violate no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-hour gate, checklist and a replay tool require modest changes and some tooling effort, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that logs capture the events Article 12(2) requires.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch logging gaps early but covers only Article 12(2) event relevance, not Article 12(3) specifics, log retention or the broader documentation needs, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using the lab's own models to self-audit logs and turning compliance into publishable work is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as publishable research and funding leverage, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, though it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research on log verification offends no norms, though the publishing-for-funding framing is slightly unusual but not objectionable.
evidence_implementability: A six-month sprint with two postdocs and existing synthetic-data pipelines is modest in cost and reasonably feasible, though real-time anomaly detection needs some development.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets integrity and completeness of logs against Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which directly relates to the logging mandate, though it addresses log quality rather than the basic recording capability itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Anomaly detection on logs would help ensure completeness and support monitoring, but it is only a partial solution since it does not build the core logging capability and relies on smaller models that may themselves be unreliable.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware baked into project scaffolds is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory internal tooling and code-review gates for compliance are common and violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two developers over one quarter to build middleware and add it to scaffolds is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though integrating with all existing systems and defining the relevant events takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a logging layer that captures the events Article 12(2) and 12(3) require, so the logging mandate is met explicitly.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a non-bypassable reusable logging layer across all high-risk templates would largely satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not cover the technical documentation and appropriateness-to-purpose judgments, so it is close to a full solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a research dataset is an unusual and imaginative reframing that few labs would offer, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandated logs into primary scientific data and a research agenda, which is paradigm breaking or at least stretching, and it addresses what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing research from operational logs is a normal academic practice, though using biometric logs may raise data protection sensitivities that a reviewer would flag as somewhat uncommon.
evidence_implementability: It needs only two postdocs and a lightweight analytics layer on an existing pipeline, though it must wait twelve months for sufficient data, so it involves some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely how to adapt R&D to exploit the mandated logs, which relates to the stated problem but is not the direct compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself meet the logging mandate, which depends on the existing compliance retrofit, so it only contributes by adding research value on top of it, which is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance reviews are a mundane, entirely expected response to a regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint process but treats compliance as standard logging practice with the lab's R&D way of working largely unchanged, though it does embed traceability as a design constraint.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review gate with compliance checklist and sign-off is a common governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires adding a checkpoint, a checklist, and remediation tracking, which is a reasonably feasible process change but not trivial across all projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring Article 12(2) event categories are designed into each system.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help ensure logging capability exists, but it is a process control that does not itself guarantee adequate logs or cover Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a longitudinal robustness research corpus is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not wholly unprecedented, since post-deployment monitoring data is commonly mined.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning mandated logs into a research dataset that feeds the lab's science, though it does not redefine what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for research and publishing preprints is a fairly uncommon strategy that raises privacy and GDPR, confidentiality and customer-data questions, but it is not offensive if handled properly.
evidence_implementability: Building an analytics pipeline over existing log streams and running scheduled probes is reasonably feasible, though it needs data governance, engineering effort and research staff.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D around mandated logging by extracting scientific value, which relates to the stated problem but is not the direct logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the Article 12 logging mandate, since it presumes the logs exist and only adds value from them, so it is a partial contribution at best.

evidence_originality: Measuring logging overhead tradeoffs and publishing the results is interesting and somewhat imaginative in framing compliance as research, but it is a fairly expected systems-research response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (compliance instrumentation as a publishable research question) that somewhat changes how R&D relates to compliance, but it still treats compliance fundamentally as logging practice, so it sits between levels 2 and 3 and fits level 2 best.
evidence_acceptability: Running controlled experiments and publishing open benchmarks is a standard, normatively unobjectionable academic practice.
evidence_implementability: A six-month project with two PhD students and existing model families is modest in scale, but it depends on the logging layer from Proposal 1 being built first, which requires some coordination.
evidence_applicability: Benchmarking logging overhead addresses an implied problem (understanding the performance cost of meeting Article 12 logging) that relates to the stated problem, but it does not itself implement the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab choose logging densities sensibly but is only a partial contribution, since it depends on a separate logging layer (Proposal 1) and does not itself deliver compliance.

evidence_originality: Formalising a minimal sufficient provenance schema borrowing from genomics and climate data-management is interesting and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (schema, cross-disciplinary synthesis) and positions the lab as methodological originator, yet still treats compliance as a logging/metadata practice rather than changing R&D's relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Academic-style schema formalisation is a legitimate, non-offensive approach, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: A literature synthesis and prototyping two or three schemas against an existing model registry is a research effort needing some staff time and changes but no radical infrastructure, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (deciding which fields to record) derived from Article 12(2) and tested on a biometric pipeline, which relates directly to the logging mandate but does not itself deliver the logs.
evidence_effectiveness: A minimal provenance schema would help define what to log but is research-stage and does not itself implement automatic logging, event recording, or the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design with SDKs and compliance gates is a well-known, expected response to this mandate, so it is common rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces process elements and shifts logging to design time, but still treats compliance as logging practice, so it is only slightly paradigm stretching (privacy/security-by-design style).
evidence_acceptability: Shared SDKs, architecture review gates, and compliance sign-offs are common, norm-compliant engineering governance practices.
evidence_implementability: It requires a cross-team SDK, mandatory review gates, and embedded compliance engineers on every squad, which is a significant but feasible organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by enabling automatic event recording over the system lifetime.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, building logging into every high-risk system via a shared SDK with review gates would directly satisfy Article 12(1) and largely solve the logging mandate, though specific Article 12(2)-(3) content is not detailed.

evidence_originality: Living documents with update triggers and compliance owners are a common, mundane governance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining living, versioned technical documentation with named compliance owners is a standard, norm-conforming compliance practice.
evidence_implementability: A versioned repository, update triggers, and named owners require some process changes but are reasonably feasible with modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the Recital 71 documentation and up-to-date record requirement, which is related to the logging mandate but is not the Article 12 automatic event logging itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping documentation current helps traceability and compliance but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance triage and prioritization of a project pipeline is a common, expected response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance project management that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A triage audit with self-assessments and sequenced remediation is a common, norm-respecting compliance management approach.
evidence_implementability: A one-page self-assessment and a four-week exercise need only modest changes and low cost, though the sprint sequencing takes some coordination.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of scarce resources and how to meet the logging mandate, and it explicitly references Article 12 paragraph 3.
evidence_effectiveness: It prioritizes resources but does not itself build logging capabilities, so it only partly solves the problem of meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance checklists in sprint planning are common and mundane, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design practice that adds a process step while leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though it does shift compliance into planning.
evidence_acceptability: A planning checklist added to existing sprints is a common, uncontroversial process that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist and a three-project pilot within existing sprint cycles require only non-radical, low-cost changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring required logging fields are identified and emitted early in development.
evidence_effectiveness: A checklist confirming architecture can emit logs helps but is only a partial solution, as it does not specify implementing logging, retention, or Article 12(3) content, and relies on self-confirmation.

evidence_originality: Log analytics with anomaly alerting for post-market monitoring is a fairly expected, sensible response that shows only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (streaming analytics, SPC, dashboards) on top of logs but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for monitoring and reporting is a common, legally aligned strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Kafka and time-series stores are mature off-the-shelf tools, but building per-system alerting rules and a dashboard requires some new infrastructure and effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(2) purposes of risk identification, post-market monitoring, and operation monitoring that the logging mandate sets out.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to using logs for Article 72 and 26(5) purposes but does not itself deliver the core logging capability or the Annex III minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging library with a schema is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal compliance library is a conventional strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over six weeks to package existing patterns into a module is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by emitting structured records matching the Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would deliver compliant logging across projects, but it covers only the Article 12(3) fields (which apply to Annex III 1(a) systems) and not the broader 12(2) event-relevance requirements, retention, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying online change-point detection to operationalize 'substantial modification' is a reasonably interesting and somewhat unusual framing, though drift detection is a well-known ML ops topic.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (sequential tests, adaptive baselines) and a research project, but still treats compliance as a monitoring/logging tool, with only a mild link to the lab's research agenda via a publishable contribution.
evidence_acceptability: Statistical monitoring of deployed systems violates no norms, though using real deployment logs requires data governance care, and it is a fairly standard strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building validated online detectors with adaptive baselines and legal thresholds for substantial modification is a significant research effort with a difficult legal-to-statistical mapping, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified element of the mandate, Art. 12(2)(a) identification of substantial modification, though the claim that Article 12 'implicitly requires' a detection mechanism stretches the text, since the Article requires logging capability rather than detection.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift detection would help identify situations of substantial modification under Art. 12(2)(a), but it covers only one logging purpose and does not deliver the logging mandate as a whole (automatic event recording, post-market monitoring, operation monitoring, Annex III minimums), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal log governance with mock regulator inspections is a standard, expected compliance response and is not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice, with a new team and audits but no change to how R&D works or relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance and audit functions are common, norm-abiding corporate strategies that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Chartering a small cross-functional team to draft retention policies and run quarterly mock audits needs some organizational change but uses ordinary, reasonably feasible measures.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate through governance and audit, directly related to the stated problem, though it mixes in retention rules the Article does not specify.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logs are retained and verifiable but does not itself build the automatic logging capability Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Experiment tracking and data-lineage versioning are well-known MLOps practices, so the idea is fairly mundane despite the append-only ledger framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a ledger and reproducibility tooling and frames compliance audits as a by-product of research workflow, mildly weaving compliance into the science but still essentially a logging/documentation practice.
evidence_acceptability: Extending experiment tracking with versioned, append-only provenance is a common, norm-respecting practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing MLflow-style tooling with some pipeline restructuring and ledger keying to dataset commits, which is reasonably feasible with moderate changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses record-keeping and traceability requirements by capturing lineage and provenance for each experiment, though it focuses on Recital 71 documentation more than Article 12 event logs of deployed systems.
evidence_effectiveness: An append-only provenance ledger would substantially support documentation and traceability, but it does not cover runtime automatic event logging of high-risk systems under Article 12(2)-(3), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging with append-only storage and CI/CD gates is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as standard logging practice with familiar tooling, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized, mandatory logging infrastructure with deployment gates is a common compliance engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared microservice with append-only storage and integrating a CI/CD gate across all product lines requires some architectural changes but uses well-established, reasonably feasible engineering.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, recording session start/end times and Article 12(2) risk triggers.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared tamper-evident logging service with a CI/CD deployment gate would, if built, satisfy the core Article 12 automatic-logging mandate across all high-risk systems, though it does not cover technical documentation or Annex III-specific fields like reference databases or verifier identities.

evidence_originality: Designing architectures whose computation graphs natively yield compliant logs, with a 'traceability budget' metric, is unusual and imaginative, though linking interpretability to logging is not entirely unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging a design property of the architectures the lab researches, which redirects what the lab studies, though it stops short of fully redefining the lab's research agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Funding research and open-source libraries to meet regulation is a socially and legally acceptable approach that offends no norms, though it is somewhat uncommon as a compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires a two-year programme with several PhD positions and a postdoc, plus uncertain research on tensor-level hooks, which is a significant, costly commitment but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D, but through an implied route (research into architectures that produce logs) rather than directly implementing Article 12 logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would yield reusable logging components and architectures that help future projects, but a two-year research programme with uncertain results only partially solves the near-term compliance need, and tensor-level logs do not necessarily satisfy Article 12's event-level requirements.

evidence_originality: Tiered hot/warm/cold log storage with latency and overhead SLAs is a standard engineering pattern, though tying it to the Annex III fields is a sensible, mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (tiered stack, query SLAs) but still treats compliance as a logging and infrastructure practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building robust log infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A prototype with benchmarking before hardware commitment is reasonably feasible with known technologies, though decade-scale retention and sub-1% overhead require some real engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement of automatic logging over the system's lifetime and the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A tiered, benchmarked log storage architecture would help satisfy the lifetime logging and traceability mandate, but it covers only the storage/retrieval part and not what events to log, governance, or other compliance aspects.

evidence_originality: Automated drift-based gating of substantial modification inside CI is a somewhat unusual and interesting idea, though similar to MLOps model-governance gates that labs commonly build.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a CI gate with drift metrics and signed records) but still treats compliance as a logging and record-keeping practice rather than changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A CI gate with Compliance owning thresholds and signed records is a conventional governance approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Diffing model versions and adding a CI check is reasonably feasible with existing tooling, though defining quantitative thresholds for substantial modification requires some legal and technical work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem, detecting substantial modification, which Article 12(2)(a) mentions only as a logging purpose, so it is not the core logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help flag modification events and keep records, but it covers only one part of the logging mandate (not automatic event logs, post-market monitoring, or operation monitoring), and quantitative drift may not capture legal substantial modification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated model cards are fairly familiar ideas, though tying them to a Recital 71 schema is a sensible but not surprising twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (a compliance schema and rendering pipeline) but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation generation from tracked metadata is a common, norm-compliant practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing MLflow tracking with a metadata schema and a scheduled rendering job, which is a modest, low-cost change to current tooling.
evidence_applicability: It targets the Recital 71 'kept up to date' documentation obligation, which is an implied related problem rather than the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would keep technical documentation current, but it does not address Article 12's automatic event logging requirement, so it only partially solves the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates and checklist sign-offs are a common, expected governance response to regulation, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A pre-market review gate with checklist and reviewers is a new process element but still treats compliance as a logging-verification practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gates are a standard, uncontroversial governance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A checklist, two trained engineer reviewers and a sign-off requirement are modest process additions that can be set up at low cost with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets verifying that logging and traceability obligations under Article 12 are met before release, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A review gate verifies logging exists but does not build the logging capability itself or cover post-market, lifetime logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in starter templates is a sensible and fairly common platform-engineering approach, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a scaffold with adapters) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized, mandatory tooling in internal templates is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing internal starter kit with a logging library is a modest engineering effort using familiar techniques at reasonable cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, including the Annex III 1(a) fields such as reference database pointers.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure new prototypes log consistently, but it does not cover existing systems, log retention, or the identification of persons verifying results, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A drop-in logging middleware/SDK that standardizes Article 12 event capture is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-logging tool that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, explicitly preserving prototyping velocity.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal logging tooling to satisfy a legal requirement violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: A decorator-based library with a JSON schema is a modest, low-cost engineering effort that requires little change to existing serving stacks, though covering 'any' endpoint adds some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would substantially meet the logging mandate for prototypes, but it covers only the logging capability, not Annex III-specific fields fully, retention, or broader documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Post-market surveillance teams consuming logs are an expected, commonly proposed response, so the idea is fairly mundane despite sensible details like pause authority.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a team and process but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A dedicated internal monitoring team with pause authority is a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though pause authority may meet some internal friction.
evidence_implementability: Hiring three staff and wiring them into an existing alerting pipeline is a moderate, reasonably feasible organizational change, though it presumes the logging middleware already exists.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to use Article 12 logs for risk identification and post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Active log review for Article 79 risks helps with Article 12(2) purposes and post-market monitoring, but it does not itself deliver the logging capability or cover the R&D-side adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalising log-sufficiency information-theoretically is an unusual, interesting idea showing imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research question and changes what the lab researches, tying the science to regulation, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance without fully breaking the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Studying data minimisation versus logging is legally and socially unobjectionable, though an academic research framing for a compliance problem is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A fundamental research programme deriving information-theoretic lower bounds and running ablation studies on existing pipelines is expensive, uncertain and difficult but not impossible, and it does not directly deliver logging.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the tension between logging content and privacy, which relates to the logging mandate, but it does not directly say how to meet Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if it worked it would only yield insight on minimal log content and would not implement logging or achieve compliance, so it is at best a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance and CI gating of required artifacts is a well-known DevOps pattern, with only a modest twist in the Article 12 linter, so it is interesting but not rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (sprint template, log-contract artifact, linter) and reorders process, but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Engineering teams commonly adopt CI gates and up-front architecture milestones, and this violates no norms, though researchers may grumble about delayed training.
evidence_implementability: Updating playbooks, adding a CI check, and writing a linter plugin are modest engineering changes, though the sprint reordering and custom linter require some effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab will meet the Article 12 logging mandate by defining event schemas up front and enforcing required log endpoints through a CI gate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, schema-first design and CI enforcement would reliably ensure that systems have automatic event logging aligned with Article 12, though it does not fully cover Annex III specifics or the substantive adequacy of the logs.

evidence_originality: A public auditability benchmark that scores reconstructability of internal state from logs alone is an unusual and imaginative idea, though benchmarks are a familiar research format.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logging into a public research benchmark and external-lab partnership, changing the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open benchmarks with external collaborators offends no norms, though the IP-creation framing is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers and three partner labs are a modest resource commitment, but designing a valid benchmark and securing external participation is a significant undertaking with some uncertainty.
evidence_applicability: It relates to the stated problem only loosely through the logging schema and Article 12(2) alignment, mainly serving scientific prestige and IP goals rather than the lab's compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: The benchmark would not make the lab's own systems log events as Article 12 requires, so it contributes at most tangentially to meeting the mandate and does not solve the core problem.

evidence_originality: Mapping the stated minimums to a typed schema with CI tests is sensible but a fairly expected engineering response, with only modest interest in making compliance testable.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a schema and CI-based verification but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Standardizing logging schemas to meet a legal requirement is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy, although logging verifier identity may raise minor privacy concerns.
evidence_implementability: One engineer drafting for a week and wiring it into two existing projects during a normal sprint is low cost and a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the paragraph-3 logging minimums for biometric systems, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A typed schema covering all four Article 12(3) minimums, emitted on every call and checked in CI, would solve the Annex III 1(a) logging mandate, though it does not cover the Article 12(2) event-relevance logging or the wider documentation duties.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance tooling is a recognizable move among labs, with the licensing and reference-point positioning adding mild interest but not real surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (an open-source framework, a specification paper) and turns compliance into reusable IP and a sector offering, which modestly changes the relationship between R&D and compliance but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building and open-sourcing a compliance logging framework violates no laws or norms and is a fairly common, sensible response, though the licensing and positioning angle is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Two researchers at 30% time over twelve months, run parallel to core research and using existing telemetry, is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment requiring some changes.
evidence_applicability: Developing a logging framework for automatic lifetime event recording directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A twelve-month schema and framework would contribute to logging capability, but it does not by itself guarantee Article 12 compliance for the lab's high-risk systems, and the proposal is oriented toward positioning and reuse, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logging conformance in CI is a fairly expected response, and a fidelity benchmark for prototype-to-production handoff is a sensible but not surprising twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and metric but still treats compliance as a logging practice verified by testing, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated conformance testing of logs is a conventional engineering practice that violates no norms, though a per-class fidelity benchmark is slightly less standard.
evidence_implementability: A conformance test harness with reference schemas and sprint-level staging checks needs some new tooling and schema definition but fits existing CI practices, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of ensuring systems technically allow automatic recording of the Article 12 event types and Annex III minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch logging gaps early but does not itself implement logging, cover retention, or address the broader compliance response, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as a first-class computational primitive co-designed with model topology is unusual and shows imagination, though not entirely unprecedented given the observability and interpretability literature.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science of architecture design and addresses what the lab researches, though it stops short of fully redefining the lab's purpose.
evidence_acceptability: Research into observable architectures and benchmarking overhead violates no legal or social norms and is well aligned with regulatory aims.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year dedicated workstream across several architecture families is expensive and uncertain, and it demands significant resources and change, which conflicts with the commitment of scarce implementation resources for near-term compliance.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of making logging efficient and integral to AI systems, which relates to the mandate but not directly to meeting the immediate compliance requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: A research programme on architectures with built-in logging could eventually yield compliant systems, but it is a multi-year exploratory effort that does not directly deliver Article 12 logging now, so it only partially contributes to the solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance logging SDK or middleware is the expected, standard engineering response to this mandate, so it is common and unsurprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves R&D ways of working largely unchanged, with only a mild shift toward compliance-by-default in the framework.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance tooling into the framework is a common, legitimate strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal logging middleware/SDK with async capture and pluggable emitters is a moderate engineering effort that fits existing pipelines without radical change, though covering every Annex III category adds some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the mandated events and data fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would automate compliant logging by default across prototypes, though it covers only logging capabilities and not retention, documentation, or the Article 12(3) specifics that apply only to certain systems, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A design-gate checklist for logging is a sensible but fairly common shift-left compliance practice, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template and review gate to the process but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Design review gates and checklists are standard engineering governance that offend no norms, though a mandatory gate may slightly irk researchers.
evidence_implementability: Adding a one-page template and sign-off to the kickoff checklist is a low-cost, non-radical process change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by specifying risk, post-market monitoring, and operational log events up front.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-code logging-contract covering Article 12(2) event categories would help ensure logs exist by design, but it covers only schema definition and not the full mandate (e.g., Annex III 1(a) minimums, implementation, retention verification), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK/middleware is a fairly common and expected response to a logging mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (declarative SDK with YAML schemas) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal tooling for compliance is a standard strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin wrapper library over existing pipelines, validated on two prototypes first, is reasonably feasible with some engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate while protecting R&D speed.
evidence_effectiveness: It would make automatic event logging easy across systems, but it does not by itself decide which events satisfy Article 12 traceability, retention, or Annex III minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mapping pipeline stages to the mandated log fields is the obvious, expected response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance engineering that adds structured logging to products without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing legally mandated logging with encryption and access controls for personal data is a standard, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires mapping pipeline stages and restructuring biometric systems to capture four fields natively, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes but more than trivial engineering work.
