evidence_implementability: One engineer for six weeks on existing infrastructure is a modest, reasonably feasible effort, though building a full biometric verification prototype with all four logging elements requires some real work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building and demonstrating the required logging elements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps de-risk and standardize logging patterns but covers only the Annex III 1(a) case and a single prototype, so it is a partial solution to the lab's overall compliance and R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Using compliance logs as a research dataset is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes the logging obligation from a storage duty into the lab's research agenda, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Mining mandated logs for internal drift research violates no norms, though data-protection and use-limitation issues are possible, and it is a somewhat uncommon use of compliance logs.
evidence_implementability: It needs a new dedicated team, log-mining pipelines and retraining feedback loops, which is reasonably feasible but a real resource commitment.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of getting value from and adapting R&D around the logging obligation, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly address meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure that the logging mandate is met (event coverage, retention, traceability), so it contributes only partially to solving the problem, although it builds on the logs and aids post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking logging overhead is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A benchmarking campaign is a new measurement process but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, though it does let architecture choices be informed by logging cost.
evidence_acceptability: Internal benchmarking is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-week sprint instrumenting five models is modest in scope, though it depends on an SDK from another proposal and on traffic replay setup.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the performance cost of logging, which relates to meeting the logging mandate but is not the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It provides data to inform design choices but does not itself implement logging or achieve compliance, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Using mandated logs as longitudinal data to study lifetime drift is unusual and imaginative, but drift monitoring is a known topic, so it is not fully surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logging into a primary data source for a new research line, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not fully redefine what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for research is a reasonable strategy that offends no norms, though privacy and data-use limits on logs would need care.
evidence_implementability: It needs two deployed prototypes with sustained usage, fine-grained loggers, and new statistical tools, which is a significant but feasible effort.
evidence_applicability: The idea exploits the logging mandate to create research value, which addresses an implied problem of adapting R&D to the mandate but does not directly specify how to meet the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps adapt R&D to the mandate and may yield drift-detection insights, but it does not ensure Article 12 compliance and is exploratory, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A pilot benchmarking log storage and retrieval over long horizons is a sensible, common engineering response to Article 12 and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The pilot introduces a log-retention middleware and tiered storage study but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Instrumenting an existing deployment and benchmarking retention is a standard, uncontroversial engineering approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing object-store infrastructure and a single deployment with modest middleware work, though it needs some engineering effort and is framed as a pilot rather than committed implementation resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 requirement for automatic lifetime logging by testing whether and how it can be done at scale, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It is a feasibility pilot on one system that informs the design pattern but does not itself deliver compliant logging across the portfolio or cover log content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as research telemetry is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, but it is a fairly foreseeable idea rather than a surprising one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science and turning compliance cost into research data, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Using compliance logs for internal analytics and monitoring is a reasonable, somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no norms, though it should account for data protection limits on repurposing logged data.
evidence_implementability: Building lightweight analytics on top of existing log streams and holding quarterly reviews requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses how to respond to the logging mandate and adapt R&D, but the benefit (research value from logs) is an implied problem rather than the direct compliance requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab get value from logging and supports post-market monitoring, but it does not itself satisfy the Article 12 logging requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the development pipeline from the start (compliance by design) is a fairly expected response, though tying it to reproducibility and measuring overhead adds some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the experimental science itself and changes how R&D relates to compliance (embedded rather than retrofitted), which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in development is a legal, normal engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight configurable logging layer in an internal framework tested on three projects is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes to pipeline and tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet Article 12 logging and reduce rework, but it does not specify which events to log per Article 12(2) or Annex III requirements, nor deployment-time logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Keeping documentation current via periodic reviews and a designated owner is a mundane, expected compliance response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a steward role and review cadence but treats compliance as standard documentation and logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation stewards and periodic reviews are common governance practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A quarterly review plus a part-time documentation steward at ten percent time is a modest, non-radical process change using existing staff.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses keeping technical documentation current and reconciled with the Article 12 logs, which is part of the record-keeping obligation, though it does not itself implement the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help maintain documentation and detect modifications via logs but is only a partial solution since it does not build the automatic logging capability itself.

evidence_originality: Log-based anomaly monitoring pipelines are a mundane, expected response to this mandate, with the differentiator framing being commonplace.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice layered on existing MLOps, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Monitoring logs for post-market surveillance is a common, legally aligned strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an observability service on existing MLOps tooling with streaming logs, scheduled queries, and alert escalation is reasonably feasible with some new infrastructure but not radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (monitor logs against thresholds) to get Y (post-market monitoring and risk identification per Articles 72 and 79), which is explicitly part of the Article 12(2) purposes.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses the logging-use and post-market monitoring parts of the mandate but does not itself ensure logs meet Article 12 content requirements (e.g., Annex III specifics) or cover R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging libraries/middleware for compliance are what an experienced evaluator would expect from labs, so the idea is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice packaged as a tool, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin middleware on top of the existing experiment-tracking stack is low-cost and non-radical, though a configurable schema per system category requires some design work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate while preserving R&D speed (do X to get logging compliance).
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver the technical capability for automatic event recording but does not itself ensure the right events, retention, Annex III-specific fields, or documentation obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized reusable logging middleware is a very common and mundane response to a logging mandate, showing little ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice packaged as a shared tool, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging library is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers building an SDK that wraps existing serving infrastructure is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though not trivial across eight projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate across the lab's high-risk projects.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic event logging for the three Article 12(2) categories, but it omits Article 12(3) specifics and the question of what constitutes relevant events and traceability, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-first design with log completeness as a validity criterion is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, though compliance-by-design is a familiar concept.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Weaving logging into the hypothesis stage and experimental validity changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into experimental design is a sensible, legally compliant approach, though treating missing logs as experimental invalidity is a somewhat unusual norm that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: It requires defining event schemas, wiring them into cluster workflows, and changing research protocols, which are real but reasonably feasible process changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly, by avoiding retrofitting of logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would give Article 12 logging for experiments that become high-risk systems, but it does not cover deployment-time logging, the Article 12(3) minimums, or retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging in shared middleware is a standard engineering approach that an experienced evaluator would expect from most labs, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging middleware is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy that offends no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a six-month sprint by three staff and reuses the existing time-series database, so it involves some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, automatic capture of the Article 12(2) event categories across all high-risk systems would satisfy the core logging mandate, though it does not cover Annex III 1(a) minimum items or the documentation requirements explicitly.

evidence_originality: Merging compliance documentation with research-integrity reproducibility records in version-controlled living docs is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but docs-as-code and model-card style approaches are fairly expected responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a unified template, living artefacts linked to reports) and begins to tie compliance to research practice, but it mainly treats compliance as documentation practice without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Unifying documentation with research-integrity standards is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Templates in existing version control with a linking requirement are low-cost and require only modest process changes.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied related problem (documentation and traceability compliance around the logging requirements) rather than the identified logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Article 12 is about automatic event logging, while this proposal addresses technical documentation (Recital 71 and Article 11), so it contributes to traceability but does not deliver the automatic logging mandate itself.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as research data for interpretability and drift studies is an interesting and somewhat imaginative dual-use idea, but labs would plausibly think of it, so it is not rare or surprising enough for the top level.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science and producing publishable outputs from compliance data, which fits paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Analyzing production logs for research is a fairly uncommon but unoffensive strategy, though it raises minor data-protection and use-limitation questions that stop short of being objectionable.
evidence_implementability: It needs one postdoc and 15% of the GPU cluster for six months using existing deployments, which are modest, reasonably feasible changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate by extracting value from the logs, which relates to the stated problem but is not a direct compliance measure.
evidence_effectiveness: It makes use of the logs but does not itself specify how to meet Article 12's logging requirements (event coverage, traceability, retention), so it contributes only partially to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by design and open-sourcing a reference implementation is a sensible, fairly expected response, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an open-source reference architecture with logging built in by design) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, though the partner-demonstration angle is minor.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source, compliance-by-design logging violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Adding schema-driven logging middleware to an existing serving stack and benchmarking overhead is reasonably feasible, though the open-source reference and pipeline integration need some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by recording the specific Annex III(1)(a) fields and building compliance into the pipeline.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate for the Annex III 1(a) case, but it covers only that case and does not address the broader Article 12 event-recording purposes (risk situations, post-market monitoring), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning log compliance into a public, shared benchmark is unusual and shows imagination, though benchmarks and open tooling are a familiar format in AI research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance a research product and a public good, positioning the lab as a reference for traceability science.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing evaluation tooling is a somewhat uncommon strategy for compliance but offends no legal or social norms and is welcomed by regulators.
evidence_implementability: Building synthetic scenarios, instrumenting open-weight models and releasing a test harness is a sizable but reasonably feasible effort for an AI lab, though it needs real resources and a validated mapping from the legal text to metrics.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of verifying that logging meets Article 12 requirements, which relates to the stated problem but is not the direct step of implementing the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark and CI test harness would help verify the lab's own logs capture Article 12(2) event categories, but it does not itself implement logging or cover the whole mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tying documentation updates to release gating is a common, mundane compliance step with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and documentation practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Release-gated documentation updates by a named owner are a common governance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a template, named owners, and a release-tag block in the versioning system needs some process changes but is reasonably feasible at modest cost.

evidence_effectiveness: Up-to-date technical files help traceability and compliance but do not implement the automatic event logging that Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates in the SDLC modeled on safety reviews are a common, mundane response to regulatory mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A release checkpoint with a checklist is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.

evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking that logging capabilities satisfy Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-deployment gate verifying Article 12(2) logging purposes would help ensure compliance but only covers verification, not the actual logging design, paragraph 3 specifics, or retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A purpose-built logging module mapped to the regulation's listed fields is the obvious, mundane response most labs would give.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a dedicated logging module to meet Article 12(3) is a common, lawful compliance strategy that offends no norms, with legal review of retention against data-protection rules.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a dedicated logging service with tamper-evident storage, QA test cases, and legal review, which is some change but reasonably feasible with standard engineering.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the four minimum fields specified in Article 12(3) for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the prescriptive minimum logging for biometric systems, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) products and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging or the lab's wider R&D, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as shared research data infrastructure is a somewhat unusual, interesting angle, but not wholly surprising since many labs would consider dual-use of logs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science (logs as experimental records), though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A unified, tamper-evident log archive with a research data lake violates no norms, though sharing logs across groups raises minor data-governance questions.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a unified schema, tamper-evident archive, and shared data lake with cross-team coordination, which is reasonably feasible but a notable engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D practice, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would satisfy the logging mandate and add research value, but it omits specifics such as Article 12(2) event coverage, retention, and the Annex III minimums, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Implementing the mandated log fields as a prototype with an auditor query test is an expected, mundane response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice, with a schema and a queryable store, and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliant logging and a demo artifact for Compliance and Legal is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over three weeks with a defined schema and a mock auditor test suite is a modest, low-cost effort that needs only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the four Article 12(3) minimum logging fields for Annex III point 1(a) systems, which is an explicit part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would satisfy the prescriptive logging requirements for biometric systems, but it covers only the point 1(a) category and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging across the lab's other systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building default-on compliance logging into an internal SDK is a sensible and fairly expected engineering response, so it is interesting but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (an SDK-embedded telemetry module parameterised by system category) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves R&D's relationship to compliance basically unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging by default in internal tooling is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing base framework with a telemetry module that emits JSON to an append-only store is a moderate engineering effort within the lab's own control, requiring some changes but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, naming specific required fields such as timestamps, reference databases, and matched inputs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would automate the Article 12 logging capability and Annex III 1(a) minimum fields during development, but it leaves out production retention, tamper-resistance, human verifier identification, and the post-market monitoring use of logs, so it only partly solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Treating logs as first-class experimental output is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, but 'shift-left' logging in pipelines is a fairly expected response and not surprising.

evidence_acceptability: Integrating logging into experiment workflows is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms, though PIs may mildly resist the added mandatory stage.

evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by generating automatic event logs including the Article 12(3) items, though it mostly targets training and validation runs rather than deployed system operation.
evidence_effectiveness: Native logging in development pipelines would help traceability but Article 12 concerns logging of the high-risk system's operation over its lifetime, so this is only a partial solution without deployment-time logging.

evidence_originality: Building logging into a default SDK template is a sensible and fairly expected 'compliance by design' response, so it is more interesting than mundane but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (middleware, JSON schemas, a default template) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: It is an ordinary engineering and compliance strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring an internal SDK into a thin middleware layer with schemas is a moderate engineering change within the lab's control and at reasonable cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, by pre-wiring the specific Article 12 minimum fields into new Annex III projects.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic recording of the Article 12(3) fields for new projects, but it does not cover existing systems, the Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or the wider documentation duties, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Public transparency reports are a familiar corporate compliance and marketing move, so the idea is common rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a reporting document but treats compliance as standard logging and documentation practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing transparency reports and attaching summaries to contracts is a common, norm-compliant practice, though disclosing logging details may raise mild security or IP concerns.
evidence_implementability: An annual report drafted by communications with engineering input and legal review is a modest, low-cost addition that requires no changes to the systems themselves.
evidence_applicability: It relates to the stated problem only indirectly, by signaling compliance and providing a customer log-retrieval description, which implies a benefit (goodwill, procurement) rather than solving the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The report does not implement or ensure the automatic logging mandate of Article 12; it only communicates about logging, so it would contribute at best marginally to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging by design with a shared SDK and CI checks is the standard, expected response and is common and mundane.

evidence_acceptability: Building compliance into engineering architecture is a common, normative strategy that violates no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared SDK and integrating it across product teams with CI/CD tests requires some changes and coordination but is reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate (do X, get compliant automatic event logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a shared logging SDK with schemas mapped to Article 12 and CI/CD testing would substantially satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address broader documentation or Article 12(2) event-relevance judgments, so it is close to a full solution of the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance checkpoints in project lifecycles are a common, expected response, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adjusts the process by adding gates and sprint checkpoints but still treats compliance as a logging practice within the lab's existing way of working.
evidence_acceptability: Adding logging-design reviews and validation gates to project lifecycles is a standard, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires modest process changes such as retrofitting planning templates and adding checkpoints, which is reasonably feasible but needs PI buy-in and some overhead.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring logging is designed and validated before testing and deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: Early logging-design review and validation gates would help ensure Article 12 logging capability is built in, but the proposal doesn't specify what logs to capture or the Article 12(2)/(3) content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-first or compliance-by-design sequencing is a commonly expected response, with a mildly interesting framing of an instrumentation-first pipeline but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (log schema gate, early review) but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing development approach, though the reordering changes the workflow somewhat.
evidence_acceptability: Reordering development so logging is built first and adding checklist gates and early code review are ordinary engineering-process changes that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires changing the pipeline order, the definition-of-ready checklist and review timing, which are some process changes but cheap and reasonably feasible without new infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by adapting R&D workflow to avoid retrofitting logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Building the logging layer first would help ensure Article 12 logging capability exists, but it covers only part of the mandate (it does not specify which events to log, retention, or Article 12(3) specifics, and it applies only to new prototypes), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Linking Article 12 event definition to interpretability research is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is a fairly expected move for a research lab and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It ties compliance logging to the lab's core interpretability research, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than just adding a logging tool.
evidence_acceptability: Experimental research on logging granularity violates no norms and regulators and stakeholders would find it reasonable, though framing it as a research programme is somewhat unusual compared with plain compliance.
evidence_implementability: Running controlled logging experiments across several architectures at varying granularities is feasible for an AI lab, but token-level activation logging is costly and the work needs significant research effort and uncertain timelines.
evidence_applicability: It targets an implied problem, the ambiguity of what counts as a relevant event in Article 12(2) across architectures, which clearly relates to the stated need to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy of loggable events validated by experiments on reconstruction fidelity would address the core question of what to log under Article 12(2), but it is a research programme that yields definitions and does not itself deliver the logging mechanism, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning logging overhead into an open benchmark is an interesting, somewhat imaginative idea, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance measurement a research output, which stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open benchmark of logging costs is somewhat unusual for compliance but offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It reallocates one postdoc and a small GPU budget for a year to instrument five existing models, which requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet logging requirements within resource limits by quantifying costs and guiding design, though the link to actually implementing logs is implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It yields cost data to inform architecture choices but does not itself implement the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning logging overhead into an open benchmark is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but benchmarking overhead is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes the compliance constraint as a research question yielding publications and reputation, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches broadly.
evidence_acceptability: Internal benchmarking and publishing a preprint is a common, norm-respecting research strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two existing postdocs, no new hires, and instrumenting current models with logging tiers over two quarters is a small, low-cost, non-radical effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the performance cost of compliant logging, which relates to meeting the logging mandate but is not the mandate's core requirements directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Measuring overhead helps design logging but does not itself implement Article 12 logging mandate content, so it contributes only partially to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: A reusable centralized logging module is the obvious, expected engineering response to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging library mandated at architecture review is a new tool and process but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging libraries and architecture-review gates are standard engineering governance that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared library and integrating it into all high-risk projects requires some engineering effort and process change but is reasonably feasible with existing practices.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate, including the Article 12(1) requirement and the paragraph 3 minimum data points.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging library with schemas and QA validation would directly deliver the automatic event recording Article 12 requires, though it does not cover the Article 12(2) event-relevance judgments or documentation obligations in full.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance documentation into a public open standard is interesting and shows some imagination, but open documentation templates (model cards, datasheets) are familiar so it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance a source of community leadership and public good, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source community standards and workshop feedback are legally and socially acceptable, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response, with no offense to sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small team drafting a schema over two quarters, piloting on three publications and releasing open source is reasonably feasible with some changes and moderate resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified, related problem (documenting and record-keeping compliance for Article 12/Recital 71) though the implied logging gap remains, so it applies to the stated problem via a clearly related need.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation template addresses Recital 71 technical documentation but does not itself deliver automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Shared logging libraries and compliance-by-default scaffolding are fairly standard engineering responses, with the block-instantiation-without-logging gate a mildly clever touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tooling approach (scaffold-enforced library) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library embedded in scaffolding is a common engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineer-weeks to spec plus wiring into an existing scaffolding CLI is modest, requiring some changes but reasonably feasible measures at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate by capturing events relevant to 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: It would ensure every prototype has automatic logging, but it does not address Article 12(3) specifics, retention, traceability appropriateness, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Lifetime-cost budgeting for compliance is a sensible but fairly mundane administrative idea, with some interest in framing it as competitiveness with pure-research bids.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a funding-template process element but treats compliance as a cost-management practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a lifetime maintenance budget line with annual review is a conventional, norm-compliant financial governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a revision of funding templates and charters by the grants office plus an annual review, which is a modest, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses funding the lifetime log storage, retention and documentation upkeep that Article 12 implies, but it is an implied funding problem rather than the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting ensures resources exist for lifetime logging but does not itself build logging capability or ensure the logs meet Article 12 content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing mandatory logs as a scientific dataset for studying drift and feeding continuous learning is an unusual, imaginative angle beyond typical compliance responses, though not wholly unprecedented (post-deployment monitoring research).
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logs into the science and creating partner-based data offerings born from compliance, but does not alter what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymised logs with deployment partners is a somewhat uncommon strategy that does not offend norms, though data-protection and partner consent concerns exist.
evidence_implementability: Aggregating anonymised event streams across partners, building dashboards and a feedback loop requires significant data-sharing agreements, privacy engineering and infrastructure, making it difficult but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (extracting value from compliance cost and adapting R&D) related to the stated problem rather than directly meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: The programme leverages logs for research but does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met (Article 12 capabilities, minimum contents); it only contributes a partial benefit to the compliance response.

evidence_originality: Gap audits are a standard, mundane first response to any new regulation and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A internal gap audit against Article 12 is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week audit with a small existing team is low-cost and non-radical, though mapping every system in two weeks is slightly ambitious.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by determining what is missing and what to fix.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit identifies gaps and remediation effort but does not itself implement logging, so it only partially solves the problem; it also centers on Article 12(3), which applies only to Annex III point 1(a) systems, not all high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: Shared centralized logging infrastructure is a common, mundane response that evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice (shared infrastructure) that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared centralized logging layer is a common, lawful engineering approach that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses idle storage nodes and existing HPC allocation with a lightweight ingestion API, requiring some integration work from each model team but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 mandate for automatic event recording (logs) for high-risk systems, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Centralized infrastructure would provide automatic recording capability, but it does not specify which events are logged to meet Article 12(2) purposes or Annex III minimum fields, nor retention or traceability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable shared logging component in existing CI is a common, mundane engineering response that evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-as-logging practice implemented as a shared library, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing shared infrastructure and existing budgets is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared module dropped into existing CI/CD pipelines and funded from current maintenance budgets involves only non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specific required log fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would implement Article 12(1) and the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, but covers only logging capture and not the broader obligations (Art 12(2) event relevance, retention, documentation, or R&D adaptation), so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning a logging obligation into a publishable benchmark for lifetime logging integrity is unusual and shows some imagination, though benchmark publishing is a familiar research move.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a research output and a scientific contribution, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, but it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing benchmarks and publishing research is socially and legally acceptable, and a lab might only worry about disclosing details of its own systems.
evidence_implementability: It needs a dedicated research group and long-horizon simulated deployment scenarios, which is a significant and costly commitment that is still feasible.
evidence_applicability: The idea is a benchmark for logging integrity over time, which relates to the logging mandate only indirectly, since it measures logging quality in general and does not state how the lab will meet its own Article 12 duties.
evidence_effectiveness: Publishing a benchmark would not make the lab's own systems compliant with Article 12, so it is at best a minor contribution and probably will not solve the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Unifying regulatory documentation with internal reproducibility records in version control is a sensible but fairly expected response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from many labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (metadata schemas, doc-steward role) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation repositories and steward roles are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing version control with schemas and a rotating steward role is low cost and requires non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets record-keeping and traceability requirements, but mainly the documentation part rather than the automatic logging mandate, so the link is to an implied sub-problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses technical documentation under Recital 71 but does not provide automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it only partially solves the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Wrapping inference with auto-stamped compliance metadata is a sensible but fairly expected developer-tooling response, with some thoughtful touches like zero researcher burden.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK/middleware) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely automating it.
evidence_acceptability: Automated logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial compliance approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: An internal SDK with context-managers and middleware over inference calls is a modest engineering effort using standard tooling, though it requires some changes to existing workflows and an event store.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified logging mandate (reference database, matched input, verifier identity) named in the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would capture the Article 12(3) fields for biometric systems, but does not address the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event logging for risk, post-market monitoring, or non-biometric systems, nor log retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-tests in CI is a well-known shift-left practice, so it is sensible but not especially surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (CI gates) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using CI gates for compliance checks is a common engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It adds schema-validation fixtures to an existing CI runner, which is a modest change, though it requires writing fixtures for each high-risk system class.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically checking that required log events are emitted during development.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch missing or malformed event emissions early, but it only verifies schema conformity and does not ensure the events are the right ones or that retention and traceability are met, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Front-loading requirements and design reviews, as in privacy-by-design or design gates, is a familiar approach, so the idea is sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a process step and template but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A short design session, a one-page template, and peer review by the compliance lead are common, uncontroversial governance practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: A half-day session and a one-page template are low-cost, non-radical additions to the prototyping process that are easy to adopt.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by defining what events to log in line with Article 12(2) criteria.
evidence_effectiveness: A design gate for log taxonomy tied to Article 12(2) would help ensure logs capture risk-relevant events, but it only covers design planning and not the technical logging implementation, retention enforcement, or Annex III-specific minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Ring-fencing headcount for compliance is a common, mundane management response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard resource allocation for compliance and leaves the lab's R&D and compliance relationship essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Dedicated compliance staffing and ring-fenced hours are a common, uncontroversial management strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Ring-fencing 8% of engineering headcount via the next quarterly resource plan and an existing sign-off mechanism is a resourcing decision that mirrors current practice, so it needs only modest changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of resourcing logging work predictably, which relates to how the lab meets the logging mandate, but it does not itself specify any logging measure.
evidence_effectiveness: Dedicated capacity helps the lab deliver logging architecture reliably, but it is only a partial solution because it defines no logging content or design and does not ensure Article 12 requirements are met.

evidence_originality: Quantifying proportionality and seeking to become the reference source is an unusual and somewhat imaginative approach compared with typical logging-implementation responses, though not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a formal decision model, regulatory engagement, academic positioning) and shifts the lab toward shaping interpretation of its obligations, but it still treats compliance as a logging-granularity question rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Submitting to a consultation and publishing a preprint are legitimate, somewhat uncommon strategies that offend no norms, though the claimed Article 71 database data and implementing acts are somewhat shaky.
evidence_implementability: A small team over two sprints is feasible, but calibrating a defensible quantitative model on limited public incident data is difficult and the output may not be adopted, so it requires some real effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (ambiguity about how much logging is proportionate) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate, rather than directly implementing logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A proportionality formula and position paper might help interpret 'appropriate to the intended purpose' but does not itself deliver logging capability or ensure the lab meets the Article 12 mandate, so it is at best a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with owners and periodic audits is a familiar, mundane compliance practice that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a governance workflow but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A governance workflow with owners and audits is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Assigning documentation owners, update triggers and quarterly audits is a modest process change using existing staff and tooling, though it takes some organizational effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of record-keeping and audit readiness tied to Article 12, though it mostly targets documentation rather than the logging mandate itself, so the link is somewhat implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation and logs aligned and audit-ready, but it does not itself implement the automatic logging capability Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing logging in rather than bolting it on is a well-known compliance-by-design practice that experienced evaluators would expect, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice with slight process reordering, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-by-design-style compliance engineering is a common, norm-respecting strategy that violates no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Designing logging in from the start with a standard interface is reasonably feasible but requires changes to engineering process and tamper-evident storage infrastructure for each deployed instance.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by implementing logging capability in the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Building automatic, tamper-evident event logging into system architecture with a defined interface would, if done, satisfy the core Article 12(1) mandate to technically allow automatic recording of events, though specifics like Annex III 1(a) fields and event relevance to Art 79/72/26(5) are only partly addressed.

evidence_originality: Mapping existing tooling to regulatory requirements is a mundane, expected first step with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance gap-mapping that treats the obligation as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance gap analysis is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week inventory by existing engineers using current tools is low-cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by identifying which Article 12 requirements are already covered and which gaps remain.
evidence_effectiveness: It is a reasonable preparatory step that avoids redundant builds but does not itself implement logging, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Treating loggability as an architectural design property is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, though 'interpretable/traceable architectures' is a known research theme and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making traceability a first-order architectural research variable and redirecting what the lab researches, which addresses the larger problem of research direction.
evidence_acceptability: Investing in research on traceable architectures offends no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat unusual to frame compliance as a research agenda.
evidence_implementability: Two senior researchers for eighteen months prototyping three architectures is a significant, uncertain research commitment, but feasible within a lab's resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making future systems inherently loggable and adapting R&D) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate or adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, 18 months of architecture prototyping and benchmarks would not deliver the Article 12 logging capability now required, so it only partially contributes to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the model objective is unusual and imaginative, though related ideas such as interpretability and self-explaining models exist, so it is not fully surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into model design and the lab's research agenda, addressing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Research on self-documenting architectures and publishing open benchmarks violates no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual response to a logging mandate.
evidence_implementability: Designing new architectures trained under joint accuracy and log-fidelity objectives is a multi-year, expensive research programme with uncertain outcomes, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets Article 12's requirement for automatic event logging over the system lifetime, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, model-emitted logs would not by themselves cover the Article 12 minimum items such as reference databases, user identification, and usage periods, nor retention, so it only partially solves the problem and is slow to deliver.

evidence_originality: Shared centralized logging services are a standard, expected engineering response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared tool but still treats compliance as logging infrastructure, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized internal logging platform is a common, legally and socially unobjectionable engineering strategy.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team within existing budget and a two-person-day SDK integration is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though centralizing schemas across diverse projects takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate across high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide the logging infrastructure but does not itself define which events to log, and covers only part of the compliance need such as risk-relevant event content and Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Budgeting compliance costs is a sensible, somewhat uncommon angle compared with technical logging responses, but it is not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (mandatory budget category) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only adding cost accounting around it.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a budget line item to proposals is a common administrative strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page template update to existing grant and charter processes is easy and low-cost, with only a modest added burden on PIs.
evidence_applicability: Funding log storage and documentation upkeep addresses an implied problem (resourcing Article 12 compliance) that relates to the stated problem but does not itself specify how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting for traceability makes sure compliance work is resourced, which helps, but it does not produce logging capability or meet the mandate on its own, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared central log repository is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as a logging/storage practice with a shared service, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised log retention on existing infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing HPC storage with a dedicated partition and lightweight API requires modest changes at low cost, though lifecycle and access-control design add some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses retaining and serving logs over system lifetime for post-market monitoring and audits, which is part of the stated logging-mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It handles storage, retention and query but not what events are logged, tamper-resistance, or Article 12 content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code tests in CI/CD are a fairly common and expected engineering response, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/process (CI conformance tests) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Pytest fixtures, mock endpoints and CI hooks are standard tooling that a lab can build at low cost with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking the Article 12 paragraph 3 fields, i.e., do X (CI tests) to get Y (verified compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: Automated CI tests verifying log fields and schema would reliably ensure logging capability is present, but they cover only verification of format, not the full logging mandate (design of event capture, retention, Article 12(2) relevance), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A traceability benchmark with a public leaderboard for logging schemas is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, but benchmark-building is a familiar research move.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new element (a benchmark and leaderboard) and ties R&D evaluation to compliance, but it still centers on logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open benchmarks with auditors and legal experts is a collaborative, norm-consistent practice, though somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Curating 200 ground-truthed scenario pairs with a small cross-disciplinary team and running an annual leaderboard is reasonably feasible, though it needs sustained effort and external coordination.
evidence_applicability: The benchmark targets Article 12(2) logging for risk identification and post-market monitoring, but it mainly builds a field-wide evaluation tool rather than directly meeting the lab's own logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark would help define appropriate traceability and test logging schemas, but it would not itself implement compliant logging in the lab's systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A gap analysis plus retrofitted log emitters is the obvious, common response expected from labs facing this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logging to meet a regulation using existing resources is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: A six-week sprint on existing infrastructure with no new hardware and costs absorbed into opex is easy and low-cost, though it needs some engineering changes to the pipelines.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by mapping existing pipelines to Article 12(1)-(3) and adding log emitters to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If carried out it would close the logging gaps and substantially satisfy Article 12, though it is limited to a gap analysis plus instrumentation and does not address retention, log governance, or the system-specific Annex III minimums in depth, so it is reasonable but only a mostly complete solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing telemetry and monitoring infrastructure for compliance logging is a fairly expected, cost-driven response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as a logging infrastructure matter and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged, though infrastructure-layer capture is a slight twist.
evidence_acceptability: Repurposing internal infrastructure for compliance is a common practice that violates no norms, though the reuse of reproducibility storage for logs needs some care over retention and access.
evidence_implementability: Using already-funded servers, data lake, and storage with lightweight agents and schema templates is low-cost and non-radical, though it requires some engineering work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate in paragraph one and the four Annex III 1(a) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide the automatic recording capability and the Annex III 1(a) fields, but it does not address the broader Article 12(2) traceability purposes, retention, or the choice of events, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logging as a research and publication topic is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but compression and selective logging are fairly familiar ideas.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element, a research thread, and reframes compliance cost as an IP and publication asset, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance a little, though it still centres on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research on efficient compliant logging is a normal activity, but selective recording could raise regulator concerns about whether it still meets Article 12, so it is a slightly unusual strategy.
evidence_implementability: It needs only one postdoc and one engineer, an internal grant and an existing testbed, so it is cheap and non-radical, though the research outcome is uncertain.
evidence_applicability: It targets Article 12's logging requirements directly by researching ways to meet the minimum logging mandate with less storage and privacy overhead, which is part of the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It is a six-month exploratory research project that might yield techniques, not a way to implement compliant logging now, so it contributes only partially to the solution and the lab still needs a baseline logging system.

evidence_originality: A dedicated tamper-evident log and document archive with a records team is a standard, expected response to record-keeping mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a platform and a records unit but treats compliance as ordinary logging and documentation practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Dedicated compliance records infrastructure is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Provisioning an internal document/log service with access control and a two-person unit requires some new infrastructure and staffing but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and keeping documentation current across system lifetimes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially support retention and upkeep of logs and documentation, but it does not by itself ensure systems technically generate the required event logs or that the content meets Article 12(2)-(3) requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware layered onto existing pipelines is the most common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice built as infrastructure, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging tooling adopted incrementally is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team building an optional layer over one quarter within existing experiment-tracking infrastructure is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by capturing the Article 12(2) event types to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to meeting the logging mandate, but being optional and incremental with no detail on Article 12(3) specifics or log retention and integrity, it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Earmarking a maintenance pool is a sensible, fairly familiar financial-governance move, somewhat interesting in how it is tied to project close-out but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A ring-fenced budget line is a new financial process, but it still treats compliance as a cost-management and logging-maintenance practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Dedicated budget reserves funded by a share of project revenue are a normal corporate practice that offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: It needs finance-office policy changes and a revenue-allocation rule, which is a reasonably feasible administrative change at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of funding lifetime logging and documentation obligations, which relates to meeting the mandate but does not itself address how to do the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Funding secures the resources for ongoing compliance, which helps, but it does not build the logging capability or ensure the technical content of Article 12 is met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated CI testing of log schema conformance is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response, with modest interest in shifting verification left.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI test harness) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Parameterised pytest cases in existing CI pipelines are low-cost and require non-radical changes, though synthetic session replay needs some setup.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need to verify that Article 12(3) logging fields are correctly recorded, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure log fields are present and consistent but does not itself deliver the logging capability or address broader Article 12 duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design and compliance review gates are fairly familiar ideas (privacy/audit by design), so it is interesting but shows only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes logging as an architectural invariant that also feeds scientific analysis, changing how R&D relates to compliance somewhat, though it remains largely within logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into model architecture and adding a code-review gate are legitimate engineering and compliance practices that offend no norms, though slightly less common than standard wrappers.
evidence_implementability: Embedding event-emitters in inference pipelines and instituting a review gate requires some architectural changes and process additions but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate by making models automatically record events, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Native logging plus a pre-deployment review gate would substantially support Article 12 compliance, but the gate checks 'on paper' and Article 12(3) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems, leaving it a strong partial solution rather than complete coverage of retention, 12(2) purposes, and post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: Treating log richness as an optimisation target in an internal competition is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly unprecedented given auditability and explainability challenges.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It explicitly reframes compliance as a design objective woven into the research itself, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: An internal competition violates no norms, though diverting scarce resources and trading off accuracy could draw some mild resistance, so it is somewhat uncommon but inoffensive.
evidence_implementability: Running three teams for six months building a novel system with new evaluation panels and third-party reconstruction criteria is a significant resource commitment and hard to define, but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It targets the implied problem of building logging-capable, auditable systems, which relates to the logging mandate but not directly to compliance of the lab's existing systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A design competition would yield architectures with rich logs, but it is a six-month exploratory exercise on one example system and does not itself ensure the lab's actual high-risk systems meet Article 12, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Middleware interceptor logging to an immutable store on an existing event bus is a common, mundane engineering response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal middleware logging layer with an immutable store is a common, norm-compliant way to meet Article 12.
evidence_implementability: Two FTEs for one quarter reusing the existing Kafka bus and current hardware is a low-cost, non-radical change with a concrete plan.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by capturing timestamp, input reference, match and verifier identity, which map onto Article 12(3) items.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the core automatic-recording requirement for Annex III systems, though it covers only part of Article 12(2) purposes like risk-situation identification and does not address R&D adaptation or documentation.

evidence_originality: A cross-team compliance pod that meets biweekly is a fairly common organizational response to regulatory mandates and shows little ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (the pod) but still treats compliance as a logging-obligation mapping practice without changing how R&D itself works.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance staff in project teams with modest internal budget reallocation is a standard practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Reallocating about 15% FTE and holding biweekly meetings within the existing budget requires only modest, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how the lab should organize to meet the logging mandate by mapping obligations and sequencing the work into sprints.
evidence_effectiveness: The pod helps identify obligations and avoid late rework but does not itself build logging capabilities or ensure technical adequacy, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Version-controlled documentation registries with owners are a common, expected compliance response, with the log-to-documentation consistency check adding only a minor twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a version-controlled repository with automated cross-checks and a named owner, which is standard compliance documentation practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation ownership and audit-ready technical files are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Setting up a registry, assigning owners and adding automated cross-checks requires some process changes and tooling but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The registry directly addresses the documentation and traceability aims in Recital 71 and ties to log consistency, though it focuses more on technical documentation than on the Article 12 logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A living documentation registry with log cross-checks would contribute to traceability and audit readiness but does not itself implement automatic event logging or the specific Article 12(2)-(3) log content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a prototype to de-risk logging requirements is a common, expected response with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A time-boxed prototype logging microservice is standard compliance engineering that treats the mandate as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A feasibility prototype against a legal requirement is a conventional strategy that violates no norms, though biometric work carries mild sensitivity.
evidence_implementability: A two-week spike by one engineer pair using an open-source model and the existing event bus is low-cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(3) logging fields for Annex III 1(a), which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The spike de-risks the most demanding clause and informs design but is only a simplified prototype, so it contributes to rather than fully solves compliance.

evidence_originality: A standing post-market log review team is a mundane, expected response to monitoring obligations with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a staffed team and anomaly scripts but treats compliance as standard logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A dedicated compliance and monitoring team is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
