evidence_implementability: Staffing four people and running weekly anomaly scripts is a modest, reasonably feasible organizational change with moderate recurring cost.
evidence_applicability: The unit directly targets using logs to identify Article 79(1) risk situations and support post-market monitoring, which are explicit purposes of the logging mandate, though it presumes logs already exist rather than addressing how to build the logging capability.
evidence_effectiveness: Continuous log review contributes to meeting monitoring and traceability aims but does not itself implement the Article 12 logging capability or the minimum logging content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying statistical process control to logs to anticipate substantial-modification determinations is an unusual and interesting idea that shows some imagination, but not a wholly surprising one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logging into publishable research and a commercial offering, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for drift monitoring and early-warning compliance signals offends no legal or social norms, though pairing it with commercial offerings is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated research track, statistical models trained on historical logs, and dashboard integration, which is a significant effort and the reliability of detecting 'substantial modification' algorithmically is uncertain, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, identifying situations of risk or substantial modification under Art. 12(2)(a), which relates to the stated mandate but is not the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help flag possible substantial modifications but does not itself deliver the core logging mandate (automatic event recording across the lifetime), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Continuous documentation tied to commits and experiment tracking is a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice with a mild automation twist and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date technical documentation is a common, expected compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning a postdoc per project and syncing a documentation repository with an existing experiment tracker needs some staffing and integration work but uses ordinary tooling, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the documentation/record-keeping obligation from Recital 71, which is closely related to but not the same as the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping documentation current helps traceability and audit readiness but does not itself implement the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a module that logs the four Article 12(3) minimum fields is the most obvious, expected response to the mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice packaged as a reusable library, leaving the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging modules and validating them against mock audits is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-quarter sprint with the platform team producing a reusable library is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes but no radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It explicitly does X (log the four mandated fields) to get Y (meet Article 12(3) for biometric systems), which is directly part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The module would directly satisfy the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging fields, but it covers only part of the broader Article 12 mandate (1, 2) and not general-purpose logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory compliance logs as a longitudinal scientific dataset is an unusual and imaginative reframing that most labs would not offer, though it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and turning the obligation into a research asset, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for internal research is somewhat unusual and raises possible data-protection and purpose-limitation concerns, but it offends no norms outright and is broadly acceptable.
evidence_implementability: Adding schema annotations and condition tags to log entries needs some engineering work and cross-team partnership, but it is reasonably feasible with existing logging infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly uses the Article 12 logs and tags them with schema annotations, so it addresses how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D, though its main aim is research value rather than compliance itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Annotated logs would still satisfy the logging mandate and add research value, but the proposal does not ensure compliance with Article 12's specific content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design gates and architecture reviews are a common, expected response, though the framing around protecting research momentum adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a process element (a gate and template) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifting it earlier in the project lifecycle.
evidence_acceptability: A design-stage gate using a charter template and internal reviewers is a common governance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It adds a one-page template to an existing charter process and a two-week review by existing staff, which is a small, non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 automatic logging mandate by ensuring logging architecture is specified before development of high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is designed in and avoids retrofitting, but it only governs architecture specification, not the actual implementation, the content of logs per Article 12(2)-(3), or ongoing compliance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default starter templates are a sensible and fairly expected approach, interesting but not surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (templates, schema mapping) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only shifting it earlier in the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Templates and checklists are a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring internal GitLab starter templates with an SDK, schema file, and checklist is a modest, reasonably feasible change using existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how the lab meets the Article 12 logging mandate by embedding required log fields (Annex III 1(a) items) into new projects, so X yields Y which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would ensure new high-risk prototypes have native logging, but it covers only new projects (not legacy systems), omits deployment-level retention and operational monitoring, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying contract testing and property-based fuzzing in CI to logging schemas is a sensible, somewhat imaginative adaptation of standard software practice, but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (versioned contracts, fuzz tests in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional engineering quality practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Schema contracts, property-based tests and CI gating use mature tooling and fit existing engineering workflows at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses a identified sub-problem of the logging mandate, keeping logs consistent and complete over the system's lifetime as required by Article 12(1), so it is related to the stated problem though it covers only schema continuity.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help guarantee schema continuity across lifecycle changes but does not decide which events to log, cover Article 12(2) relevance or 12(3) minimum content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging middleware embedded in the development template is a common, expected response to this mandate and is not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice with a reusable module, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into system architecture is a common, expected compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a reusable logging middleware and wiring it into the standard development template requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing automatic event recording (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: A built-in logging layer capturing events across the lifetime would directly satisfy the Article 12(1) mandate for the lab's systems, though it leaves the specific Article 12(3) fields and retention details unspecified.

evidence_originality: Exposing Article 12 logs to clients as a product feature is an interesting and somewhat unusual twist on compliance, but not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by turning logging into a customer-facing product and market differentiator, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Customer-scoped read-only log access under contract is a fairly common and legitimate practice, though the privacy of logged input data and personal identifiers needs care.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a thin REST API, a dashboard, and contract-scoped access on top of an existing logging pipeline, which is reasonably feasible with some added security and multi-tenant work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely how to extract value from or add benefit to compliance logging, which relates to but is not the stated mandate to log and adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: A client-facing API depends on a logging SDK from another proposal and does not itself meet the logging mandate, so it contributes only partially to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code gating in CI/CD is a well-known, mundane approach to regulatory requirements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It applies standard compliance and logging practice via existing tooling without changing how the lab works or relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal engineering gates and compliance checks in CI are a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a checklist and automated log-simulation test to existing CI/CD is a reasonably feasible change, though defining tests for the log fields takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building the required log fields into R&D outputs.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI/CD gate enforcing Article 12(3) logging fields would ensure prototypes natively have those logs, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event logging, retention, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Costing compliance into grant budgets is a sensible but fairly predictable administrative response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new financial tool but still treats compliance as a cost of logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though it adds a new process element.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting compliance costs in grant proposals is a conventional, norm-compliant financial practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A finance analyst can build a spreadsheet-style cost model from existing pilot log-volume data and add it as a mandatory grant attachment, requiring only modest process changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (budgeting for lifetime logging costs) that relates to the stated problem of how to respond to the logging mandate, but it does not itself meet the logging mandate or adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab fund and plan for compliance but only partially contributes, since it does not implement logging or ensure Article 12 conformity.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware is the standard, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little that is surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, which is mildly new at most.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging middleware built on OpenTelemetry is a common, norm-abiding engineering approach to compliance that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-engineer, six-week prototype is modest, though integrating across all projects and meeting a 2 ms latency budget requires some changes, making it reasonably feasible rather than trivially easy.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets Article 12 event categories and Annex III 1(a) fields, which are explicitly the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would substantially deliver the automatic logging capability, but it covers only logging and not documentation, retention, or deployer obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance logging into a shared internal library or template is a fairly standard, expected engineering response and is not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance and logging tool that automates practice without changing how the lab does R&D or relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal shared library embedded in standard templates is a common engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin internal middleware with config-driven mapping is reasonably feasible, though serialization, storage, and retention infrastructure require some development and adoption effort.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(1) automatic event-logging mandate across the lab's R&D projects.
evidence_effectiveness: Default automatic logging in every scaffolded prototype would largely satisfy the logging mandate, but it does not itself ensure that the logged events are the ones relevant to Article 12(2) or Article 12(3) purposes, nor retention, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Budgeting for compliance in proposals is a common, mundane administrative response and not surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and project-management practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Requiring budget lines and withholding funding for missing estimates is a common, uncontroversial project-governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a budget field to a proposal template and review forms is a simple administrative change at low cost, though reviewers must judge Annex III tier estimates.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of resourcing and planning for logging obligations, which relates to but is not directly the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting only ensures resources are earmarked and does not itself implement logging or satisfy Article 12, so it is a helpful but partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code generation in CI/CD is a known practice applied to compliance, which is interesting and sensible but not highly imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (doc-generation job in CI) but still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation within existing engineering workflows is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing build pipeline and repository metadata, requiring some tooling and discipline in metadata capture but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified related problem of keeping technical documentation up to date under Recital 71, which relates to but is not the logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Auto-generated documentation would keep technical documentation current, but it does not implement the Article 12 event logging mandate itself (automatic recording of events, Art. 12(3) specifics), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A log-completeness validator is an expected, fairly mundane response to the mandate, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-checking tool that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, though it adds a new tool element.
evidence_acceptability: Internal log self-audits for regulatory compliance are a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Automated checks over existing logs and a weekly scheduled run in the monitoring pipeline need some build effort but are reasonably feasible with no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified part of the stated problem, meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate for biometric systems, with a clear do-X-to-get-Y link.
evidence_effectiveness: A validator that checks live logs for the four Article 12(3) minimum fields would help ensure compliance for biometric systems, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and does not itself create logging or address Article 12(1)-(2) generally, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Adding a compliance checkpoint to project intake is a common governance move that an experienced evaluator would expect, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process step to intake but still treats compliance as a logging-practice checklist item mirroring the ethical-review gate, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A checklist gate mirroring existing ethical review is a common strategy that violates no norms, though PIs may grumble about added paperwork.
evidence_implementability: Updating a grant-review checklist with a one-page requirement is a non-radical, low-cost change that can be done within a month.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to adapt R&D to meet the logging mandate by doing X (gate intake on a logging section) to get Y (logging designed in from the start).
evidence_effectiveness: A funding-gate requiring a logging-architecture section ensures Article 12 is designed in for new R&D projects, but it covers only planning documentation for new proposals and not actual implementation, existing systems, or the specific Article 12(3) minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left design-time compliance with architecture decision records is a familiar, sensible engineering practice, so it is only mildly interesting rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (architecture templates and ADRs) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Architecture templates, design reviews, and ADRs are common strategies that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint refactoring five architecture documents and adding a design-review requirement is a modest, non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by embedding event-recording categories 12(2)(a)-(c) into system architecture designs.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding logging subsystems at design time would reasonably address the logging mandate for new and current systems, though it covers mainly 12(2) categories and not Annex III 12(3) specifics or the broader documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building tamper-evident logging middleware into the deployment stack is the most standard, expected response to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D working relationship to compliance unchanged, though tamper-evident middleware is a mild new tool.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging for regulatory compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Modular middleware plus retrofitting all in-flight projects requires significant engineering effort, but it is reasonably feasible with a cross-functional team.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by recording the specified events.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native tamper-evident logging would address the logging mandate in Article 12 including Annex III 1(a) items, though it covers only logging and not documentation or post-market processes, so it solves the main problem.

evidence_originality: Merging research documentation with compliance documentation is a fairly common and sensible idea that shows some practicality but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared template and process but still treats compliance as documentation practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged apart from reuse of documents.
evidence_acceptability: Consolidating documentation for peer reviewers and auditors is a sensible strategy that offends no norms, though relying on it as the sole Article 12 compliance route may draw regulator skepticism.
evidence_implementability: Restructuring existing documentation into a shared template with a quarterly refresh owned by the project lead requires modest changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified problem of documentation burden and recordkeeping overlap that relates to the compliance problem, but it conflates technical documentation with Article 12 logging, so the link to the stated logging problem is implied rather than direct.
evidence_effectiveness: Article 12 mandates automatic event logs, and a quarterly-refreshed documentation file covers only the Recital 71 technical documentation and not technical logging capability, so it contributes only partially.

evidence_originality: Releasing open-source standards from compliance work is a somewhat unusual and interesting idea but not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into an outward-facing community standard and positions the lab as a standard-setter, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, but does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a provenance schema is a somewhat uncommon but entirely inoffensive strategy, though releasing training and validation records as seed data may raise minor concerns.
evidence_implementability: A small working group drafting a schema over two sprints and publishing it under Apache 2.0 is modest in cost and requires some new effort but no radical change, though community adoption is harder.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (standardizing provenance and logging formats) related to the stated logging mandate, with its main benefit being community impact rather than the lab's own compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema extending Article 12 minimums would help structure logging but does not itself implement the lab's logging or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design gating at project intake is a sensible and fairly expected response, showing modest imagination but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging a design constraint on project funding, though it remains a procedural checklist rather than reshaping what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A checklist gate requiring a logging plan before funding is a common governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It only amends an existing grant-review checklist and adds a one-page spec reviewed by existing staff, which is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D by tying Article 12(2) event categories to project intake.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure new projects are designed with logging from the start, but it covers only a plan at intake, not the actual implementation, existing systems, or Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Phased budget allocation and risk-tiered sequencing of compliance work is a common, mundane project-management response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard retrofit logging project managed through budgeting, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Phased budgeting, risk-tiered sequencing and release-gate checklists are conventional, norm-compliant corporate practice, though deferring lower-tier systems' compliance may raise some legal risk.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a revised resource plan, a ring-fenced budget share and checklist gating, which are reasonably feasible administrative changes without radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to resource and sequence meeting the logging mandate while protecting R&D, which is part of the stated problem, though it does not specify the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by organizing resources and protecting research but does not itself deliver logging capability, so it is only a partial solution, and deferring lower-tier systems may not satisfy deadlines.

evidence_originality: Tying documentation updates to CI/CD triggers is sensible but is a common, expected compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It applies standard documentation-management practice (versioned repo, CI/CD tickets, compliance engineers) and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning engineers and wiring ticket triggers into existing CI/CD is reasonably feasible with some staffing and process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified related problem, keeping technical documentation current for post-market monitoring, which is part of the Recital 71 context but is not the logging mandate itself, so the link is implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would keep technical documentation current, which supports Recital 71 compliance, but it does not address Article 12's automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance schemas and design gates are a familiar idea in compliance-by-design, so this is a sensible but expected response with only mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new template and gate but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged, though shifting it earlier is mildly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: A design-stage compliance checkpoint with sign-off is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight YAML template and a sprint-planning gate are cheap, quick, and involve only non-radical process changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring required data points are defined and instrumented, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-build event schema mapped to Article 12(2) categories and Annex III 1(a) fields helps ensure the right events are instrumented, but it does not itself deliver the logging capability, retention, or ongoing monitoring, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A logging module that captures exactly the four mandated Annex III fields in a tamper-evident store is the obvious, expected response to Article 12(3), so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard logging component and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Audit logging that implements the regulation's own requirements violates no norms and is a common compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: An append-only logging module intercepting a pipeline is a bounded, low-cost engineering task that can be built independently of the core algorithm.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by recording the four fields Article 12(3) names.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy the specific Annex III 1(a) logging minimums, but it does not cover the general Article 12(1)-(2) event logging or broader R&D adaptation, so it is a strong yet partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a logging/dashboard toolkit for compliance is an expected response, but pairing it with publication and a procurement asset adds some interesting imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open-source toolkit, publication, product asset) and partly reframes compliance as research output and offering to clients, stretching the relationship somewhat, but the core remains logging tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Building an open-source logging toolkit and publishing a methods paper is a legitimate, norm-compliant approach, though somewhat less common than buying or standard in-house logging.
evidence_implementability: Two postdocs for one year on an existing data lake with no new headcount is reasonably feasible, though it requires a year of dedicated effort and a custom build.
evidence_applicability: The toolkit directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, explicitly covering 12(2)(a)-(c) use cases.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to meeting logging requirements but omits Annex III 12(3) specifics, retention, and lifetime documentation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a scientific failure-mode dataset is unusual and shows imagination, but it is a fairly intuitive extension of log analysis rather than truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making mandated logs a primary research corpus and shaping what the lab researches, though it stops short of a full paradigm break.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymised operational logs for internal research and publication is a plausible, somewhat unusual strategy that offends no norms, though data protection and confidentiality sensitivities would need care.
evidence_implementability: It requires building an annotation pipeline, clustering methods, and access to deployment logs (often held by deployers), which is a significant but not impossible effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (how to derive value from mandated logs when adapting R&D), which relates to but is not the core of the stated logging-mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate and mostly adds research value, so it only partially contributes to the problem of responding to Article 12.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging library with a unified schema and pluggable backends is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared SDK is a new tool but it treats compliance purely as a logging engineering practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal shared library with a pilot-then-mandate rollout is a standard practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A defined team, a two-week spike, a one-quarter timeline and a pilot are reasonable, but building and mandating a lab-wide SDK in two languages requires some changes and moderate effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by supplying the logging capability for high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help standardize event recording and reduce per-system cost, but it does not itself ensure the content is appropriate for Article 12(2) purposes, retention, or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design gates with shared libraries are a well-known and expected response, so it is sensible but not imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a review gate and reusable library as new process elements but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the relation between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review gate and shared libraries are common, norm-compliant engineering governance strategies that offend no sensibilities, though gating before training may draw some R&D pushback.
evidence_implementability: It requires a new review gate, platform team engineering of reusable libraries, and process change across projects, which is reasonably feasible but involves some real changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building automatic event recording into systems from the start.

evidence_effectiveness: Automatic logging of the Article 12(3) items in every high-risk prototype would largely meet the logging mandate if done, though it covers mostly the Annex III 1(a) minimum and not the broader 12(2) event relevance or documentation upkeep.

evidence_originality: Logging by design with release gates is a standard, expected response to the mandate and is not surprising or imaginative.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design with a CI/sprint compliance gate is a common, expected response to Article 12, so it is mundane rather than surprising.

evidence_originality: Building logging in from the start and adding a compliance review gate is a common, mundane response to this mandate.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by default via a shared middleware and CI gate is a sensible, commonly expected 'compliance by design' response, interesting but not surprising.

evidence_originality: A documentation steward with scheduled reviews and version control is a common, expected response to documentation obligations and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.

evidence_originality: A shared internal logging library with a CI/CD gate is a common, mundane engineering response that experienced evaluators would expect from most labs.

evidence_effectiveness: If built and enforced, a common logging library would satisfy the technical logging requirements across projects, though it covers only logging and not the wider documentation or post-market monitoring duties, and its scope is tied to biometric-style fields.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging via OpenTelemetry middleware is a common and expected response, with no surprising or imaginative element.

evidence_originality: Shift-left, compliance-by-default tooling is a well-known software engineering pattern and an expected response, so it is mundane rather than surprising.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates at project intake are a fairly common and expected response, so this is interesting but not surprising or imaginative.

evidence_originality: A reusable embeddable logging module is a very common and expected engineering response to Article 12, showing little that is surprising or imaginative.

evidence_originality: Compliance gap audits with per-system matrices are a standard, expected response to new regulation and show little imagination.

evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a product offering that differentiates the lab in the market, changing the relationship between R&D output and compliance obligation, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Exposing logs to clients is a common transparency strategy, though real-time exposure of verification records raises some privacy concerns that need handling, without offending norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on an existing logging layer with an API, lightweight front-end and a six-week pilot with two customers, which is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal packages Article 12 logs into a dashboard supporting deployers' Article 72 and 26(5) obligations, which relates directly to the logging mandate, though the core need to meet logging requirements is assumed to be already met by an existing logging layer.
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard helps downstream monitoring and transparency but does not itself ensure the lab's logs meet Article 12 content or lifecycle requirements, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Log monitoring dashboards with alerting and periodic reports are a common, expected response to logging mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds dashboards, alerting and reporting processes but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D works.
evidence_acceptability: Continuous compliance monitoring and filing reports for regulators is a standard, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated analyst team and real-time tooling, which is some added cost but reasonably feasible using existing logging middleware.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(2) purposes of identifying risk situations and supporting post-market monitoring, which are part of the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Analytics on logs would help meet Article 12(2) purposes and Article 72 monitoring, but it presumes the logging capability exists and does not itself deliver the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Unifying research reproducibility and compliance logging in a shared ledger is a reasonably sensible, somewhat imaginative idea, though experiment-tracking platforms are familiar so it is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves compliance logging into the research workflow itself, merging reproducibility records with compliance and positioning the lab as a reference implementation, which changes the R&D-compliance relationship without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Tamper-evident logging and reproducibility standards violate no norms and are broadly acceptable to researchers, regulators and auditors.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared platform service with CI/CD hooks across high-risk pipelines needs engineering investment and cross-team coordination, but uses existing technologies and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate with automatic event recording and queryable records for auditors.
evidence_effectiveness: A tamper-evident automatic event-log store would substantially satisfy Article 12(1) logging for the lab's pipelines, but it focuses on training/evaluation experiment logs and may not capture runtime deployment events needed for Article 12(2) and post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code in CI/CD is a known DevOps pattern, though applying formal property specs to Article 12(2) event coverage is somewhat interesting and shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a spec language, CI/CD gate, model-checking assertions) but still treats compliance as a logging-coverage practice, merely moved earlier in development.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance gates in CI/CD are a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Formalizing vague legal criteria like 'events relevant for identifying risk' into checkable specs and building a domain language and model-checking tooling is difficult and costly, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking that logging configurations cover the Article 12(2) event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help verify coverage of logging requirements but covers only Article 12(2), not Art 12(3) specifics or actual log generation, retention, or quality, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance testing in CI/CD is a fairly expected, sensible response that shows some thought but is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a CI/CD compliance gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated build gates and contract tests are common engineering strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a test harness, synthetic traffic replay, and schema assertions, which is reasonably feasible using existing CI tooling but needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required log fields and events are present.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies logging completeness and catches gaps early but does not itself build the logging capability, address retention or other obligations, or cover real-world event relevance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Front-loading compliance design at project intake is a familiar privacy/security-by-design pattern, so it is common and not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new artifact and gate but still treats compliance as logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A one-page intake gate with a rotating reviewer is a common, norm-respecting governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing intake workflow and a 0.2 FTE rotating reviewer with no new hires, so it needs only modest process changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by specifying logging architecture before development begins, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A one-page brief at intake helps ensure logging is designed in early, but it does not itself implement the Article 12 capabilities (e.g., event coverage, Annex III minimums), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance automation via CI pipelines is a fairly expected response, though linking log audit to auto-regenerated documentation shows a bit of imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (CI job, LLM summarization) but still treats compliance as a logging and documentation practice without changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Automating compliance checks and documentation is a fairly common strategy that violates no norms, though LLM-drafted regulatory documentation may raise mild eyebrows.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight microservice on existing infrastructure with rule-based validators is feasible with some changes, though LLM-assisted documentation regeneration adds some difficulty.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified requirements of Article 12(3) minimums and Recital 71 documentation upkeep, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address log completeness for Annex III 1(a) and documentation currency, but not the broader logging for Article 12(2) or the substantive content and accuracy of documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable auto-instrumenting logging SDK is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice delivered as tooling, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging library with centralized storage is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building an OpenTelemetry-compatible decorator-based SDK in three weeks, adopted via standard lockfile, is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically emitting the required log fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help with technical logging capability, but it covers only a partial solution (e.g., retention, risk-relevant events, human verifier identification, and the Annex III scope are not addressed), so it is not a full solution.

evidence_originality: Budgeting for compliance up front is a fairly familiar project-management idea, though applying it as a mandatory traceability line item in the grant cycle is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It embeds traceability into funding and milestone governance alongside scientific KPIs, changing how R&D and compliance relate (compliance built into project planning), though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting compliance as a funded line item reviewed at quarterly checkpoints is a sensible, norm-respecting management practice that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: It requires modest changes to grant and milestone-review processes and coordination with the grants office, which is reasonably feasible without major cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D processes by ensuring logging and documentation are resourced from the start.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure resources and timing for logging work but does not itself design or implement the logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance tooling is interesting and shows some imagination in turning an obligation into a research output, but it is not wholly unexpected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging a citable research contribution and a standard-setting position, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building and openly publishing a compliance reference implementation is a legal, collegial and somewhat unusual strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Three months of a postdoc and a junior developer on internal test data is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment with no new infrastructure, though it requires some diversion of staff.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement of meeting the logging mandate by building the specific Article 12(3) fields (timestamps, reference database, match inputs, verifier identity).
evidence_effectiveness: A reference logging implementation would meet the Article 12(3) minimum fields for the relevant system, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) biometric case and not the lab's broader Article 12 obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Design-time gating and scaffolding for logging is a sensible, fairly expected 'shift-left' response, with a mildly interesting stub-generation touch but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a mandatory design template and auto-generated stub code) but still treats compliance as a logging practice built into the existing development process, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory design checklists and sign-off gates are common engineering governance practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A template, a design sign-off review, and stub code generation are modest process changes that a lab can adopt with reasonable effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring logging is specified and built in during design, with the four mandatory fields stubbed out.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is designed in from the start and covers the Annex III 1(a) fields, but it does not address the full Article 12 scope (risk, post-market and operation-monitoring events) or verify log quality at runtime, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a research instrument is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging a source of scientific research and publications, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open-access research and building internal benchmarks offends no norms, though publishing findings from logs may raise some confidentiality questions, and it is a somewhat uncommon strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated research thread, a benchmark corpus, and detector training, which means significant resources and uncertain outcomes, but is feasible for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: The proposal uses Article 12 logs for drift detection and post-market monitoring, which is an implied benefit related to the logging mandate rather than a direct way of meeting it.
evidence_effectiveness: A research programme on log-based drift detection would help post-market monitoring but does not by itself ensure Article 12 compliance such as event recording capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance tooling and reusing telemetry as a research dataset is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but open-source logging libraries are a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance cost into a citable external contribution and reference implementation changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release under an EU-funded licence with regulator engagement offends no norms, though releasing raw telemetry as a dataset raises minor privacy and confidentiality sensitivities.
evidence_implementability: A two-person pod integrating into existing CI/CD in one quarter is reasonably feasible, though documentation, open release, and licensing/funding add some extra effort.
evidence_applicability: The toolkit directly implements Article 12 logging elements (timestamps, reference databases, matched inputs, verifier IDs), which is the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would deliver conformant automatic logging for the lab's pipelines, though it covers mainly paragraph 3 (Annex III 1(a)) specifics and leaves risk-event identification and post-market monitoring logic partly unaddressed.

evidence_originality: A log storage and query layer with dashboards is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise or ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (a queryable append-only log store and dashboards) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal log store with compliance dashboards is a standard strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A prototype of a columnar append-only store with an API and three dashboards is reasonably feasible with moderate engineering effort and some changes to the SDK ingestion.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by making Article 12 logs retained, queryable, and usable for Article 72 post-market monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: It contributes substantially by providing storage and consumption of logs but does not by itself ensure that the logging capabilities in Article 12(2) and 12(3) are generated, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12 compliance into a publishable research area in log-based interpretability is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making the logging obligation itself a research agenda, which is paradigm stretching and arguably addresses what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open-source provenance research and building logging tools violates no legal or social norms, though framing compliance as a research programme is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A small team building new log compression, querying and replay tools plus publishing is a significant R&D effort with uncertain results, but it is feasible with some changes and not totally impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate through tools for logs and replay, which is related to the stated problem but mainly solves an implied problem of research value rather than directly meeting logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: The tools could help with logging and traceability, but the proposal centers on research outputs and does not specify how it ensures Article 12 compliance, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Dual-use of compliance logs as research datasets is interesting and shows some imagination but is a fairly foreseeable idea among labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science, stretching the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using compliance logs also for research is a somewhat unusual but non-offensive strategy, though privacy and data-minimization concerns about repurposing logs are modest.
evidence_implementability: It requires schema design changes and cross-team collaboration, but this is reasonably feasible within existing logging infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate while adapting R&D to it, with the identified outcome of turning compliance cost into a research asset.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the logging mandate if all regulatory minimums are kept, and adds research value, but the proposal is largely about leveraging logs rather than fully specifying compliance, so it is a strong but partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Using mandated logs as an empirical resource for drift science is interesting and shows some imagination, though the idea of drift monitoring from logs is not wholly unexpected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning logging obligations into a research agenda and new partnerships, addressing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Research partnerships using deployer logs and publishing findings are legitimate, though data-sharing and confidentiality questions make it somewhat unusual rather than fully standard.
evidence_implementability: A three-year track needing industry partners, access to live-system logs, and dedicated research staff is a significant, expensive undertaking, and the brief asks for committing implementation resources rather than exploring.
evidence_applicability: It does not directly address how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate but addresses an implied problem of using logs for drift and risk detection tied to Article 79(1).
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute research insight on drift but does not itself deliver compliant logging capability, so it is at best a partial contribution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as development feedback is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, but it is a fairly expected move (monitoring data into retraining) and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving the compliance logs into the development loop, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for internal analytics is a common practice, though the privacy-aggregation and reuse of logs for purposes beyond compliance may raise slight data-protection questions, which the proposal mitigates.
evidence_implementability: It uses a lightweight ETL job on existing infrastructure and an existing experiment-tracker UI, so it requires only modest, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal reuses mandatory logs to feed development, which relates to the stated problem of how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate, though it addresses an implied benefit rather than meeting the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab get value from compliance logs and contributes to adapting R&D, but it does not itself satisfy the logging mandate's technical requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a basis for open drift-detection science is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but it is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making the logging obligation a source of research and public contribution, which is paradigm stretching but does not redirect what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks and research on compliance-derived logs violate no legal or social norms, though publishing is a somewhat unusual way to answer a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: Building synthetic drift benchmarks and evaluating detection algorithms needs a dedicated research effort with real resources, and the lab has to build the logging itself anyway, but it is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It uses Article 12(1) logs to detect drift and emerging risk, which relates to Article 12(2)(a) and (b) on risk identification and post-market monitoring, but it is a research programme and does not directly say how the lab will meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift-detection research on logs would help with monitoring and risk identification, but it does not itself implement compliant logging or satisfy the mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into citable, DOI-assigned open research artifacts is an interesting, somewhat imaginative twist that is uncommon among likely responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as a reproducibility and publication asset that positions the lab as a reference implementation, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance without altering what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing logs openly with DOIs is somewhat unusual, and may raise confidentiality or data-protection concerns, but it offends no norms and fits open-science culture.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing metadata layer within a containerised pipeline, but a category-aware schema generator, versioned repository and DOI minting amount to some real engineering changes rather than a trivial add-on.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces Article 12-compliant records, which is the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic structured logging of the Article 12 elements would meet the logging mandate, but it does not clearly address risk-situation identification or post-market monitoring, and Article 12(3) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating documentation drift as a measurable scientific phenomenon is unusual and imaginative compared with typical lab responses, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns a compliance obligation into a research topic, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations and adds new elements, but it stops short of changing what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: An internal research track on documentation practice offends no norms, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Recording documentation-update metadata on selected projects and analyzing it annually is a modest process change that is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses keeping technical documentation current (Recital 71), which is only implied by the logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem rather than the stated logging problem directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Studying documentation drift would not make the lab's systems meet the Article 12 automatic event-logging requirement, so it contributes little to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Building a query and replay tool on top of mandated logs is a sensible, somewhat interesting dual-use idea but is a fairly expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (GraphQL layer, dashboards, replay) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely repurposing logs for debugging.
evidence_acceptability: Internal tooling on logs violates no norms, though using compliance logs for debugging might raise minor data-governance questions, it is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Reusing the existing observability stack and building a thin query layer is low-cost and involves non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses post-market monitoring access to logs (Article 72) which is an implied part of the logging mandate, but does not itself establish the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps use logs for post-market monitoring requests but does not ensure the logging itself meets Article 12 content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourced logging standards are a fairly known idea among compliance responses, so this is interesting and somewhat unusual in its standard-setter framing but not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Publishing an open standard with conformance suites turns compliance into a new offering and standard-setting role for the lab, which changes the compliance relationship, but it still centres on logging and does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source, MIT-licensed standards with conformance tests violate no legal or social norms and are a common, welcome strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a schema, reference implementation, and conformance test suites plus prototyping on two systems requires considerable engineering and community adoption effort, though it is feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by providing a schema designed to satisfy those requirements and applying it to the lab's own Annex III systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would produce a logging implementation covering Article 12 for the lab's systems, but conformance depends on legal interpretation, and the standard is not guaranteed to cover all requirements or be adopted, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance logging tooling is a fairly foreseeable response, interesting but not especially surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new offering and community positioning born from compliance, shifting the relationship between R&D and obligations somewhat, though the core remains logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing compliance tooling under a permissive licence violates no legal or social norms and is a familiar, welcomed practice.
evidence_implementability: It can be built in the existing MLOps stack, but a modular, pluggable, versioned, documented open-source library with integration guides takes significant engineering and maintenance effort beyond the lab's own compliance needs.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by building a logging library that implements Article 12(1)–(3) requirements, so the lab gets compliant logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A library implementing Article 12 logging would largely meet the logging mandate if built, though it cannot by itself determine event relevance for each system's intended purpose or the Annex III 1(a) specifics without integration work.

evidence_originality: A shared internal logging middleware is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to the logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (middleware library with tests mapped to articles) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralised shared compliance tooling is a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building and maintaining an internal library with a three-person team and adopting it during integration sprints requires some changes and moderate cost but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal does X (shared middleware logging timestamps, reference-database lookups, matched inputs, verifier identities) to get Y (compliant logging), which is explicitly the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, standardised hooks capturing the Article 12 and Annex III 1(a) items would directly deliver the automatic logging capability the mandate requires, though it addresses logging only and not documentation or other duties.

evidence_originality: Retrofitting existing monitoring pipelines is the most expected, mundane response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging layered onto existing tooling, and the lab's way of working remains unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Extending existing monitoring infrastructure to meet a legal logging mandate is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing event buses and log aggregators with about two person-months of engineering per product line, which is a non-radical, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by emitting the Article 12(2) event classes and setting retention to match lifetime obligations.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver automatic event logging aligned to Article 12(2) classes, but it does not address the Annex III 1(a) minimums, tamper-evidence, or documentation, so it solves the core logging need only in part.

evidence_originality: Centralizing compliant logging in shared platform middleware is a sensible but very common engineering response that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice implemented as infrastructure, leaving the lab's R&D way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging middleware is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms, though mandating all pipelines traverse it may cause minor internal friction.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing experiment-tracking service with schemas and middleware is reasonably feasible, though a single sprint across all pipelines is optimistic and requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building automatic event recording for high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the logging capability, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a)-style fields and not documentation, post-market monitoring, or per-use-case traceability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Unifying compliance logs with reproducibility records is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, but experiment tracking for compliance is a fairly familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as the same artefact as scientific audit trails, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Default logging with no opt-out for high-risk branches violates no norms and is consistent with legal and scientific practice.
evidence_implementability: Adding lightweight hooks to existing MLflow pipelines in one sprint is feasible, though schema design and mapping require some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building automatic event logging mapped to Article 12(2) categories into the lab's pipelines.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, default structured logging mapped to Article 12(2) would substantially meet the logging mandate, but it covers training/experiment logs more than runtime logs of deployed systems and omits Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing existing experiment-tracking infrastructure for compliance logs is an obvious, expected response that most labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces no new elements and treats compliance as standard logging practice built on existing tooling, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, sensible engineering strategy that offends no norms, though mixing research and compliance records may raise minor audit-separation concerns.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing storage and tracking infrastructure with a schema extension and runtime emitters needs some changes but is reasonably feasible and low-cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building the compliance-event schema and mapping it to the specific article paragraphs.
evidence_effectiveness: Wiring runtime containers to emit structured events mapped to Art. 12(2)(a)-(c) into a log store would meet the core logging mandate, but it omits retention, integrity, Annex III 1(a) minimums, and technical documentation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Restating the statutory minimum fields with an immutable log and gap-flagging dashboard is common and mundane for this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, with only a dashboard as a modest add-on.
evidence_acceptability: Logging the statutory minimum fields with named reviewers is a standard, legally mandated practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: An immutable log and dashboard tied to existing biometric pipelines require some new tooling and integration but are reasonably feasible, not a trivial or radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the Article 12(3) minimum logging items, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimums for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it covers only that subset and not Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution to the lab's broader response.

evidence_originality: Embedding a standing compliance working group with periodic audits is a common, mundane organizational response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A dedicated compliance cell with audits is a new organizational element, but it still treats compliance as a separate logging and documentation practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A cross-functional compliance team using existing headcount with protected time violates no norms and is a standard strategy.
evidence_implementability: Using four existing staff at 20% time requires modest reallocation with no new hires, making it easy to implement at low cost.
evidence_applicability: A standing group maintaining Article 12 documentation templates and auditing prototypes for logging readiness directly addresses how the lab meets the logging mandate, though the logging implementation itself is only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Audits and templates would help ensure logging readiness, but the proposal does not specify how logging capabilities are built, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging libraries with pipeline test gates are a standard, expected response that shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as logging practice, with a new tooling element (a CI/CD gate) but no change to the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, so it is at most slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance into engineering architecture and CI/CD gates is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Developing a standardized library with configurable schemas and integrating it into pipelines requires some engineering changes and effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a logging module that captures the specific Article 12(3) records (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs) as the way to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, an embedded logging library with CI/CD test gates would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it overreaches by applying Article 12(3) to all Annex III categories and omits the verifier-identification element and Article 12(2) purposes, so it is reasonable and nearly complete.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default templates and logging middleware are a fairly common, expected response, with only mild interest from the retrofit-time framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (templates/middleware) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into internal tooling is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring an existing FastAPI template to add middleware configured by YAML is a modest engineering task using existing tools and a small team.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (use periods, reference databases, matched inputs, verifier identification) while preserving R&D velocity.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding Article 12 logging hooks in the default serving template would solve the core logging mandate for prototypes built on it, though it covers only the logging part, not documentation or non-SDK systems, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs for failure-mode discovery is unusual and shows some imagination, though log analytics for anomaly detection is a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by treating compliance-generated logs as a scientific data source and feeding findings back into redesign and open community contributions.
evidence_acceptability: Analyzing own operational logs and publishing taxonomies is a fairly uncommon but unoffensive strategy, though publishing from deployed-system logs raises some data-privacy and confidentiality questions.
evidence_implementability: It needs only two researchers at 15 percent time and an existing log lakehouse, so it is a modest, reasonably feasible addition.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, how to get value from and use compliance logs for risk identification and R&D adaptation, which relates to but is not the explicit logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Mining logs for failure taxonomies does not itself meet the Article 12 logging mandate (it presupposes logs exist), so it is at best a partial contribution that leverages logs for risk identification under 12(2)(a).

evidence_originality: Treating Article 12 logging as a tender differentiator is an unusual and interesting framing that shows some imagination, though it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by turning logging into a marketable trust product for public-sector clients, but it does not alter what the lab researches, so it stretches the paradigm without breaking it.
evidence_acceptability: Going beyond the legal minimum and marketing transparent audit trails to public clients violates no norms, though positioning compliance as a sales differentiator is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: It is a small workstream of two people that reuses the existing pipeline and an existing pilot contract, adding a signed-event journal and a dashboard, which is reasonably feasible at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems and also tackles the cost of compliance, so it applies directly to the stated problem.
