evidence_acceptability: Restructuring evaluation SOPs so outputs double as compliance records is a sensible, norm-respecting practice that offends no legal or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires rewriting the evaluation SOP and adding structured schemas to every benchmark run within a quarter and depends on a separate logging backbone, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet documentation and logging obligations and adapt R&D processes accordingly, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Evaluation artefacts cover only part of the Article 12 requirement (runtime event logs of deployed systems, use periods, and the like), so it contributes but is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open logging schema standards are an interesting, somewhat expected move for labs seeking influence, showing some imagination but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open schema specs, standards-channel publication) and a new offering born from compliance, but it still treats compliance fundamentally as logging practice rather than reshaping the lab's R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source standards contributions are a commonly accepted, norm-respecting strategy, though the standard-setting ambition is a bit unusual.
evidence_implementability: A small team drafting versioned JSON specs and publishing them is low cost and non-radical, though gaining community adoption takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (defining meaningful events and positioning the lab in the standards landscape) rather than directly delivering the lab's required logging capability.
evidence_effectiveness: Publishing open schemas would not by itself make the lab's own systems compliant with Article 12, so it is at best a partial contribution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code in CI is a fairly familiar idea that evaluators would expect, with only a mildly interesting application to Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (compliance test gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, though shifting it left into the pre-merge pipeline.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI quality gates are a common engineering practice that violate no norms and fit comfortably with compliance expectations.
evidence_implementability: A pytest fixture in an existing CI pipeline is cheap and quick to build, requiring only modest changes to current engineering workflow.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by testing for the paragraph-2 categories and the Annex III(1)(a) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably enforce that prototypes have mandated log fields, but it only tests for field presence with stub models and synthetic events, so it is a partial solution that does not cover log retention, real-world traceability, or adapting R&D.

evidence_originality: A pre-deployment compliance gap audit is a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard gap analysis that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits are a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week audit with one developer per project is a modest, non-radical effort using existing staff and code, so it is easy and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems by finding missing log fields.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit identifies gaps and feeds a remediation backlog, which contributes to compliance but does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using CI checks and contract tests to guard compliance is a sensible but fairly expected DevOps-style response; mapping diffs to logged fields adds some interest but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool to the existing pipeline but still treats compliance as logging practice, and it does not change how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated build checks for compliance are a common engineering practice and offend no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing pipeline, though parsing diffs and mapping modules to logged fields requires some nontrivial tooling work, so it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, namely keeping the logging mandate met as R&D changes the models and architecture, through a specific intervention (a schema-contract test in CI).
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate that blocks commits which reduce logging coverage would help preserve Article 12 logging over the system's lifetime, but it covers only schema regression and not the full mandate (what to log, retention, event relevance), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12 into a public benchmark with metrics like log completeness and provenance depth is unusual and shows imagination, though it is not entirely surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance a research output and creating new partnerships and offerings born from the obligation.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open benchmark with university partners and presenting at academic workshops is a legal, norm-respecting strategy, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It needs two university partnerships, benchmark design, a reference implementation and an 18-month timeline, which is reasonably feasible but a significant effort for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of operationalizing and standardizing Article 12 logging and positioning the lab, which relates to the stated problem but not directly to meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark would help define and measure traceability but does not itself ensure the lab's own systems have compliant logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance logs as a longitudinal scientific dataset with tailored statistical process control is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly unprecedented given existing post-market monitoring ideas.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and creating a new post-market research sub-discipline, which is paradigm stretching and arguably reaches what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for research and publication is uncommon and raises possible data protection and confidentiality concerns, but it offends no sensibilities when handled properly.
evidence_implementability: It needs new statistical methods, multi-year data accumulation, and pilots on live Annex III systems, which is a significant but feasible effort, though the reliance on a multi-year horizon and publication makes it harder.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D around the logging mandate by using logs as research data, which relates to the stated problem but is not the direct compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal reuses logs for drift research and assumes the logging infrastructure already exists, so it does not itself meet the logging mandate and only partially contributes to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Declarative compliance-as-code profiles are a familiar DevOps pattern applied sensibly here, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (YAML manifests, CI-driven configuration) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires building manifests, CI integration, and middleware but uses existing tooling and is reasonably feasible with some process changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by mapping required Article 12 fields to project builds, though the 'risk category to Article 12(3)' mapping is slightly overextended.
evidence_effectiveness: Pre-scoped, CI-configured logging profiles would help ensure required fields are captured, but they only partially solve the mandate since they do not address log retention, integrity, or the general Article 12(2) traceability events, and Article 12(3) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems.

evidence_originality: Reusable shared logging infrastructure is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and is not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tooling layer but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared logging middleware is a common, norm-conforming engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing MLflow infrastructure with a reusable event-schema module is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some engineering changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate while reducing per-project resource cost, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging backbone conforming to Article 12 would contribute substantially to meeting the logging mandate, but it covers only logging and not the broader compliance or Annex III specifics fully, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A versioned schema plus SDK with contract tests for the four Article 12(3) fields is a sensible but expected engineering response, so it is common rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (schema, SDK, contract tests) but still treats compliance purely as logging practice, without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging tooling to meet a legal requirement is a standard strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin SDK and JSON schema with automated tests are low-cost and fit existing pipelines, requiring non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem by implementing the four Article 12(3) mandatory logging fields for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the Annex III 1(a) minimum logging requirement but covers only that subset, not the general Article 12(1)-(2) traceability, retention, or broader R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Budgeting for compliance costs in project scoping is sensible but fairly mundane and an expected response, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (compliance-lifecycle costing in scoping) and slightly touches which research directions get pursued, but still treats compliance largely as a logging and documentation practice.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a cost line to grant-scoping checklists is a common, uncontroversial administrative practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Revising a template and checklist is a low-cost, non-radical change, though estimating lifetime costs requires some effort from PI teams.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses how the lab adapts its R&D to the logging mandate by costing lifetime compliance obligations at scoping, which is an implied problem (resource planning) related to the stated problem rather than directly meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Costing compliance up front helps the lab avoid funding gaps and informs which R&D to pursue, but it does not itself implement logging or satisfy Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated CI checks for log integrity are a sensible, somewhat expected DevOps-style response, though the hash-chain and schema validation add mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (a CI log-contract gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Engineering regression testing in CI violates no norms and is a common, uncontroversial strategy.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing CI runners with a containerised test job and synthetic requests, which is reasonably feasible with modest changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by catching regressions that would break Article 12 logging capabilities.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps keep logs conformant and tamper-evident but covers only the schema and integrity of logs, not the full Article 12 scope such as event relevance, retention, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a research dataset is unusual and shows imagination, though the idea of repurposing compliance data is not wholly unprecedented or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science and making logs a research asset, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for research is somewhat unusual and raises data-protection and purpose-limitation questions, but it does not offend sensibilities if handled properly.
evidence_implementability: Co-designing log schemas with engineering and forming a research sub-group per project requires some organizational change and extra metadata capture, but it is reasonably feasible using logs already mandated.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by exploiting its outputs, which relates to the stated problem but is not a direct compliance measure.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help produce richer logs and extract value from them, but it does not itself ensure the lab meets Article 12 requirements such as the specific minimum logging items, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI schema-validation gate for log fields is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (CI validator) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks are a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight validator in the existing CI runner with a modest time budget is easy and low cost to build.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking that emitted logs contain Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It catches schema gaps early but only checks field presence, not Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or runtime logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware is the common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard logging practice packaged as a reusable tool, treating compliance as logging and leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged apart from a shared library.
evidence_acceptability: Internal logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared SDK with a Python/C++ hot-path is a reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes to the serving layer and adoption across projects, but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by emitting the specific events Article 12 requires.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logging SDK that captures the Article 12(3) minimum fields would, if built, directly deliver the technical logging capability, though it does not itself cover retention, documentation, or the broader Article 12(2) event relevance, so it is mostly but not entirely the solution.

evidence_originality: Building a standard logging layer into the development framework is the obvious, expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable logging SDK with pre-deployment completeness tests is a new tool and process, but it still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice and does not change how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into engineering templates is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared SDK and template require some engineering effort and process change, but they are reasonably feasible for a lab, though capturing Annex III 1(a) fields in every system is a bit broad.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the Article 12 logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would largely satisfy the technical logging mandate, but it does not address documentation, retention, or the event-relevance judgments for risk monitoring, and the 'guarantees' claim is overstated, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building compliance logging into the development process by design is a fairly expected response, with an interesting reproducibility framing but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes logging from a post-hoc add-on to part of how the science is done and redefines SOPs, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging and reproducibility into standard operating procedures is a common, norm-compliant strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires reworking pipelines and SOPs through a working group before new projects are chartered, which is a reasonably feasible but real change, and the claim of no slowdown is optimistic.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (build automatic event logging into pipelines) to get Y (meet Article 12's logging and traceability mandate), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event logging built into every pipeline stage would, if done, address the logging mandate and traceability aim fairly fully, though it focuses on development-stage logs and does not specify Article 12's deployment-time event types or Annex III minimums, so it is likely a substantial but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: A cross-functional stage-gate compliance checkpoint with sign-off is a common, expected governance response to a regulatory mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checklist and review gate to the existing stage-gate process, which is standard compliance practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate reviews with legal sign-off and audit repositories are common strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing stage-gate process and requires only a checklist, a sign-off role, and evidence storage, which are non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying logging capabilities before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate verifies that logging exists and is adequate but does not build the logging capability or address R&D adaptation, so it contributes only partially to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Treating event definition as a research problem and publishing a taxonomy is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It ties compliance to what the lab researches and gives the lab a role in shaping compliance definitions, stretching the relationship between R&D and obligations beyond mere logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing a research taxonomy and engaging in standards-shaping is a legitimate, somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A small interdisciplinary group is feasible, but defining event taxonomies for emergent systems is difficult and the output is exploratory rather than a committed compliance deliverable.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of what events to log for novel architectures under Article 12(2), which relates directly to meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy would help define loggable events but is only a partial solution, as it does not build the logging itself and its adoption by regulators is uncertain.

evidence_originality: A shared logging layer wrapping existing experiment trackers is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging via middleware, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging middleware with immutable storage is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers building a thin adapter over existing trackers in one sprint is low cost and non-radical, though some integration work is needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by capturing the Article 12(3) logging items to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum fields and automatic recording, but it does not cover the Article 12(2) event-relevance for risk, post-market monitoring and operation, nor retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logging fields against regulatory requirements is a mundane, expected response, though the edge-case injection adds slight specificity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (test harness) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Sandboxed QA testing of compliance features is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a test harness with edge-case scenarios needs some dedicated effort but is reasonably feasible within existing QA capabilities.
evidence_applicability: The harness directly targets verifying the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Validating that each mandated field populates would address Article 12(3) compliance for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it covers only that paragraph and does not address the general logging in 12(1)-(2) or the R&D adaptation question, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Adding a compliance gate to design review and training engineers is the standard, expected response to a logging mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It uses existing checklists and sprint gates and treats compliance as ordinary logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal engineering gates tied to legal compliance are common and violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing design review checklist with a template and training, which is non-radical, though blocking sprints and retrofitting log coverage takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by doing X (a gated logging spec) to get Y (compliant logs), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A design-gate requiring logging for Article 12(2) and (3) events directly produces the mandated capability, though it covers only logging and not documentation, retention, or other duties, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in templates is a sensible and familiar 'compliance by default' approach, interesting but not particularly imaginative or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK/scaffold) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a standard logging SDK into prototype templates is a common, uncontroversial engineering compliance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight SDK and template integration requires some development effort but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling and no radical organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by producing automatic event logs for every system.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help with automatic recording and Article 12(3)(a) timestamps, but it covers only part of the requirements (e.g., reference database, verification persons, risk-event relevance, retention), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Dedicated compliance budgeting is a fairly standard project-management response, with only mild interest in the fixed FTE percentage and backfill mechanism.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a planning template and parallel workstream but still treats compliance as a separate logging and documentation task, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Allocating a budgeted share of engineering time to compliance and tracking it is a common, norm-compliant project-management practice.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a revised planning template and quarterly tracking, though backfilling from other projects and reallocating 12-18% of FTE takes some organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the directly stated problem of how to resource and organize the logging mandate alongside R&D, though it does not itself specify the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure compliance work gets resourced and is not deferred, but it supplies no technical logging design, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a longitudinal research corpus is interesting and shows some imagination, but drift monitoring from logs is a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning logs into a research corpus and a new research agenda on drift, which weaves logging into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Using mandated logs for internal reliability research is legally and socially unobjectionable, though somewhat unusual and with possible data-protection or confidentiality considerations around reuse of logs.
evidence_implementability: A unified schema across eight projects and time-series/SPC analysis is reasonably feasible with existing methods, but requires coordination and a sustained research effort across projects.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D to logging by deriving value from it, which relates to the stated problem but not directly to meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help build a unified log schema and extract value from logs, but it does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met (e.g., Article 12 event coverage), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A living event taxonomy is a sensible and fairly expected response to vague requirements, and it shows some thought about novel architectures but is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (event taxonomy and registry) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves how R&D works essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Registries, working groups and periodic log reviews are common governance practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a lightweight event spec per project, a cross-team working group, and quarterly reviews, which are some process changes but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly tackles the identified problem of turning Article 12(2)'s abstract event categories into concrete loggable event types so the lab can meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A per-system event registry with quarterly reviews would substantially enable compliant instrumentation, but it addresses only event definition and not retention, tamper-resistance, Annex III minimums, or other aspects of logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware with tamper-evident storage and a CI/CD contract-test gate is a sensible but expected response that many labs would propose, with only the build gate adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (middleware, SDKs, CI gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated logging with deployment gates is a common compliance strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal middleware with SDKs, retention configuration and CI gating requires some engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with standard components and one shared investment.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified event categories and minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would capture the Article 12 event categories and Annex III minimum fields across all systems, solving the logging mandate, though it does not address fields needing human input such as identifying the natural persons who verify results, nor does it address R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: A standardized logging module with pipeline enforcement is the common, expected response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice embedded in architecture, with new tooling elements (CI/CD gates, common API) but no change in how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building a standard logging middleware enforced by CI/CD gates is a common, legitimate compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a common API, integrating it across all systems and adding CI/CD gates, which is reasonably feasible but involves some platform engineering changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically capturing the required events.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a mandatory tamper-evident logging layer would largely satisfy the logging requirement, though it only partly covers the Article 12(2) risk-relevant event scope and adaptation of R&D beyond the technical layer.

evidence_originality: Treating log utility as a measurable scientific quantity with a public benchmark is somewhat unusual and interesting, but benchmark suites are a familiar research move and not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an evaluation suite and metrics) and reframes logging as a research object, but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Building a public benchmark for compliance logging violates no norms and is a collaborative, well-accepted strategy.
evidence_implementability: Constructing synthetic Annex III scenarios, defining validated metrics, and running multiple configurations requires substantial effort and community uptake, representing reasonably feasible but non-trivial changes.
evidence_applicability: The benchmark directly evaluates logging implementations against Article 12(2) traceability criteria, which is an identified part of deciding how to meet the logging mandate, though it measures rather than builds logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark helps the lab choose and improve logging configurations but does not itself implement the logging mandate, so it is only a partial contribution to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing reference logging implementations is a fairly expected response, with some interest in the biometric calibration but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an open reference toolkit and published research) and frames Article 12 as design philosophy, yet it is still essentially logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance much.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance reference implementation and publishing papers is a legally and socially unobjectionable, though somewhat unusual, strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two PhD researchers over one year building an open-source toolkit on anonymised data is a reasonably feasible, moderate-cost project requiring some changes but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: The toolkit directly implements the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, though only for Annex III point 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab (and others) meet the logging mandate for biometric systems, but it covers only one Annex III category and does not address Article 12(1)-(2) generally or the lab's broader R&D, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A release-gate compliance checkpoint with a per-project checklist is a common, expected response that shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process gate but leaves the lab's way of working and its view of compliance as a logging practice essentially unchanged, so it preserves the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance gate before production is a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though teams may grumble about delays.
evidence_implementability: Adding a milestone gate and a checklist to existing sprint and release processes is a modest change that is reasonably feasible, though it needs compliance office capacity.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by enforcing coverage of its stated purposes before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate ensuring logs cover Article 12(2)(a)-(c) before deployment would help meet the mandate, but it only verifies coverage and does not build the logging capability or address Article 12(3) or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a longitudinal research corpus for studying drift and degradation is unusual and shows some imagination, though mining logs for monitoring is a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandated logs into a scientific dataset that informs what the lab researches, going beyond treating compliance as mere logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Using operational logs for internal analysis is an unusual but legitimate strategy that does not offend norms, though privacy and purpose-limitation issues around verifier identities and input data need care.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal analytics pipeline with change-point detection and clustering over logs the lab must already keep is a reasonably feasible measure needing some new tooling and data engineering, though not trivial.
evidence_applicability: The proposal does not directly address how to meet the logging mandate but solves an implied problem of adapting R&D to the mandate by deriving value from the logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to adapting R&D by extracting value from the logs but does not itself satisfy the logging requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using Git and a wiki for documentation with periodic reviews is a common, mundane response that labs would be expected to give.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reuses existing tools and a documentation-steward role while treating compliance as standard documentation practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: The approach is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing infrastructure with near-zero incremental cost and only a light process addition such as a rotating role and quarterly reviews.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, keeping technical documentation current and traceable, which relates to the mandate but not directly to the automatic logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Centralizing technical documentation in Git and a wiki helps with Recital 71 documentation upkeep but does not address Article 12's automatic event logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance-by-design reviews are a fairly familiar response, though tying it to the lab's pattern library and co-authored traceability appendix adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (design gate and appendix) but still treats compliance as logging practice integrated into project governance rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a review step and workshop to an existing grant-review cycle is a common governance approach that offends no norms, though PIs may grumble about overhead.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing quarterly cycles, existing engineers and an existing design-pattern library, so only modest process change and a half-day workshop per project are needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by adapting R&D processes, explicitly citing Article 12(2) traceability events.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-funding design gate would help ensure logging is architected into new projects, but it covers only new projects, not existing systems, and does not itself implement logging or other Article 12 elements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware/SDK is a common, expected response from engineering organizations, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice delivered as a shared tool, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralizing shared compliance infrastructure is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A six-week, two-engineer sprint building a thin SDK adopted via existing CI/CD hooks is low-cost and non-radical, though it needs some per-group integration work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate across high-risk projects (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging component would satisfy the Article 12(1) automatic-recording requirement, but it does not itself address the Article 12(2) event relevance or Article 12(3) specific content, nor the wider R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK with CI/CD gates is a sensible but very expected response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from AI labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a reusable SDK and CI/CD gating but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into architecture is a common, norm-conforming strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated infrastructure sub-team and pipeline changes across systems, which is reasonably feasible but involves some real changes and cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate, including the specific items in 12(3), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the automatic logging requirement, but it covers mainly 12(3) fields and retention, leaving the broader traceability and R&D adaptation parts only partly addressed.

evidence_originality: Shared logging libraries wired into project templates are a common and expected engineering response, so this is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (shared SDK, scaffolder integration, schema contract) but still treats compliance as logging practice, though it moves logging into the default architecture.
evidence_acceptability: Standardised instrumentation by default is a common strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin SDK with pluggable backends and a scaffolder hook is a modest engineering effort using standard practices with low disruption.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (automatic recording of events) in the lab's R&D builds.
evidence_effectiveness: A default logging SDK baked into every prototype would deliver Article 12(1) automatic event recording across the lab, but it does not itself define which events satisfy 12(2)/(3) or address documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Budget triage by compliance cost is a fairly expected, mundane managerial response, with some interest in weighting science value over compliance effort.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes what gets funded based on compliance burden, touching what the lab researches, but it mostly treats compliance as a cost to manage within existing ways of working, a mild stretch.
evidence_acceptability: Portfolio prioritization with PI memos and advisory board ranking is a normal, uncontroversial management practice, though phasing some projects may cause friction.
evidence_implementability: A one-page memo, an advisory board ranking, and budget re-baselining are lightweight, low-cost changes achievable within existing processes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (resource allocation under retrofit costs from Article 12) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate or adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Triaging funding by compliance rework cost helps prioritize and sequence resources but does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Merging reproducibility tooling with compliance documentation is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but experiment tracking with auto-logging is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It explicitly changes the relationship between R&D practice and compliance by making the scientific record and the regulatory file the same artifact, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating documentation with experiment tracking violates no legal or social norms and is a sensible, uncontroversial strategy.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing model registry to auto-capture lineage, hyperparameters, metrics and risk annotations is a reasonable engineering change, though lab-wide restructuring requires some real effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the documentation and record-keeping obligations in Recital 71 and Article 12(1), which are part of the stated problem, though the broader benefits claimed are tangential.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with technical documentation and lifetime-persisting records, but it focuses on training-time experiment records and does not address runtime event logging for deployed systems or the specific Article 12(2)-(3) logging content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Unifying research experiment tracking and regulatory logging into one stream is sensible and somewhat interesting, but extending MLflow/W&B with compliance fields is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (schema-validated compliance columns in the tracking pipeline) and weaves logging into research workflow, though it still treats compliance fundamentally as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Append-only logging within existing research tooling and flag-based activation violate no norms and are a common type of strategy.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing MLflow/W&B pipelines with schema validation and a flag is reasonably feasible, requiring some engineering changes but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by emitting the Article 12(3) fields automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: It would largely satisfy the 12(3) logging fields for flagged systems, but it covers mainly the 12(3) minimum and training-time experiments rather than runtime logs of deployed systems, and does not address Article 12(2) purposes fully, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A secure log archive with retention tiers and integrity checks is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Encrypted storage, retention tiers, audit access and integrity checks are conventional compliance practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a lifetime log archive with an API and automated gap detection is a reasonably feasible IT project, though it takes some real engineering and storage cost.
evidence_applicability: The archive directly addresses the logging mandate by storing and indexing lifetime logs to support Article 72 post-market monitoring and traceability, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A secure, queryable, integrity-checked log archive would substantially meet retention and traceability needs, but it does not cover generating the logs or the Article 12(2)-(3) content requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK/middleware is a standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with a reusable tool but no change in how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared infrastructure with a mandatory integration requirement is a common strategy that violates no norms, though mandating it for teams may cause minor internal friction.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers for one quarter and a plug-in SDK compatible with the existing stack is a modest, concrete, non-radical investment.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate efficiently across parallel research projects.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the logging mandate technically, but it does not specify which events to log for Article 12(2) purposes, retention, or traceability content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default templates and logging decorators are a fairly common expected response, with only mild framing as a prototyping-speed benefit.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a new tooling format (template scaffold) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves R&D ways of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Templated starter repos with built-in logging are a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing MLOps starter repo with a decorator-based logging layer, which is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces automatic event logs at inference, which is the Article 12 logging mandate stated in the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by making logging default and consistent, but it covers only inference-boundary logs and not the full Article 12 scope (risk-situation events, post-market monitoring, Annex III minimums like user identification, retention), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tying log-readiness to funding-release gates is a sensible but fairly expected governance move, so it is interesting but not highly imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint to existing review processes and still treats compliance as logging practice, though linking it to budget tranches adds a modest new process element.
evidence_acceptability: Gating funds on compliance readiness is a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though blocking budget tranches may draw some project-team resistance.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing steering committee and PMO template with a thirty-minute slot and no new body, so it is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by enforcing demonstrable logs for 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: A demonstration gate would help enforce log readiness but does not itself build the logging, cover Article 12(3) or documentation needs, or ensure ongoing capture, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code via SDK and CI/CD gates is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standardized SDK and pipeline gate but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged despite the 'architectural invariant' framing.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized logging libraries and CI/CD compliance gates are common engineering practice and violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK and CI gate requires some platform-team work and changes to deployment pipelines but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a logging layer that captures the Article 12(1)-(3) events, including the Annex III(1)(a) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, an enforced SDK with CI/CD schema gates would reliably deliver the automatic logging capability the mandate requires, solving the main compliance problem, though it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance judgments beyond schema fields.

evidence_originality: Combining cryptographic minimization with Article 12(3) logging and GDPR tension is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is not wholly surprising as a response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (privacy-preserving logging schemas, a reference architecture, publication) and partly reframes compliance as publishable IP and technical authority, but it remains centered on logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging, publication, and engagement with regulators are common, norm-respecting strategies, though the retention minimization must be reconciled carefully with the mandated logging.
evidence_implementability: A nine-month project with two researchers and 5% of general research budget reallocation is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment that requires some changes but no radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(3)(b)-(d) logging requirements for biometric systems, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the logging obligation for biometric systems under Annex III 1(a) while reducing data retention risk, but it covers only that subset and not the lab's wider high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as an auxiliary training loss with differentiable audit nodes is imaginative and unusual compared with typical logging-infrastructure responses, though transparency-by-design themes exist in the interpretability literature.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science of model architecture and addresses what the lab researches, though it stops short of a complete redefinition.
evidence_acceptability: Research into transparent-by-design architectures violates no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat unusual way to respond to a logging mandate.
evidence_implementability: Embedding differentiable audit nodes and auxiliary losses into transformer and diffusion models is an open research problem needing significant redesign, retraining, and uncertain results, so it is difficult and expensive though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The idea targets the logging mandate by making inference-step records an intrinsic model property, but it addresses an implied problem (architectural traceability) rather than directly meeting Article 12's event-logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, model-internal interpretable records would not by themselves provide the lifetime event logs, timestamps, reference databases, or user identification Article 12 requires, so it only partially solves the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: A design-stage logging architecture review gate is a common, expected compliance-by-design process that many labs would propose, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a review gate and spec deliverable but still treats compliance as standard logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: An internal design review and sign-off gate is a common governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires a new gate and documentation step but uses existing sign-off and documentation processes, so it is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping design to its requirements before development.
evidence_effectiveness: A design review ensures logging is planned, but it does not itself implement logging, cover Article 12(3) specifics, or ensure ongoing compliance, so it only partly solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware with CI/CD gating is the common, expected response to Article 12, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-and-logging engineering approach that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging middleware with deployment gates is a common compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A reusable middleware built in two sprints and wired into existing CI/CD is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes, though immutable tamper-evident storage adds moderate effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-capturing events and documenting schema against Article 12(3) minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would largely satisfy the logging requirement across systems, but it covers only logging capture and not wider traceability, post-market monitoring, or identification of natural persons in verification, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code in CI is a familiar and fairly predictable response for a lab, with a sensible but not surprising application to Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool-based process (automated gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice, so it is only slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Adding automated compliance checks to CI/CD is a common, norm-respecting engineering practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing GitLab CI pipeline with a compliance job using the shared SDK test harness requires modest changes at low cost, though simulating full-lifecycle event streams takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: CI gates that check event schema, lifetime continuity and retention directly address the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Automated conformance tests would catch logging defects early and contribute substantially, but they verify logging rather than decide what to log or cover Annex III specifics, so they are only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Native instrumentation with checksums, an append-only log, and a drift alert is sensible and somewhat interesting, but it is an expected engineering response to the mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements such as a write-once log and a drift alert but still treats compliance as logging practice built into the existing product.
evidence_acceptability: Append-only logging and compliance engineering violate no legal or social norms and are common strategies, though biometric identifier logging raises minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting the matching engine and adding an append log requires some engineering changes to an existing product but is reasonably feasible without a separate service.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by capturing the Article 12(3) minimums (use period, reference database, matched input, verifier identity) in the biometric flow.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, atomic write-once logging of database version, matched inputs, and verifier IDs would satisfy the paragraph-3 requirements for the biometric line, though it does not address paragraphs 1-2 broadly or explicitly log the period of each use.

evidence_originality: Compliance checks in CI pipelines are a fairly familiar idea in DevOps, so this is interesting but not especially imaginative or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (automated CI testing) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing gates are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building per-category schemas and a sandbox harness with synthetic inputs requires some engineering effort and changes to workflow but is reasonably feasible with standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required events are emitted (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate that verifies required log events are emitted and well-formed would help ensure the logging mandate is met, but it does not address retention, content adequacy for traceability, or non-prototype obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandated logs as research data is a fairly sensible, somewhat imaginative idea but not highly surprising, since labs would plausibly think of using monitoring data for drift research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making the compliance logs a research data source, so logging is woven into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for internal research is a somewhat unusual strategy, and it raises minor data-governance and purpose-limitation questions, but it offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds one analytics pipeline on top of the existing compliance log store with a single postdoc, which is a reasonably feasible addition needing some changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: The idea mainly addresses an implied problem, how to extract research value from logging overhead, though its monthly drift indicators also serve post-market monitoring, which relates to the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met (what to log, retention, traceability), so it helps only as a partial contribution to the solution.

evidence_originality: Unified telemetry SDK with append-only logs is the obvious, expected response to Article 12 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standard compliance logging with immutable storage is a common, legally aligned strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Embedding a standardized logging SDK into inference pipelines and writing to immutable cloud storage uses existing technology, but requires cross-system engineering changes and retention costs across all high-risk systems.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, with specific mapping to paragraph 3 items (do X to get compliance logging).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, an automatic append-only logging SDK capturing timestamps, reference databases, matched inputs and verifier identities with lifetime retention would directly satisfy the core Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not address the broader R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance documentation into open-science artifacts linked to papers is somewhat unusual and interesting, but not strikingly ingenious, and open documentation is a known transparency idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making the compliance deliverable a scientific contribution woven into publication, though it keeps the lab's core research unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Open science is a norm-aligned practice, but publishing full training data provenance and risk records may offend commercial, IP and security sensibilities somewhat.
evidence_implementability: Building a versioned schema and public repository is reasonably feasible, though curating full dossiers for every paper requires significant effort and legal review.
evidence_applicability: It addresses technical documentation from Recital 71 rather than the Article 12 automatic logging mandate, so it solves an implied, related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Publishing documentation does not provide automatic event logging capabilities and so only partially contributes to meeting the mandate, while also raising confidentiality issues.

evidence_originality: A reference logger mapping the Article 12(3) fields to an append-only ledger is what an evaluator would expect from labs, with no surprising insight.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance logging implementation with a reusable template and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, though the append-only ledger is a mildly new element.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing the mandated logs with GDPR-compliant encryption is a common compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers prototyping over four sprints against an existing pipeline with standard append-only storage and encryption is a modest, reasonably feasible effort requiring some changes but no radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements the Article 12(3) minimum logging set, which is the explicit logging mandate named in the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would satisfy the Annex III(1)(a) minimum logging requirements, but it covers only that tier and not general Article 12(1)-(2) logging for other high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory continuous logging as an object of research on drift signatures is unusual and shows some imagination, though drift detection itself is a familiar topic.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns the compliance obligation into a research program and affects what the lab researches, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, but it does not fully redefine the larger problem.
evidence_acceptability: Studying logging effects and drift in sandboxed environments violates no legal or social norms and is a normal research activity.
evidence_implementability: Multi-year longitudinal deployment of instrumented models in sandboxed production-like environments with new statistical detector development is a significant, expensive, slow undertaking, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It does not address how to meet the logging mandate and only loosely relates to the problem through post-market monitoring design, a special-situation benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: The programme produces drift-detection research and does not itself implement the logging mandate or ensure compliance, so it would not solve the main problem even if done.

evidence_originality: Centralized reusable logging middleware is a common, expected response to the mandate with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-engineering approach that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance logging infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A centralized sidecar logging middleware integrated into CI/CD requires building a platform and some changes but is a reasonably feasible, standard engineering measure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12's automatic logging requirements, including the paragraph 3 minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would directly satisfy the logging mandate across deployments, though it does not address documentation, risk-specific event selection, or R&D adaptation, so it is mostly but not entirely the solution to the main problem.

evidence_originality: Adding a compliance gate to design-review checklists is a common, expected 'shift-left' response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It uses existing governance templates and review processes and treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Checklist gates and compliance-aware reviewers are common governance strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It only requires updating an existing template, training PIs in regular meetings, and assigning reviewers, which is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring Article 12 event categories are specified before implementation (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: A design-review gate requiring signed logging specs covering Article 12(2)(a)-(c) would help ensure logging capability is built in, but it addresses only the design-stage part of the mandate and not actual log implementation, Annex III 1(a) minimums, or ongoing operation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized, reusable logging layer with automatic profile activation is sensible and somewhat interesting, but it is a fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable sidecar is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the relationship between R&D and obligations unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Append-only audit logging built into shared infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: A thin wrapper around an existing experiment runner with structured JSON-Lines and an append-only store is reasonably feasible, though it requires some infrastructure investment and integration work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by automatically recording the four specified minimum event types.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would capture the Article 12(3) minimum events across projects, but it covers mainly the Annex III point 1(a) minimum and not the broader Article 12(2) risk, post-market and monitoring event relevance, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance reviews are a mundane, expected response, with only the compute-access tie adding slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a gate) but still treats compliance as a logging-requirement checkpoint without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: A internal classification gate with legal and office sign-off is a common governance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-page checklist and a sign-off step tied to compute access require some process changes and coordination but are reasonably feasible and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of knowing which Article 12 logging requirements apply before committing R&D resources, which is directly part of deciding how to respond to the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps determine which logging fields apply early and avoids wasted prototypes, but it does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy/security/logging by design is a familiar approach that labs would commonly propose, so it is sensible but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Integrating logging into the design process from the first prototype changes how R&D relates to compliance (logging woven into the science) but does not alter what the lab researches, so it is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Design-stage compliance integration and internal audits are common, norm-respecting practices with no legal or social objections.
evidence_implementability: It requires revised protocols, an event-mapping document, lightweight hooks, and quarterly audits, which are reasonable process changes with moderate overhead and no radical investment.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate through event-mapping, logging hooks, and audits against Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: Early integration and audits would substantially support Article 12 compliance for new systems but do not cover legacy systems, the specific Article 12(3) minimums, or retention and other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into open reproducibility archives and co-authored benchmark papers is an unusual, imaginative angle compared with typical logging-infrastructure responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance records a source of scientific output and new partnerships, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Tiered access with sanitized public records is a reasonably norm-respecting approach, though public release of logs raises some confidentiality and IP sensitivities that make it somewhat uncommon.
evidence_implementability: It requires building curated archives, tiered access, sanitization processes and a stewardship partnership, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial set of changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal curates mandatory documentation and logs into archives satisfying Article 12, which relates directly to the logging mandate, though its main aim (open-science impact) is only an implied benefit tied to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Structured archives would help organize compliance records, but the proposal does not specify how events are automatically logged or how Article 12(2) purposes are met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reconciling Article 12(3) logging with data minimisation via commitments, hashes and k-anonymity buckets is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle, though privacy-preserving logging is a known research area, so it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (cryptographic commitments, a two-layer pipeline) and creates partner tooling and publications, but it still treats compliance chiefly as a logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging violates no norms and is a sensible, common-sense strategy, though the legal question of whether hashes satisfy the Article 12(3) recording requirements is a mild uncertainty.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping a hashing and k-anonymity logging pipeline is feasible with existing cryptographic tools, but it demands significant specialist work and attack stress-testing, so it needs some changes and moderate resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified requirement of Article 12(3) (reference databases, matched inputs, verifier identities) and how to log it compliantly, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If it worked it would meet Article 12(3) logging for biometric systems while resolving GDPR tension, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and does not address general logging obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Cryptographically attested, version-hashed provenance middleware for biometric match logging is a somewhat unusual and interesting take, but it is a logical extension of standard logging/audit-trail practice rather than a surprising idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (immutable lineage, cryptographic attestation, open-source component) and turns compliance into a publishable contribution, yet it still fundamentally treats compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source compliance tooling with cryptographic attestation violates no norms, though binding verifier identities raises minor privacy/labor considerations that are manageable.
evidence_implementability: Building middleware with query interception, version hashing, and cryptographic verifier attestation is a substantial engineering effort but uses established techniques and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the explicit Article 12(3)(b)-(d) logging requirements (reference database, input data, verifier identity) for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would satisfy the specific minimum logging requirements for biometric systems, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) and not the period-of-use logging or the broader Article 12(1)-(2) obligations across the lab's systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy-preserving audit logging as a research thread with an open-source offering is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns a compliance obligation into publishable research and a procurement differentiator, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance (compliance-born offerings and partners) without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing research and offering open-source tools to public-sector partners offends no norms, though applying differential privacy to audit logs may raise regulator concerns about completeness.
evidence_implementability: One postdoc, existing HPC capacity, and a six-month timeline are modest and feasible, although the research outcome is uncertain and the logs must still meet the regulation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified part of the problem, the burden of meeting Article 12(3)(c)-(d) logging of sensitive data, though only for a narrow subset of high-risk systems (Annex III 1(a)).
evidence_effectiveness: It could ease one logging-related burden and create reputational value, but it is research that does not itself deliver compliant logging now and may conflict with auditability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Integrating compliance capture into existing workflows is a common, expected response, with little that is surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces process changes (log checkpoints in SOPs) but still treats compliance as logging practice, though capturing records as a by-product of the science leans slightly toward changing the relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Folding logging and documentation into existing SOPs is a common, legally sound strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing notebooks and version control with three workshops, so it needs only modest changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging and documentation mandate by capturing records during normal R&D work.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet documentation and logging duties but does not itself specify system-level automatic event logging or the Article 12(2) event content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code in CI is a well-known DevOps pattern, so applying it to Article 12 logs is sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI gating of log schemas) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though it does fold evidence into the development workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Adding compliance checks as CI gates is a common engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing GitHub Actions pipeline, but it requires writing schema checkers per high-risk category, which means some changes and reasonably feasible work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by verifying that logs contain the Article 12 fields before release.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify log conformance and cut audit overhead, but it checks only the schema during tests and does not cover runtime logging, retention, or the substantive judgment of what events matter, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance logging SDK mapped to Article 12(3) is a sensible but fairly expected response, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a reusable tool and format but still treats compliance as logging practice, with only a modest new element in the form of an SDK component.
evidence_acceptability: Building reusable compliance tooling is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
