evidence_effectiveness: It helps meet retention and retrieval needs but does not by itself ensure the logs capture the required events or cover Article 12 content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gateway-level logging middleware with declarative schemas is a sensible and fairly expected pattern, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only automating it at the infrastructure layer.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging middleware with declarative schemas is a common engineering approach that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a plugin in the existing gRPC stack plus schemas and durable storage, which is reasonably feasible but involves some engineering changes.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly addresses the stated problem by automatically capturing the Article 12(3) fields (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier IDs) for the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a structural default logging layer would meet the automatic-recording mandate across systems, though it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance judgments or systems outside the gateway, so it is nearly but not fully a complete solution.

evidence_originality: Mapping the regulation's required fields to workflows and enforcing them in backend APIs is the obvious, expected response and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging implemented via API changes, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Complying with a legal mandate through logging is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Modifying backend APIs and gating outputs on field capture across product journeys requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with known technology.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly implements the four minimum logging fields of Article 12(3), which is an identified part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, capturing all four required fields as a hard prerequisite would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) logging minimums, though it covers only that subset of Article 12 (not general logging under 12(1)-(2) or R&D adaptation).

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in CI pipelines are a fairly expected engineering response, so the idea is interesting but not rare or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A CI pytest gate is a new tool/process element but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations in any deep way.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing gates in release pipelines are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses standard tools like pytest and CI with synthetic queries and fixtures, requiring only modest changes, though building test fixtures for each model takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying the Article 12(3) fields are recorded before release.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies only the Article 12(3) minimum fields (which apply to Annex III 1(a) systems) and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging, nor production behavior, so it contributes to but does not fully solve compliance.

evidence_originality: Tagging projects by regulatory category and front-loading compliance sprints is a mundane, commonly expected planning response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a project-management re-prioritization that treats compliance as a logging task scheduled around the science, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Risk-tiered planning and compliance-first scheduling is a standard strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a tagging exercise and sprint re-planning within the existing quarterly cycle and funding envelope, which is a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets meeting Article 12 logging obligations, especially the Annex III 1(a) sub-log requirements, by sequencing engineering work to build them.
evidence_effectiveness: Sequencing and tagging projects helps plan for logging but does not itself implement the logging or cover the general Article 12(1)-(2) obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates and checklists are the most common response expected for such a mandate, so the idea is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice, a review gate with a checklist, and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A stage-gate compliance review is a common governance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist and a sign-off checkpoint are low-cost and non-radical, though they add a gate to the lifecycle and require remediation loops.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auditing systems against its specific sub-paragraphs before release.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-deployment checklist and sign-off gate would help ensure logging requirements are verified, but it checks for logging rather than building it and relies on checklist quality and human sign-off, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reserving a fixed share of project hours for compliance is a sensible but fairly common resource-planning approach that an experienced evaluator would expect, with little surprise or ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A budgeting framework reserving engineer-hours for documentation and log upkeep is a new process element but still treats compliance as a separate logging and documentation practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reserving hours for compliance is a conventional management strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A budget allocation capped at eight percent of FTE is a non-radical management change that can be adopted quickly at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of keeping documentation and log systems maintained over the system lifetime, which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses only staffing for documentation and log upkeep, not the technical logging capability, event coverage, or Article 12(2)-(3) content, so it contributes to but only partially solves the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Log analytics dashboards for monitoring are a fairly expected response, with the differentiator angle adding only slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (analytics platform, dashboards) and a mild competitive-differentiator framing, but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D works.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal log analytics and dashboards for post-market monitoring and sharing capability with authorities is a common, norm-compliant strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a queryable log repository linked to model versioning plus role-based dashboards, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes though not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the problem, using Article 12(2)(b) logs to support post-market monitoring obligations.
evidence_effectiveness: Dashboards help with post-market monitoring and risk identification but do not by themselves ensure the logging mandate (automatic event recording, Annex III minimums) is met, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using mandated logs as a longitudinal research corpus for drift science is unusual and shows some imagination, though drift detection on logs is a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving the logs into the lab's science and creating a new research offering born from the obligation, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing operational logs for research may raise data-protection and purpose-limitation concerns (GDPR), but the approach is a reasonable and fairly uncommon strategy that does not offend sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs instrumented deployments, an archiving pipeline, and multi-year research teams, which is a significant but feasible investment given that the logs must be generated anyway.
evidence_applicability: The proposal implements the Article 12 logging schema and uses the logs for drift analysis, which addresses the logging mandate only partly and treats the compliance response as a means to an implied research goal.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not on its own ensure that logs satisfy Article 12 requirements such as traceability, risk identification, and the Annex III minimums, but it does contribute by building the logging infrastructure and giving it a use in post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: A dedicated monitoring team with anomaly detection on logs is a fairly predictable, mundane response to post-market monitoring obligations.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice, adding an organizational unit and tools but not changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal surveillance of logs for compliance is a sensible and legitimate strategy that violates no norms, though data-protection concerns around log content are modest.
evidence_implementability: Staffing a standing team and building a centralized data lake with anomaly-detection pipelines requires significant organizational change and ongoing cost, though it is feasible for a well-resourced lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified purposes of the logging mandate in Article 12(2)(a)-(c), tying logs to Article 72 and 26(5), so it solves an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A central log-analysis unit would help meet the Article 12(2) purposes (risk identification, post-market monitoring, operational monitoring), but it covers only the monitoring use of logs and does not itself deliver the technical logging capability or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-source compliance tooling with a market-differentiator framing is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a market offering and reference-implementation positioning, changing the relationship between the lab's work and its obligations (new offerings born from compliance), though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance tool and running customer workshops is somewhat unusual for a lab but offends no legal or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building and documenting a log verification/export toolkit over two quarters is a reasonable, moderate effort requiring some new development but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: The toolkit directly addresses Article 12 log records and Annex III 1(a) fields, though it focuses on deployer verification/export rather than the lab's own logging capability, so it addresses a closely related implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help deployers verify and export logs but does not itself create the automatic event recording in the systems, so it is only a partial solution to meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a logging library is a fairly expected response and the dual-use credit angle shows some but limited imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a new element (an open-source toolkit) and turns compliance into a research output and grant narrative, but it still fundamentally treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building and releasing an open-source compliance tool under MIT licence and seeking grant credit violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building on existing internal tooling over one quarter is a modest, reasonably feasible effort with some changes needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by building a library that records the specified log items.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide automatic logging aligned to Article 12(3) minimums, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimums, does not address the general Article 12(1)-(2) event relevance or the lab's wider obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a machine-readable documentation standard and pushing it to ISO/IEC is a somewhat unusual and imaginative response, but standardization contributions are a recognizable approach and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open schema, standards submission, reference-role positioning) and creates new offerings from compliance, shifting the lab's relationship to compliance toward standard-setting, but it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release, validation on internal systems, and a standards-body position paper violate no norms and are fairly common, legitimate strategies, though the lab must clear IP or confidentiality concerns when sharing documentation structure.
evidence_implementability: A small cross-team group drafting a schema, validating on two systems, and submitting a paper is reasonably feasible, though standards adoption and cross-team effort require some changes and resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied, related problem (documentation and traceability from Recital 71) rather than directly the automatic logging capability, so it applies only indirectly to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal focuses on technical documentation under Recital 71 rather than Article 12's automatic event logging mandate, so even if achieved it only partially contributes to meeting the logging requirement.

evidence_originality: A lifetime-storage cost model tied to budget reallocation is a sensible but fairly expected finance-oriented response, showing some imagination without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a financial model and budget reallocation that trims research streams to fund compliance, which changes the relationship between R&D priorities and compliance obligations but does not weave logging into the science itself.
evidence_acceptability: Budget analysis and board-approved reallocation are common governance practices that violate no norms, though trimming projects may cause mild internal friction.
evidence_implementability: A twelve-week analysis and a board budget revision are within normal management capacity, requiring only moderate effort and some difficult prioritization decisions.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely resourcing the lifetime logging requirement, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Costing and funding the logging mandate helps the lab pay for compliance but does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a dedicated logging schema for the Article 12(3) minimums with write-once storage and access controls is the mundane, expected response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its R&D-compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Complying with explicit legal logging requirements through common engineering controls violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a structured log schema with write-once storage and role-based access requires some engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with known technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the specific four-item logging floor in Article 12(3), which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully meet the Article 12(3) minimums for Annex III 1(a) systems but does not address the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging for other high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution to the broader mandate.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a customer-visible trust signal for procurement is interesting and shows some imagination but is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by creating a new product and market differentiator born from the logging obligation, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Offering a read-only, consent-based log portal as part of a licensing tier is a somewhat unusual but legitimate business practice that offends no norms, though exposing personnel identifiers needs careful data-protection handling.
evidence_implementability: Building a lightweight API and web interface on top of existing middleware is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes, with added security and privacy work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making logs verifiable and exportable to deployers, relating to Article 12/26 monitoring and traceability) rather than the directly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A customer-facing dashboard exposing logs helps transparency and audit export but does not itself create the Article 12 automatic logging capability, so it is only a partial contribution (it presupposes the middleware logging exists).

evidence_originality: Centralizing compliance logging into shared middleware is a mundane, expected response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging service is a common, uncontroversial engineering and compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building over six months on existing containerised infrastructure with thin adapters is a modest, reasonably feasible change with low-to-moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X, get compliant logs) by implementing the specified Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: A central logging middleware capturing the Article 12(3) fields would meet the logging mandate for the lab's high-risk systems, though it does not cover Article 12(2) event-relevance scoping, retention, or documentation, so it is mostly but not wholly a solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware or SDK is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, offering little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A reusable logging SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance tooling is a standard, uncontroversial strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building and maintaining an SDK with configurable schemas and integrating it across all pipelines requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible for a platform team.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the required event streams and Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a standard logging SDK embedded in all high-risk systems would largely satisfy the logging requirement, though it does not itself cover the broader documentation or the judgment of which events are relevant to risk.

evidence_originality: A schema plus CI validator for mandated log fields is a sensible but fairly expected compliance engineering response, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new tooling (schema, validator, endpoint) but still treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated schema validation in CI is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It is a scoped sprint using existing CI, event bus, and human-in-the-loop checkpoint, making it low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, meeting the specific biometric logging minimums in Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: The validator covers the four Article 12(3) minimum fields for Annex III 1(a) systems, but it does not address the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging, documentation, or R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating log schemas as a publishable research contribution is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and research by making logging a scientific contribution and an offering to other labs, stretching the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open schemas and working with legal counsel is somewhat unusual but offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Designing schemas, validating on three prototypes, publishing, and consulting counsel requires significant but ordinary R&D effort, so it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting Article 12(2) logging via event-taxonomy schemas, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Schemas covering Article 12(2) would help meet the mandate but do not address the Article 12(3) minimums, the automatic-recording infrastructure, or retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Design-doc templates for compliance are a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice folded into existing design review, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a logging section to design documents with peer review at a design gate is a common, norm-compliant governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A reusable template completed at an existing design-review gate is a low-cost, non-radical change, though it requires some process adoption by project leads.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 logging mandate by specifying event schemas and the Annex III 1(a) data fields, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A design-time template ensures logging is planned but does not itself build or verify the technical logging capability, so it contributes only partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Weaving traceability into model computation for compliance is an unusual and somewhat imaginative framing, though interpretable-AI-by-design is a known research theme.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It explicitly changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the regulatory constraint into a design principle woven into the science, but it does not redirect what the lab researches at the larger level.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging into model design is a legally and socially unobjectionable, somewhat unusual strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping three novel architectures with a small team in six months is a research effort with uncertain accuracy and overhead outcomes, so it requires significant change and is difficult but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of making logging reliable and intrinsic to high-risk biometric systems, which relates to the mandate but does not directly deliver the specified log contents.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, architecture-native traceability would address only part of Article 12 (event logging, period of use, reference database, human verifier identity) and is not a full solution, so it contributes partially.

evidence_originality: Pre-release verification of compliance controls is a common and expected response, with only modest touches such as shadow-traffic edge-case scenarios.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a testing step but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Pre-release testing and checklist-based sign-off are standard QA and compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs QA scripting, synthetic and shadow-traffic scenarios, and release gating, which are reasonably feasible additions to existing QA processes without radical change.
evidence_applicability: The drills directly verify that logging captures the events Article 12(2) and 12(3) require, which is the core of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Validating logs against an Article 12 checklist before release would reasonably ensure the lab meets the logging mandate if carried out, though it checks capability and does not itself build the logging.

evidence_originality: Pre-release compliance gates are a common, expected response to regulatory mandates and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard audit checkpoint that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gates and sign-offs are a common governance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A three-person review cell and a go/no-go certificate are modest process additions requiring some changes but are reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring logging meets Article 12(2) traceability requirements before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-deployment logging review would catch gaps and help meet Article 12, but it only verifies logging and does not itself build the logging capability or cover R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with named stewards is a sensible, commonly expected response to the documentation-update requirement, and it shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a documentation steward role and version-controlled revision cycles but still treats compliance as a separate administrative practice, leaving R&D unchanged, though it introduces some new process elements.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date documentation with audit trails for notified bodies violates no norms and is a conventional compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Version-controlled repositories and assigned stewards are low-cost, non-radical changes that most labs can adopt with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It targets documentation currency from Recital 71, which relates to the record-keeping context only implicitly rather than the stated logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would meet the technical documentation upkeep requirement but does not address Article 12's automatic event logging mandate, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance testing with automated gates is a sensible, fairly common DevOps-style idea that shows little surprise or ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (an automated conformance gate in sprints) but still treats compliance as logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A sprint gate with automated tests is a common engineering practice that violates no norms, though blocking sign-off may create some friction with researchers.
evidence_implementability: Adding an automated test suite and a sprint checkpoint is a reasonably feasible set of changes, though building the replay and verification harness takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying event capture during development.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch logging gaps early and contribute substantially, but it only checks field population and consistency on prototypes and does not cover lifetime logging, retention, or the broader adaptation of R&D, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left logging in research pipelines is a sensible and fairly expected response, with only modest interest in applying it before product transition.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (logging-native research infrastructure) and slightly shifts when compliance applies, but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into research tooling is a sensible, norm-respecting practice that offends no one and preserves researcher autonomy.
evidence_implementability: Extending the existing training harness with a structured logger and versioning it alongside notebooks is a reasonably feasible measure, though it needs some changes to research workflows and carries storage and overhead costs.
evidence_applicability: Instrumenting all prototypes with Article 12-schema event logging directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would give audit-ready logging from the start, but it covers only generic provenance, version and metric logging and does not address the Annex III 3 specifics, retention or the wider compliance duties, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: A gap analysis before building is a mundane, standard compliance step with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gap audits are a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week checklist audit with liaisons and a tracker is cheap and requires only non-radical organizational changes.
evidence_applicability: The audit directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by identifying which required log fields are missing in live systems, an identified problem tied to the stated one.
evidence_effectiveness: A gap audit helps target work but does not itself build the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution (and 'four mandated data points' applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems).

evidence_originality: Building monitoring dashboards and SPC alerts on top of logs is a sensible but fairly expected response to post-market monitoring requirements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new analytics team and tooling but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal post-market monitoring analytics is a common, norm-compliant strategy that regulators and customers would welcome.
evidence_implementability: A small data science team using standard streaming and statistical process-control tools is a reasonably feasible addition requiring some new staffing and infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly uses Article 12 logs to meet the Article 12(2) purposes of identifying Article 79(1) risk situations and supporting Article 72 post-market monitoring, though it addresses the use of logs more than the mandate to produce them.
evidence_effectiveness: Analytics on logs would contribute meaningfully to monitoring and post-market duties but does not itself implement the logging capability or the Article 12(3) minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Assigning a compliance steward, using version control and holding quarterly audits is a mundane, expected compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common, uncontroversial governance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A steward per project and version-controlled repositories with quarterly audits are modest, non-radical changes that are easy to put in place at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the technical documentation described in Recital 71, which is related to but not the same as the logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Documentation lifecycle management supports traceability and compliance verification but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging that Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a longitudinal research dataset is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning logging obligations into a research program that shapes what the lab studies, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Mining mandated logs for reliability research is legally and socially acceptable, though publishing findings from operational logs raises somewhat unusual data-use and confidentiality questions, so it is a less common strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A dedicated data-science pod, sustained multi-year longitudinal analysis, and peer-reviewed publication require significant resources and access to deployer logs the lab may not control, making it expensive and difficult but feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal uses Article 12 logs for research and regulatory standing, which solves an implied related problem (adapting R&D to the mandate) but does not directly address how to meet the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would leverage logs for benefit and support risk identification but would not itself establish the logging capability or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging in research pipelines is a fairly expected idea, with the framing of audit-ready experiments showing some but modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the experimental process itself, which is paradigm stretching, though it does not alter what the lab researches or create new offerings.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in MLOps and codifying it in a handbook is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin logging agent on the existing MLOps stack with an append-only store is reasonably feasible, though it requires some changes to pipelines and mandatory procedures across the lab.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (avoiding a retrofit gap between research and deployment-grade logging) that relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, rather than the directly identified logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: Instrumenting all experiments with immutable logging would contribute substantially to meeting Article 12 traceability, but it covers lab R&D pipelines rather than deployed-system event logging for Article 12(2)-(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging/telemetry middleware is a common, mundane approach that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a logging infrastructure practice, merely centralizing it, so the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance stay essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized logging middleware for compliance is a standard, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses an existing time-series store and container orchestration with a lightweight agent, though refactoring orchestration and embedding in every system requires some changes, making it reasonably feasible to fairly easy.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(1) and (2) automatic event recording mandate, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the automatic logging capability across systems, but it does not itself ensure the event content relevant to risk, post-market and operation monitoring or Annex III specifics, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: A feasibility spike with storage tiering and TCO modeling is a mundane, expected response, though the p99 audit-query stress test adds slight specificity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard engineering due diligence on logging architecture and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Feasibility and TCO studies before committing budget are a common, uncontroversial business practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A four-week study by one senior engineer and a DBA is cheap and easy to run with no radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (cost and viability of retention and audit-query performance for the Annex III 1(a) fields) that relates to the logging mandate, though not the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A feasibility spike only answers whether lifetime logging is viable and does not itself build or deliver the logging capability, so it contributes to but does not solve the compliance problem, and the stated problem explicitly excludes exploratory funding.

evidence_originality: A log analytics dashboard with alerting and report exports is a common, expected response to this mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tool and reporting format but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: In-house compliance monitoring dashboards are a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an ingestion pipeline, rules engine and reporting is a standard data-engineering project requiring some resources and changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The dashboard directly targets Article 12(2)(a)-(b) goals of identifying risk/modification signals and supporting post-market monitoring, which are part of the stated logging mandate, though it addresses the use of logs more than the generation of logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to monitoring and evidence needs but does not itself ensure that systems technically record events or meet Article 12(3) minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a longitudinal research instrument for studying model ageing is an unusual and interesting reframing, though it stops short of being truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science and turning compliance infrastructure into a source of publishable research.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for research is a somewhat unusual strategy that offends no norms, though logged data reuse for publication could raise minor data governance questions.
evidence_implementability: Co-developing the logging layer with the ML science group and adding richer metadata requires some changes and added storage and engineering effort, but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to design the logging layer to meet the mandate and adapt R&D, though the main benefit, publishing longitudinal studies, is an implied secondary outcome.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the Article 12 minimum and support post-market monitoring, but it adds research aims and does not itself specify how the required fields such as the Annex III items are met, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building compliance in by design with a gate in the SDLC is a common and expected response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a review gate and spec step but remains standard compliance and logging practice that treats compliance as logging implementation.
evidence_acceptability: Specifying logging at the design stage with a review gate is a common, norm-compliant security/compliance-by-design practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires modest SDLC changes such as spec requirements and a review gate, which is reasonably feasible without radical cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring systems have compliant automatic logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Architectural logging hooks and schema validation against Article 12(2) would help meet the logging mandate, but they do not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or documentation, so the solution is partial.

evidence_originality: A gap analysis before remediation is the standard, expected first step for any compliance mandate and is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice with the lab's way of working unchanged and no new elements introduced.
evidence_acceptability: A internal gap audit is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week audit with one senior engineer per team is a low-cost, non-radical effort that is easy to carry out.
evidence_applicability: A gap audit against Article 12 paragraphs 2 and 3 produces an implied but related outcome (knowing the delta) that feeds the decision on how to meet the logging mandate, rather than meeting it directly.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit is a necessary diagnostic that helps size remediation but does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial contribution to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Building logging in as default middleware with CI gates is a sensible, fairly expected 'compliance by design' response, with only modest imaginative flair.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (default middleware, CI gates, schema as architectural artifact) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging via standard engineering controls violates no norms and is a common, legally sound strategy.
evidence_implementability: Adding middleware and CI checks to an existing prototyping framework is reasonably feasible with some engineering changes, though defining a canonical schema takes effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by making automatic logging a default in prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially ensure technical logging capability in prototypes, but a generic schema may not cover Annex III specifics, deployed-system lifecycle logging, or documentation duties, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shifting logging to design-time (logging by design) is a well-known, expected response to such mandates, so it is common rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance practice, just earlier in the lifecycle with a gate, and the lab's way of working and the relation of R&D to compliance remain largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A mandatory internal engineering standard for regulatory compliance is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a kickoff compliance gate and requiring logging specs in design documents is a process change with some cost and cultural adjustment but no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by specifying the required log fields and triggers in system design.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding the logging requirements from the start would substantially secure Article 12 compliance, but it covers only logging and not the wider documentation or ongoing monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by default from the first prototype is a common, expected response to Article 12 and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is standard compliance-by-design logging practice (logging middleware, design templates, architecture review gates) that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandating logging in design templates and architecture reviews is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Updating templates and adding middleware and review criteria requires some engineering changes for new projects but is reasonably feasible and avoids retrofitting.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing automatic event recording in systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Default architectural logging with review gates would largely satisfy the technical-capability requirement, though it does not address the Annex III minimum fields or log retention and use specifically, so it is close to but not fully a complete solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging as a shared service is a fairly common and expected response, though sensible rather than imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared infrastructure tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized internal logging service is a common, sensible engineering and compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring the ML-ops platform with two senior engineers for a quarter is a reasonably feasible, moderate change rather than trivial or radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X, get compliant logs) and protecting R&D budgets from repeated effort.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared tamper-evident logging layer capturing the Article 12(2) and 12(3) fields automatically would, if built, solve the main logging-mandate problem for all high-risk pipelines.

evidence_originality: A compliance gate before deployment is a common and mundane response that evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard review checkpoint that treats compliance as ordinary logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A pre-deployment compliance checkpoint is a common governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A half-day review panel of two engineers and one legal liaison added to the existing project-review cadence is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly checks whether the system technically enables automatic event recording under Article 12(2), which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A review gate only assesses the logging design and does not itself build logging capabilities or cover the Article 12(3) minimums or ongoing operation, so it contributes only partially.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-tests in CI is a fairly known DevOps practice, though applying it to Article 12 fields is moderately interesting rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/process (blocking CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing gates in CI are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Pytest fixtures with a mock logging back-end and a GitHub Actions gate are low-cost and use existing tooling, requiring only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by testing that the specific Article 12(3) event types are produced (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: CI gates verify that mandated log fields are emitted and schema-valid, which helps ensure Article 12 logging capability but does not cover the full mandate such as runtime retention, relevance of events to risk, or post-market monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-source instrumentation for automatic logging of ML lifecycle events is an interesting but fairly expected response, with some imagination in framing compliance as reusable research infrastructure.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and reframes compliance as reusable community infrastructure, but it still treats compliance fundamentally as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building an open-source automatic logging layer to satisfy Article 12 is a common, legally and socially unobjectionable strategy.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting PyTorch and JAX pipelines across training, inference, retraining and drift detection requires substantial engineering and design work but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly does X (build automatic logging capturing Article 12 events) to get Y (meeting the logging mandate), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event logging would substantially address the logging mandate but leaves the specifics of relevant event selection, retention, and non-Annex-III coverage only partially resolved, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated log validation in CI is a fairly expected tooling response, though open-sourcing it as a transparency and market play adds some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an automated validator in CI) and an open-source release that turns compliance into reputation and client offerings, which stretches the compliance relationship somewhat but the core remains logging-compliance tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Building and openly releasing a compliance tool violates no legal or social norms and is a somewhat uncommon but welcome strategy.
evidence_implementability: A schema-based field validator is a modest engineering task, though open-source release with documentation and maintenance requires some added effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of verifying that logs satisfy the specific Article 12(3) minimum fields, which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Validating Article 12(3) fields helps ensure logs meet minimum requirements but does not itself create logging capability or cover Article 12(1)-(2) broader traceability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Classifying systems by retrofit cost is a common, mundane compliance-readiness approach that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard gap-analysis and budgeting process that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Audit-and-prioritize budgeting is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-quarter internal audit run by group leads with budget integration requires modest effort and no radical change.
evidence_applicability: The audit of in-pipeline systems against Article 12 fields directly addresses how the lab should respond to the logging mandate, though it targets prioritization rather than logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Triage identifies and budgets for gaps but does not itself implement logging, so it contributes only a partial solution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Hash-chained append-only logs are a well-known technique that experts would expect, so the idea is interesting but not ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a research workstream and internal standard but still treats compliance as logging practice, with only a modest positioning claim about market leadership.
evidence_acceptability: Building tamper-evident, hash-chained logs is a common, legally and socially unobjectionable compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated team of two senior researchers plus an engineering pod and prototyping effort, which is a reasonably feasible but non-trivial resource commitment rather than a minor change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses Article 12's requirement for automatic logging over the system's lifetime by building lifetime-durable, traceable logs.
evidence_effectiveness: Tamper-evident lifetime log storage would contribute substantially to meeting the logging mandate, but it does not specify which events to log or cover the other parts such as Annex III minimum fields, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Starter templates with built-in compliance hooks are a familiar DevOps idea, so this is interesting but not surprising; also 'three tiers per Annex III risk band' is slightly loose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (templates, CI pipelines) but still treats compliance as logging and documentation practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal templates and scaffolds for compliance are a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Auditing four prior prototypes and codifying three template tiers in an internal registry is a modest, reasonably feasible effort with non-radical changes to workflow.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by pre-wiring logging hooks and documentation stubs into new projects.
evidence_effectiveness: Templates help new prototypes start with logging and documentation but do not guarantee Article 12 content adequacy, legacy systems, or the system-specific event relevance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Exposing logs to clients as a trust feature is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but transparency dashboards are a recognizable idea and not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance from an internal cost into a client-facing product offering and a procurement differentiator, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Showing client-facing logs is uncommon but offends no norms, although exposing identities of verifying persons raises some data-protection concerns that remain manageable.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight read-only API gateway over existing logging middleware, piloted with two existing clients, is reasonably feasible, though real-time exposure of sensitive data needs access control and security work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, making logs usable and visible to deployers for monitoring, which relates to the logging mandate but is not the identified problem of generating compliant logs.
evidence_effectiveness: A deployer-facing view of logs helps with Article 12 traceability and Article 26(5) monitoring, but it assumes the logging itself already exists and does not itself meet the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as a research object with tiered ablation studies and an open design guide is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though 'privacy by design'-style framing is familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and turning the obligation into publishable research, without redefining what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open design guides and doing compliance-driven engineering research violates no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat uncommon.
evidence_implementability: Building three prototype high-risk systems with ablation studies is a significant resource commitment and more exploratory research than a committed implementation, making it expensive and difficult but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate and adapt R&D, by designing logs into systems and measuring their costs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would yield design knowledge and prototypes but does not itself guarantee that the lab's actual high-risk systems meet Article 12 requirements such as the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared centralized logging service replacing per-project scripts is a common, mundane response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice centralized into one service, leaving the lab's R&D and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial engineering approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two existing FTEs building a microservice on the current container stack with phased rollout is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though consolidating many projects' logging takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-capturing the paragraph 3 minimum fields, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would cover the mandated minimum fields and consolidate logging, but it addresses mainly para 3 items and not the broader para 2 event relevance (risk identification, post-market monitoring) or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Standardizing a logging schema and enforcing it in CI is a sensible, common approach that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A unified internal schema enforced by a CI lint rule is a new process element but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal standardization with CI checks is a common engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A small working group drafting the schema in one sprint plus a CI lint rule is low-cost and non-radical, though retrofitting existing projects requires some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by covering the specified fields in 12(2) and Annex III 1(a).
evidence_effectiveness: The schema and enforcement would meaningfully deliver Article 12 logging capability across systems, but it covers only logging and not wider documentation, retention, or deployer-side obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware that implements Article 12 is the obvious, mundane response a lab would give.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, apart from adding the logging earlier in design.
evidence_acceptability: Building mandated logging into systems is a common compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging middleware built in during design with two sprints per group is a reasonably feasible set of changes, though it needs some engineering across all pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate, as it does X (embed logging) to get Y (demonstrable compliance).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, logging of the Article 12(3) items would meet the logging mandate, but it is over-scoped for systems outside Annex III 1(a) and does not address how R&D adapts, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance reviews are a common, mundane approach that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new process elements (gates, checklist, workshop) but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Go/no-go milestones and compliance training are standard strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Amending a project template, adding a one-page checklist, and running a half-day workshop this quarter is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by embedding record-keeping design into the project lifecycle.
evidence_effectiveness: Design-review gates with an Article 12 checklist would help ensure logging is built in, but they do not themselves specify or implement the logging capabilities, so the solution is only partial.

evidence_originality: Building logging in from inception to avoid retrofits is a common, expected response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance essentially unchanged, merely shifting timing earlier.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding tamper-evident logging for compliance is a common, legally conforming strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires integrating instrumentation into training and fine-tuning pipelines across all high-risk systems, but a scoped Q3 sprint prototype on two product lines is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly implements Article 12 logging (automatic event recording for risk identification, post-market monitoring, and operation monitoring), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A tamper-evident, built-in logging layer would, if implemented, satisfy the core logging mandate, though the proposal is thin on Article 12(3) specifics like personnel identification and is limited to a prototype on two product lines.

evidence_originality: Centralized shared logging middleware is the standard, expected response to a logging mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library with a design-review gate is a common, uncontroversial engineering and compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It consolidates existing partial loggers into one SDK over a quarter with phased onboarding, which is reasonably feasible with some organizational change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specific events (timestamps, reference database lookups, input data, human verification) the article lists.
evidence_effectiveness: A unified logging SDK enforced at design review would substantially deliver the automatic event recording and audit surface required, though it does not address risk-identification or post-market monitoring content beyond schema, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Making compliance logging a default in experiment code and presenting it as reproducibility hygiene is sensible but fairly expected, with only mild imagination in the reframing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Weaving logging into the experimental protocol so compliance becomes part of the science modestly changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, which is paradigm stretching, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into research workflows and reproducibility practice is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight logging layer integrated into an existing harness within two sprints is a modest, reasonably feasible change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by capturing Article 12(3) items (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs) as a default in the lab's experiment harness, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Default logging would meet much of the Article 12 logging requirement for the lab's trials, but it omits Article 12(3)(d) verifier identification and the Article 12(2) risk, post-market and operation monitoring events, and it covers R&D trials rather than deployed systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware layer is a common, expected engineering response that labs would readily propose, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging infrastructure and leaves the lab's R&D way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged, merely centralizing the build.
evidence_acceptability: Shared infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small team of three or four engineers building on the existing data stack with an API integrated at design phase is reasonably feasible, though retrofitting existing systems requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by providing automatic event recording across high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would support automatic logging with consistent capture, but it does not specify which events satisfy Article 12(2) traceability or Annex III minimums, nor retention or oversight identification, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Adding compliance gates to CI/CD is a fairly common DevOps/compliance-as-code response that experienced evaluators would expect, though the Article 12(3) schema check is a sensible specific touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling step (CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Extending existing CI pipelines with compliance checks is a standard, norm-respecting engineering practice.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing GitLab CI with no new headcount and only moderate effort to write the static-analysis and schema tests, so it is easy and low-cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by enforcing logging capability in development, i.e., do X to get Y where Y is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate verifying log-emission capability would ensure the logging mandate is technically met for prototypes, but it covers only capability checks and not retention, Article 12(2) purpose-relevance, or broader documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Making documentation a sprint deliverable with a rotating steward is a sensible but fairly standard process-management response that many labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a workflow tweak but treats compliance as a documentation practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding documentation duties in sprints is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: The proposal uses an existing Confluence-to-registry pipeline and a rotating steward role within current sprints, so it needs only modest process changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the Recital 71 technical-documentation upkeep requirement, which is related to but not the same as the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate, so it solves an implied rather than directly stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping the technical file current helps traceability and compliance, but it does not create the automatic event logs Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging-by-design with review gates and audits is a common, expected response with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a logging practice, embedding it earlier in design with a template and gates, which is standard compliance-by-design that leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into system architecture with review gates and audits is a common, norm-abiding compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires some process changes (templates, code-review gates, a traceability engineer) but is reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified events, so it solves an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Architecture-level automatic logging with release audits would, if done, largely satisfy the logging requirement, though it addresses only the logging mandate and not the R&D adaptation or the Article 12(2) event relevance beyond Annex III 1(a).

evidence_originality: Requiring compliance costs in project budgets is a common, mundane administrative measure that an evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template line item but still treats compliance as a logging and record-keeping cost, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting for compliance in project proposals is a common, norm-respecting governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Amending an internal grant-review template to add a required budget line is a non-radical, low-cost administrative change, though estimating five-year costs takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of unfunded lifetime logging obligations, which is directly part of how the lab must meet Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: It ensures funding for log retention and documentation but does not itself build logging capability or meet the technical mandate, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: A gap analysis and retrofit of existing tracking infrastructure is the most common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged, adding only log hooks to existing repositories.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure and making internal engineering changes is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over three months using existing repositories and no new tooling is a low-cost, non-radical change that is easy to implement.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (audit and patch logging) to get Y (Article 12 logging capability), which is explicitly part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Mapping and patching logging fields would help meet the logging mandate, but it addresses Article 12(3) fields, which apply only to Annex III 1(a) systems, and leaves the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event-relevance requirements and R&D adaptation largely unaddressed, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into a shared ML pipeline platform is the common, expected response to Article 12 and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Instrumenting shared pipelines with automatic hook-based loggers is a standard compliance-by-engineering practice that still treats compliance as logging and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automatic logging in existing infrastructure violates no legal, social, or business norms and is a conventional strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over one quarter using the existing framework and time-series store is a modest, low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by automatically recording events in a schema mapped to Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver the automatic event recording of Article 12(1) and support traceability, but it covers only logging, not the 12(2) event-relevance judgments, retention, or deployer-side use, and it is a retrofit, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK is a fairly expected response to Article 12, though the CI auto-generated stubs add a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (sidecar, SDK, CI stubs) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging SDK with append-only storage is a common, uncontroversial engineering approach that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a sidecar service with gRPC, Python and C++ SDKs and CI integration requires real engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with standard tools.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12(1) logging mandate by providing automatic event recording for prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic logging capability but does not itself address Article 12(2)-(3) specifics, retention, or traceability relevance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing a public log-transparency whitepaper as a competitive differentiator is somewhat unusual and interesting, but it is a recognizable transparency/marketing practice and not especially ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new element (a public quarterly document) and frames compliance as a market offering, but the underlying logging practice and R&D way of working remain unchanged, so it only slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing details of logging schemas and retention policies is a somewhat uncommon practice that may raise security or IP concerns but does not offend sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a quarterly document with compliance, engineering, and legal review is a modest, reasonably feasible process that requires little change.
evidence_applicability: The whitepaper communicates Article 12 logging implementation to clients, which relates to the stated problem only indirectly because it does not itself implement the logging mandate; it addresses an implied benefit (client assurance).
evidence_effectiveness: A document describing logging does not itself ensure automatic event capture or meet Article 12 requirements, so it would at best contribute marginally to the solution and is only a partial one.

evidence_originality: An open-source logging middleware is a fairly expected response to a logging mandate, though the community-adoption and feedback angle adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and open-release model but still treats compliance as logging practice, with only slight stretching via partner labs and usage-data feedback.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release under an EU-friendly license is a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A small team building a Python library with ONNX layers, guides and cross-architecture validation involves some real changes and effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing use periods, databases, matched inputs, and verifier IDs.
evidence_effectiveness: A working middleware would meet the logging requirements for the lab's pipelines, but it covers mainly Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and not the wider risk/post-market event relevance or documentation, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a research dataset is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making mandatory logs an input to the science, which is paradigm stretching, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing operational logs for research is somewhat unusual and raises anonymization and data-protection questions, but it does not offend sensibilities if anonymized.
evidence_implementability: It adds an ETL stage to the existing logging SDK and data warehouse and assigns one postdoc, which is a modest, reasonably feasible set of changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, how to get value from the logging obligation, which relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps with post-market monitoring and offsets the cost of logging, but it does not itself meet the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default tooling with CI enforcement is a sensible and fairly common response, with only modest imagination in framing logging as zero-cost infrastructure.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process (SDK and CI gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Shared compliance libraries and CI gates are common engineering practice and offend no norms, though developers may resist the added friction.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring prototyping templates, adding a logging abstraction, and setting up a CI gate is a reasonably feasible set of changes using standard engineering tooling, though it takes some effort across existing projects.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building the required log fields into every high-risk prototype.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, default logging hooks enforced by a CI gate would make systems technically log-capable, but they would not cover the full scope of Article 12 (risk-relevant events, post-market monitoring, retention) or the wider documentation requirements, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance gates in staging are a fairly familiar CI/CD-style idea, though applying it to Article 12 event categories is somewhat interesting.
