evidence_implementability: A small team over one quarter plus coordination with three peer labs and reference loggers for four Annex III categories is a reasonably feasible but nontrivial effort requiring some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the identified problem of what constitutes meaningful logging under Article 12 and implements it in the lab's system, though the open benchmark and publication parts address implied broader goals.
evidence_effectiveness: Deriving an event taxonomy and implementing it in the lab's own production logging pipeline would address which events to log under Article 12(2), but it does not by itself cover the full mandate (automatic recording, minimum Annex III 1(a) items, retention, R&D adaptation), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into CI/CD pipelines by default is a common, sensible approach that an experienced evaluator would expect from many labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces automatic hooks in the pipeline but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only integrated into existing tooling rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting logging into existing pipelines is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A small team modifying the existing orchestration layer and reusing existing storage is low-cost and non-radical, though retrofitting needs some engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(1) mandate for automatic event recording, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Pipeline-level logging would help meet Article 12(1) but does not specify which events satisfy 12(2) traceability or 12(3) minimum items, nor runtime logging of deployed systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Exposing Article 12 logs to deployers via an API as a sales differentiator is a somewhat interesting and moderately unusual take, but it is not highly surprising since log-access APIs and compliance-as-feature framing are fairly familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Reframing compliance logging as a product offering and competitive moat changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings (compliance-born offerings), which matches paradigm stretching without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Customer-facing log access with OAuth and anonymization is a commonly accepted business strategy that violates no norms, though data-exposure concerns are manageable.
evidence_implementability: Building secure REST endpoints, standardized schemas, and documentation on every deployed system requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with existing technology.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly implements automatic event logging and traceability per Article 12 and supports deployers' post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: An API exposing logs would help with traceability and deployer monitoring but does not itself define which events to log, ensure retention, or cover Article 12(2)(a) risk identification and anonymization may remove needed data, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as an empirical corpus for studying drift semantics is an unusual and imaginative angle, though not wholly surprising given existing drift detection work.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning logging obligations into a research resource and publishable science, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing research on logs and drift taxonomies violates no norms, though a fundamental research thread is somewhat unusual as a response to a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: Using existing sandbox prototypes to collect longitudinal logs and apply change-detection theory is feasible, though it needs sustained research effort and is not a quick compliance fix.
evidence_applicability: The proposal studies which logged events suffice to detect drift and risk under Article 12(2)(a)-(c), which relates to the logging mandate only indirectly, as an implied problem of making logs useful, rather than meeting the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It is a research program that would not make the lab compliant with the logging requirement and only partially informs what to log, so it contributes to the solution but does not solve it.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a compliance reference implementation is a sensible and somewhat unusual move with some imagination, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an open-source reference repo that positions the lab as a reference and shortens customer integration), which modestly shifts compliance toward an offering, but it is still essentially logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source compliance tooling violates no norms, though publishing may raise minor IP or liability questions for some stakeholders.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers maintaining a standalone repo with tests and documentation is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment.
evidence_applicability: It directly builds the logging capability that Article 12(3) requires, which is an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A reference logging stack covering the four Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and retention would meet the logging mandate for biometric systems, but it does not address other high-risk systems or the lab's wider R&D, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left logging with CI enforcement is a sensible but familiar pattern from DevOps and observability practice, not surprising for this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces process gates and CI checks but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing development workflow, only changing when logging is done.
evidence_acceptability: Design reviews, smoke-test gates, and CI checks are common engineering strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding two sprint checkpoints and CI schema checks is a modest process change using existing tooling, though it requires some cultural adjustment and upfront schema work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by building logging into R&D practice (do X to get compliant logging without late retrofit).
evidence_effectiveness: Defining log schemas up front and enforcing them with CI gates would make Article 12 logging capability present in every new high-risk experiment, but it covers only the logging build process and not the specific content requirements (e.g., Annex III minimums), retention, or existing systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as a longitudinal research dataset is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though drift monitoring from logs is a fairly familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science and making the obligation a source of research data.
evidence_acceptability: Using compliance logs for model monitoring and research is a sensible, norm-respecting approach, though it is somewhat unusual to frame it as a research asset (and data-protection use limits might need care).
evidence_implementability: Designing a unified event schema and automated drift-detection pipelines requires moderate engineering and data-infrastructure work but uses established tools, so it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by defining an event schema and pipelines, and adapts R&D to it, though the stated focus is on research benefit more than on the mandated contents.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help satisfy Article 12 traceability and post-market monitoring aims but is only a partial solution, as it omits specifics like retention, Annex III minimums, and identification of reviewers.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance via stage gates is a fairly expected response, sensible but not particularly imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the process by which compliance is integrated into R&D governance, weaving logging into design decisions, but it does not alter what the lab researches or create new offerings, which is a modest stretch.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance checks in design reviews is a common governance strategy that violates no norms, though making logging a binding criterion is slightly more assertive than usual.
evidence_implementability: It amends an existing stage-gate procedure and embeds one reviewer in existing panels, which is a modest, non-radical process change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by preventing late-stage failures to meet logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging capability is designed in and tested, but it does not itself specify what to log or deliver the technical logging mechanism, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized shared logging infrastructure is a common, expected response to such a mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice implemented as infrastructure, leaving the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized shared logging platform mandated as a project dependency is a common, norm-compliant engineering and compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: An existing eight-person platform team building a containerized service over two quarters is reasonably feasible but requires some organizational changes like mandatory dependency rules.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, including automatic recording and Annex III minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would deliver automatic event recording and the minimum fields, but it does not fully address Article 12(2) purpose-specific event relevance, human verifier identification workflows, or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: CI contract-test gates for log schema are a sensible but fairly expected DevOps-style response to a logging mandate, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (CI gate with contract tests) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated pre-deployment checks are a common engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a pytest suite and a pipeline gate to an existing staging pipeline is a modest, low-cost change using standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that required Article 12(3) log fields are emitted and persisted.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure log field presence and format and catches regressions, but covers only Article 12(3) fields and not the broader Article 12(2) event relevance or retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as epistemically meaningful instrumentation with information-theoretic event criteria is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not wholly unprecedented in the observability and monitoring literature.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes logging as scientific instrumentation and a research contribution, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance (logging woven into the science), though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A working group developing a taxonomy and prototyping it on existing deployments is a normal, unobjectionable research and compliance activity.
evidence_implementability: A small working group prototyping on two existing deployments is feasible, but formalizing information-theoretic criteria and validating correlation with degradation requires some real research effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by defining which events to record for risk identification and monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: A principled event taxonomy would help determine relevant events for traceability and post-market monitoring, but it does not cover retention, integrity, or the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in by design with an architecture-review gate is a common, expected response to the mandate and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a design-phase gate and checklist revision, which are new process elements, but it still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A design checklist and review gate is a common internal governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Revising a checklist and adding an architecture-review requirement is a modest, low-cost process change, though teams must build logging layers into every high-risk prototype.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by specifying the Article 12(3) logging elements at design time.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a mandatory logging specification at design would largely satisfy the logging requirements, though it covers mainly Article 12(3) fields and does not address broader aspects such as retention or the Article 12(2) event relevance, so it is reasonable and nearly complete but not fully so.

evidence_originality: A compliance gate or checklist in the development lifecycle is a very common, expected response to regulatory mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance checkpoint added to existing agile process and still treats compliance as a logging practice, though it introduces a new process element.
evidence_acceptability: Release gates and sign-offs are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist and sign-off at existing sprint reviews are low-cost and non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly targets verifying that automatic logging and retention meet Article 12 before high-risk prototypes leave the lab, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A checklist gate would help ensure logging is present but only verifies readiness, doesn't design the logging or cover the Article 12(2)-(3) content requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging libraries to amortize compliance cost are a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard shared-library approach that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized reusable compliance infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers for one quarter plus six weeks of onboarding, integrated into existing CI/CD, is a modest, reasonably feasible investment with some process change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building a reusable logging module that implements the Annex III 1(a) minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared module would deliver the required automatic event logging across projects, but it covers mainly the Annex III 1(a) minimums and says little about Article 12(2) event relevance or the other compliance needs, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log retention, integrity and monitoring dashboards are the mundane, expected response to Article 12, and the proposal has no surprising element.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as logging and records-management practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A log stewardship programme with retention tiers, encryption and audit cadence is a standard, norm-compliant governance response that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a cross-functional team, ongoing operations and a dashboard, which are reasonably feasible measures that involve some organisational change but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by covering log storage, lifetime retention and feeding post-market monitoring under Article 72.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help sustain compliance after logs are generated, but it does not address the generation of event logs or the content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Schema migration tooling is well known, and applying it to the lifetime-of-system language is a sensible but unsurprising use of it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Schema versioning and migration tooling is a conventional engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A CLI with a CI hook running schema-diff checks is standard engineering that fits existing pipelines, though auto-generating migration scripts for stored logs takes real effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12 requirement that logs be kept over the system's lifetime, and it protects the Article 12(3) minimums, so it addresses an identified part of the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would keep logs queryable and compliant across versions, but it covers only the schema-continuity part of logging and does not decide which events to log, ensure traceability, or address the wider obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI-pipeline gate with static analysis to enforce logging instrumentation is a somewhat unusual and sensible shift-left idea, but not strikingly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (AST scanner in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Build-time compliance gates are a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing lint suite and merge pipeline with a custom AST scanner is reasonably feasible, though defining code paths touching Annex III data flows requires some nontrivial work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging mandate by catching missing instrumentation (do X to get Y, where Y is part of the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure that required log events are instrumented in code, but static checks do not verify runtime logging correctness, retention, or the other Article 12 aspects, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Retention schedules with tiered cloud storage and assigned stewardship are common, mundane responses that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and data-governance practice (storage tiers, retention schedule, access roles) that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using a cloud contract and existing staff for log retention is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It relies on existing provider and staff with a contract negotiation and role assignment, so it is easy and low cost to implement.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of keeping logs across the system's lifetime and making them available to auditors, which relates to the stated logging mandate but is not the core capture requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: Retention and access governance covers only the storage and retrieval part of the logging mandate and does not address what events to log or the technical capability for automatic recording, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A standardized logging SDK enforced via a CI/CD release gate is the most expected, mundane response an AI lab would give to Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice built into existing engineering workflows, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging with release gates is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an SDK and adding a CI/CD gate requires some cross-team engineering effort and changes but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified events.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the technical logging capability requirement across systems, though it does not cover retention, post-market monitoring use, or the proportionality of events, so it is mostly but not wholly a solution.

evidence_originality: Documentation managers, version control, and quarterly audits are standard compliance practice and would be expected from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice with a modest process upgrade and leaves the lab's way of working and the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation upkeep and internal audits are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a role per project, a repository, and audit cycles, which are reasonably feasible measures involving some process changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses keeping technical documentation current, which is tied to Recital 71 and traceability but is only adjacent to the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping documentation current helps compliance and traceability but does not itself deliver automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using the Article 12(3)(d) verifier-logging clause as a window into how logging alters operator behaviour is an unusual and imaginative idea that labs would rarely propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns a logging requirement into a research agenda on human-machine verification and so changes what the lab researches, though it does not address the full compliance obligation, which fits stretching to breaking.
evidence_acceptability: A cross-disciplinary research programme with controlled experiments is a legitimate and uncontroversial approach, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires assembling a cross-disciplinary team and running controlled human-subject experiments, which is costly and slow when the lab must commit scarce implementation resources.
evidence_applicability: It relates to one narrow clause (12(3)(d), which applies only to Annex III 1(a) biometric systems) and offers only a loose benefit for the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not deliver the logging capability or meet the mandate itself, and at best it informs interface design, so it is unlikely to solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-default logging templates are a fairly expected, standard response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a reusable tooling element yet still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifting it earlier in the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into templates is a common, norm-conforming engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring existing prototype templates to include a reusable logging module with a config manifest is a modest, non-radical engineering change at low to moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing events in the Article 12(2) categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic event logging for prototypes, but it covers only the lab's builds and leaves open log retention, Annex III-specific fields, and documentation, so it is a strong partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reference architectures with UML diagrams and database schemas for compliance logging are a common, expected response, with nothing surprising in the approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice, a design doc and schema, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusable reference designs and standard database logging are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A design document and DDL script using PostgreSQL are low cost and require no radical changes for engineers to adopt.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, meeting the Article 12(3) logging requirements for Annex III point 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A reference design mapping Article 12(3)(a)-(d) to a data flow and DDL would help meet the biometric-specific logging minimums, but it covers only one high-risk category and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) mandate or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated experiment tracking and provenance-by-design is a fairly familiar MLOps idea, though framing it as research output adds some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Making compliance documentation a first-class research output woven into the science changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, stretching the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reproducibility and provenance tracking are widely accepted research practices that offend no norms, though making them a mandatory research criterion is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Integrating an experiment-tracking layer that auto-generates documentation is reasonably feasible with existing tools, though it requires pipeline changes and a lab-wide process shift.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by producing records and documentation that satisfy Article 12 and Recital 71, though it focuses on documentation more than on event logs.
evidence_effectiveness: Provenance and documentation generation would substantially help but does not by itself cover runtime automatic event logging of deployed systems required by Article 12, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI-enforced JSON schema contract for log fields is a sensible, interesting engineering move but a fairly expected way for a software lab to operationalize logging requirements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (schema registry plus CI gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Build-time validation gates are a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Schema registries and CI validation are standard tooling, though retrofitting existing pipelines and managing versioning across retraining requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by encoding the 12(3)(a)-(d) minimum fields and catching gaps early.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure required fields are present in log payloads, but it does not cover the Article 12(2) event relevance, actual runtime logging, retention, or non-Annex III 1(a) systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Standardized logging middleware with default-on and opt-out is a sensible but fairly expected response, with the auto-tagging by Article 12(2) purpose adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and an opt-out default but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building default logging infrastructure with documented opt-outs is a common, norm-compliant engineering and compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: A language-agnostic layer integrated as a default dependency across an internal framework requires some engineering effort and changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-recording events and tagging them per Article 12(2) categories.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, default-on logging with tagging would largely solve the logging-capability requirement, though it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics or the broader documentation and R&D adaptation questions.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a public open research resource is unusual and imaginative compared with typical responses, though open data sharing itself is a known concept.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging a source of community assets and scientific positioning, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing anonymized logs openly is an unusual strategy that raises confidentiality, IP, and privacy-law concerns but does not radically offend norms, and differential privacy mitigates the worst of them.
evidence_implementability: It requires a differential-privacy pipeline for complex traces, a curation process, and ongoing releases with legal review, which is a significant and expensive effort on top of basic logging.
evidence_applicability: The proposal builds on the Article 12(3) logging pipeline but its main output (a public research archive) addresses an implied benefit rather than the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, so it relates only indirectly.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure that logs meet Article 12 requirements and only adds a data-sharing layer on top of compliance, so it is at best a partial contribution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Dual-use of compliance logs for reproducibility is a sensible and somewhat imaginative idea, but integrating logging with experiment tracking is a fairly familiar MLOps move rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as a research reproducibility asset, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science workflow, but does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: The approach is a common, norm-compliant engineering and compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities, with a slightly uncommon framing.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing experiment-tracking pipeline is reasonably feasible with some engineering changes, including gating checkpoint promotion on log completeness.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by building a layer capturing Annex III 1(a) minimums and Recital 71 metadata, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a unified logging layer tied to experiment tracking would substantially satisfy the logging requirement, though it leaves some Article 12 elements (e.g., reference database checks, human verifier identification at deployment) only implicitly covered, making it a strong but not fully complete solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized reusable logging middleware is the common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging library is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, though it is a standard-ish engineering approach.
evidence_acceptability: It is a conventional engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Three engineers over two quarters with CI/CD integration is a modest, reasonably feasible effort, though it requires coordination across projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specified log fields in a standardized way.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would capture the Article 12(3) minimum items across all high-risk systems, largely solving the logging mandate, though it focuses on Annex III 1(a) fields and not broader 12(2) event relevance or documentation.

evidence_originality: Log retention and retrieval infrastructure is a fairly expected, mundane response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces storage, metadata and retrieval tooling but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Retaining encrypted logs and offering regulators a retrieval interface is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Tiered storage, release-linked metadata and a regulator-facing retrieval interface across a system's lifetime and beyond decommissioning require significant engineering and ongoing cost, though they are feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified, directly related problem of keeping and producing logs for compliance and post-market monitoring, though it is not the core logging capability requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Retention and retrieval would support post-market monitoring and incident response, but it covers only the storage side and not what to log or the other Article 12 requirements, so it is a partial solution; also the Act's retention period is set elsewhere (Art. 19/26) so 'lifetime' is over-broad.

evidence_originality: Reconciling Article 12(3) logging of matched biometric input with privacy via hash-based verifiable logging is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (privacy-preserving cryptographic logging, a standardisation white paper) but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging, DPO involvement and engaging in standardisation consultation are legitimate and norm-respecting strategies, though somewhat uncommon.
evidence_implementability: It requires cryptography research, benchmarking, and a DPO partnership, which is significant but feasible with in-house expertise, though hashing may conflict with the requirement to record the input data itself.
evidence_applicability: It targets an identified, directly related problem: meeting Article 12(3) logging for biometric systems without retaining raw biometric data, although the privacy tension is implied rather than stated in the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses only the Annex III 1(a) biometric logging subset and may not satisfy the requirement to record matched input data, so it is only a partial contribution to meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Mandatory documentation templates with owners and review checkpoints are a common, expected response, with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, apart from adding checkpoints to existing sprint reviews.
evidence_acceptability: Internal documentation governance is a common, norm-conforming compliance strategy that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: A template, named owners, and sprint checkpoints are modest process changes that most labs can adopt at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation and traceability need that is implied by and related to the logging mandate, rather than the identified logging requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A living documentation process supports Recital 71 and technical-documentation compliance but does not itself implement the automatic event logging mandated by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing research tracks for post-market monitoring is a sensible and somewhat imaginative framing but is a fairly expected response, so it shows some imagination without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving compliance tooling into the lab's research agenda, stretching the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reallocating internal compute toward compliance tooling is a legal, non-offensive strategy, though tying compliance to research goals is somewhat less common than plain compliance spending.
evidence_implementability: Redirecting about 15% of GPU-hours and hardening existing drift detectors into a production monitoring service requires some changes and engineering effort but builds on existing research and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified part of the stated problem, meeting the logging mandate's post-market monitoring purpose and adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet post-market monitoring and risk-event flagging needs under Art. 12(2)(b) but does not by itself cover the full logging mandate (Art. 12(1), 12(3), retention), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code with CI gating for compliance is a sensible but fairly expected response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from AI labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new tooling (metadata schemas, CI gates) but still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice, with no change to what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Version-controlled documentation and deployment gates are common engineering and compliance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing Git-based repository with CI checks, so it requires some schema and workflow work but is reasonably feasible at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the technical documentation and up-to-date record obligations from Recital 71 and Annex IV, though it is not the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation current and block noncompliant deployments, but it does not provide the automatic event logs required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating log compression and selective retention as a research problem is an interesting angle beyond typical just-build-logging responses, but is fairly predictable engineering and not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance cost as a publishable research contribution, linking compliance to the lab's research output and modestly changing that relationship, though it still centers on logging practice and new tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research on log efficiency validated against Article 12 traceability is a sensible, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms, though it is somewhat unusual to frame it as research.
evidence_implementability: Fifteen percent of one group's capacity for eighteen months with systems-engineering partnership is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, but it is a research effort with uncertain outcomes and delayed payoff rather than ready implementation.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the lifetime logging mandate of Article 12 by tackling storage and compute costs of retaining logs, which is an identified part of meeting the logging requirement, though cost is a secondary aspect of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Efficient retention and indexing would help sustain compliance affordably but it is only a partial solution since it does not itself define what to log or ensure the logs meet Article 12 content requirements, and selective retention could risk traceability.

evidence_originality: Dedicated compliance cost centres are mundane budgeting practice with little that is imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a budgeting matter and leaves the lab's R&D and logging practice unchanged, so it preserves the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Ring-fencing compliance costs in a budget is a common, transparent financial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Creating a budget line and a three-year cost projection is an administrative step that needs no technical change and is low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses funding for Article 12 logging, which relates to the stated problem only implicitly, since it does not itself say how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by securing resources and visibility but does not itself create logging capability or adapt R&D, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12 logging into a marketable certification dossier is a somewhat unusual and interesting angle compared with typical internal-logging responses, but compliance-as-selling-point is a familiar business idea and not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the business by creating a commercial offering born from compliance, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking since the R&D itself is not altered.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing standardised log specifications and compliance certificates for enterprise customers is a somewhat uncommon but entirely unobjectionable business strategy.
evidence_implementability: Drafting per-product certificates and piloting with two anchor clients is reasonably feasible with moderate effort, though it depends on the underlying logging being built and on customer API access to logs.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making use of and communicating logging compliance to customers) that relates to but is not the directly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself implement the logging mandate or adapt R&D to meet Article 12, so it only contributes a partial solution by leveraging logs that must exist anyway.

evidence_originality: Triaging the R&D portfolio by regulatory exposure is a sensible but fairly expected planning step, showing modest imagination without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes what the lab researches and when by re-weighting the roadmap and shifting staff based on compliance exposure, altering the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations without introducing fundamentally new elements.
evidence_acceptability: Portfolio risk triage and resource reallocation is a sensible, legal business practice that offends no norms, though somewhat less common than plain logging implementation.
evidence_implementability: A one-time mapping exercise by an analyst and Compliance Officer plus a budget-review reallocation of 8-12% of FTEs uses existing roles and processes, requiring some changes but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of anticipating which projects will carry high-risk obligations so the lab can adapt R&D, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly address building logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab prioritize and avoid retrofits but does not itself implement logging capabilities, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Event-sourced unified logging is a known architectural pattern; applying it to dual research and compliance use is sensible and somewhat interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new architecture element and merges research tracking with compliance logging, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Unifying logging on an event bus is a legitimate, widely used engineering strategy that offends no legal or social norms and supports compliance.
evidence_implementability: Rewriting the deploy pipeline and migrating training, validation, and inference events onto a Kafka store is a significant, costly engineering change, though feasible with standard technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate while adapting R&D infrastructure, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide automatic, queryable logging and reduce drift, but it does not by itself guarantee the specific content requirements, retention, or risk-event identification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Redesigning data handling to meet the enumerated logging minimums, with a cross-functional working group, is the expected and mundane response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with a GDPR retention policy added, and the lab's R&D relationship to compliance is unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common compliance strategy that reconciles with GDPR and violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires re-mapping the verification flow and adding capture points within six months, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes with a defined team and scope.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, meeting the specific logging minimums in Article 12(3), by capturing timestamps, reference databases, matched inputs, and verifier identities.
evidence_effectiveness: Capturing the Annex III 1(a) minimums natively would solve the Article 12(3) mandate for biometrics systems, but it covers only that subset and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging duty across the lab's other systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Periodic internal compliance audits with a per-system matrix are a common, expected response and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A recurring internal audit of logging against Article 12 is a standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance audits reviewed by management are a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A cross-functional quarterly review requires some staff time and coordination but is reasonably feasible with existing teams.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of verifying that logging meets Article 12(2) and 12(3) requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Audits would help detect logging gaps but do not themselves build the logging capability, so the proposal is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A standard logging middleware or decorator with an append-only log is the obvious, common response labs would be expected to give to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging practice via a shared library, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standard audit-trail logging is a common strategy that violates no norms, though the per-project version pinning and the privacy implications of input hashing are minor concerns.
evidence_implementability: Wrapping the existing serving layer with a decorator and a version-pinned library is low-cost and non-radical for an engineering team.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing specific Article 12(3)-type fields in every inference call.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging library capturing timestamps, input hashes, model version and reference-database ID would meet much of Article 12's automatic-recording requirement, but it leaves out the identification of the persons who verify results, retention, and the Article 12(2) event-relevance mapping, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as a research dataset for drift taxonomy is interesting and shows some imagination but is not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandated logs into a research dataset, which is logging woven into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Mining logs is a plausible practice, but cross-referencing verifier identities with demographic segments raises data-protection and purpose-limitation concerns that offend sensibilities somewhat.
evidence_implementability: Building an analytics pipeline with clustering and change-point detection is reasonably feasible with standard tools, though demographic linkage and privacy safeguards add difficulty.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of getting value from and supporting post-market monitoring with the mandated logs, which relates to but is not the core logging-compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate (it presupposes logs exist) but would contribute by using the logs for post-market monitoring and drift detection, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Requiring logging specs in design documents is a common, expected compliance step that shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new template and gate but still treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Design-document templates and sign-off gates are common engineering governance practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a template appendix and a review gate is a modest process change that an engineering lead can draft and roll out at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by moving logging design earlier in development.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging capability is designed in, but it only specifies the schema and does not itself guarantee that the Article 12 content requirements are met or that the logs are implemented and work, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging layer with a checklist gate is the common, expected response to this mandate and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-logging practice with a shared tool and checklist, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging infrastructure and architecture-review gates are common, uncontroversial engineering and compliance practices.
evidence_implementability: A shared middleware with a standard API and schema plus a checklist gate requires meaningful platform engineering and integration across systems but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building shared logging infrastructure that satisfies Article 12(1) and the Article 12(3) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a mandatory standardized logging layer would solve the core logging mandate, though it only partly covers Article 12(2) purpose-driven event relevance and the Article 12(3) fields apply to only one Annex III category.

evidence_originality: A centralized shared logging service with an SDK is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane rather than ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, centralized as infrastructure, and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal tooling with stewards and documentation is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two FTEs for four months and one-sprint integration per team is modest and realistic, though it requires some changes across groups.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate, with explicit reference to Article 12(2) and Recital 71.
evidence_effectiveness: A single audit-ready logging service would substantially meet Article 12 logging and documentation needs, but it does not by itself ensure that the content of the logs (event relevance, Annex III minimums) is right, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging modules embedded in pipelines are the expected, mundane response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice; it treats compliance as logging infrastructure without changing how the lab does R&D, though the engineering-default framing is slightly more than minimal.
evidence_acceptability: Building standard compliance logging into engineering pipelines is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared module with integration at an existing review gate needs some cross-project engineering changes but is reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a reusable automatic logging layer that implements Article 12(1)-(3) requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A standardised logging module integrated at the architecture gate would largely satisfy the logging mandate if implemented, though it is vague on how risk-relevant events and the Annex III-specific items (reference database, matches, verifier identity) are captured.

evidence_originality: Repurposing mandated logs as a research dataset on lifetime drift is an interesting and somewhat imaginative angle, though monitoring and drift analysis are known practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving the logs into the science, treating them as a research dataset rather than just compliance output.
evidence_acceptability: Using compliance logs for internal longitudinal analysis is a sensible, norm-respecting practice, though it requires attention to data protection and purpose limits, making it somewhat uncommon but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: Standing up an analytics group and pipeline to ingest production logs requires new staff, infrastructure, and access to deployed-system logs, which is a significant but feasible investment.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of getting value from compliance logging, which relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D, rather than directly meeting the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself deliver the logging mandate, so it only contributes a partial solution by exploiting logs once they exist.

evidence_originality: Documentation maintenance cycles are a mundane and expected response to this mandate, with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged and does not alter the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A documentation owner, quarterly reviews and a controlled repository are common governance practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning owners and setting up review cycles and a repository requires only modest, non-radical organizational changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal keeps technical documentation current, which is a Recital 71 requirement tied to record-keeping and compliance, but it does not address the Article 12 automatic logging mandate directly, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Maintaining up-to-date documentation helps with traceability and post-market monitoring but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Append-only cryptographically chained logs and compliance gates in CI/CD are well-known good practice and an expected response to this mandate, with limited surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (hash-chained logs, CI/CD compliance gates) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice without changing the lab's R&D relationship to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into engineering pipelines is a common, norm-conforming strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Rebuilding inference and training pipelines with immutable storage and deployment gates requires significant engineering change and cost, though it is feasible with existing technology.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly implements automatic event logging per Article 12(1)-(3), which is the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, tamper-evident automatic logs with CI/CD coverage checks against Article 12 requirements would essentially satisfy the mandate, though the criteria for what counts as relevant events remain loosely defined.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK/platform layer with immutable storage is a very expected, standard engineering response to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (an instrumentation SDK) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Built-in logging with compliance access is a common, norm-compatible strategy, though logging training pipelines might raise some researcher-workflow or data-privacy concerns.
evidence_implementability: Building and rolling out an SDK wrapping all inference and training endpoints across the lab requires significant engineering effort and changes, but is reasonably feasible with existing technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the automatic event-logging requirement, including timestamps, inputs, reference databases and verification actions named in Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic, default-on logging of events across all pipelines would substantially meet the Article 12 logging mandate, though it is mainly a technical logging layer and does not address risk-event identification specifics or post-market monitoring processes fully.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as research data is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, but repurposing operational telemetry for research is a fairly foreseeable idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science, so that compliance infrastructure feeds research, which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for research is a reasonably unusual strategy, though it raises possible data protection and purpose-limitation concerns that are not addressed, so it is mostly acceptable but not entirely common.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing event-bus and metrics pipelines by adding metadata tags and a curated dataset, which requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses meeting the Article 12(1) lifetime logging mandate by extending existing pipelines and tagging logs, though much of its stated benefit (a research dataset) is an added goal rather than the compliance requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Tagging and retaining logs would contribute to meeting the logging mandate, but it does not specify the Article 12(2) event types or the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution to compliance.

evidence_originality: Earmarking compliance budget in project proposals is a common, mundane project-management response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process step (budget line item) but still treats compliance as a logging cost practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting for compliance upfront is a common, uncontroversial management practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a capped budget line item to an existing grant template and quarterly review is a non-radical administrative change that is cheap to adopt.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, funding and cost surprises for compliance, which relates to but is not the direct technical logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It funds logging infrastructure but does not itself make systems log the required events, so it only partially contributes to meeting the Article 12 mandate.

evidence_originality: Earmarking compliance budget lines is a mundane, expected administrative response, though framing it as enabling infrastructure adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It preserves standard compliance practice by adding a budget line, leaving how the lab does R&D essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a compliance budget line to project charters and grant applications is a common, normal governance practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a policy update and some training for grant writers, which is a modest but real change rather than trivial, though funders' acceptance of the line is a minor uncertainty.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely resourcing for logging over the system's lifetime, which relates to meeting the logging mandate but does not directly address logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Budgeting ensures resources exist for logging design and upkeep, but it is only a partial solution because it does not specify or implement the logging capabilities themselves.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design applied to logging is a very common and expected response to this mandate, with nothing surprising in it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Building logging middleware into the reference architecture with design-stage sign-off is a new process element, but it still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged (logging-by-design is standard compliance advice).
evidence_acceptability: Architecture review gates and standing engineering directives are common governance strategies that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires embedding middleware in the platform and adding review-board sign-off to every high-risk build, which is a reasonably feasible set of process and engineering changes, though it adds some overhead.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting Article 12(1)-(3) logging requirements, with a clear do-X-to-get-Y link.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, logging built in from the start with schemas covering the Article 12(3) items would solve the main logging-mandate problem, though it does not address the scope of Article 12(2) event relevance in depth.

evidence_originality: Progressive schema enrichment gated by CI is sensible but resembles standard shift-left compliance and maturity-gate practices, so it is merely interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (tiered schemas and CI gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Staged schema tiers enforced by CI checks aligned to sprint milestones are a common engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires defining three schema tiers and adding CI checks to existing sprint milestones, which is reasonably feasible with some process changes but not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D workflows by ensuring the full log set exists before release.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging capability is present at release and avoid late bolt-on work, but it does not specify the content of the logs (e.g., Article 12(2) event relevance, Annex III minimums) or retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A compliance checklist and release gate is a very common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D workflow essentially unchanged, adding only a checkpoint.
evidence_acceptability: Internal release gates are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing release-management tooling, a checklist and a small audit team, so it is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying compliance before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-release gate verifying logging against every Article 12 sub-clause would catch deficiencies, but it only checks outputs and does not build the logging capability itself, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging as automatic middleware in the experiment pipeline is a sensible and fairly common engineering pattern (observability, MLOps tracking), showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces tooling (middleware, append-only store) but still treats compliance as a logging practice added to the existing workflow, though making it a transparent side-effect slightly stretches that.
evidence_acceptability: Automatic, built-in logging in the dev pipeline is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding middleware to an existing Docker/CI runner with an append-only store is a modest, non-radical engineering change, though capturing verifier IDs and reference-database matches automatically needs some per-system work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate with the specific Article 12 fields while preserving R&D workflow.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would produce Article 12(3) logs for every run, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) fields, not the broader 12(2) event relevance for risk, post-market monitoring, and operation, and logging prototypes is not the same as deployed-system logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered log storage for retention and retrieval is a common, mundane response to a logging mandate that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (tiered store with schema mapping) but still treats compliance purely as logging infrastructure and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A tiered log storage layer mapped to Article 12 categories is a standard, uncontroversial compliance engineering approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a columnar time-series store with hot-warm-cold tiers uses well-established technology, though it requires some dedicated engineering and storage cost, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 lifetime logging obligation at scale by storing and retrieving logs mapped to Article 12(2) categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the lifetime retention and retrieval part of logging but not the whole mandate (what events to log, traceability content, Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library with append-only storage is the obvious, common response expected from labs facing this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance engineering that treats compliance as a logging practice, with no change to how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into systems is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A shared library with automatic hooks and append-only storage needs some engineering effort and retrofitting across pipelines but is reasonably feasible with existing platform teams.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by implementing the specific logging elements the article prescribes.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared tamper-evident logging library embedded from prototyping would, if built, satisfy the core Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not cover technical documentation or all Article 12(2) event-relevance judgments.

evidence_originality: Treating log sufficiency as an information-theoretic research question is interesting and somewhat imaginative, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (formal methods, taxonomy, collaboration) and turns compliance into a research topic, but it still centers on logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A research workstream on minimal sufficient logs with legal collaboration and privacy balancing violates no norms, though it is somewhat less common than plain compliance implementation.
evidence_implementability: Building formal criteria, a taxonomy, and empirical validation with legal and systems collaborators is a significant, research-heavy effort, not a simple change, and its payoff is uncertain.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, determining what logs are sufficient under Article 12 given data minimization, which relates to the stated logging mandate but is not directly implementing it.
evidence_effectiveness: The research would inform what to log but does not itself deliver the logging capability required by Article 12, so it is at best a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code testing gates are a fairly familiar idea, though applying them to Article 12 fields is a sensible and mildly interesting application.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI conformance gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI are a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small pytest plugin in CI with a sandboxed container and synthetic inputs is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though defining event-relevance assertions takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by checking required log fields before release.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies log field presence and format but cannot ensure that the logs capture the right events or satisfy the full mandate, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: A provenance table keyed on session ID is an expected, mundane engineering response to the logging mandate, with a modest reuse angle.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new pipeline element but still treats compliance as a logging practice, with only a mild nod to reuse for debugging and drift detection.
evidence_acceptability: An immutable provenance table that logs the Article 12(3) items is a standard, legally aligned compliance approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing feature store with a write-per-inference table and storage-tier retention is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change, though per-inference synchronous writes add some engineering cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement to record reference database, matched inputs, and verifier identity, which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully satisfy the Article 12(3) logging items for biometric systems, but it covers only that subset (not Article 12(1)-(2) general event logging for other high-risk systems), so it is a partial solution to the overall mandate.

evidence_originality: A pre-built template or wrapper library for the Article 3 minimum logging fields is a very common, expected engineering response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a schema and wrapper library as a tool but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using standard templates to implement mandated logging violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: A typed schema and thin wrapper library is cheap and easy to build and drop into projects, requiring only non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement to meet the paragraph 3 logging mandate for biometric systems, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would cover only the Annex III point 1(a) minimum fields, not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event logging for risk, post-market and operational monitoring, nor other high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered storage and schema migration for log retention is a routine, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Durable log retention with archival tiers is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Tiered object storage with append-only logs and schema versioning uses standard, mature tooling and is prototypable in two weeks, requiring only some changes to deployment infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified lifetime-logging and audit-demonstration requirement, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address only the retention and retrievability part of Article 12 and not event selection, traceability content, or Annex III minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.
