evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK and CI gate is a moderate engineering effort needing platform team work and adoption across projects, but it is well within normal practice.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly delivers automatic event logging (timestamps, state snapshots, input-output capture) that Article 12 mandates, so it solves an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a shared SDK with CI enforcement would reliably produce logs across prototypes, but it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance judgments, Annex III-specific fields, or retention and oversight, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance and design reviews are a standard and expected response, so the idea is common rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a workshop and gating step but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A planning checkpoint and workshop with compliance sign-off is a common, norm-respecting governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires modest process changes and a rotating compliance engineer from an existing pool, which is reasonably feasible without major cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by embedding logging design in R&D projects.
evidence_effectiveness: Scoping logging early would help build Article 12 capabilities, but it only addresses design planning and not the specific log content, retention, or verification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Phase-gate compliance checklists with rotating reviewers are a common, mundane response to regulatory mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard documentation checkpoint bolted onto existing processes, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a documentation review to phase-gate processes is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing phase gates, PM tooling, current staff, and a half-day workshop plus a one-page checklist, so it is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation/technical-file side of Recital 71 and Annex III awareness, which is related to the mandate but only implied for the automatic logging requirement of Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: A checklist review of technical files helps with documentation compliance but does not create automatic event logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware to cut per-project compliance costs is a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging infrastructure and leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing GPU cluster and leased data lake, and a lightweight agent is a non-radical change with modest cost, though integration across projects takes some work.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 mandate for automatic event logging, capturing events, timestamps, and reference-database queries that the article names.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared middleware layer would plausibly deliver the automatic logging capability, but it does not address risk-event identification, post-market monitoring design, retention, or the identification of the persons who verify results, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralizing logging into one middleware layer on existing observability tooling is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging middleware is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Consolidating logging into a shared service is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing Kubernetes, Prometheus and Loki tooling with a one-quarter build, though each project must adapt its manifests, so there are some changes but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specified fields (timestamps, reference database, input data, verifying personnel).
evidence_effectiveness: A unified schema and single audit point would reasonably deliver the logging capabilities required, though it covers mainly Article 12(3) fields and not broader traceability or R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-by-design logging is a very common and expected response to this mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Making logging a design constraint with review gates changes how compliance relates to R&D somewhat, but it remains a logging-compliance practice within the existing development process, i.e. standard privacy/security-by-design style.
evidence_acceptability: This is a conventional, widely accepted compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Revising templates, adding review gates, and assigning logging engineers requires some process and staffing changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate through the lab's R&D process (do X to get compliant logging).
evidence_effectiveness: Building automatic event logging into every high-risk build from the start would, if done, satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it does not itself cover the specific Annex III minimum fields or retention.

evidence_originality: Version-tolerant log storage with retention tiers is a sensible but expected infrastructure response, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a storage tool but still treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Durable, access-controlled log storage for auditors is a conventional, legally aligned strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a schema-versioned columnar append-only store with tiered compression, RBAC and a query API uses mature technology but requires some dedicated engineering changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified Article 12(1) lifetime logging and Article 72 retrieval needs that are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A durable lifetime log store addresses retention and retrieval but does not itself determine which events are logged or cover the other compliance obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and version-controlled compliance documentation is a fairly well-known approach, though applying it to AI Act documentation is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and workflow elements (git-mapped docs, automated diffs) but still treats compliance as a documentation and record-keeping practice.
evidence_acceptability: Version-controlled documentation with named owner sign-off is a common, norm-respecting practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Git-based documentation with automated diffs and checklists uses familiar tooling and requires some process changes and a research-ops assignment, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses keeping technical documentation current (Recital 71 and the broader record-keeping duty), which is related to the stated problem, but it does not address the automatic event logging that Article 12 actually mandates.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping documentation synchronized with model changes helps with traceability and compliance but is only a partial solution because it does not implement the automatic event logs required by Article 12(1)-(3).

evidence_originality: A shared reusable logging middleware is the standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice packaged as a shared module, leaving the lab's way of working and relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared internal compliance infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team building a module on existing infrastructure with minimal configuration is a reasonably feasible measure, though integrating across diverse projects requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the Article 12 minimum log fields across systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A middleware that auto-captures events would substantially meet logging requirements, but it only covers the minimum fields (largely Annex III 1(a)-style) and does not address broader Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A client-facing logging transparency portal with an annual conformance report is somewhat unusual and interesting, but compliance-as-differentiator is a familiar move and it is not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates a new offering born from compliance (a client-facing transparency product), which changes how compliance relates to the lab's business, though the R&D itself is unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Transparency reporting and client dashboards are broadly acceptable business practice, though publishing log schemas and self-certifying conformance needs care about confidentiality and the meaning of 'certification'.
evidence_implementability: Building a read-only dashboard and writing an annual report is reasonably feasible, but it requires some engineering to aggregate log coverage per client deployment and handle privacy and anonymization.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the stated problem only indirectly: it communicates logging conformance to clients rather than meeting the logging mandate itself, so the benefit is an implied one (reputation, procurement).
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard and white paper presuppose that logging already exists and do not build the logging capability, so they are only a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance into a product is a known idea that is somewhat unusual among lab responses and shows some imagination, but it is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's business by turning compliance obligations into a new client offering, which fits the example of new offerings born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Productizing monitoring data is a reasonable business strategy, though exposing logs to clients raises some confidentiality and data-protection concerns, which keeps it from being fully common.
evidence_implementability: Building an API layer and portal on top of existing log streams requires real engineering effort and security work but is reasonably feasible with standard technology.
evidence_applicability: The proposal builds on the mandatory Article 12 log streams and Article 72 post-market monitoring, but its main aim is revenue, so it addresses an implied rather than directly stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A client-facing dashboard built on the logs would help with monitoring and transparency but does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met (e.g., Article 12(3) minimums, retention, traceability), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance gates are a familiar approach, though the replay tool simulating incidents against the live log stream adds a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process step and tool but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a compliance review gate to a sprint process is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-hour gate, a clause-mapped checklist and a replay tool fit into an existing sprint cadence with modest changes and cost, though building the replay tool takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that logging captures the required events during R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help verify that logs cover Article 12(2) events, but it addresses only part of the mandate (no coverage of Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or documentation), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using in-house smaller models for self-auditing of logs and turning compliance into publishable work is somewhat imaginative, though anomaly detection on logs is a familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as publishable research that supports funding, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, but it does not alter what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research sprints and log monitoring offend no norms and are legally unproblematic, although framing compliance as a research opportunity is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: A six-month sprint with two postdocs and existing synthetic-data pipelines is modest in scale and feasible, though the real-time detection modules add some difficulty.
evidence_applicability: The proposal builds modules that detect missing or anomalous log entries and benchmarks them against Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which directly addresses the logging mandate, though it targets log integrity rather than logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Integrity checking would help ensure logs are complete and trustworthy, but it only partially solves the mandate, since it doesn't create the logging capability and its detectors may themselves be unreliable.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware as a mandatory scaffold dependency is a common and expected response, not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a mandatory logging layer to meet Article 12 is a common, legally compliant engineering approach that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two developers building a reusable middleware over one quarter and making it a scaffold dependency is a reasonably feasible, moderate change rather than trivial or radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (non-bypassable logging layer covering Art. 12(2) and 12(3) events) to get Y (meeting the logging mandate), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A non-bypassable logging layer in all templates would largely satisfy the technical logging requirement, but it does not address retention, appropriate scoping to intended purpose, or documentation, so it solves the logging mandate while leaving gaps in the broader response.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory compliance logs as a scientific dataset for longitudinal drift research is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the lab's science and creating a research/publication offering born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Using operational logs for research and publication is a somewhat uncommon strategy that is not offensive, though data protection of biometric logs could raise some concern.
evidence_implementability: It needs two postdocs and a lightweight analytics layer on an existing pipeline, which is reasonably feasible but requires waiting twelve months for data and handling biometric data constraints.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by gaining value from it, which relates to the stated problem but is not about meeting the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself meet the logging mandate; it only exploits logs once they exist, so it contributes partially by leveraging compliance investment.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance checkpoints with checklists and sign-offs are a very common and expected response to such mandates, so the idea is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A design-review gate is a standard process control that treats compliance as a logging and documentation practice without changing how the lab does R&D, so it is paradigm preserving or at most introduces a new process element.
evidence_acceptability: Internal design reviews with compliance checklists and sign-offs are a common governance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a checklist, a review step, and tracking, which are modest process changes using existing roles, although the logging architecture work itself still requires engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring each system's logging architecture is specified and verified before release.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate would ensure logging designs address Article 12(2) categories before deployment, which helps substantially, but it does not itself build the logging or cover Article 12(3) specifics or the lifetime operation of the logs, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning mandated logs into a longitudinal research corpus is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logs a source of scientific work and publications, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for internal research and publishing preprints is unusual but offends no norms, though privacy and data-protection concerns over input data and personal identifiers (such as verifiers) need handling.
evidence_implementability: Building an analytics pipeline over logs the lab must already produce is a reasonably feasible add-on, though it requires some new engineering, data governance work and research effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal exploits the logging mandate to create research value, which is an implied problem related to how the lab adapts its R&D, but it does not itself address how to meet the logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab get value from compliance and adapt R&D, but it is only a partial solution because it does not specify how the logging mandate itself is met, and Article 12(3) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems.

evidence_originality: Studying logging overhead is a reasonably expected topic, though framing it as publishable research to justify the engineering investment shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element, treating compliance instrumentation as a publishable research question, which modestly shifts the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it is still centered on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open benchmarks and running ablations violates no norms and is a common academic strategy.
evidence_implementability: A six-month project with two PhD students and existing models is feasible, but it depends on the logging layer from Proposal 1 and takes dedicated effort, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the performance cost of logging, which relates to meeting the logging mandate without degrading deployed systems, rather than the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Benchmarking logging overhead helps the lab choose logging densities but does not itself deliver the Article 12 logging capability (it depends on a separate logging layer), so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Drawing on genomics and climate-science data-management practice to define minimal provenance is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though schema standardization is a familiar compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a schema, cross-disciplinary synthesis, a methodological contribution) but still treats compliance as a logging and metadata practice rather than changing the lab's R&D relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A research-driven approach to compliance using literature synthesis and prototyping violates no legal or social norms and is entirely acceptable.
evidence_implementability: Literature synthesis and prototyping two or three schemas against an existing model registry is reasonably feasible with moderate effort, though the research framing adds some uncertainty and cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely knowing which metadata fields count as sufficient for Article 12(2) traceability, which relates to the stated logging mandate but does not directly deliver logs.
evidence_effectiveness: Defining a minimal provenance schema would help decide which fields to log, but it is a research project that yields only a partial contribution and does not itself implement automatic event logging as Article 12 requires.

evidence_originality: Designing logging in from the start with a shared library and compliance sign-off is a very common, expected response to such a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces some new process elements (SDK, gates, embedded engineers) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's research direction unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-by-design style embedded compliance and review gates are common, legally sound strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared SDK, architecture review gates, and embedded compliance engineers on every squad require significant organizational and engineering change and cost, but are feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12(1) mandate for automatic event recording by building logging into system design, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, built-in logging via a shared SDK with review gates would reasonably satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not detail which events are logged for Article 12(2) or Annex III 3 specifics, so it is nearly but not fully a complete solution.

evidence_originality: Keeping technical documentation as living, versioned files with update triggers is a common and expected response to Recital 71, so it is mundane rather than ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a versioned repository and trigger rules but treats compliance as standard documentation practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation governance is a conventional strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: A versioned repository, update triggers tied to retraining events, and named owners are low-cost process changes that existing QA groups can adopt readily.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation upkeep from Recital 71, which is adjacent to but not the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not produce automatic event logs or traceability capabilities required by Article 12, so it contributes only marginally to meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Triage and prioritization audits are a standard, expected project-management response to a compliance mandate, so this is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A triage audit with self-assessments and sequenced remediation is a common, normal compliance management practice that offends no norms, though deferring lower-priority work is mildly risky only if it delays legal obligations.
evidence_implementability: A four-week one-page self-assessment and sprint sequencing is low-cost and requires only non-radical process changes, though the remediation sprints themselves still need engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of allocating scarce resources to meet the logging mandate, which relates to the stated problem but does not itself specify how to implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Prioritization helps sequence compliance work but does not itself build the logging capability, and Article 12 paragraph 3 applies only to Annex III point 1(a) systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checkpoints in planning are a common, expected response, and this one shows little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checklist step but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A planning checkpoint and checklist in existing sprints is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a one-page checklist, a QA coordinator, and a small pilot inside the existing sprint cycle, which is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by deciding on required fields early in development.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging fields are planned and architecture can emit them, but it does not itself build the logging or cover the full Article 12 requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log analytics with anomaly alerting for post-market monitoring is a fairly expected, standard engineering response, though framing compliance cost as a safety feature adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (streaming pipeline, SPC, dashboard) but still treats compliance as a logging/monitoring practice, with a mild shift toward a client-facing reporting offering.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for post-market monitoring and client reporting is a legally aligned, normal strategy, though ingesting deployer production logs raises some data-access and privacy considerations that remain manageable.
evidence_implementability: Kafka plus a time-series store and dashboards are mature off-the-shelf tools, but building per-system alerting rules and a monitoring team workflow requires some real changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets identified purposes in Article 12(2)(a)-(c) (risk identification, post-market monitoring, operation monitoring), which are part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The pipeline analyzes logs to flag Article 79(1) risks and substantial modifications and supports Article 72 and 26(5) duties, but it does not itself make systems generate compliant logs (Art. 12(1), 12(3)), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable internal logging SDK with a standard schema is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal compliance tooling is a standard strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over six weeks with a Python wrapper is low cost and a non-radical change to existing pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the specified data points consistently.
evidence_effectiveness: It would cover the Article 12(3) fields for each project, but it addresses only the logging piece and not the broader Article 12(2) traceability purposes, retention obligations, or R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using sequential change-point tests to operationalize 'substantial modification' is an interesting and somewhat imaginative link, though drift detection is a familiar monitoring approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new element (online change-point detection research) and ties the lab's R&D to a compliance need as publishable science, but it still frames the work as a logging/monitoring mechanism rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship fundamentally.
evidence_acceptability: A statistical monitoring and research project violates no legal or social norms and is a common, acceptable strategy.
evidence_implementability: Developing adaptive non-stationary detectors and validating them on real deployment logs is a significant research effort with a hard, ambiguous target (defining substantial modification), though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified element of Article 12, the recording of events for identifying substantial modification, though the claim that drift equals substantial modification is an interpretive stretch.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift detection would help flag situations relevant to Article 12(2)(a) but covers only part of the logging mandate and does not itself deliver the automatic event recording or other required log content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal log governance and mock regulator inspections are a standard, expected compliance response with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging and governance practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal compliance and audit function is a common, norm-abiding governance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Chartering a small cross-functional team with policies and quarterly mock inspections requires some organizational change and effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that systems produce and retain the required records.
evidence_effectiveness: Governance and audits help ensure logs are retained and accessible, but they do not themselves build the technical logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Experiment tracking with data lineage and reproducibility is a fairly standard MLOps response, though framing audits as a by-product is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves compliance record-keeping into the everyday science workflow so audits become a by-product, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it remains mostly logging/tracking practice.
evidence_acceptability: Experiment tracking and data lineage are common, uncontroversial practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing MLflow-style tracking with versioned ledger keyed to dataset commits requires some pipeline changes but is reasonably feasible with existing tools.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the need for traceability and records (Recital 71 documentation and logging) by capturing provenance in R&D, though it targets technical documentation more than Article 12 event logs of deployed systems.
evidence_effectiveness: An append-only provenance ledger would substantially help documentation and traceability of development, but it does not cover runtime event logging of deployed high-risk systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared append-only logging microservice with a CI/CD coverage gate is a sensible but expected engineering response to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice and adds only familiar tooling (CI/CD gate, append-only storage), leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory logging standards enforced via CI/CD are a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared microservice and retrofitting all high-risk pipelines with a CI/CD gate requires some engineering change but uses well-established technology and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by recording sessions with start/end times and Article 12(2) risk triggers.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the shared tamper-evident logging layer with a deployment gate would largely satisfy Article 12 for the lab's systems, though it does not cover post-market monitoring details or Annex III 1(a) specifics such as reference databases and verifier identities.

evidence_originality: Designing architectures for intrinsic traceability and a 'traceability budget' metric is somewhat imaginative and unusual, though traceability and interpretability research is a familiar direction.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging a design property of the architectures the lab researches, turning the obligation into a research agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Funding research and open-source libraries to meet compliance offends no legal or social norms, but a research-driven response is somewhat unusual for a compliance mandate.
evidence_implementability: A two-year programme with four funded researchers building a new traceability metric and tensor-level logging libraries is a significant, expensive, uncertain undertaking, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(1) automatic event-logging requirement and the lab's decision about how to adapt R&D to it.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on architectures and tensor-level hooks may eventually help logging, but it is long-horizon, does not deliver compliance in the near term, and Article 12 needs only ordinary logs, so it is a partial contribution at best.

evidence_originality: Tiered log storage with query SLAs is a sensible but fairly expected engineering answer to a logging mandate, with modest imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new architecture and benchmarking process but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building robust log storage for regulatory inspection is a conventional, norm-compliant engineering response with no sensibilities offended.
evidence_implementability: Tiered hot/warm/cold storage is standard technology, though decade-scale retention with sub-second queries and under 1% write overhead requires some real engineering and hardware budget.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 mandate for lifetime automatic logging and the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields by designing storage and retrieval for them.
evidence_effectiveness: A tiered storage architecture would solve retention and retrieval of logs but does not address which events to log, risk identification, or post-market monitoring content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Operationalizing substantial modification as a quantitative CI gate is an interesting and somewhat imaginative move, though automated compliance checks in CI are a recognizable idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and ties compliance thresholds into the development pipeline, but still treats compliance as a logging/monitoring practice rather than changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Gating merges with compliance-owned thresholds and signed records is an unusual but non-offensive engineering-governance practice that fits regulatory sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a CI check that diffs weight hashes and configs is reasonably feasible, though defining quantitative thresholds for a legal concept like substantial modification requires significant cross-functional work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (knowing when model changes constitute substantial modification, which relates to the logging purposes in 12(2)(a)) rather than the logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate that flags substantial-modification drift helps the lab identify risk/modification situations under Art. 12(2)(a), but it does not itself deliver the automatic event logging, traceability, or Annex III minimum log content the mandate requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated model cards from tracking metadata are a well-known approach, making this interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new pipeline and schema but still treats compliance as a documentation/record-keeping practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation generation from experiment metadata is a common, legally unproblematic practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing MLflow tracking with a compliance schema and a scheduled rendering job requires some changes but is reasonably feasible with modest cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses technical documentation and keeping it up to date (Recital 71), which is related to the record-keeping mandate but is not the automatic event logging of Article 12 itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reasonably help with the documentation upkeep obligation but only partially covers the logging mandate, as it does not produce event logs, traceability of operations, or post-market monitoring records.

evidence_originality: Pre-release compliance gates with checklists and sign-off are a very common, mundane response to regulatory mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance checkpoint that treats compliance as a process step and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance gates and audit checkpoints are a common, uncontroversial governance practice.
evidence_implementability: A checklist, two trained reviewers and a sign-off requirement are modest process additions that need no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of ensuring Article 12 logging and traceability obligations are met before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A pre-release review gate would help verify that logging capabilities exist, but it does not build the logging itself or cover post-market monitoring, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging middleware in project templates is a sensible and fairly expected engineering response, interesting but not surprising or highly imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a scaffold with adapter profiles) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance essentially intact, though building it into project creation moves slightly toward integration.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized compliance tooling embedded in templates is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing internal starter kit with a pluggable logging library is a modest engineering change at reasonable cost, though it needs some design work and adoption effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-injecting the required event capture, including Annex III 1(a) fields, into every prototype.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would make new prototypes log consistently and compliantly, but it covers only new projects and the logging capability itself, not retrofitting legacy systems, retention, or the wider documentation requirements, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A drop-in logging middleware or decorator for compliance is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (SDK/middleware) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance tooling into engineering workflows is a conventional strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A decorator-based SDK and JSON schema are standard software work that is feasible at modest cost and requires little change to existing serving stacks.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly implements the Article 12(1)-(3) logging mandate, so it solves an identified problem that is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, a universal logging layer with a schema for the paragraph-2 events would largely satisfy the logging requirement, though it covers only technical logging and not documentation or the Annex III-specific fields in full detail.

evidence_originality: A post-market surveillance team consuming logs is a fairly expected response by labs to this mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new organizational element (a team with authority) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D works.
evidence_acceptability: A internal compliance or surveillance team is a common governance approach, though pause authority over deployments is somewhat unusual yet not offensive.
evidence_implementability: Hiring three people and wiring them into an existing alerting pipeline with pause authority requires some organizational change and budget but is reasonably feasible within a quarter.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to use logs for identifying risk situations and post-market monitoring named in Article 12(2).
evidence_effectiveness: Monitoring logs for Article 79 risks and escalation would meaningfully support Article 12(2) purposes but does not itself deliver the logging capability or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Formalising log sufficiency as an information-theoretic problem with lower bounds per risk category is unusual and imaginative compared with typical logging-infrastructure responses, though not wholly unprecedented given existing privacy-utility literature.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes the lab's R&D toward a fundamental research programme on log-sufficiency, changing the relationship between research and compliance obligations and addressing what the lab researches, though it stops short of introducing wholly new elements beyond the research itself.
evidence_acceptability: Research on privacy-compliant logging violates no norms and is legally and socially acceptable, though a focus on minimising logs could raise some regulator concerns and is somewhat uncommon.
evidence_implementability: A fundamental research programme deriving theoretical bounds is difficult and uncertain, and it does not commit to near-term implementation resources, though ablation on existing pipelines is feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, what minimal logging satisfies Article 12 without over-collection, which relates to the logging mandate but does not itself deliver the lab's logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would inform proportionate logging design and guidance but would not by itself make the lab's systems compliant, so it is only a partial contribution to the solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance via CI gates and schema-first design is a fairly expected response among engineering teams, though the sprint-template packaging is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (CI gate, linter plugin, log-contract artifact) and reorders the sprint cadence, but still treats compliance as logging practice within the existing agile workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Gating builds on logging compliance is a common, norm-respecting engineering practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Updating the agile playbook, adding a log-contract artifact, and writing a CI linter plugin are modest process and tooling changes that a lab can do at low cost without radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by defining event schemas and checking emitted events against an Article 12 checklist, and it adapts R&D workflow accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably ensure log endpoints exist and match a checklist, but a linter checks for presence and schema rather than substantive adequacy such as traceability appropriate to intended purpose, retention, or Annex III specifics, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A public benchmark scoring state reconstructability from logs alone is unusual and shows imagination, though benchmarks are a familiar research format.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a research and field-level reference product with external partners, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open benchmark with external lab collaboration is a legitimate, norm-compliant research activity, though somewhat less common than standard compliance steps.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a harness with three partner labs under a shared schema is reasonably feasible, though coordinating external labs and agreeing on a schema adds some difficulty.
evidence_applicability: It addresses logging and traceability but mainly aims at a public benchmark and scientific impact, so it only implies a connection to how the lab itself meets the Article 12 mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark would not make the lab's own systems compliant; it might help evaluate log quality but only partially contributes to meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Mapping the statutory minimums into a fixed event schema is an expected, mundane response, though CI-based verifiability adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a schema and CI testing as a new tool/format but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D works.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing a typed logging schema to satisfy Article 12(3) is a standard, legally aligned compliance approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: One engineer drafting the schema in a week and wiring it into two projects during an integration sprint requires some changes to the serving path but is reasonably feasible and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement of meeting the logging mandate by mapping each paragraph-3 minimum to fields that systems must emit.
evidence_effectiveness: The schema would cover the four paragraph-3 minimums for Annex III 1(a) systems but does not address paragraphs 1-2 (risk identification, post-market monitoring, operational monitoring) or retention/documentation more broadly, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance into open-source reusable IP and a sector reference point is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but not highly surprising since open-source tooling for compliance is a foreseeable response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a source of offerings, positioning and funding for the lab, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance tool and publishing a spec paper is somewhat unusual for a lab but offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: Two researchers at 30% time over twelve months, using existing telemetry and running parallel to core research, is a reasonably feasible commitment with some changes, though building and publishing a framework is more than a trivial task.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate, with added benefits (IP, funding) that are implied rather than core.
evidence_effectiveness: A logging framework capturing lifetime events would help meet Article 12 but does not itself guarantee the required risk-relevant, post-market and Annex III-specific logging content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated conformance testing of logs against a schema is a sensible, somewhat unusual framing for prototype-to-production handoff, but it is an expected engineering response and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a log-fidelity conformance harness with metrics) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves R&D's relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal conformance testing and pass-rate metrics offend no legal or social norms and are common engineering strategies.
evidence_implementability: Defining reference schemas per system class and adding staging conformance checks requires some tooling and process changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required event types and Annex III minimums are captured.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch logging gaps early but only verifies fidelity against a schema, not the full mandate (design of logging, retention, relevance judgment), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing architectures with logging built in and mapping a cost-observability frontier is somewhat unusual and imaginative, but it is not strikingly surprising given existing work on observability and interpretability.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Making logging a first-class architectural primitive co-designed with model topology, and turning compliance into a research agenda, changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, though it stops short of redefining what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Building observability into research is a legitimate, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities, though a long exploratory program is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year, dedicated workstream redesigning architectures across transformer, diffusion, and hybrid models is a significant, expensive undertaking, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the logging mandate indirectly by seeking better ways to build logging into systems, an implied problem related to the stated one, with the publication benefit being tangential.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on architectures with native logging would help with logging capability in the long run but does not deliver Article 12 compliance for current systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable compliance logging SDK is an expected, mundane response to a logging mandate with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance essentially unchanged beyond automation.
evidence_acceptability: A shared compliance logging library is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an async logging library with pluggable emitters is a standard engineering task, though covering every Annex III category and integrating it into the prototyping framework requires some changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate, with the stated intervention (SDK) yielding the stated outcome (compliant traceability by default).
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable middleware that captures Article 12(2) event classes and 12(3) fields by default would, if built, solve the main logging mandate for the lab's high-risk builds, though it doesn't address documentation or the question of what to research.

evidence_originality: Designing logging requirements up front is a common, expected response (privacy/compliance by design) and shows little ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checklist template but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though it introduces a new process element.
evidence_acceptability: A design-gate checklist is a common, norm-compliant engineering practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page template added to the kickoff checklist with lead engineer sign-off is a low-cost, non-radical process change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by defining the log events required for risk, post-market monitoring, and operation.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is designed in early but only specifies schemas and sign-off, leaving actual implementation, retention, and Annex III specifics as a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK with declarative schemas is a fairly expected, sensible response that is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and declarative configuration format but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal logging SDK to meet a legal mandate is a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin middleware wrapper over existing pipelines with YAML schemas, piloted on two prototypes, is reasonably feasible but requires some new engineering and cross-team adoption.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (automatic recording of events) while also protecting R&D speed.
evidence_effectiveness: It would make Article 12 event logging automatic and consistent, but it addresses only logging capture and not retention, the Annex III-specific fields, or the interpretation of what is risk-relevant, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Mapping pipeline stages to mandated log fields is the obvious, standard response to Article 12(3) and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-driven logging with encryption and access controls is a common, norm-respecting strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires restructuring pipelines and adding structured logging, which is a moderate engineering effort within normal product development and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields for Annex III biometric systems, which is an explicit part of the stated logging mandate problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Natively capturing the four mandated fields with security controls would satisfy the Article 12(3) requirement, but it does not address Article 12(1)-(2) general logging or other systems, so it is a partial solution to the overall mandate.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance documentation into a publishable reproducibility standard is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (reproducibility framework, publication) and reframes compliance as scientific output, yet explicitly leaves core research questions unchanged, so it only slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Internal templates, compliance co-design and publishing a preprint are common, norm-abiding strategies, though publishing could raise minor confidentiality questions.
evidence_implementability: Co-designing a template and piloting on two projects in a quarter is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some process changes but no major cost.
evidence_applicability: It targets documentation and record-keeping related to Article 12 and thus relates to the stated problem, but the implied outcome (reproducibility standard and standing) is only loosely tied to the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal addresses documentation of algorithms and data, which is more Recital 71 technical documentation than Article 12's automatic event logging, so it would contribute only partially to meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Implementing the mandated minimum log fields as a reference schema and spec document is the obvious, expected response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It builds a reference logging schema for Article 12(3) fields, which is standard compliance logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing the legally mandated logs and documenting them for the technical file is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-engineer team building against an existing prototype with a throughput stress test is a small, low-cost, readily feasible effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specific Article 12(3) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the logging requirement for biometric ID systems, but it covers only Article 12(3) for Annex III 1(a) and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging duties or other systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging capacity as a design variable and measuring the accuracy-overhead tradeoff of auditability is an interesting, somewhat imaginative framing beyond the usual add-a-logger response, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and making auditability a research question, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking since it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance in design and publishing tradeoff research offends no norms and is only slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: It needs only a small team of three people and a prototype on existing benchmarks, but rebuilding the whole model-development pipeline is a significant change, so it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by building an event ontology mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) and embedding logging in every system.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding schema-driven logging in all new systems would largely satisfy Article 12 for future systems, but it does not cover existing systems or the Article 12(3) specifics and is partly a research exercise, so it contributes substantially without fully solving the problem.

evidence_originality: CI-based validation of log schemas is a fairly mundane, expected response, though sensibly applied to Article 12 fields.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a validator tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks for compliance are a common engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a schema validator to an existing stage-gate CI pipeline is a modest, non-radical extension using familiar tooling at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying the required Article 12(3) fields are emitted.
evidence_effectiveness: It reliably catches missing log fields but does not ensure log content is adequate for risk identification, post-market monitoring, or retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning log sufficiency into a benchmarked scientific property (recoverability of decision processes from logs alone) is unusual and imaginative compared with typical logging-infrastructure responses, though not wholly unprecedented given interpretability benchmarks.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making the logging obligation a research object and a contribution to the interpretability literature, which stretches the paradigm without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A public benchmark for auditability offends no legal or social norms and is consistent with research culture, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Building a public task suite with ground-truth causal chains and training probe models on synthetic log streams is a significant research effort with uncertain feasibility, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely how much logging granularity is enough for traceability, which relates to the mandate but does not itself implement the logging required by Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab calibrate logging and add research value, but it is only a partial contribution because it does not directly deliver compliant logs, and reconstructing decisions from logs alone is unlikely to be fully achievable.

evidence_originality: Interceptor-based, hash-chained append-only audit logs mapped to the statutory fields are a common and expected response, with only mild interest from the tamper-evident chaining.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance logging component (middleware plus fixed schema) that leaves the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Audit logging that follows Article 12(3) fields and uses an append-only ledger violates no legal or social norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: A gRPC intercepting proxy writing to a hash-chained local ledger is standard engineering with modest cost and no radical changes to the matching engine.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces the Article 12(3)(a)-(d) logs (use period, reference database, matched inputs, human verifier identity), which is the stated logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would satisfy the specific minimum logging requirements for biometric systems, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and not the Article 12(1)-(2) general logging or the lab's wider R&D adaptation.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK with a CI/CD compliance gate is a common, expected engineering response to Article 12, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice with new tooling but no change in how the lab's R&D relates to compliance, so it preserves the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Mandating shared infrastructure and compliance gates is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared SDK and a pipeline gate takes platform engineering effort and some retrofitting of existing systems, but it is reasonably feasible with standard tools.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the Article 12(3) categories and the paragraph-one capability.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would give systems the automatic logging capability Article 12 requires, but it covers only the logging mechanics and not the full compliance and R&D response such as the Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or documentation.

evidence_originality: Turning mandated logs into an open community benchmark for studying risk emergence is unusual and imaginative, and few labs would be expected to propose it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance logs a new research and community offering, a paradigm stretch rather than a break.
evidence_acceptability: Publicly releasing logs from high-risk deployments raises GDPR, confidentiality, and client-contract concerns that offend sensibilities somewhat, though anonymised open datasets are a recognised practice.
evidence_implementability: Building an anonymisation and curation pipeline for logs while preserving event sequences and releasing it publicly requires significant engineering, privacy review, and legal work, but is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It relates to the stated problem only loosely, as a use of compliance-generated logs for research, which is a special situation rather than a response to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The benchmark does nothing to meet the Article 12 logging mandate itself, so it would not solve the stated problem of how to comply, even though it builds on logs.

evidence_originality: Budget-based compliance gating is a sensible and somewhat unusual angle compared with typical technical logging responses, but it is not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes how compliance relates to R&D project selection by making logging readiness a gating criterion in funding, which stretches the relationship but does not break the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Adding compliance cost lines and weighted criteria to an internal funding rubric is a conventional governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires revising a scorecard and getting the committee and compliance officer to cooperate, which is a reasonably feasible organizational change rather than a trivial one.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of funding the logging mandate, since compliance work is otherwise squeezed out of project budgets.
evidence_effectiveness: It ensures that logging gets budgeted and prioritized, but it does not itself build the logging capabilities or guarantee their quality, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as an architectural layer with a review gate is a common, expected response to this mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance-by-design logging practice that adds a review gate but leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance gates in development is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a logging design review gate to sprints and building logging into architecture requires some process and engineering changes but is reasonably feasible and not radical.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building in the specific logging elements required by Article 12(2) and (3).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a mandatory design gate ensuring automatic capture of required log data would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address the broader documentation, retention, or R&D-adaptation aspects.

evidence_originality: Requiring compliance cost line items in business cases is a sensible but fairly predictable project-management response, with some interest in the return-unreviewed gate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (compliance-costing gate in intake) and modestly ties compliance to project approval, but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Budgeting gates in project intake are a common, uncontroversial management strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Amending a project-intake template to require a cost line item is a non-radical administrative change at low cost, though PIs must produce five-year TCO estimates.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (funding and resourcing the logging and documentation obligations) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D, rather than the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Costing compliance up front helps resource planning but does not itself deliver the logging capability or meet the Article 12 mandate, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Reusable shared logging middleware is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (middleware/SDK) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely integrating it at design time.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging layer is a common engineering and compliance strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a middleware prototype in eight weeks on existing pipeline tooling and distributing an SDK is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by auto-capturing the specified events.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help meet logging requirements across projects, but it is only a partial solution since it does not cover all Article 12 variations, intended-purpose appropriateness, or retention and use of logs.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK/middleware baked into prototypes is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with nothing surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling that leaves the lab's way of working and relationship between R&D and compliance essentially unchanged, though it adds a reusable library.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal compliance tooling with compliance input is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over six weeks integrated into an existing Docker stack is a modest, low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate by providing automatic event recording across high-risk systems, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially provide the technical logging capability, but it does not by itself ensure that event content meets purpose-specific requirements, retention, or the Annex III minimums, and it only covers prototypes, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Continuous documentation with deployment gating is a well-known compliance and DevOps-style idea and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces some new process elements like automated triggers but still treats compliance as a documentation practice, leaving the R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date versioned documentation is a conventional, regulator-friendly practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning documentation engineers and adding automated change-triggered doc flags requires some new roles and tooling but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets technical documentation upkeep from Recital 71, which relates to record-keeping but not directly to the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it addresses an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Living documentation with automated change triggers would help with traceability and compliance but does not deliver the automatic event logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a reference implementation to prove logging viability is a common, expected engineering response with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, a reference template, with the lab's way of working unchanged and no new relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building a compliant logging reference implementation and sharing design docs internally is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses the standard inference stack and well-specified fields, so it is a reasonably feasible, modest-effort build, though it requires dedicated engineering of a full pipeline prototype.
evidence_applicability: The prototype directly implements the four minimum logging fields of Article 12(3)(a)-(d), which are part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the Annex III 1(a) logging requirements for biometric systems but only a partial solution to the broader Article 12 mandate, since it is a prototype template for one system category and does not by itself cover Article 12(1)-(2) across all high-risk systems or production deployment.

evidence_originality: Using mandated logs as a scientific data source for long-horizon drift study with statistical process control is unusual and shows imagination, but drift monitoring is a known concept so it is not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logging into a research agenda on lifetime drift, changing how R&D relates to the logging obligation, though it does not redefine what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-driven research on logs is a legitimate approach, though retaining full logs long term raises some data-protection questions but nothing that offends norms.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting existing prototypes and running a months-long study with standard SPC methods is feasible with some changes and resources, though it requires deployed systems and long timelines.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the logging mandate directly by implementing the Article 12(3) minimum set and linking to Article 72 monitoring, but its main aim is a research track, so the stated problem is only partly the focus.
evidence_effectiveness: It would implement logging on prototypes and produce drift detection that aids post-market monitoring, but it does not cover the full compliance scope across systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Linking design decisions to specific Article 12 sub-paragraphs in sprint logs is a sensible but fairly expected governance move, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (traceability fields in sprint logs mapped to Article 12) but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice without changing how R&D is done.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audit trails and documentation are common strategies that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a field to sprint logs, monthly review, and version-controlled archiving are modest process changes that need little cost or new technology.
evidence_applicability: It addresses documentation and traceability, which relate to Recital 71, but Article 12 concerns automatic event logging by the system itself, so it solves an implied rather than the directly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help demonstrate compliance and design rationale at inspection but does not itself implement automatic system logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logs via fuzzing and tracking compliance as a sprint KPI is a somewhat interesting, imaginative twist, though compliance testing in CI is fairly expected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (conformance fuzzing and a compliance KPI) but still treats compliance as logging practice, with only a mild shift toward engineering metrics.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI to verify compliance is a common engineering strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing property-based testing framework with a schema validator, which is reasonably feasible, though defining what counts as a trigger and per-category schemas requires some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that emitted logs satisfy Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A nightly harness verifying logs capture Article 12(2) triggers would help confirm logging completeness, but it only validates logging and does not itself implement logging or cover documentation and other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Assigning documentation owners and scheduling periodic reviews is a common, expected compliance response with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is a standard documentation-governance process (owners, policies, review checkpoints, versioned repository) that leaves the lab's R&D way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal documentation governance violates no legal or social norms and is a conventional business practice.
evidence_implementability: A one-page policy per system, a named owner and quarterly reviews in a versioned repository are low-cost, non-radical changes that are easy to put in place.
evidence_applicability: It addresses technical documentation currency from Recital 71, which is related to record-keeping but is not the Article 12 automatic logging mandate that is the core of the stated problem, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping technical documentation current helps compliance and traceability but does not deliver automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware or SDK module is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, though it is built into the platform, and it does not change how the lab relates R&D to compliance in a deeper way.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory internal tooling for compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms, though mandating it from the first prototype may mildly burden researchers.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK module and mandating its use is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some platform changes and engineering effort but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly maps each captured field (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier identities) to the Article 12(3) requirements, which are part of the stated problem.
