evidence_acceptability: Compliance logging engineered into systems is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A dedicated platform team, SDK and two quarters of integration sprints across every product group, including retrofitting, is a significant but feasible effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by capturing the exact Article 12(3) items (timestamps, reference database, matched inputs, verifier identities).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, uniform automatic logging across all high-risk systems would meet the logging mandate and traceability, though it covers 12(2) event relevance and R&D adaptation less fully and Article 12(3) applies only to certain Annex III systems.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware is a standard, expected response to a logging mandate, though the scaffold-time integration is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK wired into scaffolding) but still treats compliance purely as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extracting existing debug-telemetry hooks into a versioned SDK and wiring it into the project generator is a modest, non-radical engineering effort using existing assets.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate across the lab's high-risk prototypes (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably deliver automatic event recording and Article 12(3) fields across prototypes, but covers only part of the compliance picture (12(2) relevance, retention, documentation, deployer needs), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Platform-level inherited logging via sidecars and base images is a sensible, commonly expected engineering response, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (middleware, sidecar, base image) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only automated and centralized.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized audit logging infrastructure violates no legal, social, or business norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing Kubernetes templates and common tooling, requiring some platform engineering and adoption effort but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (Art. 12 automatic recording of events, timestamps, input data, risk-relevant points) in the lab's R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging layer inherited by all prototypes would reasonably satisfy the automatic event-recording mandate for the lab's systems, though it covers logging only and not the wider obligations such as documentation or the Annex III-specific fields, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized shared logging platform is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged, merely centralizing the tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal logging infrastructure is a conventional approach that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Using existing container orchestration and database layers with a small three-person team and configuration-based integration makes this reasonably low-cost and feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (event recording, Article 12(3) items like reference database and verifier identification) across high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging service with timestamped events, reference-database queries and verifier tagging would cover the Article 12 logging mandate if built, but it does not address retention rules, risk-event relevance, or broader documentation, so it is a strong but mostly complete logging solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging SDK plus design-review checklist is the common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice implemented via a shared tool, leaving the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging infrastructure and design-review gates is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared logging SDK with a dedicated platform sub-group and a checklist step is a reasonably feasible set of changes requiring some resources but no radical shifts.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by building an automatic event-logging pipeline that captures risk-relevant events, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared SDK mandated through design review would, if done, satisfy Article 12(1)-(2) logging requirements, though it does not cover the Annex III 1(a) specifics like reference database or verifier identity, so it is largely but not completely a full solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into shared SDKs or middleware is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (shared middleware and schema in the SDK) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: A middleware layer and an append-only event bus are standard engineering that needs some changes and moderate effort, and the claim of near-zero integration cost is optimistic.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by producing the required log events automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic event logging for internal prototypes, but it does not cover the Article 12(3) specifics, log retention, or the post-market monitoring needs, and it applies only to systems built on the SDK, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: CI-based testing of log completeness against regulatory fields is a sensible and fairly expected DevOps-style response, only mildly interesting with edge-case generation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI test harness) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifting verification earlier.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Writing schema assertions and synthetic workloads in an existing CI pipeline is low-cost and involves non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring Article 12(3) fields are logged correctly.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies that required Article 12(3) fields are present but does not itself implement logging or address Article 12(2) and broader obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared compliance logging middleware library with pluggable emitters and schema templates is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, with the lab's way of working largely unchanged, though schema templates per Annex III category add slight new elements.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal shared tooling for compliance is a standard strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers for six weeks, extraction from an existing experiment-tracking store, and piloting on three prototypes is a modest, reasonably scoped effort with low cost.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly implements the Article 12 logging mandate (auto-emitting structured logs covering Article 12(3) fields), which is a direct part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would deliver compliant automatic logging across prototypes, but it covers mainly Article 12(3) fields and does not address broader record-keeping like technical documentation or Article 12(2) event relevance judgment, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code in CI is an interesting and sensible idea, but it is a fairly expected response that shows only some imagination rather than being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI gate with schema validation and doc-drift detection) but still treats compliance as a logging and documentation practice, leaving the R&D relationship to compliance unchanged beyond automation.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks are a common engineering strategy that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing GitLab CI with JSON Schema and doc diffing, requiring modest changes, though auto-generating documentation and testing live log output take some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by validating Article 12(3) log fields and keeping Recital 71 documentation current.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help enforce schema conformance and documentation currency, but it does not address Article 12(1)-(2) event relevance, risk identification, or the Annex III scope, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logging in CI is a sensible, fairly expected DevOps-style response; it is interesting but not particularly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/process (automated test stage) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI pipelines is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Requires writing parameterised test scripts and fixtures per profile and integrating with the event store, which is some work but reasonably feasible with existing CI infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring required events are actually recorded: do X (CI gate) to get Y (complete logs).
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate verifying that required events are emitted and persisted would reliably catch logging omissions, but it addresses only verification of logging completeness, not the full mandate (design of log content, retention, Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logging in CI is a sensible and fairly predictable response that an experienced evaluator would expect, with little surprise or ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (compliance gates in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to its obligations unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing in CI pipelines is a common engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Schema validation checks and synthetic end-to-end tests against a stub database are cheap and fit existing CI tooling with no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking that the four specified log fields are present, which is a stated part of the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: CI tests verifying the Article 12(3) fields are emitted would help ensure logging compliance, but they cover only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) event-recording or documentation duties, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware or SDK wrapper is a fairly common and expected engineering response to a logging mandate, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared service and SDK but still treats compliance as a logging practice, deliberately leaving the R&D workflow unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance logging infrastructure is a standard strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an event store with schema validation and thin wrappers requires moderate infrastructure effort but is reasonably feasible with existing serving endpoints, though adoption across projects takes some change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by mapping specific fields to Article 12(3) requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A central event-store capturing the Article 12(3)(a)-(d) fields would, if built, deliver the automatic logging the mandate requires, though it does not cover the broader Article 12(2) event relevance, documentation, or retention questions, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tamper-evident retention with query interfaces is a common, mundane response expected from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Secure log retention is a common, expected compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Segregated storage, hashing, retention schedules and a query interface are well-understood engineering requiring some new infrastructure but reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to keep and produce logs over the system lifetime for authority requests, which is part of the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Retention, integrity-protected storage and retrieval would address the log storage and traceability side of Article 12, but it does not define which events to log or cover the capture mechanism, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reconciling logging mandates with GDPR through pseudonymisation and retention limits is an interesting but fairly expected response from a legal-minded evaluator's view.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a data-handling protocol but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged, so it is slightly paradigm stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Pseudonymisation, retention limits, and restricted access are common, norm-respecting data-protection strategies.
evidence_implementability: Legal and DPO teams drafting minimisation, retention, and access rules is a reasonably feasible, low-cost measure using existing functions.
evidence_applicability: It solves an identified, directly related problem: how to meet Article 12(3) logging, especially verifier identification, without creating a data-protection violation.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address only the GDPR intersection for one Annex III category's logging fields, so it helps as a partial solution but does not deliver the overall logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Using regression tests to verify logging is a sensible but fairly expected response; the edge-case payloads (stale reference DB, concurrent verifiers) add a little specificity but not surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/process (CI assertion suite) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI testing of log completeness is a standard engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires writing parameterised test scripts and a JSON schema within existing CI infrastructure, which is a modest, low-cost change, though covering every event class and edge case takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that logs capture required event classes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure log completeness and format but does not itself create logging capability, cover retention or the Annex III specifics fully, or address broader compliance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating the logging mandate as a controlled experiment on the capability cost of auditability is interesting and somewhat unusual, but not strikingly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making the logging obligation a research question and publishing open data, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Benchmarking logging overhead and publishing results offends no legal or social norms, though it is a somewhat uncommon approach to compliance.
evidence_implementability: Implementing a minimal logging layer on two 7B models and running three benchmark suites is reasonably feasible with moderate effort and cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (understanding the performance cost of logging) related to meeting the mandate, but does not directly produce a compliance mechanism.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute evidence and a minimal logging layer but is only a partial solution, since 7B models are not frontier-scale, the compliance scope is narrow, and it does not cover full Article 12 requirements like Annex III specifics.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance gates at design review are a common, expected response, though the timing before compute allocation is a sensible touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance checkpoint that adds a review step but leaves the lab's R&D and logging practice essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A design-review compliance checkpoint is a common governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It only adds a two-hour session to an existing monthly architecture board with a designated engineer, which is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying logging architecture before training begins.
evidence_effectiveness: A single gate checking design would catch architectural gaps early but does not itself build, operate, or maintain the logs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Documentation review cycles with trigger matrices and audits are common and mundane compliance practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance governance process that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Periodic reviews, audits and sign-offs are common governance strategies that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires a cross-functional process and quarterly audits but uses existing organizational structures, so it is reasonably feasible with modest changes.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied related problem (keeping documentation up to date under Recital 71) rather than the identified logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation update cycle would keep technical documentation current, but it does not address the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A standardized internal logging SDK/middleware is the common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, merely centralized into a shared component, leaving the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory internal tooling for compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a platform SDK and enforcing it across all high-risk projects requires a substantial one-time investment and process change but is clearly feasible with reasonable measures.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by building logging that satisfies Articles 12(1)-(3), which is an identified part of the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a mandatory reusable logging layer would largely meet the logging mandate, though it does not cover the technical documentation or the R&D adaptation side, and 'appropriate to intended purpose' scoping still needs per-system judgment.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance patterns is interesting and somewhat uncommon, but not especially ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (public reference framework, shared vocabulary) and shifts compliance toward a community-facing scientific contribution, but it still centers on logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance reference framework is somewhat unusual for a lab but offends no norms or sensibilities, and it aligns with the regulation's documentation aims.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers plus legal input to build and open-source a design-pattern catalogue with code stubs is a modest, reasonably feasible effort requiring some changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by designing logging into serving infrastructure, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A reference architecture and minimum logging schemas would help the lab meet logging requirements, but it is a catalogue with stubs rather than a full implemented, verified compliance solution, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing Article 12 logging as an information-theoretic minimal-sufficiency problem with differential-privacy-aware sampling is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly unprecedented in compliance research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements and reframes compliance as a research contribution, shifting the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations somewhat, but it still centers on logging design rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Academic research on logging schemas with privacy protection offends no norms and is consistent with legal and business sensibilities, though it is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Deriving formal lower bounds and validating them on prototypes is a research program with uncertain outcomes and considerable expertise cost, making it difficult as a commitment of scarce implementation resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets how much logging is needed to meet Article 12 traceability, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, it would yield schemas that inform what to log but would not by itself deliver working compliant logging or cover all of the lab's obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance-coverage checks in CI are a sensible but fairly expected response to a logging mandate, showing little surprising imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (query tool, CI coverage report) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: An internal CI-integrated compliance-checking tool is a common engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or political norms.
evidence_implementability: Wrapping a columnar store with a CLI/notebook and CI hook requires some new tooling and process changes but is reasonably feasible with standard components.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses verifying that logging covers Article 12(2) event categories, which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help catch logging gaps early but covers only coverage verification, not the logging implementation itself, retention, or Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Budgeting compliance costs in project proposals is a fairly common, mundane governance step, though front-loading traceability costs is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (cost itemisation in proposals) but still treats compliance as logging practice, with a mild shift toward considering compliance at project selection.
evidence_acceptability: Adding cost lines to a budget/feasibility form is an ordinary administrative practice that violates no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: It only requires modifying a template and having the budget office add three lines, which is a low-cost, non-radical change, though estimating data volumes up front takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of resourcing and planning for logging obligations, which relates to how the lab adapts R&D, but does not itself address the logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab plan and fund logging but does not implement logging or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial contribution to the solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checks in CI and sprint reviews are a common DevOps shift-left practice, with only the live log playback adding mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a CI lint rule and a demo step but still treats compliance as ordinary logging practice embedded in existing workflows, leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding checklists and CI gates in engineering workflows is a conventional strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing pull-request, CI, and standup rituals with a lint rule and a short demo, so it is cheap and non-radical to implement.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by verifying that prototype logging covers the Article 12(2) event categories, so it does X to get Y, and Y is part of the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI lint check and demo step would help catch missing log emissions early but cannot ensure log content is adequate, complete, or retained, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logging into a publishable research contribution is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though academic framing of governance is not unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes traceability as a scientific research question, which changes how R&D relates to compliance, but it stops short of altering what the lab researches or its core practices.
evidence_acceptability: Academic publication and interviews with operators are common, norm-abiding activities, though sharing internal post-mortems requires some confidentiality care.
evidence_implementability: Writing a methodological paper from internal post-mortems and three interviews is feasible with modest resources, though it takes research effort and formalisation work.
evidence_applicability: The framework for adequate log-event taxonomies by system class relates directly to how the lab meets Article 12's logging mandate, though it is geared toward publication more than the lab's own compliance, so it addresses an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A published tiered specification would help the lab decide what to log and contribute to compliance, but it is only a partial solution since it does not itself implement logging or ensure conformity.

evidence_originality: Productizing compliance as a differentiator is a somewhat unusual and interesting idea, but it is a fairly familiar business move and not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance logging into a sellable client-facing assurance product changes the relationship between the lab's work and its obligations (a new offering born from compliance), which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Offering compliance documentation to clients is an uncommon but non-offensive strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs legal and product co-design of a template and a two-customer pilot built on existing logging output, which is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses how to respond to the logging mandate by packaging logs into reports, which relates to the stated problem only through an implied benefit (market value) rather than directly meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by leveraging Article 12 outputs and turning compliance into value, but it does not itself implement the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Directly implementing the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields is the most obvious, expected response to the mandate, with nothing surprising added.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice plus a retention-and-access framework, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Complying with explicit legal requirements through data governance and legal partnership violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Capturing timestamps, reference database IDs, matched inputs, and verifier identities plus a retention framework requires some new work and cross-team coordination but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specified minimum logging capabilities.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would satisfy the Article 12(3) specific logging requirements for point 1(a) systems, but it omits Article 12(1)-(2) general logging and non-biometric products, so it is a strong yet partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as research data is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logs primary research data and compliance outputs into science, which stretches the paradigm but does not change what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using mandated logs for internal research and post-market monitoring is a somewhat unusual but non-offensive strategy, with minor data-protection and publication-confidentiality caveats.
evidence_implementability: Assigning two postdocs to an existing MLOps group to build anomaly-detection on logs the lab must already collect is a modest, reasonably feasible change, though not entirely trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to adapt R&D to the logging and post-market monitoring obligations under Articles 12(2)(b) and 72, which are part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help produce post-market monitoring evidence and make use of logs, but it does not itself specify how to implement the logging mandate (event capture, retention), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance testing in CI is a fairly expected and known response, with only mild interest in codifying each Article 12 field as a test.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (CI gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance tests in CI are a widely accepted engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding unit-integration tests to an existing CI pipeline that assert log records appear is a modest, well-understood engineering change using standard tooling, though writing tests per log field takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required events are recorded before compliance review.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging coverage exists and catches gaps early but only tests with synthetic inputs and does not by itself ensure logs are adequate, retained, or traceable in deployment, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Storage benchmarking for log retention is a mundane, expected engineering step with no surprising element.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard infrastructure sizing for logging and leaves the lab's way of working and its compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal benchmarking before architecture decisions is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A synthetic workload generator and benchmarking of existing storage backends is a modest internal engineering effort using standard tools at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (sizing and cost of log storage and retrieval) that supports the logging mandate but is not itself the logging capability.
evidence_effectiveness: It only informs architecture choices and does not produce logging or define which events to record, so it contributes just a small partial piece of the solution.

evidence_originality: Budgeting compliance costs per project is a sensible but fairly expected response, with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and integrates compliance cost into project selection, mildly changing the portfolio decision process, but still treats compliance as a logging cost to be managed rather than changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a cost line item to project proposals before steering committee votes is a common, norm-compatible management practice.
evidence_implementability: A spreadsheet-plus-script calculator and a proposal template requirement are cheap and easy to build and adopt with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The cost calculator addresses an implied problem (budgeting for the resource burden of logging and deciding which projects to commit resources to), which relates to the stated problem but does not itself meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab make informed resource-allocation decisions about compliance overhead but does not implement logging or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using the logging mandate as a basis for rigorous drift-detection research is interesting and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as measurement science woven into the lab's research, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: An empirical study that publishes findings and uses test deployments offends no norms, though treating compliance as a research program is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Instrumenting existing systems with parameterized logging tiers and running perturbation experiments on test deployments is a significant, multi-year research effort, though feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely how much logging is enough to detect substantial modification under Article 12(2)(a), which relates to the mandate but does not directly implement the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: Thresholds linking log resolution to detection latency would help calibrate logging for risk and modification detection, but this is only a partial contribution and does not deliver the actual compliance capability.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging library with CI gating is the standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (SDK, CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging library with CI enforcement is a common engineering compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building an SDK in one sprint on top of an existing experiment tracker, plus a CI gate, is a reasonably feasible measure requiring some changes but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would produce Article 12 logs across pipelines and enforce them, though it addresses logging only and the Annex III minimums are flagged only for biometric projects, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Framing Article 12(2)(a) risk-event identification as a formal learnable sequence-detection problem is interesting and somewhat unusual, but anomaly/drift detection for monitoring is a familiar technical response, so it is not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logging into a research agenda and publication program, changing the relationship between the lab's R&D and its obligations, though it stops short of redefining what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Research and publication on drift and anomaly detection offend no norms or laws and are a normal lab activity.
evidence_implementability: Building labeled datasets and developing calibrated detectors with theory is a multi-year research effort requiring significant resources and with uncertain outcomes, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem of identifying risk-relevant events from logs under 12(2)(a), which relates to the stated problem but only a single sub-clause and via research rather than meeting the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Detectors for risk events might contribute to part of Article 12(2)(a) capability but do not deliver the logging mandate itself (automatic recording, minimum fields, retention), so at best a partial solution and unlikely to meet near-term compliance.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware or platform-team approach is a common, expected response to such a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice, merely centralized into one reusable tool, and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared infrastructure for compliance is a common, norm-compliant corporate strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Six senior engineers for a quarter and a pilot on two prototypes is a reasonably feasible, concretely resourced plan, though it requires some change to existing design sprints and integration with serving stacks.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by building a module that auto-captures Article 12(2) event categories and Annex III 1(a) fields to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging module would solve the core logging-compliance requirement across projects if built, though it does not address the non-logging obligations or the R&D adaptation question, and scoping 'where relevant' leaves some gaps.

evidence_originality: Mapping logged events to Article 12(2) in a pre-build sign-off is a mundane, expected compliance procedure with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template to existing stage-gate processes and treats compliance as standard process practice, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Governance sign-off gates and specification templates are common, norm-compliant practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page template embedded in an existing stage-gate review board is a low-cost, non-radical change that can be done quickly.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by ensuring each project specifies logs tied to Article 12(2), an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A spec and gate ensure logging is planned and mapped to Article 12 purposes, but it does not itself implement logging or cover Article 12(3) specifics, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A monitoring dashboard built on logs is a fairly expected response to this mandate, with little surprising or ingenious about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, with the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring dashboards for regulatory compliance are a common, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a centralized log-ingestion pipeline with alert thresholds and a dashboard is a reasonably feasible data-engineering project requiring some new work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate's stated purposes of post-market monitoring (Art. 72) and risk identification (Art. 79(1)) by using logs for those ends.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps operationalize use of logs for monitoring but does not itself ensure the systems log the required events or cover the Article 12(3) minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as an intrinsic architectural property optimized via differentiable architecture search is unusual and imaginative compared with typical lab responses like adding logging pipelines.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging part of the science and the architecture search objective, and shifts what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Nothing here offends legal or social norms, though it is an unusual strategy for compliance that treats it as research.
evidence_implementability: It requires a novel research agenda with formalizing information-theoretic log requirements as differentiable losses, which is difficult and uncertain and demands significant resources, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It targets the Article 12 logging mandate directly, including the paragraph 3(a)-(d) minimum fields, so it does relate to the stated problem, though through a research route rather than a compliance fix.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal is an exploratory research program that would not by itself deliver reliable Article 12 logging, since standard instrumentation is still needed and the architecture search outcome is uncertain, so it is unlikely to solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: Applying schema-registry and migration practice to compliance logs across model versions is a sensible, somewhat interesting angle but is a conventional data-engineering approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (registry plus migration runner) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Schema registries and migration pipelines are standard engineering practice that offend no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Schema-registry tools and CI-integrated migration runners are mature, so this requires some engineering work but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting Article 12's lifetime logging and traceability mandate as models are retrained or substantially modified, though it covers only the schema-evolution part of logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help preserve traceability across model versions but does not itself decide what events to log or satisfy the Article 12(2)-(3) content requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Retrofitting logging middleware onto existing tracking tools is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice and explicitly keeps the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure and forming a cross-team working group is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Plugging middleware into existing experiment-tracking tools with a small working group is feasible at modest cost, though retrofitting across multiple pipelines requires some engineering changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by embedding automatic event recording in existing high-risk pipelines.
evidence_effectiveness: Reusable logging middleware mapped to Article 12 requirements would largely satisfy the logging mandate if done, though it is vague about which events are captured and omits technical documentation and Annex III specifics, so it is a strong but not fully specified solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-tests in CI is a fairly expected and mundane response, though tied neatly to Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool/process element but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance tests in CI are a common engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Pytest fixtures in an existing CI pipeline are cheap and reasonably easy to add with non-radical changes to workflow.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring logs contain mandated fields, which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate verifying Article 12(3) fields would reliably catch missing log fields but does not itself design the logging or cover Article 12(1)-(2) traceability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware embedded in every project is the expected, mundane response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared tool but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's research approach and its relationship to compliance basically unchanged, though architecture-level embedding is slightly beyond purely standard practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building mandatory logging into engineering workflows is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared logging middleware library with sprint-zero compliance review requires some engineering effort and process changes but is reasonably feasible with standard software practice.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by building the required logging capability into every system.
evidence_effectiveness: A uniform logging module covering Article 12(3) items would largely satisfy the logging mandate, but it does not address broader scoping, retention, or Article 12(2) event relevance for each system, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and automated compliance documentation from CI is a fairly common, expected response, though sensibly executed.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (auto-generated tech file) but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from existing pipelines is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing CI/CD and experiment-tracking metadata with export hooks, requiring only modest changes at low cost and no new tooling or headcount.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified related problem, documentation drift and lifetime currency, which is part of the record-keeping obligation, though the logging mandate is only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would keep technical documentation current, which helps with Recital 71 but does not implement Article 12's event logging itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK with a decorator is a common and expected response to logging mandates, with little surprising or imaginative about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice packaged as tooling, leaving the lab's way of working and relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal logging middleware for compliance is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A Python decorator-based library with SQLite and Kafka back-ends is easily built with modest cost and non-radical changes to existing workflows.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by providing automatic event recording across the lab's inference paths.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared SDK that automatically records structured events including the Article 12(3) minimum fields would, if built, deliver the technical logging capability the mandate requires, though it omits retention, integrity and Article 12(2) risk-event scoping, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A dedicated documentation function with version control, update triggers and quarterly audits is the standard, expected response to documentation obligations, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a compliance unit and a version-controlled repository with update triggers, which are new process elements, but it still treats compliance as a documentation and record-keeping practice and leaves R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance team and audit process is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Three staff, a version-controlled repository and quarterly audits are reasonable, modest organizational changes that a lab can feasibly carry out.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the documentation-currency requirement from Recital 71, which is related to the record-keeping mandate, but Article 12 itself concerns automatic event logging, so the problem it solves is implied rather than the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A documentation unit would keep the technical dossier current, which helps compliance, but it does not implement the automatic event logging that Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging middleware/SDK inherited by default is a sensible and fairly expected engineering response to Article 12, so it is common rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (an internal SDK) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal compliance tooling is a standard, uncontroversial strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires dedicated staff and integration with the existing containerised stack, but this is a modest, reasonably feasible engineering effort with named resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate while preserving R&D hours, a clear do-X-to-get-Y link.
evidence_effectiveness: A default logging layer capturing the Article 12(2) event categories across all systems would substantially meet the logging mandate, though it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics or documentation duties explicitly.

evidence_originality: A focused sprint to build a logging schema and benchmark overhead is a fairly expected response, with the publishable-contribution angle adding only a little interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a research sprint and a publishable specification but still treats compliance as a logging implementation task, with only a mild nod to turning the constraint into a contribution.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging and publishing a spec violates no norms, though the publication element is slightly less common and could raise minor IP or confidentiality questions.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers for six weeks on one live system is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment with low cost and no radical organizational change.
evidence_applicability: The sprint directly designs logging schemas for the Annex III 1(a) minimums (timestamps, reference database, matched input, verifier identity), which are explicitly part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would produce a compliant, reusable logging spec for the biometric system and a portfolio template, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and Article 12(1)-(2) general logging, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging requirements as testable CI assertions is a sensible but fairly predictable DevOps move, with mild interest from the property-based edge-case generation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool/process (CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI is a legal, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms, though it is a somewhat specific application.
evidence_implementability: Adding a CI stage with property-based tests against a staging instance uses standard tooling and modest effort, though defining the event schemas and synthetic edge cases takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that Article 12(2) events are emitted correctly.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps keep logging intact across code changes but does not itself design the logging, cover Article 12(3) specifics, or ensure log retention and adequacy, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Measuring logging-first versus retrofit cost is a sensible, somewhat unusual empirical approach, but it is not especially imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an experimental benchmark) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal controlled experiment comparing engineering approaches violates no legal or social norms, though parallel duplicate teams are slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: Running parallel sprint tracks across three system types doubles engineering effort on the same spec, which is a significant but feasible cost, so it needs some changes and resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (deciding how to resource and sequence logging implementation) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It yields data to choose a design approach but does not itself implement logging or satisfy Article 12, so it only partially contributes to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: A centralized, reusable logging module integrated at design time is a common and expected engineering response, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging SDK introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, with design-review mandates only modestly changing process, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Shared compliance infrastructure and design-review gates are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a lightweight SDK once and requiring it in design reviews is reasonably feasible with some process changes and platform team effort across six projects.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate across the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A standardized logging SDK mapped to Article 12(2) event categories would contribute substantially to meeting the logging mandate but does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, documentation, or retention governance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: An internal compliance unit with dashboards and mock audits is a standard, mundane governance response that evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds an organizational unit and dashboard but still treats compliance as a separate logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal compliance and audit function is a common, norm-conforming governance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Staffing three people and building a dashboard is a modest, reasonably feasible organizational change at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: The unit reviews logs for Article 79(1) risks and supports post-market monitoring, which directly addresses the mandate to use logging for compliance, though it presumes the logging infrastructure already exists.
evidence_effectiveness: Monthly log review and mock audits would help detect risks and verify compliance, but they do not themselves meet the technical logging requirements, so the solution is only partial.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a provenance and archival tool is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing, but compliance tooling and open-source release are fairly familiar ideas, so it is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Open-sourcing a compliance logging layer as a standing lab responsibility creates a new offering born from compliance and shifts the lab's relationship to it, though it still centers on logging rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release under MIT is a common, norm-compatible strategy, though it may raise mild concerns about exposing proprietary information or about logging data protection.
evidence_implementability: Building middleware integrated with existing experiment trackers is reasonably feasible, though maintaining it as an open-source project requires ongoing resources.
evidence_applicability: The tool directly addresses the logging mandate by capturing logs and records aligned with Article 12, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially support Article 12 logging and traceability, but the Article 12(3) minimums apply only to specific biometric systems, and the proposal captures training lineage beyond what Article 12 requires, so it only partially solves the full mandate such as event relevance to risk and post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated logs as longitudinal scientific datasets for drift research is an unusual and imaginative reframing, though drift detection and SPC are known concepts.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance logs the basis of new research and partnerships, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking the question of what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Partnering with deployers on anonymized logs and publishing results is a somewhat unusual but non-offensive strategy, though data-sharing and privacy concerns exist.
evidence_implementability: It requires deployer partnerships, access to anonymized log streams over months, and new statistical frameworks, which is significant and difficult though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of using logs to identify risk situations and support post-market monitoring, which relates to the logging mandate but is not the direct problem of building compliant logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift detection on logs would help meet post-market monitoring and risk-identification purposes of Article 12(2), but it does not itself deliver the logging capability or cover the full mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auditing logs for mandated fields is a mundane, expected compliance response with nothing ingenious about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance monitoring and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal log auditing and remediation SLAs are common compliance strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: A weekly automated script checking four known fields plus an escalation SLA is a low-cost, non-radical addition to existing QA.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies completeness of the four fields but does not build logging capability or cover Article 12(1)-(2) event relevance, nor does it apply beyond Annex III 1(a) systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a public longitudinal drift research corpus is interesting and shows some imagination, though drift monitoring is a known concept and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logs a source of research and publications, which is paradigm stretching, but it does not change what the lab researches at a larger level.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research and white papers are acceptable in principle, though publishing findings derived from logs raises some confidentiality and data protection sensitivities that the proposal does not address.
evidence_implementability: It needs a multi-year program, an analysis pipeline, tagging and annual publications on top of existing infrastructure, which is reasonably feasible but needs sustained resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting value from Article 12(1) logs and supporting risk identification and post-market monitoring, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly say how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The observatory reuses logs and tags events against Article 79(1) risk categories, which supports traceability and post-market monitoring, but it does not itself establish the logging capability or the minimum content the mandate requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-tests in CI is a common, expected response, with property-based testing a mild flourish.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a test harness and conformance reports but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI pipelines is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing pytest suite and CI/CD pipeline with a small QA pair, requiring some new test work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by catching gaps in logging conformance during development.
evidence_effectiveness: A CI gate verifying log completeness and schema would reliably ensure prototypes' logging meets Article 12(3) fields, but it only verifies logging and does not build the logging or address Article 12(1)-(2) scope, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A streaming log pipeline with anomaly dashboards is a common, expected response to logging mandates and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging and monitoring infrastructure and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized log monitoring and post-market monitoring are standard, norm-compliant practices that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Deploying a streaming platform with central storage and dashboards across all production instances requires significant infrastructure and ongoing operations, but it is feasible with existing technology, so it needs some changes and reasonable investment.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the logging mandate by streaming logs centrally and supporting Article 26(5), 72 and 79(1) monitoring and reporting, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, continuous log ingestion with risk correlation and reporting would address most of the logging and monitoring obligations, though it does not itself define which events are logged or cover Article 12(3) specifics, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, mundane response that labs would be expected to give.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a logging practice added to existing pipelines and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding Article 12 logging into existing pipelines is a standard, legally sound compliance approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-week sprint per pipeline reusing existing Kafka and time-series infrastructure is a modest, non-radical change, though it still requires some engineering work per pipeline.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by mapping Article 12(2) events to logs.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, automatic event logging mapped to Article 12(2) triggers would largely meet the logging mandate, though it leaves out retention, risk-relevance judgment, and the human-verification identification fields, so it is not entirely complete.

evidence_originality: A provenance ledger for biometric logging is a mundane, expected response to the explicit requirements of Article 12(3).
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance logging module that treats the mandate as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Audit ledgers with role-based access are common compliance strategies that offend no norms, though logging identities of verifiers raises minor privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: It adds an immutable ledger alongside existing feature stores and access controls, which requires some changes but is reasonably feasible with standard data engineering.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12(3) minimum logging duties (reference database, matched input data, verifier identity) for Annex III 1(a) systems, which are part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would satisfy the paragraph 3 requirements for biometric systems, but it does not cover the Article 12(1)-(2) general logging or period-of-use recording, so it is a partial solution to the overall mandate.

evidence_originality: Stress-testing log storage with synthetic multi-year data is a sensible engineering step but fairly expected and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new test tooling (synthetic log generator, regression tests) but still treats compliance purely as logging infrastructure practice, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Internal engineering validation offends no legal, social, or political norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a synthetic generator and automated test suite requires a dedicated workstream but is reasonably feasible with standard engineering skills.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 requirement for logs to persist and be retrievable over the system's lifetime, which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It de-risks storage durability and retrieval but does not address what events to log, traceability content, or R&D adaptation, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Phase-gating compliance within sprint cadence is a common, mundane process-governance response that experienced evaluators would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template field and gate reviews but leaves the lab's R&D way of working and its standard compliance-as-process approach essentially unchanged, which is paradigm preserving.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance gates in existing workflows is a common strategy that offends no norms, though some teams may grumble about the added gating.
evidence_implementability: Revising a project template and making the Compliance Officer a standing reviewer fits existing sprint processes and requires only non-radical, low-cost changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring logging is in place before deployment and handed off to post-market monitoring, tying X (gates) to Y (logging compliance).

evidence_applicability: It addresses record-keeping for traceability, which is related to the logging mandate, but it targets released artifacts and documentation rather than the automatic event logging of a deployed high-risk system, so it addresses an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Provenance manifests would contribute to traceability and documentation but do not provide automatic runtime event logs, so they are only a partial solution to the mandate.

evidence_originality: Mining logs as a 'failure archaeology' dataset to build a taxonomy of real-world AI failures and publish an annual report is an interesting, somewhat imaginative reframing, but not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logs into a standing research program on failure modes, changing the relationship between the lab's R&D and its Article 12 obligations so logging feeds the science, though it does not alter what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal analysis of operational logs and publishing an annual report is a somewhat unusual but unoffensive strategy, with minor sensitivities around disclosing failures and data protection.
evidence_implementability: Two postdocs, an incident database and analysis of logs across the portfolio is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment, though log access, privacy and data-quality issues add some work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting value from and justifying Article 12 logs, and cites 12(2)(b) post-market monitoring, but the core stated problem of meeting the logging mandate is only indirectly addressed.
evidence_effectiveness: It would use logs for scientific insight and partly support post-market monitoring, but it does not by itself make the logging mandate met (no logging design, retention, or minimum content), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware and template-repo scaffolding is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK and template scaffolding) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving R&D's relationship to compliance largely unchanged beyond earlier integration.
evidence_acceptability: Internal shared libraries and standardized schemas are routine practice that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing production logging hooks and an existing template repo, requiring modest extraction and versioning work rather than radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by providing pre-built log emitters and event schemas for new prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared SDK would substantially ease and standardize logging but does not by itself cover required content judgments (e.g., Article 12(2) relevance, Annex III specifics, retention, oversight identification), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Immutable event-sourced logs on WORM storage with an auditor API are a well-known, standard engineering pattern for compliance logging, so the idea is competent but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces some specific tools (event sourcing, WORM, auditor API), but it treats compliance purely as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable audit logging with retention controls is a common, expected compliance strategy that violates no norms, although storing biometric match data raises some privacy concerns that retention policies address.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing SSO and standard storage technologies and applies to one product line, so it needs some new build work but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement in Article 12(3) by mapping each sub-point to a specific data field, so it is directly tied to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, the ledger would capture every Article 12(3) element (use period, reference database, matched input, verifier identity), which solves the main logging mandate for Annex III biometric systems, though it does not cover Article 12(1)-(2) for other high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: A cross-lab open logging ontology for reproducibility is an interesting and somewhat unusual reframing, but standardization consortia and open schemas are familiar and it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a shared open ontology and consortium) and links logging to scientific reproducibility, but it still treats compliance mainly as logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source standards and academic-industry consortia are common, norm-compliant strategies, though sharing log schemas could raise some minor confidentiality concerns.
evidence_implementability: Convening four to six labs, co-designing an ontology, and releasing reference implementations requires significant coordination and effort, though it is feasible with reasonable resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (shared, comparable logging formats and reproducibility) that is related to meeting the logging mandate, rather than the mandate compliance directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help standardize the Article 12(3) fields, but it does not itself implement logging in the lab's systems or address Art. 12(1)-(2) obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance stage gates with sign-off memos are the standard, expected response to a regulatory mandate and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint to existing processes but leaves the lab's R&D way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged, which is standard compliance practice.
evidence_acceptability: A stage-gate compliance sign-off is a common, uncontroversial governance practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires amending stage-gate procedures and adding a Compliance sign-off and a recurring review, which are some process changes but reasonably feasible and not costly.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by verifying Article 12(2) logging capabilities before release and after modification.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate verifying logging adequacy would help ensure Article 12 compliance, but it checks rather than builds the logging capability and does not itself deliver technical logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Releasing anonymized deployment failure logs as an open benchmark is unusual and shows some imagination, but open datasets from operational data are a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logs into a public research asset and new offering for the AI-safety community, changing the relationship between R&D and logging obligations beyond routine logging practice, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Public release of logged operational data raises confidentiality, privacy, and security concerns, and CC-BY-NC with data from high-risk deployments is somewhat sensitive but not unacceptable if anonymized after ethics review.
evidence_implementability: It requires reliable anonymization, ethics review, schema design, hosting, and legal clearance of deployment data with re-identification risk, which is significant effort but feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses only an implied benefit (external research value from logs) and does not directly address how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not make the lab's systems compliant with Article 12 and only tangentially adapts R&D, so it is unlikely to solve the stated problem.

evidence_originality: A shared compliance pod with decoupled funding is a sensible but fairly expected organizational response, with a mildly interesting funding-line twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new organizational elements (a pod, a budget line) but still treats compliance as a logging-support function rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Creating a compliance team is a normal practice, though reclassifying 15% of earmarked R&D personnel costs to a different budget line may raise funder or accounting concerns, making it somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Staffing three people and reallocating budget lines requires some organizational change and funder negotiation, but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: A dedicated cross-project team to build logging/traceability capability directly addresses how the lab meets the Article 12 logging mandate, though the link runs through an implied organizational mechanism rather than specific logging measures.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared pod would help standardize and speed logging implementation, but it specifies no logging content or technical measures, so it is only a partial solution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with a named steward and release-triggered reviews is a mundane, standard compliance approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A documentation steward and release-triggered review are common governance practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Assigning stewards and linking doc updates to release triggers is a modest process change at low cost, though the 14-day mandatory cycle adds some burden.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets technical documentation upkeep, which Recital 71 links to logging and traceability but which is not the Article 12 automatic-event-logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
