evidence_effectiveness: Version-controlled documentation with review triggers helps demonstrate compliance but does not implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Logging by design / compliance-by-design is a common, expected response and is not particularly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standard and shared middleware but still treats compliance as logging practice, though shifting it earlier into design is a modest stretch.
evidence_acceptability: A mandatory internal engineering standard for logging aligned with Article 12 is a common, lawful, uncontroversial compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It requires building shared middleware and changing the workflow from the first sprint, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by building logging into R&D work.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially meet the logging mandate for prototypes but covers only Article 12(2) and omits the Annex III 3 minimum items and retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating minimal-sufficient logging as a publishable research programme is unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the obligation into a research output and standards-influencing position rather than only a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing preprints and engaging with interpretive guidance is a somewhat unusual yet inoffensive approach, though pursuing 'minimal' logging may raise mild regulator sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two early-career researchers over twelve months using existing pilot systems is a modest, reasonably feasible allocation requiring some changes but no radical resources.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets how to meet the Article 12(2)(a)-(c) logging mandate by determining which events must be logged, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps define and reduce compliance uncertainty but is a research effort on two pilot systems that yields a partial solution, not actual implemented logging across the portfolio, and 'minimal' logging risks under-compliance.

evidence_originality: Merging regulatory documentation with open-science reproducibility is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new template and external partners and reframes compliance as a contribution to scientific infrastructure, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it doesn't change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Aligning compliance documentation with open-science norms is somewhat unusual but offends no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A six-week sprint with existing internal committee and an external working group, piloted on two projects, requires some coordination and changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation requirement from Recital 71, an implied related part of the logging/record-keeping problem, rather than the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: The template addresses Recital 71 technical documentation but does not address the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying privacy-preserving cryptographic or statistical techniques to Article 12(3)(c) match logs is an unusual and interesting angle that goes beyond typical logging-compliance responses, though privacy-preserving logging is not wholly unknown.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (homomorphic tokens, DP noising, threat models) but still treats compliance as a logging-practice question, without changing the lab's R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Seeking to satisfy logging mandates while protecting data privacy and publishing threat models offends no legal or social norms, though the noising approach could raise regulator concerns.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping two architectures and measuring tradeoffs is a reasonably feasible research effort, but homomorphic or DP techniques on biometric match logs are technically difficult and require significant expertise.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified problem, namely meeting Article 12(3)(c) logging without creating a surveillance dataset, which is part of the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would address the privacy tension created by the logging mandate but only for the biometric Annex III 1(a) case, and noising could degrade log fidelity, so it only partially solves the broader logging-mandate problem.

evidence_originality: A log retention and storage cost protocol is a common, mundane administrative response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and IT governance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A retention and storage protocol with encryption, access tiers, DPO consultation and finance validation is a conventional, norm-respecting governance approach.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a protocol using existing IT, finance and cloud contracts requires modest changes and is reasonably feasible at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied problem (managing the storage, security and cost of logs once generated) that relates to the logging mandate but is not the core requirement of enabling automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses only retention, storage cost and access for logs, and does not itself make the systems log events or fulfill the Article 12 content requirements, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware with schema versioning is a standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool and versioned schema but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how the lab relates R&D to compliance, so it is only slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared logging infrastructure is a common, legally compliant engineering approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A shared library integrated into an existing SDK requires moderate engineering work but is reasonably feasible and non-radical, and it reduces per-project effort.
evidence_applicability: The middleware directly implements the Article 12 logging mandate, capturing the Article 12(2) event types and the Annex III 1(a) minimums, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, an automatic logging library embedded in the SDK would satisfy the technical logging requirements, though it does not cover the rest of the compliance burden such as documentation or the appropriateness of logging to each system's purpose.

evidence_originality: Retention, access control, and encryption policies for logs are common and mundane compliance responses, with only a modest GDPR-alignment angle.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard internal compliance policy for log governance that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal governance policies of this kind are conventional and violate no norms, and they explicitly reconcile with GDPR.
evidence_implementability: Drafting an internal policy with retention periods, encryption, and role-based access is low-cost and uses existing compliance office and security tooling.
evidence_applicability: The policy directly addresses how the lab handles logs it must produce and keep under Article 12 and Article 72, which is part of the stated logging-mandate problem, though it covers governance rather than the logging capability itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A retention and access policy helps ensure logs are preserved and producible to authorities, but it does not create the logging capability or the event coverage required, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Design-time logging specifications and documentation templates are standard compliance practice, so the idea is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template and a gate but treats compliance as standard logging documentation, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A mandatory design-stage specification with sign-off is a common governance strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A template-based document completed during design review with a sign-off gate is a modest process addition using existing compliance and project staff, with low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by defining events tied to Article 12(2) and Annex III minimums, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure planning and documentation of logging but does not itself implement automatic logging or ensure it works, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing evaluation harnesses for post-market drift analysis and turning the resulting reports into publications is a somewhat interesting and imaginative angle, though drift monitoring itself is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance outputs into publications and grant narrative, which stretches the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using production log samples for evaluation and publication is a reasonably common and legitimate strategy, though publishing findings from deployed-system data raises mild confidentiality and data-protection concerns.
evidence_implementability: Reusing existing harnesses with 10% compute and a shared analyst is feasible with some changes, but it depends on the middleware from proposal one and on a single analyst handling the reporting.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified part of the stated problem, post-market monitoring under Article 72, which Article 12(2)(b) says logs should facilitate, so the link to the logging mandate is direct but partial.
evidence_effectiveness: Drift reports help with Article 72 post-market monitoring, but the proposal does not itself deliver the core Article 12 logging capability, and it depends on another proposal's middleware, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging library embedded in all projects is a common and expected response to the mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling that treats the mandate as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal compliance library with a ship gate is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK and mandating its integration requires engineering effort and some process changes but is reasonably feasible with standard software practice.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the automatic event-logging requirements of Article 12(1)-(3) for the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable SDK enforced at codebase level would automatically capture the mandated Article 12 events and would largely solve the logging mandate, though it does not cover other Article 12 aspects like appropriateness to intended purpose or retention, so it is reasonable and nearly complete for the logging problem.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a shared longitudinal research corpus is unusual and shows imagination, but it is not wholly unprecedented, since data-sharing and operational telemetry research exist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandated logs into a research resource and a new offering for the community, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing operational logs raises privacy, customer confidentiality, and trade-secret concerns, which may offend sensibilities somewhat, though anonymization and governance mitigate this.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year anonymized corpus with an ingestion and governance pipeline, data-protection compliance and community releases is a significant, costly undertaking, though feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, how to derive value from or adapt R&D around the logging mandate, which relates to the stated problem, but not the compliance requirement directly.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself deliver the logging capability Article 12 requires; it only exploits logs once they exist, so it contributes to the response only partially at best.

evidence_originality: Gap audits and compliance matrices are the common, mundane first step any experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice (gap analysis) that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A gap audit against regulatory requirements is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-week internal sprint using existing observability tools and staff is a low-cost, non-radical change that is easy to carry out.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by identifying which Article 12 fields are missing, though it covers only the assessment step.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by targeting engineering effort, but it only diagnoses gaps and does not itself implement logging, and it focuses on 12(3) which applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered immutable WORM logging with audit-query stress tests is a common, expected compliance engineering response, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working and R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable append-only logs, role-based access, and lifetime retention are standard, norm-compliant strategies that offend no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A three-month spike on WORM storage is reasonably feasible but requires some architectural changes and retention infrastructure for the full operational lifetime.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem by building logging for the four Article 12(3) mandatory fields.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum logging mandate, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and not the broader Article 12(1)-(2) traceability purposes, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing a logging mandate as an epistemological research question about the limits of documenting stochastic systems is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly surprising for a research lab.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and compliance by making the compliance obligation a research question and addressing what the lab researches, with new elements such as publishing community standards.
evidence_acceptability: A published research programme on documentation limits violates no laws or norms, and open publication and case studies are normal academic practice, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: A fundamental research programme with theoretical and empirical papers and open publication needs significant researcher time and uncertain outcomes, making it difficult and resource-intensive when the lab must commit scarce implementation resources.
evidence_applicability: It relates to the stated problem only indirectly via Recital 71's documentation and the idea of informing how internal documentation is written, an implied rather than identified problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, theoretical work on documentation limits would not itself deliver the automatic event logging Article 12 requires, so it only marginally informs documentation rather than solving the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Schema registries and versioned data governance are well-known data engineering practices, so applying them to compliance logs is sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a schema-registry tool and migration tooling but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Avro/Protobuf registries are mature tools, though backfill and migration tooling and cross-team discipline require some changes and effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, log evolution and audit readiness across model iterations, that relates to the logging mandate but is not stated in it.
evidence_effectiveness: Schema versioning keeps historical logs usable over the system lifetime, which helps with Article 12(1) traceability, but it does not decide what to log or cover the Article 12(2) event relevance or the Article 12(3) minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A dedicated log-review or post-market monitoring team is a standard, expected response to Articles 72 and 79 and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds an organizational unit and dashboard but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, leaving R&D ways of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance monitoring unit reviewing logs for post-market surveillance is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Staffing a small permanent cell and building a dashboard and escalation protocol requires some new headcount and tooling but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified purposes in Article 12(2)(a)-(c) of using logs for risk identification and post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with monitoring and risk detection but does not itself ensure the logging mandate is technically met (Art. 12 capabilities), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library integrated from the first commit is a standard, expected response to a logging mandate and is not especially imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling that treats the mandate as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building standardized, version-controlled logging middleware is a common engineering approach that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin library wired into the existing starter template is low-cost and non-radical, though it needs some schema design and backend work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic-logging mandate across the lab's high-risk prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging SDK tied to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) event categories would deliver the core logging capability, but it does not cover retention, Annex III-specific minimums, documentation, or the R&D adaptation side, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating traceability as a scientific axis of architecture design and ablating architectures for log informativeness is unusual and imaginative compared with typical logging-infrastructure responses, though not wholly unprecedented given interpretability research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance-relevant traceability a research objective that shapes what the lab researches, though it stops short of fully redefining the lab's mission.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open research on architecture and compliance is a legitimate scientific activity that offends no norms, though open publication is somewhat uncommon in a compliance context.
evidence_implementability: Controlled ablation studies across architectures require significant compute and researcher effort and uncertain outcomes, but they are feasible for an AI lab with some reallocation of resources.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (designing models that produce better logs) that relates to the stated logging-mandate problem rather than directly stating how to meet the mandate now.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on how architecture affects native log informativeness would help future systems meet Article 12, but it does not itself implement the logging mandate for current systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left logging via a template with pre-wired schemas is a sensible and fairly expected response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tooling element (template module and schemas) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into the development template is a common, norm-compliant engineering strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing internal prototyping framework with a pluggable emitter module is a modest change, though it takes some effort to design schemas and get engineers to adopt them.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building event capture for the Article 12(2) categories into prototypes, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the automatic event logging required by Article 12(1)-(2), but it does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, retention, or the logging of deployed production systems, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a research asset is a somewhat imaginative and relatively unusual framing, but it is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making compliance logs a feed for the science (logging woven into research), which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing logs internally is a sensible practice, but opening streams to researchers raises some data protection and access-control concerns, though anonymisation mitigates this.
evidence_implementability: Building on existing logging infrastructure with schema standardisation in two sprints and a dashboard is reasonably feasible, though cross-project standardisation and anonymisation require some changes.
evidence_applicability: Standardising log schemas for mandated automatic event recording directly addresses the logging mandate, though the research-dataset reuse is an added benefit rather than the compliance requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Standardised schemas and audit-ready logs help meet Article 12, but the proposal does not specify which events (risk situations, post-market monitoring, operation monitoring) are captured, so it only partly solves compliance.

evidence_originality: Lifetime, version-spanning log schemas are a sensible but fairly expected data-engineering response to Article 12(1), showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a unified schema and migration guide but still treats compliance as a logging practice, without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Schema design, retention planning and migration guides are standard engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing object storage and a small team, so it is largely feasible, though maintaining schema versioning across model swaps takes some ongoing effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement of logging over the system lifetime and supporting Article 72 monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A stable cross-version log architecture would help satisfy lifetime logging and post-market monitoring, but it covers storage and schema rather than the full set of required events, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the forward pass as an interpretable-by-construction architecture is unusual and shows imagination, though related to existing interpretability research.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into the science of what the lab researches (architecture design), changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of fully redefining the lab's research agenda.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme on log-emitting architectures is a somewhat unusual but legitimate approach that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Redesigning model architectures so the forward pass emits structured logs, and benchmarking them against standard ones, is a significant, difficult and expensive research effort with uncertain success.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the logging mandate by producing logs intended to satisfy Article 12 while adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: Article 12 requires event logs such as usage periods, reference databases and verifier identities, not internal activations, so this would only partly solve the mandate even if it worked, and it adds speculative research risk.

evidence_originality: Turning a regulatory ambiguity into publishable ML research on modification taxonomies and drift detection is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making regulatory science a research agenda and positioning the lab as a standard-setter, which stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open preprints and engaging regulatory guidance violates no norms, although releasing internal policy thinking publicly may raise mild concerns.
evidence_implementability: Developing and validating formal criteria and detection algorithms is a substantial research effort with uncertain outcomes, though not impossible for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the undefined boundary of substantial modification in Article 12(2)(a), which relates to the logging mandate but is not the logging implementation itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Defining substantial-modification criteria would help the lab decide when logging is triggered, but it does not itself deliver the logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A portfolio-wide logging gap audit feeding a resource reallocation decision is a sensible, fairly expected governance step, with a modestly interesting sunk-cost framing but nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standardized rubric and a reprioritisation matrix, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice exercise, though the option to restart projects hints at influencing what the lab pursues.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and resource reviews are common, uncontroversial management practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two-week gap assessments by project leads and a one-quarter consolidation are low-cost, modest process changes that are readily doable.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of deciding how to allocate R&D resources between retrofitting and restarting under Article 12, which relates directly to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit identifies gaps and prioritises resources but does not itself build logging capability, so it helps only as a partial contribution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging template/SDK is a mundane and expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK) but still treats compliance as standard logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal reusable logging SDK to satisfy Article 12(3) is a common, fully lawful compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers in one sprint extracting hooks from an existing prototype into an SDK is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12(3) logging requirements for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the Article 12(3) fields for biometric systems only, leaving Article 12(1)-(2), other high-risk categories, and non-biometric work unaddressed, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using mandatory lifetime logs as a longitudinal research dataset on model drift is an unusual and imaginative reframing of a compliance duty, though drift monitoring itself is known.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logging a source of scientific output, but it does not change what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing anonymised aggregate findings from biometric system logs is somewhat unusual and raises privacy and deployer-consent sensitivities, but is not offensive.
evidence_implementability: It needs access to logs of deployed biometric systems (likely operated by third parties), multi-year commitment and data protection handling, which is difficult though not impossible, with only one postdoc assigned.
evidence_applicability: It relates to the stated problem through Article 12 logs and 2(a) triggers, but the benefit (a research publication) is an implied outcome rather than meeting the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It yields research value but does not itself meet the logging mandate or adapt the lab's systems to it, so it only partially contributes to solving the problem.

evidence_originality: Monitoring log completeness as an observability metric is a sensible but fairly predictable DevOps application, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a streaming dashboard) but still treats compliance as logging practice, with no change to how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring of log completeness is a sensible practice that offends no norms or sensibilities, though the real-time framing is slightly less standard.
evidence_implementability: Kafka plus Grafana with alert rules is commodity tooling that needs modest setup per pilot, so it is a reasonably feasible measure with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring Article 12 event recording works in production, though it assumes the logging itself already exists.
evidence_effectiveness: The dashboard only verifies that logs are being captured and does not itself create the logging capability, define event content, or cover retention, so it contributes to compliance but is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code and CI testing for logging requirements is a sensible but fairly expected response by experienced engineering teams, so it is interesting rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an automated schema-assertion test gate in CI) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing and blocking issues are common engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding schema-assertion tests to an existing nightly build and issue tracker is low-cost and uses standard tooling, though codifying obligations takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required event categories are emitted.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging capability exists in prototypes, but it only checks schema presence, not log adequacy, retention, Article 12(3) specifics, or production behavior, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory logs as a natural experiment for drift research is an imaginative reframing that few labs would offer, though drift monitoring itself is familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making mandated logs a research platform and a source of new science, directly shaping what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Mining operational logs for peer-reviewed drift research violates no norms, though it raises mild data-protection and customer-confidentiality questions and is somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year programme with a dedicated analytics team and access to deployed-system logs requires significant resourcing and customer data-access arrangements, which is expensive and difficult but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting research value from logging, but does not itself say how to meet the logging mandate, so it relates only indirectly to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It builds on logs but does not ensure that Article 12 requirements are met, so it contributes only as a partial, tangential solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing monitoring infrastructure for compliance is a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: This is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure is a common, sensible strategy that offends no norms, though telemetry repurposed as compliance logs may raise integrity concerns.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing pipelines with a six-week gap analysis and incremental patches is low-cost and non-radical, though it depends on a shared middleware from another proposal and on telemetry being suitable.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by mapping current telemetry to the specific paragraphs of Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Mapping existing telemetry against Article 12(2) and (3) and patching the gaps would plausibly yield compliant logging for the systems covered, but it is only a partial solution because it does not address R&D adaptation, retention, or the Annex III specifics beyond gap filling.

evidence_originality: Building logging into shared tooling as a default is a sensible, commonly expected 'compliance by design' response, not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a default logging middleware in the SDK) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding default logging in engineering tooling is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing experiment-runner with middleware and project templates is a modest change, though it requires some engineering effort and an append-only store.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(1) automatic-recording mandate, which is part of the stated problem of how to meet the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve much of the technical logging requirement for prototypes, but it does not clearly cover Article 12(2) event relevance, Annex III 3(a)-(d) specifics, or retention and deployed systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code and documentation in CI/CD is a fairly well-known MLOps idea, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science workflow rather than treating it as a post-hoc step, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating compliance into engineering workflows is a sensible, norm-respecting approach that offends no sensibilities, though somewhat less common than post-hoc compliance.
evidence_implementability: Adding CI/CD hooks for automatic log and documentation generation requires some pipeline changes and cross-team co-design but uses existing MLOps tooling, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate and technical documentation requirements by automating their production in the pipeline.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help produce logs and documentation, but it does not specify Article 12 event-content requirements (risk situations, post-market monitoring, Annex III specifics), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into existing frameworks is the standard, expected response to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with no change to how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Logging for compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-person cell integrating lightweight middleware on the existing monitoring stack over two sprints is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It does X (native logging of the four mandatory fields) to get Y (compliance with the logging requirement), and Y is directly part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding logging middleware that captures the Article 12(3) fields would directly satisfy the core logging mandate, though it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance or the documentation in Recital 71, so it is reasonable but only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A CI gate that diffs model artifacts and holds deployment on substantial-modification thresholds is an interesting, somewhat imaginative engineering move, but automated compliance gates in CI/CD are a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (CI comparison service) but still treats compliance as a logging and documentation practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated release gates with sign-off are a common, norm-respecting governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a weight/schema/data-lineage diff service within an existing CI runner is reasonably feasible with some engineering effort, though defining and calibrating similarity thresholds for 'substantial modification' is nontrivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified part of the stated problem, recording events relevant to substantial modification under Article 12(2)(a), as a way of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably flag and log modifications and enforce sign-off, but it addresses only the substantial-modification part of Article 12(2)(a) and not the broader logging mandate (runtime event logs, post-market monitoring, Annex III minimums), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A drop-in logging SDK/decorator with CI enforcement is a sensible but very common engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect from AI labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK, CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal tooling and CI checks are standard engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A decorator-based internal package with SQLite/Postgres backends is reasonably feasible, though automatically capturing reference databases, matched inputs and verifier IDs across all pipelines needs some real integration work beyond a one-line change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by recording the specified fields (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would capture the Article 12 event fields automatically and enforce adoption, but it covers only logging mechanics (not retention, Annex III scope relevance, risk-event identification, or documentation), so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning Article 12(2)(a) risk-event identification into a public community benchmark challenge is an unusual, imaginative response that most labs would not give, though benchmarks themselves are familiar in ML.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making the compliance obligation a research agenda and external-facing scientific offering, with new partners and shared yardsticks born from the mandate.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing benchmarks and hosting challenges is a normal, accepted scientific practice, with only minor anonymisation and data-sharing sensitivities for real logs.
evidence_implementability: Curating labelled log sequences, defining metrics, and hosting an annual challenge require substantial ongoing effort and data-privacy work, though they are feasible for a research lab.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem, namely detecting risk situations from logs per Article 12(2)(a), rather than the lab's direct obligation to implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A public benchmark would not by itself make the lab's own systems log the required events or comply with Article 12, so it only contributes partially at best.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance testing in CI is a fairly common and expected response, with only mild interest in applying it to log schemas and replay simulations.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool-based process (CI gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice, without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI are a common engineering strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a validation stage to an existing CI pipeline with schema validators and replay simulations is a modest, non-radical change using standard tooling, though writing the Article 12 checks takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate by verifying that emitted logs satisfy Article 12 before promotion, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure log schema, timestamp, and retention compliance but does not itself design the logging capability or cover substantive requirements such as the Article 12(2) event relevance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware/SDK built into the default inference pipeline is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK with pluggable emitters) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building internal logging infrastructure for compliance is a standard, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal SDK and integrating it into the standard inference pipeline requires some engineering effort and changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by making automatic event recording the default for prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic logging for prototypes, but it is only a partial solution as it does not specify which events satisfy Article 12(2) purposes, retention, or the Annex III-specific minimums, nor does it cover non-prototype systems.

evidence_originality: CI/CD-triggered documentation updates and a document-control registry are sensible but a fairly expected compliance-tooling response, showing only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and pipeline integration but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A versioned documentation and log registry with auditable trails violates no norms and is a conventional compliance approach.
evidence_implementability: Building a CI/CD-linked document-control pipeline with alerts and retention logic requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: The registry directly targets the stated problem of meeting logging and record-keeping duties, including keeping documentation current per Recital 71 and log retention tied to Article 26(5).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would substantially deliver up-to-date documentation and managed log retention, but it does not itself specify event-logging capabilities required by Article 12(2)-(3), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing telemetry and observability tools for compliance logging is an expected, mundane response that many labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice, with a reusable middleware and inherited defaults that leave the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing observability infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, sensible engineering strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Wrapping existing OpenTelemetry collectors with schema modules needs some platform-team work and changes but is reasonably feasible and builds on deployed tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by mapping logs to the 12(2)(a)-(c) event categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide automatic event logging by default, but it addresses only the logging mandate and leaves out the Annex III specifics, log retention and the documentation obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using mandated logs as a longitudinal research dataset for drift is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though drift monitoring from production logs is a known concept.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logs into a research asset and a new research program, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than treating logging as mere practice.
evidence_acceptability: Analyzing compliance logs for drift monitoring is a legitimate, norm-consistent use, though repurposing logs for research raises mild data-governance questions that do not offend sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a shared ingestion layer, schema normalization across projects, and a dedicated research node with long-horizon data, which is a significant and costly effort though feasible.
evidence_applicability: The idea uses Article 12 logs for drift detection and post-market monitoring, which relates to the mandate only implicitly, since the stated problem is how to meet the logging mandate or adapt R&D, and the research output is an implied benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself ensure the lab's logs meet Article 12 requirements and yields a research dataset, so it contributes only partially to the compliance problem, mainly supporting post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: Log-based monitoring dashboards are a fairly expected response to the logging mandate, with the compliance-to-capability framing being interesting but not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (analytics dashboard) and reframes compliance as an operational capability, but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A read-only analytics dashboard over compliance logs is a legitimate, uncontroversial business practice that violates no norms, though repurposing it as a funding narrative is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing visualisation stack and needs one postdoc to build a read-only panel, so it is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, making logs useful for the Article 72 and 26(5) purposes that Article 12 logging is meant to serve, which relates to but is not the stated logging-mandate problem itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A dashboard built on top of the logs helps with post-market monitoring and operation monitoring, but it does not itself deliver the logging mandate (event recording, minimum Annex III fields), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using a paying client pilot to fund and generate a reusable compliance architecture is somewhat unusual and shows some business imagination, though not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a reusable template and a client-funded pilot with retained IP, which slightly changes how compliance cost is handled, but it still treats compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Paid pilots with bank partners and retained IP are common business strategies, though a bank handling biometric logs raises some data-protection considerations that are manageable.
evidence_implementability: It reuses existing registry and alerting tools with only a new capture schema and verifier-identity module, and partner funding covers engineering, though a six-month bank pilot requires some coordination and change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X, the Article 12(3) logging stack, to get compliance logging for an Annex III 1(a) system).
evidence_effectiveness: Retrofitting the biometric model to satisfy all four Article 12(3) minimum logging items and making it reusable would, if done, solve the core logging-mandate problem for that system and offer a template for others, though it covers only one system and Article 12(1)-(2) generalization is assumed.

evidence_originality: Automated testing of log coverage against regulatory categories is a sensible but fairly expected idea with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a log-conformance harness) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A QA conformance-testing tool is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A Python harness built on the existing observability stack and run nightly in staging requires only modest, non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need to confirm that Article 12(2) event categories are captured, which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify log coverage but does not itself implement logging or address the full mandate, so it only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance logging in project templates via an SDK is a fairly common, expected response, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool and schema but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only moving it earlier in the workflow without changing R&D's relationship to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory shared libraries in internal templates are a common engineering practice and offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing OpenTelemetry instrumentation and the internal template repo, so a shared library as a default scaffold dependency is a modest, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing Article 12(3) fields in every prototype.
evidence_effectiveness: It would reliably produce the required logs in prototypes, but it covers mainly Article 12(3) fields and prototypes, not the full compliance picture (retention, documentation, Article 12(2) event relevance, production systems), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A pre-design compliance gate with a checklist and sign-off is a common, expected governance response to a regulatory mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a standard review process and checklist but treats compliance as ordinary logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal gating and sign-off procedures are common business practice and offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist and sign-off requirement is cheap and easy to put in place, though blocking resource allocation adds some process friction.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate by catching Article 12(2) gaps before development begins.
evidence_effectiveness: A checklist gate would help ensure logging is considered early, but it does not itself build logging capabilities, cover Article 12(3) specifics, or ensure actual implementation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating the regulatory definition of risk-relevant events as a publishable theoretical research topic is unusual and shows some imagination, though it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a research-output angle and positions compliance as a source of scientific contribution, shifting the relationship between R&D and compliance somewhat, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Academic taxonomy work and validation on own deployments violate no norms or sensibilities, though it is somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated research effort with literature synthesis and formal methods expertise and does not deliver near-term compliance, making it a significant commitment of scarce resources.
evidence_applicability: Defining what counts as a risk-relevant event directly addresses the Article 12(2)(a) logging requirement, but it is an implied step toward meeting the logging mandate rather than the logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy would help decide what to log but is only a partial solution since it produces no logging capability, and the publishable theory may not yield operational specifications.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library baked into a base image is a sensible but fairly expected response; the compliance-by-default framing adds mild interest without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Shared compliance middleware and base-image enforcement is a common engineering practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a thin SDK on top of already-captured pipeline metadata and pinning it in a base Docker image is a modest engineering change with low cost and no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem, namely how to meet the logging mandate, by emitting the specific fields named in Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: A default-on logging SDK would directly satisfy the Article 12(1) automatic recording mandate and the Article 12(3) minimum fields for prototypes, but it does not cover the broader R&D adaptation or the Article 12(2) relevance-based event selection, so it is largely but not fully a solution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: A pre-deployment compliance review gate with an SOP and trained reviewers is a very common, expected response to a regulatory logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a checkpoint to existing project management but leaves R&D practice and the treatment of compliance as a standard logging/QA process unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal review gate violates no legal, social, or business norms and is a conventional governance strategy.
evidence_implementability: It needs only an SOP, two trained reviewers, and a workflow step in an existing tool, which is a low-cost, non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring systems meet Article 12 logging requirements before reaching clients.
evidence_effectiveness: The gate verifies logging coverage before deployment but does not itself build the logging capability or cover Article 12(1) and 12(3) or ongoing operation, so it contributes only partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Log retention and access-control policies with DPO involvement are common and mundane responses to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and data-governance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retention policies, access controls, and pseudonymisation are standard, widely accepted data-governance practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: An SOP co-authored with the DPO plus role-based access on an existing log store is a routine, low-cost change that needs no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses a stated mandate element, the Article 12(3)(d) verifier-identification logs, by governing how they are stored and accessed.
evidence_effectiveness: It handles privacy and access for one logging item but does not deliver the logging capability itself or cover Article 12(1)-(2) traceability, and it applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Framing Article 12 logging as an information-theoretic minimum-sufficient-event problem with entropy and causal-inference metrics is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly unprecedented or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (formal criteria, metrics) and turns compliance into a research program on auditability science, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations by weaving it into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Data minimization and traceability research offers no offense to legal or social norms, and aligns with regulators' interests, though it is a somewhat uncommon response.
evidence_implementability: Formalizing sufficient traceability and developing new metrics is a research effort with uncertain outcomes that requires significant expertise and time, making it difficult but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets what events must be logged to meet Article 12 and tests against the Annex III 1(a) list, which relates directly to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A research program will not by itself deliver compliant logging on a deadline and the formal criterion may not match legal requirements, so it only partially contributes to the solution.

evidence_originality: Feasibility and overhead studies for logging are a mundane, expected response to such a mandate, with nothing surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging engineering practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal engineering feasibility study with board sign-off is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs only two engineers for three months and load-test instrumentation, which is a reasonably feasible, modest change, though simulating five-year horizons takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (whether lifetime logging is viable at scale) that relates to meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, rather than directly delivering the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It produces measurements to inform architecture but does not itself implement logging or deliver compliance, so it contributes only partially to meeting the mandate; the lab needs committed implementation, not exploration.

evidence_originality: Open shared logging schemas are a reasonably known idea, though framing the community-contributed schema versions as a longitudinal dataset on operationalizing traceability adds some imaginative interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (public registry, open agent, community contributions) and partly reframes compliance as a shared public good, but still centers on logging practice and does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing compliance tooling and engaging the scientific panel violates no norms and is a well-regarded, legally unproblematic approach.
evidence_implementability: Three FTEs for one quarter is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment using standard tools like JSON-Schema, protobuf and Python, requiring no radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the logging mandate by building schemas and an agent that emit logs covering Article 12(3) fields, though much of its stated benefit (community impact, goodwill) targets other labs rather than the lab's own compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema registry and logging agent would help meet the logging requirement but only partially, since it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or integration with the lab's actual systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance checks in CI are a fairly familiar DevOps idea applied to logging, so it is interesting but not surprising or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a CI merge gate with contract tests) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated build gates are a common engineering practice that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing pytest infrastructure and containers, so it needs some new test-writing and sandbox setup but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that logs cover the Article 12(2) categories.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would reliably verify that prototypes emit required event types, but it covers only logging capability checks and not the wider compliance needs such as retention, documentation or the Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Publishing an open living-documentation standard is interesting and somewhat unusual for a lab, but documentation standards and model-card-like efforts are fairly familiar, so it shows only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (an open standard, versioning methodology, tooling) but still treats compliance as documentation practice rather than changing how R&D relates to obligations, though open release creates a modest new offering.
evidence_acceptability: Open standards and documentation work violate no legal or social norms, though open-licensing may raise some IP concerns, it is a common governance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Requires a working group, three pilots, and tooling development, which is a reasonable but non-trivial resource commitment, so some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It addresses technical documentation under Recital 71, which is related to the regulation but not the Article 12 automatic logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with documentation upkeep but does not implement automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial contribution, and much effort goes to scholarly positioning rather than compliance.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing monitoring infrastructure for compliance logging is a sensible and fairly common response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a thin annotation layer but still treats compliance as logging practice, reusing existing dashboards without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Extending existing tooling for regulatory logging is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building on existing infrastructure with a thin annotation layer in six weeks is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the Article 12(3) logging requirements, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Annotating drift telemetry may not capture Article 12(3) items like reference databases, matched inputs, or verifier identities, and it covers only the Annex III 1(a) minimum, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reconciling logging with privacy via cryptographic techniques is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is a fairly expected research direction.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (privacy techniques, formal guarantees) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though it does tie R&D output to compliance through publication.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging research is a legitimate, norm-respecting approach, though somewhat unusual in how it treats raw biometric inputs under a logging mandate, and it needs care to stay consistent with Article 12(3)(c).
evidence_implementability: Developing and prototyping cryptographic and differential-privacy schemes is a research programme that needs significant expertise and effort, and the stated problem needs committed implementation resources rather than exploration.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(3) logging fields for biometric systems, an identified part of the stated problem, though it is narrow in scope.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the 3(c) logging requirement while reducing data-minimisation conflict, but it covers only the biometric subset and leaves general logging under Article 12(1)-(2) unaddressed, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated conformance testing in CI is an interesting and sensible application, but it is a fairly expected DevOps-style response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a CI contract-test gate) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI gates are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding contract tests to an existing CI/CD pipeline is a reasonably feasible, non-radical change, though defining schemas and writing tests for each system takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by checking that required event classes are emitted.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify that systems emit required log events, which helps, but it does not address retention, log content quality in production, or the other obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered log storage with schema versioning for lifetime retention is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure practice that leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Retaining and querying logs with tiered storage is a conventional strategy that violates no legal or social norms, though long retention raises minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: A small team prototyping an internal microservice using established storage tiering and schema versioning is reasonably feasible, with moderate effort for stress testing at scale.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 lifetime logging and traceability mandate by making logs durable and queryable.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with retention and queryability over the lifetime, but it does not address which events to log, the Annex III minimums, or the broader R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware/SDK is a common, expected response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane rather than imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging SDK is a new tool, but it still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Building standard compliance tooling to avoid penalties violates no norms or sensibilities and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building and integrating an SDK across inference pipelines and validating schemas per Annex III category requires real platform engineering effort, but it is reasonably feasible and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the specific required fields (do X to get compliant logs).
evidence_effectiveness: A shared layer that auto-captures Article 12(2) and paragraph-3 events would largely satisfy the logging mandate if built, though it ignores broader issues such as retention and documentation, so it is reasonable and close to a full solution for the logging requirement.

evidence_originality: A middleware logging collector with a reusable component framing is a common, expected response to this mandate with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice implemented as a software component, leaving the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building a logging microservice to satisfy a legal requirement is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy, though biometric log data raises ordinary privacy handling concerns.
evidence_implementability: An OpenTelemetry-compatible collector with pluggable storage prototyped in two sprints and integrated into an existing pipeline is a modest, reasonably feasible engineering effort with some integration changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified requirement of meeting the paragraph 3 logging mandate, which is part of the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, the module would capture exactly the four Article 12(3) minimum logging items (use period, reference database, matched input, verifier identity), solving the core logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems, though not Article 12(1)-(2) general logging for other systems.

evidence_originality: Standardising automatic logging and auditing against Article 12 is the obvious, expected response to this mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice with a unified schema and a team, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging is a common, legally expected strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Retrofitting a unified logging schema across all high-risk systems with a dedicated cell is a significant but reasonably feasible engineering effort using known techniques, requiring some changes rather than radical ones.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the Article 12 logging capabilities.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, auditing against Article 12(2)-(3) and embedding logs would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address broader documentation or R&D adaptation, so it is solid but arguably not the complete solution.

evidence_originality: A pre-development compliance gate at project intake is a common, sensible design-for-compliance approach that experienced evaluators would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a procedural gate and logging-spec document to existing stage-gate workflow but still treats compliance as logging practice, with no change to how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate compliance checkpoints are a standard governance practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It slots into an existing stage-gate workflow with a small three-person panel, requiring only modest process change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by requiring specs that satisfy 12(2)(a)-(c) before building.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is designed in early but only specifies and reviews logging rather than implementing it, covering only a partial solution (and not the Article 12(3) specifics or actual log operation).

evidence_originality: Logging middleware with CI/CD gating is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, merely automated within existing engineering workflows, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance gates in engineering pipelines is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A reusable logging middleware wired into CI/CD is a standard engineering effort requiring some process changes but nothing radical or prohibitively costly.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (embed automatic logging via middleware) to get Y (Article 12 compliance), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Default logging fields mirroring Article 12(3) enforced before staging would address the logging mandate substantially, though it does not cover the broader Article 12(2) event-relevance judgments or R&D adaptation, so it is largely but not wholly a solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into the shared ML framework so every model inherits compliance is a sensible and fairly common engineering response, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a framework-level telemetry layer as a new element, but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working largely unchanged, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in infrastructure is a common, legally and socially unobjectionable strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two senior engineers for one quarter, middleware on an existing Kafka bus, and no new procurement make this reasonably feasible, though refactoring a core framework involves some real change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically recording events including input data, reference database, and verifier IDs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic event logging and inherit compliance for new models, but it only partially covers Article 12 aspects such as risk-relevant event selection, retention, and legacy systems, plus the broader R&D adaptation question.

evidence_originality: Templated event-schema specs that generate validation code are a sensible, somewhat unusual formalization, but they are not especially surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (per-class playbooks, living YAML specs that auto-generate validation code) but still treats compliance as a logging design practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common engineering-documentation approach that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs some upfront effort to author playbooks per system class and a tooling pipeline for code generation, but it fits into the existing design phase and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by defining which events to log and mapping them to 12(2)(a)-(c).
evidence_effectiveness: It helps decide what to log and enforces schema consistency, but it does not itself cover the logging infrastructure, retention, or the Annex III 1(a) minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-cost scoring in project intake is a fairly mundane, expected governance response, with modest interest in tying it to research selection.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (intake gate) but still treats compliance as a logging-effort cost to be budgeted, though it does somewhat influence what research gets funded.
evidence_acceptability: Adding a cost-estimation criterion to an internal prioritization committee is a common governance practice that offends no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: It only requires a template and an added committee criterion, which is a low-cost, non-radical change, though estimating Article 12 effort takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, that compliance burden consumes engineering capacity and should shape R&D choices, which relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not make any system log anything or satisfy Article 12; it only helps manage resource planning, so it is at best a partial contribution and arguably unlikely to solve the logging mandate itself.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging as a design standard with a sprint gate is a very common and expected response to this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice with a process gate, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged and treating compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance gate in development is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a standardized logging module and a sprint-review gate is a non-radical change, though it requires some engineering effort and coordination with the compliance team.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building a standard logging module and verifying it against Article 12(2)(a)-(c).
