evidence_originality: Applying chaos-engineering and pen-test methods to logging is a sensible but fairly expected security-minded response, with only modest imaginative framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (adversarial testing, an external review) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving R&D's relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Testing log integrity with QA fault injection and an external penetration review is a legitimate, norm-respecting security practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Automated fault-injection each sprint plus an annual external review requires some new tooling, a QA cell, and recurring cost, but it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, that logs must be reliable over the system's lifetime, which relates to the logging mandate though Article 12 does not explicitly require tamper-resistance testing.
evidence_effectiveness: It would strengthen log integrity and evidentiary value but does not address deciding what to log, Article 12(2) event relevance, or the full logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware is the standard, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working and relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared logging infrastructure on an existing MLOps stack is a common, norm-respecting compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building an adapter on the existing stack is a reasonably feasible measure with some changes, though schema design for Annex III fields and retrofitting across systems takes real effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal does X (embedded logging middleware) to get Y (Article 12-compliant automatic event logs), and Y is directly the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared middleware that automatically captures logs covering Art. 12(2)(a)-(c) and the paragraph 3 minimum fields would, if built, address the core logging mandate, though it does not cover documentation or R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but not fully complete solution.

evidence_originality: Folding discounted lifetime compliance costs into project ranking is unusual and shows some imagination, though NPV-style cost budgeting is a familiar tool.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making lifetime logging cost a criterion for which research projects get funded, which goes beyond logging practice but stops short of changing what the lab researches fundamentally.
evidence_acceptability: Cost-aware portfolio scoring is a common management strategy that violates no norms, though researchers may dislike penalizing exciting projects.
evidence_implementability: Adding a line item and a modified NPV formula to the grants process is a modest process change, though estimating lifetime logging costs reliably requires some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how the logging mandate's ongoing costs affect R&D decisions, which relates to the stated problem of adapting R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab plan for and budget the logging burden, but it does not itself make any system meet Article 12's logging requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware by default is a standard, expected response to a logging mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (SDK) but treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though built into scaffolds.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging library is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A thin SDK shipped as a default dependency in project scaffolds is a modest engineering effort requiring some changes but no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate across the lab's high-risk prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: It would deliver automatic event recording but does not cover Article 12(3) specifics, log content relevance, retention, or documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a client and regulator facing transparency product is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though dashboards over logs are not entirely unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates a new offering born from compliance, which changes the relationship between the lab's work and its compliance obligations without altering what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Offering role-based audit access to clients and regulators is a transparent, norm-respecting strategy, though exposing verification-person identifiers raises some data-protection considerations that need handling.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a new web interface with role-based access and integration with the logging infrastructure, which is a reasonable but non-trivial product effort that depends on another proposal's infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses logging and traceability obligations by exposing logs, verification-person identifiers and post-market monitoring data, though it is a downstream reporting layer rather than the core logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A reporting interface built on existing logging infrastructure helps with transparency and compliance posture but does not itself meet the Article 12 logging requirement, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging SDK/sidecar with a configurable schema is a sensible and very common engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool (SDK/sidecar with YAML config) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal compliance logging platform violates no norms and is a standard, uncontroversial business strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over six weeks on the existing serving stack with a validation plan on three prototypes is a modest, low-cost, non-radical effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, including the Annex III 1(a) fields, by providing automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the 'technically allow' logging requirement across prototypes but does not cover traceability design choices, retention, or Article 12(2) event relevance judgments per system, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Defining relevant events via a taxonomy of early-warning indicators is a sensible and fairly expected response, with some interest but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a research taxonomy as a new element but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the lab's R&D relationship to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A research effort to define loggable risk events from public incident data and in-house testing violates no legal or social norms and is a sensible, common-sounding compliance-supporting activity.
evidence_implementability: Surveying incident reports, building a taxonomy, and validating on in-house adversarial suites requires real research effort and a possibly sparse EU database, so it is feasible but demands some significant work and is open-ended.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of what events to log under Article 12(2)(a), which relates to the logging mandate but is only one sub-part and framed as scientific investigation rather than a compliance measure.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy of risk-signal events would help specify what to log but does not itself implement logging or cover 12(2)(b),(c) or retention, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Unifying compliance logs with research reproducibility records is a sensible and somewhat imaginative idea, but not highly surprising or unique.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves compliance logging into the research workflow by unifying it with reproducibility metadata, which changes how R&D relates to compliance, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing logging infrastructure and auditing against notified-body expectations offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires redesigning pipelines and building a common ontology mapped to notebooks and version control, which is a significant but feasible effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by mapping the Article 12(3) fields into the lab's existing systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet logging requirements and cut duplicate effort, but it leaves open questions on system-level event logging, post-market monitoring, and retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-instrumenting logging wrappers are a familiar approach that many labs would propose, with nothing particularly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard logging tool that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves R&D relationships unchanged, though it adds a new tooling element.
evidence_acceptability: Automated logging middleware is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin decorator library with Kafka or SQLite sinks, prototyped in four weeks on two model lines, is a non-radical, low-cost change using standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by automatically recording start/end times, data references, and match records named in Article 12(3).
evidence_effectiveness: It would generate the automatic event logs Article 12 requires, but it does not address which events matter for risk, post-market monitoring, or retention, nor the documentation and human-verification identity items, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Consolidating documents to reduce overhead is a common, mundane response that evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance-documentation streamlining that leaves the lab's way of working and the R&D-compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Merging documentation sets into one technical file is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A single template drafted by the quality lead and piloted on two projects before rollout is a modest, non-radical change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses how to organize record-keeping and documentation to meet the mandate, which relates directly to the stated problem, though it centers on technical documentation rather than the automatic event logging that Article 12 actually requires.
evidence_effectiveness: Consolidating documentation helps with the technical-file side of compliance but does not implement automatic event logs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Retrofitting existing systems to protect sunk costs is a common, mundane compliance response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as a logging-infrastructure upgrade and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged, so it preserves the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Retrofitting rather than rebuilding is a common, prudent business strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Deploying agents on existing hardware after a two-week gap analysis is a reasonably feasible, low-cost measure, though retrofitting diverse pipelines requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by retrofitting existing infrastructure to emit compliant logs.
evidence_effectiveness: Gap analysis plus lightweight logging agents on existing nodes would plausibly deliver Article 12 automatic event logging, but it says little about the specific content requirements (risk situations, post-market monitoring, Annex III minimums) so it is a substantial but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: A public lifetime logging-fidelity benchmark is an unusual and interesting idea with some imagination, though benchmark proposals are a familiar research form and it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates new partners and an open-science offering born from compliance, which changes how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations, but it stops short of redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks, university collaboration and peer-reviewed publication are norm-respecting academic practices, with only mild uncommonness in tying them to regulatory compliance.
evidence_implementability: Building a multi-year simulation scenario library with two university partners and peer-reviewed publication requires substantial effort and coordination, but it is feasible and does not demand radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, validating logging capability and post-market monitorability, which relates to the mandate but is not a direct response to the lab's need to implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark would help evaluate logging quality but does not itself make the lab's own systems compliant with Article 12, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Treating regulatory logging as a scientific research question with longitudinal studies is uncommon and imaginative, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance logging a research subject that feeds back into the lab's science and publications, which is paradigm stretching and arguably extends to what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open publication and research on one's own deployments are broadly accepted norms, with only minor concerns about disclosing sensitive information.
evidence_implementability: Longitudinal studies on live deployments, with varied logging granularities and peer-reviewed publication, take significant time and resources and have uncertain outcomes, which makes them difficult and unlike committing to a concrete implementation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely how to define 'appropriate to intended purpose' traceability, which relates to the logging mandate but is not the direct act of meeting it.
evidence_effectiveness: A research programme on which variables to log would inform a better logging design but would not itself deliver the Article 12 logging capability, so it is only a partial contribution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Pluggable logging middleware is a fairly expected response; the open-source goodwill angle adds mild interest but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (an SDK and open-sourcing) but still treats compliance as logging practice separated from the science, explicitly decoupling it.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal logging SDK and open-sourcing it is a fairly common, norm-respecting strategy, though open-sourcing compliance tooling is slightly uncommon and raises no sensibility concerns.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a decorator-based SDK in one sprint that writes to existing storage is low-cost and non-radical, though integrating across varied pipelines needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X to get automatic Article 12 logs) while minimizing R&D disruption.
evidence_effectiveness: It would handle automatic event recording and capture Article 12 fields, but it does not address the full mandate such as risk-relevant event identification, retention, or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating logging fields as first-class data objects in a reusable pattern is a sensible idea but a fairly expected response to the mandate, showing only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an architecture pattern and reference implementation) and moves compliance earlier into design, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building provenance and logging into architecture is a conventional, norm-compliant engineering approach with no legal or social concerns.
evidence_implementability: A two-week spike by one engineer on an existing prototype producing a reference schema is modest, though retrofitting provenance through every pipeline stage may take more work.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(3) logging fields for Annex III 1(a) biometric systems (reference database, matched inputs, verifier ID), which are part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the specific 12(3) minimums for biometric prototypes, but it omits the period-of-use logging explicitly and the general Article 12(2) event logging and other lifecycle documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Optimizing logging overhead as a research topic is a somewhat interesting and plausible response, but not especially rare or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element, an internal research track, but still treats compliance as logging practice (optimizing logging overhead) rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal research on efficient logging offends no norms, though testing sampling in place of full-fidelity logging carries mild legal sensitivity.
evidence_implementability: One postdoc and one engineer for six months is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment using existing models, requiring only some resource reallocation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the overhead cost of meeting the logging mandate, which relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: A six-month benchmarking study of sampling versus full logging informs design but does not itself implement Article 12 logging, and sampling may even conflict with the requirement to record events automatically, so it is at most a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance as a competitive differentiator is a recognized business strategy, so it is somewhat unusual for an R&D lab's response to logging and shows some imagination without being surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and the lab's offerings by turning compliance into a product and new client-facing offerings, which is paradigm stretching but does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Marketing compliance features and publishing whitepapers are common business strategies that violate no norms, provided claims of exceeding thresholds are accurate.
evidence_implementability: It requires building dashboards, exportable audit logs, and coordinating commercial and compliance teams, which means some changes and moderate effort but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the logging mandate only indirectly by commercializing logging outputs, so it solves an implied problem (monetizing compliance) related to but not the core of how to meet Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: It assumes logging infrastructure already exists and would help with exportable logs and dashboards, but it does not itself ensure the system meets the Article 12 recording requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging library with versioned schemas is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK with versioned schemas) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library is a common engineering strategy that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers building a thin decorator/middleware SDK in three sprints is a low-cost, non-radical change, though it must be retrofitted onto all pipelines.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing events, timestamps, reference database pointers, and verifier hooks.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would reasonably deliver the technical logging capabilities across pipelines, but it covers only the technical capture and not retention, appropriateness to purpose, or broader compliance, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stage-gate compliance checklists are a very common and expected response, so the idea is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance checkpoint that treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A sign-off checkpoint in an existing review board process is a common governance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It adds a checklist and two staff to an existing process, which is a non-radical, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by verifying that required log fields are captured and retained.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate verifying log completeness would help ensure Article 12 compliance before release, but it covers only part of the mandate (it checks the 12(3) fields, which apply to Annex III 1(a) systems only, and does not build the logging or address 12(2) or R&D adaptation).

evidence_originality: Logging by design with a design-review gate is a common, expected response to Article 12 and is not surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A design-gate checkpoint is a new process element, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, so it is at most slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory design-stage requirements and review gates are standard governance practice and offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a logging requirement and a design-review gate to existing engineering and compliance processes is a non-radical change that can be done at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by ensuring automatic recording and the Annex III minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: Building in logging fields from the start would largely satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate, though it only covers the logging side and not the other adaptation questions such as R&D implications or the broader obligations in Article 12(2).

evidence_originality: A shared logging service reused across projects is a common, mundane engineering response that experienced evaluators would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A centralized logging middleware is a standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged, though it consolidates the tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging infrastructure is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing monitoring stack with two engineers over eighteen months, which is reasonably feasible with some changes to build integration.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate by providing automatic event capture, lifetime storage and retrieval with Article 12(2) schemas.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the logging capability but does not cover the Annex III 12(3) specific fields explicitly or the R&D adaptation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Efficient low-overhead logging architectures are an expected response, though comparing shadow-model and post-hoc reconstruction approaches adds some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (architecture prototypes, benchmarks) but still treats compliance as a logging engineering practice, with only a mild nod to publishable research.
evidence_acceptability: Engineering compliance logging and publishing results is a common, norm-compliant strategy, though shadow-model logging may raise some privacy questions for biometric data.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping and benchmarking three architectures across deployed high-risk systems requires significant engineering effort and compute, and reconstruction or shadow-model approaches are difficult, but it is feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, including the 12(3) minimum requirements, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Benchmarking three architectures is a research and prototyping exercise that would inform a compliant logging design but does not itself deliver compliant logging across deployed systems, and the 12(3) scope covers only biometric use cases, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log retention and readability testing is a fairly expected response, though the time-travel replay framing adds slight interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a testing protocol but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Testing log durability is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A CI job and quarterly replay tests are standard engineering practice requiring modest additional effort and no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of logs remaining valid across the system lifetime, which relates directly to Article 12's lifetime recording requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logs remain usable over the lifetime but covers only one aspect of the logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open standards publication as compliance positioning is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but industry-led specifications are a known approach and not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a public offering and competitive differentiator, changing the relationship between the lab and its obligations (new partners and reputation born from compliance), which is paradigm stretching, though not breaking what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open specification and engaging regulators is a somewhat unusual but entirely inoffensive strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A small team drafting a specification over two quarters, with partner feedback, open licensing and a maintenance forum, requires some new effort and resources but is reasonably feasible given the logging architecture already exists internally.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (positioning and standardizing logging practice) related to the logging mandate rather than the identified need to implement compliant logging directly.
evidence_effectiveness: The specification would not itself make the lab's systems meet Article 12 requirements; it supports reputation and market position, so it contributes only partially to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code with CI gates and checklist sign-offs is a fairly common, sensible approach that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a docs-as-code process with CI gating but still treats compliance as a standard record-keeping practice, though it does tie documentation into the engineering workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Sign-offs, checklists and CI gating are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing Git and CI/CD infrastructure plus a one-page checklist, so it is easy and low cost to implement.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (documentation and traceability from Recital 71) rather than the stated logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Versioned technical documentation addresses Recital 71's documentation duties but does not implement the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Release gates and compliance checklists are a standard, mundane response to a regulatory mandate and show little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A pre-release compliance gate is a common, norm-conforming strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A one-page checklist, two trained reviewers, and a blocking step in the existing release workflow is a low-cost, non-radical change that can be done within a month.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required log fields exist before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: It checks that logging is present and documented but does not build the logging capability or ensure the logs are adequate over the system lifetime, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a longitudinal research dataset for drift study is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in CI/CD are a fairly familiar DevOps idea that an experienced evaluator would expect, though applying it to Article 12 log fields is moderately interesting.

evidence_originality: Building a logging pipeline for compliance is an expected response, and open-sourcing it as a reference implementation is a mildly interesting twist but not ingenious or surprising.

evidence_originality: Treating logging as an architectural variable in matched-pair training experiments is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly surprising.

evidence_originality: Treating technical documentation as a living artefact with CI/CD gating and stewards is a common, mundane compliance practice that experienced evaluators would expect from most labs.

evidence_originality: Performance-overhead profiling of logging with an open-source schema library is a sensible, somewhat expected research framing with modest imagination.

evidence_originality: Automated CI tests that assert log fields are populated is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.

evidence_originality: Repurposing compliance logs as a longitudinal science dataset on deployed-AI drift is an unusual and imaginative reframing, though drift monitoring itself is known.

evidence_originality: Instrumenting an experiment tracker with provenance metadata and auto-generating compliance documents is a fairly expected MLOps response, though the integration of research runs with Article 12 mapping is somewhat interesting.

evidence_originality: Framework-level logging hooks with tensor provenance is an interesting and somewhat imaginative engineering take, but logging wrappers and provenance tools are a fairly expected lab response to this mandate.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware with a design-gate mandate is a common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.

evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy Article 12(3) logging content while resolving the GDPR tension, but it targets only the biometric Annex III 1(a) subset and the generic Article 12(1)-(2) logging mandate for other systems is left unaddressed, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared open benchmark of risk-relevant event taxonomies is an uncommon and interesting response that shows imagination, though it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an open annotated benchmark built with external deployment partners) and turns compliance into a research and community offering, but it still centers on defining what to log, so it stretches the paradigm only moderately.
evidence_acceptability: Open research collaboration with deployment sites and open licensing is socially and legally acceptable, though sharing operation traces from biometric and critical-infrastructure systems raises some privacy and confidentiality sensitivities.
evidence_implementability: Collecting six months of traces from two Annex III sites, annotating them with multiple annotators, and releasing them openly requires significant partnership, data-access, legal and annotation effort that is expensive and difficult but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified sub-problem directly related to the mandate, namely knowing which events Article 12(2) requires to be logged, though it targets the field rather than the lab's own logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help the lab and others define relevant events but does not itself implement logging capability or satisfy the lab's obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandated log fields as first-class architectural objects and testing their accuracy and latency cost across independent labs is interesting and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging part of the science and turning a compliance constraint into publishable work, which is paradigm stretching, though it does not change what the lab researches at large.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a reference implementation and running partner-lab verification is somewhat unusual but offends no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs benchmark design, an open-source implementation, and coordination of three partner labs, which is significant effort but feasible, though it is a research programme and not a quick compliance fix.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the specific Article 12(3) logging fields (reference database, matched inputs, session times, verifier identity).
evidence_effectiveness: Designing the four Annex III 1(a) log fields as core architecture would meet the Article 12(3) mandate for biometric systems, but it covers only that system category and is framed as a research programme rather than a full compliance response, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a cross-organization open scientific corpus of AI failure taxonomies is unusual and imaginative, though similar incident-database ideas exist, so it is not entirely unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logs a public scientific resource and creating new consortium partnerships, going beyond logging practice, and it partly addresses what the lab researches (failure science).
evidence_acceptability: Sharing anonymised operational logs raises confidentiality, data-protection, and competitive concerns for deployers, but the approach is collaborative and legally pursuable, so it is somewhat unusual without offending sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires a consortium, data-sharing agreements across deployers, privacy-preserving schema design, and ongoing publication, which is a significant, expensive, and difficult undertaking though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making use of Article 12 logs for risk identification and post-market monitoring) that relates to the stated problem of how to respond to the logging mandate, rather than the direct compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself ensure the lab's systems technically record events per Article 12(1)-(3); it only builds a shared corpus on top of logging, so it would contribute to but not solve the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: A shared internal logging SDK is a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (shared SDK and schema) but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized internal tooling for regulatory compliance is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A four-person pod over two sprints using existing observability infrastructure with integration at next major iteration is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by encoding the required fields in one schema.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide compliant event recording across systems, but it covers only logging and not the broader compliance or R&D adaptation, and the Annex III 1(a) fields apply only to some systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared SDK and central audit store is a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized instrumentation within existing MLOps violates no legal or social norms and is a standard strategy.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing MLOps stack, though it requires some SDK development and integration across pipelines, so it is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the Article 12 event categories in a shared system.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, auto-capturing Article 12(2) event categories centrally would address the main logging mandate, though Annex III-specific fields and retention details are not fully covered, so it is a strong but not complete solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance checks in CI pipelines are a fairly expected, sensible response, with only modest imagination in the synthetic-load probe and diff report.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (a CI/CD gate with schema validation) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated pipeline gates are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing GitLab CI runners and JSON Schema, so it needs only modest, non-radical changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that the required events are emitted and persisted.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify that logging is complete and catch gaps early, but it does not by itself design the logging, ensure the content is appropriate to the intended purpose, or cover retention and post-deployment, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: An open benchmark built from real deployment logs with sandbox partners is unusual and shows some imagination, but benchmark releases are a familiar research format.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance logging into a public research benchmark and creates new partnerships with regulatory sandboxes, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open benchmarks and sandbox partnerships are accepted practice, though releasing deployment logs, even anonymised, raises some confidentiality and data-protection concerns without being unacceptable.
evidence_implementability: Getting real logs from deployers through two member-state sandboxes, agreeing a schema, and anonymising at scale is difficult and slow, and it depends on third parties, though it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It relates to Article 72 post-market monitoring, which is referenced in Article 12(2)(b), but it addresses an implied community-level need rather than the lab's own logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not make the lab's own systems log the events Article 12 requires, so it would at best contribute indirectly to the lab's compliance, and it mostly serves community research.

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance logs as reproducibility artifacts is interesting and shows some imagination, but the idea of experiment tracking and provenance logging is fairly familiar.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the scientific practice itself, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Treating logs as research artifacts and storing them in versioned repositories violates no legal or social norms and is a sensible, uncontroversial strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a logging middleware into ML pipelines and versioned storage requires some pipeline changes and engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D accordingly by building logging middleware into pipelines.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide the automatic event recording required by Article 12 and add research benefits, but it does not address the specific risk-identification, post-market monitoring, or Annex III minimum content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating the logging requirement as an information-theoretic question with a traceability-entropy metric is unusual and imaginative compared with typical lab responses, though not entirely surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning the logging obligation into a research agenda that shapes architecture design, which stretches the paradigm and partly addresses what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A research programme on traceability bounds violates no legal or social norms, though framing compliance as publishable theory research is somewhat unusual for a lab.
evidence_implementability: Deriving formal information-theoretic bounds and a mutual-information metric against ground-truth decision rationale for transformers and diffusion models is difficult and open-ended, requiring significant research effort with uncertain outcomes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses logging for auditability only indirectly: the bounds inform what logs are needed, which is an implied problem related to the mandate rather than the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not deliver Article 12 logging capability on its own and is exploratory, so at best it partially contributes to meeting the mandate, and the ground-truth rationale notion is questionable.

evidence_originality: Overhead benchmarking with an SLO gate is a sensible but fairly mundane engineering response, with only mild interest in tying it to architecture selection.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal performance benchmarking gating architecture selection is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A micro-benchmark harness with synthetic workloads is cheap and straightforward to build, requiring only modest changes to existing processes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (performance cost of mandatory logging affecting design choices) that relates to meeting the logging mandate, rather than the mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: Benchmarking logging overhead helps pick viable architectures but does not itself implement logging or satisfy Article 12 content requirements, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Building logging into research from the first run is a recognized 'compliance by design' idea that experienced evaluators would expect, though pre-registered log schemas add a mildly interesting twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between research and compliance by weaving logging and provenance into experimental design itself, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking since it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding logging in research protocols and pre-registration violates no norms and is aligned with regulators and scientific reviewers, though mandating it for all prototypes may chafe researchers.
evidence_implementability: It requires revising SOPs and wiring log schemas and dataset lineage into pipelines, which is a reasonably feasible set of process changes with some overhead.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate and adapting R&D by making logging present from the start of high-risk system development.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially ensure logging capability and traceability exist at deployment, but it does not specify the log contents required by Article 12(2)-(3) or lifetime operation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing experiment tracking infrastructure for compliance logging is a sensible and common-sense approach that many labs would propose, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a module to existing tooling but treats compliance as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Extending existing logging tools for compliance is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It builds on infrastructure already operated, including an append-only store, so it needs only a modest module and low cost, though some engineering work is required.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (extend the tracker to log the Article 12(3) fields) to get Y (meeting the logging mandate), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Capturing the Article 12(3) fields as automatic, immutable logs over the system lifetime would meet the core logging mandate, though Article 12(2) event relevance for risk and post-market monitoring is only partly covered.

evidence_originality: Measuring compliance overhead and compressing logs is a sensible, fairly expected response, with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a benchmarking and compression tool but still treats compliance purely as a logging practice, leaving R&D's relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Measuring logging overhead and testing compressed logs that still meet minimum requirements is a common, norm-compliant engineering practice, though sampled logs carry slight legal risk.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing GPU cluster, two postdocs, and four weeks of instrumentation on deployed systems, so it is cheap and feasible with some work on prototyping reduced-log schemes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of the compute cost of meeting the logging mandate, which relates to but is not the direct question of how to meet the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps the lab budget and reduce logging cost but does not itself deliver compliant logging, and sampled logs may conflict with Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance mapping into a citable pattern library is somewhat interesting, but regulatory-to-design mapping and compliance catalogues are fairly expected responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (a pattern library, a research workstream) and frames compliance as publishable methodology, but it still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change how R&D relates to obligations in a fundamental way.
evidence_acceptability: An internal audit and pattern library is a conventional, norm-compliant way to respond to a regulation and offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It needs a postdoc and a senior researcher for six months, which is a modest staffing commitment with no radical technical change, though auditing every active project takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate and adapt R&D, through mapping obligations to architectures, which is directly related, though the implementation step is implied rather than stated.
evidence_effectiveness: A catalogue and audit would help the lab identify and design logging obligations, but it does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A drop-in logging library is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination beyond competent engineering.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard tooling approach to logging that treats compliance as a logging practice, with only a new library as a mild new element and no change to how the lab works.
evidence_acceptability: Internal logging middleware for compliance is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A thin decorator-based SDK on append-only Parquet storage is a modest internal engineering build using standard tools, though it needs some development and schema work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate (do X, get compliant logs for Article 12).
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide automatic event logging meeting Article 12 requirements, but it covers only logging and not the broader compliance or R&D adaptation, and the 'guarantee' of compliance is overstated, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a research asset is an interesting and somewhat imaginative reframing, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science and turning compliance into a research asset, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for internal research and standardising schemas is a sensible business practice, though repurposing logs containing personal data raises some GDPR purpose-limitation concerns, making it somewhat uncommon but not offensive.
evidence_implementability: Standardising log schemas across all Annex III deployments and building a longitudinal queryable corpus requires some changes and cross-team effort but is reasonably feasible with existing data engineering.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate by leveraging logs, with schema standardisation relating directly to Article 12 but the main aim (research value) being implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help standardise logs and add research value, but it does not itself ensure the logging mandate's content requirements are met, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying differential privacy and federated computation to mandatory biometric logs is unusual and shows some imagination, though privacy-preserving logging is a recognized research area and not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (privacy-preserving cryptographic and statistical mechanisms for log fields) but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-protective logging is a legally and socially acceptable strategy, somewhat uncommon, though applying noise to mandated audit records may raise tension with regulatory auditability.
evidence_implementability: Building a prototype pipeline with differential privacy and cryptographic mechanisms, and measuring utility-privacy trade-offs against audit needs, is a significant and difficult undertaking with uncertain results, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(3) logging requirements for biometric inputs, reference databases and verifier identities, which is an identified part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, it would help meet Article 12(3) logging for biometric systems while protecting data, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) systems and is framed as exploratory research, so it is only a partial solution to the lab's logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Framing intended-purpose crystallisation as a deliberate milestone and building intellectual authority is unusual and shows some imagination, though not highly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes how R&D phases are structured relative to compliance triggers and the lab's relationship to the regulatory discourse, stretching the paradigm beyond logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing a peer-reviewed methodology paper and inviting regulatory comment violates no norms, though using publication as a compliance response is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Writing and submitting a paper within twelve months from existing project histories is reasonably feasible with modest changes to lab activity.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (when logging duties get triggered in R&D phases) related to the stated problem, but it does not itself provide logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A methodology paper would not itself implement logging capability and would only partially help the lab meet the mandate by clarifying timing of obligations.

evidence_originality: Compliance checks in CI are a fairly common DevOps idea, though applying it to Article 12 logging fields is a sensible, mildly interesting application.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a CI compliance gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, without changing the relation between R&D and compliance much.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI are a normal engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Adding a CI stage that runs a synthetic workload and validates log fields is a modest extension of existing build pipelines, though defining schemas and workloads takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the logging mandate by verifying that required Article 12 and Annex III 1(a) logs are emitted during R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure log presence and format early, but it covers only one part of the problem (it does not check log adequacy, retention, or other duties, and it applies only to Annex III 1(a) minima), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Cost estimation in project scoping is a mundane, expected response, though tying it to Article 12 parameters adds slight specificity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a template and worksheet but still treats compliance as an overhead cost to be managed, although it does slightly influence which projects get funded.
evidence_acceptability: Budget worksheets in project charters are a common management practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It only requires adding a spreadsheet and a budget line to existing templates, which is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: The idea addresses the lab's decision on how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by making recurring Article 12 costs visible at scoping, which is an implied rather than a direct problem of meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: Cost visibility helps funding decisions but does not itself deliver logging capability or compliance, so it is only a partial contribution to the solution.

evidence_originality: Open-source logging tooling for compliance is a fairly expected and interesting response, showing some but not striking imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a reusable open-source library and community contribution) but still treats compliance fundamentally as logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building and open-sourcing a compliance logging library under a permissive licence violates no legal or social norms, though releasing it publicly is somewhat less routine than purely internal compliance.
evidence_implementability: A three-person team over two quarters integrating with the existing experiment-tracking stack is a reasonably feasible, moderately resourced effort requiring some changes but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic logging mandate by building a module that records events.
evidence_effectiveness: A generic plug-in library would help with the automatic recording requirement but does not cover risk-specific event selection, Annex III minimums, retention, or use-case tailoring, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a research dataset for drift and reliability is unusual and shows some imagination, though it is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the logging obligation into a research asset and a source of new offerings like benchmarks, which stretches the paradigm but does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing logs for anonymized research and benchmarks is a somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no norms, though secondary data use raises some privacy and data-governance questions that need handling.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated data-science pod, standardized schemas across deployments, and multi-year analyses, which is a significant but feasible investment built on logs the lab must already produce.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely getting value from mandated logs and supporting post-market monitoring, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly solve the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself deliver compliant logging; it only exploits logs once they exist, so it contributes to the post-market monitoring aim but is a partial solution to the mandate.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a longitudinal drift-research corpus is an unusual and imaginative reframing that few labs would propose in response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by making logs a scientific asset and a public resource, so compliance output feeds research rather than being just a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Repurposing operational logs for research raises GDPR purpose-limitation and anonymisation concerns and customer consent issues, though it is not outright illegal if properly anonymised.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a retention, anonymisation and research-repository pipeline with platform engineering, which is significant extra work beyond basic logging but feasible with existing data engineering practices.
evidence_applicability: It builds on Article 12(1) logs and addresses the adapt-R&D part of the stated problem, but the benefit of drift research is an implied rather than directly identified compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal does not itself meet the logging mandate (what to log, Article 12(2) and 12(3) content) and only contributes a side benefit from logs that must exist anyway, so it is at most a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library with deployment gating is a common, expected response, lacking surprising elements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with a reusable module and CI checks being new tooling but not changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging SDK with CI/CD gating is a common, norm-compliant engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared SDK and CI gates requires some engineering changes and process adjustment but is reasonably feasible, not trivial and not radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by auto-recording the specified events in every high-risk system.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, a mandatory standardized logging layer would directly satisfy the Article 12 logging mandate for the lab's systems, though it focuses on Annex III 1(a)-style fields and not the broader risk-relevant event definitions, so it is near-complete rather than fully so.

evidence_originality: A cost-modeling study of log storage is a sensible but fairly expected response to lifetime retention burdens, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a measurement and forecasting process but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An internal cost study and negotiation with IT is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A six-month project with two researchers, three pilots, and existing middleware is a modest, reasonably feasible effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (affordable lifetime retention of logs) that relates to the logging mandate rather than the mandate's core requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Cost forecasting helps manage the budget side of logging but does not itself deliver the logging capability or Article 12 compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusing compliance logs as research data is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but the SPC drift-detection mechanism is fairly familiar and the idea is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by treating compliance logs as a research dataset and a source of publications and grants, turning a cost into scientific capital.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymised, aggregated operational data for monitoring and research is a somewhat uncommon strategy that offends no sensibilities, though secondary use of logs needs data-protection care.
evidence_implementability: It requires only a small two-analyst pod and building on existing log stores and a monitoring workstream already obliged, so it is a reasonably feasible modest change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of making logs useful for risk identification and post-market monitoring, which relates to the mandate but is not the core act of building compliant logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Feeding logs into post-market monitoring with SPC drift detection helps meet Article 12(2)(a)-(b) purposes but does not itself implement the logging capability or the Annex III minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in shared scaffolds or middleware is a sensible and fairly common engineering approach, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a template and middleware tooling and shifts logging earlier in development, but it still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Built-in logging with code review checks is a standard engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a middleware module to existing templates and checking its schema in code review is a modest, non-radical change using the current Python/PyTorch stack.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (do X to get compliant logs), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logger template capturing the Article 12(3) data points would meet the logging mandate for new prototypes, but it covers only Annex III 1(a) minimums, ignores Article 12(2) event relevance, and leaves existing systems and documentation unaddressed, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Requiring a design-time contract file enforced by CI is a sensible shift-left idea but is fairly familiar from schema-as-code and compliance-as-code practice, so it is interesting rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a logging contract file and a build gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moving it earlier in the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory commit templates and merge checks are common engineering governance practices that offend no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a YAML template and a CI check is a lightweight, low-cost change, though it requires some process adjustment and maintenance of the schema validator.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12(3) logging fields (reference database, matched input, verifier identity, period of use) that the lab must meet, so it does X to get Y, where Y is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It ensures logging schemas are designed up front, but a declared schema in YAML does not guarantee the runtime logs are actually captured, and it omits period-of-use detail and Article 12(1)-(2) general logging, so it is a helpful but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance documentation as code in Git is a sensible but fairly familiar docs-as-code idea, with the onboarding and funding-justification benefits being mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new format and process (versioned dossier) and reframes documentation as a knowledge asset, but still treats compliance as a documentation practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Version-controlled documentation is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building on existing Git workflows and assigning one engineer per project makes this feasible with modest changes and low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the Recital 71 technical documentation requirement (kept up to date over the system's lifetime), which is part of the stated problem, though it only indirectly addresses Article 12's automatic event logging.
evidence_effectiveness: A versioned dossier would help with documentation and traceability but does not implement automatic event logs, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Releasing a logging schema as a community benchmark is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance work as a scientific and community-contribution product and changes the lab's relationship to its obligations, though it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an anonymized schema and synthetic data after ethics review and de-identification is a somewhat uncommon but norm-respecting open-science practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Packaging a schema and synthetic dataset with a license and a short paper requires some extra work and review but is reasonably feasible for a compliance-engineering team.
evidence_applicability: The idea mainly addresses an implied problem of reputation and community benefit rather than directly meeting the logging mandate, though it is related through the Article 12 architecture.
evidence_effectiveness: It does not itself make the lab's systems compliant with the logging mandate and only contributes marginally to the problem, so it probably will not solve it.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code gating via templates and CI is a sensible, fairly expected response for a lab, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (YAML manifest, pre-commit hook, CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moved earlier in the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Developer-workflow gates and templates are common engineering practice that violate no norms, though some researchers may find them mildly burdensome.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing repo-template tooling with a YAML manifest, pre-commit hook and CI check, which is low-cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring prototypes declare Article 12(3) fields, so X leads to Y which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure logging schemas are declared and validated, but a schema manifest does not guarantee actual runtime logging or cover Article 12(1)-(2) beyond Annex III 1(a), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gap analysis and portfolio triage against regulatory requirements is a fairly expected response, though tying it to Annex III 1(a) minimums adds some specificity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by letting logging feasibility steer which research gets pursued, though it is still a review process rather than a redefinition of research.
evidence_acceptability: A structured internal portfolio review with go/no-go decisions is a fairly common business practice that offends no norms, though diverting projects is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A six-week memo process and steering committee review uses existing governance and requires only modest effort, though assessing architectures for the logging fields takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of deciding how to respond and adapt R&D to the logging mandate by assessing the specific Annex III minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: The review identifies gaps and prioritizes projects but does not itself implement logging, so it only partially solves the problem of meeting the mandate or adapting R&D.

evidence_originality: Keeping documentation up to date via change-management triggers is a standard, expected response and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Version-controlled documentation governance is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Appointing owners, defining triggers, and hooking into the existing change-management workflow requires only modest process changes at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (technical documentation currency from Recital 71) rather than the logging mandate itself, so it applies indirectly.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the documentation up-to-date expectation but does not address the automatic event logging mandate of Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance gates and checklists are a very common, mundane response expected from labs facing a regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A review gate with a checklist is standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Stage-gate reviews with compliance sign-off are a common governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A checklist, training, and a sign-off gate meeting are procedural additions needing modest resources and no radical change, though actual logging engineering still must be done elsewhere.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how the lab meets the logging mandate by verifying Article 12 obligations before systems advance, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A gate verifying compliance helps prevent non-compliant systems from shipping but does not itself build the logging capability or address R&D adaptation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A central register with scheduled reviews is a standard, mundane compliance response that evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary record-keeping administration and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Governance and documentation processes are common compliance strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Setting up a compliance team, a central register and quarterly reviews is a reasonably feasible organizational change with modest cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses keeping technical documentation and log archives current over system lifetime, which is part of the stated compliance problem, though it focuses on documentation governance more than the automatic logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A central register and review cycles would help keep records current and auditable but would not by itself deliver the technical automatic event logging that Article 12 requires, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Studying minimal-footprint logging architectures with deterministic replay seeds is a somewhat interesting, moderately imaginative angle, though a compliance-logging study is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (architecture comparison, replay seeds, a cost matrix) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only gesturing at publishability.
evidence_acceptability: An internal research project with ring-fenced staff and a whitepaper is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs modest resources (one postdoc, half an engineer, two pilot models) and no radical change, though it delays implementation by six months and the output is a study rather than a working system.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting Article 12 logging minimums efficiently, with output feeding the framework refactor.
evidence_effectiveness: A six-month study that informs the refactor and storage plan helps the lab meet the logging mandate but does not itself implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized reusable logging middleware is a very common engineering response that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared SDK is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged, so it is at most slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal platform with a registration requirement violates no legal or social norms and is a standard strategy.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing event-bus architecture and amortizes one effort across projects, though it requires some platform work and mandatory adoption, so some changes are needed.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the Article 12(3) fields automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve the core logging requirement for Annex III 1(a) systems if built, but it covers only the 12(3) fields, not the broader Article 12(2) event relevance or documentation, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing architectures with intrinsic provenance driven by Article 12 is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, but it echoes existing interpretability and explainable-by-design research and is not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal weaves logging into the science of model architecture, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance and affecting what the lab researches, which is paradigm breaking or at least stretching, though it stops short of a wholesale redefinition of the research agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Research on interpretable and traceable architectures offends no norms or legal sensibilities and is a respectable though somewhat uncommon response to regulation.
evidence_implementability: Four researchers prototyping three architectures over eighteen months is a significant, costly, and uncertain research commitment, but it is not impossible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It targets Article 12 logging sufficiency in an indirect way, solving an implied long-term problem of how to adapt R&D rather than the immediate need to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Exploratory architecture research may not yield a working design and does not directly deliver the logging capability needed now, so it would at best contribute partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating technical documentation from lab notebooks and Git history is a sensible, fairly expected response, interesting but not surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (a nightly pipeline and versioned dossier) but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation with periodic human review is a common, norm-respecting strategy, though relying on one engineer per project for review is slightly lean.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing JupyterHub and Git infrastructure with a scripted pipeline and no new team, so it is reasonably easy and low cost, though mapping to regulatory content takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 11/12 technical documentation and record-keeping obligation, but it focuses on documentation of R&D rather than the automatic event logging of the deployed system that Article 12 mandates, so it applies to an implied part of the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation current but does not provide the system-level automatic event logging that Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Research on efficient logging and turning compliance into publications is interesting but a fairly expected response, without surprising ingenuity.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (research track, reference implementation, grant leverage) and starts to turn compliance into a publishable contribution, but it still centers on logging practice rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Treating compliance as a research and open-publication opportunity is somewhat unusual but offends no legal or social norms.
