evidence_implementability: It needs only one postdoc FTE and already-reserved GPU benchmarking time, which are modest, non-radical resources, though a two-year research programme adds some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of the cost of logging under resource constraints, which relates to the stated problem but does not directly specify how to meet the Article 12 requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Low-overhead logging research would contribute to meeting the mandate but it is exploratory, does not itself deliver compliant logs, and covers only part of the problem.

evidence_originality: Log replay and gap-checking tools are fairly familiar observability practice, though framing it as a regulatory traceability simulator is somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: An internal read-only log query and audit tool breaks no legal or social norms and is a sensible compliance-verification practice.
evidence_implementability: A CLI query layer over an existing JSONL store is a modest build requiring some development but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses verifying that logging supports identifying risk situations or modifications under Article 12(2)(a), which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies traceability and flags gaps but does not itself create logging capabilities or cover post-market monitoring, operation monitoring, or Annex III requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging SDK/middleware is a very expected, mundane response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though it adds a new tool.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library with default-on logging is a common engineering approach that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires building a decorator-based SDK and integrating it into templates and the existing serving framework, which is reasonably feasible but needs some development effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by auto-instrumenting the Article 12(3) fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It would largely solve the logging-compliance need, but Article 12(3) fields apply only to Annex III 1(a) systems and it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance or log retention, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware is a fairly standard engineering approach to cross-cutting compliance, so it is sensible but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared infrastructure format but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves R&D ways of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing message bus with a three-month platform-engineering build and per-project schema configuration, which is reasonably feasible and needs only moderate changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by building a logging layer that captures the Article 12(3) items (timestamps, input data, reference-database queries, verifier identities).
evidence_effectiveness: A centralized logging layer would, if built, satisfy the automatic-recording mandate across systems, though it addresses logging only and not the wider documentation and traceability duties, and it is limited to capturing the listed events.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code and CI gating are fairly known ideas, but treating missing log schemas like compile errors in R&D prototypes shows some imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process (CI gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, though it moves logging earlier into development workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance checks in CI are a legitimate engineering practice that offends no legal or social norms, though enforcing them as merge gates is slightly less routine than plain logging.
evidence_implementability: It builds on the existing pytest suite and pre-merge webhook with a three-sprint pilot, so it needs some changes but is reasonably feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring the required fields exist in prototypes, which is explicitly part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It enforces logging fields at build time but covers only Art. 12(3) minimums (which apply to Annex III 1(a) systems), and it does not address Art. 12(1)-(2) event relevance, retention, or runtime logging, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating traceability as a design constraint in experiment templates is sensible and interesting but a fairly expected shift-left compliance idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the experimental method and grant approval, stretching the paradigm without changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance into protocols and peer review is a sensible, norm-respecting strategy, though somewhat less common than standard after-the-fact documentation.
evidence_implementability: Revising templates in two months and tying them to grant approval requires some process changes but is reasonably feasible without radical cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the stated problem by making experiment runs automatically emit the Article 12 logging artifacts (timestamps, reference databases, matched inputs, verifier identities).
evidence_effectiveness: Native log emission in the experimental workflow would substantially meet the logging mandate, but it addresses R&D-run logs more than the logging capability of deployed high-risk systems, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building compliance logging into the development toolchain (compliance by design with an append-only provenance layer) is a sensible but fairly expected response among labs, so it is interesting rather than ingenious or rare.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (a provenance bus middleware, immutable stores) and shifts logging from retrofit to default practice, but it still treats compliance as logging infrastructure rather than changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Compliance-by-design logging with append-only stores is a common, legally aligned strategy that offends no norms, though immutable logs raise minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: Building lab-wide middleware and integrating it across training, testing and deployment toolchains requires significant engineering but uses standard techniques and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly states doing X (embedding automatic logging in pipelines) to get Y (Article 12 and Annex III-compliant traceability), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic structured logging with timestamps, input references and immutable storage would substantially address the Article 12 mandate, but it focuses on development stages and may not fully cover deployed-system runtime event logging, risk-relevant event identification or post-market monitoring needs, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A log-ingesting compliance dashboard with alert rules is a fairly expected response, with the early-warning reputation framing only mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (dashboard) but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice, with the lab's R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal monitoring dashboards and compliance reporting are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A small data-engineering team building a dashboard on existing infrastructure with alert rules is reasonably feasible, needing some new work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate's stated purposes (Art. 12(2) risk identification, post-market monitoring, operation monitoring) by consuming logs and mapping alerts to them.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps use logs for monitoring and traceability, but it presumes logging capability exists and does not itself ensure systems technically record events or cover Annex III minimum fields, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Shift-left compliance design gates are a fairly familiar idea, though the framing as a thirty-minute sprint gate is somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (a go/no-go gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely shifting it earlier in the lifecycle.
evidence_acceptability: A design-gate checklist requirement is a common governance strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a one-page log spec to an existing design review checklist is a small governance amendment requiring little cost or change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by specifying which Article 12(2) events get recorded.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging is planned early, but a spec alone does not guarantee actual logging capability, correct implementation, or Article 12(3) minimums, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging SDK with a review gate is the standard, expected response to Article 12 and is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, introducing a tool but still treating compliance as logging engineering without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Building compliance logging into engineering pipelines is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A reusable logging SDK with an architecture review gate is a reasonably feasible set of engineering changes, though it requires platform team effort and adoption across all research groups.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by recording the events Article 12 specifies.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would largely satisfy the logging requirement, but it covers mainly the technical logging and not wider issues such as retention, Annex III specifics, or post-market monitoring use, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging layer is the obvious, expected engineering response to Article 12, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (SDK/middleware) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a plug-in logging SDK across all portfolio systems requires some engineering effort and integration changes but is a reasonably feasible, standard software measure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by capturing the specific events and fields the Article requires.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, standardized automatic logging with Annex III-specific fields would directly satisfy the core Article 12 logging mandate, though it does not cover documentation or other obligations.

evidence_originality: Project templates and cookiecutter generators for compliance are a fairly familiar engineering approach, though mapping Article 12 fields to code locations is a mildly interesting touch.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and process but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moved earlier in the workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Internal templates and onboarding pilots are a common strategy that violates no norms, though mandating lab-wide use may meet mild resistance.
evidence_implementability: Building a template and piloting with two teams is a reasonably feasible, modest-cost effort using existing tooling, with some process change when mandated.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate in R&D by making Article 12 fields part of project setup.
evidence_effectiveness: A scaffold pre-wiring logging and mapping Article 12 fields to code would substantially help meet the logging mandate for new prototypes, but it leaves legacy systems, retention, and post-market monitoring uncovered, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating Article 12 logging as a scientific question about drift-predictive signals via ablation studies is unusual and shows imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging itself a research agenda, weaving compliance into the science and addressing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Funding a research effort on logging design with postdocs and a PhD student is a legitimate, non-offensive strategy, though somewhat unusual as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It needs modest staffing (two postdocs, one PhD student) and instrumenting existing prototypes, which is feasible, but it commits scarce resources to open-ended research with uncertain payoff rather than a defined deliverable.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (understanding what to log meaningfully beyond minimum fields) that relates to the logging mandate but not the identified need to comply with it.
evidence_effectiveness: The research line would yield insights about which log features predict degradation, but it does not itself deliver Article 12 compliant logging for the lab's systems, so it is only a partial contribution to the stated problem.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and compliance-as-code are a known pattern that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (YAML tagging, CI hook, auto-generated living documentation) but still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it does fold documentation into the researcher workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from version-controlled metadata is a common engineering strategy that violates no norms and suits regulators and auditors.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing Git/CI infrastructure with a lightweight schema, requiring some tooling work and researcher adoption but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified related problem (keeping technical documentation current and audit-ready), yet it conflates this with Article 12 logging, so it applies to an implied rather than directly stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with the technical documentation burden and audit readiness, but it does not implement the automatic event logging Article 12 actually mandates, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A retention-policy module on an existing document system is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard archival and compliance practice that leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Records retention policies are a common, norm-conforming compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It extends an existing document-management system with a policy module run by one administrator quarterly, which is low cost and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the record-keeping and documentation-upkeep obligation in the regulation, which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Retention and retrieval of logs and documentation addresses only the lifetime-availability piece, not the core mandate of technically enabling automatic event logging with the required content (Art. 12(2)-(3)), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reframing compliance logs as scientific instruments for failure discovery is an interesting, somewhat imaginative idea, though using logs for monitoring and anomaly detection is not wholly unexpected.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science and turning an obligation into a research instrument, though it does not change what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Using logs for failure discovery and publishing findings is somewhat unusual but offends no norms, though data protection and confidentiality concerns around publishing log-derived findings are manageable.
evidence_implementability: Adding logging hooks and anomaly-detection pipelines requires some process changes and engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with existing tools.
evidence_applicability: Embedding logging hooks at design stage directly addresses meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (identifying risk situations, post-market monitoring), with the added research use as an implied benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, design-stage logging plus anomaly detection would satisfy the logging requirement and support risk identification, though it does not itself specify the minimum Annex III logging contents or retention, so it is mostly but not fully a solution.

evidence_originality: Prototyping a logging pipeline against Article 12(3) before production scoping is a sensible but fairly expected response with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance/logging practice using a prototype and checklist, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal compliance prototype validated against a checklist is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers in one sprint on existing GPU cluster is low cost and a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses meeting the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements, which is part of the stated problem, though it is a de-risking step rather than the compliance itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A prototype demonstrates feasibility and stress tests logging but does not itself deliver compliant production logging, so it only partially solves the problem and is limited to Annex III 1(a) systems.

evidence_originality: Reusing Article 12 logs as reproducibility artifacts shipped with papers is an interesting, somewhat imaginative dual-use framing, though embedding logging in pipelines is a fairly expected response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging into the science itself so compliance becomes a scientific asset, which is paradigm stretching rather than breaking.
evidence_acceptability: Co-design with legal and transparency-oriented publishing violates no norms, though shipping operational logs raises minor confidentiality concerns, making it a somewhat unusual but inoffensive strategy.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a lightweight schema into existing training and evaluation pipelines is reasonably feasible with some engineering changes, though publishing full logs adds complexity.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D, with a clear do-X-to-get-Y link to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Embedding log hooks in pipelines would help meet the logging mandate, but research-run logs may not match the high-risk deployed-system lifetime logging Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a compliance logging pipeline that captures the mandated fields is the most obvious and expected response to this mandate, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice with an append-only store and leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Implementing legally required logging is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers over three weeks on the existing stack is a modest, non-radical effort at low cost, though instrumenting four data sources requires some work.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly implements the four minimum log fields that Article 12(3) requires for Annex III point 1(a) systems, so it addresses the stated logging mandate head-on.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, it would satisfy the prescriptive Article 12(3) minimums and give a reusable template, but it covers only biometric-ID systems and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging duties across the lab's other systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Early risk-classification gates are a common and expected response to the Act, so this idea is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a process gate and questionnaire but still treats compliance as a checkpoint on top of R&D, leaving how the lab works largely unchanged, though it moves compliance earlier into project selection.
evidence_acceptability: A compliance checkpoint at project intake with a memo per project is a conventional governance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a biweekly steering review, a questionnaire and memos, which are some process changes but reasonably feasible and not costly.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of knowing which systems must meet Article 12 logging, which relates to the stated problem but is not the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: Early classification helps ensure logging is architected in, but it does not itself design or deliver the logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance documentation as a publishable methods contribution is unusual and shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance documentation as scholarly contribution and community norm-setting, which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Open release and community engagement violate no norms, though releasing compliance material as scholarship is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: A small working group using Zenodo and drafting a paper is low-cost and feasible, though acceptance at a top venue is uncertain.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses Recital 71 technical documentation, which relates to the record-keeping context, but it does not address the Article 12 logging mandate itself, so it solves only an implied, related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Publishing an open documentation template would help with documentation and the lab's standing, but it would not implement automatic event logging, so it is at best a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Publishing compliance documentation as open-science packs alongside papers is unusual and shows some imagination, though not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by turning documentation duty into an open-science publication artefact and a tender differentiator, but it does not change what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Open release of documentation with redaction and privacy counsel review violates no norms, though publishing risk summaries may raise some IP and security concerns.
evidence_implementability: A two-person editorial cell, a schema, and a publication-committee rule are reasonably feasible measures requiring some process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses technical documentation (Recital 71/Article 11) rather than the logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied, related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not produce automatic event logs under Article 12, so it contributes only marginally to meeting the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Mapping the Article 12(3) fields to a provenance ledger is a sensible, expected response and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a ledger component but still treats compliance as a logging practice, with only a mild nod to provenance as first-class metadata.
evidence_acceptability: Append-only audit logging with pseudonymisation is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It extends existing feature-store infrastructure with an append-only ledger, which is a reasonably feasible set of changes rather than a radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(3)(b)-(d) logging fields, which are part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the specific Annex III 1(a) minimum logging fields, but covers only that subset of the mandate (not Article 12(1)-(2) generally or the broader R&D adaptation), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware is a very common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect from AI labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized logging middleware is a common, norm-respecting engineering and compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Refactoring existing experiment-tracking infrastructure into a shared middleware is a reasonably feasible, moderate change that reduces per-project engineering.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a shared logging component that captures the Article 12(3) items (timestamps, reference databases, input matches) to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A mandatory logging interface would substantially meet the logging mandate, but it omits the Article 12(3)(d) verification-person identification, the Article 12(2) risk and post-market monitoring event relevance, and retention, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Retention infrastructure with WORM storage and regulator-response SOPs is a common, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: WORM storage, integrity checks and SOPs are standard compliance and logging practice that leave the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Secure log retention co-managed with IT security and regulator-facing procedures are common strategies that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Procuring WORM storage, setting up quarterly checks and drafting SOPs is reasonably feasible with some cost and changes, though lifetime-scale retention adds some expense.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the stated problem (retaining and producing logs for Article 12 compliance), with explicit reference to the Article 12(3) minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: Tamper-evident, lifetime-retention log storage with retrieval procedures would contribute to meeting the logging mandate but does not itself generate the event-recording capability, relevance-defining event selection, or the Article 12(2) traceability design, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Anomaly-detection on logs with alerting dashboards is a common, expected response to post-market monitoring, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (analytics service) but still treats compliance as logging and monitoring practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A log analytics and alerting service for post-market monitoring is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a Kafka-based microservice with rule repository and dashboards uses standard tooling and is reasonably feasible, though it requires some engineering effort and ongoing tuning.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the mandate by consuming Article 12 logs to support Article 72 monitoring and Article 79(1) risk identification, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with monitoring and risk flagging but only partially solves the logging mandate itself, since it presupposes logging capture and covers only downstream duties.

evidence_originality: Shared logging middleware or SDK is a common, mundane engineering response that evaluators would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice centralized into a shared tool, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal reusable logging SDK to meet a legal mandate is a common, norm-respecting engineering strategy.
evidence_implementability: Two to three engineers over six months to build a modular SDK is a reasonably feasible measure, though integrating across all pipelines requires some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the specified Article 12(3) items across systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A uniform logging layer would meet the Article 12(3) minimums and so contribute substantially, but it does not cover Article 12(2) event relevance or broader documentation, making it a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Log-native architectures such as attention-tracing transformers and differentiable audit-graph networks are an imaginative and unusual response, though they are related to existing interpretability and traceability work.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Treating regulatory constraint as an architectural design variable changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations and shapes what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Research into compliance-by-design architectures violates no norms or sensibilities and would be well received by regulators and the research community.
evidence_implementability: A small group prototyping two to three designs in six months is modest in resourcing, but the research outcome is uncertain and it does not yield deployable compliance, so it requires significant effort with unclear payoff.
evidence_applicability: It targets the Article 12 automatic-recording requirement directly by seeking architectures that emit logs, so it addresses an identified part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate or adapting R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal is an exploratory research program on architectures that might emit logs, so it would at most contribute to meeting the logging mandate and does not directly deliver compliant logging for the lab's systems, and the stated problem rules out exploratory funding.

evidence_originality: Embedded compliance roles are a familiar practice (like embedded security champions), so the idea is interesting but not rare or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new process element (embedded engineer, design reviews) but still treats compliance as a logging and review practice rather than changing how research itself is done.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance staff in teams is a common organizational strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It reallocates two existing contracts into a small six-month pilot, which is a modest structural change at low added cost, though embedding across all squads later needs some change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by catching log-schema gaps early in design.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure log schemas and risk flags are handled early but does not itself build the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Starter templates and scaffolds with compliance mappings are a common engineering practice, so the idea is mundane even though it is sensible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice packaged as a template, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mandating an internal template violates no legal or social norms and is a common engineering strategy.
evidence_implementability: Extracting a skeleton from an existing prototype and mandating it through the tracker is low cost and involves non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The scaffold directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by pre-wiring Article 12(3) fields into new high-risk projects.
evidence_effectiveness: It would make logging consistent and cheap for new projects, but it covers only new projects and mainly the Article 12(3) fields, so it is a partial solution that does not address existing systems, retention, or the Article 12(2) relevance logic.

evidence_originality: Applying differential privacy and federated aggregation to compress Article 12 logs is an unusual, somewhat imaginative angle beyond typical logging responses, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance as a source of licensable technical capability and publishable research, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations (new offerings born from compliance).
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging and research programmes violate no norms and are a sensible, if somewhat uncommon, strategy, though tension with required log content may raise legal questions.
evidence_implementability: Two funded researchers for eighteen months to prototype is a significant, costly commitment with uncertain research outcomes, but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets how to meet Article 12's recording duties, benchmarked against the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Privacy-preserving compression may help satisfy logging mandates while reducing data burden, but it is an eighteen-month prototype that does not itself deliver compliance now and may conflict with traceability needs, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized append-only log pipelines using Kafka are common practice, with only a mildly interesting twist in extending logging into the prototype phase.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces tooling integration but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: An append-only durable log store is a common, norm-respecting compliance engineering strategy.
evidence_implementability: Kafka with object-storage tiering and integration into existing experiment-tracking tooling is standard, well-supported infrastructure requiring some engineering work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the automatic logging mandate over the system's lifetime by building a log infrastructure.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the logging mandate's lifetime recording and traceability but only partially, since it omits specific event content under Art. 12(2)-(3), and the claim that Art. 12(1) requires prototype-phase logs is overstated.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging platform inherited by all projects is a sensible and fairly expected engineering response, interesting but not surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (a shared logging middleware platform) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance infrastructure is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses one FTE for six months and reuses existing storage, which is a reasonable, modest refactor requiring some changes but no new infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate (do X to get automatic compliant event records).
evidence_effectiveness: A reusable logging bus with Annex III 1(a) field templates would plausibly deliver Article 12 logging across prototypes, but it addresses only logging and not the wider documentation, oversight, or R&D adaptation aspects, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using automated distribution-shift tests in the model registry to flag possible substantial modifications is an interesting, somewhat unusual link between MLOps and a legal concept, but not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (drift-based modification detection) but still treats compliance as a monitoring/logging-type practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated drift monitoring and alerting is a common engineering practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Statistical comparison hooks in an existing model registry with alert routing are reasonably feasible with modest engineering effort, though defining thresholds takes some work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem related to the logging purpose (identifying substantial modifications) rather than the core logging mandate directly.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps detect potential substantial modifications (Art. 12(2)(a)) but does not itself implement the event logging mandate, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Designing the log schema up front is a sensible, fairly expected shift-left compliance practice, with the peer-deliverable framing adding only mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (a traceability-spec artifact and design-review checklist item) but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common, uncontroversial engineering-governance practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a schema step and a checklist item to existing sprints and design reviews requires modest process change at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by defining log fields against Article 12(2) and Annex III 1(a) requirements in each sprint.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help ensure systems are instrumented for logging, but it covers only design-time schema definition and not implementation, retention, or Article 12 compliance as a whole, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating the log mandate as an opportunity for longitudinal drift and reproducibility research is unusual and shows imagination, though not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as a source of scientific data, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations and creating new partnerships and offerings born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Partnering with deployers to analyze anonymised aggregated logs is a somewhat unusual but non-offensive strategy, though data-sharing and confidentiality concerns add mild friction.
evidence_implementability: A multi-year study requiring three industrial partners, access to deployed-system logs, and causal-inference expertise is a significant, expensive undertaking, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It repurposes logs for a research benefit that only loosely relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, a benefit in a special situation.
evidence_effectiveness: The study would not itself make the lab's systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate; it only uses logs for research, so it would at best contribute marginally to the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: A configurable logging sidecar in a service mesh is a fairly expected engineering response, though the prototype-to-production tiering shows modest thought.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (a sidecar with declarative YAML spec and tiered configurability) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving R&D's relationship to compliance largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: It is a common engineering approach to compliance that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a sidecar interceptor on existing service mesh with declarative config is reasonably feasible, requiring some development effort and changes but nothing radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(1) and 12(2) logging mandate by producing automatic event recording aligned with the paragraph-2 categories.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the technical logging capability, but it does not cover paragraph-3 specifics, retention duties, or broader documentation and oversight, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance documentation into a marketed client deliverable is a somewhat unusual and sensible idea but not strikingly ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It creates a new offering born from compliance and changes how compliance relates to the lab's business, which is paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Providing documentation packages to enterprise clients is a normal business practice that offends no norms, though exposing logging architecture may raise minor confidentiality considerations.
evidence_implementability: Templating documents per product family and refreshing them each release is a modest extension of existing compliance work, requiring some coordination with sales engineering.
evidence_applicability: The package addresses documentation and logging transparency tied to Recital 71, but its main outcome is marketing and client differentiation, so it applies to the logging mandate only as an implied, related benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: Bundling documentation and logging diagrams helps present compliance records clearly but does not itself implement automatic event logging, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance requirements into a public benchmark is somewhat unusual and interesting, but not strikingly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (benchmark, toolkit, open release) and begins to turn compliance into a research output, but it still centers on logging requirements rather than altering what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing open benchmarks is an unusual but inoffensive strategy for a lab and violates no norms, though it is somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: Building an open-source toolkit with a synthetic pipeline, rubric, and documentation is a sizable but reasonably feasible software and research effort requiring some changes in lab priorities.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of how to operationalise and measure Article 12(3) logging, which relates to the stated problem but mostly serves community influence rather than the lab's own compliance need.
evidence_effectiveness: A benchmark would help the community assess logging for Annex III 1(a) systems but does not itself make the lab's own systems compliant, so it is only a partial solution, and it covers only the Article 12(3) subset.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing experiment-tracking infrastructure for compliance logs is a common, pragmatic and expected response rather than an imaginative one.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice by reusing existing tooling and leaves the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing internal infrastructure for compliance logging is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A two-person pod over one quarter using existing schema and storage is low-cost and non-radical, though the gap-filling and the shift from training-time tracking to runtime logs add some uncertainty.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (extend the tracking platform to log the mandated fields) to get Y (Article 12 logging compliance), which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Mapping every Article 12(1)-(3) field onto the existing tracking platform would plausibly satisfy the logging mandate, but it omits deployment-time event logging for risk identification and post-market monitoring and does not address documentation or retention governance fully, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Merging debug and compliance logs is a sensible idea that shows some imagination but is a fairly predictable efficiency response, not truly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new format and process (shared schema co-designed with researchers) but still treats compliance fundamentally as logging practice, with only mild integration into R&D workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Combining debug and compliance logging is a sensible, legally unproblematic practice that offends no norms, though somewhat less standard than separate compliance logs.
evidence_implementability: A unified log schema co-designed in sprint zero with an append-only time-series store uses standard engineering tools and requires only modest changes to existing workflow.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate while adapting R&D practice, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A well-designed schema would address the logging mandate's technical requirements and reduce duplication, but it covers mainly the logging part and not documentation, retention, or Annex III-specific fields in detail, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building logging in from the start and pairing engineers with compliance liaisons is a common, expected response with no surprising element.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: This is standard privacy/compliance-by-design practice that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: The approach is a conventional strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding logging modules and a required spec deliverable to design documents involves some process changes but is reasonably feasible for a lab.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building the Article 12(1)-12(3) logging capabilities into systems, so doing X yields compliance with the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native logging with specification deliverables would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it does not address broader aspects such as log retention or deployer use, so it is strong but not clearly complete.

evidence_originality: Assigning a part-time internal compliance team from existing staff is a common, mundane organizational response to a new regulatory mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance staffing arrangement that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship between R&D and compliance essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Using existing staff for part-time compliance duties is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It requires only reallocating a fraction of existing staff time with a weekly stand-up and no new budget, though the workload may compete with research duties.
evidence_applicability: The idea addresses ownership of log-schema design, retention, and Article 12 audit readiness, which is directly related to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, though it is an organizational enabler rather than a logging solution itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A part-time team with one day per week each helps coordinate and sustain compliance but does not itself build the logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and documentation tied to release gates are a well-known practice, so the idea is sensible but not very imaginative or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a sprint-based process but still treats compliance as a documentation practice, merely changing its timing, so it only slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation gates in release processes are a common, norm-respecting strategy, though the release-blocking rule and the per-sprint engineer assignment may meet mild resistance.
evidence_implementability: It uses the existing code-review pipeline and sprint cadence with modest added effort, such as one engineer per sprint and a release gate, so it requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Recital 71 requirement to keep technical documentation up to date, but it does not address the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate that is the core of the stated problem, so the problem it solves is only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping documentation current helps with traceability and compliance but does not deliver automatic logging capability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing a logging toolkit and publishing a reference architecture is a fairly expected, somewhat interesting response but not ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (open toolkit, partner validation, peer-reviewed architecture) and creates shared ecosystem offerings born from compliance, which stretches the relationship somewhat, though it still centers on logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source release and academic collaboration are common, norm-compliant strategies, with minor concerns about IP and security of logs being modest.
evidence_implementability: Building middleware is feasible, but peer review, multi-institution validation, and open-source release require significant coordination and resources beyond core compliance work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building and sharing logging middleware, so X (build logging architecture) yields Y (compliance) as part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would provide a reasonable logging implementation for the lab but focuses on dissemination and does not specify how Article 12 event coverage (risk, post-market, monitoring) is satisfied, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code gating in CI is a well-known DevOps pattern, so applying it to logging is sensible but mundane to somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new pipeline tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: A CI/CD compliance gate is a common engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It adds a stage to existing GitLab CI runners using manifest parsing and a smoke test, which is a reasonably feasible, modest change though schema definitions and tests require some work.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by ensuring event recording is present in high-risk system builds.
evidence_effectiveness: It reliably enforces presence of logging instrumentation and fields but does not ensure log content adequacy, retention in deployment, or other Article 12 aspects, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code with CI/CD gating is a sensible, fairly well-known DevOps practice that is interesting but not surprising for this mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (version-controlled queryable docs, CI/CD gates, stewards) but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal documentation governance and deployment gates violate no norms and are common, accepted strategies.
evidence_implementability: It requires some process changes, tooling and steward roles, but these are reasonably feasible with existing CI/CD infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of keeping technical documentation current, which relates to the regulation's record-keeping context but not directly to the Article 12 logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It would fully address the technical documentation upkeep from Recital 71 but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution to the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-tests in CI is an interesting and sensible idea but fairly expected among engineering-minded responses, showing modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (CI log-completeness gates) but still treats compliance as logging practice, merely moving verification earlier in the dev loop.
evidence_acceptability: Automated CI checks are a common engineering strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Writing harness scripts per Annex III category with model stubs and synthetic inputs is reasonably feasible within existing CI tooling, though it requires some build effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by verifying that required events and fields are emitted.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps ensure logging completeness during development but is only a partial solution since it does not cover log retention, relevance of events to risk, or real-world deployment behavior, and synthetic tests may miss gaps.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance logging into experimental design is an interesting and somewhat unusual framing that shows some imagination, but it is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making compliance data an inseparable part of the scientific record, which is paradigm stretching, though it does not alter what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Updating SOPs and using a shared internal logging service is a normal, uncontroversial engineering and compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires SOP changes and pipeline modification across experiments plus a shared microservice, which is reasonably feasible but involves some changes and cross-team coordination.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate and adapting R&D, with 'do X (native logging in experiments) to get Y (compliant logs)' clearly stated.
evidence_effectiveness: Building Article 12(3) log fields into every experiment's pipeline would meet the logging mandate for R&D prototypes, but it covers only the logging fields for R&D runs and not deployed-system logging, event-relevance under 12(2), or human-verifier identification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a reference prototype of the Article 12(3) logging fields with an append-only store is a sensible but expected engineering response, with little surprising or imaginative content.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a forkable microservice and benchmarking but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal logging prototype is a common, norm-compliant strategy, though the biometric test data might raise minor privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: A small dev-cloud pipeline with four capture points and an append-only store is low-cost and requires no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing the Article 12(3) minimum fields.
evidence_effectiveness: It is a reasonable partial solution covering only the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields and a prototype, not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging across the lab's systems or production deployment.

evidence_originality: Open-sourcing compliance tooling is a fairly foreseeable move and interesting but not strikingly imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance engineering into a public offering and community contribution changes the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations, stretching the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing open-source compliance tooling is somewhat uncommon for labs but offends no legal or social norms and is broadly welcomed.
evidence_implementability: The lab already has an internal logging framework to extract, but documenting against Article 12, external audit and open release add significant extra effort, so this is reasonably feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly produces a logging implementation meeting Article 12 requirements, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A reference implementation would meet the lab's own logging obligation and help others, but it does not address Article 12's appropriateness to intended purpose or other R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory compliance logs as a long-horizon scientific dataset for drift detection is unusual and imaginative, though log-based drift monitoring is a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the logging obligation into a research resource and new partnerships, which is paradigm stretching, and does not change what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using deployers' logs as a research dataset is an uncommon strategy that raises data-protection and confidentiality questions (biometric data, natural persons' identities) but is not outright offensive if agreements are in place.
evidence_implementability: It requires partnering with two Annex III biometric deployment sites, ingesting their log streams, and building an analysis pipeline, which means significant data-access, legal, and coordination effort but is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses how to adapt R&D to the logging mandate by exploiting logs, which relates to the stated problem only implicitly since it does not itself say how the lab meets Article 12 obligations.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not make the lab compliant on its own, since the lab's own systems' logging is not addressed, but it contributes a partial response by leveraging the mandate for research value.

evidence_originality: Applying information-theoretic Fano-style bounds to the question of minimal sufficient logging is unusual and imaginative, and few labs would respond to this mandate that way.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns compliance into a research programme on the science of logging, which changes the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations and adds new elements such as theoretical bounds and a field vocabulary, though it does not alter what the lab broadly researches.
evidence_acceptability: Academic research and publication aimed at informing regulators offend no norms, although it is somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing staff and benchmarks, but it commits three senior researchers to a multi-year theory effort with uncertain results, which is significant resource demand and does not fit the requirement for a committed implementation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, namely knowing what to log to satisfy the 'appropriate to intended purpose' standard of Article 12(2), which relates to the stated problem but is not the direct task of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Theoretical bounds and papers would offer a design criterion and could inform proportionality, but they would not by themselves deliver compliant logging in deployed high-risk systems, so they only partly solve the problem.

evidence_originality: Testing log fields in CI is a mundane, expected response and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice using familiar tooling, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated compliance testing in CI is a common, uncontroversial engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Pytest fixtures in an existing CI pipeline are low-cost and a non-radical change, though they need some work to hook into checkpoint evaluation.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses an identified part of the problem, meeting the Article 12(3) minimum logging fields for Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies the four Annex III 1(a) log fields but does not cover the broader Article 12(1)-(2) logging capability, other systems, or production behavior, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Pre-handover compliance audits with edge-case testing are a fairly common and expected response, though the crash and clock-drift scenarios add a little interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds an internal audit and attestation step but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged, which fits slightly stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Audit and attestation practices are standard, violate no norms, and are welcomed by regulators and clients.
evidence_implementability: An internal audit team running scripted sandbox tests is reasonably feasible, though it requires some new process and staffing.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by testing the specific Article 12(3) minimums.
evidence_effectiveness: The audit would verify that Article 12(3) fields are captured and would help demonstrate compliance, but it only verifies logging rather than building it and ignores Article 12(1)-(2) general traceability, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Embedding logging in an existing experiment-tracking pipeline is the common, expected response and shows little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal builds a standardized logging API into existing MLflow and CI/CD tooling, which is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing existing infrastructure for compliance logging is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Two platform engineers extending the existing MLflow, CI/CD and time-series stack within already-allocated budget is a non-radical, low-cost change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing the specific Article 12(3) items, so it does X to get Y where Y is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A centralized automatic logging layer would meet the logging requirement if built, but Article 12(3) applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems, and the proposal does not address the Article 12(2) event-relevance purposes such as risk identification and post-market monitoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Stress-testing logging infrastructure is a sensible and fairly expected engineering validation step, with modest imagination in tying pass/fail criteria to Article 12 fields.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new test rig and probe process but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Validation testing with documented pass/fail criteria for auditors is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a dedicated multi-week test rig with continuous traffic and automated probes needs some added infrastructure and effort but is reasonably feasible with standard engineering.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 requirement that logs be recorded and remain reliable over the system's lifetime, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A long-burn durability test would help show that logs remain complete and retrievable, but it covers only verification of storage and integrity, not what events to log, the other Article 12 requirements, or the R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logs against replayed scenarios is a sensible and somewhat interesting framing, but it is an extension of standard compliance test practice and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a test harness) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Pre-release compliance testing is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building automated scenario-replay scripts is a reasonably feasible engineering task, though defining realistic risk scenarios and mapping them to legal requirements takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: The toolkit directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by testing that logs capture the required events and Annex III 1(a) data points.
evidence_effectiveness: Validating log output against traceability requirements would substantially help compliance, but it only verifies logs and does not itself build the logging capability or address the wider obligations, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Separating research from deployment with a gate is a fairly common and expected response, though the explicit sign-off framing is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a governance gate and staging process but still treats compliance as a logging practice, only separating when it applies.
evidence_acceptability: Informal notebooks before the gate and an exemption of pilot-adjacent work could draw regulator skepticism, though a stage-gate is a common governance strategy and offends no norms outright.
evidence_implementability: A two-reviewer gate and a staged logging activation are lightweight and reasonably feasible with modest process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of when logging obligations attach and how to preserve R&D freedom, which relates to but is not directly the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A staging gate would help scope logging to regulated systems, but it only partly solves the problem because it never specifies how to meet the logging mandate and its assumption that pre-deployment systems are exempt is legally shaky, since Article 12 applies to high-risk systems placed on the market or put into service.

evidence_originality: A reusable shared logging middleware is a very common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice, centralizing it in a library without changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared internal tooling to meet legal requirements is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A two-person team over six months using existing compute infrastructure is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment with no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting Article 12 logging and Annex III 1(a) minimum fields, and protects R&D budgets.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the logging mandate across projects, though it covers only logging and not the broader record-keeping or R&D adaptation, and the fit to varied systems is uncertain.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware by default is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared middleware tool but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized shared logging service is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: It uses existing container orchestration and a modest team of one senior engineer plus two staff, so it is feasible at moderate cost with some changes rather than trivially easy.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic-logging requirement across the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic default log capture across all deployments would contribute substantially to meeting Article 12, but it does not itself ensure the event-relevance, Annex III specifics, or retention content, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Named documentation owners, refresh triggers, and quarterly audits are a common, mundane compliance response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a documentation governance workflow that treats compliance as standard administrative practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A documentation governance process violates no legal, social, or business norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Assigning owners, running a shared register, and holding quarterly audits are non-radical changes that are cheap to implement, though refresh sprints at every retraining add some burden.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the technical documentation requirement in Recital 71, which is related to the stated problem, but it does not directly address the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Keeping documentation current helps traceability and conformity assessment but does not provide the automatic event logs Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as an open benchmark resource is unusual and shows some imagination, though not wholly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning mandated logs into a research asset and a publication/curation role born from compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing compliance logs for research is somewhat unusual and raises data-protection and purpose-limitation questions, but anonymisation with differential privacy keeps it from offending sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It is a six-month postdoc-led study that builds on an existing shared logging layer, and while DP aggregation and open release need effort, it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, offsetting compliance overhead and adapting R&D to the logging mandate, rather than meeting the logging requirement itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would only partially offset compliance costs and does not itself satisfy the logging mandate, so it is a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance documentation into a research-publication stream mapped onto reproducibility standards is unusual and shows some imagination, though not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes traceability as an evidence-quality standard tied to the lab's scientific output, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations rather than treating compliance as mere logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing academic papers on regulation and reproducibility offends no norms and is a legitimate, familiar scholarly activity.
evidence_implementability: Two researchers writing two papers a year is a modest, reasonably feasible commitment requiring little organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It relates to Article 12 and Recital 71 documentation and may help the lab understand traceability, but the link to meeting the logging mandate is indirect and only special-situation benefit.
evidence_effectiveness: Publishing comparative papers on documentation and reproducibility does not itself implement automatic event logging or ensure the lab's systems comply, so it solves the problem only marginally, if at all.

evidence_originality: Pooling compliance infrastructure across institutions is an interesting idea that shows some imagination, though shared-service consortia are a familiar pattern.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It brings in new partners and a shared-infrastructure arrangement, which changes how the lab relates to compliance, but it still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the research itself unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Consortium cost-sharing and MOUs with partners are a somewhat uncommon but legitimate approach, though sharing event logs (possibly containing personal data) across institutions raises data-governance questions that need careful handling.
evidence_implementability: It needs multi-party agreements, cost-sharing and interoperability standards, which means significant coordination, but a pilot on one project makes it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the long-term log storage and post-market monitoring support in Article 12(2)(b), which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It addresses storage cost and infrastructure for logs but does not itself define what events to log, ensure traceability, or cover risk identification and operation monitoring, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logs in CI is a fairly expected, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would anticipate from labs, with only modest interest in tying it to notified-body gating.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tool into the existing pipeline but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Adding automated CI tests for logging is a standard engineering practice that violates no legal, social, or business norms.
evidence_implementability: A pytest-style suite in an existing GitLab CI pipeline is low-cost and a non-radical change, though defining the expected log schemas takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring systems technically emit the required logs under Article 12 before release.
evidence_effectiveness: It would catch gaps in log emission and so contributes to meeting the logging mandate, but it does not address retention, the content of what must be logged, or other obligations, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy/compliance-by-design and shared logging libraries are well-known approaches, so this is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an SDK-level telemetry layer) and shifts logging from per-project retrofit to design-time, but it still treats compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Building logging into the development framework is a common, legally compliant strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Embedding a standardized telemetry layer in a core SDK is a reasonably feasible engineering change requiring some upfront work but no radical overhaul.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate, including the Annex III specific log items.
evidence_effectiveness: Inherited logging would substantially satisfy the logging requirement across systems, but it does not address Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or non-Annex-III tailoring, so it is a strong but partial solution.
